The Four-Column Map of the Book . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .495
Preface


This book is a work of philosophy. It is not a commentary, not a theological treatise, and not
a scientific monograph. It is an attempt to reconstruct metaphysics from the ground up, on
the basis of a single architectonic principle: that the structure of any explanatory cognition
can be analyzed through four columns—fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics, and
context—and that the classical problems of identity and manifestation can be dissolved, rather
than solved, once this four-column structure is made explicit.
    The book is written in a strictly philosophical register. Its arguments are offered to be
assessed on their own merits, and each claim is labeled with the kind of support it has and the
kind of criticism it invites. The book does not draw its premises from revelation, from authority,
from empirical data, or from mathematical formalism; but it does not deny that revelation,
authority, empirical inquiry, and formal science have their own domains of validity. Its claim is
narrower: within philosophy, its arguments stand or fall by philosophical standards. The reader
who has no acquaintance with any tradition can follow the argument from beginning to end, and
can assess it on its own terms.


The Scope of the Book

The book is a work of metaphysics. Its subject is the structure of identity and manifestation,
and the architecture within which that structure is articulated. It makes no normative, ethical,
or prescriptive claims. Every technical term it introduces—including viability—is defined as a
descriptive or structural concept, and is to be understood as such throughout. Where the book
speaks of “success,” “adequacy,” or “recoverability,” these name structural relations between an
identity and its manifestations, not values, goods, or ends.
    This does not mean that the framework is indifferent to value. It means that the framework
describes the structure within which value is possible, and leaves the determination of value to
inquiries that the framework is designed to serve, not to replace. Structure is not the whole of
what is; it is the order through which what is becomes intelligible. The book’s claim is that
this order is real, invariant, and describable. It does not claim that the order is self-sufficient,
or that nothing lies beyond it. Where the description reaches its limit—at the boundary of
philosophy—the book marks the boundary and indicates that the boundary is not the end.


Structure of the Book

The book is organized into nine parts, thirty-seven chapters, and three appendices.


Part I (Foundation). The four-column framework of cognition: fixed elements, fluid elements,
governing dynamics, and context. This is the analytical structure on which the rest of the book
is built.

                                               xvii
xviii                                                                                      Preface


Part II (Realms). The four fundamental realms and the three barzakhic realms: seven
independently real levels of being, each with its own mode of existence and its own structural
possibilities.

Part III (Fixed Elements). Identities and manifestations: the invariant structure that
persists through transformation, and the contextual appearance through which it is expressed.

Part IV (Fluid Elements). Light: the conveyor of effect between identities and manifestations,
with three essential properties (descending, ascending, reflective).

Part V (Governing Dynamics). The rules of the realms: twenty-two structural constraints
that govern how light operates in each realm.

Part VI (Arguments). The arguments for the principles established in Parts I–V: the
necessity of expression, the minimality of the four grades, the minimality of the three hubs,
the irreducibility of one-step reduction, the conservation of identity, the non-duplicability of
identity, the desire to find, the unknownness of same-category identities, and the impossibility of
super-identity.

Part VII (Resolution of Tensions). The apparent tensions that arise when the principles
are brought together—rigidity and dynamism, unity and multiplicity, intensity and breadth,
tendency and success, relation and order—and the principle of category-relative predication that
resolves them.

Part VIII (Derivative Concepts). Time and eternity, death and birth, the three-fold
distinction between self-awareness, consciousness, and awareness, and the ontological economy of
expression cost and sediment.

Part IX (Boundaries and Conclusion). The boundaries of philosophy, the relation between
philosophy and revelation, and the open questions that the framework leaves for future inquiry.

The Appendices. Three appendices follow the main body. They are proposals and structural
descriptions that build on the framework but are not part of its metaphysical body. Appendix A is
a prospectus for a dependent treatise on the architecture of moral systems (Viability Metaethics).
Appendix B is a structural description of the human subject, offered as a structural account rather
than as exegesis. Appendix C is a structural description of certain religious phenomena, offered
as a structural account rather than as a prescription. Each appendix states at its beginning that
it is not part of the metaphysical body of the book.


On the Dialogues with Philosophical Traditions
The book’s engagement with historical traditions—Ibn Sina, Suhrawardi, Ibn Arabi, Mulla Sadra,
Plato and Plotinus, Proclus, Kant and Hegel, Whitehead, the Upanishads and Buddhism, and
Preface                                                                                         xix


Kashmir Shaivism—is presented in a separate treatise, to be published independently. The
reason for the separation is a matter of philosophical principle, not of convenience. The book is
written under the following commitment:

     The validity of no philosophical principle in this book depends on confirmation from
     any outside domain. Its concepts and principles are to be assessed through structural
     precision, internal coherence, and philosophical argument.

   This commitment does not forbid comparison with traditions. It forbids using comparison
as a ground of justification. A dialogue that says “Ibn Sina held a similar view, therefore the
framework’s view is plausible” would violate the commitment. A dialogue that says “Ibn Sina
held a different view, and here is where the framework’s view differs and why” is historical
and comparative, and is permitted—but it belongs to a different genre from the systematic
reconstruction this book offers.
   The dialogues are works of comparative philosophy. They presuppose the framework and
compare it with other positions. The framework itself presupposes nothing outside philosophy,
and stands on its own arguments. Keeping the two genres in one volume would encourage a
misreading: that the framework’s authority rested, in part, on the traditions it compared itself
with. The separation removes that misreading.
   References to traditions appear in the body of the book only as footnotes, where a reader
who wishes to consult the comparative treatment is directed to the appropriate chapter of the
separate treatise. They carry no justificatory weight, and the footnote states this explicitly. The
body of the book does not depend on them.


On Balanced Philosophical Formalization
The book uses formalization, but in a restricted sense.
   Formalization here means brief notation, explicit formulation of principles, dependency tables,
and epistemic labels. It does not mean full formal proof, axiomatic derivation, or mathematical
formulation. The aim is precision of presentation, not justification.
   Three consequences follow.
   First, every principle appears first in full philosophical prose, and only then in symbolic form.
The prose is the principle; the symbol is its abbreviation. A reader who skips the symbols loses
nothing essential; a reader who skips the prose has not read the principle.
   Second, formalization is distributed through the text rather than collected in a single place. It
appears where it aids precision—at the statement of a definition, at the summary of an argument,
at the dependency map of a part. It does not appear where it would substitute for argument.
   Third, the symbols used are few, and each is introduced with its meaning. The book does not
assume the reader’s acquaintance with any formal system. Where a symbol is used, the prose
that surrounds it states what the symbol abbreviates.
   This is what “balanced” means here. The book uses formalization where formalization
serves understanding, and it withholds formalization where formalization would substitute for
understanding.
xx                                                                                        Preface


Reading Paths
The book can be read in five ways.


The philosophical reader. Read from beginning to end, in the order of the chapters. Each
part presupposes only what has come before. Each chapter is short enough to be read in one
sitting, and each ends with a transition to the next. This is the intended path.


The researcher. Read the parts relevant to your inquiry, and follow the cross-references
backward to the foundations. The dependency maps at the end of each part state which
principles depend on which, so that the reader who enters in the middle can see what the entering
point presupposes. The index of principles and the index of arguments allow the reader to locate
a specific claim in its context.


The student. Read the book in the order of the chapters, and at the end of each chapter,
attempt the question for reflection. The questions are not exercises in the pedagogical sense;
they are openings onto the problems the chapter addresses. A student who can state, in their
own words, why the question matters, has understood the chapter.


The reader interested in light. Part IV (Chapters 11–15) can be read independently by
a reader who has read Parts I–III. The part begins with a problem that is intelligible to any
reader, builds its proposal from the framework established in the earlier parts, and draws its
consequences without requiring the later parts. A reader whose interest is in light, and not in
the whole of the framework, will find in Part IV a self-contained treatment of the subject.


The reader interested in the appendices. The three appendices are self-contained proposals
and descriptions. Each can be read independently of the others, and each states at its beginning
what it is and what it is not. The reader who comes to the framework from a tradition, or who
is interested in the relation between the framework and other domains of inquiry, may find the
appendices a useful entry point. But the appendices presuppose the framework, and a reader
who has not read the main body will find them compressed.


A Note on the Title
The title names a concept that belongs entirely to the book’s metaphysics. Identity does not
admit of degrees: a thing is the same one or it is not. But the relation between an identity and
its manifestations can satisfy certain structural conditions more or less completely. We call the
structural character of that relation viability. The viability of an identity in a realm has three
structural components: the fidelity of its manifestations to its structure, the sustainability of
the cost of producing them, and the recoverability of its capacity to manifest. Viability admits
of degrees; identity does not; and the two are related as what is expressed to the structural
character of its expression.
Preface                                                                                       xxi


   The concept is defined in Chapter 6, and the book returns to it in Chapters 30, 33, 35, and
36. It is a descriptive concept: it states a condition on the relation between an identity and its
manifestations, and attaches no value, end, or good to that condition.


Saeed Hasibi
2026
Introduction: The Problem, the Method, and the Map


Scope of This Book
This book is a work of metaphysics. Its subject is the structure of identity and manifestation, and
the architecture within which that structure is articulated. Every technical term it introduces—
including viability—is defined as a descriptive or structural concept, and is to be understood as
such throughout. Where the book speaks of “success,” “adequacy,” or “recoverability,” these
name structural relations between an identity and its manifestations, not values, goods, or ends.
   The book makes no normative, ethical, or prescriptive claims. But it does not follow that
the book is indifferent to value, or that it treats the domain of value as unreal. The book
describes the structure within which value is possible; it does not supply the content of value,
and it does not replace the inquiries that do. Its claim is that this structure is real, invariant,
and describable—not that it is self-sufficient, and not that nothing lies beyond it. Where the
description reaches its limit, the book marks the limit and indicates that the limit is not the end.


A Note on Description and Prescription
The book describes structure; it does not prescribe conduct. The distinction is deliberate, and it
is worth stating at the outset so that the reader knows what kind of work the book is doing and
what kind of work it is not doing.
   A structural description is not a normative prescription, but neither is it irrelevant to one.
The description of the structure of identity and manifestation provides an ontological basis on
which a normative prescription may be built; it does not itself supply that prescription, and
it does not replace it. The relation between the two is one of grounding, not of identity: the
description states what is, the prescription states what ought to be, and the transition from the
first to the second requires a further premise that the description alone does not supply.
   The book is therefore silent on questions of ethics, value, and guidance, not because those
questions are unimportant, but because they belong to a different inquiry. The silence is not a
denial. It is the recognition that a structural philosophy, honestly practiced, knows where its
competence ends—and that the end of its competence is not the end of what is. The structural
description offered here can serve as a foundation for the inquiry into value; it cannot serve as a
substitute for it. The reader who seeks a normative theory will not find one in these pages; the
reader who seeks the structural ground on which a normative theory may be built will find it.


The Problem
For over two millennia, the problem of identity has remained the central aporia of metaphysics.
From the Ship of Theseus in ancient Greece to the doctrine of No-Self in Buddhist philosophy,
from Locke’s memory criterion to contemporary paradoxes of personal identity, philosophers
have repeatedly failed to reconcile the persistence of a thing with its continuous change.

                                               xxii
Introduction                                                                                       xxiii


      This book argues that this persistent failure stems from a foundational ontological error: the
conflation of identity with manifestation. Identity is the invariant structure that persists through
transformation; manifestation is the appearance of that structure in a receiving realm, according
to the realm’s capacity. The two are not the same; they are not even on the same level. Identity
is the source; manifestation is the expression. And between them lies the entire architecture of
reality.
      The error is not confined to a single domain of inquiry. It recurs wherever identity is confused
with its appearances: the persistence of a person with the continuity of their memories; the
identity of a city with the continuity of its buildings; the identity of a tradition with the continuity
of its texts. In each case, the confusion generates a paradox: the entity seems to persist and
not to persist at the same time. The dissolution of the paradox requires, first, the distinction
between identity and manifestation, and, second, an account of how the two are related.
      The problem is not only how an identity continues through change. It is also how one identity
appears in many realms, keeping its unity of essence, while its manifestations may differ in
structure.
      The title names a concept that belongs entirely to the book’s metaphysics. Identity does not
admit of degrees: a thing is the same one or it is not. But the relation between an identity and
its manifestations can satisfy certain structural conditions more or less completely. We call the
structural character of that relation viability. The viability of an identity in a realm has three
structural components: the fidelity of its manifestations to its structure, the sustainability of
the cost of producing them, and the recoverability of its capacity to manifest. Viability admits
of degrees; identity does not; and the two are related as what is expressed to the structural
character of its expression. Viability is a descriptive concept: it states a condition on the relation
between an identity and its manifestations, and attaches no value, end, or good to that condition.
The concept is defined in Definition 6.2, and the book returns to it in Chapters 30, 33, 35, and
36.
      The architecture that the book builds is not the whole of what is. It is the order through
which what is becomes intelligible. The book’s claim is that this order is real, invariant, and
describable; it does not claim that the order is self-sufficient, or that nothing lies beyond it. The
architecture is a description of structure, not a substitute for being.


The Method
The method of this book is systematic and architectural. Two architectures are kept apart: the
four columns are the analytical framework of cognition, and the seven realms are the ontological
architecture of being (Section 1.5). It proceeds from the most fundamental concepts to the
most derivative. The book is organized into nine parts and three appendices, each of which
presupposes only what has come before.

Part I (Foundation). Establishes the four-column framework of cognition, which provides the
analytical tools for everything that follows. The four columns are fixed elements, fluid elements,
governing dynamics, and context. The framework is supported by a removal test for necessity
and a reducibility test for sufficiency, and its central principles—the conveyor principle, the
xxiv                                                                                  Introduction


context-dependence principle, the infinity of contexts, and the impossibility of super-identity—are
argued from stated premises, each with its status declared. The part occupies six chapters,
because the framework is the first principle of the entire book and deserves the space to state
its definitions, its necessity argument, its sufficiency estimate, and its dependency map without
compression.


Part II (Realms). Develops the four fundamental realms (the four categories) and the three
barzakhic realms (the hubs), seven independently real levels of being. The fundamental realms
are the First Determination, the Structural Determination, the Relational Manifestation, and the
Material Manifestation. The barzakhic realms are the Hub of Decree, the Hub of Signification,
and the Hub of Realization; their mediating function does not make them less real. Relations
among realms are not confined to a single downward series.


Part III (Fixed Elements). Develops the fixed elements: identities and manifestations.
Identity is defined as the invariant structure that persists through transformation. Manifestation
is defined as the appearance of identity in a receiving realm according to its capacity, aptitude,
and constraints. The relation between the two is one of expression, reflection, and homogeneity
of essence.


Part IV (Fluid Elements). Develops the fluid element: light. Light is the conveyor of effect
between identities and manifestations. It has three essential properties—descending, ascending,
and reflective—and it is the condition of possibility of any network of cognition. The part occupies
five chapters. The treatment is organized around a single question: what is the structural place
of light in the four-column framework? The answer is not assumed at the outset; it is built,
chapter by chapter, from the problem to the proposal, from the proposal to its consequences.


Part V (Governing Dynamics). Develops the governing dynamics: the rules of the contexts.
Each fundamental realm has its own rules (universality, necessity, formality for the Structural
Determination; relationality, contextuality, awareness for the Relational Manifestation; causality,
temporality, discreteness for the Material Manifestation). Each barzakhic realm has its own rules
(proportion, order, harmony for the Hub of Decree; truthfulness, accuracy, fidelity for the Hub of
Signification; proportion in realization, preservation of the realized, continuation of realization
for the Hub of Realization). The terms used for the rules of the Hub of Realization are structural
terms naming the rules of that realm; they carry no ethical, normative, or prescriptive content
in this book. They are defined in Chapter 17 and are to be understood entirely within that
structural sense.


Part VI (Arguments). Develops the arguments for the principles established in Parts I–V.
The arguments include the necessity of expression, the minimality of four contexts, the minimality
of three hubs, the irreducibility of one-step reduction, the conservation of identity, the non-
duplicability of identity, the desire to find, the unknownness of same-category identities, and the
impossibility of super-identity.
Introduction                                                                                      xxv


Part VII (Resolution of Tensions). Resolves the apparent tensions that arise when the
principles are brought together. The tensions include rigidity versus dynamism, unity versus
multiplicity, intensity versus breadth, tendency versus success, and relation versus order.

Part VIII (Derivative Concepts). Develops the derivative concepts: time and eternity,
death and birth, the three-fold distinction between self-awareness, consciousness, and awareness,
and the ontological economy of expression cost and sediment.

Part IX (Boundaries and Conclusion). Fixes the boundaries of philosophical justification,
identifies the philosophical questions that remain open, and states the architecture’s concluding
structure and its open questions.

The Appendices. Three appendices follow the main body. They are proposals and structural
descriptions that build on the framework but are not part of its metaphysical body. Appendix A is
a prospectus for a dependent treatise on the architecture of moral systems (Viability Metaethics).
Appendix B is a structural description of the human subject, offered as a structural account rather
than as exegesis. Appendix C is a structural description of certain religious phenomena, offered
as a structural account rather than as a prescription. Each appendix states at its beginning that
it is not part of the metaphysical body of the book.


The Map
The reader who follows the order of the chapters will find that each part presupposes only what
has come before. The reader who wishes to consult a particular topic may begin with the relevant
chapter and follow the cross-references backward to the foundations. The book contains no
repetition: each concept is defined once, in its proper place, and referred to thereafter by chapter
and section number.
   The book is organized as a ladder. Each chapter is a rung. The reader ascends from the
foundation (the four-column framework) to the summit (the open horizons). At each rung, the
reader sees one column in one context. At the summit, the reader sees the whole.
   A note on linearity. The book is written under a strict rule of linear dependency: every
chapter refers only to chapters that precede it. A chapter does not refer forward to a chapter
that has not yet been read. Where a concept that will be developed later is needed earlier, it is
introduced at the point of first need, in the minimal form required, and its full development is
deferred without a forward reference. This is why the reader will not find, in the body of the
book, formulas of the kind “as we will see in Chapter N” where N is greater than the current
chapter. The dependency maps at the end of each part state, from the other direction, what
each part depends on.


A Note on Origins and Independence
The book offers its arguments on their own merits, and asks to be assessed in that way. No
principle of it is justified by reference to an outside theory, tradition, or result. Its concepts are
xxvi                                                                                    Introduction


defined within the book, and its arguments are stated so as to be assessed without any other
work.
   The architecture of descent and return, in which a source expresses itself through levels, is
familiar in the history of philosophy, and the reader who knows that history will see kinship. The
comparative treatment of these kinships is given in a separate treatise, for a reason of philosophical
principle: a comparison of structures is a different genre from a systematic reconstruction,
and keeping them in one volume would encourage a misreading of the framework’s authority.
References to traditions that appear in the body of the book are confined to footnotes, and they
carry no justificatory weight. The body of the book does not depend on them.


A Note on the Epistemic Status of Claims
Every major claim in this book is tagged with one of five epistemic-status labels (and a proposed
principle is marked as such, with no status yet). These labels tell the reader what kind of
argument is being offered, and therefore what kind of criticism is appropriate.

(A) (A) Axiom / Foundational Commitment. A starting point that is adopted rather
than proved. Its justification is coherence, explanatory power, and fruitfulness—not deduction.
An (A) claim can be criticized by (i) showing incoherence with other commitments, (ii) showing
a rival commitment that is more explanatory or more fruitful, or (iii) showing that the framework
could do without it.

(T) (T) Argued. An argument is given in the text—typically a reductio, a transcendental
argument, or an inference to the best explanation. A (T) claim can be criticized by attacking
its premises or its inferential step. Every (T) claim in this book depends on premises, and
where those premises are themselves commitments ((A)) the text says so; a ledger at the end of
Chapter 6, and another at the end of Part VI, list the premises on which the most important
arguments depend.

(E) (E) Estimate. A claim that is offered as approximate and subject to revision—typically a
structural estimate. An (E) claim can be criticized by showing that the architecture works as
well or better with a different structure, or that the specific structure is doing no explanatory
work.

(Q) (Q) Open Philosophical Question. A philosophical question that has no final answer yet,
but can be examined within the system. It is not handed to any other domain for measurement
or testing.

(S) (S) Speculation. A speculative extension, flagged for caution. The framework does
not claim that the speculation is true; it claims that it follows naturally from the framework’s
structure and is worth investigating.
   The reader is invited to assess each claim by the standard appropriate to its status. A (T)
claim is not refuted by saying “it is only an estimate”; an (E) claim is not refuted by saying “it
Introduction                                                                                   xxvii


is not proved.” The labels are not decorations; they are the framework’s way of being honest
about what it is doing.


A Note on the Use of Terms
The book uses a small number of technical terms, each of which is defined at its first occurrence
and collected in the Glossary. The most important are:

Identity
The invariant structure that persists through transformation.

Manifestation
The appearance of identity in a receiving realm according to the realm’s capacity, aptitude, and
constraints.

Fixed element
An entity whose invariant identity is preserved throughout the process of cognition.

Fluid element
An entity that conveys effect, connecting fixed elements to one another.

Governing dynamics
The rule that explains how fluid elements affect fixed elements.

Realm
An independently real level of being.

Context
The setting in which cognition occurs or a manifestation is realized (a cognitive context, or an
existential context, which is a realm).

Light
The conveyor of effect between identities and manifestations, with three essential properties
(descending, ascending, reflective).

Hub (barzakhic realm)
An independently real level whose mode of existence includes mediating, transforming, or
regulating relations between other realms.

Signature
The structural description of an identity’s invariance; what can be recorded, compared, and
copied (as distinct from the identity itself).

Viability
The structural character of the relation between an identity and its manifestations in a realm,
measured by fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability; a descriptive concept, not a value, an end,
or a good.
xxviii                                                                                   Introduction


    Every technical term is defined within the book, and no argument depends on the reader’s
acquaintance with any tradition. This does not mean that the terms have no history. Several of
them have close relatives in earlier philosophy; the separate treatise on the dialogues says which,
and the footnotes of the present book direct the reader there when a tradition is mentioned.
Within the book itself, the sense of each term is fixed by its definition and by nothing outside it.
    No term in this book carries normative or ethical weight. Every term is defined structurally.
Where a term used in this book has a normative use elsewhere—“justice,” “care,” “sustainability,”
“flourishing”—its sense in this book is fixed entirely by the book’s own structural definitions, and
no normative use of the term outside the book determines its sense here.


A Note on Structural and Theological Senses
Several of the book’s technical terms—most notably light, source, and first determination—have
close relatives in theological and religious vocabulary. The reader who comes to this book from
a religious tradition may recognize the words, and may be tempted to read the book’s claims
through the tradition’s meanings. The temptation is natural, and it is worth addressing directly.
    The book’s terms have a structural sense, not a theological sense. When the book speaks of
“light,” it names the structural condition of possibility of relation, not the divine essence; when it
speaks of “source,” it names the structural origin of determination, not a deity; when it speaks
of “first determination,” it names the first structural level at which determination takes form,
not a divine attribute or a cosmic principle. The terms are homonyms with their theological
relatives, not synonyms for them. The book uses the words because they are the least misleading
structural labels available, and it marks the distinction so that the homonymy is not mistaken
for identity.
    But the distinction between the structural and the theological is not the end of the matter.
The structural terms point beyond themselves. The structural light is not the divine light; but
the structural light is the condition of possibility of relation, and the divine light is, in the
traditions, the condition of possibility of manifestation. The structural source is not the deity;
but the structural source is the origin of determination, and the traditions speak of the origin of
determination as the act of the deity. The book does not claim that the structural sense is the
theological sense, and it does not claim that the two senses are unrelated. It claims that the
relation between them is a question for another inquiry—an inquiry that the book’s structural
description is designed to serve, not to replace.
    The book’s claim is therefore narrow and, at the same time, open. The narrow claim: within
the book, the terms have the structural sense the definitions give them, and no theological use
of the same words determines their sense here. The open claim: the structural sense is not a
denial of the theological sense. The book neither affirms nor denies that the structural terms
correspond to anything in the theological vocabulary of any tradition; it marks the question as
belonging to a different inquiry, and it indicates that the different inquiry is real.
    The reader who wishes to compare the book’s structural vocabulary with the theological
vocabulary of a tradition is invited to do so. The separate treatise on the dialogues undertakes part
of that comparison. But the comparison is a different genre from the systematic reconstruction
this book offers, and the book’s arguments do not depend on it. The structural sense stands on
Introduction                                                                                    xxix


its own; the theological sense, if there is one, stands on its own; and the relation between the
two is a question for another inquiry—one that the book neither undertakes nor forecloses.


A Note on the Independence of Philosophy from Science
The book is written under the following commitment:

     The validity of no philosophical principle in this book depends on confirmation from
     outside philosophy—including from science. Every principle is derived from within
     the four-column framework and from philosophical arguments.

   This commitment does not forbid the book from speaking of science. It forbids the book
from using science as a ground of justification for its principles. References to science appear in
this book in one role only: as a coherence test. A coherence test shows that a scientific inquiry
can develop itself within the philosophical framework without contradiction. It is marked in the
text by a dedicated box, headed “Coherence Test (not evidence, not justification),” and it is
never used as a premise in any argument of the book.
   The coherence test is not a concession to science. It is a discipline on the book’s own claims.
If a philosophical principle is incompatible with the way an established inquiry actually works,
the principle is defective as a principle of the structure of cognition, and the coherence test
reveals the defect. The test does not confirm the principle; it exposes the principle to a kind of
check. A principle that passes the coherence test is not thereby justified, and a principle that
fails it is not thereby refuted—but the failure is a reason to examine the principle further.
   The reader who seeks a philosophy grounded in science will not find one here; the reader
who seeks a philosophy that ignores science will also not find one. What the book offers is a
philosophy that is autonomous in its justification and coherent with the inquiries it does not
depend on. The distinction is stated once here and observed throughout.


A Note on the Structure of the Book
The book is divided into nine parts, thirty-seven chapters, and three appendices. The parts are:

   I. Foundation: The Four-Column Framework of Cognition (Chapters 1–6)

  II. Realms: The Four Fundamental and Three Barzakhic Realms (Chapters 7–8)

 III. Fixed Elements: Identities and Manifestations (Chapters 9–10)

 IV. Fluid Elements: Light (Chapters 11–15)

  V. Governing Dynamics: The Rules of the Contexts (Chapters 16–17)

 VI. Arguments (Chapters 18–26)

VII. Resolution of Tensions (Chapters 27–31)

VIII. Derivative Concepts (Chapters 32–35)
xxx                                                                                 Introduction


 IX. Boundaries and Conclusion (Chapters 36–37)

   The appendices are:

  A. Viability Metaethics: A Prospectus

  B. A Structural Anthropology: Nafs and Ruh

  C. A Structural Description of Religious Phenomena

   Each appendix is not part of the metaphysical body of the book. Each states at its beginning
what it is and what it is not.
   The back matter contains six elements: a Bibliography, organized by chapter and keyed to
the source codes used in the footnotes; a Glossary of Terms; an Index of Principles; an Index of
Arguments; an Index of Formalizations; and a Four-Column Map of the Book, which shows at a
glance which column each chapter develops.
   The Bibliography is organized by the chapter in which each source is cited, rather than
alphabetically. Every source is assigned a code of the form [Cn-m], where n is the chapter
number and m is the source number within that chapter. The same source cited in more than one
chapter receives a distinct code in each chapter. This allows the reader to locate every citation
in its chapter context, and it allows the footnotes to identify a source by code, name, and the
passage cited, without the reader needing to search the Bibliography alphabetically.


Concluding Remark
This book is offered as a proposal, not as a finished system. It invites objection, revision, and
refinement. The reader who finds a claim unconvincing is invited to strengthen the objection
and continue the inquiry. The horizon is open. The inquiry continues.
           Part I

Foundation: The Four-Column
   Framework of Cognition




             1
Chapter 1

Explanatory Cognition and the Four Questions


Scope. This chapter is a structural analysis of what it is for an explanatory cognition to be
complete. It distinguishes the architecture of cognition from the architecture of being, states
the four questions that any complete explanation must answer, and introduces the method by
which the four questions are to be established. Its claims are structural, not normative; where it
speaks of “understanding,” “explanation,” “cognition,” “element,” “rule,” or “context,” these are
structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter. The chapter’s silence
on questions of value is not a denial of their reality; it is the recognition that the structural
description is not the whole of what can be said.


1.1     The Question of Understanding
When we say that we understand something, what have we done? The question is deceptively
simple. We may say that we understand a phenomenon, a text, a person, or a proof, and in each
case we seem to be claiming the same thing: that the matter is no longer opaque to us. But
what is it that has become transparent, and what has made it so?
   The question is not about the psychology of understanding. It is not a question about what
happens in the mind when we come to grasp something. It is a structural question: what must an
account of something contain, if the account is to count as an explanation of it? The distinction
between these two questions is the beginning of the inquiry of this book.
   To see the distinction, consider a case. Someone says, “I understand why the bridge collapsed.”
What has been claimed? Not merely that the person feels a certain way about bridges, or that
the collapse has caused them to have a mental image of bending metal. What has been claimed
is that there is an account of the collapse—that something has been identified which makes the
collapse intelligible, and that the identification does not leave the main difficulty untouched.
   The question of this book is: what must such an account contain? The book’s answer,
developed over the first part, is that the account must answer four questions, and that the four
questions are distinct. The rest of the chapter states the questions, explains the scope in which
they are asked, introduces the method by which their necessity and sufficiency are to be assessed,
and distinguishes the architecture of cognition from the architecture of being.


1.2     The Four Questions
Every cognition that claims to “understand” something must answer four questions. The questions
are not posed here as a derivation from any premise; they are stated as an observation about
what any explanatory account, on inspection, must contain. Whether the four are truly necessary,

                                                 2
1.3. The Scope: Explanatory Cognition                                                             3


and whether no fifth is needed, is a matter for later argument; the present chapter states the
questions and prepares the ground for that argument.

1.2.1    What?
The first question is: what are the elements that are known? Any explanatory account must
identify the entities or terms whose relations it is about. It must say what is being related to
what. Without such identification, the account has nothing to relate; it is a description of process
without terms.

1.2.2    How?
The second question is: how are these elements connected? A list of entities is not an explanation
of how any one of them bears on another. The account must say by what the relation is carried,
or through what the effect of one element reaches another.

1.2.3    On What Basis?
The third question is: on what basis do the connections hold? The account must state the rule
or regularity that governs how the elements behave in one another’s presence. Without such a
rule, the account shows that things are connected, but not how the connection behaves, and so
cannot support prediction or counterfactual reasoning.

1.2.4    Where?
The fourth question is: where—from what standpoint—is the cognition carried out? Any
explanation is given from some position, in some frame, with some choice of what is held fixed
and what is allowed to vary. The account must make explicit the standpoint from which its
elements are individuated and its rule applied.

1.2.5    The Four Together
The four questions are: what, how, on what basis, and where. They are not four questions about
the same thing. They are four questions about four different aspects of a single explanatory
account. The first asks about terms, the second about the medium between terms, the third
about the rule of the medium, and the fourth about the frame in which terms, medium, and rule
are posed.
   If any one of these questions remains unanswered, the cognition is incomplete as an explanation.
This claim, and the further claim that no fifth question is needed, are to be argued in the chapters
that follow. For the purposes of the present chapter, the four questions are to be understood as
the questions the book will call the four columns of explanatory cognition.


1.3     The Scope: Explanatory Cognition
The four questions are questions about explanatory cognition, and the framework they lead to is
a framework for explanatory cognition. The term needs to be fixed at the outset, because the
4                                    Chapter 1. Explanatory Cognition and the Four Questions


framework does not claim to describe every mental state.

    Definition 1.1 (Explanatory Cognition)

    Explanatory cognition is cognition whose aim is to understand how some things stand to
    one another.

    Remark 1.1 (What the framework does not claim)

    The framework does not claim to describe every mental state. A momentary sensation,
    a mood, or a bare act of attention need not answer all four questions. The framework
    concerns cognition whose aim is to understand relations among things. Whenever this
    book says “cognition” without qualification, it means explanatory cognition in the sense
    of Definition 1.1.

    Example 1.1 (Two cases)

    A negotiation is an explanatory cognition when the aim is to understand how the parties
    affect one another. A city plan is an explanatory cognition when the aim is to understand
    how districts and institutions bear on one another. A bare sensation of warmth is not an
    explanatory cognition in this sense, because it does not aim to understand how anything
    stands to anything.

    The scope is limited. It is also large enough to cover the inquiries of the book: the inquiries
into identity and manifestation, into the seven realms, into light, into the rules of contexts, and
into the derivative concepts that follow from these. Every such inquiry is a cognition whose aim
is to understand how some things stand to one another. The framework of the four columns is
offered as the analytical structure of such cognition.


1.4     The Method
The four-column principle is a piece of conceptual analysis, and its justification has three parts.
The reader is invited to judge each part separately.


(i) A removal test for necessity. If dropping a column leaves a recognizable explanatory
failure, the column is necessary. The test is applied when the four-column principle is stated, in
the chapter that follows the next.


(ii) A reducibility test for sufficiency. If every candidate fifth column can be reassigned
to one of the four without loss, the four are sufficient. The test is applied in the same chapter.
Sufficiency is offered as an estimate, not as a proof, because a new kind of explanation might
always turn up.


(iii) The fruitfulness of the framework. If the framework supports the arguments and
distinctions of the chapters that follow, and if those chapters are clearer for the support, the
1.5. Two Architectures                                                                          5


framework’s fruitfulness is a reason in its favor. The argument of the whole book is the test of
this part.
   The status labels introduced in the Introduction are used here with exactly the meanings
assigned there. In particular, a (T) claim in this chapter is one that follows from the stated
definitions; the definitions themselves are commitments, and are labeled as such.

   Remark 1.2 (Why the method is not a proof from nothing)

   The removal test presupposes that we can recognize an explanatory failure when we
   see one. The reducibility test presupposes that we can recognize when a role has been
   reassigned without loss. Neither presupposition is itself proved. They are commitments of
   the method, and they are declared as such. The method does not promise certainty; it
   promises a discipline on the claims the book makes.



1.5     Two Architectures
Two questions are easily run together, and the book keeps them apart from this point on.

   1. For cognition: what roles must be told apart if something is to be understood? The four
      columns answer this question.

   2. For being: of what levels or kinds of existence does reality itself consist? The second part
      of the book answers this question, by separate arguments, with seven realms.

   The distinction is not incidental. It is one of the framework’s central commitments, and it is
stated as a principle.

   Principle 1.1 (Cognitive and Ontological Architecture Are Distinct)

   (T) The four columns are four analytical roles that any complete explanation must assign.
   From the definition of the columns alone it does not follow that reality consists of four
   kinds of entity, and it does not follow that reality consists of any particular number of
   levels.

Proof. The removal test, when it is applied, shows what an explanation must contain. A statement
about what an explanation must contain is a statement about the explanation; it becomes a
statement about the explained only with a further premise, namely that the roles are carved
out by the structure of what is explained. That premise is not part of the four-column principle.
Hence the principle is silent on how many levels of being there are. Whatever is said on that
matter must be argued on its own ground.

   Remark 1.3 (No conflict between four and seven)

   There is no conflict between a cognition that has four columns and a reality that has
   seven realms. The four columns apply to the study of any realm, and to the study of
   the relations among realms. Within the study of a single realm, its manifestations are
   the fixed elements, light is the fluid element, the rules of that realm are the governing
6                                     Chapter 1. Explanatory Cognition and the Four Questions


    dynamics, and the realm together with the cognitive standpoint is the context. Nothing
    in this chapter should be read as saying that each column is a realm, or that each realm is
    a column.

    The distinction between the two architectures is developed in detail in the parts that follow.
For the present, it is enough to see why it must be made. If the four columns were read as four
kinds of entity, the framework would become a metaphysics of four substances—a view the book
does not hold and does not need. If the seven realms were read as seven columns, the analytical
framework would become an ontology of seven levels—a view the book will argue for, but not by
making it identical with the analytical framework. The distinction allows the book to argue for
each architecture on its own terms.



1.6     The Finitude of the Subject

One further commitment is needed before the argument can proceed. It is not a principle of
the four-column framework; it is a premise about the subject who uses the framework, and it is
adopted as an axiom.

    Principle 1.2 (Finitude of the Subject)

    (A) Every cognizing subject is finite: at any time it occupies finitely many contexts, and
    in any finite span it completes only finitely many acts of reconstruction.


    Remark 1.4 (Why finitude is an axiom)

    Finitude is adopted rather than proved. Its justification is that every cognizing subject we
    know of—a person, an institution, a tradition—is bounded in what it can survey. A critic
    who denies finitude must say what an unbounded subject would be, and this book offers
    no account of such a subject.


    The axiom is used later in two places. It is used to argue for the impossibility of super-identity,
and it is used throughout the part of the book that develops the arguments in detail. A reader
who does not accept the axiom can still follow the arguments that do not depend on it; the
dependency maps at the end of each part state which arguments do.



1.7     The Boundary of Philosophy: Structure, Not Telos

The distinction between the two architectures—the architecture of cognition and the architecture
of being—raises a further question that must be settled before the argument can proceed. The
question is not what the framework describes, but what kind of question it can answer. The
framework describes structure. It does not, and by its method cannot, describe telos—the end,
purpose, or final cause for which anything exists. The distinction is stated here as an axiom, so
that the reader knows from the outset what the framework claims and what it does not.
1.7. The Boundary of Philosophy: Structure, Not Telos                                               7


   But the distinction is not a wall. It is a threshold. The framework’s silence on telos is not a
denial of telos; it is the recognition that the description of structure is not the description of the
whole. The structure is real, and the framework’s claim is that the structure is invariant and
describable. But the structure is the order of what is, and what is is not exhausted by its order.
The framework describes the order; it does not claim that the order is self-sufficient, and it does
not claim that nothing lies beyond it.

   Principle 1.3 (Philosophy Describes Structure, Not Telos)

   (A) Philosophy, as practiced in this book, describes the structure of what is: the relations
   among things, the rules that govern those relations, and the frames in which both are
   posed. It does not, and by its method cannot, establish the telos of what is: the end, the
   purpose, or the good for which anything exists. The question of telos is a real question,
   and the structure that philosophy describes points toward it; but the structure does not
   contain it, and philosophy cannot derive it from the structure alone.

   The principle is a commitment, and its status is (A). It is not derived from the four-column
framework, and it does not follow from any of the definitions stated so far. It is adopted because
the method of the book is structural: the book asks what roles an explanation must assign, and
it answers by analysis, not by appeal to purpose. A method that answers by analysis cannot, by
the same analysis, deliver a purpose. To claim otherwise would be to confuse the description of a
structure with the justification of an end. But to claim that the structure is the whole of what is
would be to confuse the order of what is with what is.
   The distinction has two sides, and both must be stated.

The first side: structural philosophy. A structural philosophy asks how things stand to
one another. It identifies the elements, the medium of their relation, the rule of the medium,
and the frame in which all three are posed (the four questions of Section 1.2). It answers by
description: it says what the structure is, and it states the conditions under which the structure
holds. Its claims are assessed by coherence, explanatory power, and fruitfulness—the criteria
stated in Section 1.4. This is the kind of philosophy the present book practices.

The second side: teleological inquiry. A teleological inquiry asks for the sake of what a
thing exists. It identifies the end toward which a structure is ordered, and it states the good
that the structure serves. Its claims are assessed by a different standard: by the adequacy of
the end it proposes, by the coherence of that end with the structure it is said to serve, and by
the authority of the source from which the end is received. This is not the kind of inquiry the
present book undertakes.
   The two inquiries are not rivals. They answer different questions about the same reality.
A structural description can be true while a teleological account is also true, and the two can
be compatible without either reducing to the other. The structural description says what the
structure is; the teleological account says what the structure is for. The first does not entail
the second, and the second does not replace the first. But the first is not complete without
the second, and the second is not intelligible without the first. The structure is the condition
8                                       Chapter 1. Explanatory Cognition and the Four Questions


of possibility of the teleological account, and the teleological account is the completion of the
structure’s meaning.

    Remark 1.5 (Why the boundary is not a weakness)

    The boundary is not a deficiency of the framework. It is a condition of its precision. A
    framework that claimed to establish both structure and telos by a single method would be
    claiming more than its method can deliver. The framework’s honesty about its boundary
    is part of what makes its structural claims assessable: the reader knows exactly what kind
    of claim is being made, and therefore what kind of criticism is appropriate. A structural
    claim is criticized by showing that the structure is misdescribed; a teleological claim is
    criticized by showing that the end is inadequate or unauthorized. The two criticisms are
    different, and the framework keeps them apart. But the boundary is a threshold, not a
    wall: it marks the point at which description gives way to indication, and indication is not
    a lesser form of knowledge but a different form.


    Remark 1.6 (What the framework does not say about telos)

    The framework does not say that telos is unreal, unknowable, or unimportant. It says
    only that telos is not established by the method of this book. Whether telos is real, and
    if so how it is known, is a question the framework leaves open. The question belongs
    to a different inquiry—whether that inquiry is revelation, intuition, practical reason, or
    religious experience—and the framework takes no position on which inquiry is the right
    one. It takes a position only on what its own method can deliver, and telos is not among
    the things its method delivers. But the framework’s silence is not a denial. The framework
    neither affirms nor denies that telos is real; it marks the question as belonging to a different
    inquiry, and it indicates that the different inquiry is real. The indication is not a proof,
    and it is not a substitute for the inquiry. It is the recognition that a structural philosophy,
    honestly practiced, knows where its competence ends—and that the end of its competence
    is not the end of what is.

    Remark 1.7 (Structure is not self-sufficient)

    The framework describes structure. But the framework does not claim that structure is
    the whole of what is. The order through which what is becomes intelligible is real, and
    the framework’s claim is that this order is invariant and describable. But the order is not
    self-sufficient: it is the order of something, and the something is not exhausted by its order.
    The framework’s silence on telos is therefore not a denial of telos; it is the recognition that
    a description of order is not a description of the whole. The structure is a condition of
    intelligibility, not a substitute for being. And the framework’s claim is that the structure
    is real, not that it is all there is.


    The boundary has a consequence for the reader. The reader who seeks a structural description
of identity and manifestation will find one in this book. The reader who seeks an account of the
end for which identity and manifestation exist will not find one here; the book points beyond itself,
1.8. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                   9


to the inquiry that undertakes that question. The pointing is not a refusal. It is the recognition
that a structural philosophy, honestly practiced, knows where its competence ends—and that the
pointing is itself a kind of claim: the claim that structure is not the whole, and that the whole is
not exhausted by what philosophy can describe.

           Finitude of the subject                                       (A)

A Question for Reflection
Can you name an explanatory account that fails to answer one of the four questions? What is it
about the account that makes the failure recognizable? And can you name a question about the
same thing that the four questions do not answer—a question about what the thing is for?

The next chapter defines the four columns as analytical roles, so that the four questions can be
used as the analytical structure of any explanatory cognition.
Chapter 2

The Four Columns Defined


Scope. This chapter defines the four analytical roles that the previous chapter introduced as
the four questions of explanatory cognition. It defines fixed element, fluid element, governing
dynamics, and context; it gives each a control question by which a proposed instance can be tested;
and it states the distinction between the two kinds of context that the framework employs. It does
not argue that the four roles are necessary, nor that no fifth is needed; those arguments belong
to the chapter that follows. Its claims are structural; where the chapter is silent on questions
of value, the silence is not a denial but a recognition that the analytical description is not the
whole of what can be said. Where the chapter speaks of “element,” “effect,” “rule,” “standpoint,”
“limit,” or “aptitude,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this
chapter.


2.1      A Scene

Consider two people in conversation. One speaks; the other listens and replies. Something has
passed between them: a meaning, an intention, a request. We understand the exchange without
difficulty, and we can describe it in ordinary language. But if we ask what an explanation of the
exchange would have to contain, the description becomes less obvious.
    Four things, at least, would have to be identified. First, the parties: the speaker and the
hearer. Second, the medium: the language they share, or the words they exchange. Third, the
rule: the conventions of turn- taking and of meaning by which a word affects a hearer. Fourth,
the setting: the negotiation, the dinner table, the courtroom, from which the exchange takes its
point.
    The four are not the same, and none is supplied by another. To know who the parties are is
not yet to know what passes between them. To know that language passes between them is not
yet to know by what rule it works. To know the rule is not yet to know from what standpoint
the parties are individuated as they are. The scene is ordinary, but the structure it exhibits is
general: every explanatory cognition, on inspection, assigns four roles, and the roles are distinct.
    This chapter defines the four roles. The definitions are not derived from the scene; the scene
is an illustration. The definitions are offered as the framework’s analytical vocabulary, and their
necessity is a matter for the next chapter.


2.2      Fixed Elements

The first role is the fixed element.


                                                10
2.2. Fixed Elements                                                                                 11


    Definition 2.1 (Fixed Element)

    A fixed element is an entity selected as an invariant term within a given explanatory
    cognition. Its fixedness is methodological: it is held stable for the purpose of explaining
    its relations, and does not by itself imply that the entity is ontologically immutable. A
    fixed element is present in the cognition as a node.

    Two things in this definition deserve emphasis.
    First, the fixedness is methodological, not ontological. To hold an entity fixed in an explanation
is to decide, for the purposes of the explanation, not to vary it. It is not to claim that the entity
cannot vary. A river may be held fixed as a boundary in political geography, and the same river
may be treated as a fluid route of transport in the geography of trade. In the first frame it is a
fixed element; in the second it is not. The fixedness is a role the entity plays in a frame, not a
property the entity has in itself.

    Remark 2.1 (Relativity of Fixedness)

    Fixedness is relative, not absolute. An element may be fixed in one context and fluid in
    another. A river is a fixed boundary in the context of political geography, and a fluid route
    of transport in the context of trade. This relativity is the context-dependence principle,
    which is stated and argued in a later chapter; here it is only named.

    Second, the fixedness of an element within a cognition must not be confused with the
ontological invariance of an identity. The former concerns the conditions of an explanation; the
latter concerns what persists through transformation. An entity may be held fixed in an analysis
while being, ontologically, changeable; and an identity is ontologically invariant whether or not
any cognition holds it fixed. The two notions are distinguished at length in the part of the book
that treats identity. For the present, it is enough to see that the fixed element is a role in an
explanation, not a metaphysical posit.

    Remark 2.2 (Control Question for a Fixed Element)

    For any proposed fixed element, ask: in which context is it held fixed, and what is being
    explained while it is held fixed? A fixed element with no answer to the first part is not yet
    a fixed element of any cognition.


    Example 2.1 (Conversation and City)

    In the context of a negotiation, the parties are fixed elements. In the context of urban
    planning, the districts and institutions of a city are fixed elements.

    The definition and its remarks are summarized in the control question: a fixed element is
whatever an explanation holds invariant while it explains the relations of that element to others.
The role is defined by what the explanation does with the entity, not by what the entity is in
itself.
12                                                          Chapter 2. The Four Columns Defined


2.3      Fluid Elements

The second role is the fluid element.

     Definition 2.2 (Fluid Element)

     A fluid element is an entity that conveys effect. A fluid element is an edge in the network
     of cognition, connecting fixed elements to one another and explaining their behavior in
     one another’s presence.


     The word “fluid” in this definition does not mean “liquid.” It means “conveying”: an element
is fluid in the framework’s sense if it carries the effect of one fixed element to another. Language,
information, force, signals, processes—all of these can be fluid elements in the appropriate context.
The framework’s use of the word is fixed by the definition and by nothing else.

     Remark 2.3 (The Fluid Element as Condition of Possibility)

     A fluid element is the condition of possibility of cognizing relations. Without a fluid
     element, fixed elements are disconnected nodes, not a network of cognition. The argument
     for this claim—that no explanation of how one fixed element bears on another is complete
     without a fluid element—is given in a later chapter. Here the claim is stated as part of
     the definition’s import.


     Remark 2.4 (Control Question for a Fluid Element)

     For any proposed fluid element, ask: what does it convey, and between which fixed
     elements? If it conveys nothing between anything, it is not functioning as a fluid element
     in that cognition.


     Example 2.2 (Conversation and City)

     In the negotiation, language conveys the effect of one party on the other. In the city, roads
     and trade convey the effect of one district on another.


     The fluid element is the second column. It is not the effect itself; it is what carries the effect.
This distinction will matter when the book turns to light, which is the framework’s name for the
fluid element in its most general role. For the present, the definition is enough: a fluid element is
what an explanation invokes when it says how one thing reaches another.



2.4      Governing Dynamics

The third role is governing dynamics.
2.5. Context                                                                                     13


   Definition 2.3 (Governing Dynamics)

   Governing dynamics is a rule that explains how fluid elements affect fixed elements.
   Dynamics determines the behavioral pattern of the network of cognition.


   Governing dynamics is not itself an element. It is a rule of effect. The distinction is not
always obvious, because in some cognitions a fluid element and a rule may coincide: a custom, for
example, is both “a thing that conveys” and “a rule of effect.” The framework’s way of handling
the coincidence is the one it uses everywhere: the role an entity plays in a given cognition decides
how it is classified there, and the same entity may play both roles in different cognitions.

   Remark 2.5 (Control Question for a Governing Dynamics)

   For any proposed governing dynamics, ask: what kind of change does it explain, and what
   would count as a violation of it? A rule that no event could violate explains nothing.


   Example 2.3 (Conversation and City)

   In the negotiation, the conventions of turn-taking and of meaning explain how an utterance
   affects its hearer. In the city, its laws and customs of exchange explain how trade affects
   the districts.

   The third column is the rule. It is what an explanation invokes when it says not merely that
one thing reaches another, but how the reaching is governed: what regularities the connection
obeys, and what would count as a departure from them. Without such a rule, the network of
cognition shows that things are connected, but not how the connection behaves.



2.5     Context

The fourth role is context.

   Definition 2.4 (Context)

   A context is the background in which cognition occurs. Context determines what counts
   as a fixed element, what counts as a fluid element, and which dynamics governs.


   Context is not itself an element. It is the condition of possibility of defining elements. The
framework’s fourth column is not one more item on the list; it is what makes the list possible.
Context is the frame within which the other three columns take the specific content they have.

   Remark 2.6 (Control Question for a Context)

   For any proposed context, ask: what limit or aptitude does it set for what can appear in
   it? A context that sets no limit and favors no appearance is an empty label.


   The word “context” is used in this book in two senses, and the distinction is kept throughout.
14                                                        Chapter 2. The Four Columns Defined


The cognitive context. A cognitive context, or frame, is any background that fixes a partition
of entities into fixed and fluid, together with a governing dynamics. A negotiation, a city plan,
and a legal case are cognitive contexts. A cognitive context is fixed by the question being asked,
and there are indefinitely many of them; the infinity of cognitive contexts is argued in a later
chapter.



The existential context. An existential context is the realm in which a manifestation or
an act of being is realized, with the capacity and the constraints of that realm. A realm is an
ontological level, not a standpoint of cognition. The book distinguishes seven such realms; the
distinction between cognitive and existential context is what keeps the study of cognition from
being confused with the study of being.

     Remark 2.7 (Two Kinds of Context)

     A cognitive context is fixed by the question being asked. An existential context is fixed
     by the identity and the receiving realm, not by the question. An existential context does
     not require a cognizing subject in order to be real: a manifestation may be realized in
     a realm without being known, observed, or reconstructed by any subject. A cognitive
     context conditions the knowledge of a manifestation; an existential context conditions its
     realization.


     Example 2.4 (Conversation and City)

     The context of negotiation defines the parties as fixed elements, language as the fluid
     element, and the conventions of exchange as dynamics. The context of urban planning
     defines districts, roads, and the laws of exchange in the same three roles.


     The fourth column is the frame. It is what an explanation invokes when it says not merely
how something is connected and by what rule, but from what standpoint the connection and the
rule are posed. Without a frame, the same entities can be partitioned into fixed and fluid in
different ways, and the rule alone does not say which partition is intended.
     The distinction between the cognitive context and the existential context is a distinction
between two orders, not a separation of two worlds. The existential context is the order of being;
the cognitive context is the order of inquiry. The two are distinct, and neither is reducible to
the other; but the first is the condition of possibility of the second. A manifestation is realized
in a realm before it is known in a frame; and the frame is the order through which the realm
becomes intelligible. The framework keeps the two apart so that the study of cognition is not
confused with the study of being—but the keeping-apart is not a denial that the two are related.
The existential context is the ground of the cognitive context, and the cognitive context is the
intelligibility of the existential context.
2.6. The Four Roles Together                                                                     15


2.6     The Four Roles Together

The four columns are not four items on a list. They are four roles in a single structure. The fixed
elements are what is related; the fluid element is the medium of relation; the governing dynamics
is the rule of the medium; the context is the frame in which all three take their specific content.




  Column                Definition                            Control Question

                        cognition                             and what is being explained?
  Fluid element         An entity that conveys effect         What does it convey, and between

   The table is not a proof that the four are necessary, nor that no fifth is needed. It is a
summary of the definitions, with the control question that tests a proposed instance. The
argument for necessity, and the estimate for sufficiency, are given in the next chapter.


   Remark 2.8 (Distinctness and Separability)

   Distinctness does not imply absolute separability. Two analytical roles may be instantiated
   by the same entity, or one role may constrain the content of another (the rules of a
   cognition may be constrained by the structure of its elements), without the roles thereby
   becoming conceptually identical. The four roles are distinct as roles; they may be carried
   by fewer than four entities in a given cognition.


   The four roles are analytical tools. They describe the structure of an explanation, not the
furniture of the world. The distinction matters, because the analytical description is not the
whole of what can be said about what is explained. The structure is the order through which
what is explained becomes intelligible; but the order is not the explained, and the explanation is
not the whole of what is explained. The four columns are the framework’s way of describing the
order; they do not claim that the order is self-sufficient, and they do not claim that nothing lies
beyond it.
