A Question for Reflection
Take an explanation you accept—of a historical event, a biological process, a legal decision. Can
you identify, in that explanation, the four roles as this chapter has defined them? Which role is
most easily identified, and which is most easily overlooked?

The next chapter argues that the four roles are jointly necessary, and offers an estimate that they
are jointly sufficient.
Chapter 3

The Four-Column Principle: Necessity and Sufficiency


Scope. This chapter argues that the four roles defined in the previous chapter are jointly necessary
for any explanatory cognition, and offers an estimate that they are jointly sufficient. It states
the four-column principle, gives the removal test for necessity, gives the reducibility test for
sufficiency, and argues that the four roles are distinct. Its claims are analytical; where the
chapter is silent on questions of value or purpose, the silence is not a denial but a recognition
that the analytical description is not the whole of what can be said. Where the chapter speaks
of “completeness,” “removal,” “reducibility,” “role,” or “distinctness,” these are structural terms;
their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and in the previous chapter.


3.1     The Question
An explanation, we said in the previous chapter, assigns four roles: fixed elements, fluid element,
governing dynamics, context. The definitions were given, and a control question was supplied for
each. But two questions remain unanswered.
   First: are the four roles necessary? Could an explanation omit one of them and still be
complete? If a role can be omitted without loss, then it is not a column of explanatory cognition,
but a convenience of some explanations.
   Second: are the four roles sufficient? Could an explanation require a fifth role that the four
do not cover? If a fifth role is needed, the framework is incomplete, and the book’s architecture
must be revised.
   This chapter addresses both questions. The first it answers by argument: the four roles
are necessary, and their necessity can be shown by removing each in turn and observing what
remains. The second it answers by estimate: the four roles are sufficient, in the sense that every
candidate fifth role examined so far has been reducible to one of the four. The estimate is offered
as an estimate, not as a proof, because the possibility of a new kind of explanation cannot be
ruled out in advance. The chapter states in advance what would refute the estimate.


3.2     The Four-Column Principle
The two questions are answered together by a single principle.

   Principle 3.1 (The Four-Column Principle)

   (T) (necessity) Every explanatory cognition requires the simultaneous presence of four
   columns: fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics, and context. If any one of
   the four is absent, the cognition is incomplete as an explanation.


                                                17
18                             Chapter 3. The Four-Column Principle: Necessity and Sufficiency


     (E) (sufficiency) No fifth column is needed: every candidate fifth column that has been
     examined reduces to one of the four.

     The principle has two halves with different statuses. The necessity half is (T): it is argued,
and the argument is given below. The sufficiency half is (E): it is an estimate, supported by a
test, and it is subject to revision if a candidate fifth column is found that cannot be reduced to
any of the four. The two halves are stated together because they concern a single claim about the
analytical structure of explanatory cognition, but the reader is invited to assess them separately.
     The principle is not a stipulation. It is not a definition of “explanation” by fiat. The necessity
half follows from what an explanation is asked to do, as the removal test shows. The sufficiency
half is an estimate about the space of possible explanations, and it is offered at exactly that
strength.


3.3      Proof of Necessity: The Removal Test
The argument for necessity proceeds by removing each column in turn, and observing what
remains. If what remains is a recognizable explanatory failure, the column is necessary. If what
remains is a complete explanation, the column is not.

Proof of Necessity (Removal Test). By the definitions of the previous chapter, an explanation
says what is related, by what the relation is carried, according to what rule, and from what
standpoint. We remove each column in turn and observe what remains.

 (a) Without fixed elements. There is nothing for effect to hold between. What remains is a flow
       with no terms, which is a description of process but not of what the process connects. The
       resulting account is a recognizable explanatory failure.

 (b) Without fluid elements. The fixed elements are a list, not a network. Nothing is said about
       how any one bears on another. The resulting account is a recognizable explanatory failure;
       the argument that this is so is the conveyor principle, which is stated and proved in the
       next chapter, and here it is only named.

 (c) Without governing dynamics. The network is unordered: it shows that things are connected,
       but not how the connection behaves, so it cannot support prediction or counterfactual
       reasoning. The resulting account is a recognizable explanatory failure.

 (d) Without context. The explanation is a rule without a standpoint. Such a rule underde-
       termines its own application: the same entities can be partitioned into fixed and fluid in
       different ways, and the rule alone does not say which partition is intended. The resulting
       account is a recognizable explanatory failure.

     Each removal yields a recognizable explanatory failure. Hence each column is necessary.

     The proof depends on a premise that is not itself proved: that we can recognize an explanatory
failure when we see one. The premise is a commitment of the method, and it is declared as such.
3.4. Support for Sufficiency: The Reducibility Test                                              19


A reader who denies it may still follow the argument that the four roles are what an explanation,
on inspection, assigns; what the reader denies is that the inspection has the force of proof. The
framework does not claim more than the inspection delivers.

   Remark 3.1 (The Removal Test Is Not a Definition)

   The removal test is not a definition of “explanation,” and it is not a derivation of the
   four columns from a prior principle. It is a test: it takes the four columns as proposed by
   the previous chapter, and it asks whether an explanation can be complete without one of
   them. The test presupposes that the four columns have been correctly identified; if they
   have not, the test may fail to reveal a column that should have been on the list. The next
   section addresses this possibility, in the form of the reducibility test.




3.4    Support for Sufficiency: The Reducibility Test

Sufficiency cannot be proved from the definitions, because a new kind of explanation might
always turn up. It is therefore offered as an estimate and supported by a test.

   Definition 3.1 (Reducibility)

   A candidate fifth column is reducible when its role in explanation can be reassigned to
   one of the four columns without loss.


   The test proceeds by examining the standard candidates for a fifth column, and asking, for
each, whether its role can be reassigned.


Candidate 1: Purpose or goal. A teleological explanation (“the knife is made in order to
cut”) states a rule of the form “the system tends toward state S.” That is a governing dynamics.
The role of purpose in the explanation is the role of a rule that governs the system’s behavior,
and the rule is one of the four columns.

   Remark 3.2 (The Analytical Reduction of Purpose)

   The reduction here is analytical, not metaphysical. The claim is that the role of purpose
   in an explanation can be reassigned to the governing dynamics column without loss of
   explanatory content. The claim is not that purposes are unreal, or that the things that
   have purposes do not really have them. A teleological explanation is a particular kind
   of explanation; the framework’s claim is that its form can be analyzed through the four
   columns, not that the reality it explains is exhausted by the analysis. The distinction
   matters, because the analytical reduction of a role is not the metaphysical reduction of a
   reality. A reader who takes the analytical reduction as a denial of purpose has misread it;
   a reader who takes it as a description of the form of teleological explanation has read it
   correctly.
20                            Chapter 3. The Four-Column Principle: Necessity and Sufficiency


Candidate 2: Time. Temporal order enters an explanation either as a feature of the dynamics
(the rule concerns how states succeed one another) or as part of the frame (the scale at which
the elements are individuated). In either case, it is carried by the third or fourth column.


Candidate 3: The observer. The standpoint of the cognizer is the content of the context
column: the question asked, the means used, the scale adopted. The observer is not a fifth
column; it is what the fourth column makes explicit.
     These three are the standard candidates. The test would fail, and the principle would have
to be revised, if an explanation accepted as complete could be exhibited whose content cannot
be redistributed over the four columns in this way.

     Remark 3.3 (The Risky Claim)

     The framework makes a risky claim, and says in advance what would refute it. A candidate
     fifth column that resists reduction to the four would refute the sufficiency half of the
     four-column principle. The framework does not offer a proof that no such candidate can
     be found; it offers an estimate, supported by the examination of the candidates that have
     been proposed, and it invites the reader to produce a counterexample.



3.5      The Distinctness of the Four Analytical Roles

The four columns are necessary only if they are also distinct. If one column could be supplied by
another, the removal test would not show what it claims to show: the removal of a column that
is not distinct from another would not produce an explanatory failure, because the other column
would supply the role.
     The distinctness of the four roles is therefore argued separately.

     Principle 3.2 (The Distinctness of the Four Analytical Roles)

     (T) The four questions are distinct: an answer to any one of them does not, by itself,
     supply the answer to any other.


Proof.      1. Knowing what the elements are does not say what, if anything, passes between
       them. Two things may be fully described, and yet nothing be said of how one bears on the
       other.

     2. Knowing that something passes between them does not say by what rule it behaves. A
       conduit may be named without any law of its working.

     3. Knowing the rule does not say from what standpoint the elements are partitioned as they
       are, since the same rule can be applied to different partitions.

     4. Knowing the standpoint does not supply the elements, the conduit, or the rule that are to
       be found from it.
3.6. The Limit of the Argument                                                                    21


  5. Hence no one of the four answers is supplied by another taken alone, and the four roles are
      distinct.



   The proof shows that the four roles are distinct as roles. It does not show that they are
distinct as entities. The distinction is important, and it is stated in the next remark.

   Remark 3.4 (Distinctness Is Not Separability)

   Distinctness does not imply absolute separability. Two analytical roles may be instantiated
   by the same entity, or one role may constrain the content of another (the rules of a
   cognition may be constrained by the structure of its elements), without the roles thereby
   becoming conceptually identical. A custom may be both a fluid element and a governing
   dynamics, depending on the question the cognition asks. What the distinctness principle
   asserts is that the roles are not interchangeable: an answer to one question does not, by
   itself, answer another.


   Remark 3.5 (The Limit of the Argument)

   The conclusion is limited. It shows that the roles are distinct and all required. It does
   not show that they are carried by four distinct kinds of thing in reality; one entity can
   play several roles in different cognitions, and this is the point of the context-dependence
   principle, which is stated in a later chapter. The framework’s claim is analytical, not
   ontological.


   Remark 3.6 (The Analytical and the Real)

   The analytical necessity of the four columns is a claim about the structure of explanation,
   not a claim about the composition of reality. The two are related, but they are not the
   same. If explanation is possible, then the structure of explanation is real; but the reality
   of the structure is not the reality of the things explained. The four columns describe
   the order through which what is becomes intelligible; they do not claim that the order is
   the whole of what is. The framework keeps the analytical and the real distinct, because
   the confusion of the two would turn a description of explanation into a metaphysics of
   substances—a view the book does not hold and does not need.



3.6     The Limit of the Argument
Two claims have been argued. The four columns are necessary, and the four roles are distinct.
Neither claim amounts to a demonstration that the four-column framework is the unique correct
framework for explanatory cognition. Three limits must be stated.
   First, the removal test presupposes that we can recognize an explanatory failure. A reader
who denies this premise denies the force of the argument, not its content; the argument itself
remains intelligible, and its conclusion remains a claim that the reader can assess on other
grounds.
22                             Chapter 3. The Four-Column Principle: Necessity and Sufficiency


     Second, the reducibility test is an estimate, not a proof. Its support consists in the examination
of the standard candidates for a fifth column; it does not exclude the possibility that a new kind
of explanation will be found that resists reduction to the four. The framework states this limit
openly and offers the estimate at exactly that strength.
     Third, the distinctness principle shows that the roles are distinct, not that they are separable.
The framework’s four columns are analytical roles, not four substances. Where a single entity
plays more than one role, the framework does not multiply entities; it distinguishes roles.
     These limits are not deficiencies of the argument. They are the conditions under which the
argument is offered, and the framework states them so that the reader knows what kind of claim
is being made. A reader who accepts the limits may still accept the framework; a reader who
rejects the framework is invited to attack it at the limits, since those are where the framework is
most vulnerable.
     The limits have a positive side, and it is worth stating. The framework’s claim is analytical,
and the analytical claim points toward the reality it analyzes. The four columns describe the
order of explanatory cognition; the order is real, and the framework’s claim is that it is invariant.
But the order is not self-sufficient. The analytical description is not the whole of what can
be said about what is explained. The framework’s silence on what lies beyond the analytical
structure is not a denial; it is the recognition that the analytical structure is the order of what is,
not the whole of what is. The framework’s claim is that the order is real and describable; it does
not claim that the order is the whole, and it does not claim that nothing lies beyond it.


3.7      Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter

            Claim                                                           Status

            Necessity of the four columns (removal test)                    (T)
            Sufficiency of the four columns (reducibility test)             (E)
            Distinctness of the four roles                                  (T)
            Reducibility (definition)                                       (A)


A Question for Reflection
Can you construct an explanation that you would accept as complete and that does not assign
one of the four roles? If so, the reducibility test has failed for that case, and the sufficiency half
of the principle is in question. If not, what is it about the explanation that makes the missing
role unrecognizable as missing?

The next chapter states and proves the conveyor principle: the claim that no explanation of how
one fixed element bears on another is complete unless it invokes a fluid element. The principle is
the first of the four columns to receive a proof of its own.

The Conveyor Principle and Non-Sequential
Connectivity


Scope. This chapter states and proves the conveyor principle: the claim that no explanation of
how one fixed element bears on another is complete unless it invokes a fluid element. It states
what would falsify the principle, and it distinguishes the principle from a stronger claim that it
does not entail—the claim that the effect must pass through every intermediate element. Its
claims are analytical; where the chapter is silent on questions of value, the silence is not a denial
but a recognition that the analytical description is not the whole of what can be said. Where the
chapter speaks of “effect,” “carrier,” “medium,” “signal,” “process,” “passage,” or “route,” these
are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and in the previous
chapters.



4.1     A Scene

Consider a lamp and a wall. The lamp is switched on; the wall is illuminated. Something has
passed from the lamp to the wall, or so we say. But what has passed, and how?
   The ordinary answer is that light has passed. But the ordinary answer is not yet an explanation.
To say that light has passed is to name a candidate for the medium; it is not yet to say how the
medium carries the effect, or what would count as the effect’s failing to arrive. And if we press
the question—what exactly is it that travels from the lamp to the wall?—the ordinary answer
begins to dissolve. Is it a stream of particles? A wave in a medium? A field that is disturbed?
Each answer has its difficulties, and each has been defended.
   The scene is not about light in particular. It is about a more general question. Whenever we
say that one thing bears on another—that the lamp illuminates the wall, that a word affects a
hearer, that a cause produces an effect—we are supposing that something passes between them.
The present chapter asks what an explanation of such passage must contain.
   The question is not new. It is as old as the problem of causation. But the framework’s answer
to it is precise, and the precision is what the chapter aims at.



4.2     The Question

In the previous chapter, the four-column principle was stated and argued. The four columns
are necessary, and the four roles are distinct. One of the four columns—the fluid element—was
defined as the entity that conveys effect. The definition was given in the chapter before that,
and a control question was supplied for it.

                                                 23
24                         Chapter 4. The Conveyor Principle and Non-Sequential Connectivity


     The present chapter asks a further question about the fluid element. The definition says what
a fluid element is; it does not yet say why an explanation must invoke one. The question is:

       Why is no explanation of how one fixed element bears on another complete, unless it
       invokes a fluid element?

     The question is not idle. An explanation that names the two fixed elements and states that
one changes when the other does—“when the switch is flipped, the wall becomes bright”—records
a correlation. It does not say how the switch bears on the wall. If the correlation is offered as a
complete explanation, something has been left out, and the present chapter identifies what.
     The chapter’s answer is the conveyor principle. The principle is stated in the next section,
proved in the section after, and distinguished from a stronger claim in the section after that.


4.3      The Conveyor Principle

     Principle 4.1 (Conveyor Principle)

     (T) No explanation of how one fixed element bears on another is complete unless it invokes
     a fluid element: a carrier, medium, signal, or process by which the effect passes.

     The principle is stated as a claim about completeness. It does not say that every explanation
must name a particular kind of fluid element; it says that every explanation of how one element
bears on another must invoke some fluid element or other. The principle is deliberately broad in
the range of what counts. A thing, a signal, a process, a medium, a field—any of these can be a
fluid element, provided it conveys effect. What the principle excludes is the explanation that
says how one thing bears on another without invoking anything by which the bearing is carried.
     The breadth is not a weakness. It is what makes the principle hard to evade. An explanation
that tries to avoid naming a fluid element will fail, not because the framework insists on a
particular kind of medium, but because the explanation will leave unanswered the question of
how. The proof of the principle, given below, makes this precise.

     Remark 4.1 (The Principle Is Not a Definition)

     The conveyor principle is not a definition of “explanation,” and it is not a stipulation that
     every explanation must contain the word “medium.” It is a claim about the structure of
     any explanation of how one thing bears on another. The claim can be denied; a reader
     who denies it is invited to produce an explanation of how, that names no carrier, and that
     is nonetheless complete. The proof below shows that the denial is difficult to sustain; it
     does not show that the denial is impossible in every conceivable case.

     Example 4.1 (Conversation)

     If language is removed from the negotiation, the two parties are disconnected nodes.
     Language is therefore the condition of possibility of the explanation of how one bears on
     the other. The example is not a proof of the principle; it is an illustration of what the
4.4. The Proof                                                                                       25


   principle says.



4.4    The Proof
The principle is proved by reductio.

Proof of the Conveyor Principle.       1. Suppose an explanation of how A bears on B is complete,
      and invokes no fluid element.

  2. Then it says only that A and B are fixed elements, and that B changes when A does.

  3. That statement records a correlation between two nodes. It does not say how A bears on
      B, since by hypothesis no route, medium, or process is specified.

  4. An explanation that does not say how is incomplete as an explanation of how.

  5. This contradicts the supposition. Hence every complete explanation of how one thing bears
      on another invokes a fluid element.


   The proof is short, and its brevity is the point. The principle is not a substantive metaphysical
claim about the furniture of the world; it is a claim about what a certain kind of explanation
must contain. The argument turns on a single distinction—between recording a correlation and
explaining how the correlation is produced—and the distinction is one that any explanation of
how must respect.

   Remark 4.2 (The Proof Is Relative to a Premise)

   The proof depends on the premise that an explanation that does not say how is incomplete
   as an explanation of how. The premise is not proved; it is what the word “how” means
   in the context of an explanation. A reader who accepts the premise accepts the proof; a
   reader who denies the premise denies the meaning of “how” that the framework employs.
   The framework does not offer an argument for the meaning; it states the meaning, and
   offers the proof as what follows from it.

   Remark 4.3 (The Principle Is Analytical, Not Causal)

   The conveyor principle is a principle about explanation, not a principle about causation.
   It says that any explanation of how one thing bears on another requires a medium; it does
   not say that every instance of one thing bearing on another requires a medium. The two
   claims are different, and the difference is the difference between the order of inquiry and
   the order of being. The framework’s claim is about the structure of inquiry: it is a claim
   about what an explanation must contain. It does not claim that reality is exhausted by
   what an explanation can contain, and it does not claim that nothing happens without a
   medium. It claims that nothing can be explained as happening without a medium. The
   distinction is crucial, because it prevents the principle from being read as a denial of direct
26                         Chapter 4. The Conveyor Principle and Non-Sequential Connectivity


     action— whether that action is human, natural, or divine.


     The proof’s premise is not a weakness of the argument. It is the way the argument makes
its claim. The conveyor principle is a claim about what an explanation of how must contain,
and the claim is established by exhibiting what an explanation that contains nothing of the kind
would look like. The reader who accepts the premise will find the argument compelling; the
reader who denies the premise will not, and the framework does not pretend otherwise.


4.5      What Would Falsify the Principle

The principle is only as strong as the breadth of the term “fluid element,” and the term is
deliberately broad. Because of that breadth, the principle could not be refuted by merely
renaming a mediator. A genuine counterexample must satisfy two conditions.

     1. It must name no mediating medium, signal, or process.

     2. It must nonetheless be accepted as complete.

     The standard candidate is unmediated action at a distance. One thing bears on another
across a gap with nothing passing between them, and the account is held to leave no further
question about how.
     The framework’s position on the candidate is stated in the next remark.

     Remark 4.4 (The Framework’s Position on Unmediated Action)

     The framework holds that an account of unmediated action at a distance always leaves
     the question of how unanswered. The account may be accepted as a description of what
     happens; it is not accepted as an explanation of how what happens is produced. Whoever
     exhibits an accepted complete account of that kind refutes the conveyor principle. The
     framework does not claim that no such account will ever be exhibited; it claims that no
     such account has been exhibited, and it states what such an account would have to be.
     The framework does not deny that unmediated action is real. It denies that unmediated
     action can be explained without a medium. The two claims are different. The first is a
     claim about what can happen; the second is a claim about what can be said about what
     happens. The framework’s principle is the second, not the first. A reader who takes the
     principle as a denial of the first has misread it; a reader who takes it as a claim about the
     second has read it correctly.


     The remark is not a dogmatic refusal to consider the candidate. It is a statement of what the
framework would need in order to revise the principle. The framework is not committed to the
principle come what may; it is committed to the principle as the best account currently available,
and it says in advance what would show the account to be wrong.
4.6. Non-Sequential Connectivity                                                                    27


4.6     Non-Sequential Connectivity

The conveyor principle requires that some fluid element carry the effect. It does not say that the
effect must traverse, one after another, every element that lies between two fixed elements in
some ordering of them. The distinction is important, and it is stated as a principle of its own.

   Principle 4.2 (Non-Sequential Connectivity)

   (T) The conveyor principle does not require that the connection between two fixed elements
   pass through all intermediate fixed elements. A fluid element may connect two fixed
   elements directly, even when other fixed elements lie “between” them in some ordering.


Argument for Non-Sequential Connectivity. The reductio that proves the conveyor principle uses
only the premise that an explanation of how A bears on B must name a carrier. Nothing in
it requires the carrier to pass through further nodes. The argument for the conveyor principle
is therefore indifferent to whether the carrier is sequential or non-sequential; the principle is
satisfied by either. A separate argument would be needed to require sequential passage, and no
such argument has been given.


   The principle is not a claim that sequential passage is impossible. It is a claim that sequential
passage is not required. In some explanations, the fluid element does pass through intermediate
elements; in others, it does not. The framework does not decide in advance which case holds. It
distinguishes the two possibilities, and it leaves the question of which holds in a given explanation
to the explanation itself.

   Remark 4.5 (Why the Distinction Matters)

   The distinction matters for the parts of the book that follow. When the book turns
   to light, it will argue that light is the fluid element in its most general role, and that
   light connects identities and manifestations directly, without requiring passage through
   every realm between them. The principle stated here is the analytical counterpart of that
   ontological claim; the two are related, but the relation is a matter for the later part. For
   the present, the principle is offered as a claim about the structure of explanation, and it is
   proved by the same kind of argument as the conveyor principle itself.


   The principle is the second half of the chapter’s contribution. The conveyor principle says
that some fluid element must carry the effect; the non-sequential principle says that the carrying
need not be a passage through every intermediate. Together, they state what the framework
requires of the fluid element column, and what it does not.
   The framework’s claim is analytical: it describes what an explanation requires, not what
reality must contain. A direct connection is a real possibility; the framework’s claim is that if
it is to be explained, the explanation must invoke a medium, even if the medium is the direct
connection itself. The distinction is the distinction between the order of inquiry and the order of
being, and it is kept throughout the book.
28                        Chapter 4. The Conveyor Principle and Non-Sequential Connectivity


4.7      The Conveyor Principle and the Four Columns
The conveyor principle is the first of the four columns to receive a proof of its own. In the
previous chapter, the necessity of the four columns was argued by the removal test; the test
presupposed that the fluid element is necessary, and the present chapter supplies the proof of
that presupposition.
     The principle’s place in the framework can be summarized as follows.

     Column                      Role in the argument of this chapter

     Fixed elements              The two terms whose relation is to be explained.
     Fluid element               The medium by which the effect of one term reaches the other.
                                 The conveyor principle asserts its necessity.
     Governing dynamics          The rule of the medium’s operation. The conveyor principle
                                 does not assert anything about it; the rule is the subject of a
                                 later part.
     Context                     The frame in which the relation is posed. The conveyor principle
                                 is silent on it; the frame is what makes the relation a relation
                                 between these terms rather than others.

     The table is a summary, not a new argument. Its purpose is to locate the conveyor principle
in the framework’s architecture: the principle is about the second column, and it presupposes the
first and fourth. The third column—the governing dynamics—is not addressed by the principle,
and the reader who wishes to know what the framework says about it will find it in the part of
the book that treats the rules of the contexts.

            What would falsify the conveyor principle                      (A)

A Question for Reflection
Can you name an explanation, accepted as complete by those who use it, that invokes no carrier
between the elements it relates? If you can, the conveyor principle is in question. If you cannot,
what is it about the explanation that makes the missing carrier unrecognizable as missing?

The next chapter turns to the context column. It argues that the fixedness or fluidity of an element
depends on the cognitive context, not on the element’s essence, and that the cognitive contexts in
which an identity can be cognized are not finite in number.
Chapter 5

Context-Dependence and the Infinity of Contexts


Scope. This chapter states and argues two principles about the context column. The first is that
the fixedness or fluidity of an element depends on the cognitive context, not on the element’s
essence. The second is that the cognitive contexts in which an identity can be cognized are
not finite in number. The chapter distinguishes the cognitive context, which the two principles
concern, from the existential context, which is the realm in which a manifestation is realized. Its
claims are analytical; where the chapter is silent on questions of value, the silence is not a denial
but a recognition that the analytical description is not the whole of what can be said. Where the
chapter speaks of “fixedness,” “fluidity,” “essence,” “frame,” “openness,” or “generation,” these
are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and in the previous
chapters.


5.1     A Scene
Consider two inquiries into the same river. The first is the inquiry of the political geographer,
who asks: where does the border lie? For that inquiry, the river is a fixed element—a boundary
that is held stable while the relations of the two banks are explained. The second is the inquiry
of the trader, who asks: how do goods travel from this bank to that? For that inquiry, the river
is a fluid element—a route that carries effect from one side to the other.
   The river is one thing; its role differs. Neither inquiry is wrong; each is correct within its own
frame. But if the two inquiries are confused—if the geographer’s river is taken to be the river,
and the trader’s river is taken to be not the river but a mere appearance—then something has
gone wrong. A role that belongs to a frame has been mistaken for a property of the thing.
   The same structure recurs. A word in a dictionary is a fixed element: an entry whose meaning
is held constant while its relations to other entries are explained. The same word in a conversation
is a fluid element: a conveyor of meaning between speakers. A coin in an economic analysis is a
fixed unit of value; the same coin in a metallurgical analysis is a fluid sample of copper. In each
case, the same entity plays different roles in different frames, and the roles are not properties of
the entity but assignments made by the question the frame asks.
   The scene poses two questions. First: if fixedness is not a property of the thing, what is it a
property of? Second: how many such frames are there—is there a finite list of them, or does the
list run on without end? The present chapter answers both questions.


5.2     The Question
The first question is this. When an explanation holds an element fixed, or treats it as fluid, is
it identifying a property the element has in itself, or is it assigning a role that depends on the

                                                 29
30                                  Chapter 5. Context-Dependence and the Infinity of Contexts


explanation? The essentialist answer is that the element is fixed, or is fluid, in virtue of what it
is, and so in every frame alike. The framework’s answer is that fixedness and fluidity are roles,
assigned by the frame.
     The question is not merely terminological. If fixedness were a property of the thing, then two
frames that assign different roles to the same thing could not both be correct; one of them would
have to be mistaken about what the thing really is. If fixedness is a role, then both frames can
be correct in their own terms, and the apparent conflict between them is a conflict between the
frames, not between the thing and itself.
     The second question is this. The framework’s principle of context-dependence says that an
element’s role depends on the frame. How many frames are there? A finite list? An infinite one?
If the list is finite, then a complete survey of the roles an element can play might, in principle, be
possible. If the list is infinite, no such survey can be completed, and the framework’s epistemic
humility has a structural ground.
     The chapter answers both questions. The answer to the first is the context-dependence
principle; the answer to the second is the principle of the infinity of contexts. The two are distinct
principles, with distinct arguments, and the chapter treats them in turn.


5.3       The Context-Dependence Principle

     Principle 5.1 (Context-Dependence)

     (T) The fixedness or fluidity of an element depends on the cognitive context, not on the
     element’s essence. A single element can be fixed in one context and fluid in another.


Proof of the Context-Dependence Principle.         1. Essentialism says: each element is fixed, or is
       fluid, in virtue of what it is, and so in every context.

     2. But a river is a fixed element (a boundary) in political geography and a fluid element (a
       route of transport) in the geography of trade. A word is a fixed element (an entry whose
       meaning is held constant) in a dictionary and a fluid element (a conveyor of meaning
       between speakers) in a conversation.

     3. So there are elements whose status differs between contexts. This contradicts the universal
       claim of essentialism.

     4. Hence fixedness and fluidity are not essential properties of elements. They are roles,
       assigned by the question a context asks: which relations it holds constant, and which it
       treats as carrying effect.



     The proof is a counterexample argument. Essentialism makes a universal claim; the counterex-
ample shows that the universal claim is false. The argument does not prove that every element’s
role varies with the frame; it proves that some do, and that is enough to refute essentialism.
5.4. From Context-Dependence to Infinity                                                              31


   Remark 5.1 (What the Principle Generalizes)

   The context-dependence principle is a special case of a broader structural claim, which the
   framework develops in its treatment of predication. The broader claim is that metaphysical
   predicates are not absolute: they are defined relative to a level or a respect. The present
   principle applies the broader claim to the level of the cognitive context: just as a predicate
   is true or false relative to a realm, an element is fixed or fluid relative to a context. The
   broader claim is argued in its own place; the present principle is one of its applications,
   and does not depend on the broader argument for its establishment.


   Remark 5.2 (Cognitive Context and Existential Context)

   The principle concerns the cognitive context. It must not be read as saying that where a
   manifestation is realized depends on how it is studied. The realm in which a manifestation
   is realized is its existential context; it is fixed by the identity and the receiving realm, not
   by the question asked. The distinction between the two kinds of context was introduced
   in the chapter that defined the four columns; the present remark applies it. The cognitive
   context fixes the roles of elements in an explanation. The existential context fixes what
   can be realized where. The two are not the same, and the context-dependence principle
   concerns the first alone.
   The distinction between the two kinds of context is a distinction between the order of
   inquiry and the order of being. The cognitive context is the order through which what is
   becomes intelligible; the existential context is the order of what is. The two are distinct,
   and neither is reducible to the other; but the first is the condition of possibility of the
   second. A manifestation is realized in a realm before it is known in a frame; and the frame
   is the order through which the realm becomes intelligible. The framework keeps the two
   apart so that the study of cognition is not confused with the study of being—but the
   keeping-apart is not a denial that the two are related. The existential context is the ground
   of the cognitive context, and the cognitive context is the intelligibility of the existential
   context.

   Remark 5.3 (Not Every Assignment of Roles Is Equally Good)

   The principle says that fixedness and fluidity are roles. It does not say that every assignment
   of roles is equally adequate. Some assignments will explain the phenomenon better than
   others; some will fail to explain it at all. The framework’s criteria of context validity,
   which are stated in a later chapter, are what discipline the use of contexts. The present
   principle is about what kind of thing fixedness is, not about which assignments are correct.



5.4    From Context-Dependence to Infinity
The context-dependence principle leaves a question open. If fixedness depends on the context,
and if the context is fixed by the question, then how many questions are there? If the number
of questions is finite, then the number of contexts is finite, and a complete survey of the roles
32                                  Chapter 5. Context-Dependence and the Infinity of Contexts


an element can play might be possible in principle. If the number of questions is infinite, no
such survey can be completed, and the framework’s epistemic claim about super-identity has a
structural ground.
     The question is not whether we, in fact, have surveyed all the contexts. The question is
whether the survey could, in principle, be completed. The next two sections argue that it cannot.
The argument has two parts. The first part states an assumption about the openness of relations.
The second part uses the assumption to generate a non-terminating sequence of contexts.


5.5      The Openness of Relations
The first part of the argument is an assumption about what happens when a manifestation is
produced in a context. The assumption is stated as a definition, and adopted as an axiom.

     Definition 5.1 (Openness of Relations)

     (A) Openness of relations: for every cognitive context C and every manifestation m that
     an identity has in C, there is a cognitive context C ′ in which m is itself a fixed element,
     related by fluid elements and dynamics that are not available in C.


     The definition says that any manifestation, once produced, can become an element in a
further context. The manifestation is not merely a label for the identity that produced it; it is a
thing in its own right, and it can be related to other things in ways the producing context did
not consider.

     Remark 5.4 (Why Openness Is Plausible)

     The assumption is plausible because a manifestation is not a mere label for the identity;
     it is the product of the identity’s interaction with a receiving realm. Once produced, it
     is a thing in its own right, and it can be related to other things in ways the producing
     context did not consider. A speech is manifested in a conversation and then becomes
     a fixed element in an analysis of rhetoric; a building is manifested in a street and then
     becomes a fixed element in the history of a city. The assumption is that this step never
     runs out. It is the framework’s version of the familiar observation that every answer in
     inquiry opens further questions.


     Example 5.1 (A Speech)

     A speaker says something in a conversation. The utterance is a manifestation of the
     speaker’s identity in the relational realm of conversation. In a subsequent inquiry, the
     same utterance is a fixed element—a text to be analyzed for its rhetorical structure. In a
     further inquiry, the analysis is itself a fixed element—a document to be studied for its
     assumptions. At each step, the previous product becomes an element of a new context.
     The example illustrates the assumption; it does not prove it.


     The assumption is adopted, not proved. Its justification is that it is plausible in light of what
5.6. The Infinity of Contexts                                                                      33


manifestations are, and that its denial would require an argument the framework does not have.
A reader who denies the assumption can still accept the context-dependence principle; what the
reader denies is the basis for the infinity of contexts.


5.6     The Infinity of Contexts
The second part of the argument uses the openness assumption to generate a non-terminating
sequence of contexts.

   Principle 5.2 (Infinity of Contexts)

   (T) Given the openness assumption of Definition 5.1, the cognitive contexts in which an
   identity can be cognized are not finite in number: no finite list of them is complete.
   (S) Whether their number is countable or uncountable is left open.

   The principle has two halves, with different statuses. The first half is (T): given openness,
the non-terminating generation argument below establishes that no finite list is complete. The
second half is (S): whether the infinite number is countable or uncountable is a question the
framework does not settle. The two halves are stated together because they concern a single
claim, but the reader is invited to assess them separately.

Proof of the Infinity of Contexts.     1. Let C0 be any cognitive context for an identity I, and
      let m0 be a manifestation of I in C0 .

  2. By openness, there is a context C1 in which m0 is a fixed element, related by new fluid
      elements and dynamics. I has a manifestation m1 in C1 , and m1 differs from m0 , since it
      is the product of I with a different context.

  3. Apply the same step to m1 , and so on. The sequence C0 , C1 , C2 , . . . never repeats: each
      Cn+1 contains an element mn that is not a fixed element of Cn or of any earlier context,
      since manifestations are context-bound products.

  4. So no finite list of cognitive contexts is complete.


   The proof depends on a premise that is not established here: that manifestations are context-
bound products. The premise is developed in the framework’s treatment of manifestation, in
a later part of the book. Here it is stated as a premise of the argument, and the argument is
offered as what follows from it.

   Remark 5.5 (The Infinity Is on the Side of the Subject)

   The infinity established here is an infinity of contexts, not an infinity of being. The
   framework does not claim that reality is infinite; it claims that the frames in which reality
   can be cognized are not finite in number. The distinction is crucial, because the two
   claims are different, and the confusion of the two would turn an epistemic claim into a
34                                  Chapter 5. Context-Dependence and the Infinity of Contexts


     metaphysical one. The infinity is on the side of the subject: it is the subject’s inquiry that
     is non-terminating, not the object of the inquiry that is inexhaustible. The framework’s
     claim is that the finite subject cannot complete the survey; it does not claim that the
     survey has no object, or that the object is beyond all survey. The object may be fully
     known to a subject that is not finite; the framework’s claim is about the finite subject,
     not about the object. The framework’s silence on the infinite subject is not a denial of
     its possibility; it is the recognition that the framework’s method is the method of finite
     inquiry, and that the limits of finite inquiry are not the limits of what is.


     Remark 5.6 (Cognitive Contexts and Ontological Levels)

     The infinity here is that of cognitive contexts. It does not imply that there are infinitely
     many fundamental levels of being. The framework’s ontology has a fixed and small
     number of levels, and the plurality of frames does not create further levels. The distinction
     between cognitive architecture and ontological architecture, which was introduced in the
     first chapter of this part, is what makes this clear: the infinity of frames is an infinity of
     standpoints of cognition, not of levels of being.


     Remark 5.7 (An Image, Not an Argument)

     A cone cut by planes at different angles yields different figures. The image illustrates how
     one structure shows different faces under different cuts. It is not an argument for the
     infinity of contexts: the number of ways of cutting a cone says nothing about the number
     of cognitive contexts. The argument is the generative one above, and its force is exactly
     that of the openness assumption.




5.7        The Two Principles in Tandem

The two principles of this chapter are distinct, but they are related, and their relation is worth
stating.
     The context-dependence principle says that fixedness is a role, not an essence. The infinity
principle says that the frames in which roles are assigned are not finite in number. Together, they
imply that an element can be fixed in some contexts and fluid in others, and that the number of
both kinds of context is infinite. No finite survey of an element’s roles can be completed, because
the roles depend on the frames, and the frames are not finite.
     This consequence will matter for the framework’s claim about super-identity. The claim is
that no finite subject can know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts. The infinity
of contexts is one of the premises of that claim; the other is the finitude of the subject. The
two premises together yield the conclusion. The argument for super-identity is given in a later
chapter; for the present, it is enough to see that the infinity principle is one of its structural
grounds.
5.8. The Limit of the Argument                                                                       35


  Principle                          What it establishes

  Context-dependence                 Fixedness and fluidity are roles, assigned by the frame,
                                     not properties of the element.
  Infinity of contexts               The frames in which roles are assigned are not finite in
                                     number; no finite list of them is complete.
  Both together                      An element can play infinitely many roles; no finite survey
                                     of its roles can be completed.


   Remark 5.8 (Epistemic Humility Is Not Skepticism)

   The framework’s epistemic humility is the recognition of the limits of finite inquiry, not a
   denial that knowledge is possible. The finite subject can know; what the finite subject
   cannot do is complete the survey. The two claims are different, and the difference matters.
   A skeptic claims that knowledge is impossible; the framework claims that knowledge is
   partial. The first is a denial of knowledge; the second is a description of its condition. The
   framework’s claim is that the partiality is structural: it belongs to the relation between a
   finite subject and an identity, not to the identity itself, and not to the object of knowledge.
   The identity may be fully known to a subject that is not finite; the framework’s claim is
   about the finite subject, not about the identity. The framework’s silence on the infinite
   subject is not a denial of its possibility; it is the recognition that the framework’s method
   is the method of finite inquiry, and that the limits of finite inquiry are not the limits of
   what is.



5.8     The Limit of the Argument
Three limits must be stated.
   First, the context-dependence principle is proved by counterexample, and counterexample
proves only that essentialism is false. It does not establish what fixedness and fluidity are in
positive terms. The framework’s positive account is that they are roles assigned by the question
a context asks; this account is stated, not proved, and a reader who prefers a different positive
account is invited to develop it.
   Second, the infinity principle depends on the openness assumption. A reader who denies
openness can accept the context-dependence principle and deny the infinity principle; the two
are related but separable. The framework adopts openness because its denial would require
an argument the framework does not have, and because the assumption is plausible in light of
what manifestations are. The framework does not claim that openness is necessary in every
conceivable framework.
   Third, the principle of infinity is a structural claim about cognitive contexts, not a claim
about the world. It does not say that the world is infinite; it says that the frames in which the
world can be studied are. A reader who is concerned that the framework is making a metaphysical
claim about infinity is invited to read the principle at its stated strength: it is a claim about the
analytical structure of cognition, not about the extent of being.
36                                  Chapter 5. Context-Dependence and the Infinity of Contexts


     These limits are not deficiencies. They are the conditions under which the argument is offered,
and they are stated so that the reader knows what kind of claim is being made.
     The limits have a positive side, and it is worth stating. The limits are limits of finite inquiry,
not limits of reality. The framework does not claim that reality is inexhaustible; it claims that
the finite subject’s survey of reality is non-terminating. The distinction is the distinction between
the order of inquiry and the order of being, and it is kept throughout the book. A reader who
takes the framework’s claim as a claim about reality has misread it; a reader who takes it as a
claim about finite inquiry has read it correctly. The framework’s claim is that the finite subject
cannot complete the survey; it does not claim that the survey has no object, or that the object is
beyond all survey. The framework’s silence on the infinite subject is not a denial of its possibility;
it is the recognition that the framework’s method is the method of finite inquiry, and that the
limits of finite inquiry are not the limits of what is.

A Question for Reflection
Can you name an element that plays a fixed role in one frame and a fluid role in another, and
whose roles in the two frames are both correct? What would it mean to say that one of the two
frames has got the element’s role wrong?

The next chapter draws the epistemic consequences of the infinity of contexts. It states and argues
the impossibility of super-identity; it states the criteria by which contexts are to be distinguished
as valid or invalid; and it defines the concept after which this book is named, viability.
Chapter 6

Super-Identity, Context Validity, and Viability


Scope. This chapter draws three consequences of the principles established in the preceding
chapters. The first is a consequence of the infinity of contexts: the impossibility of super-identity.
The second is a consequence of the context-dependence principle: the need for criteria by which
contexts are distinguished as valid or invalid. The third is a consequence of the four-column
framework as a whole: the definition of viability, the concept after which this book is named.
The chapter also distinguishes the four columns from the seven realms, and it ends with a ledger
of the claims established in this part and a dependency map of the premises on which they rest.
Its claims are analytical; where the chapter is silent on questions of value, the silence is not a
denial but a recognition that the analytical description is not the whole of what can be said.
Where the chapter speaks of “validity,” “adequacy,” “viability,” “fidelity,” “sustainability,” or
“recoverability,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.


6.1     A Scene
Suppose someone says: I have known every manifestation of this city. The claim is not idle. The
speaker means that nothing about the city—its economic life, its cultural life, its architecture, its
legal order, its residents, its history—remains outside their knowledge. If the claim is true, then
no question about the city can be put to them that they cannot answer. If the claim is false,
then some question about the city exceeds their knowledge, and the speaker has overreached.
    The claim is not, in fact, ever made in those words. But it is made in other words, all the
time. The biographer who claims to have “captured” a life; the historian who claims to have
written the “definitive” account of a period; the analyst who claims to have built a “complete
model” of a system; the reader who claims to have “understood” a text in its entirety—each of
these is a version of the same claim. What each claims is that a finite subject has surveyed an
infinite field, and that nothing remains outside the survey.
    The scene poses three questions. First: is such a claim ever true? If not, why not? Second: if
the claim is not true, what distinguishes a survey that is adequate from one that is not? Third:
what becomes of the notion of “adequate survey” once the distinction between identity and
manifestation is made? The present chapter answers these questions. The first is answered by
the argument for the impossibility of super- identity. The second is answered by the criteria of
context validity. The third is answered by the definition of viability.


6.2     The Impossibility of Super-Identity
The first question is whether a finite subject can know all manifestations of an identity in all
contexts. The chapter’s answer is that it cannot, and the answer is argued, not asserted.

                                                 37
38                                     Chapter 6. Super-Identity, Context Validity, and Viability


     Definition 6.1 (Super-Identity)

     A super-identity claim is a subject’s claim to have known, or to be able to know, all
     manifestations of an identity in all contexts, so that nothing about the identity’s expression
     remains outside its knowledge.

     The definition must be distinguished from a different and acceptable claim. A subject may
reconstruct an identity to some degree of adequacy, by finding what remains invariant across
the manifestations available to it; the result is a pseudo-identity, and nothing in this section
denies that it can be adequate. What is denied is exhaustiveness. The distinction between a
pseudo-identity and its source is developed in the part of the book that treats identity; here it is
named, and the impossibility principle concerns the stronger claim.
     Three things are easily confused, and the framework keeps them apart: the aggregation
of data or manifestations, the compatibility of the manifestations with one another, and the
numerical unity of the identity that they manifest. Collecting manifestations (aggregation) and
finding them consistent (compatibility) do not restore the numerical unity of the source. The
distinction is argued in the part of the book that treats identity; here it is named.

     Principle 6.1 (Impossibility of Super-Identity)

     (T) No finite subject can know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts. The
     super-identity claim is therefore self-undermining.

     The proof is a reductio, and it rests on four premises.

Proof of the Impossibility of Super-Identity. Premises:

 P1 Finitude of the subject (Principle 1.2): every subject occupies finitely many contexts.

 P2 Infinity of contexts (Principle 5.2): the contexts in which an identity can be cognized are
       not finite in number.

 P3 Manifestation is a product: the manifestation of I in a context is determined jointly by I
       and by the receiving realm, not by I alone.

 P4 Knowing is situated: to know a manifestation is a cognition, and every cognition occurs in
       a context (the fourth column, Principle 3.1).

     Reductio:

     1. Suppose a finite subject knows all manifestations of I in all contexts.

     2. By P3, a manifestation in C cannot be derived from I alone. Knowing I well, even perfectly,
       does not yield the manifestations in contexts that the subject has not entered.

     3. By P4, knowing the manifestation in C is a cognition occurring in a context; the subject
       must have some standing in C for this to be possible.
6.2. The Impossibility of Super-Identity                                                                39


  4. By P2, there are non-finitely many such C, and by P1 the subject has standing in only
     finitely many.

  5. Hence the subject cannot know all of the manifestations. This contradicts the supposition.



   The weight of the proof falls on P3. The other three premises are the framework’s finitude
axiom, its infinity principle, and its fourth column; P3 is the substantive premise, and the
argument is only as strong as it. The next remark states what P3 would need in order to be
refuted.

   Remark 6.1 (The Generative-Rule Objection)

   It may be objected that a subject could know the invariant structure itself, and from it
   generate every manifestation by a rule, without entering each context. The framework’s
   reply is P3: because manifestations are products of identity and receiving realm, no
   rule stated in terms of the identity alone yields them. A generative rule would need the
   receiving contexts as inputs, and these are the very thing the finite subject lacks. This
   reply is the reason P3 is given the weight of a premise in this argument. Whoever exhibits
   a rule that generates every manifestation from the identity alone, without the receiving
   contexts, refutes the principle.

   Remark 6.2 (What the Principle Does Not Say)

   The principle does not say that identity is unknowable. It says that exhaustive knowledge
   is impossible, and that claims to it are always mistaken. What remains is asymptotic
   knowledge: pseudo-identities of increasing adequacy. The impossibility is epistemic. It is
   compatible with the framework’s affirmation that identity is real, invariant, and conserved;
   what the principle denies is that any finite subject’s survey of identity can be completed.

   Remark 6.3 (The Impossibility Is on the Side of the Subject)

   The impossibility established here is an impossibility for the finite subject. It is not an
   impossibility as such. The framework does not claim that no subject whatsoever can know
   all manifestations of an identity in all contexts; it claims that no finite subject can. The
   distinction is crucial, because the two claims are different, and the confusion of the two
   would turn an epistemic claim into a metaphysical one. The impossibility is on the side of
   the subject: it is the finite subject’s survey that cannot be completed, not the object of the
   survey that is unknowable. The framework’s claim is that the finite subject’s knowledge
   is partial; it does not claim that the object is beyond all knowledge, or that no subject
   whatsoever can survey it. The object may be fully known to a subject that is not finite;
   the framework’s claim is about the finite subject, not about the object. The framework’s
   silence on the infinite subject is not a denial of its possibility; it is the recognition that the
   framework’s method is the method of finite inquiry, and that the limits of finite inquiry
   are not the limits of what is. The distinction between the order of inquiry and the order of
40                                     Chapter 6. Super-Identity, Context Validity, and Viability


     being is kept throughout the book, and it is kept here in its most decisive form: the finite
     subject’s inability to complete the survey is a fact about the subject, not a fact about the
     surveyed.


     Example 6.1 (A City)

     Someone who says “I have known every manifestation of this city” would have to have a
     standing in the economic, cultural, architectural, and legal contexts of the city, and in
     indefinitely many more, since each manifestation that one frame produces can serve as a
     fixed element of a further frame. No finite resident, planner, or historian can do this; the
     claim is not merely unproved but unavailable.

     The impossibility of super-identity is the first of the three consequences the chapter draws.
It is a consequence of the infinity of contexts, combined with the finitude of the subject. Its
importance for the framework is stated in the next section.


6.3      The Criteria of Context Validity
The impossibility of super-identity raises a danger. If every partition of entities into fixed and
fluid counts as a context, and if contexts are not finite in number, then the framework would
license arbitrary partitions: any assignment of roles would be as good as any other, and the
notion of a context would do no work.
     The framework disciplines the use of contexts by three criteria, adopted as axioms, and by a
fourth criterion proposed in this book.


6.3.1     The Three Axioms

     Principle 6.2 (Cross-Checkability)

     (A) A valid context is one whose fixed and fluid elements can be identified and distinguished
     from at least one other valid context.

     Principle 6.3 (Minimality)

     (A) A valid context is the smallest context that can still explain the phenomenon.


     Principle 6.4 (Consistency)

     (A) A valid context is consistent in all its overlaps with other valid contexts.


     The first criterion cannot be stated as “observable independently of the context,” since in a
framework in which elements are individuated by contexts that wording is not available. The
cross-checkability form asks for something the framework can supply: an element that is a fixed
element of a context must be recognizable from another valid context as the same element. This
is what blocks purely private contexts.
6.3. The Criteria of Context Validity                                                                41


   The second criterion disciplines the choice of frame. A frame that explains the phenomenon,
but does so by introducing elements or rules that are not needed, is not minimal, and so is not
valid. The criterion does not say which frame is minimal; it says that some frames are not.
   The third criterion disciplines the relation between frames. A frame that overlaps another
valid frame, and that contradicts it in the overlap, is not valid. The criterion does not require
that every frame overlap every other; it requires that where frames overlap, they agree.

   Remark 6.4 (The Three-Fold Test)

   A context is tested by three questions: (1) Can its elements be identified from some other
   valid context? (2) Is it the smallest context that explains the phenomenon? (3) Is it
   consistent in all its overlaps with other valid contexts? A context that fails one of these is
   invalid. The test is the framework’s discipline on the plurality of contexts. It does not say
   how the test is to be applied in every case; it says what the test is.



6.3.2    The Proposed Fourth Criterion

A fourth criterion is proposed. It is not yet assigned a status, because its independent definition
and support are given in a later part of the book. The framework proposes it, and states what
would put it in question.

   Principle 6.5 (Manifestational Adequacy (proposed))

   Status: proposed; not yet assigned (A) or (T). The context chosen for the study of a
   manifestation, and the realm to which a manifestation is attributed, must have the capacity
   and aptitude for the kind of appearance attributed to it.


   The criterion does not say that each context admits only one possible manifestation. Contexts
differ in aptitude, and several manifestations of one identity may be suited to one realm. It says
only that attributing to a realm an appearance of a kind that the realm cannot bear is an error
of attribution.
   The criterion is proposed because the three axioms govern the use of cognitive contexts and
say nothing of the aptitude of the realm in which a manifestation is realized. It is retained only
if the later part of the book gives it an independent definition and support.

   Remark 6.5 (Status of the Criteria)

   The three criteria are (A). A critic who rejects them is invited to propose alternatives; the
   framework’s claim is that some such criteria are necessary, not that these particular ones
   are final. The fourth criterion is proposed, not adopted; a critic who rejects it is invited to
   show that it does no work, or that its work is done by the three that precede it.
42                                     Chapter 6. Super-Identity, Context Validity, and Viability


6.4      The Definition of Viability

The impossibility of super-identity and the criteria of context validity together raise a third
question. If a subject cannot know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts, what can it
know? The answer is not nothing. It is a pseudo-identity of greater or lesser adequacy. What
distinguishes the greater from the lesser? The framework’s answer is viability, the concept after
which this book is named.
     The definition is given here, at the point where the framework meets it, rather than at the
end of the book. It is a structural definition: it states a condition on the relation between an
identity and its manifestations, and it locates that condition in the architecture of expression.

     Definition 6.2 (Viability)

     (A) The viability of an identity in a realm is the structural success of its expression there:
     the degree to which the relation between the identity and its manifestations satisfies three
     structural conditions.

       (i) Fidelity: the manifestation preserves the essential determination of the identity.

      (ii) Sustainability: the cost of producing and maintaining the manifestation does not
           exceed what the receiving realm can bear.

      (iii) Recoverability: the identity retains its structural capacity to manifest in that realm;
           the singularity at which restoring a manifestation would cost more than producing a
           new one has not been crossed.

     Viability is a structural condition. It describes what must hold for the relation between an
identity and its manifestations to be sustained. It is not itself the good, and it does not establish
what the good is. But it is the structural precondition of any good that the relation can bear: a
relation that has lost its fidelity, its sustainability, or its recoverability cannot carry the good that
the relation might otherwise have carried. The good itself is not established by the structural
description; the structural description is the ground on which the inquiry into the good can be
built. The framework’s claim is that the ground is real, invariant, and describable—not that the
ground is the whole of what can be said.
     The definition is stated at the level of the relation between an identity and its manifestations,
not at the level of the identity itself. This is the point of the next remark.

     Remark 6.6 (Viability Is Not Identity)

     Identity is rigid: it admits no degrees. Viability admits of degrees: the relation between an
     identity and its manifestations can satisfy its structural conditions more or less completely.
     The two statements do not conflict, because viability is a property of the relation between
     an identity and its manifestations in a realm, not of the identity itself. Identity is what is
     expressed; viability is the structural character of how it is expressed. The distinction is
     the distinction between the order of the expressed and the order of its expression; it is not
6.5. The Four Columns Are Not the Seven Realms                                                    43


   the distinction between the real and the unreal, or between the valuable and the valueless.
   Viability is a structural condition, not a value; but the structural condition is the ground
   on which value can be borne.

   The three components of viability are developed in the parts of the book that follow. Fidelity is
developed in the chapters on expression; sustainability is developed in the chapter on expression
cost; recoverability is developed in the chapter on death. The definition stated here is the
framework’s definition; the developments are what make the definition work.


6.5     The Four Columns Are Not the Seven Realms
Before the part concludes, one more distinction must be made. The four columns of the framework
are analytical roles; the seven realms of the framework’s ontology are existential levels. The
correspondence between the two is not an identity of the two. The distinction is stated here,
at the end of the part that introduces the columns, so that the reader enters the part that
introduces the realms with the distinction in hand.
   The correspondence is as follows.

   Four-Column         Frame- Ontological Framework
   work

   Context                        The existential contexts (the seven realms), together with
                                  the indefinitely many cognitive contexts in which they are
                                  studied.
   Fixed elements                 Identities and manifestations.
   Fluid element                  Light (one element, three essential properties).
   Governing dynamics             The rules of the realms.

   The table is a correspondence of roles to contents, not an identification of columns with levels
of being. In particular, the fact that four roles are needed in explanation is not an argument that
there are four realms, and the fact that there are seven realms does not multiply the columns.

   Remark 6.7 (No Conflict Between Four and Seven)

   The four columns apply to the study of any realm, and to the study of the relations among
   realms. Within the study of a single realm, its manifestations are the fixed elements, light
   is the fluid element, the rules of that realm are the governing dynamics, and the realm
   together with the cognitive standpoint is the context. Nothing in this part of the book
   should be read as saying that each column is a realm, or that each realm is a column.

   The correspondence between the four columns and the seven realms is a correspondence of
order, not an identity of being. The four columns describe the order through which any realm
becomes intelligible; the seven realms are the levels of being that the order describes. The order
is real, and the framework’s claim is that the order is invariant and describable. But the order is
not self-sufficient: it is the order of something, and the something is not exhausted by its order.
44                                    Chapter 6. Super-Identity, Context Validity, and Viability


The distinction is the distinction between the order of inquiry and the order of being; it is kept
throughout the book, and it is kept here at the point where the analytical framework meets the
ontological one.


6.6          The Structure Is Not Self-Sufficient
The four-column framework and the seven-realm ontology together constitute the framework’s
architecture. The architecture is a description of structure, and the framework’s claim is that the
structure is real, invariant, and describable. But the framework does not claim that the structure
is the whole of what is. The order through which what is becomes intelligible is real; the order is
not the explained, and the explanation is not the whole of what is explained.
      The framework’s silence on what lies beyond the structural description is not a denial. It is
the recognition that a description of order is not a description of the whole. The structure is
a condition of intelligibility, not a substitute for being. And the framework’s claim is that the
structure is real, not that it is all there is. A reader who takes the framework’s claim as a denial
of what lies beyond the structure has misread it; a reader who takes it as a description of the
order through which what lies beyond the structure becomes intelligible has read it correctly.

A Question for Reflection
If you were to survey the manifestations of a person you know well, what would you be able to
reconstruct, and what would remain outside the survey? What would distinguish an adequate
reconstruction from an inadequate one?

The next part turns to the realms. It develops the framework’s ontology: the four fundamental
realms and the three barzakhic realms, seven independently real levels of being. The distinction
between the four columns and the seven realms, which the present chapter has stated, is the
distinction that makes the transition possible.

Realms: The Four Fundamental and
