Chapter 7

The Four Fundamental Realms


Scope. This chapter begins the framework’s ontology. It defines the fundamental realm as a
mode of existence, states the principles of the independence and determinate capacity of realms,
defines the four fundamental realms—the First Determination, the Structural Determination,
the Relational Manifestation, and the Material Manifestation—and argues the non-necessity
of downward passage. It does not argue that there are exactly four fundamental realms; that
argument is given in a later part of the book, and the chapter says so explicitly. Its claims are
structural; where the chapter is silent on questions of value, religion, or mystical experience,
the silence is not a denial but a recognition that the structural description is not the whole of
what can be said. Where the chapter speaks of “realm,” “mode of existence,” “manifestation,”
“activity,” “interaction,” “capacity,” or “source,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed
by the definitions in this chapter. The names of the four realms are structural labels whose sense
is fixed by their definitions; where a tradition has used a similar name, the kinship is a kinship
of vocabulary, not an identity of meaning.



7.1     A Scene

Consider a melody. Played on a piano, it is a sequence of sounds: discrete events in time, each
with a beginning and an end. Written on a page, it is a pattern of notes: a structure that can be
repeated, transposed, orchestrated. Heard by a listener, it is a meaning: it evokes a mood, it
belongs to a tradition, it says something to someone. And beneath all three descriptions, there
is the melody itself—one thing, not many; the same melody whether played on piano or violin,
whether written in C or D, whether heard by one listener or another.
    The melody appears at four levels, and the levels are not the same. To say what sounds are
produced is not yet to say what the notes are, or what the notes mean, or what makes them one
melody. Each level has its own mode of being, its own kind of multiplicity, its own way of being
related to the others. The melody is one at one level and many at another, and the unity of the
higher level does not cancel the multiplicity of the lower.
    The scene poses a question that is as old as philosophy. What are these levels? Are they real,
or are they mere ways of speaking? If they are real, how many are there, and what distinguishes
one from another? If they are mere ways of speaking, what is the single reality that the speaking
is about?
    This chapter begins the framework’s answer. It does not finish the answer; the argument that
the levels are exactly four is given later, in the part of the book that argues for the minimality of
the four grades. But it begins the answer, by defining what a level of being is, and by defining
the four levels that the framework distinguishes.

                                                 49
50                                                     Chapter 7. The Four Fundamental Realms


7.2      The Question

The scene raises two questions, and the chapter treats them in turn.
     The first is: what is a level of being? The framework has already distinguished the cognitive
architecture (the four columns) from the ontological architecture (the levels of being), in the
first part of the book. The distinction was drawn, but the ontological architecture was not yet
developed. The present chapter defines its basic unit, the fundamental realm.
     The second is: what distinguishes one fundamental realm from another? The question is
not about the number of realms; it is about what makes a realm a realm of a distinct kind.
The chapter’s answer is that each realm has a distinct mode of existence, a distinct kind of
manifestation, activity, and interaction, and a distinct capacity for what can appear within it.
Two realms are distinguished when their modes of existence differ, not when their contents differ.
     The chapter’s method is structural. It defines the realm, states the principles of independence
and determinate capacity, defines the four realms one by one, and argues that relations among
realms need not be sequential. The chapter does not argue that the four are exactly four; it
states the four, and defers the argument for the number to the part of the book that develops
the minimality argument. This deferral is not a gap; it is the discipline of linear dependency.
The reader is asked to accept the four realms as defined, and to suspend the question of their
number until the argument for it is given.



7.3      The Definition of a Fundamental Realm

The first question is answered by a definition.

     Definition 7.1 (Fundamental Realm)

     A fundamental realm is an independently real mode of existence within which a specific
     mode of manifestation, activity, and interaction is possible.


     Three terms in the definition need to be fixed.
     Manifestation is used here in its structural sense: a manifestation is the appearance of an
identity in a receiving realm, according to that realm’s capacity. The term is not defined in this
chapter; it is defined in the part of the book that treats fixed elements. Here it is used to say
that a realm is a realm in which manifestations of a certain kind can occur.
     Activity is the structural occurrence proper to a realm. Each realm has a kind of activity
that is its own; the activity of a realm is not the activity of another realm transposed into it.
This is what the definition means when it says that a realm is a mode of existence “within which”
a specific mode of activity is possible.
     Interaction is a structural relation between two manifestations in the same realm. The
definition says that a realm is a realm in which interactions of a certain kind can occur, not
merely one in which manifestations can appear in isolation.
7.4. The Independence and Capacity of Realms                                                        51


   Remark 7.1 (Realm and Context)

   A realm is an ontological level: a mode of existence. A context is the setting in which a
   manifestation is realized or a cognition is carried out. The realm in which a manifestation
   is realized is its existential context; a frame of inquiry is a cognitive context. The words
   are kept apart so that a level of being is not mistaken for a standpoint of knowing. The
   distinction was drawn in the first part of the book; the present remark applies it.


   Remark 7.2 (The Names of the Four Realms)

   The names under which the four realms are introduced—“First Determination,” “Structural
   Determination,” “Relational Manifestation,” “Material Manifestation”—are structural
   labels. Each is defined by the definition that introduces it, and its sense is fixed by that
   definition alone. The names carry the structural sense the definitions give them.
   Where a tradition has used a similar name for a grade of being, a cosmic principle, or a
   deity, the kinship is a kinship of vocabulary, not an identity of meaning. The structural
   sense stands on its own; the traditional sense, if there is one, stands on its own; and
   the relation between the two is a question for another inquiry. The framework’s claim is
   narrow: within the book, the names have the structural sense the definitions give them,
   and no traditional use of the same words determines their sense here. The framework does
   not claim that the structural sense is the whole of what the names can mean; it claims
   that the structural sense is the sense the book needs, and that the sense is sufficient for
   the book’s purpose.

   The definition fixes what a realm is. The next section states what a realm’s independence
and capacity consist in.


7.4     The Independence and Capacity of Realms
Two principles state what it is for a realm to be a realm, rather than an aspect or a function of
another realm.

   Principle 7.1 (Independent Reality of the Realms)

   (A) Each realm is independently real: it has a mode of existence of its own, with rules of
   its own and structural possibilities of activity of its own, and it is not merely an aspect, a
   function, or a name for a relation among other realms.

   The principle is adopted, not proved. Its support is that, if it is denied, the rules and
structural possibilities peculiar to each realm lose their subject: there would be nothing for those
rules to be rules of. The principle would be refuted by showing that the rules of some realm
are in fact consequences of the rules of another. The framework does not claim that no such
derivation will ever be found; it claims that none has been found, and it states the principle at
that strength.
52                                                      Chapter 7. The Four Fundamental Realms


     Remark 7.3 (What Independence Does and Does Not Mean)

     Independence is not separability. The realms are ordered and are related; a realm’s
     independence means that what it is cannot be restated without remainder in terms of
     another realm’s mode of being. It does not mean that a realm can exist without the others,
     or that a realm has no relations to the others.


     Remark 7.4 (Independence Is Not Self-Sufficiency)

     The independence of the realms is independence of mode, not independence of existence.
     The realms are distinct in their modes of being, and each is real in its own right; but their
     existence is not self-grounded. The independence principle states that no realm can be
     reduced to another; it does not state that any realm is the ultimate ground of its own
     being. The framework’s claim is that the realms are distinct levels of a single order of
     determination; the order itself points beyond itself, and the framework does not claim that
     the order is self-sufficient. A reader who takes the independence principle as a claim of
     self-sufficiency has misread it; a reader who takes it as a claim of irreducibility has read it
     correctly.


     The second principle concerns what a realm can bear.


     Definition 7.2 (Realm Capacity)

     The capacity of a realm is what its mode of existence permits to appear in it and what it
     constrains.


     Principle 7.2 (Determinate Capacity of Realms)

     (A) Every differentiated realm has a determinate capacity: its mode of existence permits
     certain manifestations and constrains others.


     Determinate capacity does not mean a limited numerical quantity. It means that what a
realm can bear is not unrestricted: the realm has a structural character, and the character
excludes some appearances. The principle is used in the definition of manifestation and in the
account of cost; here it is laid down, so that the four definitions that follow can presuppose it.


     Remark 7.5 (The Two Principles Together)

     The first principle says that a realm is real in its own right. The second says that a realm’s
     mode of existence determines what can appear in it. Together, they imply that each realm
     is a real level whose character is not arbitrary: the realm is what it is, and its being what
     it is determines what can and cannot be manifested there.
7.5. The First Determination                                                                       53


   Remark 7.6 (The Order of Determination Points Beyond Itself)

   The four realms, together, constitute an order of determination: a structure through which
   what is becomes determinate, level by level. The framework’s claim is that this order
   is real, invariant, and describable. But the framework does not claim that the order is
   self-grounded. The order of determination is the order of what is determined; it is not
   the ground of determination. The framework’s silence on what grounds the order is not a
   denial of the ground; it is the recognition that a description of order is not a description
   of the ground of order. The order points beyond itself, and the framework’s claim is that
   the pointing is real, not that the pointed-to is describable within the framework’s method.
   The distinction is the distinction between the order of what is and the ground of what is;
   it is kept throughout the book.

   The four realms are now defined. Each is defined by three questions: what is its mode of
existence, what manifestation, activity, or interaction is possible in it, and what distinguishes it
from the other three. The next four sections answer these questions for each realm in turn.


7.5     The First Determination

   Definition 7.3 (First Determination)

   The First Determination is the fundamental realm of pure unity. Its mode of existence is
   that of an identity as such: there is no multiplicity, no change, and no succession in it.

   The First Determination is characterized by three marks.


Changelessness. Change requires multiplicity: a before and an after, a state and a transition.
There is no multiplicity in the First Determination; so there is no change.


Timelessness. Succession requires a before and an after. There is none in the First Deter-
mination; so there is no time. (That the First Determination is without time does not make it
merely “unlasting”; the distinction between timelessness and duration is developed in the part of
the book that treats time.)


Indivisibility. Division requires parts. There are no parts in the First Determination; so there
is no division.
   The activity possible in the First Determination is not motion or becoming. It is the being-
what-it-is of an identity without remainder. This is not an absence of activity; it is its limit case:
an activity that has no structural requirement to become anything else.

   Remark 7.7 (The First Determination Is Not the Ultimate Source)

   The First Determination is not asserted to be the ultimate source of reality. It is the first
   level at which the source’s reality takes a determinate form. The source in its essence
54                                                      Chapter 7. The Four Fundamental Realms


     is beyond all determination; its relation to the First Determination is one of grounding,
     not of identity. The word “source” here is a structural term: it names the point at which
     determination begins.
     The architecture of determination that this book describes is not self-grounded. The First
     Determination is the first level of created determination, not the uncreated ground. The
     structural description of determination points beyond itself to what grounds it, and the
     framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, not that the pointed-to is describable within
     the framework’s method. The framework describes the order of determination; it does not
     claim to describe the ground of that order. A structural description can be true while the
     essence of the source remains undescribed, and the framework claims no more than its
     method delivers.
     This is not an indifference to the ground. It is the recognition that the order of determina-
     tion is not the whole of what is, and that the ground of the order is not an item within the
     order. The framework’s claim is that the order is real, invariant, and describable; it does
     not claim that the order is self-sufficient, and it does not claim that nothing lies beyond it.
     A reader who identifies the structural source with the ultimate source has conflated the
     order with its ground; a reader who distinguishes them has read the framework’s claim
     correctly. The distinction is the distinction between the order of determination and the
     ground of determination, and it is kept throughout the book.


     Remark 7.8 (The First Determination Is Not Composite)

     The First Determination is not structured through the arrangement of distinguishable parts.
     Its unity is not compositional. The identity present at this level is determinate without
     being internally divided into distinguishable components. The structural descriptions
     used at lower levels therefore cannot be transferred to the First Determination without
     qualification. In particular, the definition of identity as an invariant structure, developed
     in the part of the book that treats identity, is to be read at this level in a qualified
     sense: structure as the principle that distinguishes and unifies, not as an arrangement of
     components. The distinction is drawn where identity is defined; here it is only named.



7.6      The Structural Determination

     Definition 7.4 (Structural Determination)

     The Structural Determination is the fundamental realm of general multiplicity. Its mode of
     existence is that of law: what is general, formal, and necessary with respect to an identity,
     apart from any particular context of appearance.

     The Structural Determination is the realm of the class of allowable transformations: the
level at which an identity is specified into laws that fix what transformations it tolerates. Its
multiplicity is that of forms, not of things; its elements are many, but they are many laws, not
many instances.
7.7. The Relational Manifestation                                                                   55


   Three features characterize the realm.


Universality. The laws apply to all manifestations of an identity, regardless of context. A law
that applies only in some contexts is not a structural law; it is a relational regularity.


Necessity. The laws could not be otherwise, given the identity they express. A law that could
be otherwise is not a structural law; it is a contingent regularity.


Formality. The laws concern the form of the manifestations, not their content. A law that
concerns content is not a structural law; it is a material law.
   The activity possible here is implication: from a law its consequences follow, and from a
universal law its instances. The activity of this realm is unfolding in the sense of entailment.

   Remark 7.9 (Ontological Distinctiveness)

   The Structural Determination differs from the First Determination in being plural: there
   are many laws, not one. It differs from the Relational Manifestation in being general: its
   multiplicity is that of forms, not of things related to one another in particular contexts. It
   differs from the realm of the Hub of Decree, which is introduced in the next chapter, in
   that it holds what is lawful in general, not what is allotted to each identity in particular.



7.7     The Relational Manifestation

   Definition 7.5 (Relational Manifestation)

   The Relational Manifestation is the fundamental realm of relational multiplicity. Its mode
   of existence is that of things that exist in relation to one another through meaning and
   significance.


   The word “meaning” here is a structural term. It names the relation between a manifestation
and the network of other manifestations in which it stands. It does not name a semantic or
evaluative content in the sense of linguistic meaning or moral worth.
   The Relational Manifestation is the realm of meaning and of structural awareness of the
other. Meaning in this realm is not a property of an isolated manifestation but a relation among
manifestations. Awareness, in the structural sense that is developed in the part of the book that
treats self-awareness, is first possible here: a manifestation can be structurally related to another
manifestation in a way that the other is taken into account.
   Three features characterize the realm.


Relationality. Manifestations exist in relation to one another. A manifestation that is not
related to any other is an isolated event, not a manifestation of the Relational Manifestation.
56                                                       Chapter 7. The Four Fundamental Realms


Contextuality. The meaning of a manifestation depends on its context. A manifestation
whose meaning is fixed independently of context is a structural unit, not a manifestation of the
Relational Manifestation.


Structural awareness. Manifestations can be structurally aware of one another: each regulates
its relation to the others through the reception of light. The term “awareness” here is a structural
term; it names a structural relation, not a phenomenal or psychological state. It is developed
in the part of the book that treats the distinction between self-awareness, consciousness, and
awareness.

     Remark 7.10 (Ontological Distinctiveness)

     The Relational Manifestation differs from the Structural Determination in that its multi-
     plicity is particular and contextual, not general. It differs from the Material Manifestation
     in that its things do not occupy places or have extension. It differs from the realm of
     the Hub of Signification, introduced in the next chapter, in that it is the realm of actual
     relations among manifestations, whereas the hub is the realm of significance as a mode of
     existence.



7.8      The Material Manifestation

     Definition 7.6 (Material Manifestation)

     The Material Manifestation is the fundamental realm of material multiplicity. Its mode of
     existence is that of things that are discrete, localized, and successive.

     It is the realm of extended things and of their succession: what is seen, heard, and touched.
The description is structural: it states the form of appearances in this realm, not an evaluative
ranking of the senses.
     Three features characterize the realm.


Causality. Events have causes, and causes produce effects.


Temporality. Events occur in time: they have a past, a present, and a future.


Discreteness. Events are separate from one another: they occupy distinct positions in space
and time.
     The activity possible here is arising, passing away, and succession of determinate things in
time and place.

     Remark 7.11 (Ontological Distinctiveness)

     The Material Manifestation differs from all others in that its multiplicity is that of separate,
     successive, located things. It differs from the realm of the Hub of Realization, introduced
7.9. The Relations Between the Realms                                                                57


   in the next chapter, in being the realm of what has been realized, not of the realizing.



7.9     The Relations Between the Realms
The four realms are related in three ways, and the three ways do not coincide.

The ordinal relation. The place of a realm in the overall order of expression: from unity,
through general multiplicity and relational multiplicity, to material multiplicity. This relation is
structural, not spatial: it says which realm is more general or more unified than which, not along
what route anything must travel.

The manifestation relation. The appearance of an identity in a realm other than its own, in
a form suited to that realm.

The influence relation. The effect of one realm, or of an identity in it, on another.
    The distinction between these three relations matters because they are easily run together.
The ordinal relation is an order of generality; it is not a route. The manifestation relation is the
appearance of an identity in a receiving realm; it is not a passage through every intermediate
realm. The influence relation is the effect of one realm on another; it is not a transposition of
one realm’s mode of existence into another.

   Remark 7.12 (“Higher” and “Lower”)

   Throughout the book, higher and lower designate ordinal positions in the architecture of
   expression. They do not designate existential routes, causal priorities, or degrees of reality.
   That one realm is higher than another says that it is more unified or more general; it does
   not say that anything must travel from it to the other, that it produces the other, or that
   the other is less real.

    The non-necessity of downward passage is a principle in its own right, and the next section
states it.


7.10         The Non-Necessity of Downward Passage

   Principle 7.3 (Non-Necessity of Downward Passage)

   (A) The presence or effect of an identity in a lower realm does not require that the identity
   pass existentially through every realm that lies between. Relations among the realms are
   not confined to a single sequential route.

    Two considerations support the principle.
    First, by the independence of the realms, each realm has its own capacity to receive; the form
that an identity takes in a lower realm is fixed by the identity and that realm’s capacity, not by
what the identity became in the intervening realms.
58                                                     Chapter 7. The Four Fundamental Realms


     Second, the three relations distinguished in the previous section are distinct, and the ordinal
relation does not by itself impose a route.
     The principle would be refuted by showing that the capacity of a lower realm to receive an
identity is constituted by the identity’s manifestations in each intermediate realm. The framework
denies that; the denial is the content of the principle.

     Remark 7.13 (What the Principle Does Not Say)

     The principle does not say that the intermediate realms are idle or dispensable. The
     barzakhic realms, introduced in the next chapter, have functions of their own, and an
     identity’s presence in a lower realm may still be regulated by the rules of the realms
     that bear on it. Regulation is not passage. The relation of this principle to the necessity
     of mediation is developed in the part of the book that establishes the irreducibility of
     one-step reduction; here the principle is stated, and the distinction between regulation
     and passage is named.


     Remark 7.14 (The Principle Leaves Direct Action Open)

     The principle is a negative claim: it says that the ordinal relation does not impose a route.
     It does not make a positive claim about what routes are actual. In particular, it does not
     deny that a direct effect can occur between any two levels of the architecture, including an
     effect that comes from beyond the architecture itself. The framework’s claim is that the
     architecture does not constrain the route that an effect may take; it does not claim that
     every effect must traverse the architecture. The distinction is the distinction between the
     order of determination and the routes of effect; the order does not impose a route, and
     the routes are not exhausted by the order. A reader who takes the principle as a denial
     of direct action has misread it; a reader who takes it as a claim that the order does not
     impose a route has read it correctly.


     Remark 7.15 (No Conflict with the Manifestation Relation)

     The manifestation relation is compatible with the non-necessity of downward passage.
     An identity appears in a lower realm in a form suited to that realm; the form is fixed
     by the identity and the receiving realm. Nothing in this requires that the identity have
     appeared in each intermediate realm on the way. The manifestation relation says what
     the appearance is; the non-necessity principle says what the appearance does not require.



7.11       What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Three things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred, and the
deferral is worth stating.
     First, the chapter does not argue that there are exactly four fundamental realms. It defines
four, and it leaves the argument for the number to the part of the book that develops the
minimality of the four grades. The four-column framework, which was established in the first
7.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                 59


part of the book, does not entail that there are four realms; the distinction between the analytical
roles and the ontological levels was made precisely so that the two numbers could be argued
separately. The reader who asks “why four?” is asked to wait for the argument.
   Second, the chapter does not develop the rules of the four realms. The rules of the Structural
Determination, the Relational Manifestation, and the Material Manifestation are named here,
and their content is examined in the part of the book that treats governing dynamics. The rules
of the First Determination are given there too. The chapter’s purpose is to define the realms,
not to state their rules.
   Third, the chapter does not introduce the three barzakhic realms. Those are the subject
of the next chapter, and the present chapter is complete without them. The seven realms are
four fundamental and three barzakhic; the present chapter establishes the four, and the next
establishes the three.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know well—a person, a place, a work of art. Can you identify, in the thing,
the four modes of multiplicity that the chapter distinguishes: its pure unity, its general features,
its relational meaning, and its material existence? Which of the four is most easily overlooked,
and why?

The next chapter introduces the three barzakhic realms: independently real levels whose mode of
existence includes mediating, transforming, or regulating relations between other realms. With the
three, the framework’s ontology is complete: seven realms, four fundamental and three barzakhic.
Chapter 8

The Three Barzakhic Realms


Scope. This chapter completes the framework’s ontology. It defines the barzakhic realm as an
independently real level whose mode of existence includes mediating, transforming, or regulating
relations between other realms; it states the principle of the independent reality of the barzakhic
realms; it defines the notion of mixed nature; and it defines the three hubs—the Hub of Decree,
the Hub of Signification, and the Hub of Realization—together with the structural relations
between them and the four fundamental realms. Every term in the chapter is structural: where it
speaks of “realm,” “mode of existence,” “mediation,” “allotment,” “signification,” or “realization,”
the sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter. The names of the three hubs are structural
labels whose sense is fixed by their definitions; where a tradition has used a similar name, the
kinship is a kinship of vocabulary, not an identity of meaning. The word “barzakhic” is likewise
a structural label for the mode of existence that mediates between realms; where the traditions
have used the word for an intermediate state, the kinship is a kinship of vocabulary, not an
identity of meaning. The chapter’s argument does not depend on any traditional use of the
words, and the framework’s claim is structural.


8.1     A Scene
Consider three cases of mediation, and notice how different they are.
   A potter makes a bowl. The clay is one thing; the bowl is another. But between the clay and
the bowl there is a measure: how much clay, how thick the wall, how wide the rim, how deep the
body. The measure is not the clay, and it is not the bowl; it is the allotment within which the
clay becomes the bowl. Without the measure, the clay remains clay; with the measure, the clay
takes the form of a bowl. The potter’s craft is the craft of allotting measure.
   A letter is translated. The letter is one thing; the translation is another. But between the
letter and the translation there is a signification: what the letter means, what each sentence
carries, what the whole is about. The signification is not the letter, and it is not the translation;
it is the meaning that the translation will carry. A translation without signification is a row of
words; a translation with signification is a letter in a new language. The translator’s craft is the
craft of carrying signification.
   An architect builds a house. The plan is one thing; the house is another. But between the
plan and the house there is a realization: the plan becomes stone, wood, glass, room, threshold.
The realization is not the plan, and it is not the house; it is the plan becoming concrete. A plan
without realization is a drawing; a plan with realization is a house. The builder’s craft is the
craft of realizing.
   Three cases, and each shows a different kind of mediation. The potter allots measure; the
translator carries signification; the builder realizes. The three are not the same. To allot measure

                                                 60
8.2. The Question                                                                                  61


is not to carry signification, and to carry signification is not to realize. And yet each of the three
is a mediation between a source and its reception, and each is a level of its own, distinct from
the source and from the reception.
   The scene poses a question. What are these three levels? Are they real, or are they merely
ways of speaking about the crafts? If they are real, how many are there, and how do they
relate to the four realms that the previous chapter defined? The present chapter answers these
questions. Its answer is that the three levels are the three barzakhic realms—the Hub of Decree,
the Hub of Signification, and the Hub of Realization—and that each is an independently real
level whose mode of existence includes mediating between the four fundamental realms.


8.2       The Question
The previous chapter defined the four fundamental realms—the First Determination, the Struc-
tural Determination, the Relational Manifestation, and the Material Manifestation—and it
argued the non-necessity of downward passage. The four realms, so defined, are the framework’s
fundamental levels: each is a mode of existence, and the four stand in an order of expression
from unity to material multiplicity.
   The present chapter completes the framework’s ontology. Between the four fundamental
realms there are three transitions: from unity to general multiplicity, from general multiplicity to
relational multiplicity, and from relational multiplicity to material multiplicity. Each transition
is a structural gap that expression must cross. The present chapter’s claim is that the three
transitions are regulated by three independently real levels, and that those levels are the three
barzakhic realms.
   The question is: what are the barzakhic realms, and how do they relate to the four fundamental
realms?
   Two aspects of the question must be distinguished.


The definitional aspect. What is a barzakhic realm, and what are the three? The chapter
defines the barzakhic realm, defines the mediation it performs, defines its mixed nature, and
defines the three hubs that are the framework’s specific barzakhic realms.


The structural aspect. How do the barzakhic realms relate to the four fundamental realms?
The chapter states the principle of their independent reality, locates them in the order of
expression between the fundamental realms, and states the non-necessity of sequential passage
through them.
   The chapter proceeds as follows. It states a scene of three kinds of mediation. It states the
question. It defines the barzakhic realm and the mediation it performs. It states the principle
of the independent reality of the barzakhic realms and defines their mixed nature. It defines
the three hubs. It states the relations between the barzakhic and the fundamental realms, and
the non-necessity of sequential passage through the hubs. It closes with the continuations that
belong to later parts of the book and with the epistemic status of its claims. The argument
that exactly three hubs are required, and the argument that the hubs are irreducible to the
62                                                        Chapter 8. The Three Barzakhic Realms


fundamental realms, are given in the part of the book that treats the arguments; the present
chapter defines what the later arguments are about.


8.3      The Definition of a Barzakhic Realm
The chapter’s first task is to define the barzakhic realm. The definition is structural: it names
the mode of existence that distinguishes a barzakhic realm from a fundamental realm.

     Definition 8.1 (Barzakhic Realm)

     (A) A barzakhic realm is an independently real ontological level whose mode of existence
     includes mediating, transforming, or regulating relations between other realms.

     Three parts of the definition need to be fixed.
     Independently real. The realm is a level of being in its own right, with rules and structural
possibilities of its own; the term is defined in the previous chapter, in the principle of the
independent reality of the realms.
     Mode of existence. The way in which the realm is: its structural character, the kind of activity
that is proper to it, and what it permits to appear within it.
     Mediating, transforming, or regulating. The specific character of the barzakhic realm: it is
not merely a level; it is a level whose mode of existence includes a function that pertains to
the relation between other realms. The function is part of what the realm is, not an accidental
relation that the realm happens to bear.
     The definition locates the barzakhic realm by its mode of existence, not by its contents. Two
realms are distinct when their modes of existence differ, not when the things that appear in them
differ. A barzakhic realm is therefore not a place where certain things happen; it is a mode of
existence whose structure is that of mediation.

     Remark 8.1 (The Names of the Barzakhic Realms)

     The names under which the three barzakhic realms are introduced—“the Hub of Decree,”
     “the Hub of Signification,” “the Hub of Realization”—are structural labels. Each is defined
     by the definition that introduces it, and its sense is fixed by that definition alone. The word
     “hub” is used because the realm is the point at which the transition between two realms is
     regulated; the word carries no mechanical or spatial suggestion. Where a tradition has
     used a similar name, the kinship is a kinship of vocabulary, not an identity of meaning.
     The structural sense stands on its own; the traditional sense, if there is one, stands on
     its own; and the relation between the two belongs to an inquiry that the framework is
     designed to serve, not to replace.



8.4      The Definition of Mediation
A barzakhic realm mediates; the notion of mediation is what the definition of the barzakhic
realm presupposes, and it is stated here as a definition of its own.
8.5. The Independence of the Barzakhic Realms                                                       63


   Definition 8.2 (Mediation)

   Mediation is the structural regulation, conditioning, or transformation of a relation between
   two realms by a realm whose mode of existence includes that function.

   Mediation is the specific activity of a barzakhic realm. It is not passage, and it is not influence.
The three are easily confused, and the framework keeps them apart.
   Mediation is the regulation of a relation between two realms by a third realm whose mode of
existence includes that regulation. The mediating realm is present in the relation as a condition,
not as a term.
   Passage is existential traversal of a realm: the identity, or its effect, being present as such in
each realm it traverses. The mediating realm does not require the identity to pass through it; its
presence as a condition is compatible with the identity’s non-passage.
   Influence is the effect of one realm, or of an identity in it, on another. The mediating
realm may exercise influence, but its mediation is not reducible to the influence it exercises; the
mediation is the structural regulation of the relation, not the causal effect.

   Remark 8.2 (Mediation Is Not Passage)

   The distinction between mediation and passage is structural, not verbal. If passage were
   required, an identity manifested in the Material Manifestation would have to be manifested
   in the Relational Manifestation, in the Hub of Realization, in the Hub of Signification, in
   the Structural Determination, and in the Hub of Decree. If mediation alone is required,
   the identity may be manifested directly in the Material Manifestation, with the three
   hubs regulating the manifestation without the identity appearing in each of them. The
   framework holds the second, and the argument is given in the part of the book that treats
   the irreducibility of one-step reduction.



8.5     The Independence of the Barzakhic Realms
A barzakhic realm mediates; a mediating function, taken by itself, might suggest that the realm
is dependent on the realms it mediates between. The present section states the principle that
forecloses this reading, and defines the notion of mixed nature that makes the principle precise.

   Principle 8.1 (Independent Reality of the Barzakhic Realms)

   (A) The three barzakhic realms are independently real: each has a mode of existence of
   its own, and its mediating function is a feature of its mode of existence, not a reduction of
   it to a function of the realms it mediates.

   The principle is adopted as a commitment of the framework. Its support is the structure of
the barzakhic realms as the chapter defines them: the function is part of the mode of existence,
not an external relation that the realm happens to bear. The principle is developed in two further
places: in the part of the book that argues for the irreducibility of the barzakhic realms, and in
the part of the book that resolves the apparent tension between relation and order. In the first of
64                                                       Chapter 8. The Three Barzakhic Realms


these, the argument is that the rules of a hub are not derivable from the rules of its neighbors; in
the second, the distinction between function and dependence is stated as a principle of its own.

     Definition 8.3 (Mixed Nature)

     A barzakhic realm has a mixed nature when its mode of existence shows features of both
     of its neighboring realms without being identical with either.


     Each of the three hubs has a mixed nature, and the mixture is specific to each hub. The
Hub of Decree shows the features of the First Determination (its unity) and of the Structural
Determination (its multiplicity of forms), without being either. The Hub of Signification shows the
features of the Structural Determination (its generality) and of the Relational Manifestation (its
contextuality), without being either. The Hub of Realization shows the features of the Relational
Manifestation (its relational character) and of the Material Manifestation (its concreteness),
without being either.
     The mixed nature is what makes a hub a mediator. If a hub partook of only one of its
neighbors, it could not regulate the relation between the two; it would be on one side of the gap.
By partaking of both, it can hold the relation between them: it is neither one nor the other, and
it is the level at which the transition from one to the other is regulated.

     Remark 8.3 (The Mixed Nature Is Not a Composite)

     The mixed nature of a barzakhic realm does not make it a composite of its two neighbors.
     The hub is one level, with a mode of existence of its own; its mixed nature is a feature
     of that mode of existence, not a composition of two modes. The hub is not two realms
     joined; it is one realm whose mode of existence includes, without exhausting itself in, the
     features of both neighbors. The unity of the hub is the unity of a distinct level.


     Remark 8.4 (The Mixed Nature Is Not Dependence)

     The mixed nature of a hub is not dependence on its neighbors. To partake of the features
     of two realms is not to be constituted by them; it is to have a mode of existence that, in
     its own structure, includes features that resemble the features of both. The hub is real in
     its own right; its mixed nature is the structural character of that reality. The principle of
     the independent reality of the barzakhic realms forecloses the reading of mixed nature as
     dependence.




8.6      The Hub of Decree

The first of the three barzakhic realms is the Hub of Decree. It regulates the transition from the
First Determination to the Structural Determination.
8.7. The Hub of Signification                                                                      65


   Definition 8.4 (Hub of Decree)

   (A) The Hub of Decree is the barzakhic realm of the determination of measure. Its mode
   of existence is the allotment to each identity of the extent, the limit, and the proportion
   within which it will express itself.


   The Hub of Decree is the realm in which the unified source is apportioned into the multiplicity
of forms. The source, in its own realm, is without internal distinction; in the Structural
Determination, it becomes a plurality of laws. The Hub of Decree is the level at which the
apportioning happens: the extent to which the source will be manifested, the limit beyond which
it will not, and the proportion in which its aspects will be distributed.
   The hub is what makes the unity of the First Determination legible in the plurality of the
Structural Determination. Without the apportioning of measure, the unity of the source has
no structure in which to be expressed; the plurality of forms has no principle by which to arise.
The Hub of Decree is the level at which the two are joined: the unity of the source becomes the
measure of the multiplicity of forms.
   Three features characterize the realm, and they are developed in the part of the book that
treats the rules of the barzakhic realms. Proportion: the specification of unity into multiplicity
preserves the unity of the source in the very act of differentiating it. Order: the specification
follows the structural articulation of the realms—the more unified before the more multiple,
the more general before the more particular. Harmony: the multiplicity that the specification
produces is structurally coherent.

   Remark 8.5 (The Hub of Decree Is Not the First Determination)

   The Hub of Decree is not the First Determination. The First Determination is pure unity,
   without multiplicity; the Hub of Decree is the level at which unity is apportioned into
   multiplicity. The two are distinguished by their mode of existence: the First Determination
   has no multiplicity; the Hub of Decree is the structural apportioning by which multiplicity
   is produced.


   Remark 8.6 (The Hub of Decree Is Not the Structural Determination)

   The Hub of Decree is not the Structural Determination. The Structural Determination is
   the realm of general multiplicity, of laws that apply universally, necessarily, and formally;
   the Hub of Decree is the level at which the measure is allotted to each identity, before the
   laws are general. The two are distinguished by their mode of existence: the Structural
   Determination is the realm of what is general and formal; the Hub of Decree is the realm
   of what is apportioned and particular.



8.7    The Hub of Signification

The second of the three barzakhic realms is the Hub of Signification. It regulates the transition
from the Structural Determination to the Relational Manifestation.
66                                                       Chapter 8. The Three Barzakhic Realms


     Definition 8.5 (Hub of Signification)

     (A) The Hub of Signification is the barzakhic realm of signification as a mode of existence.
     Its mode of existence is that of structures standing as signs.


     The Hub of Signification is the realm in which the general laws of the Structural Determination
become significant for the relational multiplicity of the Relational Manifestation. A structure, in
its generality, is a form; in the Hub of Signification, it becomes a sign: something that carries
meaning for the realm into which it will be received. The hub is the level at which structure is
contextualized into meaning.
     The hub is what makes the generality of the Structural Determination legible in the contex-
tuality of the Relational Manifestation. Without the signification of structure into meaning, the
general laws have no relation to the things that appear in the relational realm; the relational
things have no general structure by which to be understood. The Hub of Signification is the level
at which the two are joined: the generality of the laws becomes the meaning of the relational
manifestations.
     Three features characterize the realm, and they are developed in the part of the book that
treats the rules of the barzakhic realms. Truthfulness: the signification carries the structural
features of the structure it signifies. Accuracy: the signification preserves the distinctions among
the structural features of what it signifies. Fidelity: the signification preserves the identity of the
structure signified.

     Remark 8.7 (The Hub of Signification Is Not the Structural Determination)

     The Hub of Signification is not the Structural Determination. The Structural Determination
     is the realm of general laws, without particular content; the Hub of Signification is the
     realm at which the general laws carry meaning for particular relations. The two are
     distinguished by their mode of existence: the Structural Determination is the realm of
     what is formal; the Hub of Signification is the realm of what is significant.


     Remark 8.8 (The Hub of Signification Is Not the Relational Manifestation)

     The Hub of Signification is not the Relational Manifestation. The Relational Manifestation
     is the realm of actual relations among manifestations, with their contextuality and their
     structural awareness; the Hub of Signification is the realm of significance as a mode of
     existence, before the relations are actual. The two are distinguished by their mode of
     existence: the Relational Manifestation is the realm of things that exist in relation to one
     another; the Hub of Signification is the realm of structures standing as signs.



8.8      The Hub of Realization

The third of the three barzakhic realms is the Hub of Realization. It regulates the transition
from the Relational Manifestation to the Material Manifestation.
8.9. The Relations Between the Barzakhic and Fundamental Realms                                   67


   Definition 8.6 (Hub of Realization)

   (A) The Hub of Realization is the barzakhic realm of actualization. Its mode of existence
   is the realizing of what is possible as something concrete.


   The Hub of Realization is the realm in which the relational multiplicity of the Relational
Manifestation becomes concrete in the Material Manifestation. What is meaningful, in the
relational realm, becomes real, in the material realm; the hub is the level at which meaning is
actualized. The realization is not the meaning; it is the meaning becoming concrete.
   The hub is what makes the relationality of the Relational Manifestation legible in the
discreteness of the Material Manifestation. Without the realization of meaning in matter, the
relations have no concrete existence; the material things have no relational significance. The
Hub of Realization is the level at which the two are joined: the relational meaning becomes the
concrete existence of the material things.
   Three features characterize the realm, and they are developed in the part of the book that
treats the rules of the barzakhic realms. Proportion in realization: the realization distributes
the conditions of realization proportionally to the structural requirements of what is realized.
Preservation of the realized: the realization preserves the structural conditions on which the
realized depends. Continuation of realization: the realization preserves the conditions of further
realization across stages.

   Remark 8.9 (The Hub of Realization Is Not the Relational Manifestation)

   The Hub of Realization is not the Relational Manifestation. The Relational Manifestation
   is the realm of actual relations among manifestations; the Hub of Realization is the realm
   at which the relations become concrete. The two are distinguished by their mode of
   existence: the Relational Manifestation is the realm of what is relational; the Hub of
   Realization is the realm of what is being realized.


   Remark 8.10 (The Hub of Realization Is Not the Material Manifestation)

   The Hub of Realization is not the Material Manifestation. The Material Manifestation is
   the realm of discrete, localized, and successive things; the Hub of Realization is the realm
   at which actualization happens. The two are distinguished by their mode of existence:
   the Material Manifestation is the realm of things that are; the Hub of Realization is the
   realm that makes what is possible concrete.




8.9     The Relations Between the Barzakhic and Fundamental
        Realms

The three hubs are related to one another, and their relations to the four fundamental realms
follow a single structure. The structure is that of the three transitions from unity to multiplicity.
68                                                        Chapter 8. The Three Barzakhic Realms


The first transition. The Hub of Decree regulates the transition from the First Determination
to the Structural Determination. It apportions the source into the multiplicity of forms.


The second transition. The Hub of Signification regulates the transition from the Structural
Determination to the Relational Manifestation. It contextualizes general structure into meaning.


The third transition. The Hub of Realization regulates the transition from the Relational
Manifestation to the Material Manifestation. It realizes relational meaning in material form.
     The order of the three transitions is the order of expression: from unity, through decree,
to general multiplicity; through signification, to relational multiplicity; through realization, to
material multiplicity. The three hubs are the three levels of mediation through which the unified
source is expressed in the differentiated multiplicity of the seven realms. The relations are
bidirectional: a hub regulates the relation between its two neighboring realms in either direction.
A manifestation may ascend as well as descend; the hub regulates the relation, not a route.

     Remark 8.11 (The Three Transitions and the Seven Realms)

     The three transitions, taken together with the four fundamental realms, yield the seven
     realms of the framework’s ontology. The order of the realms is: First Determination, Hub
     of Decree, Structural Determination, Hub of Signification, Relational Manifestation, Hub
     of Realization, Material Manifestation. The order is the order of expression, and the three
     hubs are the three levels of mediation through which the unified source is expressed in the
     differentiated multiplicity. The seven realms are not a series of concentric circles; they are
     seven modes of existence, related by the order of expression.


     Remark 8.12 (The Three Transitions Are Not Sequential Passage)

     The three transitions are structural, not sequential. An identity manifested in the Material
     Manifestation does not have to pass through the Relational Manifestation, the Hub of
     Signification, and the Structural Determination on the way. The non-necessity of downward
     passage, argued in the previous chapter, holds for the barzakhic realms as well: the hubs
     regulate the relation between realms without requiring the identity to be present in each
     of them. The mediation is the presence of the hub as a condition; it is not the presence of
     the identity as a term.



8.10       Limits and Continuations
Three continuations belong to later parts of the book, and they are indicated here so that the
reader knows where the present chapter’s account is taken up.
     First, the argument for the minimality of the three hubs is given in the part of the book that
treats the arguments. The present chapter defines the three hubs; the argument that exactly
three are required, and that no fewer will do, is developed in the part that treats the minimality
of the three hubs. The argument proceeds from the number of distinctions between the four
grades of multiplicity: four grades, three distinctions, three functions of mediation.
8.11. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                 69


   Second, the argument for the irreducibility of the barzakhic realms is given in the part of the
book that treats the arguments. The present chapter states the principle of the independent
reality of the barzakhic realms; the argument that their rules are not derivable from the rules
of their neighbors, and that the three hubs are therefore irreducible to functions of the four
fundamental realms, is developed in the part that treats the irreducibility of the barzakhic realms.
   Third, the rules of the three hubs are stated in the part of the book that treats the governing
dynamics. The present chapter defines the three hubs and names the rules that characterize
them; their detailed statement—proportion, order, harmony for the Hub of Decree; truthfulness,
accuracy, fidelity for the Hub of Signification; proportion in realization, preservation of the
realized, continuation of realization for the Hub of Realization—is given in the part that treats
the rules of the barzakhic realms.
   The three continuations are the framework’s forward extensions, and the chapter states them
so that the reader knows where the account is taken up. The rules named above are structural
labels; their sense is fixed by the definitions in the part of the book that treats them, and no
traditional use of the same words determines their sense here.

A Question for Reflection
Consider something you know that is mediated between two other things—a gift between two
people, a message between two languages, a law between the legislator and the citizen. Can you
distinguish, in the mediation, the three levels the chapter has distinguished: the allotment of
measure, the signification of meaning, and the realization of what has been signified? Which
level is most easily collapsed into another, and why? What does the collapse miss that the
framework’s distinction preserves?

The next part of the book turns to the fixed elements. It defines identity and manifestation,
the two structural terms that the seven realms have presupposed throughout. With identity and
manifestation both defined, the framework’s account of what is related is complete.
           Part III

Fixed Elements: Identities and
       Manifestations




              70
Chapter 9

Identities


Scope. This chapter is a structural analysis. It defines identity, distinguishes it from signature and
from pseudo-identity, argues for its rigidity, conservation, and non- duplicability, and applies the
account to the classical puzzles of personal identity. It makes no normative, ethical, psychological,
or evaluative claim. Where the chapter speaks of “value,” “what matters,” “flourishing,” or “a
life going well”—as it does only to mark the boundary of the framework’s subject—these terms
name questions that belong to an independent normative inquiry and are not addressed in this
book. Every claim in this chapter is a claim about the structure of identity and its relation to
the appearance of identity in other realms.



9.1     A Scene

Consider a ship. It leaves harbor with planks of wood, a mast, a sail. Over the years, its planks
are replaced one by one. A plank rots; a new plank is fitted in its place. The mast is replaced;
the sail is replaced; the rudder is replaced. After a century of repairs, every plank of the original
ship has been replaced. The ship in the harbor is made of entirely new wood. Is it the same ship?
   Consider a person. She is born, grows, learns, forgets, changes her beliefs, changes her habits,
changes her name. She remembers some things from her childhood and forgets others; she feels
continuous with the child she was and also estranged from her. Is she the same person? If
so, what makes her the same, given that nothing about her—not a single atom, not a single
belief—has remained unchanged?
   The two questions have the same form. In both cases, a thing persists through change, and
the persistence seems both obvious and impossible. It seems obvious because we speak of the
ship as the same ship, the person as the same person. It seems impossible because everything
about the ship and the person has changed. The paradox is not a puzzle about language; it is a
question about what makes a thing the same thing across time, when everything about it has
become different.
   The scene is not new. It is the Ship of Theseus, and it is as old as philosophy. But the
framework’s answer to it is not the traditional one. The traditional answers say either that
the identity is the matter (the original planks), or the form (the design), or the continuity (the
gradual replacement), or the memory (the psychological connections). The framework’s answer
is that none of these is the identity; the identity is that which remains invariant under a specified
class of allowable transformations, and the puzzle is dissolved, not solved, once the distinction
between identity and its appearances is made.



                                                 71
72                                                                            Chapter 9. Identities


9.2      The Question

The scene raises a question that the framework must answer before it can proceed. The previous
parts of the book have spoken of “identities and manifestations” as the fixed elements of the
four-column framework, and of the seven realms as the contexts in which identities are manifested.
But the book has not yet said what an identity is. It has used the term; it has not defined it.
     The question is: what is identity? The question is not merely terminological. It is the question
of what makes a thing the same thing across change, and the question of what distinguishes
a thing from its appearances. If the framework’s answer is correct, the classical puzzles of
identity—the Ship of Theseus, the gradual replacement of a body’s cells, the persistence of a
person through memory and forgetting—are dissolved rather than solved. If the framework’s
answer is wrong, the puzzles remain, and the framework’s use of “identity” throughout the book
is in question.
     The chapter’s method is structural. It defines identity, distinguishes it from the notions with
which it is easily confused (signature, pseudo- identity), argues for its rigidity, its conservation,
and its non- duplicability, and applies the account to the classical puzzles. It does not argue for
the existence of identity; that is a commitment of the framework, and it is stated as such. It
argues for what identity must be if it is to do the work the framework requires of it.



9.3      The Definition of Identity

The first thing to be said about identity is that it is not a substance, not a property, not a thing.
It is a pattern of invariance across a space of possible transformations. To say that a thing has
an identity is to say that there is a class of transformations under which it remains the same.

     Definition 9.1 (Identity)

     An identity is that which remains invariant under a specified class of allowable transfor-
     mations.

     The definition raises an immediate question. The phrase “specified class of allowable trans-
formations” invites the further question: who specifies the class? If the observer specifies it,
identity becomes subjective, and the framework’s claim that identity is real is in question. If the
structure specifies it, the definition risks circularity: the class of allowable transformations is
defined by the identity, and the identity is defined by the class.
     The framework’s answer is that the class of allowable transformations is internal to the
identity itself. A structure is not first given and then subjected to transformations; the structure
is the pattern of invariance across a space of possible transformations. To grasp a structure is
to grasp the transformations it tolerates. The observer does not choose the class; the observer
discovers it through the process of reconstruction. The discovery is fallible, and the criteria by
which it is checked are given later in this chapter.
     Two further definitions are needed to make the first precise.
9.3. The Definition of Identity                                                                       73


   Definition 9.2 (Defining Invariants)

   (A) The defining invariants of an identity are the features that constitute its determination:
   those that distinguish it from its alternatives and are fixed by what it is. They are taken
   as primitive in the framework.


   Definition 9.3 (Identity-Preserving Transformation)

   An identity-preserving transformation is a transformation whose resulting state remains
   within the range of structural possibilities compatible with the identity’s defining invariants.


   The defining invariants are primitive in the framework. They are not obtained by asking
which transformations preserve identity; they are what the allowable transformations are defined
in terms of. This is a commitment of the framework, and its cost is stated: the framework
offers no observer-independent procedure for listing an identity’s defining invariants. An observer
reaches them only fallibly, by reconstruction, and the criteria of adequacy given later in this
chapter are the check on that reconstruction, not a derivation of the invariants.

   Remark 9.1 (Why the Class of Allowable Transformations Is Not Defined
   Circularly)

   The allowable range cannot be defined merely by saying that identity is preserved; that
   would define the class by the very identity it is meant to fix. It is specified through the
   defining invariants: a transformation is allowable when it respects them. The defining
   invariants are not themselves obtained by asking which transformations preserve identity;
   they are taken as primitive. What would put the commitment in question is a case in
   which two accounts of the defining invariants of one identity are both fully adequate by
   the criteria of adequacy and yet incompatible.


   Definition 9.4 (Signature)

   The signature of an identity is the structural description of its invariance: what can be
   read off, compared, recorded, and reproduced about the pattern. Signatures are what
   reconstruction recovers, and what copying copies.


   Remark 9.2 (Identity and Signature)

   Two things must be kept apart. The signature is a pattern; it can be shared by many
   things and it can be duplicated. The identity is the invariance as enacted by a single source,
   “this” invariance rather than another of the same kind. Everything that an observer can
   establish is a fact about signatures. The claim that identity is more than its signature is a
   commitment of the framework, and it is defended later in this chapter.


   The definition and its remarks are summarized as follows. Identity is invariance under
allowable transformations. The allowable transformations are fixed by the identity’s defining
invariants, which are primitive. The signature is the structural description of the invariance;
74                                                                              Chapter 9. Identities


the identity is the invariance as enacted by one source. The distinction between identity and
signature will be used repeatedly in what follows.


9.4       Invariance Is Not Composition

The definition speaks of “structure” and of what remains invariant. The word invites a picture
of an arrangement of parts, and that picture does not fit every realm. It would make the First
Determination, which is pure unity, either composite or no identity at all. The distinction
between invariance and composition must be stated.

     Principle 9.1 (Invariance Is Not Composition)

     (T) That an identity is invariant does not entail that it is composed of several parts.
     “Structure,” in the definition of identity, means the principle that distinguishes the identity
     and holds it one, and not necessarily an arrangement of components.


Proof.      1. To be invariant under a class of transformations is to be unchanged by each member
       of the class. That is a statement about the relation of the thing to the transformations,
       and it says nothing about whether the thing has parts.

     2. A thing without parts can be unchanged under every transformation of a class (for the
       class may be empty or trivially satisfied).

     3. Hence invariance does not entail composition.

     4. In realms of multiplicity, the principle of distinction and unity may show itself as an
       arrangement and ratio of parts. In the realm of pure unity, it cannot, and “structure” there
       names the principle itself.



     Example 9.1 (A Melody)

     A melody transposed to another key has every one of its notes changed, and is still the
     same melody. A melody in which a single interval is altered may not be. A change of
     composition (which notes) is therefore neither sufficient to show that the identity is lost
     nor sufficient to show that it persists. What decides is whether the defining invariants
     (here, the relations among the intervals) are kept. Not every compositional change is
     allowable, and not every compositional change is a change of identity.


     The principle removes the apparent conflict between the pure unity of the First Determination
and a structural definition of identity. The definition uses “structure” in the wide sense; the
narrower sense of arrangement is available only where there is plurality. In the realm of pure unity,
the structure is the principle of distinction and unity itself, not an arrangement of components.
9.5. Identity Across Realms                                                                        75


9.5     Identity Across Realms
An identity is not located in a single realm only. The framework’s ontology has seven realms,
four fundamental and three barzakhic, and an identity may be present in its realm of origin,
manifested in another realm, and effective on a third. Three situations must be told apart, and
the framework uses the distinctions throughout.

Presence in the realm of origin. An identity is present in its realm of origin as that which
it is: in the First Determination as pure unity; in the Structural Determination as the class of
allowable transformations that fixes how it can manifest; in the Relational Manifestation as a
relation; in the Material Manifestation as a material form. The realm of origin is the realm in
which the identity’s mode of existence is structurally located.

Manifestation in another realm. The same identity appears in another realm in a form
suited to that realm’s capacity. The appearance is a manifestation in the minimal sense that
this chapter will use: the determinate appearance of the identity in the receiving realm. The full
definition and treatment of manifestation is given in the next chapter; here the term is used in
this minimal sense, and it is marked as such.

Effect on another realm without passage through the realms between. An identity
may have an effect on another realm, or be present to it, without having to be present or
manifested in each realm that lies between. This is the non-necessity of downward passage, which
was argued in the part of the book that treated the realms.
   The identity is one in all three situations; what differs is the realm, and the kind of relation.
The distribution of an identity across realms does not contradict the context-dependence principle,
which was stated in the first part of the book: the principle concerns the cognitive context, not
the existential realm. An identity is held fixed as the invariant in its own frame; in a frame
whose question concerns a higher realm it may be studied as a manifestation of a higher identity.
These are two cognitive roles of one thing, not two things.

   Remark 9.3 (A Minimal Working Term)

   The term “manifestation” is used in this chapter in the minimal sense of “determinate
   appearance of an identity in a receiving realm.” The full definition—the appearance of an
   identity in a receiving realm according to the realm’s capacity, aptitude, and constraints—is
   given in the next chapter. The reader who has followed the argument to this point has
   what is needed to follow the use of the term in this chapter; the reader who wishes the
   full definition will find it in its place.



9.6     Three Features of Identity
Three features of identity follow from the definition, or are added to it as commitments. They
are stated here, with an indication for each of whether it follows from the definition, whether it
is an independent commitment, and whether an argument is offered.
76                                                                           Chapter 9. Identities


Relational. Identity is not a property that a thing has in isolation; it is a relation between a
thing and a class of transformations—the relation of invariance. The feature follows from the
definition, and no separate argument is needed.


Hierarchical. Identity is not a single, flat property; it is a hierarchy of invariances. A thing
may be invariant under a narrow class of transformations (its specific identity) and also under a
broader class (its generic identity). The feature follows partly from the definition: nested classes
of transformations give nested invariances. It is partly an independent commitment: that such
nesting is the general case. The commitment is supported by example, not proved.


Dynamic. Identity is not a static property that a thing has once and for all; it is a dynamic
achievement, maintained through the ongoing process of expression. The identity of a thing is
not given; it is enacted. The feature does not follow from the definition; it is an independent
commitment, and it is supported in the part of the book that treats the resolution of tensions.
