     A feature is not established merely because the definition is. Only the first is. The second
and third are commitments of the framework, stated as such, and the reader who wishes to
challenge them knows where to press.

     Remark 9.4 (Dynamic and Rigid)

     The third feature may look at odds with the rigidity of identity defended later in this
     chapter. The two statements concern different things. What is dynamic is the enactment,
     that is, the ongoing expression through which the identity shows itself. What is rigid is
     the invariant that is enacted. The difference is an instance of a broader structural claim
     about predication, which the framework develops in its own place; here the distinction is
     named, and the reader is asked to suspend the fuller treatment until it is given.



9.7      Pseudo-Identity
The definition of identity, together with the distinction between identity and signature, leaves
open what an observer can know. The observer does not have access to the identity itself;
9.7. Pseudo-Identity                                                                               77


the observer has access to manifestations, and from them constructs an approximation. The
approximation has a name.

   Definition 9.5 (Pseudo-Identity)

   A pseudo-identity is the observer’s approximation of an identity, constructed from the
   available manifestations.

   A pseudo-identity is not a falsehood; it is a working model: the best approximation the
observer can achieve, given the available manifestations and the costs of reconstruction. It
is a hypothesis about the identity, subject to revision in light of new manifestations. In the
vocabulary of the previous section, a pseudo-identity is an estimate of a signature.
   A pseudo-identity can be more or less adequate. Its adequacy is measured by three criteria.


Consistency. Observers working in different contexts, who carry out the process of reconstruc-
tion, must arrive at the same pseudo-identity, up to isomorphism.


Stability. The pseudo-identity must be stable under small perturbations of the observer’s
context or cognitive apparatus.


Fruitfulness. A system that operates according to the pseudo- identity must be able to operate
within its environment, predict future manifestations, and preserve the structural viability of its
expressions.
   These criteria do not prove that a pseudo-identity is adequate in an absolute sense. They
provide a fallibilist account of adequacy, of the same kind that scientific theories have. They
also have a second use in this chapter: they are the evidence base for the conservation principle,
stated later.

   Remark 9.5 (Signatures and Pseudo-Identities)

   The relation between the notions introduced so far is this: the identity is the invariance
   enacted by one source; its signature is the structural description of that invariance; a
   pseudo-identity is an observer’s estimate of the signature. Observers deal only with the
   last two. This is why identity is never exhausted by any record of it.


   Remark 9.6 (Four Things That Must Not Be Run Together)

   A representation that falls short of the identity is not a rival identity. Four cases differ.

      1. Cognitive error: a mistake in reconstruction, correctable by further manifestations.

      2. Incomplete representation: a pseudo-identity that is accurate as far as it goes but
         does not exhaust the signature. Every pseudo-identity is incomplete in this way.

      3. Misattribution: assigning a manifestation to an identity of which it is not a manifes-
         tation.
78                                                                            Chapter 9. Identities


         4. An independent identity: a different source with an identity of its own.

     A pseudo-identity may be a cognitive error or an incomplete representation; it is not, by
     being so, an independent identity that rivals the original. Calling a reconstruction “pseudo”
     states its epistemic standing, and gives it no ontological standing of its own.



9.8       The Fallacy of Super-Identity
The previous part of the book established the impossibility of super-identity: no finite subject
can know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts. The present section concerns a different
and earlier mistake, one that arises even when the subject sets out to know only some of them:
the belief that identity can be reconstructed by aggregating manifestations taken from different
contexts into a single record.

     Principle 9.2 (Fallacy of Super-Identity)

     (T) A record formed by aggregating manifestations drawn from contexts whose elements are
     not mutually translatable is not a reconstruction of the identity. It is a context-confounded
     record: an object that corresponds to no identity at all.


Proof.      1. To reconstruct an identity is to find what remains invariant across its manifestations.

     2. Each manifestation is the product of the identity and the context in which it appears. It
       therefore contains two components, contributed by the identity and by the context, and
       these are not separated in the manifestation as given.

     3. Invariants are isolated by comparing manifestations while the context varies and the
       identity is held constant: what survives the variation is attributed to the identity. Mere
       concatenation does not compare; it only collects.

     4. A concatenated record therefore mixes the identity’s contribution with the contributions of
       every context it has absorbed, and gives no way of telling which is which.

     5. Hence concatenation does not reconstruct the identity. A record that treats the mixture as
       an identity has no corresponding identity; call it a spurious composite: a record without a
       corresponding invariant.



     The fallacy of super-identity is the counterpart, at the level of method, of the impossibility
of super-identity. The impossibility principle is epistemic and says that no subject can know
everything. The fallacy principle is ontological in its reach: it says that the aggregate is the
wrong kind of object. A subject can commit the fallacy with a small amount of data; and a
subject can avoid it with a large one. The distinction between context and perspective, which is
drawn in the next chapter, shows where the fallacy lies: it is not in having a partial perspective,
which is unavoidable, but in treating a concatenation across contexts as a single whole.
9.8. The Fallacy of Super-Identity                                                                79


9.8.1    Aggregation, Compatibility, and Numerical Unity
The fallacy is not only a fault of gathering conflicting information. Three things are separate,
and the distinction is developed here.

Aggregation. Collecting manifestations.

Compatibility. The absence of conflict among them.

Numerical unity. The oneness of the source identity.
   Even an aggregate of manifestations that are wholly compatible with one another does not,
by being so, produce or restore the source. From aggregation and compatibility it does not follow
that the numerical unity of the source is reached. The source is not the sum or the consistent
sum of its appearances.

   Principle 9.3 (Non-Reduction of Identity to Manifestations)

   (T) An identity is not identical with the aggregate of its manifestations, nor with their
   compatible aggregate.

Proof.    1. A manifestation is the product of the identity and a receiving realm, and is not the
     identity.

  2. An aggregate of products is a plurality of products. A plurality of things is not, as such, a
     single thing of another kind.

  3. Compatibility among the products is a relation among them and does not bring in the
     thing that they are products of.

  4. Hence the identity is not the aggregate, nor the compatible aggregate.


   The status of this principle is (T) relative to the premise that manifestations are products. It
must not be confused with a claim about knowledge. That we know an identity only through
its manifestations is not a claim that it is nothing but them; and that one manifestation is
insufficient to know the identity is not a claim that the manifestation is unreal or defective in
being. Knowing and being are kept apart here.

   Remark 9.7 (The Golden Record Illusion)

   The fallacy is closely related to what we may call the Golden Record Illusion: the belief
   that there is, or could be, a single record that contains all attributes of an entity across
   all contexts. The illusion is pervasive in contemporary data-driven culture, where the
   ideal is often to collect “all the data” and construct a “complete model” of the entity.
   The four-column framework treats this ideal as ill-posed. There is no Golden Record, not
   because we lack the resources to construct it, but because collecting attributes does not
   isolate an invariant, and an invariant is what an identity is. More data of the same kind
80                                                                           Chapter 9. Identities


     makes the confounded record larger, not more adequate as a reconstruction.



9.9      Identity Rigidity and Conservation
Two further principles state what identity is not: it is not a matter of degree, and it is not lost
through time.


9.9.1     Identity Rigidity

     Principle 9.4 (Identity Rigidity)

     (A) Identity does not admit of degrees. A structure either is invariant under the specified
     transformations, or it is not.


Argument from the Logic of Identity.       1. Strict sameness is an equivalence relation: if a is the
       same as b, and b is the same as c, then a is the same as c.

     2. A relation that comes in degrees (“more or less the same”) is not transitive. A chain of
       small differences can connect two things that are very unlike. This is the structure of the
       sorites.

     3. So a degree-based “sameness” is not strict sameness. It is resemblance, which is a matter
       of degree and has no tendency to settle whether something is the same one.

     4. Hence identity, as strict sameness under the allowed class of transformations, admits no
       degrees. The apparent degrees of ordinary language (“not himself today,” “no longer the
       same”) are degrees of manifestation, or of resemblance between signatures, not of identity.


     Remark 9.8 (The Contrast with Properties)

     Rigidity must be distinguished from the degrees of properties. Properties admit of degrees:
     a room can be more or less warm, a person more or less tall. Identity is not a property;
     it is the condition of persistence itself, and as such it is not a matter of degree. The
     framework’s way of speaking of “degrees” belongs to viability, which is a structural feature
     of the relation between identity and manifestation, not of identity.


     Remark 9.9 (Rigidity of Identity Is Not Rigidity of Manifestation)

     Two propositions must be kept apart: (i) identity is invariant in itself, which belongs to
     the definition of identity; (ii) identity appears in the same way under all conditions and
     relations, which does not follow from (i). Hence the rigidity of identity does not mean the
     rigidity of its manifestations. Manifestations may differ widely while the identity does not
     change. The distinction is developed in the part of the book that resolves the apparent
     tension between rigidity and dynamism.
9.9. Identity Rigidity and Conservation                                                           81


9.9.2    Identity Conservation

   Principle 9.5 (Identity Conservation)

   (A) Identity is invariant under all temporal transformations of its manifestations. Manifes-
   tations may vary with time; identity itself is conserved.


   The principle is adopted, and two arguments support it. They are distinct, and they support
different things.



First argument: transcendental, to the presumption of sameness. We have experiences
of temporal continuity: we remember the past, anticipate the future, and recognize objects and
persons across time. Such experiences are possible only if we presume that what is remembered,
anticipated, or recognized is the same one across the interval. Hence the presumption of sameness
is a transcendental condition of temporal experience, and cannot be coherently denied by one
who is describing such experience.
   The conclusion is a statement about a presumption, and a presumption might be a useful
construct rather than a fact. The first argument therefore establishes less than the principle
asserts. It does not, by itself, tell us that identity is really conserved. The gap is closed, to the
extent that it can be closed, by the second argument.



Second argument: abductive, to the reality of the invariant. Reconstructions of
the same thing, carried out independently by observers in different contexts, converge on a
single pseudo-identity up to isomorphism; the result is stable under perturbation; and it yields
successful predictions (the three criteria of adequacy stated earlier). The best explanation of this
convergence is that the observers are tracking something that is the same across the contexts and
across time: an invariant. The rival explanation, namely that the convergence reflects shared
convention or psychological projection, predicts convergence only among observers who share
the convention, and does not explain why predictions made from the pseudo-identity succeed in
domains the convention never touched. Hence it is reasonable to hold that there is an invariant
that persists through time.

   Remark 9.10 (The Three Moments of Temporal Experience)

   The transcendental argument can be put in terms of three moments of temporal experience.
   In memory, I remember a past event as mine. In anticipation, I anticipate a future event
   as one that will happen to me. In recognition, I recognize an object or a person as the
   same one across time. The three are aspects of one structure, and all three presuppose
   the presumption of sameness. The abductive argument is what supports the further claim
   that the presumption is correct.
82                                                                               Chapter 9. Identities


9.10       Non-Duplicability of Identity
Identity is rigid and conserved. The third principle states what is perhaps the most counterintu-
itive: identity cannot be copied.

     Principle 9.6 (Non-Duplicability)

     (A) Identity cannot be copied. Signatures, pseudo-identities, and information can be
     duplicated; identity cannot. A copy of a system reproduces its signature. If the copy
     expresses at all, it expresses an identity of its own.

     Definition 9.6 (Duplication)

     Qualitative duplication produces a second thing that shares the first thing’s signature.
     Numerical duplication of an identity would produce two distinct things, each of which is
     that very identity.

Argument: The Logic of Numerical Identity.           1. Suppose I1 and I2 are numerically distinct,
       and each is identical to the identity I.

     2. Identity is symmetric and transitive: from I1 = I and I2 = I it follows that I1 = I2 .

     3. This contradicts the supposition that they are distinct. Hence numerical duplication of an
       identity is impossible.

     4. What copying does produce is qualitative duplication. Since copies of a signature exist,
       and an identity cannot be copied, an identity is not the same as its signature. If it were,
       copying the signature would copy the identity.


     Steps (1)–(3) are a point of logic and carry little weight by themselves. The philosophical
content is in step (4). It asserts that a thing’s identity is more than its pattern, so that two things
with exactly the same pattern are two, not one, and have two identities. This is the doctrine of
primitive thisness: an individuating feature that is not qualitative, and that distinguishes one
thing from an exact qualitative duplicate.1 The framework adopts the doctrine as a commitment
((A)), and states what it costs: it is a non-reductionist view of identity in Parfit’s classification,
because it holds that there is a further fact about identity over and above facts about continuity
and similarity.2 Consequently, in a case where the signature is perfectly copied, nothing observable
settles which of the resulting systems, if any, carries the original identity.
     The commitment is supported by three considerations. First, it explains why the rigidity
of identity holds: strict sameness is not a matter of resemblance. Second, it is consistent with
the best-known case against the identity of indiscernibles, Black’s two exactly similar spheres,
in which two things share every qualitative feature and yet are two.3 Third, it explains why
1
     [C09-1] Adams, “Primitive Thisness and Primitive Identity,” Journal of Philosophy 76, no. 1 (1979):
     5–26
2
     [C09-2] Parfit, Reasons and Persons (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1984)
3
     [C09-3] Black, “The Identity of Indiscernibles,” Mind 61, no. 242 (1952): 153–164
9.11. The Classical Puzzles of Personal Identity                                                       83


reconstruction can converge on a signature without ever delivering the identity: the signature is
what can be read off, and the identity is what is enacted by a source. The cost is the one stated
above: the identity- facts in duplication cases are not settled by observation.

    Remark 9.11 (Cloning, Teleportation, and Fission)

    The consequences for the classical puzzles, stated with their statuses.
    Cloning ((T)). A clone reproduces a genetic signature. It is not the original and does not
    carry the original’s identity; if it expresses at all, it expresses an identity of its own, with
    its own manifestations and its own structural trajectory.
    Teleportation ((E)). If a machine scans a body, destroys it, and builds an exact copy
    elsewhere, the copy has the original’s signature. The framework’s commitment is that
    copying does not transfer the identity, so the copy is a new system. This verdict is a
    consequence of the doctrine of primitive thisness and cannot be decided by observation; it
    is offered as the framework’s answer, not as an empirical result.
    Fission ((S)). If a system divides into two systems that both continue its signature, then
    by the logic of identity the original identity can continue in at most one of them, or in
    neither. The framework does not say that the question has no answer, but that nothing
    observable fixes it. It is a case where the further fact is real and inaccessible.


9.11      The Classical Puzzles of Personal Identity
The framework’s account of rigidity, conservation, and non-duplicability bears on the classical
puzzles of personal identity. The section treats “personal identity” as a standard metaphysical
topic concerning the persistence of a person over time. It makes no claim about what a person
is worth, what a good life is, or what obligations persons have; those questions belong to an
independent normative inquiry and are not addressed here.
    The framework does not claim to resolve the puzzles from the outside. It claims to dissolve
the metaphysical puzzle by relocating it: the question “what is identity?” receives a determinate
answer, and the difficulty returns as an epistemic question about how identity can be known.

Locke’s memory criterion. Locke defined personal identity as continuity of consciousness and
memory.4 Butler objected that this is circular: memory presupposes personal identity, since to
remember is to remember one’s own past, and so memory cannot constitute it.5 The framework
agrees with the objection. Memory is a manifestation, an expression of identity, and not what
identity consists in. Reid pressed a further difficulty, the case of the brave officer: a boy is flogged;
as an officer he captures a standard and remembers the flogging; as a general he remembers
capturing the standard but not the flogging.6 By Locke’s criterion the general is the officer and
the officer is the boy, yet the general is not the boy, which violates transitivity. The framework’s
4
    [C09-4] Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, ed. P. H. Nidditch (Oxford: Oxford
    University Press, 1979), II.xxvii.9
5
    [C09-5] Butler, “Of Personal Identity,” Dissertation appended to The Analogy of Religion (London,
    1736)
6
    [C09-6] Reid, Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man, ed. Derek R. Brookes (University Park:
    Pennsylvania State University Press, 2002), III.4
84                                                                             Chapter 9. Identities


rigidity principle diagnoses the case: strict sameness is transitive, and memory-connectedness is
a graded, non-transitive relation of manifestation, so the two cannot be the same relation.


The gradual replacement puzzle. If the parts of a ship, or the cells of a body, are replaced
over time, at what point does the object cease to be the same one? The framework answers
that the identity is not the parts but the invariance under the allowed class of replacements.
Different contexts fix different classes. In a functional context the repaired ship is the same
ship; in a material context the ship rebuilt from the original planks is. The puzzle arises from
requiring one answer across contexts, which is a mild form of the very demand that the principle
of super-identity rejects. The framework does not choose between the two answers; it says that
each is correct in its own context and that none is correct across all contexts.


Fission and duplication. These are treated in the previous section. The framework’s answer
is stated there together with its theoretical cost.

     Remark 9.12 (Four Continuities That the Puzzles Confuse)

     The rival answers to the puzzles can be located by asking which of four things each treats
     as sufficient for “being the same one”:

         1. continuity of structure (the invariant pattern persists);

         2. continuity of manifestation (the appearances follow one another smoothly);

         3. continuity of relation (the thing stands in the same relations to others);

         4. numerical unity of the identity (it is one and the same source).

     The memory criterion takes (2) for (4). The replacement puzzle contrasts (1) in different
     contexts. The brave-officer case separates (2), which is not transitive, from (4), which is.
     A theory that treats one of the first three as if it were the fourth has confused a level of
     identity with identity.


     Remark 9.13 (What Is Dissolved and What Remains)

     What the framework removes is the metaphysical puzzle of what identity consists in. It
     does so by the doctrine of primitive thisness, which is a substantial commitment, and which
     is not shared by the reductionist views of Parfit and Lewis, nor by animalist views such as
     Olson’s.a What remains is an epistemic puzzle: since observers deal only with signatures
     and pseudo-identities, there are cases in which no evidence can decide an identity-fact.
     The framework accepts this consequence openly. A reader who finds the theoretical cost
     unacceptable has located the place where the framework should be challenged.
     a
         [C09-7] Olson, The Human Animal: Personal Identity Without Psychology (Oxford: Oxford
         University Press, 1997)

9.12     What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Three things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
   First, the chapter does not give the full definition of manifestation. The term has been used
in a minimal working sense, and its full treatment—the appearance of an identity in a receiving
realm according to the realm’s capacity, aptitude, and constraints—is given in the next chapter.
The reader who wishes to see how manifestation is defined, and how the relation between identity
and manifestation is structured, will find it there.
   Second, the chapter does not develop the notion of category-relative predication. The
distinction between what is rigid and what is dynamic, and the distinction between what is
invariant in an identity and what varies in its expression, are instances of a broader structural
claim, which the framework develops in its treatment of the resolution of tensions. The reader
who wishes to see how the claim is argued will find it there.
   Third, the chapter does not develop the arguments for conservation and non-duplicability
beyond their statement. The arguments have been given in outline; their full development, with
the objections and replies, is given in the part of the book that treats the arguments. The present
chapter has stated the principles; the later part will defend them.

A Question for Reflection
Take a thing you have known for a long time—a friend, a place, a practice. What has remained
the same across the time you have known it, and what has changed? If you were asked to say
what the thing is, would you point to what has remained, or to what has changed? What does
your answer tell you about the relation between identity and its manifestations?
86                                                                          Chapter 9. Identities


The next chapter turns to manifestations. It defines manifestation as the appearance of an identity
in a receiving realm according to the realm’s capacity, aptitude, and constraints; it argues that a
manifestation is a product of the identity and the receiving realm; and it distinguishes context
from perspective. With identity and manifestation both defined, the framework’s treatment of the
fixed elements is complete.
Chapter 10

Manifestations


Scope. This chapter is a structural analysis. It defines manifestation, distinguishes essential
from non-essential features, argues that a manifestation is a product of the source identity and
the receiving realm, distinguishes context from perspective, and states the principle of essential
homogeneity. It completes the framework’s treatment of the fixed elements: with identity defined
in the previous chapter and manifestation defined here, the two fixed elements are in place. Its
claims are structural; where the chapter is silent on questions of value or religion, the silence
is not a denial but a recognition that the structural description is not the whole of what can
be said. Where the chapter speaks of “capacity,” “aptitude,” “constraint,” “effect,” “nature,”
“conflict,” “homogeneity,” or “perspective,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the
definitions in this chapter. The word “aptitude” does not name a value or an end; it names the
structural suitability of a realm for a kind of appearance.


10.1         A Scene
Consider a daughter, forty years old, a surgeon. Three people look at her, and each sees something
different.
    Her mother sees the child she raised: the small hands, the face that once cried at nightmares,
the girl who learned to ride a bicycle. The daughter is now a surgeon, married, with a practice
of her own. But what the mother sees is not the surgeon; it is the daughter, whom the mother
has known since before the daughter knew herself.
    Her colleague in the operating room sees a hand, steady and precise; a judgment, quick and
reliable; a voice, calm under pressure. The colleague does not see the child; the colleague sees
the professional, the one whose competence has been tested and proven.
    Her patient, waking from anesthesia, sees a face, blurred; a voice, reassuring; a name, half-
remembered. The patient does not see the mother’s daughter or the colleague’s professional; the
patient sees the one who saved her life, or the one who failed to.
    Three appearances, one person. The appearances are not merely different perspectives on the
same facts. Each is real; each makes visible something the others cannot. And none is reducible
to another. The mother’s love is not the colleague’s respect, and neither is the patient’s gratitude.
Each appearance is shaped by the relation between the daughter and the one who sees her—by
the mother’s memories, by the colleague’s shared work, by the patient’s dependence.
    The scene poses a question that the previous chapter left open. The previous chapter defined
identity as that which remains invariant under a specified class of allowable transformations. It
distinguished identity from signature and from pseudo-identity. But it did not yet say what an
appearance of an identity is. If the daughter’s identity is one, and her appearances are many and
different, what is the structure of the relation between the one and the many? Is she nothing

                                                 87
88                                                                    Chapter 10. Manifestations


more than her appearances, or is there something she is, which they manifest? And if there is
something she is, how can appearances so different all be appearances of it?


10.2       The Question
The scene raises three questions, and the chapter treats them in turn.
     The first is: what is a manifestation? The previous chapter used the term in a minimal
working sense—the determinate appearance of an identity in a receiving realm—and promised
that the full definition would be given here. The definition must state what a manifestation is,
what its components are, and how it is related to the identity it manifests.
     The second is: what distinguishes the features of a manifestation that belong to the identity
from the features that belong to the receiving realm? The daughter’s steadiness under pressure is
a feature of her identity; the specific appearance of that steadiness to a colleague is a feature of
the receiving context. The chapter must provide the criterion by which the two kinds of feature
are distinguished.
     The third is: is the receiving realm passive or active in the production of a manifestation?
Is it a neutral vessel that receives whatever the identity pours into it, or does its own capacity
shape what appears? The scene suggests the latter: the mother’s love makes visible what another
cannot see. The chapter must state the framework’s answer to this question, and state its status.
     The chapter’s method is structural. It defines manifestation, defines essential feature, states
the principle of the active capacity of the receiving realm, states the principle of essential
homogeneity, and distinguishes context from perspective. It does not develop the full account of
cost and sediment; those are treated in a later part of the book. It does not develop the broader
structural claim about predication; that too is treated later. The chapter’s task is to complete
the treatment of the fixed elements, and to prepare the ground for the treatment of the fluid
element.


10.3       The Definition of Manifestation

     Definition 10.1 (Manifestation)

     A manifestation is the contextually realized appearance of an identity according to the
     ontological capacity, aptitude, and constraints of the receiving realm.

     What is new in this definition is that the receiving realm is not only the place where an
appearance happens to occur. Its capacity, aptitude, and constraints take part in determining
the form of the appearance. The vocabulary used from now on is fixed.


Source identity. The identity that appears.


Receiving realm. The realm in which it appears. The seven realms, four fundamental and
three barzakhic, were defined in the earlier part of the book that treated them; any of them can
be a receiving realm for an identity whose realm of origin is another.
10.3. The Definition of Manifestation                                                              89


Capacity and aptitude of the realm. What kinds of appearance the realm can bear, and
what it is structurally suited to. The terms are structural: they name what a realm can receive
and what it is suited to receive, not a value, a purpose, or an end.


Form of manifestation. The determinate appearance that results.


Manifestational effect. The effect of the manifestation in the receiving realm.
   The definition is stated at the level of the relation between an identity and a realm. It does
not describe the identity in itself, nor the realm in itself, but what happens when the one appears
in the other. The relation is what the definition captures; the two terms are its conditions.

   Remark 10.1 (Manifestation Is Not Illusion)

   The structural account is not a claim that manifestation is an illusion. A manifestation is
   real at its own level: it is a determinate appearance in a receiving realm, with its own mode
   of existence and its own relations to other manifestations in that realm. The framework’s
   claim is that the manifestation is real as a product, not that it is unreal because it is not
   the source. The distinction is the distinction between the reality of the source and the
   reality of the product; it is not the distinction between the real and the unreal. A reader
   who takes the definition of manifestation as a claim that manifestations are appearances in
   the sense of illusions has misread it; a reader who takes it as a claim that manifestations
   are real products of a real source has read it correctly.


   Remark 10.2 (Source and Higher Realm)

   “Source” in this book means the source identity of a manifestation. It does not mean a
   higher realm. By the non-necessity of downward passage, which was argued in the part of
   the book that treated the realms, an identity may be manifested in a realm that is not
   adjacent to its own, so the source of a manifestation need not be the realm immediately
   above the one in which it appears. The realm in which an identity’s mode of existence is
   structurally located is a different matter, and is said so when meant.
   The source, in the structural sense, is the identity that appears. It is not the ultimate
   source of the identity, and the framework does not claim to describe the ultimate source.
   The structural source points beyond itself: the identity is what appears, and the identity is
   what it is because of a ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the
   distinction between the structural source and the ultimate source; it is kept throughout
   the book. A reader who takes the structural source as the ultimate source has conflated
   the order of determination with its ground; a reader who distinguishes them has read the
   framework’s claim correctly.


   Remark 10.3 (Three Features of Manifestation)

   Three features follow from the definition.
   Contextual. A manifestation is always a manifestation in a realm. The realm influences
90                                                                      Chapter 10. Manifestations


     what aspects are expressed and how.
     Partial. No single manifestation exhausts the identity. This is why super-identity is
     impossible, as was argued in the first part of the book.
     Plural. An identity is expressed in many manifestations. Plurality is a structural condition
     of expression, not a structural deficiency.
     The plurality of manifestations is not a falling-away from the identity; it is the condition
     under which the identity is expressed. What the traditions call the manifestation of the
     one in the many is, in the framework’s vocabulary, the structural plurality of expression.
     The two are not the same, and neither reduces to the other; but they are structurally
     parallel. The framework’s claim is structural: it says that the plurality is a condition of
     expression, not that the plurality is a defect. A reader who takes the plurality as a sign
     that the identity is not one has misread it; a reader who takes it as a sign that the identity
     is expressed has read it correctly.



10.4       Essential and Non-Essential Features

The first question of the chapter was: what distinguishes the features of a manifestation that
belong to the identity from those that belong to the receiving realm? The answer requires a
distinction between two kinds of feature.

     Definition 10.2 (Essential Feature)

     An essential feature of an identity is a feature that belongs to its defining invariants.
     A non-essential feature is one that may vary among the manifestations of the identity
     without altering its essential determination.


     The definition uses the notion of defining invariants, which was introduced in the previous
chapter. The defining invariants are the features that constitute an identity’s determination and
distinguish it from its alternatives; they are taken as primitive in the framework. An essential
feature is one that belongs to them; a non-essential feature is one that does not.
     It follows that an identity without one of its essential features would not be the identity
it is. But that counterfactual is a consequence of the definition, and is not used to define
the term; to define essential features by it would make the definition circular with that of an
identity-preserving transformation.

     Remark 10.4 (The Criterion of Essence)

     The definition tells us what an essential feature is, but not how to identify one. The
     framework’s criterion is internal: an essential feature is one whose removal would put the
     identity in question. The removal may be conceptual (we cannot conceive the identity
     without this feature) or structural (the feature is a condition of the identity’s persistence).
     The two are not the same; the conceptual removal is a mark, not a test, and the structural
     removal is what the framework takes as the criterion. The framework does not offer
10.5. Manifestation as a Node in a Realm                                                          91


   an observer-independent procedure for listing the essential features of an identity; the
   observer reaches them fallibly, by reconstruction, and the criteria of adequacy stated in
   the previous chapter are the check on that reconstruction.


   Remark 10.5 (The Distinction Is a Consequence, Not an Addition)

   The distinction between essential and non-essential features is not an addition to the
   definition of manifestation. It is what the definition already implies: if a manifestation
   is the appearance of an identity in a realm, then some features of the appearance are
   contributed by the identity, and some by the realm. The distinction names the two
   contributions. It is stated separately because the naming is useful, not because the
   distinction is new.



10.5     Manifestation as a Node in a Realm
In its own realm, a manifestation is a fixed element in the network of that realm. From the
standpoint of a frame concerned with a higher realm, it may be studied as a fluid element, since it
appears differently as the frame varies. The two roles are the ones the framework’s four columns
distinguish; the same manifestation can play either role, depending on the question the frame
asks.
   The point is an instance of the context-dependence principle, which was stated and argued
in the first part of the book: the fixedness or fluidity of an element depends on the cognitive
context, not on the element’s essence. What the principle says of elements generally, it says of
manifestations in particular. A manifestation is a fixed element in one frame and a fluid element
in another; neither role is more real than the other.

   Remark 10.6 (Two Independences That Must Not Be Mixed)

   A manifestation can be a real and independent entity in the order of the realm in which it
   appears. It is not independent of its source as an identity. The first is independence of
   realm; the second would be independence of identity. The first is affirmed; the second is
   denied.
   A manifestation is a structural element in its realm, with its own mode of existence and its
   own relations to other manifestations in that realm. It is not, for that, a second identity.
   It has the reality of a product, not the reality of a source. The distinction between the
   two kinds of reality is what the framework’s account of manifestation is meant to preserve.
   The distinction is the distinction between the reality of the product and the reality of
   the source. Both are real; neither is an illusion. The product is real at its own level; the
   source is real at its own level. The framework’s claim is that the two levels are distinct,
   not that one is real and the other is not. A reader who takes the distinction as a denial of
   the reality of the product has misread it; a reader who takes it as a distinction between
   two levels of reality has read it correctly.
92                                                                   Chapter 10. Manifestations


10.6       Manifestation as a Product of Interaction

A manifestation is not an independent column. It is the product of an interaction in which three
things take part: the source identity, the aptitude of the receiving realm, and the action and
interaction between the two.
     That a manifestation is a product of the source and the receiving realm is not a definitional
triviality. It is a substantive claim, and it was used as a premise in the argument for the
impossibility of super-identity in the first part of the book. The claim is a commitment of the
framework, and it is supported by the fact that one identity appears differently in realms of
different capacity. It would be refuted by a case in which the appearance in a realm is fixed by
the source alone.


10.6.1      The Active Role of the Receiving Realm

The receiving realm is not a neutral vessel. Its capacity bears on what can appear; its constraints
exclude some forms and favor others. This is not an addition to the identity’s appearance by an
outside force: it is part of what it is for the appearance to be in that realm.
     The point can be put in a slogan: a manifestation is not the identity plus the realm, but
the identity as manifested in the realm. The two contributions are not separable, and the
manifestation is not the sum of two independent parts. It is one thing, produced by the
interaction of two conditions, and its form reflects both.

     Remark 10.7 (The Active Role of the Realm Is Not Creation)

     The active role of the receiving realm is not a creation of the manifestation. The realm
     does not produce the identity, and it does not produce the manifestation from nothing. It
     is the condition under which the identity appears in a determinate form. The distinction
     is the distinction between a condition of appearance and a creator of appearance. The
     framework’s claim is that the realm is the first, not the second. A reader who takes the
     active role as a creation has misread it; a reader who takes it as a condition has read it
     correctly.
     The distinction matters because it preserves the structural asymmetry between the source
     and the receiving realm. The source is the identity; the realm is the condition. The
     identity is not produced by the realm, and the realm is not produced by the identity.
     The two are distinct conditions of one manifestation. The framework’s claim is that
     the manifestation is the product of both, and that neither is the whole cause of the
     manifestation. The framework does not claim that the manifestation is created by the
     realm, and it does not claim that the manifestation is created by the source alone. It
     claims that the manifestation is the structural result of the interaction between the two.


     The framework states the point as a principle, but the principle is proposed, not adopted,
because its independent definition and support are not yet given.
10.7. The Relation Between Identity and Manifestation                                            93


   Principle 10.1 (Contextual Manifestational Capacity (proposed))

   Status: proposed; not yet assigned (A) or (T). The form that a manifestation takes in a
   realm is fixed jointly by the source identity and by the capacity of the realm, and realms
   differ in capacity.

   The principle states what the definition of manifestation presupposes, but a definition cannot
also be the argument for itself. What is still lacking is (i) an independent account of what
“capacity” is, not defined as the structural capacity to produce what is observed, and (ii) an
argument that capacity is not merely the name of the difference in appearances. Until these are
supplied, the principle is examined in the text and not counted as a principle of the book. It is
retained here because the definition of manifestation presupposes it, and because the treatment
of cost, in a later part of the book, will give it the independent account it needs.


10.7     The Relation Between Identity and Manifestation
The relation between identity and manifestation is not identity, and it is not opposition. It is
one of expression. Four propositions state it.


First proposition: a manifestation is not the identity. It is a new entity in its own realm.
The daughter’s appearance to her mother is not the daughter; it is the appearance.


Second proposition: a manifestation is not unrelated to the identity. It makes the
identity visible, legible, recognizable; this is what makes it a manifestation of that identity
rather than an unrelated event. The daughter’s appearance to her mother is recognizable as the
daughter; it is not a random event.


Third proposition: manifestations of one identity may differ in structure. Two
manifestations of the same identity, in different realms or in one, may have different structures.
The daughter’s appearance to her mother and her appearance to her patient differ in structure.


Fourth proposition: a manifestation is homogeneous in essence with its source.
Whatever its structure, it must not have a feature that conflicts with the essential determination
of its source. The daughter’s appearance to her patient, however different, must not be an
appearance in which the daughter is not recognizable at all; if it were, it would not be a
manifestation of the daughter.
   The four propositions together locate manifestation in a conceptual space: not the identity,
not unrelated to the identity, not necessarily similar in structure to other manifestations, and yet
bound by the essential determination of the source.
   The relation is one of expression, and expression points beyond itself. The manifestation
expresses the identity; the identity is what is expressed; and the identity is what it is because of
a ground that the manifestation does not contain. The manifestation shows the identity, but
it does not exhaust the identity; and the identity is real, but its reality is not the reality of
94                                                                        Chapter 10. Manifestations


the manifestation. The distinction is the distinction between the expressing and the expressed;
it is kept throughout the book, and it is the structural ground of the framework’s account of
manifestation.


     Level             Question

     Identity          What is the source of the appearance?
     Manifestation     What of it is realized in the receiving realm?
     Manifestational What change does it bring about in the receiving realm?
     effect


     The table is a conceptual separation, not a principle. Its use is that the effect of a manifestation
does not show the whole of the manifestation, and the manifestation does not reveal the whole of
the identity. The three are distinct levels; confusion among them is the source of several errors,
including the fallacy of super-identity, which the previous chapter argued against.



10.8          Essential Homogeneity

The fourth proposition of the previous section requires a principle of its own, because it is the
criterion by which a manifestation is recognized as a manifestation of its source rather than of
another.

     Principle 10.2 (Essential Homogeneity of Manifestation)

     (A) A manifestation is essentially homogeneous with its source insofar as it preserves the
     source’s essential determination. Structural variation among manifestations of one identity
     is permissible where it does not introduce a feature incompatible with that determination;
     a manifestation cannot have a feature that conflicts with an essential feature of its source.


     The principle is empty unless it says what counts as the essential determination of an identity
and as a conflict with it. The criterion adopted is this.
     The essential determination of an identity is the totality of its defining invariants, as those
were defined in the previous chapter. A feature conflicts with that determination when it is
incompatible with an essential feature. Hence differences of form, scale, or mode in non- essential
features are allowed; incompatibility with an essential feature is not.
     The criterion is internal: it uses only the defining invariants of the identity. The principle
is (A), because it is not a consequence of the definition of manifestation alone; it adds that
manifestations are bound by the essential determination of the source. What would refute it is a
manifestation that is acknowledged to be of an identity and yet has a feature incompatible with
an essential feature; the framework would then hold either that the thing is not a manifestation
of that identity (a case of misattribution, of the kind the previous chapter distinguished) or that
the principle fails.
10.9. Context and Perspective                                                                        95


   Remark 10.8 (Structural Difference Is Not Change of Nature)

   That manifestations differ in structure does not mean that the essential determination of
   the identity changes. The daughter’s structure as a professional and her structure as a
   daughter are different, and the daughter’s essential determination is not thereby two. The
   point is one of the instances of a broader structural claim, which the framework develops
   in the part of the book that treats the resolution of tensions; here it is named, and the
   reader is asked to suspend the fuller treatment until it is given.
   The structural difference is not a change of nature; it is the richness of expression. What the
   traditions call the manifestation of the one in the many is, in the framework’s vocabulary,
   the structural variation of manifestations under the same essential determination. The two
   are not the same; the framework’s claim is structural. But they are structurally parallel,
   and the framework’s claim is that the structure is real, invariant, and describable. A
   reader who takes the structural variation as a change of nature has misread it; a reader
   who takes it as an expression of one nature under many conditions has read it correctly.




10.9     Context and Perspective

A terminological clarification is needed here and later. Realm, context, and perspective are
different things, and the framework uses the three terms with fixed senses.


   Definition 10.3 (Context)

   An existential context is the realm in which a manifestation is realized, with its capacity
   and constraints; a cognitive context is the frame in which something is cognized. An
   existential context is not chosen by an observer.


   The distinction between the two kinds of context was drawn in the first part of the book.
The present definition restates it for the purposes of the present chapter.


   Definition 10.4 (Perspective)

   A perspective is the structural position of an observer within a cognitive context: the
   point from which, the means by which, and the conceptual structure through which a
   manifestation is apprehended. A perspective is located at a position, is partial in what it
   can apprehend, and is revisable in light of further manifestations.


   A manifestation may be realized in one realm and still be understood in different ways
from different perspectives. A difference in understanding is not, as such, a difference in the
manifestation. To treat the one as the other is to confuse the epistemic with the ontic.
96                                                                       Chapter 10. Manifestations


     Remark 10.9 (The Fallacy of Super-Identity Concerns Contexts, Not Perspec-
     tives)

     The fallacy of super-identity, argued in the previous chapter, and the broader structural
     claim about predication, which the framework develops in the part of the book that treats
     the resolution of tensions, concern contexts, not perspectives. The fallacy is not that
     an observer has a partial perspective (that is inevitable); it is that manifestations from
     contexts that cannot be translated into one another are gathered into a single flat record.
     The distinction between context and perspective is what allows the fallacy to be stated
     precisely, and what allows the framework to say that partial perspectives are not a defect
     of cognition but a structural condition of it.
     The partiality of the perspective is not a deficiency; it is the condition under which a finite
     subject can cognize at all. The framework’s claim is that the partiality is structural: it
     belongs to the relation between a finite subject and an identity, not to the identity itself.
     The identity may be fully known to a subject that is not finite; the framework’s claim is
     about the finite subject, not about the identity. The distinction is the distinction between
     the limits of finite inquiry and the limits of what is; it is kept throughout the book.



10.10         Manifestation and the Four Columns
With the definition of manifestation in place, the framework’s use of the four columns can be
stated for the specific case of a manifestation.


     Four-Column Framework            Manifestation

     Fixed element                    Identity (in its own realm).
     Fixed element (studied as        Manifestation itself.
     fluid in some frames)
     Fluid element                    Light (the conveyor of effect).
     Governing dynamics               The rules of the realm.
     Context                          The realm in which the manifestation is realized.

     The table is analytical, not substantial. The four columns are analytical roles; the table does
not say that a manifestation breaks down into four independent entities. The manifestation is
not a fifth column: it is the product of the source identity and the receiving realm. The table
states how the four columns apply to the study of a manifestation, not what a manifestation is
composed of.


10.11         What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
     First, the chapter does not give an independent account of the notion of capacity. The
principle of contextual manifestational capacity, stated above, is proposed, not adopted. The
10.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                  97


independent account is given in the part of the book that treats cost, where the notion of what a
realm can bear is developed with the account of expression cost and sediment.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of the relation between manifestation
and effect. The manifestational effect is named in the definition of manifestation, but its treatment
is deferred to the part of the book that treats derivative concepts, where the notions of returning
light and sediment give the effect a fuller structural description.
    Third, the chapter does not develop the broader structural claim about predication, of which
the distinction between structural difference and change of nature is an instance. The claim is
developed in the part of the book that treats the resolution of tensions. The present chapter has
named the distinction; the later part argues for it.
    Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have fully described the relation of manifestation. It
claims to have described the structure of the relation, and the structure points beyond itself
to the source that manifests. The framework’s claim is that the structure is real, invariant,
and describable; it does not claim that the structure is the whole of what is, and it does not
claim that nothing lies beyond it. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of
manifestation and the ground of manifestation; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is stated
here as the chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Take a person you know well. Consider three of their appearances: to you, to someone who does
not know them, to themselves. What is preserved across the three? What is different? And what
does the answer tell you about the relation between the person’s identity and the appearances in
which it is manifested?

With this chapter, the framework’s treatment of the fixed elements is complete. Identity and
manifestation have both been defined, and the relation between them has been stated. The next part
turns to the fluid element: light. Light is the conveyor of effect between identity and manifestation;
without it, the relation that this chapter has described would have no medium in which to be
realized.
       Part IV

Fluid Elements: Light




          98
Chapter 11

Light: The Problem and the Map


Scope. This chapter opens the framework’s treatment of the fluid element. It begins with an
experience, states why light is a philosophical problem and not merely a topic for empirical
inquiry, maps the human answers to the question “what is light?” into four structural patterns,
and identifies the common presupposition that underlies them. It does not yet propose a definition
of light; it prepares the ground for the proposal that follows. Its claims are structural; where
the chapter is silent on questions of religion or mystical experience, the silence is not a denial
but a recognition that the structural description is not the whole of what can be said. Where
the chapter speaks of “light,” “experience,” “metaphor,” “substance,” or “relation,” these are
structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.


11.1     A Scene
Close your eyes. In the dark, objects are—you reach out, you touch a table. The table is there:
its edge, its grain, its coolness. But it is not seen. Then you open your eyes. The same table, the
same distance, the same hand. But something has been added: the table is seen. What is that
added thing?
   The question seems simple. The table did not change; the hand did not move; the distance is
the same. What changed is that the table is now visible. But “visible” is not a thing added to
the table, as a fourth leg would be. It is a relation—between the table, the eye, and something
else, something that was absent when the eyes were closed and present when they opened. What
is that something else?
   The ordinary answer is: light. The room was dark; now it is lit. But the ordinary answer
names a candidate for the something else; it does not yet say what the candidate is. When
we press the question—what is light, such that its presence makes the table visible and its
absence leaves the table in the dark?—the ordinary answer begins to dissolve. Is light a stream
of particles? A wave in a medium? A field? A condition of visibility that is not itself visible?
Each answer has its difficulties, and each has been defended.
   The scene is small, but the question it raises is not. It is the question of what makes relation
possible—not only the relation between the eye and the table, but any relation at all. If the
framework’s four columns are correct, the second column is the fluid element: the entity that
conveys effect between the fixed elements. What is that entity? The present part of the book
answers: it is light, in a sense that must be defined with philosophical precision. The present
chapter prepares the definition by showing why the question is a philosophical question, and by
mapping the answers that have been given.



                                                99
100                                                 Chapter 11. Light: The Problem and the Map


11.2        The Question
The framework’s treatment of the fixed elements was completed in the previous part. Identity
was defined as the invariance under a specified class of allowable transformations; manifestation
was defined as the contextually realized appearance of an identity in a receiving realm, according
to that realm’s capacity, aptitude, and constraints. The relation between the two was stated: a
manifestation is not the identity, and is not unrelated to it; it makes the identity visible, legible,
recognizable.
      But the relation has a gap. If the manifestation is the appearance of the identity in a realm,
what carries the effect of the identity into the manifestation, and what carries the manifestation
back to the identity? The relation is not automatic; it is not a mere logical implication. It
is a relation in which something passes—from the identity to its manifestation, and from the
manifestation to its source, and from one manifestation to another in the same realm. What is
that something?
      The four-column framework has a name for it: the fluid element. The conveyor principle,
stated and proved in the first part of the book, says that no explanation of how one fixed element
bears on another is complete unless it invokes a fluid element. The present part of the book asks
what the fluid element is, in its most general role. The answer is light.
      The question is not: what is light in the physicist’s sense? That is a question for empirical
inquiry, and the book does not address it. The question is: what is light in the framework’s
sense—the conveyor of effect between identities and manifestations? The answer must be a
philosophical definition, not an empirical description. It must state what light is, in a way that is
precise enough to be argued about, and general enough to cover the role the framework assigns
to it.
      The chapter’s method is threefold. First, it maps the human answers to the question “what
is light?” into structural patterns, and shows that the patterns are not accidental. Second, it
identifies the common presupposition that underlies all four patterns. Third, it shows that the
presupposition is the source of the tension among them—and that the tension is what motivates
the proposal of the next chapter. The chapter does not yet propose a definition. It prepares the
ground.


11.3        Why Light Is a Philosophical Problem
Before the map, a preliminary question: why is light a philosophical problem at all? Why not
leave the question to physics, which has studied light for centuries and has produced a body of
theory of extraordinary precision?
      The answer is not that physics is wrong. The answer is that physics answers a different
question. Physics asks how light behaves: how it propagates, how it interacts with matter, how it
is emitted and absorbed. It answers this question with mathematical precision, and the answers
are among the most successful in the history of science. But physics does not ask what light is,
in the sense the framework requires. It describes the behavior; it does not state the being.
      The distinction is not a criticism of physics. It is a distinction between two kinds of question.
The question “how does light behave?” is an empirical question; the question “what is light?”
11.3. Why Light Is a Philosophical Problem                                                      101


is a philosophical one. The two are related, but neither is reducible to the other. A complete
physics of light would not answer the philosophical question, and a complete philosophy of light
would not replace the physics. The framework’s claim is that the philosophical question is real,
that it has been asked since before philosophy had a name, and that the answers to it have been
multiple.

   Principle 11.1 (Light Is a Philosophical Problem)

   (T) The question “what is light?” cannot be answered by empirical methods alone, because
   light is the condition of possibility of experience—and a condition is not itself an object of
   experience.



Argument for the Principle.      1. Empirical methods answer questions about objects of experi-
     ence.

  2. Light is the condition of possibility of experience: without light, no object is visible, and
     the visible is the paradigm of the empirical.

  3. A condition of possibility is not itself an object of experience. The eye sees by light, but
     does not see light, except by reflection or scattering, which is light as an object, not light
     as the condition.

  4. Hence the question “what is light?” cannot be answered by empirical methods alone.




   The argument is not a proof that light is unknowable. It is a proof that the question of what
light is cannot be settled by the methods that presuppose light. The philosophical question
remains, and the framework addresses it.

   Remark 11.1 (The Question Is Not Merely Terminological)

   The philosophical question “what is light?” is not a question about the essence of light in
   isolation. It is a question about the structural place of light within the architecture of
   relation. The framework’s answer will be a structural answer: light is the condition of
   possibility of relation, not a thing that enters into relations. But the structural answer
   is not a denial that light points beyond itself. The condition of possibility of relation
   is a real condition, and its reality is the reality of an order that points beyond itself to
   what grounds the order. The framework’s claim is that the structural place of light is
   real, invariant, and describable; it does not claim that the structural place is the whole of
   what light is, and it does not claim that nothing lies beyond the structural place. The
   distinction is the distinction between the structure of light and the ground of light; it is
   kept throughout the part.
102                                               Chapter 11. Light: The Problem and the Map


   Remark 11.2 (The Diversity of Answers Is Not Accidental)

   The diversity of answers to the question “what is light?”—across traditions, across centuries,
   across disciplines—is not accidental. It is a sign that light is, before being a “thing” in the
   world, a structural condition for understanding the world. When a condition is mistaken
   for a thing, the answers multiply, because each answer captures an aspect of the condition
   while missing the others. The multiplication is the symptom; the condition is the cause.
   The traditions that speak of light as transcending the categories of substance and relation
   are not confused; they are pointing to the condition that the categories cannot capture.
   The framework’s claim is that the condition is real, and that its reality is the reality of an
   order that the categories presuppose but cannot exhaust.



11.4      Four Structural Patterns
The human answers to the question “what is light?” can be classified into four structural patterns.
The patterns are not historical; they are structural. In every period, all four are present. The
classification is offered as a map, not as a history.


Light as experience. The first pattern answers the question “how is seeing possible?” It
treats light as the condition of visual experience, and studies it through the phenomenology of
perception, the psychology of vision, or the analysis of what it is like to see. The pattern is
present in every period; in the modern period it appears in phenomenology and in the psychology
of perception.


Light as metaphor. The second pattern answers the question “what does it illuminate?”
It treats light as a figure for something else—for knowledge, for truth, for the good, for the
divine. The pattern is present in every period; it is the dominant pattern in mystical, poetic, and
theological traditions, and it recurs in philosophical traditions whenever light is used to figure
the intelligible. The word “metaphor” in the name of the pattern is a structural label; it does
not mean that the pattern is arbitrary or merely ornamental. The pattern treats light as a figure
for something that the categories of substance and relation cannot capture—a figure that points,
rather than a figure that substitutes.


Light as substance. The third pattern answers the question “what is it made of?” It treats
light as a thing with a nature of its own—a subtle substance, a stream of particles, a stuff of
which reality is made. The pattern is present in every period; it is the dominant pattern in
cosmological and physical traditions, and it recurs in metaphysical traditions whenever light is
treated as a constituent of being.


Light as relation. The fourth pattern answers the question “what does it mediate?” It treats
light as a medium, a carrier, a connection—something that holds between two things and makes
their relation possible. The pattern is present in every period; it is the dominant pattern in
11.4. Four Structural Patterns                                                                   103


optical and physical traditions, and it recurs in philosophical traditions whenever light is treated
as a condition of relation rather than a thing in relation.


  Pattern                  Question                       Typical Examples

  Experience               How is seeing possible?        Phenomenology of perception; psychol-
                                                          ogy of vision
  Metaphor                 What does it illuminate?       Mystical, poetic, and theological tradi-
                                                          tions; figures of the intelligible
  Substance                What is it made of?            Cosmological and physical traditions;
                                                          metaphysical traditions that treat light
                                                          as a constituent of being
  Relation                 What does it mediate?          Optical and physical traditions; philo-

   The table is structural, not historical. Its rows are not periods; they are patterns. A single
thinker may exemplify more than one pattern; a single period may exemplify all four. The
classification is not a claim about who held what, but about what kinds of answer have been
given.

   Remark 11.3 (On the Naming of Examples)

   The examples named in the table are not offered as a history, and the framework does not
   engage them in dialogue. Where the book mentions a tradition or a thinker, the mention
   serves two purposes only: to show that the pattern is not the invention of the framework,
   and to direct the reader who wishes the comparative treatment to the separate treatise
   in which it is given. The mention carries no justificatory weight, and no principle of this
   book depends on it.


   Remark 11.4 (The Metaphor Pattern Is Not Mere Metaphor)

   The second pattern is called “metaphor” because the word is the least misleading structural
   label for it. But the label must not be read as a claim that the pattern is ornamental or
   arbitrary. The traditions that speak of light as a figure for the divine, for truth, or for the
   good are not engaged in a decorative exercise; they are pointing to something that the
   categories of substance and relation cannot capture. The framework’s claim is that the
   pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not exhausted by the figure. The word
   “figure” names the relation between the light of experience and the light that the traditions
   call divine; it does not identify the two. The distinction is the distinction between the
   figure and the figured; it is kept throughout the part, and it is the structural ground of
   the framework’s account of the metaphor pattern.
