11.5        The Common Presupposition
The four patterns differ in what they say about light. They do not differ in what they presuppose
about it. All four take light to be something that is in space and time—a wave that propagates,
a particle that moves, a field that oscillates, a condition that is realized in a particular place and
moment. This common presupposition is so deeply embedded that it is rarely noticed. Yet it is
the source of the tension among the patterns.
      The presupposition can be stated in a sentence. Light is a thing in space-time. The sentence
is not a definition; it is a diagnosis. It states what the four patterns share, and it identifies what
the next chapter will put in question.
      If light is a thing in space-time, it must be either a substance or an accident, either a process
or a relation. And each of these categories fails to capture the whole. If light is a substance,
its being a relation—its role as the conveyor of effect—is unexplained. If it is an accident, its
independent existence is unexplained. If it is a process, its stability is unexplained. If it is a
relation, its physical reality is unexplained. The deadlock is not an accident of the four patterns;
it is the consequence of their common presupposition.

   Remark 11.5 (The Presupposition Is Not a Mistake)

   The presupposition is not a mistake. It is the natural presupposition of any inquiry that
   treats light as an object of study. The physicist who studies light as a wave or a particle is
   not wrong; the physicist is studying light as an object, and an object is what the physicist’s
   methods presuppose. The framework’s claim is not that the physicist is mistaken, but that
   the presupposition is not the only possible one, and that a philosophical treatment of light
   may require a different starting point. The next chapter proposes such a starting point.


   Remark 11.6 (The Common Presupposition Is Not the Only One)

   The common presupposition is not the only presupposition possible. The traditions that
   speak of light as transcending space and time are not committing an error; they are
   working with a different presupposition, one on which light is not a thing among things
   but a condition that precedes the distinction among things. The framework’s claim is
   not that the traditional presupposition is the correct one, and it is not that the common
   presupposition is the correct one. It is that the tension among the patterns is generated
   by the common presupposition, and that a philosophical treatment of light may require
   examining whether the common presupposition is the only one available. The framework’s
   own proposal, in the next chapter, is a proposal at a different level: it does not adopt the
   traditional presupposition, and it does not simply repeat the common one; it attempts
   to state the structural place of light in a way that does justice to both the common
   presupposition and the traditional one, without reducing either to the other.



11.6        What the Map Shows
Four observations follow from the map.
11.7. A Coherence Test                                                                             105


First observation: multiplicity is patterned. The four patterns recur across history, not
randomly, but structurally. The recurrence is not a sign of confusion; it is a sign that the question
has a structure that the answers are trying to capture.


Second observation: no pattern eliminates another. Each pattern captures an aspect of
light, and leaves another aside. The experience pattern captures light as the condition of seeing;
it leaves aside light as a thing studied. The metaphor pattern captures light as a figure of the
intelligible; it leaves aside light as a physical phenomenon. The substance pattern captures light
as a constituent of being; it leaves aside light as a relation. The relation pattern captures light
as a conveyor; it leaves aside light as a thing.


Third observation: no pattern is complete. All four are incomplete, and this very
incompleteness motivates the proposal of the next chapter. The proposal is not the elimination
of one pattern in favor of another; it is the change of level at which the question is asked.


Fourth observation: all patterns share a common presupposition. All four take light
to be something in space-time. The presupposition is the source of the tension among them, and
it is the presupposition that the next chapter will put in question.
   The fourth observation is the most important. It shows that the four patterns, for all their
differences, share a common ground—and that the common ground is what must be examined if
the tension among the patterns is to be resolved. The next chapter examines it, and proposes a
definition of light that does not rest on it.

   Remark 11.7 (The Structural Light Points Beyond Itself)

   The proposal of the next chapter will define light as a structural condition of relation. The
   definition is a structural definition: it states what light is in the framework’s vocabulary,
   and it does not claim to state what light is in itself. The structural definition is not a denial
   of what the traditions call the light of the divine; it is the recognition that the structural
   sense and the traditional sense are different senses, and that the relation between them is
   a question for another inquiry. But the structural definition is also not a self-sufficient
   account of light. The structural light is a condition of relation, and the condition of
   relation is a real condition; its reality points beyond itself to what grounds the condition.
   The framework’s claim is that the structural sense is real, invariant, and describable; it
   does not claim that the structural sense exhausts what light is, and it does not claim that
   nothing lies beyond the structural sense. The distinction is the distinction between the
   structure of light and the ground of light; it is kept throughout the part, and it is the
   structural ground of the framework’s silence on what light is in itself.



11.7      A Coherence Test
The chapter’s map is a philosophical classification, not an empirical claim. It does not depend
on any scientific theory, and it is not offered as evidence for any scientific theory. But it may be
106                                                  Chapter 11. Light: The Problem and the Map


asked whether the map is coherent with the way scientific inquiry actually works. The question
is a coherence test, not a justification; the framework’s principles are not derived from science,
and their validity does not depend on it.

   Coherence Test (not evidence, not justification)

   What this test shows. That the “relation” pattern is not the invention of the framework,
   but is present in the way modern physics treats light.
   The test. Modern physics treats light in at least three ways: as an electromagnetic
   wave, in Maxwell’s theory;a as a quantum of radiation, in Einstein’s account;b and as
   an excitation of a quantum field, in quantum field theory.c In each of the three, light is
   treated as a relation of a kind: a disturbance of a field, a carrier of energy, a conveyor of
   effect. The vocabulary of the three theories is not the vocabulary of the framework, and
   the framework does not adopt it. But the pattern is the same: light is treated as what
   holds between other things, not as a thing among them.
   What this test does not show. It does not show that the framework’s definition of light
   is correct. It does not show that physics confirms the framework, or that the framework
   confirms physics. It shows only that the “relation” pattern is present in modern physics,
   as it is present in the other periods the map has surveyed. A scientific inquiry can develop
   itself within the framework without contradiction on this point; the framework does not
   depend on the inquiry, and the inquiry does not depend on the framework.

inquiry treats the same topic.


11.8        What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
      First, the chapter does not propose a definition of light. It maps the answers that have
been given, and identifies the presupposition they share. The definition is proposed in the next
chapter, and the present chapter prepares the ground for it.
      Second, the chapter does not argue that light is the fluid element. The argument that light is
the fluid element, in the framework’s sense, is developed in the chapters that follow. The present
chapter assumes the identification only to the extent needed to state the question.
      Third, the chapter does not engage in dialogue with the traditions it mentions. Where a
tradition is named, the mention serves the two purposes stated in a remark above: to show
that the pattern is not the invention of the framework, and to direct the reader to the separate
11.9. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                   107


treatise. The comparative treatment of the traditions is a different genre from the systematic
treatment this book offers, and it is given elsewhere.
    Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have settled the question of what light is in itself. It
claims to have mapped the answers and identified the common presupposition. The next chapter
proposes a structural definition; the structural definition, too, will not claim to settle what light
is in itself. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of light and the ground of
light; it is kept throughout the part, and it is stated here as the chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Can you name a situation in which light as substance explains better than light as relation—or
vice versa? What does the answer tell you about the presupposition the four patterns share?

The next chapter proposes a philosophical definition of light that goes beyond the tension among
the patterns—not by eliminating one, but by changing the level at which the question is asked.
The definition is offered as a proposal, not as a result; it is to be assessed by its coherence and its
fruitfulness, not by its conformity to any existing theory.
Chapter 12

Light as Trans-Categorical Substance


Scope. This chapter proposes a philosophical definition of light. It argues that the four categories
available to philosophy—substance, accident, process, relation—each fail to capture light, and
that a new category is needed: the trans-categorical substance. It defines the trans-categorical
substance, argues that light is one, and states the principle that light is the condition of possibility
of relation. It answers five standard objections. Its claims are structural; where the chapter is
silent on questions of religion or mystical experience, the silence is not a denial but a recognition
that the structural description is not the whole of what can be said. Where the chapter speaks
of “substance,” “accident,” “process,” “relation,” “condition,” or “legibility,” these are structural
terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.



12.1      A Scene

Consider a window. Through it, you see the street: the passers-by, the trees, the sky. But you
do not see the glass. The glass is there—it separates the inside from the outside, it holds the
frame, it keeps out the wind. But what you see through it is not the glass; it is the street. The
glass becomes visible only at the edges, or when it is dirty, or at night, when it reflects the room
behind you. What you see, ordinarily, is not the medium but what the medium makes visible.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose someone asks you: what is the glass? You can answer
many things. It is a solid; it is made of silica; it has a certain refractive index; it can be broken,
melted, replaced. Each answer names a property of the glass. But none of them says what makes
the glass a medium—what makes it possible to see the street through it. The properties describe
the glass as a thing among things. The medium- being of the glass is not a property among its
properties; it is what makes the properties available to a viewer at all.
   The glass is not light, but the scene has the same structure. Light is the medium through
which things are seen. Like the glass, it makes vision possible without being seen (except
indirectly, by reflection or scattering). And like the glass, when we ask what it is, the ordinary
answers name its properties—its speed, its wavelength, its energy— without capturing what
makes it a medium. The medium-being of light is not a property among its properties; it is what
makes relation possible.
   The scene poses a question. What kind of thing is light, such that it can be a medium
without being a thing among things? The categories that philosophy has used to classify things—
substance, accident, process, relation—each seem to capture something about light, and each
seems to miss something. The present chapter argues that the categories are adequate for things
among things, but not for the medium through which things among things are related. A new
category is needed, and the chapter proposes one.

                                                  108
12.2. The Question                                                                                109


12.2      The Question

The previous chapter mapped the human answers to the question “what is light?” into four
structural patterns and identified the common presupposition they share: light is a thing in
space-time. The chapter argued that the presupposition is the source of the tension among the
patterns, and that the tension motivates a change of level.
   The present chapter proposes the change. It does not eliminate one pattern in favor of
another; it changes the category in which the question is asked. The question is no longer “what
kind of thing is light?” but “what kind of being is light, such that the categories of thinghood
are not adequate to it?”
   The chapter’s method is threefold. First, it exhibits the deadlock: each of the four categories,
when applied to light, captures an aspect and misses another. Second, it proposes a new category—
the trans-categorical substance—and defines it. Third, it argues that light is a trans-categorical
substance, and draws the consequence: light is the condition of possibility of relation. The
chapter ends with five standard objections and their replies, and with the limits of what the
proposal establishes.
   The proposal is offered as a proposal. It is not derived from the four patterns, and it is
not proved by them. It is offered as a category that the patterns point toward, and it is to be
assessed by its coherence with the rest of the framework and by its fruitfulness in the chapters
that follow. The reader who rejects the proposal is invited to propose a different resolution of the
deadlock; the reader who accepts it is invited to see whether the chapters that follow bear it out.


12.3      The Deadlock

The previous chapter showed that four structural patterns exist for understanding light—
experience, metaphor, substance, relation—and that none is complete. The incompleteness
is not a defect of the patterns; it is a consequence of the categories in which they are formulated.
Each pattern applies one of the available categories to light, and each category, when applied,
captures an aspect while missing another.
   The four categories, and what each misses when applied to light, are as follows.


Substance. If light is a substance—a thing with a nature of its own—then its being a relation is
unexplained. Light is what holds between the eye and the object, the source and the illuminated
surface, the emitter and the absorber. If it is a substance, it is one thing among others, and its
role as the conveyor of relation is accidental to it. But the role is not accidental; it is what light
is for in every pattern that treats it as a medium.


Accident. If light is an accident—a property of a substance—then its independent existence
is unexplained. Light propagates through empty space; it travels from the sun to the earth;
it carries energy and momentum. If it is a property of a substance, it cannot exist without
the substance whose property it is. But light does exist without such a substance, or so every
physical theory since Maxwell has held.
110                                             Chapter 12. Light as Trans-Categorical Substance


Process. If light is a process—an occurrence, a becoming— then its stability is unexplained.
Light has a constant speed; its frequency and wavelength are conserved in propagation; its
quantum character is invariant across contexts. If it is a process, it is a becoming without a
stable nature. But the stability is what every theory of light presupposes.


Relation. If light is a relation—a connection between two things—then its physical reality
is unexplained. Light carries energy; it exerts pressure; it can be absorbed and emitted; it is a
physical phenomenon in every sense. If it is a relation, it is a connection between things, and
a connection is not itself a thing. But light is a thing, in the sense that it enters into causal
interactions as a term, not merely as a connection.
      The deadlock is not an accident of the four patterns. It is the consequence of their common
presupposition: that light is a thing in space-time, and that things in space-time are classified
by the four categories. If the presupposition is correct, the deadlock is irresolvable. If the
presupposition is not the only possible one, the deadlock may be dissolved by changing the
category in which the question is asked.

   Remark 12.1 (The Deadlock Is a Structural Diagnosis)

   The deadlock is not a claim that the four categories are inadequate in general. It is a
   claim that they are inadequate for light. The categories work for things among things: a
   stone is a substance, a color is an accident, a fire is a process, a marriage is a relation.
   The claim is that light is not a thing among things, and that the categories therefore do
   not apply to it without remainder. The next section proposes a category that does apply.
   The deadlock is not a sign that light is unreal. It is a sign that the categories of thinghood
   are inadequate to what light is. The framework’s claim is that light is real, and that its
   reality is the reality of a condition of relation, not the reality of a thing in relation. A
   reader who takes the deadlock as a sign that light is unreal or unknowable has misread it;
   a reader who takes it as a sign that the categories are inadequate has read it correctly.



12.4        The Need for a New Category

   Principle 12.1 (The Trans-Categorical Character of Light)

   (A) Light goes beyond the existing philosophical categories— substance, accident, process,
   relation. A new category is needed: the trans-categorical substance.


      The principle is adopted, not proved. It is supported by the deadlock: each of the four
categories, when applied to light, captures an aspect and misses another. It would be refuted
by showing that one of the four categories, or a combination of them, captures light without
remainder. The framework does not claim that no such combination will ever be found; it claims
that none has been found, and it proposes a category that captures what the four miss.
      The new category is not a fifth category in the same series. It is not a substance, an accident,
a process, or a relation, added to the list as a fifth item. It is the condition of possibility of the
12.5. The Definition                                                                              111


list—what comes before the distinction among the four, not what comes after it. The distinction
is stated in the definition that follows.


12.5        The Definition

   Definition 12.1 (Trans-Categorical Substance)

   (A) A trans-categorical substance is a substance that comes before the distinction
   substance/accident/process/relation—not after it. That is, it is the condition of possibility
   of that distinction, not its result.


   The definition appears paradoxical. How can something come before the categories while
itself being understood through categories? The answer requires a shift in how we use language.
   The trans-categorical substance is not understood through a categorical definition, which
would place it within a category. It is understood through analogical indication and ostension.
Just as one cannot define the nature of sight by a proposition, but only by pointing to the act
of seeing, so too light can only be indicated by the structural role it plays in making relation
possible.
   When we call light a “substance,” we use the term analogically. It is not a substance among
other substances; it is the precondition for any substance to be related to another. The word
“substance” is retained because light is not an accident of something else, not a process that
occurs in something else, and not a relation between something else. It is what makes the
relating of substances possible, and in that sense it is substantial—but its substantiality is not
the substantiality of a thing among things.

   Remark 12.2 (The Structural Light and the Light of the Traditions)

   The word “light” is used in this book in a structural sense. The structural sense names the
   condition of possibility of relation. Where the traditions speak of light as the divine essence,
   or as the mode of its self-disclosure, the framework does not claim that its structural sense
   exhausts what the traditions mean. The structural sense and the traditional sense are not
   the same; the framework’s claim is that the structural sense is the sense the book needs,
   and that the book’s argument does not depend on the traditional sense.
   But the structural sense is not self-sufficient. The structural light is the condition of
   possibility of relation; the condition is real, and its reality points beyond itself to what
   grounds the condition. The traditions speak of the ground of the condition as the divine
   light; the framework does not describe the ground, and does not claim to describe it. The
   distinction is the distinction between the structure of light and the ground of light; it is
   kept throughout the book.
   What the book claims is narrow: within the book, “light” has the structural sense the
   definitions give it, and no traditional use of the word determines its sense here. What
   the book does not claim is that the structural sense is the whole of what light can mean.
   The book’s silence on the traditional sense is not a denial; it is the recognition that a
112                                          Chapter 12. Light as Trans-Categorical Substance


  structural description is not a description of the whole. The reader who wishes to compare
  the structural sense with the traditional sense is invited to do so; the comparison is a
  question for another inquiry, and the framework neither undertakes it nor forecloses it.


  Remark 12.3 (The Structural Light Is Not Self-Sufficient)

  The structural light is the condition of possibility of relation. A condition is real, and its
  reality is not in question. But a condition is not self-grounded. The condition of possibility
  of relation is the condition under which relation is legible; it is not the ground of its
  own being. The structural light points beyond itself to what grounds the condition. The
  framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described
  by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the condition and the ground
  of the condition; it is kept throughout the book.
  The traditions speak of the ground of the condition as the divine light, the source of
  all manifestation. The framework does not claim that its structural light is that source,
  and it does not claim that the source is unreal. It claims that the structural light is a
  real condition, and that the condition points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the
  structural light with the divine light is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them
  is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity
  is a question for another inquiry. What the framework claims is structural: light is the
  condition of possibility of relation, and the condition is real, and the condition is not
  self-sufficient. The claim is enough to ground the framework’s account of relation; it is not
  enough to ground an account of the divine. The framework does not claim to ground such
  an account, and it does not claim that no such account is possible.


  Remark 12.4 (How to Speak of the Trans-Categorical)

  The definition is not a stipulation that forbids all speech about light. It is a stipulation
  about the kind of speech that is appropriate. Categorical speech—“light is a substance,”
  “light is a relation”—is analogical when applied to light, and the analogy must be marked.
  Non-categorical speech—“light is the condition of possibility of relation,” “light makes
  relation legible”—is literal, because it names the structural role without placing light in a
  category. The framework uses both kinds of speech, and marks which is which.


  Remark 12.5 (Why “Substance” and Not Another Word)

  The word “substance” is retained because the alternatives are worse. To call light an
  “accident” would make it dependent on something else; to call it a “process” would make
  it a becoming without stability; to call it a “relation” would make it a connection between
  things rather than what makes connection possible. “Substance” is the least misleading of
  the four, provided its use is analogical. The framework adopts it with that qualification,
  and the qualification is part of the definition.
12.6. Light as the Condition of Possibility of Relation                                            113


   Remark 12.6 (The Definition Points Beyond Itself)

   The definition is a structural definition. It states what light is in the framework’s vocabulary,
   and it does not claim to state what light is in itself. The structural definition is not a
   denial of what light is in itself; it is the recognition that the framework’s method can
   deliver only the structural sense, and that the structural sense is not the whole of what
   light can be. The definition is precise in what it says, and it is silent in what it does not
   say. The silence is not a defect; it is the condition of the definition’s precision. The reader
   who takes the definition as a claim about what light is in itself has misread it; the reader
   who takes it as a structural description that points beyond itself has read it correctly.


   The definition is now in place. The next section argues that light is a trans-categorical
substance, and draws the consequence: light is the condition of possibility of relation.


12.6     Light as the Condition of Possibility of Relation

   Principle 12.2 (Light as Condition of Possibility of Relation)

   (T) Light is not a relation—it is the condition of possibility of relation. Without light, no
   relation is legible. But light itself is not legible—it is legible-making.


   The principle is argued, not asserted.

Argument for the Principle.       1. Every relation is between two terms.

  2. For a relation to be legible—for it to be recognizable as a relation between these terms—there
     must be something that connects the two terms.

  3. This “something” cannot itself be a relation. If it were, it would need another relation to
     connect it to the terms it relates, and that relation would need another, and so on without
     end. This is a regress.

  4. So there must be something that comes before relation—its condition of possibility.

  5. This “something” is what we call “light.”



   The argument is a reductio of the view that light is a relation. If light were a relation, the
regress would be unavoidable. The only way to avoid the regress is to hold that light is the
condition of possibility of relation, not a relation among relations.
   The principle’s force depends on the premise that legibility requires a connector. The premise
is not proved; it is what the word “legible” means in the context of the argument. A reader who
accepts the premise accepts the argument; a reader who denies the premise denies the meaning
of “legible” that the framework employs.
114                                             Chapter 12. Light as Trans-Categorical Substance


   Remark 12.7 (What “Legible” Means Here)

   “Legible” in this chapter is a structural term. It names the recognizability of a relation as
   a relation between these terms. A relation is legible when it can be read off the terms it
   relates—when the terms, in their relation, are recognizable as related. The term is not
   a metaphor for psychological comprehension; it is a structural condition. Light is what
   makes a relation legible, in this sense, and light itself is not legible in the same sense,
   because it is what makes legibility possible.

      The consequence is stated in the principle’s second sentence: light itself is not legible; it is
legible-making. The eye sees by light, but does not see light (except by reflection or scattering,
which is light as an object, not light as the condition). The relation is legible by light, but light
is not legible in the same way, because it is what makes legibility possible. This is the structure
that the definition of trans-categorical substance was meant to capture.


12.7        Objections and Replies
Five standard objections are addressed.

Objection 1: “This definition is not scientific.” Correct. The definition is philosophical.
Science says “how”; philosophy says “whatness.” The definition does not claim to replace the
physics of light; it claims to state what light is, in a sense that physics presupposes but does not
address. The reader who seeks a scientific definition will not find one here; the reader who seeks
a philosophical one will find it, and is invited to assess it by philosophical standards.

Objection 2: “This definition is vague.” Vagueness is a feature of the trans-categorical, not
a defect. Just as seeing is not definable by a category, light is not definable by a category. The
definition is precise in what it says: light comes before the distinction among the four categories,
and is the condition of possibility of relation. It is vague in what it does not say: what light is in
itself. The vagueness is not a failure to be precise; it is the precision of saying what can be said,
and not saying what cannot.

Objection 3: “This definition is not testable.” Testability is the criterion of science, not
of philosophy. Philosophy is assessed by coherence and fruitfulness, not by empirical test. The
definition is coherent with the framework’s other principles, and it is fruitful in the chapters that
follow. A reader who insists on testability is applying a criterion from one domain to another;
the framework does not adopt the criterion, and it says so.

Objection 4: “What does this definition add to science?” Nothing. It adds nothing
to science, because science is an instrument. It adds to understanding, not to computation.
The definition does not make predictions; it does not suggest experiments; it does not replace
any scientific theory. What it does is state what light is, in a sense that the scientific theories
presuppose but do not articulate. The addition is to philosophy, not to science; the reader who
seeks a scientific addition will not find one, and the framework does not claim to offer one.
12.8. Relation to Other Accounts of Light                                                       115


Objection 5: “This definition is not theological.” Correct. The definition is not theological,
and it does not claim to be. The book’s “light” is the structural condition of possibility of
relation, and the structural condition is not the divine essence. The two are distinct, and the
framework keeps them distinct. But the distinction is not a separation: the structural light is
the condition of possibility of relation, and the traditions speak of the divine light as the source
of all manifestation. The framework does not claim that the structural light is the divine light; it
claims that the structural light points beyond itself to what grounds it, and that the ground is
not described by the framework. The reader who seeks a theological account of light will not
find one here; the reader who seeks a structural account will find it, and is invited to compare it
with the theological accounts in the separate treatise.

   Remark 12.8 (The Objections Are Not Refutations)

   Each objection names a respect in which the definition is not what the objector expected.
   None of them shows that the definition is wrong. A definition can be philosophical without
   being scientific, vague without being defective, untestable without being unjustified,
   useless for science without being useless for philosophy, and structural without being
   either theological or a denial of the theological. The objections are answered, not refuted,
   because they are not refutations; they are statements of what the definition is not, and
   the framework agrees with each of them.


   Remark 12.9 (The Two Senses Are Not in Competition)

   The structural sense of “light” and the traditional sense are not rivals. They answer
   different questions: the structural sense answers “how is relation possible?”, the traditional
   sense answers “what is the source of all manifestation?” A reader can hold both without
   contradiction, provided the two are kept distinct. The book keeps them distinct, and it
   marks the distinction so that the identity is not mistaken for the pointing. The distinction
   is not a rejection of the traditional sense; it is a recognition that the book’s method can
   deliver only the structural sense, and that the traditional sense, if there is one, belongs to
   another inquiry.
   But the structural sense is not unrelated to the traditional sense. The structural light
   is the condition of possibility of relation, and the traditional light is the source of all
   manifestation; the two are structurally parallel, and the parallel is not an accident. The
   framework’s claim is structural; it does not claim to describe the traditional sense, and
   it does not claim that the two senses are the same. It claims that the structural sense
   points toward the traditional sense, and that the pointing is real. The distinction is the
   distinction between the structure of light and the ground of light; it is kept throughout the
   book, and it is the structural ground of the framework’s silence on what light is in itself.



12.8     Relation to Other Accounts of Light
The framework’s account of light is not the first philosophical account. Several traditions have
treated light as a central concept, and the reader who knows those traditions will see kinship.
116                                                Chapter 12. Light as Trans-Categorical Substance


The comparative treatment of the traditions is given in a separate treatise, and the present book
does not engage in dialogue with them. The reason is stated in the Preface: a comparison of
structures is a different genre from a systematic reconstruction, and keeping them in one volume
encouraged a misreading of the framework’s authority.1
      What is new in the framework’s definition, relative to the traditions that the separate treatise
surveys, can be stated in a sentence. In the traditions, light is either a substance (Suhrawardi),
a manifestation (Ibn Arabi), or a mode of existence (Mulla Sadra). In the framework, light
comes before the categories—not within one of them. The distinction is structural, and the
framework states it in the definition of trans-categorical substance. The reader who wishes to
see the comparison in detail is directed to the separate treatise; the present book’s argument
does not depend on it.
      But the distinction is not a negation. The traditions are right to treat light as central; the
framework’s contribution is the structural formulation of that centrality, not the denial of it.
What the traditions call the divine light is, in the framework’s vocabulary, the ground of the
structural light; the framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim to describe
it. The distinction between the two is the distinction between the structural sense and the
traditional sense; it is kept throughout the book. The reader who wishes to see the relation
between the two is directed to the separate treatise; the present book’s argument is structural,
and it does not depend on the traditional sense.


12.9        What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
      First, the chapter does not argue that light does not travel. The previous chapter used the
ordinary language of light’s travel (“from the sun to the earth”), and the present chapter has not
yet put that language in question. The question of whether light travels—and the proposal that
it does not—is the subject of the next chapter. The present chapter’s definition is compatible
with either answer; the next chapter argues for one.
      Second, the chapter does not develop the epistemological consequences of the definition. The
consequence that we are encompassed in light, and that complete knowledge of light is therefore
impossible, is developed in a later chapter. The present chapter has stated the definition; the
later chapter draws its consequences.
      Third, the chapter does not develop the relation between light and energy. The concept of
energy, and its status as a relational feature rather than a column, is developed in a still later
chapter. The present chapter has stated that light is the condition of possibility of relation; the
later chapter states what energy is, in relation to light.
      Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described what light is in itself. It claims to have
described the structural place of light, and the structural place points beyond itself to the ground
that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the structure

A Question for Reflection
If light is the condition of possibility of relation, can we speak of a “relation to light”—or is that
a category mistake? What would it mean to be related to what makes relation possible? And if
the word “light” is used in both a structural and a traditional sense, does the question of their
relation belong to philosophy, or to another inquiry?

“move”—because motion requires time, and time is a category of material manifestation. The
next chapter argues that light does not travel, but is an active connection structure.

Scope. This chapter sharpens the definition of the previous chapter. If light is a trans-categorical
substance, it cannot “move” in the ordinary sense, because motion requires time, and time is a
category of material manifestation. The chapter defines the active connection structure, argues
that light is one, proves that light does not travel, distinguishes two senses of “fluidity,” and
re-reads the three properties of light in the light of the new definition. Its claims are structural;
where the chapter is silent on questions of religion or mystical experience, the silence is not a
denial but a recognition that the structural description is not the whole of what can be said.
Where the chapter speaks of “structure,” “edge,” “activation,” “route,” “descent,” or “travel,”
these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.



13.1      A Scene

Consider a flashlight and a shadow. In a dark room, you switch on the flashlight, and a circle of
light appears on the wall. Move the flashlight slowly, and the circle moves across the wall. Move
it quickly, and the circle moves quickly. What moves?
   The shadow moves; the circle of illumination moves. But does the light move? We say “the
light moves across the wall,” and the sentence seems obvious. But consider: the light on the wall
at one moment and the light on the wall at the next moment are not the same light. They are
successive patterns of illumination, each produced by the flashlight’s relation to the wall at a
given moment. Nothing has traveled from one part of the wall to another; what has changed is
the relation between the flashlight and the wall, and the pattern of illumination reflects that
change.
   The scene can be described in two ways. In the first, the light travels: it leaves the flashlight,
crosses the room, and lands on the wall. In the second, the light does not travel: the flashlight’s
relation to the wall activates a pattern of illumination, and moving the flashlight deactivates
one pattern and activates another. The two descriptions agree on what happens—the circle of
light moves—and disagree on what “the light” is doing. In the first, the light is a traveler. In
the second, the light is a structure of illumination, whose edges are activated and deactivated
according to the flashlight’s position.
   The scene poses a question. Which description is correct? Or, better: which description is
appropriate to what light is? The ordinary language of light’s travel is so deeply embedded that
the second description sounds strange. But the strange description may be the more accurate
one, and the ordinary one may be a projection of a category that does not apply. The present
chapter argues that the second description is the correct one—not because the first is false, but
because the first imports a category (motion) that does not apply to light.

                                                118
13.2. The Question                                                                                   119


13.2      The Question
The previous chapter defined light as a trans-categorical substance: a substance that comes
before the distinction among substance, accident, process, and relation, and is the condition of
possibility of that distinction. The definition was adopted as a proposal, and the principle that
light is the condition of possibility of relation was argued.
   The present chapter asks a question that the definition raises. If light is trans-categorical,
it cannot be in any one of the four categories. But motion is one of the most obvious features
of light: it travels from the sun to the earth, from a lamp to a wall, from a star to a telescope.
Motion is the category of things that change place over time. If light moves, then light is subject
to time, and time is a category of material manifestation. If light is subject to time, light is not
trans- categorical; it is a thing among things, and the previous chapter’s definition is in question.
   The question is therefore not a small one. It is the question of whether the definition of the
previous chapter can survive the most obvious fact about light. The chapter’s answer is that it
can, and that the fact is not what it seems. Light does not travel; what travels is the pattern of
illumination, and the pattern is not the light. The light is the structure that makes the pattern
possible; the structure does not move; its edges activate.
   The chapter’s method is threefold. First, it exhibits the problem: the apparent conflict
between light’s fluidity and light’s stability. Second, it defines the active connection structure,
and argues that light is one. Third, it proves that light does not travel, distinguishes two senses
of “fluidity,” and re-reads the three properties of light in the light of the new definition. The
chapter ends with a statement of what it does not establish, and with the epistemic status of its
claims.


13.3      The Problem: Fluidity vs. Motion
The four-column framework defines the fluid element as the entity that conveys effect. The
conveyor principle, proved in the first part of the book, says that no explanation of how one fixed
element bears on another is complete without a fluid element. Light, in the framework’s sense, is
the fluid element: it is what conveys effect between identity and manifestation.
   But the word “fluid” is usually understood as “flowing” and “in motion.” A fluid is what
flows; it is what moves from one place to another. If light is fluid in this sense, it flows; if it flows,
it moves; if it moves, it travels; and if it travels, it contains time within itself.
   The argument can be stated compactly:

   1. If light moves, it travels.

   2. If light travels, time is part of what light is.

   3. But light is trans-categorical, and time is a category of material manifestation.

   4. Therefore light cannot move in the sense that requires time.

   The conclusion is not that light is motionless in the way a stone is motionless. A stone is
motionless because it is at rest; its rest is defined against motion. Light is not at rest; it is not in
120                                             Chapter 13. Light: Active Structure, Not Traveler


the category of things that can be at rest or in motion. The category of motion does not apply
to it. To say that light does not travel is not to say that it is stationary; it is to say that the
vocabulary of station and motion is not the vocabulary in which light is to be described.
      The problem, then, is this. The framework needs light to be the fluid element—the conveyor
of effect. But if fluidity means motion, light cannot be the fluid element without being subject to
time, and light cannot be subject to time without ceasing to be trans-categorical. The framework
is caught between two requirements: light must be fluid, and light must be trans-categorical.
The next section proposes a solution that satisfies both.

   Remark 13.1 (The Problem Is Not Merely Terminological)

   The problem is not merely a matter of words. One might think that the framework could
   simply redefine “fluid” to mean “conveying” rather than “flowing,” and the problem would
   disappear. But the redefinition would be empty unless it could be applied. What does
   it mean for light to convey without flowing? What kind of structure is a structure of
   conveyance that does not move? The next section answers these questions by defining the
   structure. The definition is what makes the redefinition substantive, and the definition is
   what the rest of the chapter develops.



13.4         The Solution: Active Connection Structure
The framework’s solution is to distinguish two things that are easily run together: a structure
that moves, and a structure whose edges are activated. Light is the second kind of structure, not
the first.

   Definition 13.1 (Active Connection Structure)

   (A) An active connection structure is a structure that:

       (a) always is—not that it is built and then moves;

       (b) is a structure of connection—not a path of connection;

       (c) has edges that are activated or deactivated according to rules;

       (d) itself does not move—its connections change.


      The definition is stated as a commitment ((A)). It is not derived from anything more basic;
it is the framework’s proposal for the kind of structure that light is. The definition is supported
by its fruitfulness in what follows: if light is an active connection structure, then the three
properties of light (descending, ascending, reflective) can be re-read as three directions of one
structure, the problem of fluidity vs. motion is solved, and the trans-categorical definition of the
previous chapter is preserved. If light is not such a structure, these things are not possible, and
the framework needs a different account.
      The metaphor of the scaffold is used for illustration, but the formal term is “active connection
structure.” The scaffold suggests a pre- existing framework of connection, not a physical object
13.5. Why Light Does Not Travel                                                                   121


located in space. To avoid spatial baggage, the formal term is preferred, and the metaphor is
retained only for illustration.

   Remark 13.2 (The Scaffold Metaphor)

   The word “scaffold” suggests a structure that is built and then used. But the definition
   says the structure “always is,” not that it is built. The scaffold metaphor is meant to
   evoke the idea of a pre-existing framework of connection; it is not meant to suggest a
   construction process. The reader who finds the metaphor misleading should prefer the
   formal term.

   The definition is now in place. The next principle states what light is, in terms of the
definition.

   Principle 13.1 (Light Is an Active Structure)

   (A) Light is an active structure—not a traveler. Light does not move; the edges of the
   structure, according to the rules of the realms, connect different nodes to one another.


   The principle is the framework’s identification of light with the structure of the definition. It
is not derived from the definition; it is the framework’s claim that light is what the definition
describes. The principle is supported by the same considerations as the definition: if light is an
active structure, the problem of fluidity vs. motion is solved, and the trans-categorical definition
is preserved. If light is not an active structure, the framework needs a different account, and the
reader who denies the principle is invited to propose one.

   Remark 13.3 (What “Stability” Means Here)

   The principle says that light does not move. It does not say that light is static in the way
   a stone is static. The stability of light is the stability of a structure: the structure is what
   it is, and its edges activate according to rules that are themselves stable. The rules do not
   change; the activations change. The stability is in the structure and the rules, not in the
   activations. The reader who confuses the stability of the structure with the stability of
   the activations will find the principle paradoxical; the reader who distinguishes them will
   find it clear.



13.5      Why Light Does Not Travel
The previous section defined the active connection structure and identified light with it. The
present section states the principle that follows, and proves it.

   Principle 13.2 (Non-Travel of Light)

   (T) Light does not travel.


Argument for the Principle.       1. Travel requires time.
122                                             Chapter 13. Light: Active Structure, Not Traveler


  2. Time is the order of succession of the stages by which changes are realized in a realm.

  3. Light is beyond time, because it is the condition of possibility of any relation, and time is
        a category of the related (of material manifestation).

  4. Therefore light does not travel.


      The proof depends on the premise that time is a category of material manifestation. The
premise is argued in the part of the book that treats time; here it is stated as a premise of the
argument. The reader who accepts the premise accepts the conclusion; the reader who denies it
denies the framework’s treatment of time, which is developed elsewhere.
      The proof also depends on the premise that light is the condition of possibility of any relation.
This premise is the principle of the previous chapter, argued there. The two premises together
yield the conclusion that light does not travel.

   Remark 13.4 (The Structural Light Points Beyond Itself)

   The structural light is an active connection structure; its edges activate according to rules;
   the structure itself does not travel. The structure is real, and its reality is the reality of a
   condition of relation. But the structure is not self-grounded. The condition of relation is
   the condition under which relation is legible; it is not the ground of its own being. The
   structural light points beyond itself to what grounds the structure. The framework’s claim
   is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework.
   The distinction is the distinction between the structure and the ground of the structure; it
   is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the structure as the divine light, the source of
   all manifestation. The framework does not claim that its structural light is that source,
   and it does not claim that the source is unreal. It claims that the structural light is a
   real structure, and that the structure points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the
   structural light with the divine light is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is
   free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a
   question for another inquiry. What the framework claims is structural: light is an active
   connection structure, and the structure is real, and the structure is not self-sufficient. The
   claim is enough to ground the framework’s account of relation; it is not enough to ground
   an account of the divine. The framework does not claim to ground such an account, and
   it does not claim that no such account is possible.


   Remark 13.5 (Why This Is Not a Denial of Physics)

   Physics describes light as propagating at a finite speed. The framework does not deny this.
   What the framework denies is that the propagation is a motion of light in the ordinary
   sense. Physics describes the behavior of light in time; the framework describes what light
   is. The two are compatible, because they answer different questions. The framework’s
   claim is philosophical; the physicist’s claim is empirical. Neither replaces the other, and
13.5. Why Light Does Not Travel                                                                   123


   neither contradicts the other. The reader who takes the framework’s claim as a denial
   of physics has misread it; the reader who takes it as a different kind of claim has read it
   correctly.
  The physical description is a real description at its own level. The propagation that physics
   describes is real; the speed that physics measures is real. The framework does not claim
   that the physical description is a mere appearance or a useful fiction. It claims that the
   physical description and the framework’s description answer different questions, and that
   both can be true. The distinction is the distinction between two levels of description, not
   the distinction between the real and the unreal.


   Remark 13.6 (Why This Is Not a Denial of Carriers of Light)

  The framework’s claim is that light itself —in the structural sense defined in the previous
   chapter—does not travel. The claim is not that nothing associated with light travels.
  The framework does not deny that there may be beings or entities that carry light, and
   that move as they carry it. The traditions have spoken of such carriers—angels, in the
   Islamic and Christian vocabularies, are said to be created from light, and to descend and
   ascend. Whether such carriers exist, and what their relation to structural light is, is a
   question the framework does not address, and does not foreclose. It belongs to a different
   inquiry—theology, or the interpretation of revelation—and the framework’s silence on it is
   not a denial.
  The distinction is worth stating explicitly, because the framework’s claim that “light does
   not travel” can be misread as a claim that nothing travels. The framework’s claim is
   narrower: structural light, the condition of possibility of relation, does not travel; its edges
   activate. Whether there are carriers of light that travel is a separate question, and the
   framework does not address it. The reader who identifies structural light with a carrier
   of light has conflated two different things: the condition of possibility of relation, and a
   being that bears relation. The framework distinguishes them, and marks the distinction
   so that the conflation is not made.


   Remark 13.7 (Motion Is Our Language)

  We say “light goes from the sun to the earth,” because time and motion are categories of
   material manifestation, and we can speak only within material manifestation. But light
   itself, in the structural sense, is beyond these categories. The sentence “light goes from
   the sun to the earth” is not false; it is a description of the appearance of light in the
   material realm, in the categories of the material realm. The philosophical claim is that
   the appearance is not the reality. Light does not go; the structure of light activates an
   edge between the sun and the earth, and the activation appears to us as a going. The
   appearance is real; the going is the appearance of the activation.
  This does not mean that nothing moves. It means that what moves, if anything moves, is
   not the structural light itself. If there are carriers of light—beings that bear light from
   one place to another— they may move, and their movement may be described in the
124                                            Chapter 13. Light: Active Structure, Not Traveler


    ordinary language of motion. The framework does not deny this; it does not address it.
    The framework’s claim is about the structural light, not about every entity that might be
    associated with light. The reader who reads the remark as a claim that nothing moves
    has read it too broadly; the reader who reads it as a claim about structural light has read
    it correctly.




13.6          Two Senses of “Fluidity”

The problem of the earlier section was that “fluidity” seems to imply motion, and motion is
incompatible with light’s trans-categorical character. The solution is to distinguish two senses of
“fluidity.”


          Kinetic Fluidity                     Structural Fluidity

          Having flow                          Having the capacity to convey
          Moving                               Being a medium
          Traveling                            Establishing connection
          Requires time                        Independent of time


      The first sense is the ordinary one: a fluid is what flows, and flowing requires motion and
time. The second sense is the framework’s: a fluid is what conveys, and conveying does not
require motion or time. The two senses are not the same, and the framework uses the second.
When the framework says that light is the fluid element, it means that light is what conveys
effect, not that light flows from one place to another.
      The distinction is not a verbal trick. It names two different structures. Kinetic fluidity is
a structure of matter: a liquid flows because its molecules move past one another. Structural
fluidity is a structure of relation: a medium conveys because it connects the terms it relates. The
two structures are different, and the word “fluid” applies to both only because both involve a
kind of passing. The passing of a liquid is a motion; the passing of a medium is a conveying.
The framework’s use of “fluid” is the second.

    Remark 13.8 (Why Not Use a Different Word)

    The framework retains the word “fluid” because it is the word the four-column framework
    uses for the second column. To call the column something else would require a revision of
    the framework’s vocabulary, and the revision would obscure the connection between the
    present chapter and the chapters that introduced the column. The word is retained with
    a stipulation: “fluid” in this book means “conveying,” not “flowing.” The stipulation is
    part of the definition, and the reader who remembers it will find the framework’s use of
    the word consistent.
13.7. Fluidity as Role, Not Essence                                                             125


13.7      Fluidity as Role, Not Essence

The distinction between kinetic and structural fluidity raises a further question. Is structural
fluidity a property of light—something light has in itself—or is it a role that light plays in the
framework’s analysis?


   Principle 13.3 (Structural Fluidity)

   (T) “Fluid element” is an analytical role—not an ontological essence. Light, in the four-
   column framework, plays the role of conveyor—so it is the fluid element. This role is
   independent of whether light moves or not.


   The principle follows from the context-dependence principle, stated in the first part of the
book: the fixedness or fluidity of an element depends on the cognitive context, not on the
element’s essence. Light is the fluid element in the framework’s analysis because it plays the
role of conveyor. It would play this role whether or not it moved; the role is analytical, not
ontological.
   The principle is important for the same reason that the context- dependence principle is
important. It blocks the inference from “light is the fluid element” to “light is essentially fluid.”
The first is a claim about the framework’s analysis; the second is a claim about light’s nature. The
framework makes the first claim and not the second. Light is what it is, in the trans-categorical
sense of the previous chapter; its being the fluid element is the framework’s way of locating it in
the analysis, not a property it has in itself.


   Remark 13.9 (The Analytical and the Ontological)

   The distinction between analytical role and ontological essence is one of the framework’s
   recurring distinctions. It is the distinction between the four columns, which are analytical
   roles, and the seven realms, which are ontological levels. It is the distinction between
   the fixedness of an element in a context and the invariance of an identity in its realm.
   The present principle applies the distinction to the fluid element: light plays the role of
   conveyor, and the role does not make light essentially fluid. The reader who keeps the
   distinction in mind will find the framework’s claims about light easier to follow.




13.8      Descent vs. Travel

A further distinction is needed, between two ways in which light can be said to “go” from a
higher level to a lower one. The two are easily confused, and the confusion is the source of the
apparent conflict between the framework’s claim that light does not travel and the ordinary
language of light’s descent.
126                                            Chapter 13. Light: Active Structure, Not Traveler


             Descent                         Travel

             Structural                      Kinetic
             In the levels of being          In space
             Simultaneous                    Gradual
             Does not require time           Requires time
             Light descends                  Light travels


      Descent is structural: it is the appearance of light in the mode of a lower realm, without the
light going from one realm to another. Travel is kinetic: it is the motion of a thing from one
place to another, requiring time and space. The framework’s claim is that light descends, not
that it travels. The descent is not a motion; it is an appearance.

   Principle 13.4 (Descent Is Structural)

   (A) The descent of light is not its motion from a higher level to a lower one, but its
   appearance in the mode of the lower level. Light in each realm appears in the mode of
   that realm—without going from one realm to another.


      The principle is the framework’s account of how light is present in the lower realms. It is
not derived from the previous principles; it is a further commitment, and it is supported by the
non-necessity of downward passage, argued in the part of the book that treated the realms. If
light does not have to pass through every realm between, its presence in a lower realm must
be explained by something other than passage. The principle explains it by appearance: light
appears in the mode of the lower realm, without going from one realm to another.

   Remark 13.10 (Descent and the Non-Necessity of Downward Passage)

   The principle is a special case of the non-necessity of downward passage. The general
   principle says that an identity’s presence in a lower realm does not require passage through
   every realm between. The present principle says the same for light: light’s presence in a
   lower realm does not require passage through every realm between. The two are related
   but distinct: the first concerns identities, the second concerns light. The reader who has
   followed the argument to this point will see that the two are instances of a single structural
   claim, applied to two kinds of entity.
   The structural descent is not a denial of direct action. The descent describes the structural
   mode in which light is present in a lower realm; it does not claim that the mode is
   the only possible mode of presence. If there is a direct action that comes from beyond
   the architecture, it is not described by the framework, and it is not denied by it. The
   framework’s claim is structural: the descent is the mode of appearance of light in a lower
   realm, and the mode does not exhaust the possible modes of presence. The distinction
   is the distinction between the structure of descent and the ground of presence; it is kept
   throughout the book.
13.9. The Three Properties Re-Read                                                             127


13.9      The Three Properties Re-Read
The previous chapter mentioned, in passing, that light has three properties: descending, ascending,
and reflective. The present section re-reads these properties in the light of the active-structure
definition.
   The re-reading is stated in a table.

  Property      Old Reading                          New Reading

  Descending    Light goes from identity to mani- The structure-edge from identity to mani-
                festation                            festation is activated
  Ascending     Light returns from manifestation     The structure-edge from manifestation to
                to identity                          identity is activated
  Reflective    Light flows among manifestations     The structure-edge between two manifes-
                                                     tations is activated

   The old reading uses the language of motion: “goes,” “returns,” “flows.” The new reading
uses the language of activation: “the structure-edge is activated.” The two readings describe
the same phenomena; they differ in the category they use. The old reading uses the category of
motion, which does not apply to light. The new reading uses the category of activation, which
does.
   The three properties are not three kinds of light, and not three modes of light. A kind or a
mode would be a separate entity; a property is an aspect of the same entity. The three properties
are three directions of a single structure: the edge from identity to manifestation, the edge from
manifestation to identity, and the edge between two manifestations. The structure is one; the
edges are three; the directions are three.

   Remark 13.11 (The Three Properties Are Not Three Things)

   The reader who has followed the argument to this point may wonder whether the three
   properties are three separate entities. They are not. They are three directions of one
   structure, distinguished by what they connect. The descending edge connects identity
   and manifestation; the ascending edge connects manifestation and identity; the reflective
   edge connects manifestation and manifestation. The structure is one; the edges are three;
   the directions are three. The unity of the structure is what makes the three properties
   properties of one thing, not three things.

   Remark 13.12 (The Cycle of Light)

   The three properties together form a cycle: an identity manifests, and its manifestation
   refers back to it, and manifestations are related to one another. The cycle is not described
   as having a beginning in time; the question of its time is taken up in the part of the book
   that treats time. Here the cycle is stated as a structural feature of the active connection
   structure, not as a temporal process. The reader who reads the cycle as a temporal process
   has misread it; the reader who reads it as a structural feature has read it correctly.
128                                            Chapter 13. Light: Active Structure, Not Traveler


   Remark 13.13 (The Cycle Points Beyond Itself)

   The cycle of light is a structural feature of the active connection structure. It describes
   the way in which the structure’s edges activate and deactivate, and the way in which
   the activations form a coherent whole. The cycle is real, and its reality is the reality
   of the structure. But the cycle is not self-grounded. The cycle is the cycle of an active
   connection structure; it is not the ground of the structure. The structural light, and its
   cycle, point beyond themselves to what grounds the structure. The framework’s claim is
   that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework.
   The distinction is the distinction between the cycle and the ground of the cycle; it is kept
   throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the cycle as the divine light, the source of all
   manifestation. The framework does not claim that its cycle of light is that source, and it
   does not claim that the source is unreal. It claims that the cycle is a real structure, and
   that the structure points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the cycle with the divine
   light is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework
   takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



13.10        A Coherence Test
The chapter’s claim is that light does not travel, but is an active connection structure. The claim
is philosophical, not empirical. But it may be asked whether the claim is coherent with the way
physics describes light. The question is a coherence test, not a justification.

   Coherence Test (not evidence, not justification)

   What this test shows. That the framework’s claim that light does not travel is not at
   odds with the way physics describes light’s propagation.
   The test. Physics describes light as propagating at a finite speed: approximately 3 × 108
   meters per second in vacuum. This description is a description of light’s behavior in time.
   It does not say what light is; it says how light behaves. The framework’s claim is about
   what light is: light is an active connection structure, not a traveler. The two claims are
   about different things. Physics describes the behavior; the framework describes the being.
   A description of behavior is compatible with a description of being that does not use the
   category of motion, just as a description of a person’s walk is compatible with a description
   of the person’s identity that does not use the category of walking.
   What this test does not show. It does not show that the framework’s claim is correct.
   It does not show that physics confirms the framework, or that the framework confirms
   physics. It shows only that the framework’s claim and the physicist’s claim can both be
   true, because they answer different questions. A reader who takes the framework’s claim
   as a denial of physics has misread it; a reader who takes it as a different kind of claim has
   read it correctly.

      The test is offered at exactly the strength stated. It is not a justification of the framework,
13.11. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                     129


and it is not a derivation of the framework’s claim from physics. It is a check on coherence: a
demonstration that the framework’s claim is not at odds with the way at least one contemporary
inquiry describes the same topic.


13.11      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
   First, the chapter does not develop the epistemological consequences of the claim that light
does not travel. The consequences—that we are encompassed in light, and that complete
knowledge of light is therefore impossible—are developed in the next chapter. The present
chapter has stated the structural claim; the next chapter draws its epistemological consequences.
   Second, the chapter does not develop the relation between light and energy. The concept
of energy, and its status as a relational feature rather than a column, is developed in a later
chapter. The present chapter has stated that light is an active structure; the later chapter states
what energy is, in relation to light.
   Third, the chapter does not develop the full account of the three properties. The properties
are named, and their re-reading is stated, but the detailed treatment of each—how the descending
edge is distinct from the ascending edge, how the reflective edge relates to the other two, how
the three together form the cycle of light—is deferred to a later part of the book. The present
chapter has introduced the re-reading; the later part develops it.
   Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described what light is in itself. It claims to have
described the structural place of light, and the structural place points beyond itself to the ground
that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the structure
of light and the ground of light; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is stated here as the
chapter’s explicit limit.
