A Question for Reflection
If light does not travel, how can we speak of “the light of the sun reaching us”—is this a category
mistake? If it is, what does the sentence “the light of the sun reaches us” actually say? Does it
say something false, or something true in a language that is not the language of the framework?
130                                          Chapter 13. Light: Active Structure, Not Traveler


What would it mean to translate it into the framework’s language? And if there are carriers
of light that travel, would their traveling be a counterexample to the framework’s claim, or a
different kind of claim altogether?

The next chapter draws the epistemological consequences of the definition. If light is an active
structure, and if we are in relation to light in every act of cognition, then we are encompassed in
light—not floating in it. The consequence is that complete knowledge of light is impossible, and
the chapter states why.
Chapter 14

The Place of Light


Scope. This chapter locates light in the framework’s architecture. It argues that light is the
medium of relation, not a term of relation—it belongs to the second of the two pairs into which
the four columns divide. It argues that light is the foundational fluid element, appearing in the
mode of each cognitive apparatus. And it argues that we are encompassed in light, not floating in
it, with the consequence that complete knowledge of light is impossible. Its claims are structural;
where the chapter is silent on questions of religion or mystical experience, the silence is not a
denial but a recognition that the structural description is not the whole of what can be said.
Where the chapter speaks of “medium,” “term,” “apparatus,” “encompassment,” or “window,”
these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.



14.1      A Scene

Consider a fish in water. The fish swims; the water surrounds it; the fish breathes the water; the
water is the medium in which the fish moves and lives. But the fish does not know the water
as we know it. The fish has no standpoint outside the water from which to see the water as an
object. The water is not one of the things the fish encounters; it is the condition under which the
fish encounters things at all. If the fish could speak, it would not say “here is water”; it would
say “here is what there is”—and the water would be invisible in its speech.
   Now consider us, in relation to light. We see by light; we do not see light. Light is the
medium in which things appear to us, but it is not one of the things that appear. When we
study light, we study it as an object—as a wave, a particle, a field—and in doing so we treat it
as one of the things that appear. But the light by which we study it is the light we are trying to
study, and that light is not one of the things that appear. It is the condition under which things
appear.
   The fish and the water, we and the light: the two scenes have the same structure. In both,
a medium makes appearance possible without itself appearing. The medium is not one of the
things; it is what makes the things possible. And the relation between the knower and the
medium is not the relation between the knower and an object; it is the relation between the
knower and the condition of the knower’s objects.
   The scene poses three questions. First: where does light stand in the framework’s architecture?
Is it a term of relation, alongside the identities and manifestations it relates, or is it the medium
of relation, belonging to a different level? Second: if light is the medium, how does it relate to the
various apparatuses of cognition—the sciences, the arts, the ordinary practices of understanding—
that study the world? Third: what is our relation to light, if we are in it as the fish is in water?
The present chapter answers these questions.

                                                 131
132                                                                Chapter 14. The Place of Light


14.2       The Question
The previous chapter argued that light is an active connection structure, not a traveler. It defined
the structure, identified light with it, proved that light does not travel, and re-read the three
properties of light (descending, ascending, reflective) in the light of the definition. The definition
is now in place.
      The present chapter asks a further question: where does light stand, in the framework’s
architecture? The question is not about what light is; the previous chapters have answered
that. It is about where light belongs—which column, which pair of columns, which level of the
hierarchy of cognitive apparatuses, and what our relation to it is.
      Three aspects of the question must be distinguished.

The structural aspect. The four columns are divided into two pairs: fixed elements with
context, and dynamics with fluid element. Which pair does light belong to? Is light a term of
relation, alongside the fixed elements, or is it the medium of relation, belonging to the other
pair? The answer locates light in the analytical framework.

The ontological aspect. Light is the fluid element. But there are many fluid elements—
language, information, force, chemical bonds, metabolic processes. Is light one of these, or is
it the foundational fluid element of which the others are specific manifestations? The answer
locates light in the hierarchy of cognitive apparatuses.

The epistemic aspect. What is our relation to light? Do we stand outside it and study it
as an object, or are we encompassed in it? The answer locates us in relation to light, and has
consequences for what we can know about it.
      The chapter treats the three aspects in turn. It argues that light belongs to the second pair,
that it is the foundational fluid element, and that we are encompassed in it. The three arguments
are distinct, and each is offered at its own strength.


14.3       The Two Pairs of Columns
The four columns are not four isolated roles. They form two structural pairs, and the pairing is
not arbitrary. It follows from the structure of relation itself.

       Pair             Columns                          Role

       Pair 1           Fixed elements + Context         The terms of the relation: what is re-
                                                         lated, and where.
       Pair 2           Dynamics + Fluid element         The medium of the relation: how the
                                                         relation works, and by what it is con-
                                                         veyed.

      The two pairs answer two different questions. Pair 1 answers: what is related? Pair 2 answers:
how is the relation carried? Neither pair answers the question of the other. Without Pair 1,
there is nothing to relate; without Pair 2, there is no relation to speak of.
14.4. Light Belongs to Pair 2                                                                  133


Pair 1: fixed elements and context. Pair 1 determines the terms of the relation. Without
fixed elements, there is nothing to relate. Without context, the fixed elements have no frame
of reference. The two are mutually dependent: fixed elements without context are undefined;
context without fixed elements is empty. The pair is the structural condition of there being terms
to relate.

Pair 2: dynamics and fluid element. Pair 2 determines the medium of the relation. Without
dynamics, the fluid element is unordered. Without fluid element, dynamics is meaningless—there
is nothing for the rule to govern. The two are mutually dependent: fluid element without
dynamics is undirected; dynamics without fluid element is empty. The pair is the structural
condition of the relation’s being carried.

   Principle 14.1 (Pair 2 as the Medium of Relation)

   (A) Dynamics and fluid element form the medium of the relation. Without fluid element,
   dynamics is meaningless. Without dynamics, fluid element is unordered. The two are
   mutually dependent.

   The principle is adopted, not proved. It is supported by the structure of relation itself: any
relation between two terms must have a medium through which the relation is established, and
the medium is distinct from the terms. It would be refuted by showing that a relation can hold
without a medium, which the conveyor principle (stated and proved in the first part of the book)
denies.

   Remark 14.1 (Why This Pairing?)

   The pairing follows from the structure of relation. Every relation has two aspects: (1)
   terms—what is related, which are the fixed elements situated in a context; (2) medium—
   how the relation is established and governed, which is the fluid element governed by
   dynamics. The four columns are the analytical decomposition of these two aspects. Pair 1
   gives the terms; Pair 2 gives the medium. There is no third aspect, and no further pair.

   The pairing is now in place. The next section draws the consequence for light.


14.4         Light Belongs to Pair 2
Light is the fluid element. It follows that light belongs to Pair 2, not Pair 1. The consequence is
not trivial; it has three implications.

First implication: light is not a term of relation. Light is the medium of relation, not
one of the terms related. It is not what is related; it is what conveys the relation. When we say
that light connects an identity and its manifestation, we do not mean that light is a third term
alongside the identity and the manifestation; we mean that light is the medium in which the
connection is carried. The distinction is the distinction between being in a relation and being
the relation’s medium.
134                                                               Chapter 14. The Place of Light


Second implication: light is inseparable from dynamics. Without the rules of the
realms—the governing dynamics—light is unordered. The rules determine what connections light
carries, in what modes, under what conditions. Light without dynamics is a capacity to convey
with nothing to convey and no rule to convey it by. The two must be understood together.

Third implication: light is the condition of possibility of the relation between fixed
elements and context. Without light, the fixed elements are disconnected islands, and the
context is an empty frame. The two terms are not related; they are merely co-present. Light is
what makes the relation possible—not the relation itself, but its condition.

   Remark 14.2 (Light Is Not the Relation)

   The third implication must be read carefully. Light is the condition of possibility of
   relation, not the relation itself. The relation between an identity and its manifestation is
   one thing; the light that makes the relation legible is another. The relation is between two
   terms; the light is what makes the relation legible. To identify the two is the mistake that
   the previous chapter argued against, when it distinguished light as condition of possibility
   from light as relation.

      The three implications together locate light in the analytical framework. Light is the medium
of relation, not a term of relation; it is inseparable from dynamics; and it is the condition of
possibility of the relation between fixed elements and context. The next section turns from the
analytical framework to the hierarchy of cognitive apparatuses.


14.5       The Hierarchy of Cognitive Apparatuses
The framework distinguishes two kinds of cognitive apparatus: primary and secondary. The
distinction is structural, not evaluative: neither kind is more fundamental than the other in itself.
What distinguishes them is the generality of their fixed elements and the foundational character
of their fluid elements.

   Definition 14.1 (Primary Cognitive Apparatus)

   (A) A primary cognitive apparatus is one whose fixed elements are general and whose
   fluid element is foundational. Its dynamics has a general formalization, and its context is
   foundational.

   Definition 14.2 (Secondary Cognitive Apparatus)

   (A) A secondary cognitive apparatus is one whose fixed elements are specific and whose
   fluid element is derived. Its dynamics has specific rules, and its context is composite.

      The two definitions are structural. They distinguish two kinds of apparatus by the generality
of their fixed elements and the foundational character of their fluid elements. The distinction is
not a ranking; it is a classification.
      The hierarchy of apparatuses is as follows.
14.6. Light as the Foundational Fluid Element                                                    135


     Level            Apparatus              Fluid Element            Dynamics

     Ontological      Seven realms           Light (foundational)     Rules of the realms
     Primary          General cognition      Light (foundational)     General rules
     Secondary        Specific cognition     Derived conveyors        Specific rules


   The table distinguishes three levels. At the ontological level, light is the foundational fluid
element, and the rules of the seven realms govern its operation. At the primary level, a cognitive
apparatus whose fixed elements are general and whose fluid element is foundational operates
under general rules. At the secondary level, a cognitive apparatus whose fixed elements are
specific operates with derived conveyors under specific rules.

   Remark 14.3 (“Primary” Does Not Mean “More Fundamental”)

   The word “primary” is a structural label, not an evaluative one. Primary apparatuses
   are those whose fixed elements are general; secondary apparatuses are those whose fixed
   elements are specific. The distinction is not a ranking of importance. A primary apparatus
   is not more fundamental than a secondary one; it is simply more general. The ontological
   level, at which the seven realms and the foundational light are defined, is more fundamental
   than either, and it is not itself an apparatus.




14.6     Light as the Foundational Fluid Element

The hierarchy of apparatuses raises a question. Light is the fluid element, but there are many
fluid elements. Is light one of them, or is it the foundational one, of which the others are specific
manifestations?

   Principle 14.2 (Light as Foundational Fluid Element)

   (A) Light, in the framework’s sense, is not one of the fluid elements—it is the foundational
   fluid element that appears in the mode of each apparatus. What appears as a chemical
   bond, a metabolic process, or a flow of water in secondary apparatuses are specific
   conveyors— structural analogues of foundational light, manifested in their respective
   apparatuses.


   The principle is adopted, not proved. It is supported by the structural parallel between light
and the specific conveyors: in each case, the conveyor is what carries effect between the fixed
elements of its apparatus, and the conveyor appears in the mode of the apparatus in which it
operates. It would be refuted by showing that a specific conveyor cannot be understood as a
manifestation of foundational light—that is, by showing that the specific conveyor has features
that foundational light cannot take in any mode.
136                                                               Chapter 14. The Place of Light


   Principle 14.3 (Appearance in the Mode of the Apparatus)

   (T) Light in each cognitive apparatus appears in the mode of that apparatus—without
   becoming many lights. Just as light in each realm takes the color of that realm, light in
   each apparatus takes the color of that apparatus.


Argument for the Principle.       1. Light is the foundational fluid element, appearing in the mode
        of each apparatus.

  2. An appearance in the mode of an apparatus is an appearance shaped by the apparatus’s
        specific character: the fixed elements it relates, the rules that govern it, the context in
        which it operates.

  3. The shaping does not multiply the light. The color that a light takes in a realm is not a
        new light; it is the same light in a different mode. So too, the mode that light takes in an
        apparatus is not a new light; it is the same light in a different mode.

  4. Hence light in each apparatus appears in the mode of that apparatus, without becoming
        many lights.


      The argument depends on the analogy between the color of light in a realm and the mode of
light in an apparatus. The analogy is not a proof; it is a structural parallel. The reader who
accepts the parallel accepts the argument; the reader who denies it denies the framework’s way
of speaking of light’s appearance in diverse contexts.

   Remark 14.4 (The Analogue, Not the Identity)

   What appears as a chemical bond, a metabolic process, or a flow of water in secondary
   apparatuses are not light in the framework’s sense. They are structural analogues of light,
   manifested in their respective apparatuses. The distinction is important: to say that light
   is the foundational fluid element is not to say that every specific conveyor is light. It is to
   say that every specific conveyor is what foundational light looks like when it appears in
   the mode of a specific apparatus.


   Remark 14.5 (The Foundational Fluid Element Points Beyond Itself)

   Light is the foundational fluid element, and the framework’s claim is that this foundation is
   real, invariant, and describable. But the foundational fluid element is not self-grounded. It
   is the foundation of the hierarchy of apparatuses; it is not the ground of its own being. The
   foundational light points beyond itself to what grounds the hierarchy. The framework’s
   claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the
   framework. The distinction is the distinction between the foundational light and the
   ground of the foundational light; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the foundational light as the divine light, the source
   of all manifestation. The framework does not claim that its foundational light is that
14.7. Encompassment in Light                                                                     137


   source, and it does not claim that the source is unreal. It claims that the foundational
   light is a real foundation, and that the foundation points beyond itself. The reader who
   identifies the foundational light with the divine light is free to do so; the reader who
   distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because
   the identity is a question for another inquiry.



14.7        Encompassment in Light
The hierarchy of apparatuses locates light ontologically. The present section turns from ontology
to epistemology. What is our relation to light, given that light is the foundational fluid element?
   The framework distinguishes two possible relations: floating in a medium and being encom-
passed by it. The distinction is structural, not metaphorical.

            Floating                             Encompassed

            Being in an external environment     Being taken up into
            Preserving full independence         Without full independence
            A fish in water                      Air in the lungs
            The environment is external          The environment is pervading

   Floating is a relation of exteriority: the medium surrounds the thing, but the thing is
independent of it. A fish floats in water; it is in the water, but the water is not in the fish. The
medium is external. The fish preserves its independence from the medium.
   Encompassment is a relation of pervasion: the medium is not merely around the thing, but
in it, and the thing is taken up into the medium. Encompassment is a relation of dependence
without exteriority.

   Principle 14.4 (Encompassment in Light)

   (A) We are not floating in light—we are encompassed in light. Light has taken us up—not
   that we have taken up light.

   The principle is adopted, not proved. It is supported by the argument that follows: light is
the condition of possibility of relation, and we are in relation in every act of cognition, so we are
in light in every act of cognition. The support is stated below; the principle is offered at that
strength.

Argument for Encompassment.         1. Light is the condition of possibility of relation (from the
      previous chapter).

  2. We, in every act of cognition, are in relation.

  3. Therefore we, in every act of cognition, are in light.

  4. But this “being in light” is not “being in an external environment”—it is “being taken up
      by the condition of possibility.”
138                                                              Chapter 14. The Place of Light


  5. Therefore we are encompassed in light—not floating in it.



      The argument turns on step (4). Steps (1)–(3) show that we are in light whenever we are in
relation; step (4) shows that this “in” is not the “in” of being in an environment. The distinction
is the distinction between the fish’s water and the air in the lungs. The fish is in the water,
but the water is external; we are in light, and light is what makes our cognition possible. The
relation is not exteriority; it is encompassment.

   Remark 14.6 (Encompassment Is Not Identity)

   To say that we are encompassed in light is not to say that we are light. The air in the
   lungs is not the lungs; the fish in water is not the water. We are encompassed in light as
   the light is in us, not as the light is us. The distinction is the distinction between being
   taken up into a condition and being identified with the condition. The framework affirms
   the first, not the second.


   Remark 14.7 (Encompassment Is Not a Prison)

   The encompassment is not a restriction on knowledge; it is the condition under which
   knowledge is possible. The fish is not imprisoned in the water; the water is what makes
   the fish’s motion possible. We are not imprisoned in light; the light is what makes our
   cognition possible. The framework’s claim is that the encompassment is structural: it
   belongs to the relation between a finite subject and the condition of its cognition. The
   condition is not an obstacle; it is the ground of the possibility of cognition. The reader
   who takes the encompassment as a limitation has misread it; the reader who takes it as
   the condition of possibility of cognition has read it correctly.
   But the encompassment is not self-sufficient. The condition of cognition points beyond
   itself to what grounds the condition. The light that encompasses us is the structural
   condition of relation; it is not the ground of its own being. The structural light points
   beyond itself to what grounds it; and what grounds it is not described by the framework.
   The distinction is the distinction between the encompassment and the ground of the
   encompassment; it is kept throughout the book.



14.8       The First Consequence: Impossibility of Complete Knowl-
           edge of Light
The principle of encompassment has consequences. The first is that we cannot know light
completely.

   Principle 14.5 (Impossibility of Complete Knowledge of Light)

   (T) We cannot know light completely—because we are encompassed in it. Complete
   knowledge requires standing outside the object of knowledge—and we cannot stand outside
14.8. The First Consequence: Impossibility of Complete Knowledge of Light                          139


   light.


Argument for the Principle.       1. Complete knowledge requires standing outside the object of
     knowledge, from a standpoint from which the object can be surveyed as a whole.

  2. We are encompassed in light. To stand outside light would be to stand outside the condition
     of our own cognition.

  3. We cannot stand outside the condition of our own cognition.

  4. Therefore we cannot know light completely.


   The argument is a reductio of the claim to complete knowledge of light. The claim is
impossible, not because we lack the resources, but because the relation between the knower and
the known is not the relation of exteriority that complete knowledge would require. We can know
light in its modes—as it appears in this or that apparatus, under this or that condition—but we
cannot know light as it is in itself, because the “in itself” would require a standpoint we cannot
occupy.

   Remark 14.8 (The Same Structure as the Impossibility of Super-Identity)

   The principle has the same structure as the impossibility of super- identity, which was
   argued in the first part of the book. In both cases, the impossibility is epistemic: we cannot
   know all of something, because our relation to it is partial. In the case of super-identity, the
   partiality is the partiality of perspectives on an identity; in the case of light, the partiality
   is the encompassment of the knower in the condition of knowledge. The two are related
   but distinct: super-identity concerns identities in their manifestations; encompassment
   concerns light as the condition of cognition.
   The impossibility is the impossibility of the finite subject. It is not an impossibility as such.
   The framework does not claim that no subject whatsoever can know light completely; it
   claims that no finite subject can. The distinction is the distinction between the limits of
   finite inquiry and the limits of what is; it is kept throughout the book. The object may
   be fully known to a subject that is not finite; the framework’s claim is about the finite
   subject, not about the object. The framework’s silence on the infinite subject is not a
   denial of its possibility; it is the recognition that the framework’s method is the method
   of finite inquiry.


   Remark 14.9 (What We Can Know)

   The principle does not say that we cannot know light at all. It says that we cannot
   know light completely. What we can know is the modes of light—how it appears in this
   apparatus, under this condition, with these effects. We can study light as an object, in
   the ways physics studies it; we can study light as a condition, in the ways philosophy
   studies it. What we cannot do is survey light as a whole, from a standpoint outside it.
140                                                               Chapter 14. The Place of Light


    The partial knowledge is real knowledge; the complete knowledge is impossible.
    The partial knowledge is not a deficient form of complete knowledge; it is the form of
    knowledge available to a finite subject, and it is real. The modes of light are real, and the
    knowledge of the modes is real. The incompleteness of the knowledge is not a failure of
    the knowledge; it is the structural character of the knowledge available to a finite subject.
    The framework’s claim is that the partial knowledge is real, and that the completeness is
    impossible for the finite subject. The distinction is the distinction between the partial and
    the complete, not the distinction between the real and the unreal.



14.9       The Second Consequence: Light as the Only Window

The second consequence of encompassment is that light is the only structural window through
which what lies beyond the material realm reaches us.

    Principle 14.6 (Light as the Structural Window)

    (A) Within the structure of finite cognition, light is the only window through which what
    lies beyond the material realm reaches us—and that too in its descended version in material
    manifestation.

      The principle follows from the non-necessity of downward passage, stated in the part of
the book that treated the realms. If an identity’s presence in a lower realm does not require
passage through every realm between, then the identity’s relation to the lower realm is carried by
something other than passage. That something is light. The light that reaches us from a higher
level is the appearance of the higher level in the mode of our own realm; it is not the higher level
itself.

    Remark 14.10 (The Window Is a Structural Description)

    The word “window” is a structural metaphor. It does not mean that light is transparent;
    it means that light is what allows the higher levels to be legible from within the lower.
    Just as a window allows the outside to be seen from within, light allows the higher levels
    to be inferred from within the lower. The inference is not direct knowledge; it is what the
    next section distinguishes from knowledge.
    The principle is a structural description, not a claim of exclusivity. The framework does
    not claim that no other access to what lies beyond the material realm is possible; it claims
    that, within the structure of finite cognition, light is the window. Whether there are other
    modes of access—revelation, intuition, mystical experience—is a question the framework
    does not address, and does not foreclose. The framework’s claim is structural: within
    the structure of finite cognition, the window is light. The distinction is the distinction
    between the structural window and the modes of access; it is kept throughout the book.
14.10. The Third Consequence: Estimate, Not Knowledge                                          141


14.10        The Third Consequence: Estimate, Not Knowledge
The third consequence of encompassment is that what we have of higher levels is estimate, not
knowledge.

   Principle 14.7 (Estimate, Not Complete Knowledge)

   (T) We can estimate, from the properties of light in material manifestation, something
   about higher levels—but our estimate is not complete knowledge. The estimate is real
   knowledge at its own level; it is not complete knowledge of the source.


   The principle is a consequence of the two previous ones. If we are encompassed in light, we
cannot know light completely; if light is the structural window to higher levels, then what we
have of higher levels is what we have of light, in its descended version. And what we have of
light is not complete knowledge; it is estimate. The estimate may be more or less adequate; it
may be refined by further study; but it does not become complete knowledge by being refined. It
remains estimate.
   But the estimate is not nothing. It is real knowledge at its own level. The distinction is the
distinction between the completeness of knowledge and the reality of knowledge; the framework’s
claim is that the estimate is real, and that the completeness is impossible for the finite subject.
The estimate is the form of knowledge available to the finite subject about what lies beyond the
structural window; it is not a deficient form of complete knowledge, and it is not a substitute for
complete knowledge. It is what it is: an estimate, at the level at which the finite subject can
know.

   Remark 14.11 (Estimate and Inference)

   Estimate is not the same as inference. An inference proceeds from premises to a conclusion
   by a rule; an estimate proceeds from what is given to something beyond what is given,
   by analogy and indication. The two are related: inference can be used within estimation,
   to make the estimation sharper. But the estimation itself is not inference; it is a way of
   speaking about what is given, that acknowledges its partiality.
   The estimate points beyond itself. What the estimate estimates is not contained in the
   estimate; it is the source that the estimate reaches toward. The estimate is real, and its
   reality is the reality of a structural reach toward what lies beyond the structure. The
   framework’s claim is that the reach is real, and that what is reached is not described by
   the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the estimate and the estimated;
   it is kept throughout the book.



14.11        A Coherence Test
The chapter’s central claim is that light is the foundational fluid element, appearing in the mode
of each cognitive apparatus. The claim is philosophical, not empirical. But it may be asked
whether the claim is coherent with the way different domains of inquiry actually work. The
142                                                                Chapter 14. The Place of Light


question is a coherence test, not a justification.

   Coherence Test (not evidence, not justification)

   What this test shows. That the hierarchy of cognitive apparatuses—primary and
   secondary, with light as the foundational fluid element—is not at odds with the way at
   least some established inquiries describe their own structure.
   The test. Consider three inquiries: physics, chemistry, and ecology. Physics studies
   general fixed elements (matter, fields) under general rules (the laws of physics). Chemistry
   studies specific fixed elements (atoms, molecules) under specific rules (the laws of chemical
   combination); its fluid element—the chemical bond—is a specific conveyor, not the general
   conveyor that physics studies. Ecology studies specific fixed elements (species, populations)
   under specific rules (the laws of ecosystem dynamics); its fluid elements—flows of water,
   air, energy—are specific conveyors, not the general conveyor that physics studies.
   What the test shows (continued). In each case, the apparatus has a fixed element,
   a fluid element, a dynamics, and a context. The fluid element differs in generality: in
   physics it is general; in chemistry and ecology it is specific. The specific fluid elements are
   structural analogues of the general one: a chemical bond conveys effect between atoms as
   light conveys effect between identities; a flow of water conveys effect between species as
   light conveys effect between manifestations. The analogy is structural, not substantial:
   the specific conveyors are not light, but they are what light looks like when it appears in
   the mode of the specific apparatus.
   What this test does not show. It does not show that the framework’s claim is correct.
   It does not show that physics, chemistry, and ecology confirm the framework, or that the
   framework confirms them. It shows only that the framework’s hierarchy of apparatuses is
   coherent with the way these inquiries describe their own structure. A scientific inquiry can
   develop itself within the framework without contradiction on this point; the framework
   does not depend on the inquiry, and the inquiry does not depend on the framework.

      The test is offered at exactly the strength stated. It is not a justification of the framework,
and it is not a derivation of the framework’s claim from the sciences. It is a check on coherence:
a demonstration that the framework’s hierarchy is not at odds with the way at least some
established inquiries describe the same structure.


14.12        What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
      First, the chapter does not argue for the existence of the seven realms. The seven realms
were argued for in the earlier part of the book that treated the realms; the present chapter
takes them as given, and asks where light stands in relation to them. The reader who is not yet
persuaded of the seven realms will find that the present chapter’s argument does not depend on
the persuasion; it depends only on the distinction between the analytical framework and the
ontological architecture, which is established in the first part of the book.
      Second, the chapter does not develop the relation between light and energy. Energy is
14.13. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                               143


mentioned in passing as one of the things that the specific conveyors convey, but its status—as a
relational feature rather than a column—is developed in the next chapter. The present chapter
locates light; the next chapter distinguishes light from what light conveys.
   Third, the chapter does not develop the full implications of encompassment. The three
consequences—impossibility of complete knowledge, light as the structural window, estimate
not complete knowledge—are stated, but their further implications are left for later parts of the
book. The present chapter has stated the principle and its immediate consequences; the later
parts develop them.
   Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described what light is in itself. It claims to have
described the structural place of light, and the structural place points beyond itself to the ground
that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the structure
of light and the ground of light; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is stated here as the
chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
If we are encompassed in light, can we speak of an “experience of light”—or is experience always
experience of something other than light? What would it mean to experience what makes
experience possible?

The next chapter draws the final consequences of the definition. It distinguishes light from what
light conveys, by defining energy as a relational feature rather than a column; it argues that light
is the condition of possibility of any explanation; and it states the framework’s understanding of
what the fluid element is, in its most general role.
Chapter 15

Consequences: Energy and Explanation


Scope. This chapter draws the final consequences of the framework’s treatment of light. It defines
energy as a relational feature, not a column; it distinguishes light from energy; it argues that
every explanation requires a conveyor, that without light no explanation is possible, and that
light is the condition of possibility of every fluid element; it gathers the formal skeleton, the
dependency map, and the open questions of the part; and it closes the part with a statement of
what the framework has established about light. Its claims are structural; where the chapter is
silent on questions of religion or mystical experience, the silence is not a denial but a recognition
that the structural description is not the whole of what can be said. Where the chapter speaks
of “energy,” “gradient,” “explanation,” “conveyor,” or “condition,” these are structural terms;
their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.



15.1      A Scene

Consider a light bulb. When it is switched on, it glows. We say that it uses energy, or that it
produces light. What is the relation between the two? Is energy the same as light? Or is light a
form of energy? Or is energy what light carries, without being what light is?
   The ordinary language is not clear on this point. We speak of “the energy of the light” and of
“the light of the sun” as if they were two things, and we speak of “light energy” as if they were
one. The two ways of speaking are not always distinguished, and the confusion is not trivial. If
energy and light are the same, then a theory of light is a theory of energy; if they are distinct,
then a theory of light must say what energy is, and how it is related to light. The present chapter
takes the second path: it distinguishes light from energy, and it defines energy as what light
carries, not as what light is.
   Now consider a second scene. An ecologist is asked to explain an ecosystem. She describes
the species that live in it, their relations, their patterns of reproduction and death. But if she
omits the flows of water, air, and energy that sustain the species, what remains? A list of species.
Nothing connects them; nothing explains how they live together. The species are there, but the
ecosystem is not. The explanation is incomplete, and it is incomplete because the conveyor of
effect—the water, the air, the energy—has been left out.
   The two scenes are about different things, but they share a question. In the first, the question
is what energy is, and how it is related to light. In the second, the question is what is required
for an explanation to be complete. The two questions are related: the answer to the second
requires the concept of the conveyor, and the concept of the conveyor requires the distinction
between light and energy. The present chapter answers both questions, and with them closes the
framework’s treatment of the fluid element.

                                                144
15.2. The Question                                                                                145


15.2      The Question

The previous chapters of this part have developed the framework’s account of light. Light was
defined as a trans-categorical substance (the chapter before the last), as an active connection
structure rather than a traveler (the last chapter), and as the foundational fluid element appearing
in the mode of each cognitive apparatus (the chapter before this one). The account is now in
place.
   Two questions remain.
   The first is about energy. The framework has spoken of light as the conveyor of effect; it has
not yet said what energy is. Is energy the same as light? Is it a property of the receiving realm?
Is it something else? The question is not terminological. If energy is not distinguished from light,
the framework collapses the two; if energy is distinguished from light, the framework must say
what energy is, and how it is related to what light is.
   The second question is about explanation. The framework has argued that every explanation
requires a fluid element (the conveyor principle). It has not yet asked whether the requirement
can be generalized: is light the condition of possibility of any explanation, or only of some? The
question is not idle. If light is the condition of any explanation, the framework’s claim about
light is stronger than it has been so far; if light is the condition only of material explanation, the
framework’s claim is narrower. The chapter argues for the stronger claim, at the strength stated.
   The chapter treats the two questions in turn. The first part distinguishes light from energy,
and defines energy as a relational feature. The second part argues that every explanation
requires a conveyor, that without light no explanation is possible, and that light is the condition
of possibility of every fluid element. The chapter ends with the formal skeleton of the part,
the dependency map, the open questions, and a statement of what the part has and has not
established.


15.3      Three Candidate Readings of Energy

The first question is: what is energy? Three readings are candidates.


First reading: energy is light (in the general sense). On this reading, energy and light
are the same thing under two names. Light is the conveyor of effect; energy is what light is. The
reading has the virtue of simplicity, but it has a difficulty: it conflates the carrier with what the
carrier carries. Light carries energy, but the energy is not the light. A beam of light can be dim
or bright; its brightness is the quantity of energy it carries, not the light itself. If energy were
the light, the beam could not be dim or bright without being more or less light, which is not the
way the framework uses the term.


Second reading: energy is the capacity of the context. On this reading, energy is the
potential of the realm—what the realm can provide, in the way of conditions for realization. The
reading has the virtue of locating energy in the context, where the conditions of realization are;
but it has a difficulty: it conflates actualization with capacity. The realm’s capacity is what it
146                                          Chapter 15. Consequences: Energy and Explanation


can bear; the energy is what is actually carried, in a given realization. The two are not the same,
and the reading conflates them.



Third reading: energy is a relational feature. On this reading, energy is a feature of the
relation among identity, manifestation, and realm—specifically, the quantity of the relation in the
dimension of actualization. The reading has the virtue of locating energy neither in the carrier
nor in the context alone, but in the relation among the three. It is the reading the framework
adopts.

   Remark 15.1 (Why Three Readings, Not Two)

   The three readings correspond to the three columns in which energy might be located:
   the fluid element (first reading), the context (second reading), or the relation among the
   columns (third reading). The framework considers all three because each has a prima
   facie plausibility, and because the choice among them has consequences for the rest of the
   framework. The reader who is persuaded by a different reading is invited to develop it;
   the framework’s claim is that the third reading is the one that fits the framework’s other
   principles, not that the first two are unintelligible.




15.4        The Proposed Reading: Energy as Relational Feature

   Definition 15.1 (Energy)

   (A) Energy is the quantity of the relation between identity, manifestation, and realm—in
   the dimension of actualization. It is neither the carrier (light) nor the capacity (context),
   but the quantity of the actualized relation.


      The definition is stated as a commitment. It is not derived from anything more basic; it is
the framework’s proposal for what energy is. The definition is supported by the following: if
energy is the quantity of the actualized relation, then the three readings of the previous section
can be located as partial views (the first identifies energy with the carrier, the second with the
capacity, and the third with the relation), and the framework can say what is right and what is
wrong in each. If energy is not such a quantity, the framework’s account of energy is in question,
and a different account is needed.
      The definition uses three terms. Identity is the source of the manifestation, as defined in the
previous part. Manifestation is the contextually realized appearance of the identity in a receiving
realm, as defined in the previous part. Realm is the ontological level in which the manifestation
is realized, as defined in the part before that. The relation among the three is what the definition
quantifies. Actualization is the dimension in which the relation is quantified: the relation is not
quantified as a possibility, but as what has actually been realized.
15.5. Energy in the Three Columns                                                               147


   Principle 15.1 (Energy as Relational Feature)

   (A) Energy is not a column. It is a relational feature that appears in three columns. It is
   the quantity of the relation between identity, manifestation, and realm—in the dimension
   of actualization.

   The principle is a consequence of the definition. If energy is the quantity of a relation, and if
a relation is not a column but a feature of the columns it relates, then energy is not a column. It
appears in the columns—in the fixed elements, in the fluid element, in the context— but it is
not itself one of the columns. The appearance in each column is the subject of the next section.

   Remark 15.2 (Energy Is Not a Substance)

   The definition must not be read as saying that energy is a substance of which the relation
   is a property. Energy is not a thing that the relation has; it is the quantity of the relation
   itself. The relation is actual; its quantity is energy. The quantity is not a substance; it is
   a measure. The framework’s claim is that energy is a measure of the actualized relation,
   not a substance that underlies the relation. The distinction is important: the first is a
   structural claim, the second is a metaphysical posit the framework does not make.



15.5     Energy in the Three Columns
The principle says that energy appears in three columns. The appearance in each is as follows.

    Column             Appearance of Energy            Explanation

    Fixed       ele- Property of material manifes- The quantity of realized capacity in a
    ments              tations                         manifestation.
    Fluid element      Content conveyed by light       The quantity of effect that light con-
                                                       veys.
    Context            Quantity of capacity con- The quantity of cost that actualization
                       sumed from the realm            pays.

   The three appearances are not three kinds of energy. They are three aspects of one quantity,
seen from the standpoint of the three columns. In the fixed elements, energy is the realized
capacity of the manifestation; in the fluid element, it is the effect that light conveys; in the
context, it is the cost that actualization pays. The three are the same quantity, described in
three ways.

   Remark 15.3 (The Three Appearances Are Not Additive)

   The three appearances are not three quantities that add up to a total. They are three
   descriptions of one quantity, and the descriptions are not independent. If the realized
   capacity in a manifestation is a certain amount, the effect that light conveys is the same
   amount, and the cost that actualization pays is the same amount. The three descriptions
   are three ways of saying the same thing; they are not three things. The reader who adds
148                                          Chapter 15. Consequences: Energy and Explanation


   them has misread them; the reader who sees them as one quantity described in three ways
   has read them correctly.



15.6        Light Primary, Energy Secondary

The definition of energy and the principle that energy appears in three columns together imply a
priority: light is primary, energy is secondary.

   Principle 15.2 (Light Primary, Energy Secondary)

   (T) Light is primary (the foundational fluid element); energy is secondary (the relational
   feature of the actualization of light). Light is the carrier; energy is the quantity carried.


Argument for the Principle.        1. Light is the foundational fluid element (the principle of the
        previous chapter).

  2. Energy is the quantity of the actualized relation among identity, manifestation, and realm
       (the definition of the previous section).

  3. The actualized relation is carried by light: without light, the relation would not be
        actualized.

  4. Hence light is what carries; energy is what is carried.

  5. Hence light is primary; energy is secondary.



      The argument turns on step (3). If light is the conveyor of effect, and if the effect is what is
quantified as energy, then the light carries what is quantified. The carrier is primary in the order
of the framework’s analysis: it is what makes the carrying possible. The quantity is secondary:
it is what the carrying carries. The priority is structural, not evaluative; it is the priority of
condition over conditioned, not of importance over unimportance.

   Remark 15.4 (Why the Priority Matters)

   The priority is not a small point. If energy were primary, then light would be a kind of
   energy, and a theory of energy would be more fundamental than a theory of light. If light
   is primary, then energy is a feature of light’s operation, and a theory of light is more
   fundamental than a theory of energy. The framework holds the second. The consequence
   is that the framework’s account of light does not depend on its account of energy; the
   account of energy depends on the account of light. The reader who keeps the priority in
   mind will find the framework’s order of exposition natural; the reader who reverses it will
   find the framework’s claims puzzling.
15.7. Every Explanation Requires a Conveyor                                                     149


15.7     Every Explanation Requires a Conveyor
The first part of the chapter distinguished light from energy. The second part turns to explanation.
The question is: is light the condition of possibility of any explanation, or only of some?

   Principle 15.3 (Every Explanation Requires a Conveyor)

   (T) Every explanation, in every realm, requires a fluid element— and without it, no
   explanation is possible. In material manifestation, this fluid element is light in the general
   sense, including water, air, electromagnetic waves, and any other conveyor of effect.


Argument for the Principle.      1. Every explanation says how some things stand to one another.

   2. To say how things stand to one another is to say what passes between them—what conveys
      the effect of one on another.

   3. What conveys the effect is the fluid element.

   4. Hence every explanation requires a fluid element.



   The argument is the conveyor principle, applied to every realm rather than only to the material
realm. The conveyor principle, stated and proved in the first part of the book, establishes the
requirement for explanations of how one fixed element bears on another. The present argument
extends the requirement to every explanation: in every realm, not only in material manifestation,
the explanation of how things stand requires a conveyor.
   The extension is supported by the same considerations that support the conveyor principle.
In the relational realm, the conveyor is the light as connection; in the structural realm, it is
the light as lawful unfolding; in the barzakhic realms, it is the light as apportioning, signifying,
realizing. The vocabulary differs from realm to realm, but the structural requirement is the same.


15.8     Without Light, No Explanation
The principle that every explanation requires a conveyor has a consequence: without light, no
explanation is possible.

   Principle 15.4 (Without Light, No Explanation)

   (T) Without light, the fixed elements are not connected to one another—and without
   connection, neither dynamics has meaning nor explanation. Every explanatory discourse
   in material manifestation is impossible without a conveyor of effect.


Argument for the Principle.      1. Without light, the fixed elements are not connected (from the
      definition of light as the conveyor of effect).

   2. Without connection, the fixed elements are a list, not a network.
150                                          Chapter 15. Consequences: Energy and Explanation


  3. A list is not an explanation: it says that things are there, but not how they stand to one
        another.

  4. Hence without light, no explanation is possible.



      The argument is short, and its shortness is the point. The principle is not a substantive claim
about the world; it is a claim about what an explanation requires. An explanation that does not
connect its elements is not an explanation; and an explanation that connects them requires a
conveyor. The conveyor is light, in the framework’s sense. Without light, the connection is not
made, and the explanation is not complete.

   Remark 15.5 (The Principle Is Not a Claim About the World)

   The principle must not be read as saying that without light, nothing exists. Things
   exist without being explained; the world exists without being understood. The principle
   is about explanation, not about existence. Its claim is that an explanation without a
   conveyor is incomplete, not that a world without a conveyor is impossible. The distinction
   is important: the framework’s claim is analytical, not ontological. The reader who reads
   the principle as a claim about the world has misread it; the reader who reads it as a claim
   about explanation has read it correctly.
   But the analytical claim is not unrelated to the world. Explanation is part of the world;
   the conditions of explanation are part of the structure of the world. The distinction is
   the distinction between an analytical claim and an existential claim, not the distinction
   between explanation and the world. The framework’s claim is that the structure of
   explanation is real, invariant, and describable; it does not claim that the structure of
   explanation is the whole of the world, and it does not claim that nothing lies beyond it.
   The distinction is the distinction between the structure of explanation and the ground of
   explanation; it is kept throughout the book.



15.9        Light as the Condition of Every Fluid Element
The previous principle says that light is required for explanation. A stronger principle says that
light is the condition of possibility of every fluid element.

   Principle 15.5 (Light as the Condition of Possibility of Every Fluid Element)

   (A) Light is not only one of the fluid elements—it is the condition of possibility of every
   fluid element. Without light, the concept of “conveyor of effect” is empty—because
   conveying effect requires a gradient of energy—and without light, there is no gradient.

      The principle is stronger than the previous one. The previous principle says that light is
required for explanation; the present principle says that light is required for the very concept of a
fluid element to have content. The argument for the stronger principle is stated in the principle
itself: conveying effect requires a gradient of energy, and without light there is no gradient.
15.9. Light as the Condition of Every Fluid Element                                               151


   The argument is compressed, and it needs to be unpacked. A gradient of energy is a difference
in the quantity of energy across the terms that are related. The difference is what makes the
effect pass from one term to another: the higher-energy term affects the lower-energy term, and
the effect is the passage of energy from higher to lower. Without the difference, there is no
passage; without passage, there is no conveyor; without conveyor, the concept of a fluid element
is empty.
   The difference is carried by light. Light is what makes the difference legible: without light,
the terms are not related, and the difference is not there to be measured. Hence light is the
condition of possibility of the gradient, and the gradient is the condition of possibility of the
conveyor. The two together make light the condition of possibility of every fluid element.

   Remark 15.6 (The Condition Points Beyond Itself)

   The condition of possibility of every fluid element is a real condition; its reality is not in
   question. But the condition is not self-grounded. The condition is the condition under
   which a fluid element can convey effect; it is not the ground of its own being. The structural
   light points beyond itself to what grounds the condition. The framework’s claim is that
   the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The
   distinction is the distinction between the condition and the ground of the condition; it is
   kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the condition as the divine light, the source of
   all manifestation. The framework does not claim that its structural light is that source,
   and it does not claim that the source is unreal. It claims that the structural light is a
   real condition, and that the condition points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the
   structural light with the divine light is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them
   is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity
   is a question for another inquiry. What the framework claims is structural: light is the
   condition of possibility of every fluid element, and the condition is real, and the condition is
   not self-sufficient. The claim is enough to ground the framework’s account of explanation;
   it is not enough to ground an account of the divine. The framework does not claim to
   ground such an account, and it does not claim that no such account is possible.


   Remark 15.7 (The Principle Is a Commitment)

   The principle is (A): it is adopted as a commitment of the framework, not proved from
   the framework’s other principles. It is supported by the argument just given, but the
   argument depends on the premise that conveying effect requires a gradient of energy, and
   that premise is itself a commitment. The framework adopts the premise because it is
   coherent with the rest of the framework’s account of light and energy; it would be refuted
   by showing that conveying effect does not require a gradient, or that the gradient can be
   carried by something other than light. The reader who wishes to challenge the principle
   knows where to press.
   The commitment is not a final claim; it is a structural claim. The commitment to the
152                                          Chapter 15. Consequences: Energy and Explanation


   foundation is not self-grounded. The commitment points beyond itself to what makes the
   commitment possible. The framework’s silence on the ground of the commitment is not a
   denial of the ground; it is the recognition that the ground is not describable at the level of
   structure. The distinction is the distinction between the structure and the ground of the
   structure; it is kept throughout the book.



15.10        A Coherence Test
The chapter’s claim is that light is the condition of possibility of every fluid element, and therefore
of every explanation. The claim is philosophical, not empirical. But it may be asked whether the
claim is coherent with the way at least some explanatory discourses actually work. The question
is a coherence test, not a justification.

   Coherence Test (not evidence, not justification)

   What this test shows. That the principle “light is the condition of possibility of every
   explanation” is coherent with the way at least one explanatory discourse—ecology—actually
   works.
   The test. Consider an ecological explanation of a forest. Without water, air, and the
   flows of energy, there is no current—and without current, no ecosystem. Only a list of
   species remains, without connection, without dynamics, without explanation. The species
   are there; the ecosystem is not. The explanation is incomplete, and it is incomplete
   because the conveyors of effect—the water, the air, the energy—have been left out. If the
   conveyors are restored, the explanation becomes complete: the species are connected by
   the flows, and the flows explain how the species live together.
   What this test does not show. It does not show that the framework’s claim is correct.
   It does not show that ecology confirms the framework, or that the framework confirms
   ecology. It shows only that the framework’s claim is coherent with the way ecological
   explanation actually works: an ecological explanation without conveyors is incomplete,
   and the framework’s claim is that this is so because conveyors are conditions of possibility
   of explanation in general. A scientific inquiry can develop itself within the framework
   without contradiction on this point; the framework does not depend on the inquiry, and
   the inquiry does not depend on the framework.

      The test is offered at exactly the strength stated. It is not a justification of the framework,
and it is not a derivation of the framework’s claim from ecology. It is a check on coherence: a
demonstration that the framework’s claim is not at odds with the way at least one explanatory
discourse actually works.

   Remark 15.8 (The Formal Skeleton Is Not the Whole)

   The formal skeleton is a summary of the part’s principal claims, not a summary of the
   part’s whole content. The skeleton states the claims and their formal forms; it does not
   state the arguments, the qualifications, the coherence tests, or the open questions. The
   skeleton is a map of the part, not the part itself. The reader who takes the skeleton as the
   whole of the part has mistaken the map for the territory; the reader who takes it as an
   orientation to the part has read it correctly.
   The skeleton is also not self-sufficient. The claims it summarizes are structural claims;
   they describe the structure of light and of explanation. The structure is real, and the
   framework’s claim is that the structure is invariant and describable. But the structure
   points beyond itself to the ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is
   the distinction between the structure and the ground of the structure; it is kept throughout
   the book, and it is the structural ground of the framework’s silence on what light is in
   itself.

15.13        The Open Questions of Part IV
The part leaves several questions open. They are philosophical questions, and they are marked
with the appropriate status. They fall into four groups.

Questions about the structure of light.

  • Q1. Descent without travel. If light does not travel, what exactly is “descent”? The
        framework’s answer is that descent is the appearance of light in a lower realm in the mode
        of that realm, not motion toward it. Whether this answer is fully adequate is left open. (Q)

  • Q2. Succession in higher realms. If time is a category of material manifestation, what
        is “succession” in higher realms? The framework’s first answer is that succession in higher
        realms is structural, like logical succession, not temporal. The development of this answer
        is left to the part of the book that treats time. (Q)

  • Q3. Sediment as active edge. If light is an active structure, what is “sediment”? The
        framework’s first answer is that sediment is an active structural edge that has remained
        active and has not been integrated—not light that has settled, but a structural edge that
        has remained in an active state. The development of this answer is left to the part of the
        book that treats sediment. (Q)

Questions about relation and experience.

  • Q4. Relation to light. If light is the condition of possibility of relation, can we speak of
        a “relation to light”—or is that a category mistake? The framework states the question
        but does not settle it. (Q)

  • Q5. Experience of light. If we are encompassed in light, can we speak of an “experience
        of light”—or is experience always experience of something other than light? The framework
        states the question but does not settle it. (Q)

  • Q6. Circularity of explanation. If light is the condition of possibility of any explanation,
        can any explanation explain light— or is every explanation of light circular? The framework
        states the question but does not settle it. (Q)

Questions about energy and higher realms.

  • Q7. Energy and light in higher realms. If energy is a relational feature in material
        manifestation, what is its counterpart in higher realms? The framework’s first answer is
        that the counterpart is a structural analogue, not energy as a quantity of matter. The
        development of this answer is left to a later part. (Q)
15.14. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                     157


Questions about the ground beyond the structure.

   • Q8. The ground of light. If light is the condition of possibility of every fluid element,
      what is the ground of this condition? The framework states that the structural light is real,
      and that it points beyond itself; it does not describe the ground, and it does not claim to
      describe it. Whether the ground is the divine light of the traditions, or something else, is a
      question the framework does not settle, and does not foreclose. The question belongs to a
      different inquiry, and the framework leaves it there. (Q)

   The eight questions are the part’s open frontier. They are not deficiencies of the framework;
they are the questions that the framework, having stated its claims, has not yet settled. A reader
who wishes to continue the inquiry will find here the places where the inquiry is most alive.


15.14      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
   First, the chapter does not settle the open questions it has listed. The questions are stated,
and the framework’s first answers are indicated, but the full treatment is deferred to later parts
of the book. The reader who wishes to see how the questions are answered is directed to those
parts.
   Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of energy in the framework’s other
parts. The definition of energy given here is the general one; the application of the definition to
specific contexts (expression cost, sediment, death and birth) is developed in later parts. The
present chapter has defined energy; the later parts apply the definition.
   Third, the chapter does not develop the full account of explanation in the framework’s other
parts. The claim that every explanation requires a conveyor is stated here; the argument that
this is so, in each of the seven realms, is developed in the parts that treat those realms. The
present chapter has stated the general claim; the later parts develop it in detail.
   Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of light. It claims to have
described the structural place of light, and the structural place points beyond itself to the ground
that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the structure
of light and the ground of light; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is stated here as the
chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
If light is the condition of possibility of any explanation, can any explanation explain light—or is
every explanation of light circular? What would a non-circular explanation of light look like, and
is it possible?

With this chapter, the framework’s treatment of the fluid element is complete. Light has been
defined, located, and distinguished from what it carries. The next part turns to the governing
dynamics: the rules that govern how light operates in each realm, and that determine what light
conveys in each context. The fluid element is light; the rules of its operation are the subject of
the part that follows.
