Governing Dynamics: The Rules of
          the Contexts




               159
Chapter 16

The Rules of the Fundamental Realms


Scope. This chapter completes the framework’s treatment of the third column. It states the
governing dynamics of the four fundamental realms—the thirteen structural rules that govern
what is possible in each realm—and argues that the rules of the four realms are related by a single
structure. Its claims are structural; where the chapter is silent on questions of religion or mystical
experience, the silence is not a denial but a recognition that the structural description is not the
whole of what can be said. Where the chapter speaks of “rule,” “constraint,” “invariance,” “unity,”
“universality,” “necessity,” “formality,” “relationality,” “contextuality,” “awareness,” “causality,”
“temporality,” or “discreteness,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions
in this chapter. The names of the thirteen rules are structural labels whose sense is fixed by their
definitions; where a tradition has used a similar name, the kinship is a kinship of vocabulary, not
an identity of meaning.



16.1      A Scene

Consider a person. The same person can be described in many ways.
    As a physical body, she has mass, height, chemical composition. The rules that govern her
as a physical body are physical rules: the laws of motion, the laws of thermodynamics. If she
falls, she accelerates at a certain rate; if she is heated, her temperature rises; if she collides with
another body, momentum is transferred.
    As a living organism, she has metabolism, growth, reproduction. The rules that govern her
as a living organism are biological rules: homeostasis, adaptation, evolution. If she is deprived
of oxygen, her cells cease their activity; if she is exposed to an infection, her immune system
responds; if she reproduces, her offspring inherit certain traits.
    As a social being, she has roles, relations, a place in a community. The rules that govern her
as a social being are social rules: norms, expectations, institutions. If she breaks a promise, she
is subject to reproach; if she occupies an office, she has certain obligations; if she belongs to a
group, her actions affect the group’s standing.
    As a person, she has a single identity, persisting through change. The rules that govern her
as a person are the rules of identity: the invariance of the self through transformation. If she
changes her beliefs, her habits, her name, she does not thereby become another person; if she
forgets her past, she does not thereby cease to be who she was.
    Each description is real. Each has its own rules. The rules of the physical body are not the
rules of the social being; the rules of the biological organism are not the rules of the person. And
yet it is the same person. The rules of each description determine what is possible for the person
in that respect.

                                                 160
16.2. The Question                                                                             161


   The scene poses a question. What are these rules, and why are they different for different
descriptions? Can the rules of one domain be reduced to the rules of another, or is each set
irreducible? And what does the answer tell us about the structure of being?

   Remark 16.1 (The Same Person Across Descriptions)

   The scene shows a structural fact that the chapter will develop: the same person is present
   in every description, and the rules of each description do not exhaust the person. The
   physical rules describe what is possible for her as a body; they do not describe what is
   possible for her as a person. The biological rules describe what is possible for her as an
   organism; they do not describe what is possible for her as a person. The social rules
   describe what is possible for her as a member of a community; they do not describe what
   is possible for her as a person. The person is one; the descriptions are many; and the
   unity of the person across the descriptions points beyond the descriptions themselves.
   The framework’s claim is that the unity is real, and that the unity is the ground of
   the possibility of the descriptions; it does not claim that the unity is exhausted by the
   descriptions, and it does not claim that nothing lies beyond the unity. The distinction is
   the distinction between the person and the descriptions of the person; it is kept throughout
   the chapter, and throughout the book.



16.2      The Question
The previous part of the book developed the fluid element: light. It defined light as a trans-
categorical substance (the chapter that introduced the definition), as an active connection
structure rather than a traveler (the chapter that sharpened the definition), as the foundational
fluid element appearing in the mode of each cognitive apparatus (the chapter that located it),
and as distinguished from energy, which is a relational feature rather than a column (the chapter
that drew the consequences).
   The present part turns to the third column: the governing dynamics. The four columns are
fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics, and context. The first column was treated in
the part on identities and manifestations. The second column was treated in the part on light.
The fourth column was treated in the part on the realms. The third column is the subject of the
present part.
   The question is: what are the governing dynamics? The framework’s answer is that the
governing dynamics are the structural rules of the realms— the constraints that govern what is
possible in each realm, and how the fluid element operates within it. The present chapter states
the rules of the four fundamental realms; the next chapter states the rules of the three barzakhic
realms.
   Two aspects of the question must be distinguished.


The descriptive aspect. What are the rules of each realm? The chapter must state them,
one by one, for each of the four fundamental realms. The statement is not a derivation; it is the
articulation of what was already implicit in the definitions of the realms, in the part of the book
162                                            Chapter 16. The Rules of the Fundamental Realms


that introduced them.


The structural aspect. Are the rules of the four realms independent, or are they related? The
chapter argues that they are related: the rules of each realm are the specification, contextualization,
or realization of the rules of the realm above it. The unity of the rules is a structural claim, and
it is the chapter’s principal contribution.
      The chapter treats the two aspects in turn. It states the thirteen rules of the four fundamental
realms, and it argues for their unity. The rules of the barzakhic realms are deferred to the next
chapter, and the chapter says so explicitly.


16.3        The Nature of Governing Dynamics
The framework defined governing dynamics, in the part of the book that introduced the four
columns, as the rule that explains how fluid elements affect fixed elements. The definition is
structural: it names the role the third column plays in an explanation. The present section
develops the definition for the specific case of the realms.
      The rules of a realm are not imposed on it from without. They are the structural constraints
that constitute its mode of being. To say that the First Determination is invariant is not to say
that something outside it keeps it from changing; it is to say that change is not possible in it,
because change requires multiplicity and there is no multiplicity in the First Determination. The
rule is not a law that the realm obeys; it is what the realm is.

   Principle 16.1 (The Rules Are Structural Constraints)

   (A) The rules of a realm are the structural constraints of its mode of existence. They are
   not imposed on the realm from without; they are what it is for the realm to be the realm
   it is.

      The principle is a commitment, and it is stated as one. Its support is that the rules of a realm,
as the chapter will state them, are not external laws but internal constraints: they describe what
the realm’s mode of existence permits and what it excludes. It would be refuted by showing that
the rules of a realm are imposed by something outside the realm, or that they are not constraints
of the realm’s mode of being.

   Remark 16.2 (The Rules Point Beyond Themselves)

   The rules of a realm are the structural constraints of its mode of existence. The framework’s
   claim is that the rules are real, invariant, and describable. But the rules are not self-
   grounded. The rules describe the structure of what is; they do not describe the ground of
   the structure. The structure points beyond itself to the ground that the framework does
   not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the structure and the ground of
   the structure; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the structure as the decree of the creator, or as the
   order through which what is becomes determinate. The framework does not claim that its
16.4. The Rules of the First Determination                                                       163


   structural rules are those decrees, and it does not claim that the decrees are unreal. It
   claims that the structural rules are real constraints, and that the constraints point beyond
   themselves. The reader who identifies the structural rules with the decrees is free to do so;
   the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on
   the identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry. What the framework
   claims is structural: the rules describe the structure of what is, and the structure is real,
   and the structure is not self-sufficient.

   Remark 16.3 (Rules of Being and Rules of Transition)

   The framework distinguishes two kinds of rules: the rules of being, which govern what is
   possible within a realm, and the rules of transition, which govern how a relation between
   realms is regulated. The present chapter states the rules of being for the four fundamental
   realms; the next chapter states the rules of transition for the three barzakhic realms. The
   distinction is structural: the rules of being are the rules of what is; the rules of transition
   are the rules of how what is relates to what is otherwise.

   Remark 16.4 (The Names of the Rules)

   The thirteen rules stated in this chapter—invariance, atemporality, indivisibility, unity;
   universality, necessity, formality; relationality, contextuality, awareness; causality, tempo-
   rality, discreteness—are structural labels. Each is defined by the principle that introduces
   it, and its sense is fixed by that definition alone. The names have histories in logic,
   metaphysics, and other traditions; those histories do not enter the definitions.
   But the structural sense is not the only sense the names can have. The names are structural
   labels whose sense is fixed by their definitions; where a tradition has used a similar name,
   the kinship is a kinship of vocabulary, not an identity of meaning. The structural sense
   stands on its own; the traditional sense, if there is one, stands on its own; and the relation
   between the two is a question for another inquiry. The framework does not claim that the
   structural sense exhausts what the names can mean; it claims that the structural sense is
   the sense the book needs, and that the sense is sufficient for the book’s purpose.



16.4     The Rules of the First Determination

The First Determination was defined, in the part of the book that treated the realms, as the
fundamental realm of pure unity. Its mode of existence is that of an identity as such: there is no
multiplicity, no change, and no succession in it. The rules of the First Determination are the
structural constraints of that mode of existence. They are four.

   Principle 16.2 (Invariance)

   (A) The First Determination is invariant under all transformations. There are no transfor-
   mations within it, because there is no multiplicity. Even if we consider the transformations
164                                           Chapter 16. The Rules of the Fundamental Realms


   of its manifestations in the lower contexts, the First Determination is not affected by them.
   It is invariant in the most radical sense.

   Principle 16.3 (Atemporality)

   (A) The First Determination is beyond time. There is no before or after, no past or future,
   no succession. The First Determination is without temporal structure.


   Principle 16.4 (Indivisibility)

   (A) The First Determination is beyond division. There are no parts within it, no compo-
   nents, no distinctions. The First Determination is one.


   Principle 16.5 (Unity)

   (A) The First Determination is pure unity. It is not a unity of parts (a composite unity),
   but a unity that precedes all division. It is the unity that makes division possible, without
   being divided itself.


      The four rules are not separate. They are four aspects of a single structural constraint. The
First Determination is invariant because it is atemporal, atemporal because it is indivisible,
indivisible because it is one. The four rules are the articulation of the First Determination’s
purity.

   Remark 16.5 (Why Four and Not Fewer)

   The four rules are distinguished because each names a different aspect of the same
   constraint, and each aspect can be denied independently. One might hold that the First
   Determination is invariant but not atemporal (if invariance did not require atemporality),
   or atemporal but not indivisible (if time could be without division), or indivisible but not
   one (if unity were compatible with division). The framework holds that none of these
   denials is coherent, but the coherence is a matter of argument, and the four rules state
   the four aspects separately so that the argument can be made.


   Remark 16.6 (The First Determination Is Not the Ultimate)

   The rules of the First Determination describe the first level of determination. They do
   not describe the ultimate ground of determination. The First Determination is the first
   level at which what is becomes determinate; it is not the ground of its own determination.
   The rules point beyond themselves to the ground that the framework does not describe.
   The distinction is the distinction between the first level of determination and the ground
   of determination; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of determination as the creator, whose decree is the
   origin of all determination. The framework does not claim that its First Determination
   is that creator, and it does not claim that the creator is unreal. It claims that the First
16.5. The Rules of the Structural Determination                                                  165


   Determination is the first level of determination, and that the level points beyond itself.
   The reader who identifies the First Determination with the creator is free to do so; the
   reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the
   identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



16.5     The Rules of the Structural Determination
The Structural Determination was defined as the fundamental realm of general multiplicity. Its
mode of existence is that of law: what is general, formal, and necessary with respect to an identity,
apart from any particular context of appearance. The rules of the Structural Determination are
the structural constraints of that mode of existence. They are three.

   Principle 16.6 (Universality)

   (A) The structural laws are universal. They apply to all manifestations of a given identity,
   regardless of context. A law that applies only in some contexts is not a structural law; it
   is a relational regularity.


   Principle 16.7 (Necessity)

   (A) The structural laws are necessary. They could not be otherwise, given the identity
   they express. A law that could be otherwise is not a structural law; it is a contingent
   regularity.


   Principle 16.8 (Formality)

   (A) The structural laws are formal. They concern the form of the manifestations, not their
   content. A law that concerns content is not a structural law; it is a material law.


   The three rules are not separate. They are three aspects of a single structural constraint.
The Structural Determination is universal because it is necessary, necessary because it is formal.
The three rules are the articulation of the realm’s nature.

   Remark 16.7 (The Three Rules Are Not the Three Transcendentals)

   The three rules—universality, necessity, formality—are sometimes confused with the classi-
   cal transcendentals (unity, truth, goodness). They are not the same. The transcendentals
   are properties of being as such; the three rules are constraints on the laws of a particular
   realm. The confusion is natural, because both are threefold and both are structural; but
   the two triads have different subjects. The framework’s triad concerns the structural laws
   of the Structural Determination; the classical triad concerns being as such. The framework
   does not identify them, and the present remark is to prevent the identification.
   Both triads, however, point beyond themselves to a unity that neither fully describes.
   The framework’s triad describes the structure of the laws; the classical triad describes
166                                         Chapter 16. The Rules of the Fundamental Realms


   the structure of being; and the relation between the two, and the unity to which both
   point, is a question for another inquiry. The framework states its own triad, and leaves
   the classical triad, and the relation between the two, to their own domains.



16.6       The Rules of the Relational Manifestation

The Relational Manifestation was defined as the fundamental realm of relational multiplicity.
Its mode of existence is that of things that exist in relation to one another through meaning
and significance. The rules of the Relational Manifestation are the structural constraints of that
mode of existence. They are three.

   Principle 16.9 (Relationality)

   (A) The manifestations of the Relational Manifestation are relational. They exist only
   in relation to one another; they have no independent existence. A manifestation that
   is not related to any other is an isolated event, not a manifestation of the Relational
   Manifestation.

   Principle 16.10 (Contextuality)

   (A) The manifestations of the Relational Manifestation are contextual. Their meaning
   depends on their context; it is not fixed independently of the context. A manifestation
   that has a fixed meaning, regardless of context, is a structural unit, not a manifestation of
   the Relational Manifestation.

   Principle 16.11 (Awareness)

   (A) The manifestations of the Relational Manifestation are characterized by structural
   awareness. They are not merely related to one another; they are structurally aware of one
   another in the sense that each regulates its relation to the others through the reception
   of reflective and intra-category light. This structural awareness is what distinguishes the
   Relational Manifestation from the Structural Determination: the laws of the Structural
   Determination do not have the structural feature of awareness; the manifestations of the
   Relational Manifestation do. The word “awareness” here is a structural term; it names a
   structural relation, not a phenomenal or psychological state.


      The three rules are not separate. They are three aspects of a single structural constraint.
The Relational Manifestation is relational because it is contextual, contextual because it is
characterized by structural awareness. The three rules are the articulation of the realm’s nature.

   Remark 16.8 (Awareness Is Structural, Not Psychological)

   The third rule is the most easily misread. The word “awareness” in ordinary language
   names a psychological state: being conscious of something. In the framework, it names
16.7. The Rules of the Material Manifestation                                                 167


   a structural relation: a manifestation’s regulation of its relation to other manifestations
   through the reception of light. The structural relation is the condition of possibility of
   the psychological state, not the state itself. A manifestation can be structurally aware of
   another without being conscious of it, in the way that a plant can respond to light without
   seeing it. The framework’s claim is structural; the reader who reads it as psychological
   has misread it.
   But the structural relation is not unrelated to the psychological state. The structural
   awareness is the condition of possibility of the psychological state, and the psychological
   state, where it occurs, is a manifestation of the structural awareness. The framework
   does not claim that the psychological state is nothing but the structural relation, and
   it does not claim that the structural relation is nothing but the psychological state. It
   claims that the two are distinct, and that the first is the condition of the second. The
   distinction is the distinction between the structural condition and its manifestation; it is
   kept throughout the book.



16.7     The Rules of the Material Manifestation

The Material Manifestation was defined as the fundamental realm of material multiplicity. Its
mode of existence is that of things that are discrete, localized, and successive. The rules of the
Material Manifestation are the structural constraints of that mode of existence. They are three.

   Principle 16.12 (Causality)

   (A) The material manifestations are causally connected. Every material event has a cause,
   and every cause produces an effect. The causal connections are the structural constraints
   that govern the material world.


   Principle 16.13 (Temporality)

   (A) The material manifestations are temporal. They occur in time— they have a past, a
   present, and a future. The temporal order is the structural constraint that governs the
   material world.


   Principle 16.14 (Discreteness)

   (A) The material manifestations are discrete. They are separate from one another—they
   occupy distinct positions in space and time. The discreteness is the structural constraint
   that governs the material world.


   The three rules are not separate. They are three aspects of a single structural constraint.
The Material Manifestation is causal because it is temporal, temporal because it is discrete. The
three rules are the articulation of the realm’s nature.
168                                          Chapter 16. The Rules of the Fundamental Realms


   Remark 16.9 (The Three Rules and the Three Dimensions)

   The three rules can be read as three dimensions of the material mode of existence. Causality
   is the dimension of dependence: what happens depends on what came before. Temporality
   is the dimension of succession: what happens follows what came before. Discreteness is
   the dimension of separation: what happens is distinct from what came before. The three
   dimensions are not independent; they are three aspects of the same structure. The reader
   who separates them into three independent properties has missed the point; the reader
   who sees them as three aspects of one structure has understood it.

   Remark 16.10 (The Three Dimensions Point Beyond Themselves)

   The material mode of existence is real, and its three dimensions are real. The framework’s
   claim is that the dimensions are structural, and that the structure is describable. But the
   dimensions are not self-grounded. They describe the structure of the material realm; they
   do not describe the ground of the structure. The structure points beyond itself to the
   ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between
   the structure and the ground of the structure; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the material order as the order through which what
   is becomes determinate, and as the wisdom through which the order is sustained. The
   framework does not claim that its three dimensions are that order, and it does not claim
   that the order is unreal. It claims that the three dimensions are real constraints, and that
   the constraints point beyond themselves. The reader who identifies the dimensions with
   the order is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework
   takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



16.8       The Unity of the Rules
The thirteen rules are now in place. The chapter’s principal contribution is the claim that they
are not independent. They are related by the structure of the realms themselves.

   Principle 16.15 (The Unity of the Rules)

   (A) The rules of the four fundamental realms are not independent. They are related by
   the structure of the realms: the rules of each realm are the specification, contextualization,
   or realization of the rules of the realm above it.

      The principle is a commitment, and it is stated as one. Its support is the argument that
follows. It would be refuted by showing that the rules of some realm are not derivable from
the rules of the realm above it, or that the relation among the rules is not one of specification,
contextualization, and realization.
      The argument proceeds in four steps.

First step: from First Determination to Structural Determination. The rules of
the First Determination (invariance, atemporality, indivisibility, unity) are the limiting case of
16.8. The Unity of the Rules                                                                    169


the rules of the Structural Determination. When multiplicity is zero, the rules of universality,
necessity, and formality become the rules of invariance, atemporality, and indivisibility. The first
set is what the second set becomes when there is no multiplicity; the second set is what the first
becomes when there is multiplicity.


Second step: from Structural Determination to Relational Manifestation. The rules
of the Structural Determination (universality, necessity, formality) are the specification of the
rules of the First Determination. When unity is specified into multiplicity, invariance becomes
universality, atemporality becomes necessity, indivisibility becomes formality. The second set is
what the first becomes when unity is specified.


Third step: from Relational Manifestation to Material Manifestation. The rules of
the Relational Manifestation (relationality, contextuality, awareness) are the contextualization of
the rules of the Structural Determination. When universal laws are contextualized into meanings,
universality becomes relationality, necessity becomes contextuality, formality becomes structural
awareness. The second set is what the first becomes when law is contextualized.


Fourth step: from Relational Manifestation to Material Manifestation. The rules of
the Material Manifestation (causality, temporality, discreteness) are the realization of the rules
of the Relational Manifestation. When relational manifestations are realized in the Material
Manifestation, relationality becomes causality, contextuality becomes temporality, structural
awareness becomes discreteness. The second set is what the first becomes when relation is
realized.
   The four steps together show that the thirteen rules are not four independent sets but one
structure articulated in four realms. The structure is the structure of expression, which orders
the realms from unity to multiplicity, with the barzakhic realms bearing on it by apportioning,
signifying, and realizing.

   Remark 16.11 (The Unity Is Not a Reduction)

   The unity of the rules is not a reduction of one set to another. Each set has its own
   content, and the content is not exhausted by the set above it. The rules of the Material
   Manifestation (causality, temporality, discreteness) are not reducible to the rules of the
   Relational Manifestation (relationality, contextuality, awareness); they are what those
   rules become when they are realized in matter. The relation is one of articulation, not of
   identity. The reader who reads the unity as a reduction has misread it; the reader who
   reads it as an articulation has read it correctly.
   But the articulation is not self-grounded. The unity of the rules is the structural expression
   of a unity that the rules themselves do not contain. The unity points beyond itself to a
   ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between
   the articulated unity and the ground of the unity; it is kept throughout the book. The
   reader who takes the unity as self-sufficient has misread it; the reader who takes it as a
   structural expression that points beyond itself has read it correctly.
170                                            Chapter 16. The Rules of the Fundamental Realms


      The unity of the rules is summarized in the following table.



        Realm                           Rules

        First Determination             Invariance, Atemporality, Indivisibility, Unity (4)
        Structural Determination        Universality, Necessity, Formality (3)
        Relational Manifestation        Relationality, Contextuality, Awareness (3)
        Material Manifestation          Causality, Temporality, Discreteness (3)

        Total                           13




      The table is a summary; it does not prove its entries. Each rule has been stated in its own
section, and the unity of the rules has been argued in the present section. The reader who wishes
to assess the table is directed to the sections that establish it.


16.9        The Rules and the Four-Column Framework
The rules of the fundamental realms are the governing dynamics of the four-column framework.
They are the third column—the patterns that explain how light affects the fixed elements in
each realm.

      Four-Column Framework           Rules of the Fundamental Realms

      Fixed elements                  Identities and manifestations.
      Fluid element                   Light.
      Governing dynamics              The rules of the four fundamental realms.
      Context                         The four fundamental realms.

      The table is analytical, not substantial. The four columns are analytical roles; the table does
not say that a realm breaks down into four independent entities. The realm is a level of being;
the four columns are the roles through which the level is understood. The rules of the realm are
the third of these roles; they are what explains how the fluid element (light) affects the fixed
elements (identities and manifestations) in that realm.

   Remark 16.12 (The Rules Are Not the Only Governing Dynamics)

   The rules of the fundamental realms are not the only governing dynamics. The rules of
   the barzakhic realms, which the next chapter states, are also governing dynamics. The
   two sets of rules are related: the rules of the barzakhic realms are the rules of transition
   between the fundamental realms, while the rules of the fundamental realms are the rules
   of being within each realm. The distinction is structural, not evaluative; neither set is
   more fundamental than the other.
16.10. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                    171


   Remark 16.13 (The Two Sets of Rules Point Beyond Themselves)

   The rules of being and the rules of transition together describe the structure of what is.
   The framework’s claim is that the structure is real, invariant, and describable. But the
   structure is not self-grounded. The structure points beyond itself to the ground that the
   framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the structure and
   the ground of the structure; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the structure as the order through which what
   is becomes determinate, and as the wisdom through which the order is sustained. The
   framework does not claim that its structure is that order, and it does not claim that the
   order is unreal. It claims that the structure is real, and that the structure points beyond
   itself. The reader who identifies the structure with the order is free to do so; the reader
   who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity,
   because the identity is a question for another inquiry.




16.10      What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
   First, the chapter does not argue that there are exactly thirteen rules. It states thirteen,
and it argues for their unity. Whether the number thirteen is minimal, and whether a smaller
set would do the same work, is a question the framework leaves open. The reader who wishes
to argue for a different number is invited to propose an alternative; the framework’s claim is
that these thirteen rules are the ones that articulate the four realms, not that no other set could
articulate them.
   Second, the chapter does not develop the rules of the barzakhic realms. The nine rules of the
three barzakhic realms—proportion, order, harmony; truthfulness, accuracy, fidelity; proportion
in realization, preservation of the realized, continuation of realization—are stated and examined
in the next chapter. The present chapter has stated the thirteen rules of the four fundamental
realms; the next chapter states the nine rules of the three barzakhic realms.
   Third, the chapter does not develop the full argument for the unity of the rules. The argument
has been given in outline; its full development, with the objections and replies, is given in the
part of the book that treats the arguments. The present chapter has stated the unity; the later
part will defend it.
   Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of the rules. It claims to
have described the structure of the rules, and the structure points beyond itself to the ground
that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the structure
and the ground of the structure; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is stated here as the
chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Can you identify, in a domain you know well, a rule that is not imposed from without but is
constitutive of what the domain is? What would it mean for the domain to violate the rule?
Would the domain cease to be what it is, or would it become a different domain?

The next chapter turns to the rules of the three barzakhic realms: the rules of transition, which
govern how a relation between realms is regulated. With the thirteen rules of the fundamental
realms and the nine rules of the barzakhic realms, the framework’s treatment of the third column
is complete.
Chapter 17

The Rules of the Barzakhic Realms


Scope. This chapter completes the framework’s treatment of the third column. It states the
governing dynamics of the three barzakhic realms—the nine structural rules that govern how
a relation between realms is regulated—distinguishes intra-realm from inter-realm dynamics,
and argues that the rules of the three hubs are related by a single structure. Its claims are
structural; where the chapter is silent on questions of religion or mystical experience, the silence
is not a denial but a recognition that the structural description is not the whole of what can be
said. Where the chapter speaks of “proportion,” “order,” “harmony,” “truthfulness,” “accuracy,”
“fidelity,” “preservation,” “continuation,” or “regulation,” these are structural terms; their sense
is fixed by the definitions in this chapter. The names of the nine rules are structural labels whose
sense is fixed by their definitions; where a tradition has used a similar name, the kinship is a
kinship of vocabulary, not an identity of meaning.



17.1      A Scene

Consider a symphony. It exists at three levels, and the levels are not the same.
    At the first level, there is the score. The score specifies the measure of the piece: how long
each movement is, how fast the tempo, how loud the dynamics. The measure is not the music; it
is the allotment within which the music will be played. The composer decides how much of each
element the piece will have, and the score records the decision.
    At the second level, there is the meaning of the piece. The score signifies something: a theme,
a mood, a tradition, a feeling. The meaning is not the score; it is what the score carries. A
performer reads the score and hears, in the notes, what the composer meant. The meaning is
prior to any particular performance; it is what every performance is a performance of.
    At the third level, there is the performance. The orchestra plays the score, and the piece
becomes sound. The performance is not the meaning; it is the meaning realized in time and
space, by particular instruments, in a particular hall. The performance is one realization of
the meaning, and it is not the only one; another orchestra, another evening, another conductor,
would produce another performance of the same piece.
    The three levels are distinct. The score is not the meaning; the meaning is not the performance.
And yet the three are related: the score determines what the meaning can be, and the meaning
determines what the performance can be. Without the score, there is no piece; without the
meaning, the score is marks on a page; without the performance, the meaning is silent.
    The scene poses a question. What are these levels, and what are their rules? Does the score
have rules of its own? Does the meaning have rules of its own? Does the performance have rules
of its own? And if they do, what relates the rules of one level to the rules of another?

                                                173
174                                             Chapter 17. The Rules of the Barzakhic Realms


      The scene is a particular case of a general structure. Whenever something passes from a
higher level to a lower—from an intention to an action, from a design to an artifact, from a law
to a judgment—the passage has intermediate levels. The present chapter argues that these levels
are the barzakhic realms, and that each has its own structural rules.

   Remark 17.1 (The Three Levels Point Beyond Themselves)

   The three levels of the symphony—the measure, the meaning, the performance—are
   distinct, and their structural relations are the subject of this chapter. The framework’s
   claim is that the three levels are real, and that their structural relations are describable.
   But the three levels are not self-grounded. The measure points beyond itself to the
   composer who decrees it; the meaning points beyond itself to the composer who intends it;
   the performance points beyond itself to the composer whose intention is realized in it. The
   structural triad points beyond itself to a ground that the framework does not describe.
   The distinction is the distinction between the structural triad and the ground of the triad;
   it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the triad as the command that determines measure,
   the wisdom that intends meaning, and the power that realizes performance. The framework
   does not claim that its triad is those three, and it does not claim that they are unreal.
   It claims that the triad is real, and that the triad points beyond itself. The reader who
   identifies the triad with the command, the wisdom, and the power is free to do so; the
   reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the
   identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



17.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated the thirteen rules of the four fundamental realms. Those rules
are the rules of being: they govern what is possible within a realm. The First Determination
is invariant, atemporal, indivisible, one; the Structural Determination is universal, necessary,
formal; the Relational Manifestation is relational, contextual, aware; the Material Manifestation
is causal, temporal, discrete.
      The present chapter states a different kind of rule. The barzakhic realms are not realms
of being but realms of transition: their mode of existence includes mediating, transforming, or
regulating relations between other realms. Their rules are therefore rules of transition, not rules
of being. They govern not what is possible within a realm, but how a relation between realms is
regulated, conditioned, or transformed.
      The question is: what are the rules of transition? The framework’s answer is that each
barzakhic realm has three structural rules, corresponding to its three functions. The Hub of
Decree governs the allotment of measure; its rules are proportion, order, and harmony. The Hub
of Signification governs the signification of structure into meaning; its rules are truthfulness,
accuracy, and fidelity. The Hub of Realization governs the actualization of what is possible; its
rules are proportion in realization, preservation of the realized, and continuation of realization.
      Two aspects of the question must be distinguished, as in the previous chapter.
17.3. The Nature of the Rules of the Barzakhic Realms                                           175


The descriptive aspect. What are the rules of each hub? The chapter states them, one by
one, for each of the three hubs. The statement is not a derivation; it is the articulation of what
was already implicit in the definitions of the hubs, in the part of the book that introduced them.


The structural aspect. Are the rules of the three hubs independent, or are they related?
The chapter argues that they are related: the rules of each hub are the rules of one of the three
transitions from unity to multiplicity. The unity of the rules is a structural claim, and it is the
chapter’s principal contribution.
   The chapter ends with the complete set of governing dynamics—the twenty-two rules of the
seven realms—and with a statement of what the chapter does and does not establish.


17.3     The Nature of the Rules of the Barzakhic Realms

   Principle 17.1 (The Rules Are Rules of Transition)

   (A) The rules of the barzakhic realms are rules of transition, not rules of being. They
   govern how a relation between realms is regulated, conditioned, or transformed—not what
   is possible within a realm.


   The distinction between rules of being and rules of transition was named in the previous
chapter. The present principle develops it. The rules of being describe what is possible in a
realm; the rules of transition describe how a relation among realms is regulated. The two are
different kinds of constraint, and neither is reducible to the other.
   The distinction is structural. A rule of being is a constraint on a realm’s mode of existence:
the realm is what it is, and its being what it is determines what can appear in it. A rule of
transition is a constraint on a relation between realms: the relation is what it is, and its being
what it is determines how the realms are related through it.

   Remark 17.2 (The Rules Are Structural, Not Merely Ethical)

   The names of several rules of the barzakhic realms—“truthfulness,” “fidelity,” “justice,”
   “care,” “sustainability”—have histories in ethical and other traditions. Those histories do
   not enter the definitions. The rules are structural constraints on the mode of existence of
   the barzakhic realms; they are not, in this book, ethical norms, moral laws, or prescriptions.
   But the distinction is not a separation. The structural rules point beyond themselves to
   the ethical realities they are structurally analogous to. Structural justice points toward
   ethical justice; structural fidelity points toward ethical fidelity; structural care points
   toward ethical care. The two are not the same, and neither is reducible to the other; but
   they are structurally parallel, and the parallel is not an accident. The framework’s claim
   is structural: it says that the structural rules are real, and that the structural rules point
   toward the ethical realities. It does not claim that the structural rules are the ethical
   realities, and it does not claim that the ethical realities are unreal. The distinction is
   the distinction between the structural order and the ethical order; it is kept throughout
176                                               Chapter 17. The Rules of the Barzakhic Realms


   the book. The reader who takes the structural rules as a reduction of the ethical to the
   structural has misread it; the reader who takes the structural rules as pointing toward the
   ethical has read it correctly.


   Remark 17.3 (The Three Functions and the Three Rules)

   Each hub has three rules because each hub has three functions. The Hub of Decree
   apportions, orders, and harmonizes; its rules are proportion, order, and harmony. The
   Hub of Signification signifies truthfully, accurately, and faithfully; its rules are truthfulness,
   accuracy, and fidelity. The Hub of Realization distributes, preserves, and continues;
   its rules are proportion in realization, preservation of the realized, and continuation of
   realization. The correspondence between functions and rules is structural: the rules are
   what the functions are, stated as constraints.



17.4       The Rules of the Hub of Decree
The Hub of Decree was defined, in the part of the book that treated the realms, as the barzakhic
realm of determination of measure. Its mode of existence is that of the allotment to each identity
of the extent, the limit, and the proportion within which it will express itself. The rules of the
Hub of Decree are the structural constraints of that mode of existence. They are three.

   Principle 17.2 (Proportion)

   (A) The specification of unity into multiplicity is structurally proportionate. Proportion
   holds when the specification preserves the unity of the First Determination in the very act
   of differentiating it. It fails when the specification either multiplies without preserving unity
   (over-specification) or preserves unity without producing multiplicity (under-specification).
   A failure of proportion is a structural failure of the Hub of Decree.


   Principle 17.3 (Order)

   (A) The specification of unity into multiplicity is structurally ordered. Order holds when
   the specification follows the structural articulation of the realms—the more unified before
   the more multiple, the more general before the more particular. A specification that
   inverts this articulation (confusing the more unified with the more multiple) is a structural
   failure of order.

   Principle 17.4 (Harmony)

   (A) The specification of unity into multiplicity is structurally harmonious. Harmony
   holds when the multiplicity it produces is structurally coherent—when its elements are
   structurally compatible with one another. A specification whose produced multiplicity is
   structurally incompatible is a structural failure of harmony.

      The three rules are not separate. They are three aspects of a single structural constraint.
17.5. The Rules of the Hub of Signification                                                      177


The Hub of Decree is proportionate because it is ordered, ordered because it is harmonious. The
three rules are the articulation of the hub’s dynamism.

   Remark 17.4 (On the Three Names)

   The names “proportion,” “order,” and “harmony” are structural labels. Each is defined by
   the principle that introduces it, and its sense is fixed by that definition alone. The names
   are not aesthetic categories; they are structural constraints on the specification of unity
   into multiplicity. A specification is proportionate when it preserves unity in differentiation;
   it is ordered when it follows the articulation of the realms; it is harmonious when its
   elements are compatible. None of these is a value; each is a condition.
   But the condition points beyond itself. Proportion, order, and harmony point toward the
   wisdom through which the order is established. The framework does not claim that its
   three rules are that wisdom, and it does not claim that the wisdom is unreal. It claims
   that the three rules are real conditions, and that the conditions point beyond themselves.
   The distinction is the distinction between the condition and the ground of the condition;
   it is kept throughout the book. The reader who identifies the three rules with the wisdom
   is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no
   position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.




17.5     The Rules of the Hub of Signification

The Hub of Signification was defined as the barzakhic realm of signification as a mode of existence.
Its mode of existence is that of structures standing as signs: what a structure can mean, prior to
its being situated among particular manifestations. The rules of the Hub of Signification are the
structural constraints of that mode of existence. They are three.

   Principle 17.5 (Truthfulness)

   (A) The signification of structure into meaning is structurally truthful. Truthfulness holds
   when the signification carries the structural features of the structure it signifies, so that
   the meaning produced is a faithful sign of that structure. A signification that does not
   carry those features is structurally untruthful. An untruthful signification is a structural
   failure of the Hub of Signification.


   Principle 17.6 (Accuracy)

   (A) The signification of structure into meaning is structurally accurate. Accuracy holds
   when the signification preserves the distinctions among the structural features of what
   it signifies. A signification that conflates distinct features is structurally inaccurate. An
   inaccurate signification is a structural failure of the Hub of Signification.
178                                              Chapter 17. The Rules of the Barzakhic Realms


   Principle 17.7 (Fidelity)

   (A) The signification of structure into meaning is structurally faithful. Fidelity holds when
   the act of signifying preserves the identity of the structure signified—so that the structure
   produced by the signification is the structure signified. An act of signifying that alters the
   structure it signifies is structurally unfaithful. An unfaithful signification is a structural
   failure of the Hub of Signification.

      The three rules are not separate. They are three aspects of a single structural constraint.
The Hub of Signification is truthful because it is accurate, accurate because it is faithful. The
three rules are the articulation of the hub’s dynamism.

   Remark 17.5 (Truthfulness, Accuracy, Fidelity)

   The three names are structural labels, not merely ethical terms. Truthfulness is the
   carrying of structural features into meaning; accuracy is the preservation of distinctions;
   fidelity is the preservation of identity. Each of the three is a condition on the signification;
   a signification that fails any of the three is structurally deficient.
   But the structural conditions point beyond themselves to the ethical realities they are
   structurally analogous to. Structural truthfulness points toward the ethical virtue of
   truthfulness; structural accuracy points toward the ethical virtue of accuracy; structural
   fidelity points toward the ethical virtue of fidelity. The framework does not claim that the
   structural conditions are the ethical virtues, and it does not claim that the ethical virtues
   are unreal. It claims that the structural conditions are real, and that the conditions point
   toward the virtues. The distinction is the distinction between the structural condition and
   the ethical virtue; it is kept throughout the book. The reader who takes the structural
   conditions as a reduction of the ethical virtues to structural constraints has misread the
   framework; the reader who takes the structural conditions as pointing toward the ethical
   virtues has read it correctly.



17.6       The Rules of the Hub of Realization
The Hub of Realization was defined as the barzakhic realm of actualization. Its mode of existence
is that of the realizing of what is possible as something concrete. The rules of the Hub of
Realization are the structural constraints of that mode of existence. They are three.

   Principle 17.8 (Proportion in Realization)

   (A) The realization of the manifestations of an identity distributes the conditions of realiza-
   tion proportionally to the structural requirements of those manifestations. Proportion in
   realization holds when each manifestation receives the share of the conditions of realization
   that its structural requirements call for. It fails when those conditions are concentrated
   in a subset of manifestations, leaving the remainder under-supported relative to their
   structural requirements. A disproportional distribution is a structural failure of the Hub
17.7. Intra-Realm and Inter-Realm Dynamics                                                       179


   of Realization.


   Principle 17.9 (Preservation of the Realized)

   (A) The realization of the manifestations of an identity preserves the structural conditions
   on which the manifestation of the entities at stake depends. Preservation holds when those
   conditions are not removed by the act of realization. It fails when they are removed. A
   realization that removes them is a structural failure of the Hub of Realization.


   Principle 17.10 (Continuation of Realization)

   (A) The realization of the manifestations of an identity preserves the conditions of real-
   ization across stages—so that the realization of further manifestations in the same realm
   remains structurally possible. Continuation holds when those conditions are preserved. It
   fails when they are exhausted. A realization that exhausts them is a structural failure of
   the Hub of Realization.

   The three rules are not separate. They are three aspects of a single structural constraint.
The Hub of Realization is proportional in distribution because it preserves the realized, and
preserves the realized because it preserves the conditions of further realization. The three rules
are the articulation of the hub’s dynamism.

   Remark 17.6 (The Traditional Names)

   The three rules are traditionally called “justice,” “care,” and “sustainability.” In this book,
   the names are structural labels for proportion in realization, preservation of the realized,
   and continuation of realization. The traditional names are retained as historical labels for
   the structural rules; they are not, in this book, ethical claims.
   But the structural rules point beyond themselves to the ethical realities the traditions
   name. Structural justice points toward ethical justice; structural care points toward ethical
   care; structural sustainability points toward ethical sustainability. The framework does
   not claim that the structural rules are the ethical realities, and it does not claim that the
   ethical realities are unreal. It claims that the structural rules are real, and that the rules
   point toward the ethical realities. The distinction is the distinction between the structural
   order and the ethical order; it is kept throughout the book. a
   a
       [C17-1] For the comparative treatment of the traditional names and their relation to the
       framework’s structural rules, see the separate treatise on the dialogues. The comparison is
       historical and comparative; it carries no justificatory weight.

   Remark 17.7 (Why the Distinction Matters)

   Intra-realm dynamics are the rules of what occurs in a realm among its own elements.
   Inter-realm dynamics are the rules of the relations among realms. The same rule may
   serve in both. For example, fidelity concerns the relation of a sign to the structure it
   signifies, and in doing so regulates a relation across realms. The distinction is kept so
   that the rules of a barzakhic realm are not read as rules of passage only. The hub has
   an internal structure, and its rules govern that structure as well as its relations to other
   realms.

   Remark 17.8 (Status of the Distinction)

   The assignment of rules to the two kinds is an estimate ((E)): it is a structural estimate.
   A different division that did the same work would not conflict with the framework. The
   framework’s claim is that some such distinction is needed, not that this particular division
17.8. The Unity of the Rules of the Barzakhic Realms                                            181


   is final.


17.8      The Unity of the Rules of the Barzakhic Realms
The nine rules are now in place. The chapter’s principal contribution is the claim that they are
not independent. They are related by the structure of the transition from unity to multiplicity.

   Principle 17.11 (The Unity of the Rules of the Barzakhic Realms)

   (A) The rules of the three barzakhic realms are not independent. They are related by the
   structure of the transition from unity to multiplicity: the rules of each hub are the rules
   of one of the three transitions between the four fundamental realms.

   The principle is a commitment, and it is stated as one. Its support is the argument that
follows. It would be refuted by showing that the rules of a hub are not the rules of a transition,
or that the relation among the three hubs is not one of three transitions.
   The argument proceeds in three steps.

First step: from First Determination to Structural Determination. The rules of the
Hub of Decree (proportion, order, harmony) are the rules of the first transition—from the First
Determination to the Structural Determination. They govern the specification of unity into
general multiplicity.

Second step: from Structural Determination to Relational Manifestation. The
rules of the Hub of Signification (truthfulness, accuracy, fidelity) are the rules of the second
transition—from the Structural Determination to the Relational Manifestation. They govern the
contextualization of general multiplicity into relational multiplicity.

Third step: from Relational Manifestation to Material Manifestation. The rules
of the Hub of Realization (proportion in realization, preservation of the realized, continuation
of realization) are the rules of the third transition—from the Relational Manifestation to the
Material Manifestation. They govern the realization of relational multiplicity into material
multiplicity.
   The three steps together show that the nine rules are not three independent sets but one
structure articulated in three transitions. The structure is the structure of refraction, which
transforms unity into multiplicity through the barzakhic realms.

   Remark 17.9 (The Unity Is Not Merely an Ethical Unity)

   The unity of the rules of the barzakhic realms is a structural unity. The framework
   does not claim that the three hubs together constitute a moral order, or that their rules
   prescribe how anything ought to be. The unity is the unity of three transitions, each of
   which has its own structural constraints. The reader who reads the unity as an ethical
   claim has misread it; the reader who reads it as a structural claim has read it correctly.
182                                             Chapter 17. The Rules of the Barzakhic Realms


   But the structural unity is not self-grounded. The unity points beyond itself to the ground
   that the framework does not describe. The traditions speak of the ground of the unity as
   the order through which what is becomes determinate, and as the wisdom through which
   the order is sustained. The framework does not claim that its structural unity is that
   order, and it does not claim that the order is unreal. It claims that the structural unity is
   real, and that the unity points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between
   the structure and the ground of the structure; it is kept throughout the book.

   Remark 17.10 (The Three Hubs Point Beyond Themselves)

   The three hubs, taken together, describe the structure of transition from unity to multi-
   plicity. The structure is real, and the framework’s claim is that the structure is invariant
   and describable. But the structure is not self-grounded. The three hubs are the levels of
   mediation within the structure; they are not the ground of the structure. The structure
   points beyond itself to the ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction
   is the distinction between the structure of transition and the ground of the structure; it is
   kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the structure as the command through which measure
   is apportioned, the wisdom through which meaning is signified, and the power through
   which what is possible is realized. The framework does not claim that its three hubs are
   those three, and it does not claim that they are unreal. It claims that the three hubs are
   real levels of the structure, and that the levels point beyond themselves. The reader who
   identifies the three hubs with the command, the wisdom, and the power is free to do so;
   the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the
   identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.

      The unity of the rules is summarized in the following table.

17.9        The Complete Set of Governing Dynamics
With the thirteen rules of the fundamental realms and the nine rules of the barzakhic realms, the
framework’s complete set of governing dynamics is in place. The set is stated in the following
table.


         Realm                           Rules

         Hub of Decree                   Proportion, Order, Harmony (3)

   The order of the table is the order of expression, from unity to multiplicity. The four
fundamental realms alternate with the three hubs, reflecting the structure of transition: each
hub sits between two fundamental realms and governs the transition between them.

   Remark 17.11 (The Complete Set Is Not the Final Set)

   The complete set of governing dynamics is complete in the sense that it covers all seven
   realms. It is not complete in the sense that it is final. The rules may be refined, extended,
   or revised as the framework develops. The framework states the set at the strength it has:
   it is the set of rules that the framework, at its present stage, has articulated, and it is
   offered for criticism and revision.
   The complete set is also not self-sufficient. The set describes the structure of the seven
   realms; it does not describe the ground of the structure. The set points beyond itself
   to the ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction
   between the structure and the ground of the structure; it is kept throughout the book, and
   it is the structural ground of the framework’s silence on what the rules are in themselves.


   Remark 17.12 (The Set Is a Commitment)

   The complete set is ((A)): it is adopted as a commitment of the framework, not proved
   from the framework’s other principles. Its support is the argument of the two chapters of
   the present part. It would be refuted by showing that a rule of the set is not a structural
   constraint of its realm, or that a structural constraint of some realm is missing from the
   set. The reader who wishes to challenge the set knows where to press.

17.10        The Rules and the Four-Column Framework
The rules of the barzakhic realms are governing dynamics of the four-column framework, as the
rules of the fundamental realms are. They are the third column—the patterns that explain how
light is regulated in each barzakhic realm.

      Four-Column Framework           Rules of the Barzakhic Realms

      Fixed elements                  Identities and manifestations.
      Fluid element                   Light (regulated).
      Governing dynamics              The rules of the three barzakhic realms.
      Context                         The three barzakhic realms.

      The table is analytical, not substantial. The four columns are analytical roles; the table does
not say that a hub breaks down into four independent entities. The hub is a level of being; the
four columns are the roles through which the level is understood. The rules of the hub are the
third of these roles; they are what explains how the fluid element (light) is regulated in that hub.

   Remark 17.13 (The Two Sets Together)

   The rules of the barzakhic realms are not the only governing dynamics. The rules of the
   fundamental realms, stated in the previous chapter, are also governing dynamics. The
   two sets together constitute the framework’s complete set of governing dynamics: thirteen
   rules of being and nine rules of transition, twenty-two in all. The two sets are related: the
   rules of the fundamental realms are the rules of what is within each realm; the rules of the
   barzakhic realms are the rules of how realms are related through the hubs.



17.11        What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
      First, the chapter does not argue that there are exactly three hubs. It states three, and it
argues for their unity. The argument that three functions of mediation are required—and that
no fewer will do—is given in the part of the book that treats the arguments. The reader who
wishes to see the argument is directed there.
      Second, the chapter does not argue for the irreducibility of the barzakhic realms. The
argument that the three hubs are independently real levels, not reducible to functions of the
fundamental realms, is also given in the part of the book that treats the arguments. The present
chapter has stated the rules of the hubs; the later part argues for the hubs themselves.
      Third, the chapter does not develop the relation between the rules of the barzakhic realms
and the other parts of the framework. The rules of the hubs are stated, and their unity is argued,
but how they interact with the rules of the fundamental realms, with the fluid element, and with
the fixed elements, is left for later parts. The present chapter has completed the statement of
the governing dynamics; the later parts apply them.
      Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of the rules of transition. It
claims to have described the structure of the rules, and the structure points beyond itself to the
17.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                               185


ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the
structure and the ground of the structure; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is stated here
as the chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Can you identify, in a process of transmission you know well, the three levels the chapter
distinguishes: the allotment of measure, the signification of meaning, and the realization of
the transmitted thing? Which level is most easily overlooked, and why? What does its being
overlooked tell you about the relation between the three levels?

With this chapter, the framework’s treatment of the third column is complete. The twenty-two
rules of the seven realms are in place. The next part turns to the arguments: the reasons why
the principles established in the parts that precede this one should be accepted, not merely stated.
The rules of being and the rules of transition are stated; the arguments for them are the subject
of the part that follows.
