Chapter 18

The Necessity of Expression


Scope. This chapter opens the part of the book that gives the arguments for the principles
established in the preceding parts. It states the principle of expression, gives two independent
arguments for it, and offers a third that is conditional and is retained only as a statement of
what expression is a condition of. It distinguishes the necessity of the tendency to express from
the degree of structural fidelity with which any particular manifestation is realized. Its claims
are structural; where the chapter is silent on questions of value or psychology, the silence is not
a denial but a recognition that the structural description is not the whole of what can be said.
Where the chapter speaks of “tendency,” “realization,” “degree of structural fidelity,” “finding,”
or “hindrance,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.



18.1     A Scene

Consider a seed. Inside the seed, there is a tree—not the tree as it will be, but the tree as it
can be: the structure, the pattern, the form that the seed carries. The seed does not choose to
become a tree; it becomes a tree when the conditions are right. And even when the conditions
are not right, the seed does not lose the tendency to become a tree; it waits, and the tendency
remains. If the seed is planted, it sprouts; if it is not, it remains a seed, with the tendency
unrealized but not absent.
   The seed’s tendency is not a choice, and it is not a mechanism imposed from without. It is
what the seed is: an identity that expresses itself in a manifestation, when the conditions for
expression are present. The tree that grows is not the seed; it is the seed’s expression, a new
entity in its own realm. And yet the tree is not unrelated to the seed; it is the seed made visible,
the identity enacted in a new form.
   The scene is not a metaphor for something else; it is a case of the structure the present chapter
will state. The seed is an identity; the tree is a manifestation; the growth is the expression that
connects them. The expression is not a choice the seed makes; it is what the seed is. An identity
is not something that has expression as an option; it is something whose being is expressed.
   The scene poses a question. What is the structure of this tendency? Is it a contingent feature
of some identities, or a structural necessity of every identity? Does it admit of degrees—does
the seed express itself more or less completely depending on conditions—and if so, how does the
necessity of the tendency relate to the degrees of its realization? The present chapter answers
these questions. Its answer is the principle of expression.




                                                187
188                                                     Chapter 18. The Necessity of Expression


18.2       The Question
The preceding parts of the book have established the framework’s principal structures. Part
I established the four-column framework: fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics,
context. Part II established the seven realms: four fundamental and three barzakhic. Part
III established the fixed elements: identity, defined as invariance under a class of allowable
transformations, and manifestation, defined as the contextually realized appearance of an identity
in a receiving realm. Part IV established the fluid element: light, defined as the trans-categorical
substance that is the condition of possibility of relation. Part V established the governing
dynamics: the twenty-two rules of the seven realms.
      The present part turns from the statement of principles to their argument. Each chapter in
this part gives the arguments for one of the principles established earlier. The present chapter
gives the arguments for the principle of expression.
      The question is: why must an identity express itself? The framework has spoken of expression
throughout the preceding parts—in the definition of manifestation, in the account of light, in
the rules of the realms. But it has not yet given the argument that expression is necessary. The
present chapter gives it.
      Three things must be distinguished.

The principle. That every identity tends toward expression, and that this tendency is struc-
tural, not contingent. The principle is the chapter’s central claim.

The arguments. Two independent arguments are given, and a third is offered as conditional
and not independent. Each argument has its own premises, and each can be assessed separately.

The distinction. The distinction between the necessity of the tendency to express and the
degree of structural fidelity with which any particular manifestation is realized. The distinction
is what allows the framework to say both that expression is necessary and that a manifestation
may be realized at a lower or higher degree of fidelity.
      The chapter treats the three in turn. It states the principle, gives the two independent
arguments, gives the conditional argument and explains why it is not independent, and draws
the distinction between tendency and fidelity. It ends with what it does not establish and with
the epistemic status of its claims.


18.3       The Principle of Expression

   Principle 18.1 (Expression as Structural Necessity)

   (A) Every identity, by its very nature, tends toward expression. Expression is not a
   contingent choice but a structural necessity. Expression necessarily involves three moments:
   manifestation descent (the identity appears in another realm), plurality (the identity can
   appear in several manifestations), and ontological novelty (each manifestation is a reality
   of its own in the realm where it is realized). These three moments are not temporally
18.3. The Principle of Expression                                                             189


   successive but structurally inseparable.

   The principle makes three claims.

First claim: expression is intrinsic. Identity is not something that can express itself or not;
identity is its expression. To be an identity is to be in the structural act of expressing itself—
across contexts, through light, in manifestation. The claim is not that the identity chooses to
express itself, nor that something outside the identity compels it. The claim is that expression
is what the identity is: an identity without expression would not be an identity at all, but an
abstraction.

Second claim: expression is necessary as a tendency. Expression is not a possibility that
some identities have and others lack; every identity tends toward expression. That the tendency
is necessary does not make the realization of any particular manifestation at a particular degree
of structural fidelity necessary. The necessity is not a contingent fact about the world; it is a
structural feature of identity itself.

Third claim: expression is structural. Expression is neither imposed from without nor
motivated from within; it is the structure of the relation between identity and its manifestations.
It is not a choice that the identity makes; it is the form of the identity’s being.
   The principle is (A): it is adopted as a foundational commitment of the framework. It is not
derived from any of the framework’s other principles; it is one of the principles on which the
others rest. Its support is the two arguments given in the next sections, and its fruitfulness in
the chapters that follow. It would be refuted by showing that an identity can exist without the
tendency to express itself—a case the framework does not know how to construct.

   Remark 18.1 (The Tendency Points Beyond Itself)

   The tendency to express is a real structural feature of identity; the framework’s claim
   is that the tendency is intrinsic, necessary, and structural. But the tendency is not
   self-grounded. The tendency is the tendency of an identity; it is not the ground of its own
   being. The tendency points beyond itself to what grounds the identity, and through the
   identity to what grounds the tendency. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real,
   and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction is the
   distinction between the tendency and the ground of the tendency; it is kept throughout
   the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the tendency as the praise that every creature
   offers to its source, and as the inclination that the creator has placed in every creature
   toward its own perfection. The framework does not claim that its structural tendency is
   that praise, and it does not claim that the praise is unreal. It claims that the tendency
   is a real structural feature, and that the feature points beyond itself. The reader who
   identifies the structural tendency with the praise of the creatures is free to do so; the
   reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the
190                                                     Chapter 18. The Necessity of Expression


   identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



18.4        The Three Moments of Expression

The principle states that expression involves three moments. They are not temporally successive;
they are structurally inseparable.


First moment: manifestational descent. The identity appears in a realm other than its
own, in a form fitted to that realm. Descent means appearance in another realm; it does not
mean passage through every realm between, as the non-necessity of downward passage (argued
in the part of the book that treated the realms) established. The barzakhic realms regulate,
apportion, and realize what appears, but they are not stations through which every appearance
must travel.


Second moment: plurality. The identity can appear in several manifestations. A single man-
ifestation could not be recognized as the expression of an identity: it would be indistinguishable
from the identity or from an unrelated thing. Plurality is the structural condition under which a
manifestation can be recognized as an expression of an identity.


Third moment: ontological novelty. Each manifestation is a reality of its own in the realm
where it is realized. It is not a copy of the identity; it is not the identity; it is a new entity of
that realm. The novelty is what makes the manifestation a manifestation, not a repetition of the
identity.
      The three moments are not separable. Without manifestational descent there would be no
expression: the identity would remain unexpressed in its own realm. Without plurality there
would be no way to recognize an appearance as the expression of an identity. Without ontological
novelty the appearance would be only a repetition of the identity and not a manifestation in a
realm. The three are three aspects of one expression, not three stages of a process.

   Remark 18.2 (The Three Moments Are Structural, Not Temporal)

   The reader who reads the three moments as a sequence—first descent, then plurality, then
   novelty—has misread them. The three are structurally inseparable; each is a condition of
   the others, and none precedes the others in time. A manifestation is at once a descent, one
   of a plurality, and a novelty. The distinction among the three is analytical, not temporal.
   The three moments, taken together, describe the structure of expression. The structure is
   real, and the framework’s claim is that the structure is invariant and describable. But the
   structure is not self-grounded. The structure points beyond itself to the source that is
   expressed and to the ground that makes the expression possible. The distinction is the
   distinction between the structure of expression and the ground of expression; it is kept
   throughout the book.
18.5. First Argument: From Intelligibility                                                    191


18.5      First Argument: From Intelligibility
The first argument for the principle of expression is from the intelligibility of identity.

Argument from Intelligibility.     1. An identity is a structure that persists through transforma-
      tion.

   2. To persist through transformation, an identity must be expressed in its transformations—it
      must be manifested in some form.

   3. An identity that did not express itself would not persist through transformation; it would
      have no transformations, and therefore no persistence.

   4. Conclusion: expression is a condition of the very concept of identity.


   The argument shows that expression is not an additional feature of identity, added to it from
outside. It is a constitutive feature: to be an identity is to be the kind of thing that expresses
itself. An identity that never expressed itself would not be an identity at all; it would be an
abstraction, a pattern with no instances. The concept of identity requires expression, because
identity is defined as invariance under transformation, and invariance is not intelligible without
transformations in which the invariance is exhibited.
   The argument’s premise (1) is the definition of identity, established in the part of the book
that treated the fixed elements. The argument’s premise (2) is what the present chapter adds:
that persistence through transformation requires manifestation. The two premises together yield
the conclusion. The reader who accepts the definition accepts premise (1); the reader who accepts
that invariance requires transformations in which it is exhibited accepts premise (2).

   Remark 18.3 (The Argument Is Not a Proof That Everything Manifests)

   The argument shows that expression is a condition of the concept of identity. It does not
   show that every identity is, in fact, manifested in every realm, or that every identity is
   manifested at all. It shows that an identity that never expressed itself would not be an
   identity in the framework’s sense. Whether a given identity is manifested in a given realm
   is a separate question, answered by the conditions of that realm and by the identity’s
   tendency.


   Remark 18.4 (The Argument Points Beyond Itself)

   The argument shows that expression is a condition of the concept of identity. The argument
   is a structural argument: it establishes that the structure of identity requires expression.
   But the structure of identity is not self-grounded. The structure points beyond itself to
   what grounds the identity, and through the identity to what grounds the expression. The
   framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described
   by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of identity and
   the ground of identity; it is kept throughout the book.
192                                                        Chapter 18. The Necessity of Expression


   The traditions speak of the ground of identity as the source from which every identity
   comes, and to which every identity returns. The framework does not claim that its
   structural identity is that source, and it does not claim that the source is unreal. It claims
   that the structure of identity is real, and that the structure points beyond itself. The
   reader who identifies the structural identity with the source is free to do so; the reader
   who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity,
   because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



18.6        Second Argument: Transcendental
The second argument for the principle of expression is transcendental. It proceeds from the
possibility of experience to its condition.

Transcendental Argument.          1. We have experiences of manifestation—of appearances, states,
        and properties.

  2. Such experiences are possible only if there is a relation between the manifestation and that
        which manifests itself.

  3. This relation is expression: the manifestation is the expression of the identity.

  4. Therefore, expression is a transcendental condition of the possibility of manifestation.

  5. Since manifestation is actual, expression must be actual.


      The argument is transcendental in the Kantian sense: it proceeds from what is given in
experience to the conditions under which the given is possible. What is given is manifestation—
the appearance of things, the states and properties we encounter. The condition of the given
is expression—the relation between the appearance and what appears. The argument’s force
is that the given cannot be what it is without the condition; the manifestation cannot be a
manifestation without being the manifestation of something.
      The argument’s premise (1) is the fact of experience; it is not argued for, but it is the starting
point of any transcendental argument. The argument’s premise (2) is what the framework adds:
that experience of manifestation requires a relation between the manifestation and that which
manifests itself. The reader who denies premise (2) denies that manifestation is manifestation of
anything; the reader who accepts it accepts the conclusion.

   Remark 18.5 (The Two Arguments Are Independent)

   The first argument proceeds from the concept of identity; the second proceeds from the
   fact of experience. The two are independent: one can accept the first and reject the second,
   or accept the second and reject the first. The framework offers both because each has its
   own force, and because the two together strengthen the case for the principle. A reader
   who rejects one of the two arguments can still accept the principle on the strength of the
18.7. Third Argument: Conditional                                                                193


   other.
   But the two arguments are not unrelated. Both arguments point beyond themselves to
   the same structure: expression is the structure of identity, and identity is the structure of
   what is. The structure is real, and the framework’s claim is that the structure is invariant
   and describable. But the structure is not self-grounded. The structure points beyond itself
   to the ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction
   between the structure and the ground of the structure; it is kept throughout the book.



18.7        Third Argument: Conditional
The third argument is of a different kind, and the difference must be stated. It is offered as a
conditional, and it is not offered as independent support for the principle.

Conditional Argument from the Desire to Find.         1. If every identity stands in the structural
     relation of finding in the reflection of its expression in another identity’s expression,

  2. then that relation can obtain only if identities express themselves in forms other identities
     can encounter.

  3. Hence, given that relation, expression is a structural condition of the possibility of finding
     among identities.


   The argument is conditional: it does not assert that the relation of finding obtains; it asserts
that if the relation obtains, expression is its condition. The conditional is true, but its truth
does not establish the antecedent. The framework argues for the antecedent—the structural
relation of finding—in a later chapter. The argument here is offered only as a statement of what
expression is a condition of: the possibility of finding among identities.

   Remark 18.6 (Why This Is Not Independent Support)

   The argument cannot be used as independent support for the principle of expression,
   because the relation of finding is itself derived from the principle of expression. To use
   the relation to support the principle would be circular: the principle would be supported
   by a consequence of itself. The framework states the conditional to be explicit about the
   relation between expression and finding, not to strengthen the case for expression. The
   support of the principle rests on the first two arguments; the conditional is a clarification,
   not a proof.
   The relation of finding, too, points beyond itself. The relation of finding is a structural
   relation among identities; it is not the ground of the relation. The relation points beyond
   itself to the source that makes finding possible, and to the ground that makes the source
   real. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground
   is unreal. It claims that the relation of finding is real, and that the relation points beyond
   itself. The distinction is the distinction between the relation and the ground of the relation;
194                                                     Chapter 18. The Necessity of Expression


   it is kept throughout the book.


      The distinction between the two independent arguments and the conditional is important.
The framework does not claim three independent proofs of the principle; it claims two, and
one conditional that clarifies what expression is a condition of. A reader who counts three
independent arguments has miscounted; a reader who counts two independent arguments and
one conditional has counted correctly.



18.8       Tendency and Structural Fidelity

The principle of expression states that every identity tends toward expression. It does not state
that every manifestation is realized at the same degree of fidelity. The distinction between the
tendency and the degree of fidelity is what allows the framework to say both that expression is
necessary and that manifestations differ.

   Definition 18.1 (Tendency to Express)

   The tendency to express is necessary. Every identity, by its nature, tends toward expression.
   This tendency cannot be structurally unrealized; it can only be structurally hindered.


   Definition 18.2 (Degree of Structural Fidelity)

   The degree of structural fidelity of an expression is not necessary. An identity can be
   realized at varying degrees of structural fidelity—it can be manifested in forms that
   preserve more or less of its essential determination, and, at the limit, in forms that do not
   preserve it at all.


      The distinction resolves two tensions that might otherwise appear in the framework.


First tension: necessity and non-realization. The framework says that expression is
necessary, and it also says that a manifestation may fail to be realized in a given realm. The two
statements appear to conflict. The distinction resolves the conflict: expression is necessary at the
level of tendency, but not at the level of realization at a particular degree of structural fidelity.
The tendency cannot be structurally unrealized; the realization at a particular degree can.


Second tension: rigidity and dynamism. The framework says that identity is rigid (it
admits no degrees), and it also says that expression is dynamic (it varies with the receiving
realm). The two statements appear to conflict. The distinction resolves the conflict: identity is
rigid with respect to its manifestations, but dynamic with respect to the higher contexts in which
it is expressed. The rigidity belongs to the identity; the dynamism belongs to the expression.
18.9. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                      195


   Remark 18.7 (What “Degree of Structural Fidelity” Measures)

   The degree of structural fidelity measures the extent to which a manifestation preserves
   the essential determination of its source. It is not a measure of value, importance, or
   success in any evaluative sense. It is a measure of a structural relation: how much of the
   source’s essential determination is preserved in the manifestation. A manifestation at a
   low degree of fidelity is not thereby a defective manifestation; it is a manifestation whose
   structural relation to its source is at a certain degree. The framework does not attach
   value to the degree; it states the degree as a structural fact.
   The degree of structural fidelity points beyond itself. The degree measures the structural
   relation; it does not measure the fulfillment of the relation. The fulfillment of the relation
   is not a degree among degrees; it is the ground of the degrees. The framework does not
   describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the
   degrees are real, and that the degrees point beyond themselves to the fulfillment that the
   framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the degree and
   the fulfillment of the degree; it is kept throughout the book.


   Remark 18.8 (Hindrance Is Not Failure)

   A tendency may be structurally hindered—the conditions for its realization may not be
   present—without the tendency being destroyed. The seed that is not planted retains its
   tendency to become a tree; the tendency is hindered, not eliminated. The framework’s
   claim is structural: the tendency is not unrealizable, but it may be unrealized in a given
   case. The distinction between hindered tendency and unrealized tendency is the distinction
   between a tendency that has not yet expressed itself and a tendency that has failed to
   express itself. The framework does not use the language of failure; it speaks of hindrance,
   not of defect.
   The hindered tendency, too, points beyond itself. The tendency is not destroyed by
   hindrance; it is preserved by the ground that sustains it. The framework does not describe
   the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the tendency is
   real, and that the tendency, even when hindered, points beyond itself. The distinction is
   the distinction between the tendency and the ground of the tendency; it is kept throughout
   the book.



18.9     What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
   First, the chapter does not argue for the antecedent of the conditional argument. The
conditional argument assumes that the relation of finding obtains among identities, and it does
not argue for that relation. The argument for the relation of finding is given in a later chapter.
The present chapter has stated the conditional; the later chapter establishes its antecedent.
   Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of the three moments of expression. The
moments are named, and their inseparability is stated, but the detailed treatment of each—how
196                                                        Chapter 18. The Necessity of Expression


manifestational descent differs from passage, how plurality is the condition of recognition, how
ontological novelty relates to the definition of manifestation—is deferred to the parts of the book
that develop those topics. The present chapter has introduced the moments; the later parts
develop them.
      Third, the chapter does not develop the full account of the degree of structural fidelity. The
definition is given, and its role in resolving the two tensions is stated, but the detailed treatment
of how the degree is measured, and how it relates to viability, is developed in a later part. The
present chapter has distinguished tendency from fidelity; the later part develops the distinction.
      Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of expression. It claims to
have described the structure of expression, and the structure points beyond itself to the ground
that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the structure
and the ground of the structure; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is stated here as the
chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know that has never been expressed—a thought you have not spoken, a
feeling you have not shown, a plan you have not carried out. Is it really an identity, in the
framework’s sense, if it has never been manifested? What does the framework’s answer to this
question tell you about the relation between the tendency to express and the realization of
expression?

The next chapter turns to the minimality of the four grades of multiplicity. It argues that four
qualitatively distinct grades are required in the analysis of expression, and that no fewer will
do. The argument for the four grades is the framework’s answer to the question of why the
fundamental realms are four and not some other number.
Chapter 19

The Minimality of the Four Fundamental Grades


Scope. This chapter argues that four qualitatively distinct grades of multiplicity are required
in the analysis of expression, and that no fewer will do. It does not claim that there are only
four levels of being; the framework’s ontology has seven. The chapter’s claim is analytical, not
ontological: it is about the grades the analysis of expression requires, not about the levels reality
contains. Its claims are analytical; where the chapter is silent on questions of religion or value,
the silence is not a denial but a recognition that the analytical description is not the whole
of what can be said. Where the chapter speaks of “grade,” “multiplicity,” “form,” “content,”
“relation,” “matter,” “meaning,” or “value,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the
definitions in this chapter.


19.1      A Scene
Consider a single word. The word justice can be considered in four ways, and each consideration
is different.
    First, the word as a mark on a page: black ink on white paper, occupying a certain space,
in a certain font. The word as a mark is one thing among many, with a position, a duration, a
physical presence. If the page is burned, the mark is gone.
    Second, the word as a form: the sequence of letters j-u-s-t-i-c-e, in that order, spelled
according to the conventions of English. The form is not the ink; the same form can be written
in pencil, printed in a book, typed on a screen, or traced in the air. The form persists across its
material realizations; it is not tied to any one of them.
    Third, the word as a meaning: what the word signifies, in the network of English words,
the concept it names, the role it plays in legal, ethical, and political discourse. The meaning
is not the form; the same meaning can be expressed by other forms (in other languages, by
paraphrase, by gesture). The meaning is relational: it is what it is by virtue of its place among
other meanings.
    Fourth, the word as a unity: what makes the mark, the form, and the meaning one word,
rather than three unrelated things that happen to be associated. The unity is not the mark, not
the form, not the meaning; it is what holds them together as one.
    Four ways of considering one word, and each is distinct from the others. The mark is physical;
the form is formal; the meaning is relational; the unity is what makes the other three one thing.
To collapse any two of them—to say that the mark is the form, or that the form is the meaning,
or that the meaning is the unity—is to lose something the analysis needs.
    The scene poses a question. Are these four ways of considering the word reducible to fewer?
Could the mark and the form be one, or the form and the meaning, or the meaning and the unity?
The present chapter argues that they cannot. The four grades are minimal: each is required, and

                                                197
198                                Chapter 19. The Minimality of the Four Fundamental Grades


none is reducible to another. The argument is the framework’s answer to the question of why
the fundamental realms are four and not some other number.

   Remark 19.1 (The Four Grades Point Beyond Themselves)

   The four grades of the word—the mark, the form, the meaning, and the unity—are distinct,
   and the chapter argues that the analysis of expression requires all four. The framework’s
   claim is that the four grades are real analytical distinctions, and that the analysis is
   describable. But the four grades are not self-grounded. The four grades are the grades
   of the analysis; they are not the ground of the analyzed. The unity that holds the mark,
   the form, and the meaning together is not exhausted by the analysis of the four grades;
   the unity points beyond the analysis to the ground that the analysis does not describe.
   The distinction is the distinction between the analysis of the grades and the ground of the
   unity; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the unity as the source from which every determinate
   thing comes, and as the order through which the determinate thing is what it is. The
   framework does not claim that its four grades are that source or that order, and it does
   not claim that the source or the order is unreal. It claims that the four grades are real
   analytical distinctions, and that the distinctions point beyond themselves. The reader
   who identifies the four grades with the order is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes
   them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity
   is a question for another inquiry.



19.2        The Question
The previous chapter stated and argued the principle of expression: every identity tends toward
expression, and expression is structural, not contingent. The chapter distinguished the necessity
of the tendency from the degree of structural fidelity with which any particular manifestation is
realized.
      The present chapter asks a further question. If expression is the appearance of an identity in
a realm, what kinds of realm are required for expression to occur? The framework’s answer is
that four qualitatively distinct grades of multiplicity are required, and that no fewer will do. The
four grades correspond to the four fundamental realms: the First Determination (no multiplicity),
the Structural Determination (multiplicity of form), the Relational Manifestation (multiplicity of
relation), and the Material Manifestation (multiplicity of matter).
      Two aspects of the question must be distinguished.


The minimality aspect. Are four grades required, or could fewer do the same work? The
chapter argues that four are required, and that merging any two adjacent grades would remove a
distinction that expression needs.


The maximality aspect. Are four grades sufficient, or is a fifth required? The chapter
argues that no fifth grade has been shown to be necessary, and that the standard candidates are
19.3. Grades of Multiplicity                                                                     199


reducible to one of the four. The claim of maximality is an estimate, not a proof.
   The chapter ends with a distinction that is essential to the argument: the distinction between
analytical minimality (the four grades required by the analysis of expression) and ontological
multiplicity (the seven realms that the framework’s ontology contains). The distinction is what
prevents the chapter’s claim from being read as a claim about how many levels of being there are.


19.3     Grades of Multiplicity
The chapter’s argument turns on a distinction between two kinds of difference. The first is
quantitative: how many things there are. The second is qualitative: what kind of multiplicity
the things exhibit. The distinction is stated in a definition.

   Definition 19.1 (Grade of Multiplicity)

   A grade of multiplicity is a qualitatively distinct way in which many things can stand to
   one another, as opposed to a merely quantitative difference of how many there are.

   The distinction between quantitative and qualitative difference is not a novelty. It is the
distinction between asking “how many?” and asking “of what kind?” The two questions are
different, and an answer to one does not answer the other. A collection of three things and a
collection of three thousand things may exhibit the same grade of multiplicity (both are material
multiplicities, say); a collection of three things and a collection of three other things may exhibit
different grades (one material, one relational). The number is not the grade.
   The framework’s claim is that expression requires four grades. The four are: no multiplicity
(the First Determination), multiplicity of form (the Structural Determination), multiplicity of
relation (the Relational Manifestation), and multiplicity of matter (the Material Manifestation).
The four are defined by the distinctions among them, and the argument for their necessity turns
on those distinctions.


19.4     The Argument for Four
The argument for the minimality of four grades is a reductio of the alternative. It proceeds by
supposing that two adjacent grades are not distinguished, and showing that the merger removes
a distinction expression needs.

Argument for the Minimality of Four Grades. Premises:

  P1 Expression is the appearance of unity in multiplicity (the principle of expression, argued in
      the previous chapter).

  P2 Multiplicity has qualitative grades, not only quantitative ones. ((A))

  P3 The qualitative grades that expression requires are: no multiplicity (pure unity); multiplicity
      of form (what is general and lawful, without particular content); multiplicity of relation
     (particular content in structural connection, without extension); and multiplicity of matter
     (content with location and succession). ((A))
200                                Chapter 19. The Minimality of the Four Fundamental Grades


      Argument:

  1. Suppose two adjacent grades were not distinguished.

  2. Merging no-multiplicity and form would remove the distinction between there being nothing
        plural and there being at least a minimal plurality of laws.

  3. Merging form and relation would remove the distinction between the general and the
        contextual: form is general, relation is contextual.

  4. Merging relation and matter would remove the distinction between what has structural
        meaning and what has location: relation is not extended, matter is.

  5. Each merger removes a distinction that expression needs. Hence the four grades are needed.



      The argument is as strong as P2 and P3. It is relative to them; they are commitments and
are stated as such. A reader who denies P2 denies that multiplicity has qualitative grades, and
with that denial the argument fails. A reader who denies P3 denies the specific list of grades,
and with that denial the argument’s conclusion is in question. The framework adopts P2 and P3,
states them as commitments, and offers the argument as what follows from them.

   Remark 19.2 (The Argument Points Beyond Itself)

   The argument establishes that the analysis of expression requires four grades. The
   argument is analytical: it shows what the analysis of expression requires. But the analysis
   is not self-grounded. The analysis is the analysis of expression; it is not the ground of the
   expression. The analysis points beyond itself to the identity whose expression is analyzed,
   and to the ground that makes the identity real. The framework’s claim is that the analysis
   is real, invariant, and describable; it does not claim that the analysis is the whole of what
   is analyzed, and it does not claim that the ground is nothing. The distinction is the
   distinction between the analysis and the ground of the analysis; it is kept throughout the
   book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the analysis as the wisdom through which what
   is becomes determinate, and as the order through which the determinate thing is what
   it is. The framework does not claim that its four grades are that wisdom or that order,
   and it does not claim that the wisdom or the order is unreal. It claims that the four
   grades are real analytical distinctions, and that the distinctions point beyond themselves.
   The reader who identifies the four grades with the wisdom is free to do so; the reader
   who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity,
   because the identity is a question for another inquiry.

   Remark 19.3 (The Argument Is Not a Proof from Nothing)

   The argument does not prove the four grades from premises that need no support. It
   proves the four grades from P2 and P3, which are themselves commitments. The reader
19.5. The Limit of the Claim of Maximality                                                      201


   who accepts the commitments accepts the conclusion; the reader who denies one of them
   denies the conclusion, and the framework does not pretend otherwise. The argument’s
   value is not that it establishes the four grades without assumptions; it is that it makes the
   assumptions visible, and shows exactly what follows from them.


   Remark 19.4 (Why Four and Not Five)

   The argument establishes that four grades are required. It does not establish that no fifth
   is required. The question of a fifth grade is the subject of the next section. The present
   section’s claim is minimal: four grades are needed, and merging any two adjacent grades
   removes a distinction expression needs. The claim that no more than four are needed is a
   separate claim, with a separate argument.



19.5     The Limit of the Claim of Maximality
The previous section argued that four grades are required. The present section considers whether
a fifth is required. The chapter’s answer is that no fifth grade has been shown to be necessary.

Argument Against a Fifth Grade.       1. A further grade would be a way many things stand to
     one another that is not any of the four.

  2. The standard candidates are reducible to one of the four: temporal multiplicity is a
     dimension of matter; axiological determination, if it is a grade of multiplicity at all, is a
     kind of relation; mathematical multiplicity is a multiplicity of form.

  3. So no further grade of multiplicity has been shown to be required.


   The argument is not a proof that no fifth grade can be found. It is an argument that no fifth
grade has been found, and that the standard candidates are reducible to one of the four. The
claim is an estimate, not a proof; it would be refuted by a grade of multiplicity that cannot be
reduced to the four.

   Remark 19.5 (The Maximality Claim Is an Estimate)

   The claim that no fifth grade is required is (E): it is an estimate, not a proof. It says that
   no further grade is known to be required, not that no further grade could be required.
   The framework offers the claim at exactly that strength, and invites the reader to propose
   a candidate that resists reduction. A candidate that does so would refute the estimate; a
   candidate that does not would strengthen it.


   Remark 19.6 (What Would Refute the Estimate)

   A grade of multiplicity that cannot be reduced to any of the four would refute the estimate.
   The framework does not claim that no such grade could be found; it claims that none
202                                Chapter 19. The Minimality of the Four Fundamental Grades


   has been found, and that the standard candidates have been considered. The reader who
   wishes to challenge the estimate knows where to press: at the reducibility of the standard
   candidates, or at the possibility of a candidate not yet considered.



19.6        Analytical Minimality and Ontological Multiplicity
The chapter’s claim has been that four grades are minimal for the analysis of expression. The
claim must not be confused with a different claim: that there are four levels of being. The
framework’s ontology has seven realms, four fundamental and three barzakhic. The distinction
between the two numbers is essential, and the present section states it.
      Three numbers have appeared in the framework so far: four columns, four grades of multiplicity,
and seven realms. They concern three different things.

       Number           What It Counts                       Where Argued

       Four columns     Analytical roles of an explanation   The first part of the book.
       Four grades      Qualitatively distinct grades of     The present chapter.
                        multiplicity   (the   fundamental
                        realms)
       Seven realms     Independently real levels of being: The second part of the book, and
                        four fundamental, three barzakhic    the chapter that argued for the
                                                             minimality of the three hubs.

      The table is not a proof; it is a map. Its use is to show that the three numbers are not in
competition. The four columns are analytical roles; the four grades are the grades of multiplicity
the analysis requires; the seven realms are the independently real levels of being. The three
numbers answer three different questions, and the answer to one does not constrain the answer
to another.

   Remark 19.7 (Why the Distinction Matters)

   The distinction matters because the chapter’s claim could be misread. If the claim
   “four grades are minimal” were read as “there are four levels of being,” the framework’s
   ontology would be reduced to four realms, and the three barzakhic realms would be
   excluded. The exclusion would be a mistake: the three barzakhic realms are not further
   grades of multiplicity; they are levels whose mode of existence includes the regulation of
   relations between other realms. The minimality of the four is a claim about what must be
   distinguished in the analysis of expression, not a claim that being consists of four levels.
   The distinction is the distinction between the analysis and the reality analyzed; it is not
   the distinction between the analysis and what the analysis is about. The analysis is about
   reality; the analysis is not the reality. The framework’s claim is that the analysis is real,
   invariant, and describable; it does not claim that the analysis is the whole of reality, and it
   does not claim that nothing lies beyond it. The distinction is kept throughout the book.
19.7. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                      203


   Remark 19.8 (Analytical, Not Ontological)

   The claim of the chapter is analytical: it says that the analysis of expression requires
   four distinctions. It does not say that reality contains only four kinds of thing, nor that
   the four grades are the only ways in which things can be plural. It says only that the
   analysis of expression requires these four distinctions, and that no fewer will do. The
   ontological claim—that there are seven realms—is argued elsewhere, and is consistent with
   the analytical claim. The two claims concern different things, and the framework keeps
   them apart.


   Remark 19.9 (The Analysis Points Beyond Itself)

   The analysis is not self-grounded. The analysis is the analysis of expression; it is not
   the ground of the expression. The analysis points beyond itself to the identity whose
   expression is analyzed, and to the ground that makes the identity real. The framework’s
   claim is that the analysis is real, invariant, and describable; it does not claim that the
   analysis is the whole of what is analyzed, and it does not claim that the ground is nothing.
   The distinction is the distinction between the analysis and the ground of the analysis; it is
   kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the analysis as the wisdom through which what is
   becomes determinate, and as the order through which the determinate thing is what it
   is. The framework does not claim that its analysis is that wisdom or that order, and it
   does not claim that the wisdom or the order is unreal. It claims that the analysis is real,
   and that the analysis points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the analysis with the
   wisdom is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework
   takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.


   Remark 19.10 (The Minimality Is Not a Metaphysics)

   The claim that four grades are minimal for the analysis of expression is a claim about the
   structure of analysis, not a claim about the structure of being. The two are related, but
   they are not the same. If analysis is possible, then the structure of analysis is real; but
   the reality of the structure of analysis is not the reality of the analyzed. The framework
   keeps the analytical and the ontological distinct, because the confusion of the two would
   turn a description of analysis into a metaphysics of grades of being—a view the book does
   not hold and does not need.



19.7     What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
   First, the chapter does not argue that no fifth grade can be found. The argument against a
fifth grade is an argument that no fifth grade has been found, and that the standard candidates
are reducible to one of the four. The claim is an estimate, and it would be refuted by a candidate
that resists reduction. The chapter has stated the estimate at exactly that strength.
204                                Chapter 19. The Minimality of the Four Fundamental Grades


      Second, the chapter does not argue for the independence of the four realms. The claim that
the four grades are minimal is a claim about the analysis of expression; it is not the claim that
the four realms are independently real. The independence of the realms was argued in the part
of the book that treated the realms. The present chapter has argued for the minimality of the
grades; the independence of the realms is a separate claim.
      Third, the chapter does not develop the relation between the four grades and the three
barzakhic realms. The barzakhic realms are not grades of multiplicity; they are levels of
transition. Their relation to the four grades is developed in the part of the book that treats the
barzakhic realms. The present chapter has distinguished the four grades from the seven realms;
the later part develops the relation.
      Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of the four grades. It claims
to have described the analytical necessity of the four grades, and the analysis points beyond
itself to the ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction
between the analysis and the ground of the analysis; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is
stated here as the chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know well—a sentence, a gesture, a law. Can you distinguish, in the thing,
the four grades the chapter has distinguished: its material existence, its form, its meaning, and its
unity? Which of the four is most easily reduced to another, and why? What does the reduction
miss that the framework’s distinction preserves?

The next chapter turns to the minimality of the three hubs. It argues that three functions of
mediation are required in the analysis of expression, and that each corresponds to an irreducible
level of being. With the argument for the four grades and the argument for the three hubs, the
framework’s case for the number of realms is complete.
Chapter 20

The Minimality of the Three Hubs


Scope. This chapter argues two things that are related but distinct. First, that three functions of
mediation are required in the analysis of expression, and that no fewer will do. Second, that
each of the three functions corresponds to an irreducible level of being— the three barzakhic
realms. The two claims have different arguments, and the chapter keeps them apart. Its claims
are structural; where the chapter is silent on questions of religion or value, the silence is not a
denial but a recognition that the structural description is not the whole of what can be said.
Where the chapter speaks of “function,” “mediation,” “allotment,” “signification,” “realization,”
“necessity,” “possibility,” or “meaning,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the
definitions in this chapter and in the parts of the book that treated the realms and their rules.


20.1     A Scene
Consider a craftsman making a chair. Between the design in his mind and the chair in his shop,
there are three levels, and the three are distinct.
   At the first level, there is the measure. How much wood will the chair use? What will its
dimensions be? How thick will the legs be, how wide the seat? The measure is not the design; it
is the allotment of proportions within which the design will become a chair. A design that could
be realized in a thousand sizes must be narrowed to one size, and the narrowing is the measure.
   At the second level, there is the meaning. What will the chair signify? Will it be a dining
chair, a throne, a stool? Will it carry the mark of a tradition, a style, a purpose? The meaning
is not the measure; a chair of the right proportions can mean a hundred things. The meaning is
what the chair can signify in the network of practices and relations into which it will enter.
   At the third level, there is the realization. The chair is actually built. The wood is cut, joined,
sanded, finished. The chair becomes a thing in the world, with weight, with texture, with a place
in the room. The realization is not the meaning; a chair that means something may never be
built, and a chair that is built may not mean what was intended. The realization is the chair
becoming concrete.
   Three levels, and each is distinct from the others. The measure is not the meaning; the
meaning is not the realization. And yet all three are required if the chair is to exist. Without the
measure, the design would be indeterminate, and no chair could be made. Without the meaning,
the chair would be an object without a place in the practices that give it its purpose. Without
the realization, the chair would be a design and a meaning, but not a chair.
   The scene poses a question. What are these three levels? Are they real, or are they merely
ways of speaking about the process of making a chair? If they are real, how many are there, and
why exactly three? The present chapter argues that the three levels are real, that they are the
three barzakhic realms, and that exactly three are required.

                                                205
206                                              Chapter 20. The Minimality of the Three Hubs


      The chapter’s argument has two parts. First, it argues that three functions of mediation are
required. Second, it argues that each function corresponds to an irreducible level of being. The
two arguments are distinct, and the chapter keeps them apart.

   Remark 20.1 (The Three Levels Point Beyond Themselves)

   The three levels of the chair—the measure, the meaning, the realization—are distinct, and
   the chapter argues that each is required. The framework’s claim is that the three levels
   are real structural distinctions, and that the analysis of expression requires all three. But
   the three levels are not self-grounded. The three levels are the levels of the craft; they are
   not the ground of the craft. The measure points beyond itself to the one who measures;
   the meaning points beyond itself to the one who intends; the realization points beyond
   itself to the one who realizes. The structural triad points beyond itself to a ground that
   the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the structural
   triad and the ground of the triad; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the triad as the command that determines measure,
   the wisdom that intends meaning, and the power that realizes what is intended. The
   framework does not claim that its triad is those three, and it does not claim that they are
   unreal. It claims that the triad is real, and that the triad points beyond itself. The reader
   who identifies the triad with the command, the wisdom, and the power is free to do so;
   the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the
   identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



20.2       The Question
The previous chapter argued that four grades of multiplicity are required in the analysis of
expression. The four grades are: no multiplicity (the First Determination), multiplicity of
form (the Structural Determination), multiplicity of relation (the Relational Manifestation), and
multiplicity of matter (the Material Manifestation). The four grades are the four fundamental
realms.
      The present chapter asks a further question. Between the four grades, there are three
distinctions. Between no-multiplicity and form; between form and relation; between relation and
matter. Each distinction is a gap that expression must cross: the manifestation of the higher
grade in the lower is not the identity of the two, and the gap between them is where mediation
is required.
      The question is: how many functions of mediation are required to bridge the three gaps?
And: are these functions mere functions, or do they correspond to independently real levels of
being? The chapter’s answer is that three functions are required, one for each gap, and that each
function corresponds to an irreducible level of being—the three barzakhic realms.
      Two aspects of the question must be distinguished.


The functional aspect. Are three functions of mediation required, or could fewer do the
same work? The chapter argues that three are required, and that two would leave one distinction
20.3. The Argument from the Distinctions Between the Grades                                   207


without a function.


The ontological aspect. Are the three functions mere functions—activities that could be
carried out by the four fundamental realms themselves—or do they correspond to levels of being
that are irreducible to the four? The chapter argues that they correspond to irreducible levels,
and that the three barzakhic realms are independently real.
   The two aspects have different arguments, and the chapter keeps them apart. The functional
argument establishes that three functions are needed; the ontological argument establishes that
the functions are not reducible to the fundamental realms. The first does not establish the
second, and the chapter is explicit about this.


20.3     The Argument from the Distinctions Between the Grades

The first argument establishes that three functions of mediation are required. It proceeds from
the distinctions between the four grades.

Argument from the Distinctions Between the Grades.         1. The four grades of multiplicity are
     qualitatively different (the previous chapter).

  2. Between two qualitatively different grades there is a distinction that expression must cross:
     the manifestation of the higher in the lower is not the identity of the two.

  3. There are three such distinctions between four ordered grades.

  4. Each is a distinction of a different kind (the next section shows this).

  5. Hence three distinct functions of mediation are required, and two would leave one distinction
     without a function.



   The argument is a counting argument. Four grades, three distinctions between them; each
distinction requires its own function of mediation; hence three functions. The argument’s force
depends on the third and fourth premises. The third is arithmetic: four grades have three
distinctions between them, not two and not four. The fourth is the subject of the next section:
the three distinctions are of different kinds, and each requires a different function.

   Remark 20.2 (What This Argument Establishes)

   The argument establishes a need for functions of mediation: that something must regulate
   or make possible the crossing of each distinction. It does not establish that each such
   function is carried by an independent level of being. That would need a further premise,
   and the argument from gaps does not supply it. The next two sections address the further
   premise; the present section establishes only the need for three functions.
208                                               Chapter 20. The Minimality of the Three Hubs


   Remark 20.3 (Why Three Functions and Not One)

   The argument shows why three functions are required, not one. If the three distinctions
   were of the same kind, one function could serve all three; but the next section argues that
   they are of different kinds. The distinctions differ in what they distinguish: unity from
   form, form from relation, relation from matter. Each distinction is a different problem,
   and each requires a different solution.



20.4       The Argument from the Modal Categories
The second argument establishes that the three functions are of different kinds, and that they
are irreducible to one another.

Argument from the Modal Categories.          1. The distinction between unity and form is that be-
        tween what is and what is lawful for it: the allotment of a measure within law.

  2. The distinction between form and relation is that between what is lawful in general and
        what is structurally meaningful in a context: signification.

  3. The distinction between relation and matter is that between what is structurally meaningful
        and what is concretely so: realization.

  4. Allotment, signification, and realization are not reducible to one another. Allotment fixes
        how much within law; signification fixes what a structure can mean; realization fixes what
        becomes concrete. One can vary while the others stay.

  5. Hence three, and not fewer, kinds of mediating function are required.


      The argument turns on step (4). If the three functions were reducible to one another, the
three distinctions could be bridged by one function; but they are not reducible. Allotment is the
fixing of a measure within law—how much, within what bounds. Signification is the carrying of
structure into meaning—what a structure can signify, prior to its being situated in a context.
Realization is the actualization of what has been signified—its becoming concrete. The three are
different kinds of mediation, and each is what the other two are not.
      The irreducibility is argued by variance. One function can vary while the others stay. A
measure can be fixed while the meaning is not yet determined; a meaning can be determined
while the realization has not occurred; a realization can occur while the measure and the meaning
remain what they were. The independence of variation shows that the three functions are not
one function under three names.

   Remark 20.4 (A Structural Reading of the Three Functions)

   The three functions are distinguished by the structural aspect of expression each concerns.
   The Hub of Decree concerns the structural measure of what can be realized: the extent
   and limit within which a manifestation can occur. The Hub of Signification concerns
20.5. The Irreducibility of the Barzakhic Realms                                                 209


   the structural meaning that a structure carries: what it can signify, prior to its being
   situated among particular manifestations. The Hub of Realization concerns the structural
   realization of what has been signified: the conditions under which it becomes concrete.
   The three aspects are distinct, and each can vary while the others stay.


   Remark 20.5 (The Argument Is Relative to Its Premises)

   The argument is as strong as its premises. Premises (1), (2), and (3) describe the three
   distinctions; premise (4) is the irreducibility claim. A reader who denies premise (4) denies
   that the three functions are irreducible, and with that denial the argument for three
   functions fails. The framework does not claim that the denial is impossible; it claims that
   the denial is false, and the variance argument is its reason for holding so.
   But the premises are not self-grounded. The premises point beyond themselves to the
   structure that they describe, and to the ground that makes the structure real. The
   framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal.
   It claims that the premises are real structural premises, and that the premises point
   beyond themselves. The distinction is the distinction between the premises and the ground
   of the premises; it is kept throughout the book.



20.5      The Irreducibility of the Barzakhic Realms
The two arguments above concern functions. The independence of the three hubs as realms is
a stronger claim, and it needs a separate argument. The distinction between the two claims is
essential, and it is the subject of the present section.

   Principle 20.1 (The Irreducibility of the Barzakhic Realms)

   (A) The three barzakhic realms are independently real levels of being. Their mediating
   function does not reduce them to functions of the four fundamental realms.

Argument for the Irreducibility of the Barzakhic Realms.       1. Suppose the function of realiza-
      tion (or of signification, or of decree) were merely a function of the four fundamental realms,
      carried out by one or both of the neighbors.

  2. Then the rules of that function would be derivable from the rules of the neighbors.

  3. But the rules of each hub—proportion, order, harmony; truthfulness, accuracy, fidelity;
      proportion in realization, preservation of the realized, continuation of realization—are rules
      of how a relation between realms is to be regulated. The rules of a fundamental realm are
      rules of what is in that realm. A rule of regulating a relation is not a rule of the things
      related.

  4. Hence the rules of a hub are not derivable from those of its neighbors, and the supposition
      fails.
210                                             Chapter 20. The Minimality of the Three Hubs


      The argument depends on step (3): that rules of regulation are not derivable from rules of
what is regulated. It would fail if a derivation of the hub’s rules from the neighbors’ rules were
produced. If such a derivation were produced, the three hubs would be reduced to functions of
the four fundamental realms, and the ontology would have four levels instead of seven.

   Remark 20.6 (What Would Refute the Argument)

   The argument is (T) relative to step (3), which is a commitment ((A)). The framework
   does not claim that no such derivation will ever be found; it claims that none has been
   found, and it states the principle at that strength. Whoever exhibits a derivation of the
   hub’s rules from the rules of its neighbors refutes the principle.


   Remark 20.7 (Two Claims, Two Arguments)

   The functional claim and the ontological claim are different, and their arguments are
   different. The functional argument establishes that three functions are required; it does
   not establish that the functions are carried by independently real levels. The ontological
   argument establishes that the functions are not reducible to the fundamental realms; it does
   not establish that three functions are required. The two together yield the framework’s
   claim: three functions, each carried by an independently real level. If only the functional
   argument were given, the framework would have three functions and no levels to carry them;
   if only the ontological argument were given, the framework would have three irreducible
   levels and no account of why three. The two arguments are both needed, and neither is
   sufficient alone.
   The two arguments together point beyond themselves to a structure that neither argument
   alone describes: the structure of mediation through which the unified source is expressed
   in the differentiated multiplicity. The structure is real, and the framework’s claim is that
   the structure is invariant and describable. But the structure is not self-grounded. The
   structure points beyond itself to the ground that the framework does not describe. The
   distinction is the distinction between the structure and the ground of the structure; it is
   kept throughout the book.


   Remark 20.8 (A Note on the Number Three)

   The number three is not read off from any tradition. It is derived from the number of
   distinctions between the four grades: four grades, three distinctions, three functions. The
   argument asks what structural functions of mediation there are, and whether each is
   irreducible. The number falls out of the argument, rather than being assumed.
   The number three is also not a final number. The framework argues that three functions
   are required, and that three are sufficient for the analysis of expression. It does not argue
   that no further barzakhic realms could exist; it argues that none is required by the analysis.
   The distinction is the distinction between what is required and what is possible; it is kept
   throughout the chapter, and it is stated here as the chapter’s explicit limit.
20.6. A Coherence Test                                                                        211


   Remark 20.9 (The Three Functions Point Beyond Themselves)

   The three functions of mediation—allotment, signification, realization—are real structural
   functions, and the framework’s claim is that each is required and that each is irreducible.
   But the three functions are not self-grounded. The three functions are the functions of
   mediation; they are not the ground of the mediation. The three functions point beyond
   themselves to the ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the
   distinction between the functions and the ground of the functions; it is kept throughout
   the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the three functions as the command through which
   measure is apportioned, the wisdom through which meaning is signified, and the power
   through which what is possible is realized. The framework does not claim that its three
   functions are those three, and it does not claim that they are unreal. It claims that
   the three functions are real structural functions, and that the functions point beyond
   themselves. The reader who identifies the three functions with the command, the wisdom,
   and the power is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the
   framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another
   inquiry.



20.6     A Coherence Test
The chapter’s claim is that three functions of mediation are required, and that each corresponds
to an irreducible level of being. The claim is philosophical, not empirical. But it may be asked
whether the claim is coherent with the way at least some domains of inquiry describe their own
structure. The question is a coherence test, not a justification.

   Coherence Test (not evidence, not justification)

   What this test shows. That the framework’s claim—that three functions of mediation
   are required between a source and its realization—is coherent with the way at least one
   domain of inquiry describes its own structure.
   The test. Consider the way a legal system describes its operation. A law is enacted (the
   measure: what is allotted, within what bounds). The law is interpreted (the meaning:
   what it signifies in the network of legal relations). The law is applied (the realization:
   what becomes concrete in a particular case). The three levels are distinct in the way the
   framework’s three hubs are distinct: the enactment of a law is not its interpretation, and
   the interpretation of a law is not its application. Each level can vary independently of the
   others: a law can be enacted without being interpreted, interpreted without being applied,
   applied without being re-enacted.
   What this test does not show. It does not show that the framework’s claim is correct.
   It does not show that the legal system confirms the framework, or that the framework
   confirms the legal system. It shows only that the framework’s claim is coherent with the
   way at least one domain of inquiry describes its own structure: the domain distinguishes
212                                               Chapter 20. The Minimality of the Three Hubs


   the measure, the meaning, and the realization of a law, as the framework distinguishes
   the three functions of the barzakhic realms. A domain of inquiry can develop itself within
   the framework without contradiction on this point; the framework does not depend on the
   domain, and the domain does not depend on the framework.



      The test is offered at exactly the strength stated. It is not a justification of the framework,
and it is not a derivation of the framework’s claim from legal practice. It is a check on coherence:
a demonstration that the framework’s claim is not at odds with the way at least one domain of
inquiry actually works.




20.7        What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.

      First, the chapter does not develop the rules of the three hubs. The rules are named—
proportion, order, harmony; truthfulness, accuracy, fidelity; proportion in realization, preservation
of the realized, continuation of realization—and their irreducibility is argued, but their detailed
statement and their articulation into a unity are the subject of the part of the book that treated
the governing dynamics. The present chapter has argued for the functions and the levels; the
rules are a separate matter.

      Second, the chapter does not argue for the relation between the three hubs and the four
grades beyond what the argument from distinctions requires. The three hubs sit between the
four grades; the chapter has argued that three functions are required and that each corresponds
to an irreducible level, but it has not developed the full account of how each hub relates to the
realms on either side of it. That account is developed in the part of the book that treats the
barzakhic realms.

      Third, the chapter does not settle the open question of whether there could be barzakhic
realms beyond the three. The framework’s claim is that three are required; it is not the claim
that no further barzakhic realms could exist. The framework has argued for three, and it has not
ruled out that a further argument might establish more. The claim is stated at that strength.

      Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of the three hubs. It claims
to have described the analytical necessity of the three hubs, and the analysis points beyond itself
to the ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between
the analysis and the ground of the analysis; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is stated
here as the chapter’s explicit limit.
