A Question for Reflection
Consider a process you know well—a promise being kept, a design being realized, a law being
applied. Can you distinguish, in the process, the three levels the chapter has distinguished: the
allotment of measure, the signification of meaning, and the realization of what has been signified?
Which of the three is most easily collapsed into another, and why? What does the collapse miss
that the framework’s distinction preserves?

The next chapter turns to the irreducibility of one-step reduction. It argues that a unified
identity cannot appear in a differentiated multiplicity without the mediating functions of the
barzakhic realms. The present chapter has argued that three functions are required and that
each is irreducible; the next chapter argues that the mediation they provide is necessary for any
appearance at all.
Chapter 21

The Irreducibility of One-Step Reduction


Scope. This chapter argues that unmediated reduction to full multiplicity is impossible, and that
appearance in a differentiated multiplicity requires mediation by the functions of the barzakhic
realms. It distinguishes the claim that mediation is required from the claim that passage through
every intermediate realm is required, argues for the first, and rejects the second. Its claims are
structural; where the chapter is silent on questions of religion or value, the silence is not a denial
but a recognition that the structural description is not the whole of what can be said. Where the
chapter speaks of “unity,” “multiplicity,” “mediation,” “function,” “distinction,” “apportioning,”
“signification,” or “realization,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions
in this chapter and in the parts of the book that treated the realms and their rules.



21.1      A Scene

Consider a translation. A poem is written in one language, and it is translated into another.
The poem is one thing: a single work, a unified whole, a pattern of sound and sense that the
poet intended. The translation is many things: many words, many decisions, many small choices
about which word to use, which rhythm to preserve, which image to keep and which to sacrifice.
Between the one and the many, something must happen.
    Three things, at least, must happen. First, the translator must decide the measure: how
much of the poem’s form to preserve, how much to adapt, how literal to be, how free. The
measure is not the poem; it is the allotment within which the translation will be made. Second,
the translator must determine the meaning: what each line signifies, what the poem as a whole
is about, what the network of allusions and associations is. The meaning is not the measure; a
translation of the right length and rhythm can mean a hundred things. Third, the translator
must realize the translation: the words must be written, in a particular order, with particular
punctuation, in a particular edition. The realization is not the meaning; a translation that means
the right thing may never be published, and a translation that is published may not mean what
the translator intended.
    The three — measure, meaning, realization — are distinct, and each is required. Between the
poem and its translation, all three must happen. But notice: the poem does not “travel through”
intermediate translations. There is no chain of increasingly translated versions through which
the poem must pass. The poem goes from source to translation in one step, mediated by the
three determinations, but without passing through intermediate poems.
    The scene poses a question. What is required for a unified thing to appear as a multiplicity?
Is mediation required, or is the appearance immediate? And if mediation is required, is passage
through every intermediate stage also required, or is the passage of a different kind? The present

                                                 214
21.2. The Question                                                                             215


chapter argues that mediation is required, and that passage is not. The two claims are easily
confused, and the chapter’s principal contribution is to keep them apart.

   Remark 21.1 (The Three Determinations Point Beyond Themselves)

   The three determinations of the translation—measure, meaning, realization—are distinct,
   and the chapter argues that each is required. The framework’s claim is that the three
   determinations are real structural distinctions, and that the analysis of mediation requires
   all three. But the three determinations are not self-grounded. The three determinations
   are the determinations of the mediator; they are not the ground of the mediator. The
   measure points beyond itself to the one who apportions; the meaning points beyond itself
   to the one who intends; the realization points beyond itself to the one who realizes. The
   structural triad points beyond itself to a ground that the framework does not describe.
   The distinction is the distinction between the structural triad and the ground of the triad;
   it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the triad as the command through which measure
   is apportioned, the wisdom through which meaning is signified, and the power through
   which what is intended is realized. The framework does not claim that its triad is those
   three, and it does not claim that they are unreal. It claims that the triad is real, and that
   the triad points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the triad with the command, the
   wisdom, and the power is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do
   so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a question for
   another inquiry.



21.2     The Question
The previous chapters of this part have argued for the framework’s structural claims. The
necessity of expression was argued; the minimality of the four grades was argued; the minimality
of the three hubs was argued, together with the irreducibility of the barzakhic realms to the
fundamental ones.
   The present chapter addresses a different question. The three hubs have been argued to be
independently real, and their functions to be irreducible. But what work do they do, exactly? The
framework’s answer is that they mediate the appearance of a unified identity in a differentiated
multiplicity. Without their mediation, the appearance would be impossible.
   The question is: why is mediation required? And: is the mediation of the kind that requires
passage through every intermediate realm, or is it of a different kind?
   Two propositions are easily taken for one, and the chapter’s first task is to distinguish them.

 (A) An identity cannot appear in a plurality without any structural distinction or mediating
     structure.

 (B) An identity, to appear in a lower realm, must pass through every realm between.

   The two propositions look similar. Both say that something must happen between an identity
and its appearance in a lower realm. But they say different things, and they have different
216                                        Chapter 21. The Irreducibility of One-Step Reduction


consequences. Proposition (A) says that mediation is required; proposition (B) says that passage
is required. The framework argues (A) and rejects (B). The distinction is the chapter’s central
claim.
      The chapter’s method is threefold. First, it distinguishes (A) from (B), and explains why
they are not the same. Second, it argues for (A): that unmediated reduction to full multiplicity is
impossible. Third, it argues against (B): that mediation does not require passage through every
intermediate realm. The chapter ends with what it does not establish and with the epistemic
status of its claims.


21.3       Two Propositions, Not One
The two propositions are easily taken for one, and the confusion has consequences. If (B) were
the only way to make sense of (A), then the framework’s claim that mediation is required would
commit it to the claim that passage is required. But the framework denies passage elsewhere:
the non-necessity of downward passage, argued in the part of the book that treated the realms,
says that an identity’s presence in a lower realm does not require passage through every realm
between.
      The framework therefore needs to distinguish (A) from (B), and to argue for (A) without
committing itself to (B). The distinction is structural: (A) is about what makes the appearance
possible; (B) is about the route the appearance takes. The first concerns the conditions of
appearance; the second concerns the itinerary of appearance. The two are different, and the
framework affirms the first while denying the second.

   Remark 21.2 (Why the Distinction Is Not Merely Verbal)

   The distinction is not merely verbal. A verbal distinction would be one that makes no
   difference to what follows. The distinction between (A) and (B) makes a decisive difference:
   if (B) were true, an identity manifested in the Material Manifestation would have to be
   manifested in every realm between its realm of origin and the Material Manifestation. If
   (A) alone is true, the identity may be manifested directly in the Material Manifestation,
   with the mediation of the barzakhic functions but without appearing in every intermediate
   realm. The two views have different consequences for what the framework says about
   manifestation, and the framework argues for the second.



21.4       The Argument from the Unity of Identity
The argument for (A) proceeds from the unity of identity and the differentiation of multiplicity.

Argument from the Unity of Identity.        1. An identity, in its own realm, is unified.

   2. The multiplicity of a lower realm is differentiated.

   3. A unified identity cannot appear as a fully differentiated multiplicity without a structural
        distinction that makes the differentiation, the apportioning, and the realization possible.
21.4. The Argument from the Unity of Identity                                                  217


  4. Such structural distinctions are the functions of the barzakhic realms.

  5. Hence appearance in a differentiated multiplicity requires mediation by those functions.



   The argument’s force is in step (3). If the identity were already differentiated in its own
realm, it could appear as a differentiated multiplicity without mediation; the differentiation
would already be there. But the identity is unified, and the multiplicity is differentiated, and
the transition from one to the other is not automatic. Something must make it possible: the
structural distinctions that allow the unified identity to appear as a differentiated multiplicity,
without ceasing to be one.
   The argument’s premises (1) and (2) are the framework’s accounts of the unity of identity
and the differentiation of multiplicity, argued in the parts of the book that treated the realms
and the fixed elements. The argument’s premise (4) identifies the structural distinctions with the
functions of the barzakhic realms, argued in the previous chapter. The argument’s conclusion
follows from the four premises.

   Remark 21.3 (The Argument Points Beyond Itself)

   The argument establishes that appearance in a differentiated multiplicity requires mediation.
   The argument is structural: it shows what the structure of appearance requires. But
   the structure is not self-grounded. The structure of appearance is the structure of the
   appearance; it is not the ground of the appearance. The structure points beyond itself to
   the identity whose appearance is mediated, and to the ground that makes the identity real.
   The framework’s claim is that the structure is real, invariant, and describable; it does
   not claim that the structure is the whole of what appears, and it does not claim that the
   ground is nothing. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of appearance
   and the ground of appearance; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of appearance as the command through which what is
   intended becomes what is, without the intention passing through intermediate stages. The
   framework does not claim that its structure is that command, and it does not claim that
   the command is unreal. It claims that the structure is real, and that the structure points
   beyond itself. The reader who identifies the structure of appearance with the command is
   free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no
   position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.


   Remark 21.4 (The Argument Does Not Establish Passage)

   The argument establishes that mediation is required; it does not establish that passage is
   required. Step (5) says that appearance requires mediation by the barzakhic functions. It
   does not say that the appearance requires the identity to be present in each barzakhic
   realm in turn. The functions can mediate without the identity passing through them.
   The translator mediates the poem without the poem passing through intermediate poems;
   the barzakhic functions mediate the appearance without the identity passing through
218                                       Chapter 21. The Irreducibility of One-Step Reduction


   intermediate realms. The argument establishes (A), not (B).
   The distinction between mediation and passage is structural. But the structure is not
   self-grounded. The structure points beyond itself to the ground that the framework does
   not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of mediation and
   the ground of mediation; it is kept throughout the book.

   Remark 21.5 (The Unity of Identity Is Not Numerical Isolation)

   The argument’s first premise says that an identity, in its own realm, is unified. It does
   not say that the identity is isolated from its manifestations, or that the unity is the kind
   of unity that excludes relation. The unity is the unity of a source, not the isolation of
   a thing. The identity is one, and its manifestations are many, and the relation between
   them is what mediation makes possible. The reader who reads the first premise as a claim
   about isolation has misread it; the reader who reads it as a claim about unity has read it
   correctly.
   The unity of the source points beyond itself. The unity is not self-grounded; the unity is the
   unity of a source that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction
   between the unity of the source and the ground of the source; it is kept throughout the
   book. The traditions speak of the ground of the source as the one from whom every source
   comes; the framework does not claim that its unity is that one, and it does not claim that
   the one is unreal. It claims that the unity is real, and that the unity points beyond itself.



21.5     Mediation Is Not Itinerary
The argument’s conclusion is that mediation is required. It does not say that passage is required.
The distinction is stated in a remark, and the remark is the chapter’s principal contribution to
the framework’s account of the barzakhic realms.

   Remark 21.6 (Mediation Is Not Itinerary)

   The conclusion is that mediating functions are necessary. It is not that every manifestation
   must visit each realm in succession. A manifestation in the Material Manifestation requires
   that apportioning, signification, and realization be in effect; it does not require that the
   identity be present, as a manifestation, in each realm between. The necessity of existential
   mediation is therefore not the necessity of a sequential path. The two are kept apart, and
   (B) is rejected.
   The mediation is structural; the structure is real, and the framework’s claim is that the
   structure is invariant and describable. But the structure is not self-grounded. The structure
   points beyond itself to the ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is
   the distinction between the structure of mediation and the ground of mediation; it is kept
   throughout the book. The traditions speak of the ground of mediation as the command
   that determines without passage; the framework does not claim that its structure is that
   command, and it does not claim that the command is unreal. It claims that the structure
21.6. The Status of the Argument and an Image                                                     219


   is real, and that the structure points beyond itself.

   The distinction between mediation and passage was stated in the part of the book that
treated the barzakhic realms, and the present remark applies it. Mediation is the regulation,
conditioning, or transformation of a relation between realms by a realm whose mode of existence
includes that function. Passage is existential traversal of a realm—the identity, or its effect, being
present as such in each realm it traverses. The first is what the barzakhic realms do; the second
is what they do not require of the identity they mediate.
   The distinction is structural, not verbal. If passage were required, an identity manifested in
the Material Manifestation would have to be manifested in the Relational Manifestation, and in
the Hub of Realization, and in the Hub of Signification, and in the Structural Determination,
and so on. If mediation alone is required, the identity may be manifested directly in the Material
Manifestation, with the barzakhic functions regulating the manifestation without the identity
appearing in each hub. The framework holds the second, and the present chapter’s argument
supports it.

   Remark 21.7 (The Translator Again)

   The translator mediates the poem. The poem does not pass through intermediate poems.
   The three determinations (measure, meaning, realization) are in effect; the poem appears
   in a new language; and the poem was never present, as a poem, in the intermediate stages.
   The image is not an argument; it is an illustration of what the argument establishes. The
   reader who finds the image persuasive will find the argument clear; the reader who does
   not will find the argument still standing on its own.
   The translator, too, points beyond itself. The translator is the mediator; the translator
   is not the ground of the mediation. The translator points beyond itself to the poet who
   intends, and to the ground that makes the poet’s intention real. The distinction is the
   distinction between the mediator and the ground of the mediation; it is kept throughout
   the book. The traditions speak of the ground of mediation as the source from whom every
   mediation comes; the framework does not claim that its translator is that source, and it
   does not claim that the source is unreal. It claims that the mediation is real, and that the
   mediation points beyond itself.



21.6      The Status of the Argument and an Image
The argument’s status is (T): it is argued, relative to the commitments on which it rests. Its
premises (1) and (2) are the framework’s accounts of unity and differentiation; premise (4) is the
identification of the structural distinctions with the barzakhic functions, argued in the previous
chapter. The conclusion follows from these premises, and the framework does not claim more
than that.
   The argument would be refuted by showing that a unified identity can appear as a fully
differentiated multiplicity without any mediating structure. The framework does not claim
that no such appearance is possible; it claims that none has been exhibited, and it argues from
220                                        Chapter 21. The Irreducibility of One-Step Reduction


the nature of unity and differentiation that none can be. The reader who wishes to challenge
the argument knows where to press: at the possibility of unmediated appearance, or at the
identification of the mediating structure with the barzakhic functions.

   Remark 21.8 (An Image: The Converter)

   A converter receives what is of one form and produces what is of another form, without
   collapsing the two into one. The image illustrates what a function of mediation does. It
   carries no weight in the argument, and no evaluative or teleological reading of “converter”
   is intended. The reader who finds the image helpful will find the argument clearer; the
   reader who does not will find the argument still standing.
   The converter, too, points beyond itself. The converter is the mediator; the converter is
   not the ground of the mediation. The converter points beyond itself to the source of what
   is converted, and to the ground that makes the conversion real. The distinction is the
   distinction between the converter and the ground of the conversion; it is kept throughout
   the book.

      The image is offered as an aid to understanding, not as a substitute for the argument. The
argument stands on its own; the image is a way of seeing what the argument establishes. The
framework uses images when they help and disclaims them when they do not; the present image
is offered in that spirit.

   Remark 21.9 (The Irreducibility Points Beyond Itself)

   The irreducibility of one-step reduction is a real structural claim; the framework’s claim is
   that appearance in a differentiated multiplicity requires mediation, and that the mediation
   is not a sequential passage. The claim is structural, and the structure is describable. But
   the structure is not self-grounded. The structure of mediation points beyond itself to the
   ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between
   the structure of mediation and the ground of mediation; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of mediation as the one who mediates without being
   mediated, and as the source from whom every mediation comes. The framework does not
   claim that its structure is that one, and it does not claim that the one is unreal. It claims
   that the structure is real, and that the structure points beyond itself. The reader who
   identifies the structure with the one is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is
   free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a
   question for another inquiry.



21.7        What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
      First, the chapter does not argue that no mediation is ever bypassed. It argues that mediation
is required for appearance in a differentiated multiplicity. Whether a particular appearance is
mediated by all three functions, or only by some, is a question the framework leaves open. The
21.8. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                 221


present chapter has argued that mediation is required; the later parts develop the details.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of how the barzakhic functions operate
in each particular case. The functions are named (apportioning, signifying, realizing), and their
necessity is argued, but the detailed account of how each functions in a given appearance is
deferred to the parts of the book that treat the specific realms and their rules.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether mediation can ever fail. If mediation
is required, what happens when it does not occur? The framework’s answer is that appearance
does not occur—the identity remains unmanifested in the realm—but the full treatment of this
case is left for the parts of the book that treat manifestation and its failures.
    Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of mediation. It claims to
have described the structure of mediation, and the structure points beyond itself to the ground
that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of
mediation and the ground of mediation; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is stated here
as the chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a case in which something appears in a new form—a thought becoming a word, a design
becoming a building, a law becoming a judgment. Does the appearance require passage through
every intermediate form, or does it require only mediation by the three determinations? What
does the answer tell you about the relation between the unified source and its differentiated
appearance?

The next chapter turns to the conservation of identity. It argues that identity is invariant under
all temporal transformations of its manifestations, and distinguishes the persistence of the identity
itself from the continuity of its manifestation and the continuity of its capacity to manifest. The
present chapter has argued that mediation is required for appearance; the next chapter argues
that, once an identity has appeared, it is conserved through the changes of its appearances.
Chapter 22

The Conservation of Identity


Scope. This chapter argues for the conservation of identity across time, and distinguishes three
things that must not be taken for one: the persistence of the identity itself, the continuity of its
manifestation, and the continuity of its capacity to manifest. Its claims are structural; where the
chapter is silent on questions of religion or value, the silence is not a denial but a recognition
that the structural description is not the whole of what can be said. Where the chapter speaks
of “persistence,” “continuity,” “conservation,” “invariance,” “transformation,” “experience,” or
“presupposition,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter
and in the part of the book that treated identity.


22.1      A Scene
Consider a song. A song is written; it is played; it is recorded; it is covered by another
artist; it is sampled; it is rearranged. Each performance is different: different tempo, different
instrumentation, different key, different voice. A jazz version and a folk version and an orchestral
version may share almost nothing in their sound. And yet, if the song is the same song, something
has persisted across all the performances. What is it?
    It is not the notes. The notes are different in each version. It is not the words, if there are
words; they may be translated, paraphrased, or dropped entirely. It is not the tempo, not the
key, not the instrumentation. And yet the song is not nothing. The jazz version is recognizable
as a version of the same song; the folk version is recognizable as another version of the same song;
the orchestral version is recognizable as a third. Something is conserved across the performances,
and the something is what makes them performances of one song rather than three unrelated
pieces.
    The something is not a thing among the performances. It is not the first performance,
of which the others are copies. It is not an ideal performance, of which the actual ones are
approximations. It is the identity of the song: what remains invariant across the allowable
transformations through which the song is expressed. The identity is not heard; what is heard is
the manifestation. But the identity is what makes the manifestation a manifestation of one song
rather than another.
    The scene poses a question. What is conserved across time, when a thing persists through
change? And is the conservation of the identity the same as the persistence of its manifestations?
The present chapter answers these questions. Its answer is the principle of conservation, and
its principal contribution is the distinction among three things that are easily confused: the
persistence of the identity itself, the continuity of its manifestation, and the continuity of its
capacity to manifest.


                                                222
22.2. The Question                                                                             223


   Remark 22.1 (Conservation Points Beyond Itself)

   The song’s conservation is a real structural feature; the framework’s claim is that the
   identity is conserved across the changes of its manifestations. But the conservation is not
   self-grounded. The conservation is the conservation of an identity; it is not the ground of
   its own being. The conservation points beyond itself to what grounds the identity, and
   through the identity to what grounds the conservation. The framework’s claim is that
   the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The
   distinction is the distinction between the conservation and the ground of the conservation;
   it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of conservation as the preservation of the one who
   preserves, and as the permanence of the one who alone is permanent. The framework does
   not claim that its structural conservation is that preservation, and it does not claim that
   the preservation is unreal. It claims that the conservation is a real structural feature, and
   that the feature points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the structural conservation
   with the preservation is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so;
   the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a question for
   another inquiry.



22.2     The Question
The part of the book that treated the fixed elements stated and argued for the conservation of
identity. It distinguished identity from signature and from pseudo-identity; it defined identity as
invariance under a class of allowable transformations; and it gave two arguments for conservation:
a transcendental argument, which proceeds from the presupposition of sameness in temporal
experience, and an abductive argument, which proceeds from the convergence of independent
reconstructions on a single pseudo-identity.
   The present chapter develops the case further. It adds a third argument, the argument from
temporal invariance, which proceeds from the rigidity of identity. It develops the transcendental
argument beyond the sketch given earlier, and it states what the argument does and does not
show. And it draws the distinction that the part of the book that treated the fixed elements
named but did not develop: the distinction among the persistence of identity, the continuity of
manifestation, and the continuity of the capacity to manifest.
   The question is: what is conserved, when an identity is conserved? The question is not idle.
Three things are easily run together, and the running-together is a source of confusion in the
framework’s subsequent parts. The three things are these.

First thing: the persistence of the identity itself. The identity is conserved across time.
This is the principle of conservation, and it is what the present chapter argues for.

Second thing: the continuity of manifestation. The identity keeps appearing. It is
manifested, again and again, in successive manifestations. The continuity of manifestation is not
the persistence of the identity; a thing may be conserved even when its manifestations cease.
224                                                     Chapter 22. The Conservation of Identity


Third thing: the continuity of the capacity to manifest. The identity can still appear.
Its capacity to manifest in a given realm is intact. The continuity of capacity is not the persistence
of the identity; a thing may be conserved even when its capacity to manifest is lost.
      The three are different. The first is the subject of the present chapter’s argument; the second
and third are the subjects of the parts of the book that treat death and birth, and sediment.
The reader who runs the three together will find that the framework’s claims about conservation,
death, and capacity appear to conflict; the reader who keeps them apart will find that the claims
are compatible, and that they answer different questions.


22.3        Three Things Not to Conflate
The distinction among the three things is essential, and the present section develops it.

The persistence of the identity itself. The identity is conserved: it remains the same
identity across the changes of its manifestations. The conservation is not the continuity of the
manifestations; it is the invariance of what the manifestations manifest.

The continuity of manifestation. The identity may be manifested continuously, or intermit-
tently, or at a single moment. The continuity of manifestation is a feature of the appearances,
not of the identity. A song that is never performed is still a song; its identity is conserved, though
its manifestations are not continuous.

The continuity of the capacity to manifest. The identity may retain the capacity to
manifest in a given realm, or it may lose it. The capacity is not the manifestation; it is the
structural possibility of the manifestation. A seed that is never planted retains its capacity to
grow a tree; the capacity is present though the manifestation is not.

   Remark 22.2 (Why the Three Are Easily Confused)

   The three are easily confused because, in ordinary cases, they occur together. When a
   person persists through time, her identity is conserved, her manifestations are continuous,
   and her capacity to manifest is intact. The three coincide, and the coincidence invites
   the inference that they are the same. But they come apart in cases that the framework
   must be able to describe: a person who is conserved but whose manifestations cease; a
   person who is conserved but whose capacity to manifest in a given realm is lost. The
   framework’s account of conservation, death, and capacity is built to handle these cases,
   and the distinction among the three is what makes the account possible.
   The coincidence of the three, where it occurs, points beyond itself. The coincidence is
   not self-grounded; the coincidence is grounded in what makes the three possible. The
   framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal.
   It claims that the coincidence is real, and that the coincidence points beyond itself. The
   distinction is the distinction between the coincidence and the ground of the coincidence; it
   is kept throughout the book.
22.4. The Principle of Conservation                                                            225


   Remark 22.3 (The Three Are Structural, Not Evaluative)

   The distinction among the three is structural, not evaluative. The framework does not claim
   that the persistence of identity is more important than the continuity of manifestation, or
   vice versa. It claims that the three are different structural facts, and that the framework’s
   account of identity, death, and capacity depends on keeping them distinct. A reader who
   reads the distinction as a ranking has misread it; a reader who reads it as a structural
   separation has read it correctly.



22.4     The Principle of Conservation
The principle of conservation was stated in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements.
It is restated here, because the present chapter’s arguments bear on it.

   Principle 22.1 (Identity Conservation)

   (A) Identity is invariant under all temporal transformations of its manifestations. Manifes-
   tations may vary with time; identity itself is conserved.

   The principle is (A): it is adopted as a commitment of the framework. It is supported by
three arguments, given in the sections that follow. It would be refuted by showing that an
identity can change under temporal transformations—that is, by showing that an identity can
become a different identity through time. The framework does not claim that no such case can
be constructed; it claims that none has been constructed that survives the distinction between
identity and manifestation, and it argues that none can be.
   The principle’s content is precise. It says that identity is invariant under temporal transfor-
mations, not that it is invariant under every transformation whatsoever. An identity may change
in its non-temporal dimensions—it may be manifested in different realms, in different modes,
with different degrees of fidelity—without thereby ceasing to be the identity it is. The temporal
transformations are a subclass of the allowable transformations; the principle says that identity
is invariant under the temporal ones, as it is invariant under all the allowable ones.

   Remark 22.4 (The Ground of Conservation)

   The conservation of identity is a real structural feature; the framework claims that the
   identity is conserved across the changes of its manifestations. But the conservation is
   not self-grounded. The conservation is the structure of persistence; it is not the ground
   of the persistence. The conservation points beyond itself to what holds the identity in
   being. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is
   not described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the structure
   of conservation and the ground of conservation; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of conservation as the one in whose hand is the holding
   of every thing, and as the one who alone is permanent. The framework does not claim
   that its structural conservation is that holding, and it does not claim that the holding is
226                                                      Chapter 22. The Conservation of Identity


   unreal. It claims that the conservation is a real structure, and that the structure points
   beyond itself. The reader who identifies the structure with the holding is free to do so;
   the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the
   identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



22.5       First Argument: From Temporal Invariance
The first argument proceeds from the rigidity of identity, together with a premise about the class
of allowable transformations.

Argument from Temporal Invariance.           1. Identity is rigid: it is invariant under the specified
        class of allowable transformations (the principle of identity rigidity, argued in the part of
        the book that treated identity).

  2. That conservation across time follows needs a premise: that change over time is a trans-
        formation of the kind in the class, and that the class includes temporal transformations.
       ((A))

  3. Time is one among several kinds of transformation of manifestations; it is not special, and
        the class of allowable transformations of an identity is fixed by the identity itself.

  4. Given (2), an identity that is invariant under its allowable transformations is invariant
        under temporal ones.

  5. Hence identity is conserved across time, as an identity.


      The argument’s force is in step (2). Without it, the principle of identity rigidity says that
identity is invariant under the transformations in its class, and says nothing about time. The
step from invariance in a class to persistence through time is not automatic: time must be
shown to belong to the class. The present argument supplies the premise, and the premise is
adopted as a commitment ((A)). A reader who denies that time belongs to the class of allowable
transformations denies the argument’s conclusion; a reader who accepts it accepts the conclusion.
      The argument is not a proof from nothing. It proceeds from the rigidity of identity and from
the premise about the class. Both are commitments; both are stated as such. The argument’s
value is that it makes the commitments visible, and shows what follows from them.

   Remark 22.5 (Why the Premise Is Needed)

   Without the premise, rigidity says that identity is invariant under the transformations in
   its class, and says nothing about time. The step from invariance in a class to persistence
   through time is not automatic: time must be shown to belong to the class. The premise
   does not claim that time is the only kind of transformation in the class; it claims that
   time is one kind, and that the class includes it. The framework does not argue for the
   premise; it adopts it, on the ground that time is a transformation of manifestations like
22.6. Second Argument: Transcendental                                                       227


   any other, and that the class of allowable transformations is defined by the identity, not
   by the kinds of transformation that happen to be instantiated. The reader who finds the
   premise plausible will find the argument persuasive; the reader who does not will find the
   argument incomplete.


   Remark 22.6 (The Invariance of Identity Is Not the Numerical Persistence of
   One Source)

   The argument shows that identity is invariant under temporal transformations. It does
   not, by itself, show that the invariant is numerically one across time. The distinction
   between the invariance of a pattern and the numerical unity of a source was drawn in the
   part of the book that treated identity; the present argument presupposes the distinction,
   and the next section’s argument bears on the numerical unity. The two are related, but
   they are not the same, and the present chapter keeps them apart.



22.6     Second Argument: Transcendental
The second argument is transcendental. It proceeds from the possibility of temporal experience
to its presupposition.

Transcendental Argument for Conservation.       1. There are experiences of temporal continuity:
     remembering, anticipating, recognizing across time.

  2. Such experiences are possible only if what is remembered, anticipated, or recognized is
     structurally presupposed to be the same across the interval.

  3. Hence the structural presupposition of the sameness of the subject of the experience is a
     condition of the possibility of such experiences.

  4. A condition of the possibility of such experiences cannot be coherently denied by one who
     is describing such experiences.

  5. Hence the presumption of sameness is a transcendental condition of temporal experience.



   The argument is the transcendental argument stated in the part of the book that treated
the fixed elements, developed here in more detail. Its force is that the experiences of memory,
anticipation, and recognition are unintelligible without the presupposition of sameness. When I
remember an event as mine, I presuppose that the “I” who remembers is the “I” to whom the
event happened. When I anticipate an event as one that will happen to me, I presuppose that
the “I” who anticipates is the “I” to whom the event will happen. When I recognize a thing as
the same thing across time, I presuppose that the thing is the same thing. In each case, the
presupposition of sameness is a condition of the experience.
   The argument’s conclusion is limited, and the next section states the limit.
228                                                    Chapter 22. The Conservation of Identity


   Remark 22.7 (The Three Moments of Temporal Experience)

   The transcendental argument can be put in terms of three moments of temporal experience.
   In memory, I remember a past event as mine. In anticipation, I anticipate a future event
   as one that will happen to me. In recognition, I recognize an object or a person as the
   same one across time. The three are aspects of one structure, and all three presuppose
   the presumption of sameness. The argument’s force depends on this structure; a reader
   who has the experiences and finds them unintelligible without the presupposition will find
   the argument persuasive; a reader who denies the structure will not.



22.7       The Limit of the Transcendental Argument
The transcendental argument has a limit, and the limit must be stated. It is the principal
contribution of the present section.
      What follows from the argument is limited. From the premise that the experience of continuity
requires the structural presupposition of one subject, it follows that the concept of a persisting
identity is structurally necessary for experience. It does not follow that an identity actually
persists in every realm and after every kind of transformation. The argument is (T) for the first
and does not reach the second.
      The gap between the two is the gap between a presumption and a fact. A presumption
might be a useful construct rather than a fact; a concept might be structurally necessary for
experience even if nothing in reality answers to it. The transcendental argument shows that we
must presume sameness; it does not show that sameness is real.

   Remark 22.8 (What the Gap Requires)

   The gap is closed, to the extent that it can be closed, by the abductive argument stated
   in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements, and developed further below. The
   abductive argument proceeds from the convergence of independent reconstructions on a
   single pseudo-identity; its conclusion is that the best explanation of the convergence is
   that the observers are tracking something that is the same across contexts and across time.
   The abductive argument does not prove that identity is real; it makes it reasonable to hold
   that there is an invariant that persists. The two arguments together—the transcendental,
   which establishes the structural necessity of the presumption, and the abductive, which
   establishes the reasonableness of holding the presumption to be correct—constitute the
   framework’s case for conservation.
   But the closing of the gap points beyond itself. The abductive argument shows that the
   presumption is reasonable; it does not show the ground of the presumption’s reality. The
   reality of the invariant, if it is real, is grounded in what makes the invariant to be what it
   is. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is
   unreal. It claims that the presumption is reasonable, and that the presumption points
   beyond itself to the ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is
   the distinction between the presumption and the ground of the presumption; it is kept
22.8. The Abductive Argument Revisited                                                        229


   throughout the book.


   Remark 22.9 (Why the Limit Is Stated)

   The limit is stated because the framework’s honesty about what it establishes is part of
   what it is. A transcendental argument that claimed to prove the reality of identity would
   be overreaching; a framework that claimed more than its arguments support would be
   vulnerable to the charge of dogmatism. The framework states its limits, and it offers
   the abductive argument as the supplement that closes the gap to the extent that the
   gap can be closed. The reader who finds the two arguments together persuasive has the
   framework’s case; the reader who does not has located the place where the framework is
   most vulnerable.
   The limit points beyond itself. The limit is the limit of the finite argument; it is not the
   limit of what is. The framework does not claim that nothing lies beyond the limit, and
   it does not claim that the limit is a defect of the framework rather than a feature of the
   relation between the finite argument and its object. The distinction is the distinction
   between the limit of the argument and the limit of what is; it is kept throughout the book.


   Remark 22.10 (Conservation Is Not the Persistence of Manifestation)

   That an identity is conserved does not mean that its manifestations are conserved: a
   manifestation in a realm may cease while the identity is conserved. The distinction is the
   structural point on which the framework’s account of death rests. A song whose every
   performance has ceased is still the song; a person whose every manifestation in a given
   realm has ceased is still the person, in the sense the principle of conservation gives to
  “still.” The reader who reads conservation as the persistence of manifestation has misread
   it; the reader who reads it as the persistence of the identity has read it correctly.
   But the conservation is not self-grounded. The conservation is the structure of persistence;
   the structure points beyond itself to what holds the identity in being. The framework
   does not describe the holding, and it does not claim that the holding is unreal. It claims
   that the conservation is a real structure, and that the structure points beyond itself. The
   distinction is the distinction between the structure of conservation and the ground of
   conservation; it is kept throughout the book.



22.8     The Abductive Argument Revisited
The abductive argument was stated in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements.
It is developed here in more detail, because it is the argument that closes the gap left by the
transcendental argument.

Abductive Argument for Conservation.       1. Reconstructions of the same thing, carried out in-
     dependently by observers in different contexts, converge on a single pseudo-identity up to
     isomorphism; the result is stable under perturbation; and it yields successful predictions.
230                                                    Chapter 22. The Conservation of Identity


  2. The best explanation of this convergence is that the observers are tracking something that
        is the same across the contexts and across time: an invariant.

  3. The rival explanation—that the convergence reflects shared convention or psychological
        projection—predicts convergence only among observers who share the convention, and
        does not explain why predictions made from the pseudo-identity succeed in domains the
        convention never touched.

  4. Hence it is reasonable to hold that there is an invariant that persists through time.



      The argument is abductive: it proceeds from the convergence of reconstructions to the best
explanation of the convergence. Its strength is the strength of inference to the best explanation;
it does not prove that the invariant is real, but it makes the reality of the invariant the best
explanation of the convergence that the framework observes.
      The argument’s premise (1) is what the framework’s account of reconstruction shows: inde-
pendent observers, working in different contexts, converge on a pseudo-identity that is stable and
predictive. Premise (2) is the abductive step: the best explanation of the convergence is that
there is an invariant. Premise (3) is the comparison with the rival explanation. The argument’s
conclusion is reasonable belief, not proof.

   Remark 22.11 (The Two Arguments Together)

   The transcendental argument and the abductive argument together constitute the frame-
   work’s case for conservation. The transcendental argument establishes that the presumption
   of sameness is structurally necessary for temporal experience. The abductive argument
   establishes that it is reasonable to hold the presumption to be correct. Neither argument
   is sufficient alone: the transcendental argument shows only that we must presume; the
   abductive argument shows only that the presumption is reasonable. The two together
   show that we must presume sameness, and that the presumption is reasonable. The
   framework’s claim is the combination; a reader who accepts both has the framework’s case
   for conservation.
   The two arguments point beyond themselves. They establish the necessity and the
   reasonableness of the presumption; they do not establish the ground of the presumption’s
   truth. The framework does not claim that its arguments are the ground of the truth, and it
   does not claim that the ground is unreachable. It claims that the arguments establish what
   they establish, and that what they establish points beyond itself. The distinction is the
   distinction between the argument and the ground of the argument; it is kept throughout
   the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the presumption as the one who is the same yesterday,
   today, and forever, and as the one in whose knowledge the identities of things are held.
   The framework does not claim that its arguments are that one, and it does not claim that
   the one is unreal. It claims that the arguments are real, and that the arguments point
   beyond themselves. The reader who identifies the arguments with the one is free to do so;
22.9. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                       231


   the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the
   identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.




22.9      What This Chapter Does Not Establish


Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.

   First, the chapter does not argue for the temporal invariance premise beyond stating it as
a commitment. The premise—that time belongs to the class of allowable transformations—is
adopted, not proved. Its support is the argument’s coherence with the framework’s other principles;
its refutation would be a demonstration that time is not a transformation of manifestations like
any other. The chapter has stated the premise; the debate over it is left open.

   Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of how the three arguments work
together. The temporal invariance argument, the transcendental argument, and the abductive
argument each have their own force; the chapter has stated all three, and has shown how the
transcendental and the abductive together close the gap left by the temporal invariance argument
alone. The full synthesis of the three is left for the parts of the book that develop the framework’s
overall case.

   Third, the chapter does not develop the consequences of conservation for the framework’s
account of death, birth, and capacity. The three-fold distinction among persistence, manifestation,
and capacity was stated; its application to death, birth, and the loss of capacity is developed in
the parts of the book that treat those topics. The present chapter has argued for conservation;
the later parts apply it.

   Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of conservation. It claims
to have described the structure of conservation, and the structure points beyond itself to the
ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the
structure of conservation and the ground of conservation; it is kept throughout the chapter, and
it is stated here as the chapter’s explicit limit.
