A Question for Reflection
Consider something that has persisted across a long time and through significant change—a
friendship, an institution, a language. What is the identity that has been conserved? Is it
something you can point to, or is it the invariant that makes the changing manifestations
recognizable as manifestations of one thing? What does your answer tell you about the relation
between conservation and manifestation?

The next chapter turns to the non-duplicability of identity. It argues that identity cannot be
numerically duplicated—that signatures, pseudo-identities, and information can be copied, but
that identity cannot. The present chapter has argued that identity is conserved across time; the
next chapter argues that, once an identity is conserved, it cannot be multiplied into two.
Chapter 23

The Non-Duplicability of Identity


Scope. This chapter argues that identity cannot be numerically duplicated—that signatures,
pseudo-identities, and information can be copied, but that identity cannot. It gives the direct
argument from the logic of numerical identity, argues that the principle holds whether or not
the identity of indiscernibles is accepted, separates the principle from qualitative similarity, and
answers three standard objections. Its claims are structural; where the chapter is silent on
questions of value or psychology, the silence is not a denial but a recognition that the structural
description is not the whole of what can be said. Where the chapter speaks of “copying,”
“duplication,” “signature,” “thisness,” or “matters,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed
by the definitions in this chapter and in the part of the book that treated identity. The word
“matters” appears only to mark the boundary of the framework’s subject: it names a question
that belongs to an independent normative inquiry, not to the present book.


23.1      A Scene
Consider two copies of the same book. The first is the author’s manuscript; the second is a
printed copy, made from the manuscript by a process that reproduces every mark, every word,
every punctuation, on paper of the same quality, with the same binding. Turn the pages; the
two are indistinguishable. If someone mixed them up, no one could tell which was which. Are
they the same book?
    The question has a natural answer and an unsettling one. The natural answer is: they are
the same book, because they say the same thing, they have the same words, they carry the same
meaning. The unsettling answer is: they are two books, because one was written by the author
and the other was printed from it. The first is the author’s; the second is a copy. They share
their signature—their words, their meaning, their form—but they are not the same object, and
not the same act of writing.
    The unsettling answer is the framework’s answer. What is shared between the two copies is
the signature: the structural description of the invariance that the book exhibits. What is not
shared is the identity: the invariance as enacted by one source. The author’s manuscript has the
identity of the author’s act; the printed copy has the identity of the printed copy. The two share
their pattern, but not their thisness.
    Now consider a harder case. Suppose a machine could scan a living person—her body, her
memories, her habits, her character—and build an exact copy elsewhere, atom by atom. The
copy would be indistinguishable from the original: it would remember the same childhood, love
the same people, hold the same beliefs, fear the same things. If the original were destroyed in
the scan, would the copy be the original? If the original were not destroyed, would there be two
of her?

                                                 233
234                                                Chapter 23. The Non-Duplicability of Identity


      The scene is a standard one in the philosophy of personal identity, and the framework’s
answer to it is the same as its answer to the two books. What the machine reproduces is the
signature: the pattern of memories, habits, and character. What it does not reproduce is the
identity: the invariance as enacted by one source. The copy is a copy; if it expresses at all, it
expresses an identity of its own, with its own manifestations and its own structural trajectory.
      The scene poses a question. What is the difference between copying a signature and duplicating
an identity? And why is the second impossible, while the first is not? The present chapter answers
these questions. Its answer is the principle of non-duplicability, and its principal contribution is
the argument that separates the principle from the disputes over qualitative similarity and the
identity of indiscernibles.

   Remark 23.1 (Non-Duplicability Points Beyond Itself)

   The non-duplicability of identity is a real structural feature; the framework’s claim is that
   the identity cannot be copied, and that the signature can. But the non-duplicability is not
   self-grounded. The non-duplicability is the structural expression of the uniqueness of each
   identity; it is not the ground of the uniqueness. The non-duplicability points beyond itself
   to what makes each identity uniquely itself. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is
   real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction is the
   distinction between the structure of non-duplicability and the ground of the uniqueness; it
   is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the uniqueness as the uniqueness of each soul
   before its source, and as the singularity that no other can share. The framework does
   not claim that its structural non-duplicability is that uniqueness, and it does not claim
   that the uniqueness is unreal. It claims that the non-duplicability is a real structural
   feature, and that the feature points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the structural
   non-duplicability with the uniqueness before the source is free to do so; the reader who
   distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because
   the identity is a question for another inquiry.




23.2        The Question

The previous chapter argued for the conservation of identity: identity is invariant under all
temporal transformations of its manifestations. The present chapter asks a further question. If
identity is conserved across time, can it be multiplied across space? Can there be two things
that are numerically one identity—two things, each of which is that very identity?
      The question is not idle. In ordinary language, we speak of “the same book” in two copies,
“the same song” in two performances, “the same person” in two photographs. The framework’s
claim is that this ordinary way of speaking is correct if it means that the signature is the same,
and incorrect if it means that the identity is the same. The two are easily confused, and the
present chapter’s task is to separate them.
      Two aspects of the question must be distinguished.
23.3. The Principle and the Definition                                                         235


The logical aspect. Is numerical duplication of an identity possible? The chapter’s answer is
that it is not, and the argument is from the logic of identity itself. The argument is short and
decisive: numerical duplication of an identity would require two distinct things, each of which is
that very identity, and the logic of identity excludes this.


The metaphysical aspect. What is it about identity that makes it non-duplicable? The
chapter’s answer is that identity is more than its signature—that a thing’s identity is the
invariance as enacted by one source, not the pattern that the source exhibits. The claim is a
commitment ((A)), and the chapter states its cost.
   The chapter proceeds as follows. First, it states the principle and defines its terms. Second,
it gives the direct argument from the logic of numerical identity. Third, it gives the dilemma
argument from the identity of indiscernibles, which shows that the principle holds whether or
not the identity of indiscernibles is accepted. Fourth, it separates the principle from qualitative
similarity. Fifth, it states the commitment on which the principle rests. Sixth, it draws the
consequences for cloning, teleportation, and fission. Seventh, it answers three standard objections.
The chapter ends with what it does not establish and with the epistemic status of its claims.



23.3      The Principle and the Definition

   Principle 23.1 (Non-Duplicability)

   (A) Identity cannot be copied. Signatures, pseudo-identities, and information can be
   duplicated; identity cannot. A copy of a system reproduces its signature. If the copy
   expresses at all, it expresses an identity of its own.


   The principle is (A): it is adopted as a commitment of the framework. It is supported by the
arguments that follow, and its cost is stated in a later section. It would be refuted by a case in
which an identity is numerically duplicated—that is, a case in which two distinct things are, each
of them, the same identity. The framework does not claim that no such case can be described; it
claims that no such case can be coherently described, and the arguments below are the reason
for holding so.
   The principle turns on a distinction between two kinds of duplication, which is stated in a
definition.

   Definition 23.1 (Duplication)

   Qualitative duplication produces a second thing that shares the first thing’s signature.
   Numerical duplication of an identity would produce two distinct things, each of which is
   that very identity.


   The distinction is structural. Qualitative duplication is duplication of a signature: the second
thing exhibits the same pattern as the first, and the pattern is what can be read off, compared,
recorded, and copied. Numerical duplication would be duplication of an identity: the second
236                                                 Chapter 23. The Non-Duplicability of Identity


thing would not merely exhibit the same pattern as the first; it would be the same source, the
same thisness, the same enactment of the pattern. The first is possible; the second is not.

   Remark 23.2 (The Principle Does Not Deny Copying)

   The principle does not deny that copying occurs. It denies that copying duplicates identity.
   A copy of a system reproduces its signature; the signature is real, and the copy is a real
   second thing. What the copy does not reproduce is the identity. The distinction is between
   the signature, which is shareable, and the identity, which is not. The reader who reads
   the principle as a denial of copying has misread it; the reader who reads it as a denial of
   the duplication of identity has read it correctly.



23.4        First Argument: The Logic of Numerical Identity
The first argument for the principle is a point of logic. It proceeds from the meaning of numerical
identity.

Argument from the Logic of Numerical Identity.            1. Suppose I1 and I2 are numerically dis-
        tinct, and each is identical to the identity I.

   2. Identity is symmetric and transitive: from I1 = I and I2 = I it follows that I1 = I2 .

   3. This contradicts the supposition that they are distinct. Hence numerical duplication of an
        identity is impossible.



      The argument is short, and its brevity is the point. Numerical identity is an equivalence
relation: it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. If two things are each identical with a third,
they are identical with each other, and so they are not two things. The logic of numerical identity
excludes the possibility that two distinct things are each the same identity, because it excludes
the possibility that two distinct things are identical with each other.
      The argument’s steps (1)–(2) are a point of logic and carry little weight by themselves.
The philosophical content of the principle is in the further claim that identity is more than
signature—that a thing’s identity is not exhausted by the pattern it exhibits. The next section
develops this claim, and the section after that states its cost.

   Remark 23.3 (The Argument Is Not the Whole Principle)

   The logic of numerical identity shows that two distinct things cannot be the same identity.
   It does not show that identity is more than signature. A reader who holds that identity is
   nothing over and above signature could accept the logic of numerical identity and still
   hold that copying a signature copies the identity—that is, that a copy of a signature is
   a second thing that is the same identity. The further claim that identity is more than
   signature is what rules this out, and the claim is a commitment ((A)), not a logical point.
   The next two sections develop the commitment and state its cost.
23.5. Second Argument: The Dilemma from Indiscernibles                                             237


23.5      Second Argument: The Dilemma from Indiscernibles
The second argument is a dilemma. It shows that the principle holds whether or not the identity
of indiscernibles is accepted.
    The identity of indiscernibles (PII) is the principle that two things sharing all their qualitative
features are one thing. It is contested; Black argued against it with a world of two exactly similar
spheres.1 The principle of non-duplicability does not depend on how this dispute comes out.

Argument from the Identity of Indiscernibles.        1. First horn: PII holds. Then two things
       cannot share all qualitative features. A copy of a signature therefore differs from the
       original in some respect (at least in its relations or its position), so it is a second thing
      with its own features, and not a second instance of the same thing.

    2. Second horn: PII fails. Then there can be two things that share every qualitative feature, as
       in Black’s spheres. They are two, and so have two identities (the argument of the previous
       section). An exact qualitative duplicate is still not a numerical duplicate.

    3. In both horns, copying does not yield a second thing that is the original identity.

    4. Conclusion: identity cannot be duplicated, whether or not PII is true.


    The argument removes the dependence of the principle on PII. Its force is that the two horns
exhaust the possibilities: either PII holds or it does not, and in either case the principle follows.
The argument does not establish the principle from PII; it establishes that the principle does not
need PII. The next section states what the principle does need.

    Remark 23.4 (What the Dilemma Shows and Does Not Show)

    The dilemma shows that the principle of non-duplicability is independent of the dispute
    over the identity of indiscernibles. It does not show that the principle is independent of
    every commitment. What the principle does depend on is stated in the next section: the
    commitment that identity is more than its signature. The dilemma is a step toward the
    principle, not the whole of its case.



23.6      The Independence from Qualitative Similarity
A further independence must be stated. The principle of non-duplicability is independent of
the degree of qualitative similarity between things. It is neither strengthened nor weakened by
finding two things more or less alike.

    Principle 23.2 (Independence from Qualitative Similarity)

    (T) The principle of non-duplicability is independent of the degree of qualitative similarity
    between things: it is neither strengthened nor weakened by finding two things more or

1
    [C23-1] Black, “The Identity of Indiscernibles,” Mind 61, no. 242 (1952): 153–164
238                                                  Chapter 23. The Non-Duplicability of Identity


    less alike.

Argument for the Independence.          1. Two entities may be qualitatively similar, up to being
        alike in every qualitative respect.

    2. Two manifestations may have similar or identical forms.

    3. Similarity of entities, or of forms, is a relation among products or appearances.

    4. Numerical unity of identity is a fact about a source.

    5. From a fact about products one cannot, without a further premise, infer a fact about the
        number of sources.

    6. Hence similarity, however complete, is not numerical unity of identity.


      The argument’s force is in step (5). Products and appearances can be similar to any
degree; the number of sources is not determined by the degree of similarity. Two things can
be indistinguishable in every qualitative respect and still be two things, with two sources and
two identities; and two things can be quite different in their appearances and still be two
manifestations of one source. The similarity of appearances is not the unity of the source.

    Remark 23.5 (A Useful Corollary)

    Two manifestations with the same form need not be manifestations of one identity; and
    two manifestations with quite different structures may be manifestations of one. The count
    of identities is not read off the likeness of appearances. The corollary is the framework’s
    principal use of the principle: it blocks the inference from the likeness of manifestations to
    the sameness of the identity, and from the difference of manifestations to the difference of
    the identity. The reader who makes either inference has conflated the signature with the
    identity; the reader who avoids both has kept them apart.



23.7        The Commitment: Identity Is More Than Signature
The principle of non-duplicability rests on a commitment: that identity is more than its signature.
The commitment must be stated, and its cost must be stated with it.
      What the commitment asserts is that a thing’s identity is not exhausted by the pattern it
exhibits. A thing’s signature is the structural description of its invariance: what can be read off,
compared, recorded, and copied. A thing’s identity is the invariance as enacted by one source:
not the pattern, but the enactment. Two things with exactly the same pattern are two, not one,
because the enactment is two.
      This is the doctrine of primitive thisness: an individuating feature that is not qualitative,
and that distinguishes one thing from an exact qualitative duplicate.2 The framework adopts the
2
      [C23-2] Adams, “Primitive Thisness and Primitive Identity,” Journal of Philosophy 76, no. 1 (1979):
      5–26
23.7. The Commitment: Identity Is More Than Signature                                            239


doctrine as a commitment ((A)). It is a non-reductionist view of identity, in Parfit’s classification,
because it holds that there is a further fact about identity over and above facts about continuity
and similarity.3 Consequently, in a case where the signature is perfectly copied, nothing observable
settles which of the resulting systems, if any, carries the original identity.
    The commitment is supported by three considerations.

First consideration. It explains why the rigidity of identity holds: strict sameness is not a
matter of resemblance, and the invariance of identity is not the invariance of a pattern shared by
many.

Second consideration. It is consistent with the best-known case against the identity of
indiscernibles, Black’s two exactly similar spheres, in which two things share every qualitative
feature and yet are two.4

Third consideration. It explains why reconstruction can converge on a signature without
ever delivering the identity: the signature is what can be read off, and the identity is what is
enacted by a source.
    The cost of the commitment is the one stated above: the identity-facts in duplication cases
are not settled by observation. The framework accepts this cost, and states it as the price of
the commitment. A reader who finds the cost unacceptable has located the place where the
framework should be challenged.

    Remark 23.6 (Primitive Thisness Points Beyond Itself)

    The doctrine of primitive thisness is a real structural claim; the framework’s claim is that
    a thing’s identity is not exhausted by its signature, and that the enactment of the pattern
    by a source is the further fact that distinguishes one thing from its exact qualitative
    duplicate. But the thisness is not self-grounded. The thisness is the thisness of a source;
    it is not the ground of its own being. The thisness points beyond itself to what makes
    each source uniquely itself. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that
    what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction
    between the thisness and the ground of the thisness; it is kept throughout the book.
    The traditions speak of the ground of the thisness as the fixed essence that each thing
    has in the knowledge of its source, and as the individuation that no other can share. The
    framework does not claim that its structural thisness is that fixed essence, and it does
    not claim that the fixed essence is unreal. It claims that the thisness is a real structural
    feature, and that the feature points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the structural
    thisness with the fixed essence is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to
    do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a question
    for another inquiry.



3
    [C23-3] Parfit, Reasons and Persons (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1984)
4
    [C23-4] Black, “The Identity of Indiscernibles,” Mind 61, no. 242 (1952): 153–164
240                                                 Chapter 23. The Non-Duplicability of Identity


   Remark 23.7 (The Commitment Is Not Derived)

   The commitment is not derived from the logic of numerical identity, or from the dilemma
   over indiscernibles, or from the argument for independence from qualitative similarity.
   Each of those arguments establishes something, but none of them establishes that identity
   is more than its signature. The commitment is the premise that gives the principle of
   non-duplicability its content, and the framework says so openly instead of replacing it by
   an argument that would turn out circular. It is supported by the three considerations
   above, and it would be refuted by showing that a framework without it explains the same
   things as well.
   The commitment is not self-grounded. The commitment points beyond itself to what makes
   the thisness possible. The framework does not describe the ground of the commitment,
   and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the commitment is a real
   structural commitment, and that the commitment points beyond itself. The distinction is
   the distinction between the commitment and the ground of the commitment; it is kept
   throughout the book.


   Remark 23.8 (The Three Levels That Must Not Be Merged)

   The principle concerns three different things, and the argument must treat them separately.

       1. Duplication of an identifiable form or structure. A form or structure can be repro-
         duced; this is duplication of signature.

       2. Qualitative similarity between two entities. Two entities may be alike in every
         qualitative respect.

       3. Numerical duplication of one identity. One identity appearing as two distinct things,
         each of which is that identity.

   The first is possible; the second is possible; the third is not. The three are easily confused,
   and the confusion is a source of many of the standard puzzles of personal identity. The
   framework’s claim is that the three are distinct, and that only the third is excluded by
   the principle of non-duplicability.



23.8      Consequences: Cloning, Teleportation, Fission
The principle of non-duplicability has consequences for the classical puzzles of personal identity.
They are stated here with their epistemic statuses.


Cloning ((T)). A clone reproduces a genetic signature. It is not the original and does not
carry the original’s identity; if it expresses at all, it expresses an identity of its own, with its
own manifestations and its own structural trajectory. The claim follows from the principle of
non-duplicability and the commitment that identity is more than signature; it is (T) relative to
those commitments.
23.9. Objections and Replies                                                                     241


Teleportation ((E)). If a machine scans a body, destroys it, and builds an exact copy elsewhere,
the copy has the original’s signature. The framework’s commitment is that copying does not
transfer the identity, so the copy is a new system. This verdict is a consequence of the doctrine of
primitive thisness and cannot be decided by observation; it is offered as the framework’s answer,
not as an empirical result. Its status is (E): it is an estimate, and it would be revised if the
framework’s account of signature and identity were revised.


Fission ((S)). If a system divides into two systems that both continue its signature, then by
the logic of identity the original identity can continue in at most one of them, or in neither. The
framework does not say that the question has no answer, but that nothing observable fixes it. It
is a case where the further fact is real and inaccessible. The status is (S): a speculative extension,
flagged for caution.
   These consequences may seem counterintuitive. They are the theoretical cost of the doctrine,
and the book states them in order that the cost is visible. A reader who finds the consequences
unacceptable has located the place where the framework should be challenged.

   Remark 23.9 (The Consequences Point Beyond Themselves)

   The consequences for cloning, teleportation, and fission are structural claims, and the
   framework’s claim is that they follow from the commitments about identity, signature,
   and copying. But the consequences are not self-grounded. The consequences point beyond
   themselves to the uniqueness of each identity, which is grounded in what makes each
   identity uniquely itself. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim
   that the ground is unreal. It claims that the consequences are real structural consequences,
   and that the consequences point beyond themselves. The distinction is the distinction
   between the consequences and the ground of the consequences; it is kept throughout the
   book.

   Remark 23.10 (The Consequences Are Not Empirical Results)

   The consequences for cloning, teleportation, and fission are not empirical results. They do
   not follow from any experiment; they follow from the framework’s commitments about
   identity, signature, and copying. The framework does not claim that the consequences are
   verified; it claims that they are what follows from the commitments, and that a reader
   who accepts the commitments should accept the consequences. The reader who does not
   accept the consequences has a reason to reject one of the commitments; the framework’s
   task is to make the commitments explicit, so that the reader knows which one to reject.



23.9       Objections and Replies
Three standard objections are addressed.


Objection 1: “If a perfect copy is made and the original is destroyed, the copy
remembers being me, acts as I did, and is regarded as me by everyone. So it is
242                                                  Chapter 23. The Non-Duplicability of Identity


me.” The copy has the signature of the original and, by the principle, an identity of its own.
Everything the objector cites—the memory-manifestations, the behavioral- manifestations, the
social recognition—is a fact about signatures, not about identity. The framework’s claim is that
identity involves a further fact that these do not settle. The reply concedes that no observation
can decide between the two cases; that is the theoretical cost of the view, stated above.

Objection 2: “A further fact that no observation can reach is mysterious, and
perhaps meaningless.” It would be meaningless if the framework offered no reason to posit
it. It offers three: it explains why strict sameness is not a matter of degree, why reconstructions
converge on a signature without delivering the identity, and why exact copies are two. The
doctrine is therefore labeled (A) and is not offered as a result. A reader who finds the three
reasons insufficient has a reason to reject the doctrine; the framework does not claim more for it
than the three reasons support.

Objection 3: “Parfit has shown that identity is not what matters.” Parfit’s claim is a
claim about what has value in survival— a normative question that belongs to an independent
inquiry.5 The framework does not address that question, and its claim about identity is
independent of it. What the framework states is structural: identity and viability are distinct,
and a duplication of signatures can occur without a duplication of identity. The framework does
not follow Parfit in dissolving the question of identity itself, but it also does not require that the
question of identity settle the question of what has value in survival.

    Remark 23.11 (The Objections Are Addressed, Not Refuted)

    Each objection names a respect in which the framework’s account is not what the objector
    expected. None of them shows that the account is wrong. A reader who finds the account
    counterintuitive has located a point at which the framework’s commitments are most
    visible; a reader who accepts the account has accepted the commitments, and should
    accept the consequences. The objections are addressed, not refuted, because they are not
    refutations; they are statements of what the account is not, and the framework agrees
    with each of them.
    The objections point beyond themselves. The objections arise from questions that cannot
    be settled at the level of structure; they point toward questions that belong to other
    inquiries. The framework does not answer those questions, and it does not dismiss them.
    It marks them as belonging to other inquiries, and it states its own structural claim at the
    strength its arguments support.

    Remark 23.12 (What Has Value in Survival Is Not Addressed)

    Parfit argued that in cases of fission what matters in survival is not identity but psy-
    chological continuity and connectedness. Lewis proposed that before fission there were
    already two persons who shared their earlier stages. These are questions about what has


5
      [C23-5] Parfit, Reasons and Persons (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1984)
23.10. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                    243


   value in survival—a normative question that belongs to an independent inquiry. The
   framework does not address it. What the framework states is structural: identity and
   viability are distinct, and a duplication of signatures can occur without a duplication of
   identity. Whether viability has value, and what value it has, is not a question this book
   answers. The distinction between the structural question and the normative question is
   stated in the part of the book that treats the boundaries of philosophy.
   The distinction between the structural question and the normative question is not a
   dismissal of the normative question. The normative question is real, and it belongs to
   an inquiry the framework is designed to serve, not to replace. The framework’s silence
   on the normative question is not a denial of its importance; it is the recognition that
   the structural description is not the whole of what can be said. The distinction is kept
   throughout the book, and it is stated here as the chapter’s explicit limit.




23.10      What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.

   First, the chapter does not argue for the commitment that identity is more than its signature.
The commitment is (A), and it is supported by the three considerations stated above. A reader
who rejects the commitment rejects the principle of non-duplicability with it, and the framework
does not pretend otherwise. The full defense of the commitment is the subject of the chapters
that follow, where the objections are developed and answered.

   Second, the chapter does not settle the question of what has value in survival. The question
is normative, and the framework does not address it. The chapter has stated the structural
claims about identity, signature, and copying; the normative question is a separate inquiry.

   Third, the chapter does not develop the full account of the relation between non-duplicability
and the other principles of the framework. The principle of non-duplicability is related to the
principle of conservation (argued in the previous chapter) and to the principle of super-identity
(argued in the first part of the book). The relations are stated in the dependency maps of the
parts; the full development is left for the parts of the book that treat them.

   Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of thisness. It claims to
have described the structure of non-duplicability, and the structure points beyond itself to the
ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the
structure of non-duplicability and the ground of the thisness; it is kept throughout the chapter,
and it is stated here as the chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a case in which something you value is perfectly copied—a photograph, a recording,
a text. What is shared between the original and the copy, and what is not? What does your
answer tell you about the difference between the signature and the identity?

The next chapter turns to the desire to find. It states a theorem about the structural relation
by which an identity is rendered legible in the reflection of its expression in another identity’s
expression. The present chapter has argued that identity cannot be duplicated; the next chapter
argues that identity can be rendered legible in the expression of another—and that this rendering-
legible is the condition of finding among identities.
Chapter 24

The Desire to Find


Scope. This chapter states a theorem about the structural relation by which an identity is
rendered legible in the reflection of its expression in another identity’s expression. Its claims are
structural; where the chapter is silent on questions of psychology or value, the silence is not a
denial but a recognition that the structural description is not the whole of what can be said. The
terms “desire” and “finding,” which appear in the title and in the theorem, are used in a purely
structural sense, defined in this chapter; neither names a mental state, a motivation, a want, a
value, or an end. Where the chapter speaks of “finding,” “desire,” “reflection,” “expression,” or
“legibility,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and
in the parts of the book that treated light and expression.



24.1       A Scene

Consider two people in conversation. One speaks; the other listens. The speaker says something
about herself—not a fact about the world, but something that reveals what she is like, what she
cares about, what she fears, what she hopes for. The listener hears the words and, in hearing
them, understands something about the speaker. The understanding is not the words; the words
are the expression. The understanding is the recognition of what the expression expresses.
    What happens in the listener? The listener does not enter the speaker’s mind; the listener
does not have direct access to the speaker’s identity. The listener has the words, and from
the words the listener forms an impression—a partial, fallible, revisable impression of what the
speaker is like. The impression is not the speaker; it is a reconstruction, from the expression, of
the identity that the expression manifests.
    Now consider the reverse. The speaker, in speaking, is also listening to herself. She hears her
own words; she sees, in the listener’s response, something of what she has said. The listener’s
response is another expression, and the speaker, in hearing it, comes to understand her own
expression better. What she said, and how it was received, and what the reception reveals
about what she meant—the three are not separate. The listener’s response is a reflection of the
speaker’s expression, and in the reflection the speaker finds her expression rendered legible in a
new way.
    The scene is not about psychology. It is about a structural relation that holds between
expressions, whether or not the expressions belong to persons in conversation. Whenever one
expression reflects another, the reflection renders the reflected expression legible as the expression
of its source. And whenever an expression is rendered legible in this way, something has been
found—not the identity itself, which is never directly accessible, but the identity as it appears in
the reflection of its expression.

                                                 245
246                                                               Chapter 24. The Desire to Find


      The scene poses a question. What is the structure of this relation? Is it a contingent
feature of some expressions, or a structural necessity of every expression? And does the relation
carry any implication for what an identity is, or for how identities stand to one another? The
present chapter answers these questions. Its answer is a theorem: that every identity stands in a
structural relation of finding.

   Remark 24.1 (Finding Points Beyond Itself)

   The relation of finding is a real structural relation; the framework’s claim is that every
   identity stands in it, and that the relation is a consequence of the principles of expression,
   conduit, and reflection. But the relation is not self-grounded. The relation of finding
   is the relation by which an identity is rendered legible in the reflection of another; it is
   not the ground of that legibility. The relation points beyond itself to what makes the
   identity legible, and to what makes the reflection reflect. The framework’s claim is that
   the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The
   distinction is the distinction between the relation of finding and the ground of finding; it
   is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of finding as the innate disposition (fitrah) that the
   creator has placed in every soul toward its source, and as the knowledge (ma’rifah) by
   which the soul recognizes its origin in the reflection of the signs. The framework does
   not claim that its structural finding is that disposition, and it does not claim that the
   disposition is unreal. It claims that the finding is a real structural relation, and that
   the relation points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the structural finding with
   the disposition is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the
   framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another
   inquiry.



24.2        The Question

The preceding chapters of this part have argued for several structural claims. The necessity of
expression was argued (the chapter on expression). The minimality of the four grades was argued
(the chapter on grades). The minimality of the three hubs was argued (the chapter on hubs). The
irreducibility of one-step reduction was argued (the chapter on mediation). The conservation of
identity was argued (the chapter on conservation). The non-duplicability of identity was argued
(the chapter on duplication).
      The present chapter asks a different kind of question. The previous chapters have argued for
what identity is, and for what it does, and for what it cannot do. The present chapter asks how
identities stand to one another—specifically, how an identity is rendered legible in the expression
of another identity. The question is not about what an identity is; it is about a structural relation
among identities, given what they are.
      The question is: is there a structural relation by which every identity is rendered legible in
the reflection of its expression in another identity’s expression? The framework’s answer is that
there is, and that the relation is a consequence of the principles already established: the principle
24.3. The Theorem                                                                                  247


of expression, the conveyor of light, and the reflective nature of light.
   The chapter’s method is threefold. First, it states the theorem, and defines the terms “finding”
and “desire” in the structural sense they will have in the argument. Second, it proves the theorem
from the three principles. Third, it draws the consequences: the dependence of the theorem on
the principle of expression (which means the theorem cannot be used to support the principle),
and the distinction between finding through manifestation and finding through a successive
downward route (the first of which is required, the second of which is not).


24.3     The Theorem

   Theorem 24.1 (The Desire to Find)

   (T) Given the principle of expression, the conduit of light, and the reflective nature of
   light, every identity stands in a structural relation of finding: it is, by its nature, such that
   it is rendered legible in the reflection of its expression in the expression of another identity.

   The theorem has three premises and one conclusion. The premises are the principle of
expression (argued in the chapter on expression), the conduit of light (argued in the part of
the book that treated light), and the reflective nature of light (argued in the same part). The
conclusion is that every identity stands in the structural relation of finding. The theorem is
(T): it follows from its premises, and the premises are established elsewhere in the book. The
theorem’s status is therefore the status of its premises, and the reader who wishes to challenge it
knows where to press.
   The theorem’s conclusion must be read carefully. It does not say that every identity is, in
fact, found by another identity. It says that every identity stands in the relation of finding:
that the relation is structurally available, whatever the contingent facts about which identities
actually encounter which expressions. The distinction is between the structural possibility and
its actualization; the theorem asserts the first, not the second.

   Remark 24.2 (The Theorem Is Structural, Not Empirical)

   The theorem is not an empirical claim about how often identities are actually found. It is
   a structural claim about the relation between expression and legibility. It says that an
   identity’s expression is, by its nature, legible in the reflection of another expression; it
   does not say that every identity is, in fact, reflected in another’s expression, or that every
   reflection is adequate. The distinction is between what the structure requires and what
   the contingent facts deliver. The reader who reads the theorem as an empirical prediction
   has misread it; the reader who reads it as a structural claim has read it correctly.



24.4     The Proof
Proof of the Theorem.      1. By the principle of expression, every identity tends to express itself.

  2. By the principle of the conduit, expression occurs through light.
248                                                                 Chapter 24. The Desire to Find


  3. By the principle of reflection, light reflects by its nature.

  4. Therefore the expression of an identity is reflected.

  5. The reflection of an expression renders the expression legible as the expression of its source;
        this rendering-legible is what the book means by finding.

  6. Conclusion: the structure of the unity of expression and reflection is the structure of finding.
        It is not an additional commitment: it follows from the three principles.


      The proof is short, and its brevity is the point. The theorem is not a new foundation; it
is a consequence of three principles already established. The argument proceeds by combining
the three: expression requires light (premise 1 and 2), light reflects (premise 3), and reflection
renders the expression legible (premise 5). The combination yields the conclusion: every identity,
by its nature, stands in the relation of finding.
      The proof’s force is in step (5). The step states what the book means by “finding”: the
rendering-legible of an expression in the reflection of another expression. The definition is not
arbitrary; it is the structural characterization of what happens when one expression reflects
another. The reader who accepts the definition accepts step (5); the reader who denies it has a
different notion of finding, and the framework’s claim is not addressed to that notion.

   Remark 24.3 (The Proof Is Not Circular)

   The proof does not assume the conclusion. It assumes the three principles, and it derives
   the conclusion from them. The derivation is not trivial—it requires the identification of
   the reflection of an expression with the rendering-legible of the expression—but it is not
   circular. The principles do not depend on the conclusion; the conclusion depends on the
   principles. The proof is a genuine derivation, not a restatement of its premises.



24.5        “Desire” Is Structural
The theorem’s title uses the word “desire,” and the word must be fixed. In this book, “desire” is
a structural term. It names the direction of the relation by which an identity is rendered legible
in what reflects its expression. It is not a mental state, a conation, a want, or a value, and the
theorem does not move from the structure of identity to the psychology of a subject.
      The point is important enough to state twice. The theorem is not about what a subject
wants. It is not about the motivation to be understood, or the longing to be known, or the
wish to find oneself in another. It is about a structural relation that holds between expressions,
whether or not any subject has the corresponding motivation. An identity that expressed itself
would stand in the relation of finding whether or not anyone wanted it to; an identity that did
not express itself would not stand in the relation, whatever the motivation.
      The word “desire” is retained because the relation has the structure of a direction: the identity
is, as it were, oriented toward its own legibility in the reflection of another. The orientation is
structural, not psychological. The framework uses the word because the structural direction is
24.5. “Desire” Is Structural                                                                     249


the closest thing, in the framework’s vocabulary, to what the word “desire” names in ordinary
language; the framework does not adopt the ordinary meaning, and it does not transfer the
ordinary meaning’s implications.

   Remark 24.4 (The Term “Finding” Is Structural Too)

   The term “finding” is likewise structural. It names the relation by which the reflection
   of an expression renders the expression legible as the expression of its source. It is not a
   psychological event—not an act of discovery, not a moment of recognition, not a feeling
   of having found. It is a structural relation: the expression is rendered legible, in the
   reflection, as the expression of its source. Whether anyone experiences the rendering is a
   separate question; the relation holds whether or not it is experienced.
   The relation, too, points beyond itself. The relation of finding is the relation by which
   an identity is rendered legible; it is not the ground of that legibility. The relation points
   beyond itself to what makes the identity legible, and to what makes the reflection reflect.
   The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not
   described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the relation and
   the ground of the relation; it is kept throughout the book.


   Remark 24.5 (No Psychological or Evaluative Claim)

   The chapter makes no psychological or evaluative claim. It does not say that identities
   want to be found, or that finding is good, or that the relation of finding is more important
   than other relations among identities. It says that the relation of finding holds structurally,
   given the principles of expression, conduit, and reflection, and it leaves the psychological
   and evaluative questions to other inquiries. The framework’s honesty about this limitation
   is part of what the chapter is.
   The silence is not a denial. The framework does not say that the psychological and
   evaluative questions are unreal or unimportant; it says that they belong to other inquiries,
   and that the structural description is not the whole of what can be said. The distinction
   is the distinction between the structural description and the inquiries it serves; it is kept
   throughout the book.


   Remark 24.6 (The Desire Points Beyond Itself)

   The structural desire is a real feature of the relation of finding; the framework’s claim is
   that every identity is oriented toward its own legibility in the reflection of another. But
   the desire is not self-grounded. The desire is the desire of an identity; it is not the ground
   of its own being. The desire points beyond itself to what places the orientation in the
   identity, and to what makes the orientation possible. The framework’s claim is that the
   pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The
   distinction is the distinction between the desire and the ground of the desire; it is kept
   throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the desire as the innate disposition (fitrah) that
250                                                              Chapter 24. The Desire to Find


   the creator has placed in every soul toward its source, and as the natural inclination
   that draws every creature toward its perfection. The framework does not claim that its
   structural desire is that disposition, and it does not claim that the disposition is unreal.
   It claims that the desire is a real structural feature, and that the feature points beyond
   itself. The reader who identifies the structural desire with the disposition is free to do so;
   the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the
   identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



24.6       The Dependence of the Theorem
The theorem depends on the principle of expression, and the dependence has a consequence: the
theorem cannot be used to support the principle.
      The point was made in the chapter on expression, where the conditional argument from the
desire to find was stated and set aside. The present section restates it, because the theorem is
the fuller statement of what the conditional argument was about.
      The principle of expression is established by two independent arguments (the argument from
intelligibility and the transcendental argument), and by the conditional argument from the desire
to find. The conditional argument was set aside in the chapter on expression, on the ground
that it is not independent: it depends on the relation of finding, which is itself derived from the
principle of expression. The present chapter gives the derivation of the relation of finding, and so
makes the dependence explicit.
      The dependence is not a defect of the theorem. It is a consequence of the framework’s
structure. The theorem is a theorem about expression and reflection, and both of these are
grounded in the principle of expression. To use the theorem to support the principle would be to
use a consequence to support its own premise, and the framework does not do that. The chapter
states the theorem as a consequence, not as a foundation; the reader who wishes to assess the
framework’s case for expression is directed to the chapter on expression.

   Remark 24.7 (The Direction of Dependence)

   The dependence runs from the principle of expression to the theorem, not from the theorem
   to the principle. The principle is the premise; the theorem is the conclusion. The relation
   is one of grounding, not of mutual support. The reader who accepts the principle should
   accept the theorem; the reader who does not accept the principle is not addressed by the
   theorem. The distinction is between what the theorem establishes and what establishes
   the theorem; the theorem establishes a consequence, and the principle establishes the
   theorem.
   The dependence, too, points beyond itself. The dependence is the structural relation
   between the premise and the conclusion; it is not the ground of the relation. The
   dependence points beyond itself to what makes the premise and the conclusion cohere,
   and to what makes the coherence possible. The framework’s claim is that the pointing
   is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction
24.7. Manifestation as a Condition of Finding                                                   251


   is the distinction between the dependence and the ground of the dependence; it is kept
   throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the dependence as the wisdom through which the
   premises and the conclusions are joined, and as the order through which the coherence of
   things is what it is. The framework does not claim that its structural dependence is that
   wisdom, and it does not claim that the wisdom is unreal. It claims that the dependence
   is a real structural relation, and that the relation points beyond itself. The reader who
   identifies the structural dependence with the wisdom is free to do so; the reader who
   distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because
   the identity is a question for another inquiry.


   Remark 24.8 (The Theorem Points Beyond Itself)

   The theorem describes the structure of finding; it is a structural claim, and the framework’s
   claim is that the structure is real, invariant, and describable. But the structure is not
   self-grounded. The structure is the structure of the relation between expression and
   legibility; it is not the ground of the relation. The structure points beyond itself to what
   makes the identity express, and to what makes the expression reflect. The framework’s
   claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the
   framework. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of finding and the
   ground of finding; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of finding as the source from whom every expression
   comes, and to whom every finding returns. The framework does not claim that its
   structural finding is that source, and it does not claim that the source is unreal. It claims
   that the structure of finding is real, and that the structure points beyond itself. The reader
   who identifies the structure with the source is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes
   them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity
   is a question for another inquiry.




24.7     Manifestation as a Condition of Finding

The theorem has an implication, and the implication must be stated with care. Finding requires
expression. If same-realm identities could find one another directly—without any expression—
expression would not be needed for finding. They find one another only through what each
expresses.
   The implication is that manifestation is a condition of finding. An identity is found through
its manifestation; the manifestation is what is reflected, and the reflection is what renders the
identity legible. Without manifestation, there would be nothing to reflect, and without reflection,
nothing would be found.
   Two things must be separated, and the distinction is the section’s principal contribution.
252                                                               Chapter 24. The Desire to Find


First thing: finding through manifestation. An identity is rendered legible through its
manifestation. The manifestation is the expression; the reflection of the manifestation is what
renders the expression legible. The first is retained: it is what the theorem establishes.


Second thing: finding through a successive downward route. Finding might be thought
to require the identity to be manifested in every realm between the source and the finding, as if
the identity had to travel downward through each realm in turn. The theorem does not require
this, and the framework does not hold it. The identity may be manifested directly in the realm in
which the finding occurs, without passing through every realm between. This is the non-necessity
of downward passage, applied to the relation of finding.
      The two things are often run together. The run-together is the source of a misunderstanding:
that the relation of finding requires a sequential descent. The framework’s claim is that finding
requires manifestation, but not that it requires sequential descent. The manifestation may be
direct; the finding may be immediate; the reflection may be of an expression that was not
preceded by intermediate expressions.

   Remark 24.9 (Why the Distinction Matters)

   The distinction matters for the parts of the book that follow. When the book treats love, or
   knowledge, or recognition among identities, it will speak of finding through manifestation,
   not of finding through successive descent. The distinction is what allows the framework
   to say that finding is structural, without committing itself to a sequential metaphysic of
   descent. The reader who conflates the two will find the framework’s claims about finding
   puzzling; the reader who keeps them apart will find them clear.
   The distinction also opens a space for what the framework does not describe. If finding is
   through manifestation and not through successive descent, then the relation of finding
   is compatible with a direct action that does not pass through the intermediate realms.
   The framework does not describe such a direct action, and it does not deny it. It claims
   that finding, structurally, requires manifestation; it does not claim that the structural
   requirement exhausts the possible modes of finding. The distinction is the distinction
   between the structure of finding and the modes of finding; it is kept throughout the book.



24.8       What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
      First, the chapter does not develop the full account of what finding consists in. The theorem
states that every identity stands in the structural relation of finding; it does not develop what
the relation amounts to, in the way of content, in any particular case. The development is left to
the parts of the book that treat recognition, love, and the relations among identities.
      Second, the chapter does not settle the question of whether every identity is, in fact, found.
The theorem says that every identity stands in the relation of finding; it does not say that the
relation is actualized for every identity. Whether a given identity is actually found depends on
contingent facts about expression, reflection, and encounter; the theorem states the structural
24.9. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                253


condition, not the contingent outcome.
   Third, the chapter does not develop the relation between finding and viability. The two
are related: viability is the structural character of the relation between an identity and its
manifestations; finding is the structural relation by which an identity is rendered legible in the
reflection of its expression. Whether the two relations are the same, or whether one is a condition
of the other, is a question the chapter leaves open. The framework’s claim is that both relations
hold; their relationship is developed in later parts of the book.
   Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of finding. It claims to have
described the structure of finding, and the structure points beyond itself to the ground that the
framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of finding
and the ground of finding; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is stated here as the chapter’s
explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a moment in which you understood something about a person from what they said or
did. What was rendered legible in that moment? Was it the person’s identity, or the person’s
expression, or both? What does your answer tell you about the difference between finding and
knowing?

The next chapter turns to the unknownness of same-category identities. It states a theorem about
the structural condition under which reflection among identities in the same realm is possible,
and it distinguishes intrinsic from temporary unknownness. The present chapter has argued that
every identity stands in the relation of finding; the next chapter argues that the relation requires
the identities to be, in a certain structural sense, unknown to one another.
