The Unknownness of Same-Category Identities


Scope. This chapter states a theorem about the structural condition under which reflection
among identities in the same context is possible, and it distinguishes two kinds of unknownness.
Its claims are structural; where the chapter is silent on questions of emotion, love, or value, the
silence is not a denial but a recognition that the structural description is not the whole of what
can be said. Where the chapter speaks of “finding,” “direction,” “individuation,” “reflection,” or
“unknownness,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter
and in the parts of the book that treated light, expression, and the theorem of finding. The
words “love” and “desire,” where they appear, name the relation the tradition has described; the
framework states the structural condition of that relation, and leaves the psychological, ethical,
and aesthetic dimensions of the relation to independent inquiries.



25.1      A Scene

Consider two mirrors facing each other. Each reflects the other, and in the reflection each shows
what the other is. But notice what happens at the limit: if the two mirrors were perfectly
aligned, with nothing between them, and if each could see the other as clearly as it sees itself,
the reflection would collapse. The mirrors would cease to be two mirrors and would become, in
effect, one surface reflecting itself. The image of the other would be the image of the self, and
the image of the self would be the image of the other. There would be nothing left to reflect,
because there would be nothing between the two that could be reflected.
   The collapse does not happen with two ordinary mirrors, because the two mirrors are
separated: by distance, by angle, by the air between them, by the frame that holds them. The
separation is what makes the reflection possible. If the separation were removed—if the two
mirrors were fused into one—the reflection would cease. The two mirrors would be one mirror,
and one mirror cannot reflect itself.
   Now consider two identities in the same context. Each expresses itself; each is rendered
legible in the reflection of its expression in the other’s expression. This is the relation of finding,
stated in the previous chapter. But the relation of finding requires that the two identities remain
distinct. If the two were fused into one—if each had direct access to the other, without the
mediation of expression—there would be no reflection between them, because reflection requires
a relation between distinct terms. The two would be one, and one cannot find itself in the
reflection of another.
   The scene poses a question. What is the structural condition under which the relation of
finding is possible between two same-context identities? The framework’s answer is that the
condition is unknownness: each must be, in a certain structural sense, unknown to the other.

                                                 254
25.2. The Question                                                                              255


The unknownness is not a defect; it is the condition of possibility of the relation. The present
chapter states the theorem and draws its consequences.

   Remark 25.1 (Unknownness Points Beyond Itself)

   The unknownness of same-context identities is a real structural condition; the framework’s
   claim is that the relation of finding requires the two identities to remain distinct, and that
   their distinctness is, in the structural sense the chapter defines, unknownness. But the
   unknownness is not self-grounded. The unknownness is the structural expression of the
   distinctness of two identities; it is not the ground of the distinctness. The unknownness
   points beyond itself to what makes each identity uniquely itself, and to what makes the
   distinctness of two identities possible. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real,
   and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction is the
   distinction between the structure of unknownness and the ground of the distinctness; it is
   kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the distinctness as the uniqueness of each soul
   before its source, and as the singularity that no other can share. The framework does not
   claim that its structural unknownness is that uniqueness, and it does not claim that the
   uniqueness is unreal. It claims that the unknownness is a real structural condition, and that
   the condition points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the structural unknownness
   with the uniqueness before the source is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them
   is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a
   question for another inquiry.




25.2       The Question

The previous chapter stated and proved the theorem of finding: every identity, by its nature,
stands in the structural relation of finding, because expression requires light and light reflects.
The theorem established that the relation of finding holds; it did not yet ask what the relation
requires of the identities it relates.
   The present chapter asks that question. What must be true of two identities, for the relation
of finding to hold between them? The framework’s answer is that they must be distinct, and
that their distinctness, in the structural sense the chapter will define, is unknownness. Each
must be unknown to the other in a way that expression can bridge and reflection can render
legible. If the two were directly known to one another, expression would be superfluous, and the
relation of finding would have nothing to do.
   The question is not about what an identity is, or about whether it can be found. It is about
the structural condition under which the relation of finding is possible. The answer is a condition
on the relation, not on the identities themselves. The condition is unknownness.
   Two things must be distinguished at the outset, because the word “unknownness” is easily
misread.
256                                  Chapter 25. The Unknownness of Same-Category Identities


First: unknownness is structural, not epistemic. It is not the state of a subject who
has not yet learned something. It is a structural feature of the relation between two distinct
identities: each is not directly accessible to the other, and the inaccessibility is what makes
expression necessary.


Second: unknownness is not a defect. It is not a lack that expression might eventually
fill. It is the condition of possibility of expression, and therefore of finding. If it were removed,
expression would be superfluous, and finding would be impossible.
      The chapter treats the theorem in the next two sections, distinguishes two kinds of unknown-
ness in the section after, and draws the structural implication for the relation of finding in the
section after that.


25.3       The Theorem

   Theorem 25.1 (Unknownness)

   (T) The unknownness of same-context identities is the structural condition of possibility
   of reflection, not a defect. If the other were directly known, there would be no mirror;
   there would be no reflection. Unknownness is the structural condition of individuation,
   and individuation is the structural condition of reflection among distinct identities.

      The theorem has two parts. The first part is negative: unknownness is not a defect. The
second part is positive: unknownness is the structural condition of possibility of reflection. The
two parts are not the same claim. The first says that unknownness should not be read as a lack;
the second says what unknownness does. Together, the two parts state what the framework
means when it says that unknownness is structural.
      The theorem is (T): it is argued from the principle of expression (argued in the chapter on
expression) and the theorem of finding (argued in the previous chapter). The argument is given
in the next section. The theorem’s status is therefore the status of its premises; a reader who
accepts the principle of expression and the theorem of finding should accept the theorem of
unknownness, and a reader who rejects one of the premises has a reason to reject the theorem.

   Remark 25.2 (The Theorem Is About Same-Context Identities)

   The theorem concerns identities in the same context. Its claim is not that identities
   in different contexts are unknown to one another, though they may be, but that the
   unknownness of identities in the same context is what makes reflection possible among
   them. The qualification “same-context” matters because the relation of finding, as the
   previous chapter stated it, holds among identities that can encounter one another through
   their expressions. Identities in different contexts may not encounter one another at all,
   and the question of whether reflection is possible among them is a further question that
   the present theorem does not address.
25.4. The Proof                                                                                 257


25.4     The Proof
Proof of the Theorem of Unknownness.        1. If the other were directly known, there would be
     no need for expression; expression would be superfluous.

  2. But expression is necessary (by the principle of expression).

  3. Therefore, the other must be unknown, so that expression is necessary.

  4. And because expression is reflective (by the principle of reflection), the unknownness of the
     other is what makes reflection possible.

  5. Conclusion: unknownness is the structural condition of possibility of reflection.



   The proof’s force is in the first two steps. Step (1) states the consequence of direct knowledge:
if the other were directly known, nothing would need to be expressed, because the other would
already be present to the knower. Step (2) states the principle of expression: every identity tends
toward expression, and expression is necessary. The conjunction of the two yields step (3): the
other must be unknown, or expression would be superfluous.
   Step (4) adds the reflective character of expression, established in the theorem of finding.
If expression is reflective—if the expression of one identity is reflected in the expression of
another—then the unknownness of the other is what the reflection works with. The reflection
renders the expression legible; the legibility is legibility to a knower who does not have direct
access to the source. The unknownness is what makes the rendering legible possible.

   Remark 25.3 (The Proof Is Relative to the Principle of Expression)

   The proof depends on the principle of expression, and it cannot be used to support the
   principle. The dependence is the same as the dependence of the theorem of finding on the
   principle of expression, stated in the previous chapter. The present theorem is a further
   consequence of the same principle, and its status is the same: (T) relative to the principle,
   and not independent of it. A reader who wishes to assess the present theorem is directed
   to the chapter on expression, where the principle is established.



25.5     Unknownness and Manifestational Partiality
The theorem states that unknownness is structural. Two kinds of unknownness must be distin-
guished, and the distinction is the chapter’s principal contribution to the framework’s account of
relations among identities.


First kind: intrinsic unknownness. The other is unknown by the structure of individuation
itself. The unknownness cannot be removed by more manifestation, because it is not a shortage
of manifestation; it is the structural fact that one identity is not another. The unknownness
of the theorem is intrinsic in this sense. No amount of expression, however complete, can turn
258                                  Chapter 25. The Unknownness of Same-Category Identities


one identity into another, and no amount of reflection, however faithful, can render one identity
directly present to another.


Second kind: temporary unknownness. The other is unknown for now, because of limited
capacity, limited manifestation, or limited occasion. The unknownness can in principle be reduced:
with more manifestation, more capacity, or more occasion, the other can become more fully
known. The temporary unknownness is real, but it is not structural in the sense the theorem
requires. It is a contingent fact about the present state of a relation, not a condition of the
relation’s possibility.
      The two are easily run together, and the running-together is a source of confusion. Intrinsic
unknownness is what the theorem asserts; temporary unknownness is what the theorem does
not deny, but does not require. A relation in which the two identities are as fully known to one
another as their capacities allow is still a relation in which intrinsic unknownness holds. The
fullness of knowledge is not the removal of unknownness; it is the fullness of the expression that
the unknownness makes possible.

   Remark 25.4 (Partiality Is a Structural Feature, Not a Defect)

   That a manifestation gives only a partial knowledge of its source does not make the
   manifestation a defective instance of its kind. The partiality is structural: a manifestation
   is the appearance of an identity in a receiving realm, and the receiving realm’s capacity
   determines how much of the identity can appear. The partiality is not a shortage that a
   better manifestation could eliminate; it is what it is to be a manifestation. The framework’s
   account of manifestation, stated in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements,
   established this point; the present remark applies it to the relation of finding among
   same-context identities.
   The partiality points beyond itself. The partiality is the partiality of the finite manifestation;
   it is not the partiality of what is. The partiality points beyond itself to the fullness that
   the finite manifestation cannot contain, and that the framework does not describe. The
   distinction is the distinction between the partiality of the manifestation and the fullness
   of what is manifested; it is kept throughout the book.


   Remark 25.5 (Unknownness Is Not Ignorance)

   The word “unknownness” might suggest ignorance—the state of a subject who does not
   know what could be known. The theorem’s unknownness is not ignorance. Ignorance is
   the temporary state that the second kind of unknownness names; it can in principle be
   reduced. The theorem’s unknownness is intrinsic and structural; it is not a state of the
   subject but a feature of the relation. A subject can be as knowledgeable as possible and
   still stand in the relation of intrinsic unknownness to another identity, because the relation
   is between distinct identities, not between a subject and an object it might come to know.
   The distinction is important, and the framework keeps it throughout.
   The distinction, too, points beyond itself. The intrinsic unknownness is the structural
25.6. Finding Requires Distinctness                                                              259


   expression of the distinctness of two identities; it is not the ground of the distinctness.
   The unknownness points beyond itself to what makes each identity uniquely itself, and
   to what makes the relation of two distinct identities possible. The framework does not
   describe the ground of the distinctness, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal.
   The distinction is the distinction between the structure of unknownness and the ground of
   the distinctness; it is kept throughout the book.



25.6      Finding Requires Distinctness
A structural implication of the theorem is stated in this section. It is stated in structural terms
only, and the framework attaches no value to it.
    If two same-context identities were directly fused, there would be no reflection between them,
because reflection requires a relation between distinct terms. Finding, in the structural sense
of the previous chapter, is the rendering-legible of one identity’s expression in the reflection of
another’s expression; it therefore requires that the two identities remain distinct. The framework
does not say that distinctness is a good, an end, or a value; it says that distinctness is the
structural condition under which the relation of finding is possible between two same-context
identities.

   Remark 25.6 (Distinctness, Not Fusion, Is the Condition of Finding)

   The point is worth stating with care. A reader might think that finding would be more
   complete if the two identities were fused—if each had direct access to the other, without
   the mediation of expression. The framework’s claim is the opposite: fusion would eliminate
   the relation of finding, not complete it. If the two were fused, there would be nothing
   to find, because there would be no other. The relation of finding is a relation between
   distinct terms; the distinctness is what makes the relation possible, and its removal is what
   makes the relation impossible. The reader who reads the framework as saying that fusion
   is the ideal of finding has misread it; the reader who reads it as saying that distinctness is
   the condition of finding has read it correctly.
   The distinctness is a real structural condition; but the distinctness is not self-grounded.
   The distinctness is the distinctness of two identities; it is not the ground of the identities.
   The distinctness points beyond itself to what makes each identity uniquely itself, and
   to what makes the relation of two distinct identities possible. The framework does not
   describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. The distinction
   is the distinction between the distinctness and the ground of the distinctness; it is kept
   throughout the book.


   Remark 25.7 (What the Tradition Has Called “Love”)

   What the tradition has called “love” is, in this framework, a particular form of the
   structural relation of finding under the condition of distinctness. The framework states
   the structural condition of the relation: two distinct identities, each expressing itself, each
260                                  Chapter 25. The Unknownness of Same-Category Identities


   rendered legible in the reflection of the other’s expression, under the condition of the
   unknownness that makes the rendering legible possible.
   But the structural condition points beyond itself. The structural condition is the condition
   of the relation; it is not the reality of the relation. The structural condition points beyond
   itself to the reality that the tradition has called love, and that the framework does not
   describe. The framework does not claim that its structural condition is that reality, and it
   does not claim that the reality is unreal. It claims that the structural condition is real,
   and that the condition points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the
   structural condition of the relation and the reality of the relation; it is kept throughout
   the book. The reader who identifies the structural condition with the reality of love is
   free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no
   position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.


   Remark 25.8 (The Framework Does Not Undertake the Inquiry Into Love)

   The framework does not undertake the inquiry into love. It states a structural condition
   under which the relation of finding among same-context identities is possible; it does not
   develop the psychological, ethical, or aesthetic dimensions of the relation the tradition has
   called love. Those dimensions belong to independent inquiries, and the framework does
   not address them. What the framework does is state the structural condition, and the
   reader who wishes to develop the other dimensions is invited to do so within the condition
   the framework has stated.
   The silence is not a denial. The framework does not say that the psychological, ethical, or
   aesthetic dimensions of love are unreal or unimportant; it says that they belong to other
   inquiries, and that the structural description is not the whole of what can be said. The
   distinction is the distinction between the structural condition and the inquiries it serves;
   it is kept throughout the book.



25.7      The Two Structural Directions of Finding
The structural relation of finding has two directions, and the distinction is worth stating because
the two are easily confused.


First direction: the ascending direction. The structural direction of returning light, from
a manifestation toward its source. It is the direction in which a manifestation is related to the
identity it expresses. When a listener hears a speaker’s words and understands something about
the speaker, the understanding is in the ascending direction: from the expression back to the
source.


Second direction: the reflective direction. The structural direction of reflective light, from
one manifestation to another in the same realm. It is the direction in which two same-context
identities are related through their expressions. When a listener responds to a speaker, and the
25.7. The Two Structural Directions of Finding                                                  261


speaker hears the response and comes to understand her own expression better, the exchange is
in the reflective direction: from one expression to another, in the same realm.
   The ascending and the reflective directions are not two separate relations; they are two
directions of a single structural relation of finding, whose structure was stated in the previous
chapter. Both are directions of light (as the part of the book that treated light established);
the difference is only in what they relate: the ascending direction relates a manifestation to its
source, and the reflective direction relates one manifestation to another in the same realm.

   Remark 25.9 (The Two Directions Are One Relation)

   The distinction between the two directions is analytical, not substantial. The relation
   of finding is one relation, and the two directions are two ways the relation can run. In
   any given encounter, the relation may run in one direction, or in the other, or in both. A
   conversation in which one person understands the other, and the other comes to understand
   herself through the first person’s response, runs in both directions. The framework’s claim
   is that the two directions are directions of one relation, not two relations; the reader who
   reads them as two has misread the framework’s account.


   Remark 25.10 (The Two Directions Point Beyond Themselves)

   The two directions of finding are real structural directions; the framework’s claim is that
   the relation of finding can run in the ascending direction or in the reflective direction,
   and that the two are directions of one relation. But the directions are not self-grounded.
   The directions are the directions of the relation of finding; they are not the ground of the
   relation. The directions point beyond themselves to what makes the relation of finding
   possible, and to what makes the relation run in one direction or another. The framework’s
   claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the
   framework. The distinction is the distinction between the directions of finding and the
   ground of finding; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the directions as the source from whom the ascending
   light comes, and to whom it returns, and as the light that makes the reflective light reflect.
   The framework does not claim that its structural directions are those, and it does not
   claim that they are unreal. It claims that the directions are real structural directions,
   and that the directions point beyond themselves. The reader who identifies the directions
   with the source is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the
   framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another
   inquiry.


   Remark 25.11 (No Claim About Emotion or Value)

   The description of the two directions is structural. It says that the relation of finding
   can run in the ascending direction or in the reflective direction, and it says what each
   direction relates. It does not say that one direction is more valuable than the other, or
   that either direction is accompanied by emotion, motivation, or any psychological state.
262                                   Chapter 25. The Unknownness of Same-Category Identities


   Those questions belong to independent inquiries, and the framework does not address
   them.
   The silence is not a denial. The framework does not say that emotion and value are
   unreal or unimportant; it says that they belong to other inquiries, and that the structural
   description is not the whole of what can be said. The distinction is the distinction between
   the structural description and the inquiries it serves; it is kept throughout the book.




25.8        What This Chapter Does Not Establish


Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.

      First, the chapter does not develop the full account of what the relation of finding amounts to,
in the way of content, in any particular case. The theorem states the structural condition under
which the relation is possible; the development of the content is left to the parts of the book that
treat the relations among identities, and to independent inquiries into the psychological, ethical,
and aesthetic dimensions of those relations.

      Second, the chapter does not settle the question of whether intrinsic unknownness can ever be
removed. The theorem states that it cannot be removed by more manifestation, but it does not
rule out that some other structural change might remove it. Whether such a change is possible
is a question the framework leaves open, and it marks the question as one of the open questions
of the framework.

      Third, the chapter does not develop the relation between the two directions of finding beyond
the distinction stated above. How the two directions interact in a given encounter, whether one
direction presupposes the other, and what the conditions of each direction are—all these are
questions that the framework leaves for later parts. The present chapter has stated the two
directions; the later parts develop them.

      Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of unknownness. It claims
to have described the structure of unknownness, and the structure points beyond itself to the
ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the
structure of unknownness and the ground of the distinctness; it is kept throughout the chapter,
and it is stated here as the chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a person you know well. Is there something about them that you know with certainty,
and something about them that remains unknown no matter how long you have known them?
What is the difference between the two? Does the unknownness diminish your knowledge, or is it
what makes your knowledge possible?

The next chapter turns to the impossibility of super-identity, treated in detail. It gives a second,
independent argument for the impossibility, adds a strengthening from the conveyor principle,
distinguishes three kinds of failure of reconstruction, and answers three standard objections. The
present chapter has stated the structural condition under which the relation of finding is possible;
the next chapter states the structural impossibility of the kind of knowledge that would remove the
condition.
Chapter 26

The Impossibility of Super-Identity (Detailed)


Scope. This chapter gives a fuller treatment of the impossibility of super-identity, which was
stated and argued in the part of the book that treated the foundation. It gives a second,
independent argument for the impossibility; it adds a strengthening from the conveyor principle;
it distinguishes three kinds of failure of reconstruction; it draws three structural consequences;
and it closes the part of the book that gives the arguments, with a ledger of the premises on
which the part’s conclusions depend. It makes no normative, ethical, religious, or evaluative
claim. Where the chapter speaks of “failure,” “limit,” “plurality,” or “view from nowhere,” these
are structural or epistemic terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and in the
parts of the book that treated the foundation and the arguments.



26.1      A Scene

Consider a catalog that attempts to list every book in a library. The catalog is itself a book in
the library. If it is complete, it must list itself. But when it lists itself, the listing is a new entry,
and the catalog is no longer the catalog it was: it is a catalog that lists itself, which is different
from the catalog before it listed itself. To be complete, the new catalog must list the new entry,
which is a new listing, and so on without end.
   The catalog cannot be complete—not because the librarian is lazy, but because the task
is self-undermining. Every attempt to complete the catalog generates a new item outside the
attempt. The incompleteness is not a shortage of effort; it is a structural feature of the task
itself. No matter how many entries the catalog contains, the entry for the catalog itself is always
one more.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose the librarian does not give up, but tries to include the
new entry in a second catalog. The second catalog must list the first catalog and the second
catalog. The second catalog is itself a book, so it must list itself. And so on. Each attempt to
complete the task generates a further task; each further task generates another; the regress is
not a sign of failure, but the structure of the task.
   The scene poses a question. What is the structure of this regress? Is it a peculiarity of
catalogs, or is it a general feature of any attempt to complete a survey? The present chapter’s
answer is that it is general: it is the structure of any attempt at super-identity—the claim to
have known all manifestations of an identity in all contexts. The scene is a particular case of a
general impossibility, and the present chapter states the impossibility in its general form.




                                                  264
26.2. The Question                                                                               265


26.2      The Question

The part of the book that treated the foundation stated and argued the impossibility of super-
identity (the principle that no finite subject can know all manifestations of an identity in all
contexts). The argument was a reductio from four premises: the finitude of the subject, the
infinity of contexts, the premise that manifestation is a product of identity and receiving realm,
and the premise that knowing is situated in a context. The argument established the principle,
and the part of the book that treated the fixed elements drew a further consequence: the fallacy
of super-identity, the error of treating an aggregate of manifestations as a reconstruction of the
source.
   The present chapter does three things that the earlier treatment did not. It gives a second,
independent argument for the impossibility—one that does not depend on the premise that
manifestation is a product. It adds a strengthening from the conveyor principle, which shows
that the impossibility arises even within a single context. And it distinguishes three kinds of
failure of reconstruction, so that the reader can see not only that the super-identity claim is false,
but also how the attempts to reconstruct an identity can go wrong.
   The question is: what is the structure of the impossibility, and what does it tell us about
the limits of reconstruction? The chapter’s answer has four parts: the diagonal argument, the
configuration-dependence strengthening, the distinction among three kinds of failure, and the
three structural consequences. The chapter ends with a ledger of the premises on which the
part’s arguments depend—an audit that closes the part of the book that gives the arguments.



26.3      The Principle Restated

The principle was stated and argued in the part of the book that treated the foundation. It is
restated here, because the present chapter’s arguments bear on it.

   Principle 26.1 (Impossibility of Super-Identity)

   (T) No finite subject can know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts. Moreover,
   the impossibility is not a matter of degree of effort: any attempt to complete the survey
   generates new contexts that lie outside it.


   The principle has two claims. The first is the impossibility itself: no finite subject can know
all manifestations in all contexts. The second is the character of the impossibility: it is not a
shortage that more effort could remedy, but a structural feature of the task. The second claim is
what the present chapter’s arguments establish. The first was established by the earlier reductio;
the second is what the diagonal argument and the configuration-dependence strengthening show.
   The distinction between the two claims matters. A reader who accepts only the first might
think that the impossibility is contingent—a fact about our present limitations, which a more
powerful subject could overcome. A reader who accepts the second sees that the impossibility
is structural: no finite subject, however powerful, can complete the survey, because the survey
itself generates contexts outside itself.
266                                    Chapter 26. The Impossibility of Super-Identity (Detailed)


26.4         A Second Argument: The Diagonal Construction
The second argument for the impossibility is independent of the original reductio. The original
reductio used the premise that manifestation is a product of identity and receiving realm. The
present argument does not; it uses only the openness of relations and the situatedness of knowing.
The two arguments reach the same conclusion by different routes, and either one is sufficient to
establish the principle.

The Diagonal Argument.          1. Suppose a finite subject S has surveyed a collection of contexts
        C1 , . . . , Cn and claims that these are all the contexts in which the identity I is manifested.

  2. The survey is itself a cognition, carried out in some context CS (the fourth column, argued
        in the part of the book that treated the foundation).

  3. By openness (the definition of openness stated in the part of the book that treated the
        foundation), the manifestations of I in the surveyed contexts, and the survey’s own results,
        are fixed elements of further contexts, related by fluid elements and dynamics not available
        in C1 , . . . , Cn .

  4. Some of these further contexts are not among C1 , . . . , Cn , since each contains an element
        that is not a fixed element of any surveyed context.

  5. So the survey is incomplete, and completing it generates the same situation again.

  6. Hence the claim to have surveyed all the contexts is false.


      The argument has the form of a diagonal construction: whatever list of contexts is offered, a
context outside the list can be constructed from the list itself. The construction uses the list’s
own content (the manifestations it surveys) as a fixed element of a new context, and the new
context is outside the list. This is the structural form of the regress that the scene displayed in
the case of the catalog.
      The argument is independent of the original reductio in one of its main premises. The original
reductio used the premise that manifestation is a product of identity and receiving realm (P3 in
the earlier argument). The present argument does not use it. It uses the openness of relations
and the situatedness of knowing, which are established in the earlier parts of the book. A reader
who accepts these two premises and rejects P3 can still accept the present argument; the two
arguments together make the case for the principle stronger, because they do not share all their
premises.

   Remark 26.1 (The Argument Is Not a Proof That Every Survey Fails)

   The argument shows that any claim to have surveyed all contexts is false. It does not
   show that no survey is useful, or that no partial survey can be adequate for its purposes.
   The distinction is between the completeness of the survey and its adequacy. A survey of
   C1 , . . . , Cn may be adequate for many purposes; it is only the claim to completeness that
   the argument refutes. The framework’s claim is structural: complete reconstruction is
26.5. A Strengthening: Configuration-Dependence                                               267


   impossible, partial reconstruction is possible, and the degree of adequacy is a separate
   question from the completeness of the survey.


   Remark 26.2 (The Earlier Version Is Withdrawn)

   An earlier version of this section argued that fluid elements are “in motion” and that
   to know one completely a subject must be present in all its positions. That argument
   is withdrawn, since it ignores that a finite subject can know a rule of motion without
   being present at every position. The present argument depends instead on the claim that
   every survey generates contexts outside itself, and it does not invoke the motion of fluid
   elements.



26.5     A Strengthening: Configuration-Dependence

The diagonal argument shows that super-identity is impossible because contexts are non-finitely
many. The present section shows a stronger claim: super-identity is impossible even within a
single context, because a context’s configuration changes with time and with the other identities
in it. The claim is stated in a definition.

   Definition 26.1 (Configuration-Dependence)

   (A) The manifestation of an identity I in a context C depends on what passes through
   the fluid element of C, and this in turn depends on the whole configuration of C: on what
   other fixed elements are present, and in what state.


   The definition is a consequence of the conveyor principle, applied to the specific case of
manifestations in a context. If the manifestation of I in C is conveyed by the fluid element of C,
and if what the fluid element conveys depends on the configuration of C, then the manifestation
depends on the configuration. The dependence is structural, not contingent.


The Strengthened Argument.        1. By the conveyor principle, every manifestation of I in C is
      conveyed by a fluid element of C.

  2. By configuration-dependence, what the fluid element conveys depends on the configuration
      of C.

  3. The configuration of C changes with time and with the other identities in it.

  4. So the set of manifestations of I in a single context C is not fixed once and for all, and
      cannot be exhaustively listed at any one time.

  5. Hence super-identity is impossible not only because contexts are non-finitely many, but
      also because even a single context yields manifestations that vary with its configuration.
268                                  Chapter 26. The Impossibility of Super-Identity (Detailed)


      The strengthened argument shows that the impossibility is deeper than the diagonal argument
alone reveals. Even if the number of contexts were finite—even if there were only one context—
the super-identity claim would still fail, because the context’s configuration changes, and the
manifestations vary with it. The impossibility is not a consequence of the number of contexts; it
is a consequence of the nature of manifestation.

   Remark 26.3 (Configuration-Dependence Is Not the Denial of Rules)

   Configuration-dependence does not deny that the fluid element operates according to rules.
   It says that what the fluid element conveys depends on the configuration, not that there is
   no rule by which it conveys. The rules are the dynamics of the context; the configuration
   is what the rules operate on. A rule of motion can be known without the configuration
   being known; but the manifestation, which is what the rule produces, depends on both
   the rule and the configuration. The distinction is between knowing the rule and knowing
   the outcome; the framework’s claim is that the outcome depends on the configuration,
   and the configuration changes.



26.6       Three Kinds of Failure of Reconstruction
An attempt to reconstruct an identity from its manifestations can fail in three structurally different
ways. The distinction is the chapter’s principal contribution to the diagnosis of reconstruction,
and it allows the reader to see not only that super-identity is impossible, but also how the
attempts go wrong.

First kind: structural error from a shortage of manifestations. There are too few
manifestations for the invariant to be isolated. The remedy is more manifestations, under varied
contexts. The error is quantitative: the reconstruction would be adequate if it had more data.
This is the kind of failure that the ordinary methods of inquiry are designed to remedy.

Second kind: structural error from incompatibility of manifestations. The man-
ifestations conflict, because some of them are not manifestations of the identity (a case of
misattribution, of the kind distinguished in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements)
or are taken from contexts not mutually translatable (the fallacy of super-identity, argued in the
same part). The remedy is to sort and separate them. The error is structural: the reconstruction
would be adequate if the incompatible manifestations were removed.

Third kind: structural error from the false assumption that an aggregate can replace
the source. Even a rich and compatible aggregate does not reproduce the identity. No remedy
of quantity helps; the error is about what kind of object a reconstruction is. A reconstruction
is a pseudo-identity, an estimate of a signature; it is not the identity, and no accumulation of
estimates makes it the identity. This is the kind of failure that the framework’s account of
identity makes visible, and that the ordinary methods of inquiry do not address.
      The three kinds of failure are not the same, and they have different remedies. The first
is remediable by more data; the second by better sorting; the third is not remediable at all,
26.7. Three Consequences of the Impossibility                                                    269


because it is not a failure of the reconstruction but a structural feature of the relation between
reconstruction and source.

    Remark 26.4 (Why the Third Kind Is the Most Fundamental)

    The first two are errors of method, and can be reduced. The third is an error of conception,
    and persists however much is gathered. The impossibility of super-identity states what is
    impossible; the three kinds of failure state how an attempt goes wrong. The distinction is
    structural; no evaluative ranking of the three is intended. A reader who treats the third
    kind as a remediable error has misread the framework’s account; a reader who sees it as
    the structural limit of reconstruction has read it correctly.



26.7      Three Consequences of the Impossibility
The impossibility of super-identity has three structural consequences. They are stated here, with
their epistemic status.

First consequence: the structural limit of reconstruction. No subject can occupy a
view that captures reality as it is in itself, independent of any context. The phrase “view from
nowhere” is a standard epistemological expression for such a view; it is not a theological claim.1
What a finite subject can achieve is a pseudo-identity of increasing adequacy, not an exhaustive
acquaintance with the source. The limit is structural, not contingent: it is what the relation
between a finite subject and an identity is. ((T))

Second consequence: the structural plurality of perspectives. The plurality of perspec-
tives is a structural consequence of the relation between a finite subject and an identity, not a
defect. Different perspectives are partial, but not arbitrary: they are located at a position, and
each is answerable to the criteria of adequacy and of context validity stated in the part of the
book that treated the foundation. The plurality is not a sign that no perspective is better than
another; it is a sign that every perspective is partial, and that the partiality is structural. ((T))

Third consequence: the fallacy of super-identity. Any attempt to aggregate manifesta-
tions across contexts into a single flat record is not a reconstruction of identity. The fallacy was
stated and argued in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements; the present chapter’s
arguments reinforce it, by showing that the aggregation is not merely incomplete but structurally
incapable of reaching its target. ((T))
    The three consequences are not separate. They are three aspects of one structural fact: the
relation between a finite subject and an identity is not the relation of a knower to an object it can
exhaust. The first names the limit; the second names what replaces the impossible completeness;
the third names the error of treating the replacement as if it were the completeness.



1
    [C26-1] Nagel, The View from Nowhere (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1986). The phrase is used
    as a standard epistemological expression, not as a claim about a divine perspective.
270                                  Chapter 26. The Impossibility of Super-Identity (Detailed)


   Remark 26.5 (The Consequences Are Structural, Not Evaluative)

   The three consequences are structural, not evaluative. The framework does not claim
   that the limit of reconstruction is a deficiency to be lamented, or that the plurality of
   perspectives is a good to be celebrated, or that the fallacy of super-identity is a sin to
   be avoided. It claims that the three are structural features of the relation between finite
   subjects and identities, and that the framework’s account of knowledge, perspective, and
   reconstruction is built on them. The reader who reads the consequences as evaluations
   has misread them; the reader who reads them as structural facts has read them correctly.

26.9     What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Three things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
   First, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the three kinds of failure exhaust
the ways in which reconstruction can go wrong. The three are the ones the framework has
identified; whether a fourth exists is a question the framework leaves open. The framework’s
claim is that the three are structurally distinct and that each has a different remedy, not that no
further kind could be found.
   Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of the structural plurality of perspectives.
The plurality is stated as a consequence of the impossibility; its development—how perspectives
are located, how they are assessed, how they relate to one another—is left to the parts of the
book that treat the resolution of tensions and the boundaries of philosophy. The present chapter
has stated the consequence; the later parts develop it.
   Third, the chapter does not develop the relation between the impossibility of super-identity
and the framework’s other principles beyond what the load-bearing premise table states. The
relations are stated in the table and in the dependency maps of the earlier parts; the full account
of how the impossibility interacts with the framework’s other claims is left to the parts of the
book that treat the system as a whole.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a subject you know well—a discipline, a tradition, a person’s life. What would it mean
to know all of it? What would the attempt to know all of it generate that would be outside
the attempt? What does the answer tell you about the difference between knowing a thing and
knowing everything about it?

With this chapter, the part of the book that gives the arguments is complete. Each principle of the
preceding parts has received its argument; each argument has stated its premises, its inferential
step, and its status; and the part has closed with a ledger of the premises on which its conclusions
depend. The next part turns to the resolution of apparent tensions. The principles are in place;
the next part shows that they do not conflict with one another, and that the apparent conflicts
are consequences of running together distinctions the framework has drawn.

Scope. This chapter gives a fuller treatment of the impossibility of super-identity, which was
stated and argued in the part of the book that treated the foundation. It gives a second,
independent argument for the impossibility; it adds a strengthening from the conveyor principle;
it distinguishes three kinds of failure of reconstruction; it draws three structural consequences;
and it closes the part of the book that gives the arguments, with a ledger of the premises on
which the part’s conclusions depend. Its claims are structural; where the chapter is silent on
questions of religion or value, the silence is not a denial but a recognition that the structural
description is not the whole of what can be said. Where the chapter speaks of “failure,” “limit,”
“plurality,” or “view from nowhere,” these are structural or epistemic terms; their sense is fixed
by the definitions in this chapter and in the parts of the book that treated the foundation and
the arguments.


27.1      A Scene
Consider a catalog that attempts to list every book in a library. The catalog is itself a book in
the library. If it is complete, it must list itself. But when it lists itself, the listing is a new entry,
and the catalog is no longer the catalog it was: it is a catalog that lists itself, which is different
from the catalog before it listed itself. To be complete, the new catalog must list the new entry,
which is a new listing, and so on without end.
   The catalog cannot be complete—not because the librarian is lazy, but because the task
is self-undermining. Every attempt to complete the catalog generates a new item outside the
attempt. The incompleteness is not a shortage of effort; it is a structural feature of the task
itself. No matter how many entries the catalog contains, the entry for the catalog itself is always
one more.
   Now consider a harder case. Suppose the librarian does not give up, but tries to include the
new entry in a second catalog. The second catalog must list the first catalog and the second
catalog. The second catalog is itself a book, so it must list itself. And so on. Each attempt to
complete the task generates a further task; each further task generates another; the regress is
not a sign of failure, but the structure of the task.
   The scene poses a question. What is the structure of this regress? Is it a peculiarity of
catalogs, or is it a general feature of any attempt to complete a survey? The present chapter’s
answer is that it is general: it is the structure of any attempt at super-identity—the claim to
have known all manifestations of an identity in all contexts. The scene is a particular case of a
general impossibility, and the present chapter states the impossibility in its general form.



                                                  273
274                                   Chapter 27. The Impossibility of Super-Identity (Detailed)


27.2        The Question
The part of the book that treated the foundation stated and argued the impossibility of super-
identity (the principle that no finite subject can know all manifestations of an identity in all
contexts). The argument was a reductio from four premises: the finitude of the subject, the
infinity of contexts, the premise that manifestation is a product of identity and receiving realm,
and the premise that knowing is situated in a context. The argument established the principle,
and the part of the book that treated the fixed elements drew a further consequence: the fallacy
of super-identity, the error of treating an aggregate of manifestations as a reconstruction of the
source.
      The present chapter does three things that the earlier treatment did not. It gives a second,
independent argument for the impossibility—one that does not depend on the premise that
manifestation is a product. It adds a strengthening from the conveyor principle, which shows
that the impossibility arises even within a single context. And it distinguishes three kinds of
failure of reconstruction, so that the reader can see not only that the super-identity claim is false,
but also how the attempts to reconstruct an identity can go wrong.
      The question is: what is the structure of the impossibility, and what does it tell us about
the limits of reconstruction? The chapter’s answer has four parts: the diagonal argument, the
configuration-dependence strengthening, the distinction among three kinds of failure, and the
three structural consequences. The chapter ends with a ledger of the premises on which the
part’s arguments depend—an audit that closes the part of the book that gives the arguments.


27.3        The Principle Restated
The principle was stated and argued in the part of the book that treated the foundation. It is
restated here, because the present chapter’s arguments bear on it.

   Principle 27.1 (Impossibility of Super-Identity)

   (T) No finite subject can know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts. Moreover,
   the impossibility is not a matter of degree of effort: any attempt to complete the survey
   generates new contexts that lie outside it.

      The principle has two claims. The first is the impossibility itself: no finite subject can know
all manifestations in all contexts. The second is the character of the impossibility: it is not a
shortage that more effort could remedy, but a structural feature of the task. The second claim is
what the present chapter’s arguments establish. The first was established by the earlier reductio;
the second is what the diagonal argument and the configuration-dependence strengthening show.
      The distinction between the two claims matters. A reader who accepts only the first might
think that the impossibility is contingent—a fact about our present limitations, which a more
powerful subject could overcome. A reader who accepts the second sees that the impossibility
is structural: no finite subject, however powerful, can complete the survey, because the survey
itself generates contexts outside itself.
27.4. A Second Argument: The Diagonal Construction                                                  275


   Remark 27.1 (The Impossibility Is on the Side of the Subject)

   The impossibility established here is an impossibility for the finite subject. It is not an
   impossibility as such. The framework does not claim that no subject whatsoever can know
   all manifestations of an identity in all contexts; it claims that no finite subject can. The
   distinction is crucial, because the two claims are different, and the confusion of the two
   would turn an epistemic claim into a metaphysical one. The impossibility is on the side of
   the subject: it is the finite subject’s survey that cannot be completed, not the object of the
   survey that is unknowable. The framework’s claim is that the finite subject’s knowledge
   is partial; it does not claim that the object is beyond all knowledge, or that no subject
   whatsoever can survey it. The object may be fully known to a subject that is not finite;
   the framework’s claim is about the finite subject, not about the object. The framework’s
   silence on the infinite subject is not a denial of its possibility; it is the recognition that the
   framework’s method is the method of finite inquiry, and that the limits of finite inquiry
   are not the limits of what is. The distinction between the order of inquiry and the order of
   being is kept throughout the book, and it is kept here in its most decisive form: the finite
   subject’s inability to complete the survey is a fact about the subject, not a fact about the
   surveyed.

The second argument for the impossibility is independent of the original reductio. The original
reductio used the premise that manifestation is a product of identity and receiving realm. The
present argument does not; it uses only the openness of relations and the situatedness of knowing.
The two arguments reach the same conclusion by different routes, and either one is sufficient to
establish the principle.

The Diagonal Argument.         1. Suppose a finite subject S has surveyed a collection of contexts
      C1 , . . . , Cn and claims that these are all the contexts in which the identity I is manifested.

  2. The survey is itself a cognition, carried out in some context CS (the fourth column, argued
      in the part of the book that treated the foundation).

  3. By openness (the definition of openness stated in the part of the book that treated the
      foundation), the manifestations of I in the surveyed contexts, and the survey’s own results,
      are fixed elements of further contexts, related by fluid elements and dynamics not available
      in C1 , . . . , Cn .

  4. Some of these further contexts are not among C1 , . . . , Cn , since each contains an element
      that is not a fixed element of any surveyed context.

  5. So the survey is incomplete, and completing it generates the same situation again.

  6. Hence the claim to have surveyed all the contexts is false.

      The argument has the form of a diagonal construction: whatever list of contexts is offered, a
context outside the list can be constructed from the list itself. The construction uses the list’s
own content (the manifestations it surveys) as a fixed element of a new context, and the new
context is outside the list. This is the structural form of the regress that the scene displayed in

      The argument is independent of the original reductio in one of its main premises. The original
reductio used the premise that manifestation is a product of identity and receiving realm (P3 in

and the situatedness of knowing, which are established in the earlier parts of the book. A reader
who accepts these two premises and rejects P3 can still accept the present argument; the two
arguments together make the case for the principle stronger, because they do not share all their
premises.

   Remark 27.2 (The Argument Is Not a Proof That Every Survey Fails)

   The argument shows that any claim to have surveyed all contexts is false. It does not
   show that no survey is useful, or that no partial survey can be adequate for its purposes.
   The distinction is between the completeness of the survey and its adequacy. A survey of
   C1 , . . . , Cn may be adequate for many purposes; it is only the claim to completeness that
   the argument refutes. The framework’s claim is structural: complete reconstruction is
   impossible, partial reconstruction is possible, and the degree of adequacy is a separate
   question from the completeness of the survey.


   Remark 27.3 (The Argument Depends on the Openness of Relations)

   The argument depends on the openness of relations, and it does not invoke the motion
   of fluid elements. The openness of relations says that any manifestation, once produced,
   can become a fixed element in a further context; the argument uses this structural fact to
   generate, from any survey, a context outside the survey. A finite subject can know a rule
   of motion without being present at every position; what the finite subject cannot do is
   complete the survey, because the survey itself generates the context that lies outside it.
   The distinction is the distinction between knowing a rule and completing a survey; the
   framework’s claim is about the second, not the first.


   Remark 27.4 (The Diagonal Argument Points Beyond Itself)

   The diagonal argument establishes that the finite subject’s survey of contexts cannot be
   completed. The argument is structural: it shows the structure of the finite survey. But
   the structure is not self-grounded. The structure of the survey is the structure of the finite
   subject’s inquiry; it is not the ground of the inquiry. The structure points beyond itself to
   what makes the inquiry possible, and to what makes the object of inquiry possible. The
   framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described
   by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of the survey
   and the ground of the survey; it is kept throughout the book.
27.5. A Strengthening: Configuration-Dependence                                               277


   The traditions speak of the ground of the survey as the knowledge that encompasses all
   things, and as the one from whom nothing is hidden. The framework does not claim that
   its structural survey is that knowledge, and it does not claim that the knowledge is unreal.
   It claims that the survey is a real structural relation, and that the relation points beyond
   itself. The reader who identifies the structural survey with the encompassing knowledge is
   free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no
   position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



27.5     A Strengthening: Configuration-Dependence
The diagonal argument shows that super-identity is impossible because contexts are non-finitely
many. The present section shows a stronger claim: super-identity is impossible even within a
single context, because a context’s configuration changes with time and with the other identities
in it. The claim is stated in a definition.

   Definition 27.1 (Configuration-Dependence)

   (A) The manifestation of an identity I in a context C depends on what passes through
   the fluid element of C, and this in turn depends on the whole configuration of C: on what
   other fixed elements are present, and in what state.

   The definition is a consequence of the conveyor principle, applied to the specific case of
manifestations in a context. If the manifestation of I in C is conveyed by the fluid element of C,
and if what the fluid element conveys depends on the configuration of C, then the manifestation
depends on the configuration. The dependence is structural, not contingent.

The Strengthened Argument.        1. By the conveyor principle, every manifestation of I in C is
      conveyed by a fluid element of C.

  2. By configuration-dependence, what the fluid element conveys depends on the configuration
      of C.

  3. The configuration of C changes with time and with the other identities in it.

  4. So the set of manifestations of I in a single context C is not fixed once and for all, and
      cannot be exhaustively listed at any one time.

  5. Hence super-identity is impossible not only because contexts are non-finitely many, but
      also because even a single context yields manifestations that vary with its configuration.


   The strengthened argument shows that the impossibility is deeper than the diagonal argument
alone reveals. Even if the number of contexts were finite—even if there were only one context—
the super-identity claim would still fail, because the context’s configuration changes, and the
manifestations vary with it. The impossibility is not a consequence of the number of contexts; it
is a consequence of the nature of manifestation.

   Remark 27.5 (Configuration-Dependence Is Not the Denial of Rules)

   Configuration-dependence does not deny that the fluid element operates according to rules.
   It says that what the fluid element conveys depends on the configuration, not that there is
   no rule by which it conveys. The rules are the dynamics of the context; the configuration
   is what the rules operate on. A rule of motion can be known without the configuration
   being known; but the manifestation, which is what the rule produces, depends on both
   the rule and the configuration. The distinction is between knowing the rule and knowing
   the outcome; the framework’s claim is that the outcome depends on the configuration,
   and the configuration changes.


   Remark 27.6 (The Limit Points Beyond Itself)

   The limit established by configuration-dependence is a real structural limit; the framework’s
   claim is that the finite subject cannot exhaustively list the manifestations of an identity
   even in a single context, because the context’s configuration changes. But the limit is not
   self-grounded. The limit is the limit of the finite subject’s survey; it is not the limit of
   what is. The limit points beyond itself to what makes the configuration what it is, and to
   what makes the manifestation what it is. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is
   real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction is
   the distinction between the limit of the survey and the ground of what is surveyed; it is
   kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of what is surveyed as the one who knows the
   configuration of all things, and as the one from whom the changes of configuration are not
   hidden. The framework does not claim that its structural limit is that knowledge, and it
   does not claim that the knowledge is unreal. It claims that the limit is a real structural
   limit, and that the limit points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the limit with
   the knowledge is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the
   framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another
   inquiry.




27.6      Three Kinds of Failure of Reconstruction

An attempt to reconstruct an identity from its manifestations can fail in three structurally different
ways. The distinction is the chapter’s principal contribution to the diagnosis of reconstruction,
and it allows the reader to see not only that super-identity is impossible, but also how the
attempts go wrong.


First kind: structural error from a shortage of manifestations. There are too few
manifestations for the invariant to be isolated. The remedy is more manifestations, under varied
contexts. The error is quantitative: the reconstruction would be adequate if it had more data.
This is the kind of failure that the ordinary methods of inquiry are designed to remedy.
27.7. Three Consequences of the Impossibility                                                 279


Second kind: structural error from incompatibility of manifestations. The man-
ifestations conflict, because some of them are not manifestations of the identity (a case of
misattribution, of the kind distinguished in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements)
or are taken from contexts not mutually translatable (the fallacy of super-identity, argued in the
same part). The remedy is to sort and separate them. The error is structural: the reconstruction
would be adequate if the incompatible manifestations were removed.


Third kind: structural error from the false assumption that an aggregate can replace
the source. Even a rich and compatible aggregate does not reproduce the identity. No remedy
of quantity helps; the error is about what kind of object a reconstruction is. A reconstruction
is a pseudo-identity, an estimate of a signature; it is not the identity, and no accumulation of
estimates makes it the identity. This is the kind of failure that the framework’s account of
identity makes visible, and that the ordinary methods of inquiry do not address.
   The three kinds of failure are not the same, and they have different remedies. The first
is remediable by more data; the second by better sorting; the third is not remediable at all,
because it is not a failure of the reconstruction but a structural feature of the relation between
reconstruction and source.

   Remark 27.7 (Why the Third Kind Is the Most Fundamental)

   The first two are errors of method, and can be reduced. The third is an error of conception,
   and persists however much is gathered. The impossibility of super-identity states what is
   impossible; the three kinds of failure state how an attempt goes wrong. The distinction is
   structural; no evaluative ranking of the three is intended. A reader who treats the third
   kind as a remediable error has misread the framework’s account; a reader who sees it as
   the structural limit of reconstruction has read it correctly.
   The third kind, too, points beyond itself. The third kind is the structural limit of the
   relation between reconstruction and source; it is not the whole of what the relation is.
   The limit points beyond itself to what makes the reconstruction possible, and to what
   makes the source possible. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does not
   claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the limit is real, and that the limit points
   beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the limit and the ground of the
   limit; it is kept throughout the book.




27.7     Three Consequences of the Impossibility

The impossibility of super-identity has three structural consequences. They are stated here, with
their epistemic status.


First consequence: the structural limit of reconstruction. No subject can occupy a
view that captures reality as it is in itself, independent of any context. The phrase “view from
280                                    Chapter 27. The Impossibility of Super-Identity (Detailed)


nowhere” is a standard epistemological expression for such a view; it is not a theological claim.1
What a finite subject can achieve is a pseudo-identity of increasing adequacy, not an exhaustive
acquaintance with the source. The limit is structural, not contingent: it is what the relation
between a finite subject and an identity is. ((T))

Second consequence: the structural plurality of perspectives. The plurality of perspec-
tives is a structural consequence of the relation between a finite subject and an identity, not a
defect. Different perspectives are partial, but not arbitrary: they are located at a position, and
each is answerable to the criteria of adequacy and of context validity stated in the part of the
book that treated the foundation. The plurality is not a sign that no perspective is better than
another; it is a sign that every perspective is partial, and that the partiality is structural. ((T))

Third consequence: the fallacy of super-identity. Any attempt to aggregate manifesta-
tions across contexts into a single flat record is not a reconstruction of identity. The fallacy was
stated and argued in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements; the present chapter’s
arguments reinforce it, by showing that the aggregation is not merely incomplete but structurally
incapable of reaching its target. ((T))
      The three consequences are not separate. They are three aspects of one structural fact: the
relation between a finite subject and an identity is not the relation of a knower to an object it can
exhaust. The first names the limit; the second names what replaces the impossible completeness;
the third names the error of treating the replacement as if it were the completeness.

    Remark 27.8 (The Consequences Are Structural, Not Evaluative)

    The three consequences are structural, not evaluative. The framework does not claim
    that the limit of reconstruction is a deficiency to be lamented, or that the plurality of
    perspectives is a good to be celebrated, or that the fallacy of super-identity is a sin to
    be avoided. It claims that the three are structural features of the relation between finite
    subjects and identities, and that the framework’s account of knowledge, perspective, and
    reconstruction is built on them. The reader who reads the consequences as evaluations
    has misread them; the reader who reads them as structural facts has read them correctly.
    The three consequences point beyond themselves. The three consequences are real struc-
    tural consequences; they are not the ground of the relation between finite subjects and
    identities. The consequences point beyond themselves to what makes the relation possible,
    and to what makes the finite subject possible. The framework does not describe the
    ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the consequences
    are real structural consequences, and that the consequences point beyond themselves. The
    distinction is the distinction between the consequences and the ground of the consequences;
    it is kept throughout the book.

27.9        What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
      First, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the three kinds of failure exhaust
the ways in which reconstruction can go wrong. The three are the ones the framework has
identified; whether a fourth exists is a question the framework leaves open. The framework’s
claim is that the three are structurally distinct and that each has a different remedy, not that no
further kind could be found.
      Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of the structural plurality of perspectives.
The plurality is stated as a consequence of the impossibility; its development—how perspectives
are located, how they are assessed, how they relate to one another—is left to the parts of the
book that treat the resolution of tensions and the boundaries of philosophy. The present chapter
has stated the consequence; the later parts develop it.
      Third, the chapter does not develop the relation between the impossibility of super-identity
and the framework’s other principles beyond what the load-bearing premise table states. The
relations are stated in the table and in the dependency maps of the earlier parts; the full account
of how the impossibility interacts with the framework’s other claims is left to the parts of the
book that treat the system as a whole.
      Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of the limit. It claims to
have described the structure of the limit, and the structure points beyond itself to the ground
that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the limit and
the ground of the limit; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is stated here as the chapter’s

A Question for Reflection
Consider a subject you know well—a discipline, a tradition, a person’s life. What would it mean
to know all of it? What would the attempt to know all of it generate that would be outside
the attempt? What does the answer tell you about the difference between knowing a thing and
knowing everything about it?

With this chapter, the part of the book that gives the arguments is complete. Each principle of the
preceding parts has received its argument; each argument has stated its premises, its inferential
step, and its status; and the part has closed with a ledger of the premises on which its conclusions
depend. The next part turns to the resolution of apparent tensions. The principles are in place;
the next part shows that they do not conflict with one another, and that the apparent conflicts
are consequences of running together distinctions the framework has drawn.

Resolution of Tensions
