Chapter 28

Rigidity and Dynamism


Scope. This chapter opens the part of the book that resolves the apparent tensions among the
framework’s principles. It states the two concepts—rigidity and dynamism—whose combination
appears to be a contradiction; it identifies the source of the apparent conflict; it argues that
the conflict is not real, but comes from running together two distinct respects of one thing; it
states and argues the principle that resolves it, category-relative predication; and it draws the
consequences. Its claims are structural; where the chapter is silent on questions of value, the
silence is not a denial but a recognition that the structural description is not the whole of what
can be said. Where the chapter speaks of “persistence,” “constancy,” “responsibility,” “integrity,”
or “dynamism,” these are structural terms, and the sense of each is fixed by the definitions in
this chapter.


28.1     A Scene
Consider a cathedral. Its foundation was laid in the twelfth century, in the Romanesque style:
heavy walls, small windows, rounded arches. Two centuries later, a Gothic choir was added:
flying buttresses, large windows, pointed arches. A century after that, a Baroque altar was
installed, with gilded columns and a painted ceiling. In the nineteenth century, a restoration
removed some of the Baroque additions and rebuilt the roof. In the twentieth century, a modern
heating system was installed, and the stained glass was removed for safekeeping during a war
and then returned.
   Each generation changed the cathedral. Each generation added, removed, or replaced
something. The cathedral of today is not the cathedral of the twelfth century: it has parts
the twelfth-century builders never imagined, and it lacks parts they built and later generations
removed. And yet, when a pilgrim comes to the cathedral today, she comes to the cathedral
her ancestors came to. The guidebook speaks of “the cathedral” without qualification, as if the
building were one thing across eight centuries of change. The identity is one; the manifestations
are many.
   The scene poses a question. The cathedral is the same cathedral across all the changes—rigid,
invariant, one. And the cathedral is different in every generation—dynamic, changing, many.
How can both be true? Is the sameness an illusion, and the changes the only reality? Or is the
sameness real, and the changes only apparent? Or is there a third possibility: that the sameness
and the changes are real, but that they are not the same kind of thing, and that the apparent
contradiction comes from treating them as if they were?
   The scene is one instance of a tension that runs through the framework. The framework says
that identity is rigid—that it admits no degrees, that it does not change. And the framework
says that identity is dynamic—that it expresses itself, that its manifestations vary, that it is in a

                                                285
286                                                         Chapter 28. Rigidity and Dynamism


state of continual expression. The two claims appear to conflict. The present chapter argues
that they do not, and states the principle that shows why.

   Remark 28.1 (The Cathedral Points Beyond Itself)

   The cathedral is the same cathedral across eight centuries of change; the framework’s
   claim is that the sameness is real, and that the sameness is the sameness of an identity
   that is conserved through the changes of its manifestations. But the sameness is not
   self-grounded. The sameness is the sameness of a structure; it is not the ground of its
   own persistence. The sameness points beyond itself to what holds the cathedral in being
   through the changes, and to what makes the changes possible without destroying the
   sameness. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to
   is not described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the sameness
   and the ground of the sameness; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the sameness as the preservation of the one who
   preserves, and as the constancy of the one in whose knowledge the identities of things are
   held. The framework does not claim that its structural sameness is that preservation, and
   it does not claim that the preservation is unreal. It claims that the sameness is a real
   structural feature, and that the feature points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the
   structural sameness with the preservation is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes
   them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity
   is a question for another inquiry.




28.2       The Question

The preceding parts of the book have established the framework’s principal principles. In
particular, the part of the book that treated the fixed elements established that identity is rigid:
it is invariant under all allowable transformations of its manifestations, and it admits no degrees
(the principle of identity rigidity). The part of the book that gave the arguments established that
expression is necessary: every identity tends toward expression, and expression is a structural
necessity (the principle of expression). And the part of the book that argued for the necessity of
expression distinguished the necessity of the tendency from the degree of structural fidelity with
which any particular manifestation is realized.
      Each of these principles is argued in its place, and each is established to the strength its
argument gives it. The question of the present chapter is not whether they are true, but whether
they can be held together. If identity is rigid, how can it be dynamic? If identity expresses itself,
and expression is a process of change, how can the identity that expresses itself be unchanged?
      The question is not idle. If the two principles cannot be held together, the framework has a
contradiction at its center, and one of the two principles must be given up. The present chapter
argues that they can be held together, and that the appearance of contradiction comes from
running together two things that the framework distinguishes.
      Two aspects of the question must be distinguished.
28.3. The Two Concepts                                                                             287


The conceptual aspect. What are the two concepts, exactly? The chapter states them
precisely, so that the apparent conflict can be located in the concepts themselves rather than in
a vague sense that something is wrong.


The structural aspect. What makes the two concepts compatible? The chapter argues
that the compatibility is a consequence of a general structural principle—category-relative
predication—which the framework has used elsewhere and which it now states explicitly.
   The chapter proceeds as follows. It states the two concepts. It identifies the source of the
apparent conflict. It argues that the conflict is not real. It states the resolving principle and
argues for it. It states the scope of the resolution and what would challenge it. It draws the
consequences. It closes with what it does not establish and with the epistemic status of its claims.



28.3     The Two Concepts

The two concepts are stated in definitions.

   Definition 28.1 (Rigidity)

   (A) Identity is rigid: it is invariant under all allowable transformations of its manifestations,
   and it admits no degrees. A structure either is invariant under the specified transformations,
   or it is not. (The definition restates the principle of identity rigidity, argued in the part of
   the book that treated identity.)


   Definition 28.2 (Dynamism)

   (A) Identity is dynamic: it is in a state of expression, continually manifesting, multiplying
   its manifestations, and bringing about new ones. Its expressions vary; its manifestations
   arise, change, and cease. (The definition restates the principle of expression, argued in the
   part of the book that gave the arguments.)


   The two definitions are stated as commitments, because each restates a principle established
earlier. The rigidity definition restates the principle of identity rigidity; the dynamism definition
restates the principle of expression. Neither is new in this chapter; the chapter’s task is not to
establish them, but to show that they can be held together.
   The apparent conflict is easy to state. Rigidity says: identity does not change. Dynamism
says: identity expresses itself, and expression is a process of change. If both are true, identity
does not change and does change. That is a contradiction, and a contradiction cannot be true.
   The apparent conflict is not a verbal quibble. It is a real tension, and it has been felt by every
reader who has followed the framework to this point. The reader who has accepted the rigidity of
identity, and has also accepted the necessity of expression, has accepted two principles that seem
to contradict each other. The present chapter’s task is to show that the seeming is only seeming.
288                                                          Chapter 28. Rigidity and Dynamism


28.4       The Source of the Apparent Conflict

The apparent conflict has a source, and the source can be identified. It is not that one of the two
principles is false; it is that both principles use the word “identity” without saying of what in the
identity they speak. The predicate “rigid” is said of identity; the predicate “dynamic” is said of
identity. If the two predicates are said of the same subject in the same respect, they contradict.
If they are said of different respects of the same subject, they do not.
      The distinction is the distinction between two respects of one thing. Consider an analogy
from ordinary language. A house can be old and new at the same time: old in its foundations,
new in its roof. The two predicates are said of the same house, but in different respects. There is
no contradiction, because the respects differ. The apparent conflict between “old” and “new”
would be a real conflict only if the predicates were said of the same respect—if the house were
old and new in its foundations, or old and new in its roof.
      The analogy is not an argument, but it locates the source of the apparent conflict. The
predicates “rigid” and “dynamic” are said of identity in two different respects: rigid with respect
to its manifestations, dynamic with respect to its expression. If the respects are distinguished,
the contradiction disappears; if they are run together, the contradiction is inevitable.

   Remark 28.2 (The Same and the Respect)

   The distinction between “the same subject in different respects” and “different subjects” is
   essential. If “rigid” and “dynamic” were said of different subjects—rigidity of the identity,
   dynamism of the manifestations, and the two subjects were entirely separate—there would
   be no tension at all, but there would also be no account of how the two relate. The tension
   arises because the two predicates are said of the same subject, and the resolution shows
   how the same subject can be both. The framework’s claim is not that the two are said of
   different things, but that they are said of the same thing in different respects. The reader
   who reads the resolution as a separation of the two has misread it; the reader who reads it
   as a distinction of respects has read it correctly.


   Remark 28.3 (The Respect Is Not Chosen by the Observer)

   The respect is not chosen by the observer, at will. It is fixed by the structure of the thing
   spoken of, and by the position of the thing in the framework’s architecture. The identity
   is rigid with respect to its manifestations because the structure of identity is invariance; it
   is dynamic with respect to its expression because the structure of expression is enactment.
   The respects are not a matter of perspective; they are a matter of what the thing is. The
   observer’s task is to identify the respects, not to create them.
   The two respects, too, point beyond themselves. The rigidity of the identity with respect
   to its manifestations is a real structural respect; it is not the ground of the identity.
   The dynamism of the expression is a real structural respect; it is not the ground of the
   expression. The two respects point beyond themselves to what makes the identity and the
   expression possible, and to what makes their relation possible. The framework’s claim is
28.5. Is the Conflict Real?                                                                    289


   that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework.
   The distinction is the distinction between the respects and the ground of the respects; it
   is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the respects as the one who is unchanging in his
   essence and creative in his act, and as the one whose constancy is the ground of the
   constancy of what is. The framework does not claim that its structural respects are
   that one, and it does not claim that the one is unreal. It claims that the respects are
   real structural respects, and that the respects point beyond themselves. The reader who
   identifies the respects with the one is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is
   free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a
   question for another inquiry.



28.5      Is the Conflict Real?
The source of the apparent conflict has been identified. The question is now whether the conflict
is real, or whether it is the appearance that comes from running together the two respects.
   The chapter’s answer is: it is not real. The conflict is the appearance that comes from running
together two distinctions the framework has already drawn. The two distinctions are these.


First distinction: what the identity is and how it expresses itself. The identity is what
it is: an invariant structure under a class of allowable transformations. Its expression is what
it does: it manifests itself, in various ways, in various realms. The first is rigid; the second is
dynamic. They are not the same, and the rigidity of the first does not exclude the dynamism of
the second. They are two aspects of one thing: what the identity is, and how it enacts what it is.


Second distinction: a difference of structure among manifestations and a change in
the identity. The manifestations of one identity may differ in structure—one may be material,
another relational, another structural. The difference is a difference in the manifestations,
not a change in the identity. The manifestations are products; the identity is the source. A
change in the products is not a change in the source. The framework’s principle of essential
homogeneity (established in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements) ensures that
the manifestations do not conflict with the identity’s essential determination; the manifestations
can differ in structure without the identity changing.
   If the two distinctions are kept, the apparent conflict disappears. The identity is rigid in
what it is; its expression is dynamic in how it enacts what it is. The manifestations differ in
structure; the identity does not change. There is no contradiction, because the two predicates
are said of different respects of one thing.
   The claim is not that the conflict is merely verbal. It is that the conflict is the appearance
that comes from a real distinction—the distinction between what the identity is and how it
expresses itself. The distinction is real; the conflict is the appearance that arises when the
distinction is not seen.
290                                                          Chapter 28. Rigidity and Dynamism


   Remark 28.4 (Why the Conflict Is Felt)

   The conflict is felt because the ordinary language of identity does not distinguish the two
   respects. We say “she is the same person” and “she has changed a great deal,” and the
   two sentences seem to conflict only if we read them as speaking of the same respect. When
   we distinguish the respects—she is the same person in her identity, and she has changed a
   great deal in her manifestations—the sentences are seen to be compatible. The felt conflict
   is the residue of the ordinary language’s failure to mark the distinction. The framework’s
   task is to mark it, and the present chapter marks it.
   The felt conflict, too, points beyond itself. The conflict is felt because the ordinary language
   does not mark the distinction; the distinction is real, and the language is partial. The felt
   conflict points beyond itself to what makes the distinction real, and to what makes the
   language partial. The framework does not describe the ground of the distinction, and it
   does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the felt conflict is real, and that
   the felt conflict points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the felt
   conflict and the ground of the distinction; it is kept throughout the book.



28.6       The Resolving Principle

The resolution of the apparent conflict is stated in a principle. It is the general principle of which
the resolution is a particular case, and it will be used in the chapters that follow to resolve the
other apparent tensions of the framework.

   Principle 28.1 (Category-Relative Predication)

   (A) Metaphysical predicates such as rigidity, dynamism, unity, multiplicity, temporality,
   and atemporality are not absolute. They are defined relative to a realm and to a respect.
   An identity is rigid with respect to its manifestations, and its expression is dynamic with
   respect to the realms in which it manifests. This is not a contradiction; it is a structural
   feature of the seven-realm architecture.

      The principle is adopted, not proved. Its support is the structure of the framework’s
architecture: the realms are distinct levels, and the respects are the roles an entity plays in
different levels. A predicate that is appropriate to one level may not be appropriate to another;
the same entity may have different predicates relative to different levels. The principle states
that this is the general case, not the exception.
      The principle’s status is (A), and the reader should know what that means. The principle is a
commitment, and its justification is its fruitfulness: the chapters that follow use it to resolve the
other apparent tensions of the framework, and the resolutions they achieve are the evidence for
the principle’s adequacy. A reader who accepts the principle will find the resolutions persuasive;
a reader who rejects it will find them circular, because they presuppose the principle. The
framework states the principle openly, so that the reader knows what the resolutions depend on.
      The principle has three components, which the reader should keep distinct.
28.6. The Resolving Principle                                                                     291


First component: predicates are not absolute. A predicate such as “rigid” is not a
property that a thing has simpliciter. It is a property relative to a realm and a respect. The
same thing can have different predicates relative to different realms or respects.


Second component: the realm is part of the predicate’s sense. To say that an identity
is rigid is to say that it is rigid with respect to its manifestations in a realm. The realm is not an
external condition on the predicate; it is part of what the predicate means.


Third component: the respect is part of the predicate’s sense. To say that an identity
is dynamic is to say that it is dynamic with respect to its expression. The respect is not an
external condition on the predicate; it is part of what the predicate means. The two components
together specify what the predicate is a predicate of: an identity in a realm, in a respect.

   Remark 28.5 (Category-Relative Predication Points Beyond Itself)

   The principle of category-relative predication is a real structural principle; the framework’s
   claim is that metaphysical predicates are not absolute, and that the predicates are defined
   relative to a realm and a respect. But the principle is not self-grounded. The principle is
   the structure of predication; it is not the ground of the architecture that makes predication
   possible. The principle points beyond itself to what makes the realms what they are, and
   to what makes the respects what they are. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is
   real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction is the
   distinction between the principle and the ground of the architecture; it is kept throughout
   the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the architecture as the one through whom the levels
   are what they are, and as the one in whose knowledge the respects of things are what they
   are. The framework does not claim that its principle is that one, and it does not claim
   that the one is unreal. It claims that the principle is a real structural principle, and that
   the principle points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the principle with the one is
   free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no
   position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.


   Remark 28.6 (The Principle Is General)

   The principle is not stated only for rigidity and dynamism. It is the general principle of
   category-relative predication, and the chapters that follow apply it to the other apparent
   tensions: unity and multiplicity, intensity and breadth, tendency and success, relation and
   order. Each of these tensions is resolved by the same move: the two predicates are said of
   different respects of one thing, and the distinction of respects removes the contradiction.
   The principle is the framework’s tool for resolving this class of tensions, and the reader
   who understands the present chapter will understand the chapters that follow.
292                                                            Chapter 28. Rigidity and Dynamism


28.7       The Argument

The argument for the resolution proceeds in four steps.


Resolution of the Apparent Conflict.           1. Rigidity. The identity does not change under the
        allowable transformations of its manifestations. It is the same identity through all of them.
       (The principle of identity rigidity.)

   2. Dynamism. The identity expresses itself, and manifestations arise, vary, and cease. The
        dynamism is in the expression, not in the invariant that is expressed. (The principle of
        expression.)

   3. Structural difference is not change of nature. Manifestations of one identity can differ in
        structure. That does not mean that the identity’s nature changes, since every manifestation
        must be homogeneous in essence with its source (the principle of essential homogeneity,
        established in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements).

   4. Conclusion. Identity is rigid as an identity; its expression is dynamic. They are two
        predicates of two respects of one thing.



      The argument’s force is in step (3). If structural difference were change of nature, the
manifestations of one identity could not differ without the identity changing, and the tension
between rigidity and dynamism would be real. The principle of essential homogeneity is what
blocks this: it allows the manifestations to differ in structure, so long as they do not conflict
with the identity’s essential determination. The difference is real; the change is not. The identity
is conserved; the manifestations vary.
      The argument’s steps (1) and (2) restate the two principles whose combination appeared to
be a contradiction. Step (3) is the principle that shows the combination is not a contradiction.
Step (4) states the conclusion. The argument is not a new proof of either of the two principles;
it is the demonstration that they are compatible, given the framework’s other principles.

   Remark 28.7 (The Argument Is Not Circular)

   The argument does not assume what it sets out to prove. It assumes the two principles
   (rigidity and dynamism), and the principle of essential homogeneity, and it derives the
   compatibility of the two from them. The derivation is not trivial—it requires the distinction
   of respects that the resolving principle states—but it is not circular. The two principles
   do not depend on their own compatibility; their compatibility depends on the distinction
   of respects, which the resolving principle makes explicit. The reader who accepts the three
   principles should accept the compatibility; the reader who rejects one of them has a reason
   to reject the compatibility, and the framework does not pretend otherwise.
28.8. Scope and Vulnerability                                                                    293


   Remark 28.8 (The Resolution Points Beyond Itself)

   The resolution of the apparent conflict is a real structural resolution; the framework’s
   claim is that the identity is rigid with respect to its manifestations, and that its expression
   is dynamic with respect to the realms in which it manifests, and that the two are not
   in conflict. But the resolution is not self-grounded. The resolution is the resolution of a
   tension within the structure; it is not the ground of the structure. The resolution points
   beyond itself to what makes the structure possible, and to what makes the tension within
   the structure possible. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what
   is pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between
   the resolution and the ground of the structure; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the structure as the one in whom there is no change,
   and as the one whose constancy is the ground of the constancy of what is. The framework
   does not claim that its resolution is that one, and it does not claim that the one is unreal.
   It claims that the resolution is a real structural resolution, and that the resolution points
   beyond itself. The reader who identifies the resolution with the one is free to do so; the
   reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the
   identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



28.8     Scope and Vulnerability

The resolution is valid for the respects named, and the scope must be stated with precision.
   The resolution says that identity is rigid with respect to its manifestations, and that its
expression is dynamic with respect to the realms in which it manifests. It does not say that
anything in an identity changes; it denies that rigidity excludes dynamic expression. The two
claims are compatible, and the resolution shows how.
   The resolution rests on two commitments: that identity is rigid ((A), established in the part
of the book that treated identity), and that manifestations are products of identity and receiving
realm ((A), established in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements). The resolution’s
force is no greater than the force of these commitments; a reader who rejects either of them has
a reason to reject the resolution, and the framework does not pretend otherwise.
   The resolution is not relativism. The realm and the respect are fixed by the architecture,
not chosen by an observer. The framework’s claim is that the architecture has the structure the
framework describes, and that the predicates are appropriate to the structure. A reader who
reads the resolution as a form of relativism has misread it; a reader who reads it as a structural
claim has read it correctly.
   The resolution would be put in question by two things.


First challenge. A case in which the change in manifestations could not be located in the
expression and not in the identity—that is, a change that cannot be separated from the invariant,
such that to speak of the invariant at all would be empty. The framework does not claim that
no such case can be constructed; it claims that none has been constructed that survives the
294                                                         Chapter 28. Rigidity and Dynamism


distinction between identity and manifestation, and it argues that none can be. The reader who
wishes to challenge the resolution knows where to press.

Second challenge. A manifestation that is acknowledged to be of an identity and yet has
a feature that the identity’s invariance excludes. The framework holds that this is a case of
misattribution (a case in which the manifestation is not of that identity) or a case in which the
resolution fails. The reader who exhibits such a case has located a limit of the resolution; the
framework does not claim that no such case can be exhibited, and it states the resolution at
exactly the strength its arguments support.

   Remark 28.9 (The Two Challenges Are Different)

   The first challenge is conceptual: it questions whether the distinction between identity and
   expression can be drawn at all. The second challenge is empirical: it questions whether
   the distinction, once drawn, is borne out in particular cases. The two challenges require
   different responses, and the framework responds to each in its own terms. The first is
   answered by the arguments of the present chapter and the chapters that precede it; the
   second is answered case by case, as the framework is applied to particular domains. The
   present chapter has stated the resolution; the application is left to the reader and to the
   chapters that follow.



28.9     Consequences
The resolution has four consequences. They are stated here, with their status.

First consequence: persistence through change. The same entity can be said to persist
through all its transformations, rather than gradually becoming another. The persistence is the
persistence of the identity; the transformations are the transformations of the manifestations.
The two are compatible, and the resolution shows how. ((T))

Second consequence: numerical sameness across time. The identity manifested yesterday
is numerically the same identity as the one manifested today; it is not a new identity replacing
the earlier one. The claim is a structural restatement of the conservation principle; it carries no
claim about obligations, duties, or accountability. ((T))

Third consequence: no degrees in identity. Identity admits no degrees; what admits of
degrees is the structural viability of the relation between an identity and its manifestations, not
the identity itself. The framework does not speak of “the self” as a graded entity; it speaks of an
identity and of the degrees of structural fidelity of its manifestations. ((T))

Fourth consequence: the constancy of light. The light that flows from an identity is the
same light, whatever manifestations it generates. The light is the conveyor of effect; the effect
varies; the light does not. This is the framework’s way of saying that the medium of expression
is constant even when the expression varies. ((E))
28.10. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                   295


   The four consequences are not separate. They are four aspects of one structural fact: the
identity is invariant, the manifestations vary, and the relation between them is the relation of
expression. The first names the persistence; the second names the numerical unity; the third
names the rigidity; the fourth names the constancy of the medium. Together, they state what
the resolution of the apparent conflict amounts to.

   Remark 28.10 (The Consequences Are Structural, Not Evaluative)

   The four consequences are structural, not evaluative. The framework does not claim that
   persistence is more valuable than change, or that numerical sameness is more important
   than structural variation. It claims that the four are structural features of the relation
   between identity and manifestation, and that the framework’s account of persistence,
   unity, rigidity, and constancy is built on them. A reader who reads the consequences as
   evaluations has misread them; a reader who reads them as structural facts has read them
   correctly.
   The four consequences point beyond themselves. The consequences are the structural
   features of the relation between identity and manifestation; they are not the ground of the
   relation. The consequences point beyond themselves to what makes the relation possible,
   and to what makes the features what they are. The framework does not describe the
   ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the consequences
   are real structural consequences, and that the consequences point beyond themselves. The
   distinction is the distinction between the consequences and the ground of the consequences;
   it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the relation as the one who is the same yesterday,
   today, and forever, and as the one whose constancy is the ground of the constancy of
   what is. The framework does not claim that its consequences are that one, and it does
   not claim that the one is unreal. It claims that the consequences are real structural
   consequences, and that the consequences point beyond themselves. The reader who
   identifies the consequences with the one is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them
   is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a
   question for another inquiry.



28.10      What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
   First, the chapter does not develop the full account of category-relative predication. The
principle is stated, and its application to the tension between rigidity and dynamism is argued,
but the principle’s application to the other apparent tensions of the framework is deferred to the
chapters that follow. Those chapters apply the same principle to different tensions, and their
arguments depend on the present chapter’s statement of the principle. The present chapter is
the foundation; the chapters that follow are the applications.
   Second, the chapter does not develop the relation between category-relative predication and
the framework’s account of the seven realms. The realms are the levels relative to which the
296                                                           Chapter 28. Rigidity and Dynamism


predicates are defined, but the full account of how the realms provide the respects is deferred to
the parts of the book that treat the realms in detail. The present chapter has stated that the
respects are fixed by the architecture; the later parts develop what the architecture is.
      Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the distinction between identity
and expression can be drawn in every particular case. The distinction is a structural claim, and
it is argued in general; its application to particular cases is a matter for the analysis of those
cases. The present chapter has argued for the distinction in general; the application is left to the
reader and to the chapters that follow.
      Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of the unity of identity across
change. It claims to have described the structure of the unity, and the structure points beyond
itself to the ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction
between the structure of the unity and the ground of the unity; it is kept throughout the chapter,
and it is stated here as the chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a person you have known for many years. In what respect is she the same person
she was when you met her? In what respect has she changed? If the two respects were not
distinguished, would the two answers contradict each other? What does your answer tell you
about the relation between rigidity and dynamism?

The next chapter turns to the tension between unity and multiplicity. The resolution uses the
same principle—category-relative predication—applied to a different tension. The present chapter
has established the principle; the next chapter applies it.
Chapter 29

Unity and Multiplicity


Scope. This chapter resolves the apparent tension between the unity of an identity and the
multiplicity of its manifestations. It uses the principle of category-relative predication, established
in the previous chapter, and applies it to a different tension. It states the two concepts; it
identifies the source of the apparent conflict; it argues that the conflict is not real, but comes
from running together two distinct kinds of plurality and two distinct kinds of unity; it states
and argues the resolving principle—recursive manifestation—and draws its consequences. Its
claims are structural; where the chapter is silent on questions of value, the silence is not a denial
but a recognition that the structural description is not the whole of what can be said. Where the
chapter speaks of “knowledge,” “reconstruction,” “reality,” or “possibility,” these are structural
or epistemic terms, and the sense of each is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.



29.1      A Scene

Consider a river. It has been flowing for a thousand years. The water that passes through it
today is not the water that passed through it yesterday, nor the water that passed through it
in the time of the earliest settlements on its banks. The stones in its bed have been worn and
replaced. The banks have shifted; some have eroded, others have been built up. The fish are not
the same fish; the reeds are not the same reeds. If you step into the river today, you step into
water that no one has ever stepped into before.
   And yet the river is one river. It has a name; it has a course; it has a place on the map; it
has a history that is taught in schools. When a traveler says she has seen the river, she has seen
the river that her ancestors saw, though not a single drop of the water is the same. The unity of
the river is not the unity of its water; the plurality of the water is not a plurality of rivers. The
river is one and its waters are many, and the two statements do not conflict.
   The scene is old. It is the river of Heraclitus, into which one cannot step twice. It is the
oldest image of the problem of the One and the Many, and it has been felt by every generation
of philosophers. The river is one; the waters are many. How can both be true? If the river is one,
how can its waters be many? If the waters are many, how can the river be one?
   The scene poses the question that the present chapter answers. The answer, in brief, is that
the unity of the river is the unity of a source, and the plurality of the waters is the plurality of
its manifestations. The two are not the same, and the apparent conflict comes from treating
them as if they were. The present chapter states the answer, and states why the answer does not
require the river to be two.



                                                 297
298                                                              Chapter 29. Unity and Multiplicity


   Remark 29.1 (The River Points Beyond Itself)

   The river is one across a thousand years of change; the framework’s claim is that the unity
   is real, and that the unity is the unity of a source whose manifestations are many. But the
   unity is not self-grounded. The unity is the unity of a structure; it is not the ground of its
   own persistence. The unity points beyond itself to what holds the river in being through
   the changes, and to what makes the changes possible without destroying the unity. The
   framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described
   by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the unity and the ground of
   the unity; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the unity as the one who is the same across the
   changes, and as the one whose permanence is the ground of the permanence of what is.
   The Quranic verse that the traditions cite in this connection is the verse of the passing of
   all things: “Every thing is passing away, except His face” (Qur’an 28:88). The framework’s
   structural reading is that the unity of the source is real, and that the manifestations are
   many, and that the source is what remains while the manifestations pass. The verse is
   cited as structural evidence, not as a ground of justification. The framework does not
   claim that its structural unity is the face of the one, and it does not claim that the face is
   unreal. It claims that the unity is a real structural feature, and that the feature points
   beyond itself.




29.2        The Question

The previous chapter established the principle of category-relative predication: metaphysical
predicates such as rigidity, dynamism, unity, multiplicity, temporality, and atemporality are not
absolute, but are defined relative to a realm and a respect. The chapter used the principle to
resolve the tension between rigidity and dynamism, and it stated that the principle would be
used in the chapters that follow to resolve the other apparent tensions of the framework.
      The present chapter uses the principle to resolve the tension between unity and multiplicity.
The tension is the ancient problem of the One and the Many: how can an identity be one and its
manifestations be many, without the one becoming the many or the many becoming the one?
      The question is not idle. The framework says that identity is one: it is a single source, a single
invariance, a single thisness. And the framework says that manifestations are many: they are
multiple, they arise and pass away, they differ in structure and in realm. If the two statements
cannot be held together, the framework has a contradiction at its center, and one of them must
be given up. The present chapter argues that they can be held together, and that the appearance
of contradiction comes from running together two distinctions the framework has drawn.
      Two aspects of the question must be distinguished.



The conceptual aspect. What are the two concepts, exactly? The chapter states them
precisely, so that the apparent conflict can be located in the concepts themselves.
29.3. The Two Concepts                                                                           299


The structural aspect. What makes the two concepts compatible? The chapter argues that
the compatibility is a consequence of a specific structure—recursive manifestation—which the
framework has used implicitly and which it now states explicitly.
   The chapter proceeds as follows. It states the two concepts. It identifies the source of the
apparent conflict. It argues that the conflict is not real. It states the resolving principle and
argues for it. It states the scope of the resolution and what would challenge it. It draws the
consequences. It closes with what it does not establish and with the epistemic status of its claims.



29.3     The Two Concepts

The two concepts are stated in definitions.

   Definition 29.1 (Unity)

   (A) An identity is one: it is a single source, a single invariance, a single thisness. Its
   unity is the unity of a source, not the unity of an aggregate. (The definition restates the
   framework’s account of identity, established in the part of the book that treated identity.)


   Definition 29.2 (Multiplicity)

   (A) The manifestations of an identity are many: they are multiple, they arise and pass
   away, they differ in structure and in realm. Their multiplicity is the multiplicity of
   products, not the multiplicity of sources. (The definition restates the framework’s account
   of manifestation, established in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements.)


   The two definitions are stated as commitments, because each restates a principle established
earlier. Neither is new in this chapter; the chapter’s task is not to establish them, but to show
that they can be held together.
   The apparent conflict is easy to state. Unity says: the identity is one. Multiplicity says: the
manifestations are many. If both are true, the identity is one and its manifestations are many.
That is not yet a contradiction; a contradiction would require that the identity be one and many
in the same respect. But the ordinary way of speaking invites the contradiction: we say “the
river is one” and “the river’s waters are many,” and we speak as if “the river” and “the river’s
waters” were the same thing. If they were the same thing, the contradiction would be real; if
they are not, the contradiction is only apparent.
   The apparent conflict is not a verbal quibble. It is a real tension, and it has been felt by every
reader who has followed the framework to this point. The reader who has accepted the unity of
identity, and has also accepted the multiplicity of manifestations, has accepted two principles
that seem to contradict each other. The present chapter’s task is to show that the seeming is
only seeming.
300                                                           Chapter 29. Unity and Multiplicity


29.4       The Source of the Apparent Conflict
The apparent conflict has a source, and the source can be identified. It comes from running
together two distinctions, either of which, if kept, would remove the conflict.

First distinction: the plurality of manifestations and the plurality of identities. The
manifestations of one identity are many; the identities are one. These are two different pluralities.
If they are run together, the many manifestations are mistaken for many identities, and the one
identity is lost in the multiplicity of its appearances. The river’s many waters are not many
rivers; they are many appearances of one river.

Second distinction: the unity of a source and the unity of an aggregate. The unity of
an identity is the unity of a source; it is not the unity of an aggregate. An aggregate is one thing
only in the sense that its parts are collected under a name; a source is one thing in the sense
that it is a single invariance, a single thisness. If the two unities are run together, the unity of
the source is mistaken for the unity of the aggregate, and the source is treated as if it were the
sum of its manifestations. The river’s unity is not the unity of the sum of its waters; it is the
unity of the source from which the waters flow.
      The two distinctions are the framework’s tools for resolving the tension. They were drawn
in the part of the book that treated identity (the distinction between identity and signature)
and in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements (the distinction between identity
and manifestation). The present chapter applies them to the specific tension between unity and
multiplicity.

   Remark 29.2 (The Two Distinctions Are Not the Same)

   The first distinction is between two kinds of plurality: the plurality of manifestations
   and the plurality of identities. The second is between two kinds of unity: the unity of a
   source and the unity of an aggregate. The two distinctions are related—the plurality of
   manifestations belongs with the unity of a source, and the plurality of identities belongs
   with the unity of an aggregate—but they are not the same, and the framework keeps them
   apart. The reader who runs them together will find the resolution incomplete; the reader
   who keeps them apart will find it complete.


   Remark 29.3 (The Source Is Not a Thing Behind the Appearances)

   The unity of a source is not the unity of a thing behind the appearances. The framework
   does not posit a hidden entity whose appearances are the manifestations; it posits a
   structural source whose invariance is what the manifestations manifest. The source is
   not hidden; it is what the manifestations exhibit. The manifestations do not conceal the
   source; they express it. The reader who reads the source as a hidden thing has misread
   the framework’s account; the reader who reads it as the invariance that the manifestations
   exhibit has read it correctly.
   The source, too, points beyond itself. The source is the invariance that the manifestations
29.5. Is the Conflict Real?                                                                       301


   exhibit; it is not the ground of its own being. The source points beyond itself to what
   makes the source the source it is, and to what makes the manifestations the manifestations
   they are. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the
   ground is unreal. It claims that the source is a real structural source, and that the source
   points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the source and the ground
   of the source; it is kept throughout the book.



29.5      Is the Conflict Real?
The source of the apparent conflict has been identified. The question is now whether the conflict
is real, or whether it is the appearance that comes from running together the two distinctions.
   The chapter’s answer is: it is not real. The conflict is the appearance that comes from treating
the many manifestations as if they were many identities, and treating the one identity as if it
were the sum of its manifestations. Once the two distinctions are kept, the conflict disappears.
   The claim is not that the conflict is merely verbal. It is that the conflict is the appearance
that comes from a real distinction—the distinction between what an identity is and what its
manifestations are. The distinction is real; the conflict is the appearance that arises when the
distinction is not seen.
   The unity of the identity and the multiplicity of its manifestations are compatible because
they are said of different things. The identity is one; the manifestations are many. To say that
the identity is one is not to say that it is one manifestation, or that its manifestations are one. To
say that the manifestations are many is not to say that the identity is many, or that the identity
is the sum of its manifestations. The two statements say different things, and they are both true.
   The compatibility is not a triviality. It would be a triviality if the identity and its manifesta-
tions were obviously different things, as a river and its waters are obviously different. But the
framework’s account of manifestation has established that the manifestations are products of the
identity and the receiving realm; they are not separate things alongside the identity, but the
identity’s own expression in the realm. The compatibility is a structural fact about the relation
between identity and manifestation, and the framework’s task is to state it.

   Remark 29.4 (The Conflict Is Felt Because the Relation Is Close)

   The conflict is felt because the relation between identity and manifestation is close: the
   manifestations are the identity’s own expression, not separate things. If they were entirely
   separate, no one would think to confuse them; but because they are the identity’s expression,
   they are easily mistaken for the identity itself. The felt conflict is the residue of this
   closeness. The framework’s task is not to separate the identity from its manifestations—
   they are not separate—but to distinguish them, so that the one is not mistaken for the
   many and the many are not mistaken for the one.
   The felt conflict, too, points beyond itself. The conflict is felt because the language does
   not distinguish the two; the distinction is real, and the language is partial. The felt conflict
   points beyond itself to what makes the distinction real, and to what makes the language
302                                                          Chapter 29. Unity and Multiplicity


   partial. The framework does not describe the ground of the distinction, and it does not
   claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the felt conflict is real, and that the felt
   conflict points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the felt conflict
   and the ground of the distinction; it is kept throughout the book.




29.6       The Resolving Principle: Recursive Manifestation

The resolution of the apparent conflict is stated in a principle, and the principle introduces a
specific structure that the framework uses here and in what follows.

   Definition 29.3 (Recursive Manifestation)

   Recursive manifestation is the structure by which a manifestation that is realized in one
   realm can itself be the occasion for further manifestations of the same identity, in the
   same realm or another, without the identity being multiplied.


      The definition states a structure, not a process. The structure is that of a manifestation
serving as the occasion for further manifestations. The occasions are not temporal stages; they
are structural positions. A manifestation, once realized, is an element of the realm in which it is
realized, and as an element it can enter into relations that occasion further manifestations of the
same identity. The identity is not multiplied by this; it remains one, and its manifestations are
many.

   Principle 29.1 (Distinction of Plurality of Manifestations from Plurality of
   Identities)

   (T) The plurality of the manifestations of one identity is not a plurality of identities, and
   recursive manifestation is not numerical multiplication of the identity.


      The principle states what the definition presupposes: that the recursive structure does not
multiply the identity. The definition states the structure; the principle states what the structure
is not. Together, they make the framework’s resolution of the tension precise.

   Remark 29.5 (Realms and Manifestations)

   The realms are independently real levels of being; they are not manifestations of one
   another. The recursive manifestation is a structure within the relation between an identity
   and its manifestations, not a relation between realms. The distinction is essential: the
   realms are ontological levels, and the recursive manifestation is the structure by which
   the manifestations of one identity are occasioned. The reader who reads the recursive
   structure as a relation between realms has misread it; the reader who reads it as a relation
   within the process of manifestation has read it correctly.
29.7. The Argument                                                                             303


   Remark 29.6 (Recursive Manifestation Points Beyond Itself)

   The recursive structure of manifestation is a real structural feature; the framework’s claim
   is that a manifestation, once realized, can be the occasion of further manifestations of the
   same identity, without the identity being multiplied. But the recursive structure is not
   self-grounded. The recursion is the recursion of manifestations; it is not the ground of
   the identity. The recursion points beyond itself to what makes the identity one, and to
   what makes the manifestations many. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real,
   and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction is the
   distinction between the recursion and the ground of the identity; it is kept throughout the
   book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the identity as the one from whom every identity
   comes, and as the one who is one and not many. The framework does not claim that its
   recursive structure is that one, and it does not claim that the one is unreal. It claims
   that the recursion is a real structural feature, and that the feature points beyond itself.
   The reader who identifies the recursion with the one is free to do so; the reader who
   distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because
   the identity is a question for another inquiry.

   The resolving principle is now in place. The next section states the argument for it.


29.7       The Argument
The argument for the resolution proceeds in five steps.

Resolution of the Apparent Conflict.     1. A manifestation is a product of a source identity
     and a receiving realm, and is not an identity (the framework’s account of manifestation,
     established in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements).

  2. So many manifestations of one source are many products of one source; the number of
     products does not fix the number of sources.

  3. A manifestation may itself be the occasion of further manifestations; each further one is
     again a product of the same source and a receiving realm.

  4. Hence the manifestations may be many, and recursively so, while the identity remains one.

  5. The unity of the identity is therefore not the unity of an aggregate and not the unity of a
     thing underlying its manifestations; it is the numerical unity of a source.


   The argument’s force is in step (2). If the manifestations were not products of the identity—if
they were the identity itself, or separate things alongside the identity—the plurality of the
manifestations would be a plurality of identities, and the contradiction would be real. The
framework’s account of manifestation is what blocks this: the manifestations are products, not
the identity, and the number of products does not fix the number of sources.
304                                                          Chapter 29. Unity and Multiplicity


      Step (3) adds the recursive structure. A manifestation, once realized, can be the occasion
of further manifestations. The recursion does not multiply the identity; it multiplies the
manifestations. The identity remains one, and the manifestations form a recursive plurality
whose number does not touch the unity of the source.
      The argument’s conclusion is the framework’s resolution of the tension. The unity of the
identity and the multiplicity of its manifestations are compatible, because they are said of
different things: the identity is one source; the manifestations are many products. The two are
not the same, and the argument shows how they can both be true.

   Remark 29.7 (The Argument Is Relative to Its Premises)

   The argument depends on the premise that manifestations are products of identity and
   receiving realm, and on the premise that a manifestation can be the occasion of further
   manifestations. The first premise is established in the part of the book that treated the
   fixed elements; the second is stated in the definition of recursive manifestation. A reader
   who denies either premise has a reason to reject the resolution, and the framework does
   not pretend otherwise. The argument’s value is not that it proves the resolution without
   assumptions; it is that it makes the assumptions visible, and shows exactly what follows
   from them.
   The premises, too, point beyond themselves. The premises are the structural conditions
   of the resolution; they are not the ground of the relation between unity and multiplicity.
   The premises point beyond themselves to what makes the relation possible, and to what
   makes the unity and the multiplicity what they are. The framework does not describe the
   ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the premises are
   real structural premises, and that the premises point beyond themselves. The distinction is
   the distinction between the premises and the ground of the relation; it is kept throughout
   the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the relation as the one who is one and from whom
   the many come, and as the one in whose knowledge the one and the many are what they
   are. The framework does not claim that its premises are that one, and it does not claim
   that the one is unreal. It claims that the premises are real structural premises, and that
   the premises point beyond themselves.


   Remark 29.8 (An Illustration)

   One source is expressed in many manifestations, each of which is something in its own
   right, and some of which are occasions for further manifestations; and still the source
   is one. The illustration is not an argument. It is a way of seeing what the argument
   establishes. The river is one; its waters are many; and the waters, in their motion, occasion
   further movements of the same river. The identity of the river does not multiply with the
   multiplicity of the waters.
29.8. Scope and Vulnerability                                                                  305


29.8     Scope and Vulnerability
The resolution is valid for the respects named, and the scope must be stated with precision.
   The resolution says that the unity of the identity and the multiplicity of its manifestations
are compatible because they are said of different things. It does not say that the identity is more
real than its manifestations, or that the manifestations are less real than the identity. Both are
real, in their own respects. The framework holds a stratified realism, in which the one and the
many are both real. The resolution’s claim is structural: the two are compatible because they
are distinct, not because one reduces to the other.
   The resolution rests on the commitment that manifestations are products of identity and
receiving realm ((A), established in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements), and on
the definition of recursive manifestation ((A), stated above). The resolution’s force is no greater
than the force of these commitments; a reader who rejects either of them has a reason to reject
the resolution, and the framework does not pretend otherwise.
   The resolution would be put in question by two things.


First challenge. A criterion for counting identities that makes manifestations, as such, count-
able as identities. If such a criterion could be given, the plurality of manifestations would be a
plurality of identities, and the resolution would fail. The framework does not claim that no such
criterion can be given; it claims that none has been given that survives the distinction between
identity and manifestation, and it argues that none can be.


Second challenge. An abandonment of the commitment that identity is more than signature,
in a way that makes the unity of a source identical with the unity of a pattern. If identity were
nothing over and above its signature, the unity of the identity would be the unity of a pattern,
and the unity of a pattern is not the unity of a source. The framework holds the commitment,
and the resolution depends on it; a reader who rejects the commitment has a reason to reject the
resolution.

   Remark 29.9 (The Resolution Is Not Reduction)

   The resolution does not reduce the many to the one, or the one to the many. It shows
   that the two are compatible by distinguishing them. The one is the source; the many are
   the products; the two are not the same, and neither reduces to the other. The reader
   who reads the resolution as a reduction of the many to the one has misread it; the reader
   who reads it as a distinction of the two has read it correctly. The framework’s position is
   stratified realism: the one and the many are both real, in their own respects.
   The resolution, too, points beyond itself. The resolution is the structural distinction of
   the one and the many; it is not the ground of the relation between the one and the many.
   The resolution points beyond itself to what makes the one and the many possible, and to
   what makes the relation possible. The framework does not describe the ground, and it
   does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the resolution is a real structural
   resolution, and that the resolution points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction
306                                                           Chapter 29. Unity and Multiplicity


   between the resolution and the ground of the relation; it is kept throughout the book.



29.9       Consequences
The resolution has three consequences. They are stated here, with their status.


First consequence: the reality of multiplicity. The many are real in their own realms.
The manifestations are not illusions, not appearances of an underlying reality that alone is real;
they are real products of real sources, with their own modes of existence and their own structural
relations. The multiplicity of the manifestations is not a sign that the identity is not one; it is a
sign that the identity is expressed. ((T))


Second consequence: the unity of identity. The unity of identity is the unity of a source.
It is not the unity of an aggregate, nor the unity of a pattern, nor the unity of a thing behind
the appearances. It is the numerical unity of a source, established in the part of the book that
treated identity. The unity does not require the manifestations to be one, and the multiplicity of
the manifestations does not require the identity to be many. ((T))


Third consequence: the structural possibility of reconstruction. Since an identity is
expressed in its manifestations, a finite subject can reconstruct a pseudo-identity of it through
those manifestations; the reconstruction is always partial, as the impossibility of super-identity
established. The reconstruction is a statement about the epistemic accessibility of an identity,
not a claim that knowledge is a good or an end. The framework’s account of reconstruction
depends on the resolution of the tension, because the reconstruction is the reconstruction of a
unity from a multiplicity, and the resolution is what makes the reconstruction intelligible. ((T))
      The three consequences are not separate. They are three aspects of one structural fact: the
identity is one, the manifestations are many, and the relation between them is the relation of
expression. The first names the reality of the many; the second names the unity of the one; the
third names the epistemic access to the one through the many.

   Remark 29.10 (The Consequences Are Structural, Not Evaluative)

   The three consequences are structural, not evaluative. The framework does not claim that
   the many are more valuable than the one, or that the one is more important than the
   many. It claims that the three are structural features of the relation between identity and
   manifestation, and that the framework’s account of multiplicity, unity, and reconstruction
   is built on them. A reader who reads the consequences as evaluations has misread them; a
   reader who reads them as structural facts has read them correctly.
   The consequences point beyond themselves. The consequences are the structural features
   of the relation between identity and manifestation; they are not the ground of the relation.
   The consequences point beyond themselves to what makes the relation possible, and to
   what makes the features what they are. The framework does not describe the ground,
29.10. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                       307


   and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the consequences are
   real structural consequences, and that the consequences point beyond themselves. The
   distinction is the distinction between the consequences and the ground of the consequences;
   it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the relation as the one who is one and from whom the
   many come, and as the one in whose knowledge the one and the many are what they are.
   The framework does not claim that its consequences are that one, and it does not claim
   that the one is unreal. It claims that the consequences are real structural consequences,
   and that the consequences point beyond themselves.




29.10         What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.

   First, the chapter does not develop the full account of the recursive structure of manifestation.
The definition of recursive manifestation is stated, and the argument uses it, but the detailed
account of how the recursion proceeds—what the occasions are, how they relate to one another,
what conditions the recursion must satisfy—is deferred to the parts of the book that treat the
specific realms and their rules. The present chapter has stated the structure; the later parts
develop it.

   Second, the chapter does not develop the relation between the resolution and the framework’s
account of the seven realms. The realms are the levels in which the manifestations are realized;
the resolution depends on their reality and their distinctions. The full account of the relation
between the resolution and the realms is deferred to the parts of the book that treat the realms
in detail.

   Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the distinction between the plurality
of manifestations and the plurality of identities can be drawn in every particular case. The
distinction is a structural claim, and it is argued in general; its application to particular cases is
a matter for the analysis of those cases. The present chapter has argued for the distinction in
general; the application is left to the reader and to the chapters that follow.

   Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of the unity. It claims to
have described the structure of the unity, and the structure points beyond itself to the ground
that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of
the unity and the ground of the unity; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is stated here as
the chapter’s explicit limit.
