A Question for Reflection
Consider something you know that is one and many—a language, a tradition, a family. In what
sense is it one? In what sense is it many? If the two senses were not distinguished, would the
two answers contradict each other? What does your answer tell you about the relation between
unity and multiplicity?

The next chapter turns to the tension between intensity and breadth. The resolution uses the
same principle—category-relative predication—applied to a different tension. The present chapter
has applied the principle to the tension between unity and multiplicity; the next chapter applies it
to the tension between two measures of the relation between a manifestation and its source.
Chapter 30

Intensity and Breadth


Scope. This chapter resolves the apparent tension between two measures of the relation between
a manifestation and its source: intensity and breadth. It uses the principle of category-relative
predication, established in the part of the book that opened the resolution of tensions, and applies
it to a different tension. It states the two measures; it identifies the source of the apparent conflict;
it argues that the conflict is not real, but comes from using one scale for two different measures;
it states and argues the resolving principle—a structural duality—and draws its consequences.
Its claims are structural; where the chapter is silent on questions of value, the silence is not a
denial but a recognition that the structural description is not the whole of what can be said. The
two measures are named by structural terms, not evaluative ones, so that the analysis is not
confused with a ranking or a valuation.


30.1      A Scene
Consider a portrait and a biography of the same person. The portrait is a single painting: one
image, one moment, one pose. The biography is a volume of chapters: many events, many
relations, many phases of a life across decades. Turn from one to the other, and something has
been gained and something lost.
   What has been gained is articulation. The biography makes explicit what the portrait leaves
implicit: the person’s childhood, her education, her friendships, her work, her failures, her old
age. The portrait shows her face; the biography shows her life. The biography articulates the
person across many features, and each feature is a facet of what the person is.
   What has been lost is unity. The portrait is one image: the whole person is present in it,
gathered, held together. The biography is many pages: no single page holds the whole person,
and the whole person is not present in any one of them. The unity of the portrait is the unity of
a single image; the biography has no such unity, because its articulation across many features
disperses what the portrait gathers.
   The scene is one instance of a structural relation. Whenever a source is expressed in a
manifestation, the manifestation exhibits two measures at once: how completely it confirms the
source as a whole, and how widely it articulates the source’s implicit features. The portrait
exhibits the first measure at a high degree and the second at a low degree; the biography exhibits
the second at a high degree and the first at a low degree. The two measures are not the same,
and the trade-off between them is structural, not contingent.
   The scene poses a question. Are the two measures two aspects of one quantity, so that gaining
in one is losing in the other by definition? Or are they two distinct measures, each of which can
vary independently of the other? The present chapter argues for the second: the two measures
are structurally distinct, and the apparent trade-off is not a consequence of a single scale but of

                                                  309
310                                                           Chapter 30. Intensity and Breadth


the difference between two scales. The chapter’s principal contribution is the distinction between
the two measures, and the argument that the apparent tension between them is resolved once
the distinction is made.

   Remark 30.1 (The Two Measures Point Beyond Themselves)

   The two measures—intensity and breadth—are real structural measures of the relation
   between a manifestation and its source; the framework’s claim is that every expression
   exhibits both, and that the two are distinct. But the measures are not self-grounded. The
   measures are the measures of the expression; they are not the ground of the expression.
   The measures point beyond themselves to what makes the expression possible, and to what
   makes the source possible. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that
   what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction
   between the measures and the ground of the expression; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the measures as the perfection that no expression
   can exhaust, and as the beauty that every manifestation reflects without containing. The
   framework does not claim that its structural measures are that perfection, and it does
   not claim that the perfection is unreal. It claims that the measures are real structural
   measures, and that the measures point beyond themselves. The reader who identifies the
   measures with the perfection is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to
   do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a question
   for another inquiry.



30.2       The Question

The preceding chapters of this part have used the principle of category-relative predication to
resolve the tension between rigidity and dynamism (the chapter that opened the part) and the
tension between unity and multiplicity (the chapter that followed). Each resolution has the same
form: the two predicates that appeared to conflict are said of different respects of one thing, and
the distinction of respects removes the contradiction.
      The present chapter uses the principle to resolve a third tension. The tension is between two
measures of the relation between a manifestation and its source: intensity and breadth. The
measures appear to trade off against each other: a manifestation that is high in intensity seems
to be low in breadth, and a manifestation that is high in breadth seems to be low in intensity.
If the two measures are two aspects of one quantity, the trade-off is necessary; if they are two
distinct measures, the trade-off is not necessary but contingent, and the tension is resolved.
      The question is not idle. The framework says that a manifestation is the appearance of an
identity in a receiving realm, and that the receiving realm’s capacity limits what can appear.
The limitation seems to force a trade-off: if the realm can bear only so much, a manifestation
that articulates many features must confirm the whole less completely, and a manifestation that
confirms the whole more completely must articulate fewer features. The apparent trade-off is a
consequence of the realm’s limited capacity, and it seems to make the two measures two aspects
of one quantity.
30.3. The Two Measures                                                                         311


   The present chapter argues that the trade-off is not necessary, and that the two measures are
structurally distinct. The capacity of the realm limits both measures, but it does not make them
one measure. The distinction between the two measures is what resolves the tension, and the
distinction is a consequence of the framework’s account of manifestation, not an addition to it.
   Two aspects of the question must be distinguished.

The conceptual aspect. What are the two measures, exactly? The chapter states them
precisely, so that the apparent conflict can be located in the measures themselves.

The structural aspect. What makes the two measures compatible? The chapter argues that
the compatibility is a consequence of a structural duality: the two measures are two aspects of
one expression, not two quantities on one scale.
   The chapter proceeds as follows. It states the two measures. It identifies the source of the
apparent conflict. It argues that the conflict is not real. It states the resolving principle and
argues for it. It states the scope of the resolution and what would challenge it. It draws the
consequences. It closes with what it does not establish and with the epistemic status of its claims.


30.3     The Two Measures
The two measures are stated in a definition.

   Definition 30.1 (Intensity and Breadth)

   (A) The intensity of a manifestation is the degree to which it confirms the source as a
   whole, in its unity (the completeness of reflection). Its breadth is the extent to which the
   implicit articulation of the source is made explicit in diverse features.

   The definition states two measures, not one. Intensity measures confirmation of unity; breadth
measures articulation of features. The two are not the same, and the definition does not reduce
one to the other.
   Intensity, as the definition states it, is the degree to which the manifestation confirms the
source as a whole. A manifestation that confirms the source as a whole is one in which the source
is present, gathered, held together. The portrait is an example: the whole person is present in
the image, even though the image is small. The confirmation is not the articulation; it is the
gathering of the source into a single appearance.
   Breadth, as the definition states it, is the extent to which the implicit articulation of the
source is made explicit in diverse features. A manifestation that articulates many features is one
in which the source is spread across many aspects, each of which is a facet of what the source
is. The biography is an example: the person’s articulation across many events and relations is
made explicit, even though no single page holds the whole person. The articulation is not the
confirmation; it is the spreading of the source across many appearances.
   The two measures can vary independently. A manifestation can be high in intensity and low
in breadth (the portrait); high in breadth and low in intensity (the biography); high in both (a
complete life-work, if such a thing exists); low in both (a fragmentary sketch). The independence
312                                                            Chapter 30. Intensity and Breadth


is structural: the two measures answer different questions, and an answer to one does not answer
the other.

   Remark 30.2 (The Two Measures Are Not the Same as the Two Pairs)

   The two measures are not the same as the two pairs of the four-column framework. The
   two pairs are fixed elements with context (Pair 1) and dynamics with fluid element (Pair 2);
   they are analytical roles in an explanation. The two measures are degrees of the relation
   between a manifestation and its source; they are structural features of that relation. The
   two distinctions are different, and the chapter keeps them apart. A reader who confuses
   them will find the chapter’s argument puzzling; a reader who keeps them apart will find it
   clear.


30.4        The Source of the Apparent Conflict
The apparent conflict has a source, and the source can be identified. It is the use of one scale for
two different measures.
      The argument is simple. If intensity and breadth were measures of one quantity, the two
would trade off by definition: a manifestation that gains in one would lose in the other, because
the total quantity is fixed. If they are measures of two distinct quantities, the two can vary
independently: a manifestation can gain in one without losing in the other, and a manifestation
can lose in one without gaining in the other. The trade-off that appears in the portrait and the
biography is not a trade-off in one quantity; it is a difference in the two quantities that the two
manifestations realize.
      The use of one scale for two measures is the source of the apparent conflict. The two sentences
“the portrait is more unified” and “the biography is more articulated” are said in the ordinary
language as if they were speaking of one scale: the portrait is high on the scale, the biography is
low on the scale. But the two sentences are speaking of two scales, not one. The portrait is high
on the intensity scale and low on the breadth scale; the biography is low on the intensity scale
and high on the breadth scale. The apparent conflict is the residue of the ordinary language’s
use of one word (“more”) for two measures.
      The source of the apparent conflict is not the framework’s account of manifestation. The
framework has said that a manifestation is the appearance of an identity in a receiving realm,
and that the receiving realm’s capacity limits what can appear. The limitation does not force a
trade-off in one quantity; it limits both measures, and the two measures can vary independently
within the limitation. The apparent conflict comes from the ordinary language, not from the
framework.

   Remark 30.3 (The Two Scales Are Not Commensurable)

   The two scales are not commensurable. There is no common unit in which both intensity
   and breadth can be measured, and no exchange rate by which one can be converted into the
   other. A manifestation that is high in intensity and a manifestation that is high in breadth
   are not two points on one scale; they are two points on two scales. The incommensurability
30.5. Is the Conflict Real?                                                                     313


   is structural: it follows from the difference between the two measures, not from a defect
   in the measures. A reader who looks for a common unit will not find one; a reader who
   accepts the incommensurability will find the resolution clear.
   The incommensurability points beyond itself. The incommensurability is the incommensu-
   rability of the two measures; it is not the ground of the measures. The incommensurability
   points beyond itself to what makes the two measures possible, and to what makes the
   relation between them possible. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does
   not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the incommensurability is real, and that
   the incommensurability points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between
   the incommensurability and the ground of the measures; it is kept throughout the book.



30.5     Is the Conflict Real?
The source of the apparent conflict has been identified. The question is now whether the conflict
is real, or whether it is the appearance that comes from using one scale for two measures.
   The chapter’s answer is: it is not real. The conflict is the appearance that comes from
treating the two measures as if they were one. Once the two measures are distinguished, the
conflict disappears.
   The claim is not that the conflict is merely verbal. It is that the conflict is the appearance
that comes from a real distinction—the distinction between the degree to which a manifestation
confirms the source as a whole and the extent to which it articulates the source’s features. The
distinction is real; the conflict is the appearance that arises when the distinction is not seen.
   The two measures are compatible because they are measures of different things. Intensity
measures the confirmation of unity; breadth measures the articulation of features. To say that a
manifestation is high in intensity is not to say that it is high in breadth, or low in breadth, or
anything about its breadth. To say that a manifestation is high in breadth is not to say that it
is high in intensity, or low in intensity, or anything about its intensity. The two statements say
different things, and they are both true.
   The compatibility is not a triviality. It would be a triviality if the two measures were
obviously different, as height and weight are obviously different. But the framework’s account
of manifestation has established that the manifestation is the appearance of the source in a
receiving realm, and the receiving realm’s capacity limits what can appear. The limitation makes
it tempting to think that the two measures are two aspects of one quantity; the temptation is
what the present chapter resists. The two measures are two aspects of one expression, not two
quantities on one scale.

   Remark 30.4 (Why the Conflict Is Felt)

   The conflict is felt because the two measures are measures of the same manifestation. If
   they were measures of different manifestations, no one would think to compare them; but
   because they are measures of the same manifestation, they are easily compared, and the
   comparison invites the inference that they are on one scale. The felt conflict is the residue
314                                                           Chapter 30. Intensity and Breadth


   of this closeness. The framework’s task is not to separate the two measures from the
   manifestation—they are measures of the same manifestation—but to distinguish them, so
   that the one is not mistaken for the other.
   The felt conflict, too, points beyond itself. The conflict is felt because the language does
   not distinguish the two scales; the distinction is real, and the language is partial. The felt
   conflict points beyond itself to what makes the two scales possible, and to what makes the
   language partial. The framework does not describe the ground of the distinction, and it
   does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the felt conflict is real, and that
   the felt conflict points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the felt
   conflict and the ground of the distinction; it is kept throughout the book.



30.6       The Resolving Principle: A Structural Duality
The resolution of the apparent conflict is stated in a principle, and the principle introduces a
specific structure: a structural duality between the two measures.

   Principle 30.1 (Structural Duality of Expression)

   (A) Intensity and breadth are two measures of one expression, not two quantities on one
   scale. They are structurally distinct: each can vary independently of the other, and neither
   is reducible to the other. The duality is structural, not evaluative; it states a feature of
   the relation between a manifestation and its source, not a value, an end, or a good.

      The principle is adopted, not proved. Its support is the definition of the two measures and
the argument that follows. It would be refuted by showing that intensity and breadth cannot
vary independently—that every increase in one is always accompanied by a decrease in the other,
in every case. The framework does not claim that no such case can be constructed; it claims
that none has been constructed that survives the distinction between the two measures, and it
argues that none can be.
      The principle has two components, which the reader should keep distinct.


First component: structural distinctness. The two measures are structurally distinct:
each is defined by what it measures, and the definitions do not reduce one to the other. Intensity
measures confirmation of unity; breadth measures articulation of features. The two definitions
are different, and the difference is what makes the two measures distinct.


Second component: independent variability. The two measures can vary independently:
a manifestation can gain in one without losing in the other, and can lose in one without gaining
in the other. The independence is what the chapter’s argument establishes, and the independence
is what the principle states.
      The two components together yield the structural duality. The measures are distinct, and
the distinctness allows them to vary independently. The apparent trade-off is not a trade-off in
one quantity; it is a difference in two quantities that the two manifestations realize.
30.6. The Resolving Principle: A Structural Duality                                             315


   Remark 30.5 (The Principle Is General)

   The principle is not stated only for intensity and breadth. It is the principle of structural
   duality, and it applies to any pair of measures that are measures of different aspects of
   one expression. The chapter applies it to intensity and breadth; the framework uses it
   elsewhere for other pairs of measures. The principle is the framework’s tool for resolving
   this class of tensions, and the reader who understands the present chapter will understand
   its application to other pairs.
   The principle, too, points beyond itself. The principle is the structure of the duality; it is
   not the ground of the expression. The principle points beyond itself to what makes the
   expression possible, and to what makes the measures possible. The framework does not
   describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the
   principle is a real structural principle, and that the principle points beyond itself. The
   distinction is the distinction between the principle and the ground of the expression; it is
   kept throughout the book.



   Remark 30.6 (The Structural Terms)

   The two measures are named by structural terms, and the structural terms are not
   evaluative. “Intensity” names the degree to which a manifestation confirms the source as
   a whole; “breadth” names the extent to which the manifestation articulates the source’s
   features. Neither term carries an implicit evaluation: neither suggests that less intensity is
   bad or that more breadth is good, or vice versa. The structural terms leave the evaluation
   to other inquiries, and they keep the chapter’s argument distinct from a ranking or a
   valuation. The reader who imports an evaluative sense into the terms has misread the
   chapter; the reader who reads them as structural measures has read it correctly.
   The structural terms, too, point beyond themselves. The terms name the measures; they
   do not name the ground of the measures. The terms point beyond themselves to what
   makes the measures possible, and to what makes the relation between them possible.
   The framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is
   unreal. It claims that the terms are real structural terms, and that the terms point beyond
   themselves. The distinction is the distinction between the terms and the ground of the
   measures; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the measures as the names through which the source
   is known, and as the attributes through which the source is described. The framework
   does not claim that its structural measures are those names, and it does not claim that
   the names are unreal. It claims that the measures are real structural measures, and that
   the measures point beyond themselves. The reader who identifies the measures with the
   names is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework
   takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.
316                                                             Chapter 30. Intensity and Breadth


30.7       The Argument
The argument for the resolution proceeds in five steps.

Resolution of the Apparent Conflict.         1. In its own realm an identity is not articulated into
        diverse features, or is so only in the way that the realm allows.

  2. In a realm of greater multiplicity its implicit articulation is made explicit.

  3. The receiving realm limits what it can bear of the source’s unity. So the manifestation
        confirms a lower degree of the source as a whole.

  4. The first (step 1 to step 2) is an increase of breadth; the second (step 3) is a reduction of
        intensity. They are different measures.

  5. Hence the apparent conflict is resolved by distinguishing them.


      The argument’s force is in step (4). If the increase of breadth and the reduction of intensity
were the same change, the two measures would be one measure, and the trade-off would be
necessary. The framework’s account of manifestation is what blocks this: the two changes are
different, and the two measures are distinct. The increase of breadth is the articulation of the
source’s implicit features; the reduction of intensity is the limitation of the source’s unity by the
receiving realm’s capacity. The two changes happen together in many cases, but they are not
the same change.
      Step (5) states the conclusion: the apparent conflict is resolved by distinguishing the two
measures. The distinction is the framework’s tool for the resolution, and the argument shows
that the distinction is required by the framework’s account of manifestation.

   Remark 30.7 (What Exactly Is Reduced, and What Added)

   Four questions, answered.

        1. What is reduced? Intensity of confirmation: the degree to which the manifestation
           confirms the source’s unity as a whole. Not the identity, which is conserved.

        2. What is added? Articulation: diverse features through which the source is made
           legible in the receiving realm.

        3. Can an increase of breadth come with a reduction of fidelity? Yes. A manifestation
           may be more articulated and yet carry features that conflict with the nature of the
           source. That is distortion, not a manifestation that satisfies the fidelity condition.

        4. Is every increase of breadth an increase in the degree to which the manifestation
           expresses the source? No. It is such only if the added features are homogeneous in
           essence with the source (the principle of essential homogeneity, established in the
           part of the book that treated the fixed elements). Otherwise the increase of breadth
           is an increase of the manifestation’s articulation that does not satisfy the fidelity
           condition.
30.8. Scope and Vulnerability                                                                  317


   Remark 30.8 (The Argument Is Relative to Its Premises)

   The argument depends on the definition of the two measures (stated in the present chapter)
   and on the framework’s account of manifestation (established in the part of the book that
   treated the fixed elements). A reader who denies either premise has a reason to reject the
   resolution, and the framework does not pretend otherwise. The argument’s value is not
   that it proves the resolution without assumptions; it is that it makes the assumptions
   visible, and shows exactly what follows from them.
   The premises, too, point beyond themselves. The premises are the structural conditions of
   the resolution; they are not the ground of the relation between manifestation and source.
   The premises point beyond themselves to what makes the relation possible, and to what
   makes the two measures what they are. The framework does not describe the ground,
   and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the premises are real
   structural premises, and that the premises point beyond themselves. The distinction is
   the distinction between the premises and the ground of the relation; it is kept throughout
   the book.



30.8     Scope and Vulnerability

The resolution is valid for the respects named, and the scope must be stated with precision.
   The resolution says that intensity and breadth are two measures of one expression, not two
quantities on one scale. It does not say that every manifestation realizes both measures at the
same degree, or that the two measures are equally realized in every manifestation. It says that
the measures are distinct, and that the distinctness is what resolves the apparent conflict.
   The resolution rests on the definition of the two measures ((A), stated above), and on the
framework’s account of manifestation ((A), established in the part of the book that treated the
fixed elements). The resolution’s force is no greater than the force of these commitments; a
reader who rejects either of them has a reason to reject the resolution, and the framework does
not pretend otherwise.
   The resolution is not relativism. The two measures are fixed by the structure of the relation
between manifestation and source, not by the observer’s choice. The framework’s claim is that
the relation has the structure the framework describes, and that the measures are appropriate to
the structure. A reader who reads the resolution as a form of relativism has misread it; a reader
who reads it as a structural claim has read it correctly.
   The resolution would be put in question by two things.


First challenge. A case in which a manifestation increases in intensity as it increases in
breadth in every instance, so that no reduction of intensity is ever general. If such a case could
be given, the two measures would always vary together, and the distinctness would be illusory.
The framework does not claim that no such case can be constructed; it claims that none has
been constructed that survives the distinction between the two measures, and it argues that
none can be.
318                                                          Chapter 30. Intensity and Breadth


Second challenge. A case in which intensity and breadth cannot be separated at all, so that
the two measures are always one. If such a case could be given, the structural duality would fail,
and the two measures would be two aspects of one scale. The framework holds that the two can
be separated, and it states the resolution at exactly the strength its arguments support.

   Remark 30.9 (The Resolution Is Not a Ranking)

   The resolution does not rank the two measures. It does not say that intensity is more
   important than breadth, or that breadth is more important than intensity. It says that
   the two are distinct, and that the distinctness resolves the apparent conflict. A reader
   who looks for a ranking will not find one; a reader who accepts the distinctness will find
   the resolution clear. The framework’s claim is structural, not evaluative.
   The absence of ranking, too, points beyond itself. The absence of ranking is the structural
   consequence of the distinctness of the two measures; it is not the ground of the measures.
   The absence of ranking points beyond itself to what makes the measures possible, and to
   what makes their relation possible. The framework does not describe the ground, and it
   does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the absence of ranking is real,
   and that the absence points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the
   absence of ranking and the ground of the measures; it is kept throughout the book.


   Remark 30.10 (The Resolution Is Not a Promise of Compensation)

   The resolution does not promise that a reduction of intensity is made up by an increase
   of breadth. The two measures are not interchangeable, and the resolution does not offer
   a common currency. A manifestation that is high in breadth and low in intensity is not
   thereby compensated for its low intensity; it is simply a manifestation that realizes the
   two measures at different degrees. The reader who reads the resolution as a promise of
   compensation has misread it; the reader who reads it as a distinction of two measures has
   read it correctly.
   The non-compensation, too, points beyond itself. The non-compensation is the structural
   fact that the two measures are distinct; it is not the ground of the relation. The non-
   compensation points beyond itself to what makes the measures possible, and to what
   makes their relation possible. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does
   not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the non-compensation is real, and that
   the non-compensation points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the
   non-compensation and the ground of the measures; it is kept throughout the book.



30.9     Consequences
The resolution has three consequences. They are stated here, with their status.


First consequence: no terminal state of expression. Expression does not come to a state
in which the reduction of intensity is eliminated and the breadth retained. The two measures
are distinct, and the distinctness is structural; no expression can realize both at their maximal
30.9. Consequences                                                                              319


degree, because the receiving realm’s capacity limits both. The first consequence is a restatement
of the impossibility of super-identity, applied to the specific case of the two measures. ((T))


Second consequence: the structural role of fidelity. Fidelity enters the definition of
viability as a structural condition on the relation between an identity and its manifestations. It
is not a claim about which manifestations are better; it is a structural condition on the relation.
A manifestation that satisfies the fidelity condition preserves the essential determination of its
source; a manifestation that does not satisfy it does not. The distinction between satisfying and
not satisfying is structural, not evaluative. ((T))


Third consequence: the two measures are independent of the fidelity condition. A
manifestation can be high in intensity and low in breadth, or high in breadth and low in intensity,
and either manifestation can satisfy or fail the fidelity condition. The independence is structural:
the two measures and the fidelity condition answer different questions, and an answer to one does
not answer the others. The consequence is what allows the framework to speak of manifestations
that are high in one measure and low in another without evaluating them. ((T))
   The three consequences are not separate. They are three aspects of one structural fact: the
two measures are distinct, the fidelity condition is a separate condition, and the three answer
different questions. The first names the limit of expression; the second names the structural role
of fidelity; the third names the independence of the measures from the fidelity condition.

   Remark 30.11 (The Consequences Are Structural, Not Evaluative)

   The three consequences are structural, not evaluative. The framework does not claim that
   a manifestation high in intensity is more valuable than one high in breadth, or that a
   manifestation that satisfies the fidelity condition is a better thing than one that does not.
   It claims that the three are structural features of the relation between manifestation and
   source, and that the framework’s account of expression, fidelity, and viability is built on
   them. A reader who reads the consequences as evaluations has misread them; a reader
   who reads them as structural facts has read them correctly.
   The consequences point beyond themselves. The consequences are the structural features
   of the relation between manifestation and source; they are not the ground of the relation.
   The consequences point beyond themselves to what makes the relation possible, and to
   what makes the features what they are. The framework does not describe the ground,
   and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the consequences are
   real structural consequences, and that the consequences point beyond themselves. The
   distinction is the distinction between the consequences and the ground of the relation; it
   is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the relation as the perfection that no expression
   can exhaust, and as the beauty that every manifestation reflects without containing. The
   framework does not claim that its consequences are that perfection, and it does not
   claim that the perfection is unreal. It claims that the consequences are real structural
   consequences, and that the consequences point beyond themselves.

30.10        What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
      First, the chapter does not develop the full account of how the two measures are to be
compared in a given case. The definition of the two measures is stated, and the argument for
their distinctness is given, but the operational question of how to measure intensity and breadth
in a particular manifestation is left for the parts of the book that develop the framework’s
applications. The present chapter has distinguished the two measures; the later parts develop
their measurement.
      Second, the chapter does not develop the relation between the two measures and the fidelity
condition. The independence of the measures from the fidelity condition is stated, but the
detailed account of how the three interact—how a manifestation can satisfy the fidelity condition
while realizing the two measures at different degrees—is deferred to the parts of the book that
treat expression, cost, and viability.
      Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the two measures exhaust the
structural features of the relation between manifestation and source. The two are the ones the
framework has identified; whether a third exists is a question the framework leaves open. The
framework’s claim is that the two are structurally distinct and that the distinctness resolves the
apparent conflict, not that no further measure could be found.
      Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of the two measures. It
claims to have described the structure of the two measures, and the structure points beyond
itself to the ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction
between the structure of the measures and the ground of the measures; it is kept throughout the
chapter, and it is stated here as the chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection

Consider a thing you know that is expressed in two ways—a story told in a sentence and in a
novel, a person seen in a photograph and in a biography, a place visited in a day and lived in for
a year. Which expression is more intense, and which is broader? Does the difference tell you
something about the thing itself, or only about the expressions? What does your answer tell you
about the relation between intensity and breadth?
30.11. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                            321


The next chapter turns to the tension between tendency and success. The resolution uses the
same principle—category-relative predication—applied to a different tension. The present chapter
has distinguished two measures of the relation between manifestation and source; the next chapter
distinguishes the necessity of the tendency to express from the degree to which any manifestation
realizes the structural condition of fidelity.
Chapter 31

Tendency and Success


Scope. This chapter resolves the apparent tension between the necessity of the tendency to
express and the degree to which any manifestation realizes the structural condition of fidelity. It
uses the principle of category-relative predication, established in the part of the book that opened
the resolution of tensions, and applies it to a different tension. The terms “success” and “failure”
are used here in a purely structural sense: success names the degree to which a manifestation
satisfies the fidelity condition of viability, and failure names the limit case in which that degree
is zero. Neither term carries a value, an end, or a good; no normative or ethical claim is made
in this chapter. Where the chapter speaks of “tendency,” “success,” “failure,” “realization,” or
“degree of structural fidelity,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in
this chapter and in the parts of the book that treated expression and viability.


31.1      A Scene
Consider two acorns from the same oak. They are, as far as anyone can tell, identical: same size,
same shape, same genetic structure, same capacity to become a tree. One is planted in rich soil,
with sun and rain and room to grow. The other is planted in shallow soil, in the shadow of a
wall, where the rain rarely reaches and the sun is blocked for most of the day.
    Both acorns tend toward the same thing: to become an oak. The tendency is not a choice,
and it is not a mechanism imposed from without. It is what the acorn is: an identity that
expresses itself in a tree, when the conditions for expression are present. If the conditions are
right, the tendency is realized; if they are not, the tendency is hindered, but not destroyed.
    Now consider what happens. The first acorn grows into a tall, full oak, with a broad canopy
and deep roots. The second grows into a small, stunted tree, with thin branches and shallow
roots. Both are oaks; both grew from acorns; both realize the same tendency. But the degree to
which they realize it differs enormously. The first realizes the tendency fully; the second realizes
it partially. Neither is a failure in the sense of not having the tendency; both are oaks, and both
grew. But one grew more completely than the other.
    The scene poses a question. The tendency is the same in both acorns; the realization is not.
Is the difference in realization a difference in the tendency? If the tendency were the same, should
not the realization be the same? And if the realization differs, does that mean the tendency was
not really the same after all?
    The scene is one instance of a structural relation. Whenever an identity tends toward
expression, the tendency is necessary, and the realization is graded. The two are not the same,
and the apparent tension between them—how can the tendency be necessary if its realization is
not?—is resolved once the two are distinguished. The present chapter states the distinction and
argues that the apparent tension is not real.

                                                 322
31.2. The Question                                                                              323


   Remark 31.1 (The Two Acorns Point Beyond Themselves)

   The two acorns have the same tendency and a different realization; the framework’s claim
   is that the tendency is necessary, and that the realization is graded, and that the two are
   compatible because they are said of different respects of the relation between identity and
   manifestation. But the two acorns are not self-grounded. The tendency is the tendency
   of an identity; it is not the ground of the identity. The realization is the realization in a
   realm; it is not the ground of the realm. The two acorns point beyond themselves to what
   makes the tendency possible, and to what makes the realization possible. The framework’s
   claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the
   framework. The distinction is the distinction between the two acorns and the ground of
   the tendency; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the tendency as the disposition that the creator
   has placed in every creature toward its perfection, and as the measure that is allotted to
   each creature within which it can grow. The framework does not claim that its structural
   tendency is that disposition, and it does not claim that the disposition is unreal. It claims
   that the tendency is a real structural feature, and that the feature points beyond itself.
   The reader who identifies the structural tendency with the disposition is free to do so; the
   reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the
   identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



31.2     The Question
The preceding chapters of this part have used the principle of category-relative predication to
resolve the tension between rigidity and dynamism (the chapter that opened the part), the
tension between unity and multiplicity (the chapter that followed), and the tension between
intensity and breadth (the chapter that followed that). Each resolution has the same form:
the two predicates that appeared to conflict are said of different respects of one thing, and the
distinction of respects removes the contradiction.
   The present chapter uses the principle to resolve a fourth tension. The tension is between
the necessity of the tendency to express and the degree to which any manifestation realizes the
structural condition of fidelity. The tension appears in two forms.

First form: necessity and non-realization. The framework says that expression is necessary:
every identity tends toward expression. And the framework says that a manifestation may fail to
be realized in a given realm. The two statements appear to conflict. If expression is necessary,
how can it fail to be realized? If it can fail to be realized, in what sense is it necessary?

Second form: rigidity and grading. The framework says that identity is rigid: it admits
no degrees. And the framework says that expression comes in degrees: a manifestation can be
realized at a higher or lower degree of structural fidelity. The two statements appear to conflict.
If identity is rigid, how can expression come in degrees? If expression comes in degrees, is not
the identity thereby graded?
324                                                           Chapter 31. Tendency and Success


      The present chapter argues that neither form of the tension is real, and that the appearance
of conflict in both comes from running together distinctions that the framework has already
drawn. The distinctions are these: the distinction between the necessity of the tendency and the
necessity of the outcome, and the distinction between the rigidity of the identity and the grading
of the expression.
      Two aspects of the question must be distinguished.


The conceptual aspect. What are the two concepts, exactly? The chapter states them
precisely, so that the apparent conflict can be located in the concepts themselves.


The structural aspect. What makes the two concepts compatible? The chapter argues that
the compatibility is a consequence of the distinction between the tendency and the outcome,
which the framework has already drawn and which it now states explicitly.
      The chapter proceeds as follows. It states the two concepts. It identifies the source of the
apparent conflict. It argues that the conflict is not real. It states the resolving principle and
argues for it. It states the scope of the resolution and what would challenge it. It draws the
consequences. It closes with what it does not establish and with the epistemic status of its claims.


31.3       The Two Concepts
The two concepts are stated in definitions, which restate the definitions given in the chapter on
expression.

   Definition 31.1 (Tendency to Express)

   (A) The tendency to express is necessary. Every identity, by its nature, tends toward
   expression. This tendency cannot be structurally unrealized; it can only be structurally
   hindered. (The definition restates the one given in the chapter on expression.)


   Definition 31.2 (Degree of Structural Fidelity)

   (A) The degree of structural fidelity of an expression is not necessary. An identity can
   be realized at varying degrees of structural fidelity—it can be manifested in forms that
   preserve more or less of its essential determination, and, at the limit, in forms that do not
   preserve it at all. (The definition restates the one given in the chapter on expression.)


      The two definitions are stated as commitments, because each restates a definition established
earlier. Neither is new in this chapter; the chapter’s task is not to establish them, but to show
that they can be held together.
      The apparent conflict is easy to state. The tendency to express is necessary: every identity
tends toward expression, and the tendency cannot be structurally unrealized. The degree of
structural fidelity is not necessary: an identity can be realized at varying degrees, and, at the
limit, not realized at all. If both are true, the tendency is necessary and its realization is not.
That is the apparent conflict.
31.4. The Source of the Apparent Conflict                                                       325


   The apparent conflict is not a verbal quibble. It is a real tension, and it has been felt by
every reader who has followed the framework to this point. The reader who has accepted the
necessity of expression, and has also accepted the graded character of realization, has accepted
two principles that seem to contradict each other. The present chapter’s task is to show that the
seeming is only seeming.

   Remark 31.2 (The Tendency Points Beyond Itself)

   The tendency to express is a real structural direction; the framework’s claim is that
   every identity, by its nature, tends toward expression, and that the tendency cannot
   be structurally unrealized. But the tendency is not self-grounded. The tendency is the
   tendency of an identity; it is not the ground of the identity. The tendency points beyond
   itself to what places the direction in the identity, and to what makes the direction possible.
   The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not
   described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the tendency and
   the ground of the tendency; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the tendency as the innate disposition (fitrah) that
   the creator has placed in every soul toward its source, and as the natural inclination
   that draws every creature toward its perfection. The framework does not claim that its
   structural tendency is that disposition, and it does not claim that the disposition is unreal.
   It claims that the tendency is a real structural direction, and that the direction points
   beyond itself. The reader who identifies the structural tendency with the disposition is
   free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no
   position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



31.4     The Source of the Apparent Conflict
The apparent conflict has a source, and the source can be identified. It comes from running
together two distinctions, either of which, if kept, would remove the conflict.


First distinction: the necessity of the tendency and the necessity of the outcome.
The tendency is necessary; its outcome is not. The tendency is a structural direction of what an
identity is; the outcome is a result of what the tendency meets in a receiving realm. The two
are different kinds of structural fact. If they are run together, the necessity of the tendency is
mistaken for the necessity of the outcome, and the tendency is treated as if it guaranteed the
realization. The tendency does not guarantee the realization; it guarantees that the identity is
the kind of thing that tends toward expression, and that the tendency can only be hindered, not
eliminated.


Second distinction: a rigid identity and a graded expression. The identity is rigid; its
expression is graded. The rigidity belongs to the identity; the grading belongs to the expression.
The two are different levels of the same relation. If they are run together, the rigidity of the
identity is mistaken for the rigidity of the expression, and the expression is treated as if it must
326                                                            Chapter 31. Tendency and Success


be as rigid as the identity. The expression is not rigid; it is graded. The identity is not graded; it
is rigid. The two are compatible because they are distinct.
      The two distinctions are the framework’s tools for resolving the tension. They were drawn
in the chapter on expression, where the necessity of the tendency was distinguished from the
degree of structural fidelity, and in the chapter on rigidity and dynamism, where the rigidity of
the identity was distinguished from the dynamism of the expression. The present chapter applies
them to the specific tension between tendency and success.

   Remark 31.3 (The Two Distinctions Are Not the Same)

   The first distinction is between two kinds of necessity: the necessity of the tendency and
   the necessity of the outcome. The second is between two kinds of property: the rigidity
   of the identity and the grading of the expression. The two distinctions are related—the
   first is about necessity, the second is about degrees—but they are not the same, and the
   framework keeps them apart. The reader who runs them together will find the resolution
   incomplete; the reader who keeps them apart will find it complete.


   Remark 31.4 (The Tendency Is Not a Guarantee)

   The tendency to express is not a guarantee that expression will be realized. It is a
   structural direction: the identity is the kind of thing that tends toward expression, and the
   tendency cannot be structurally eliminated. But the realization depends on conditions the
   tendency does not control: the capacity of the receiving realm, the other identities present,
   the structural conditions of the moment. The tendency is necessary; its realization is
   conditional. The reader who reads the tendency as a guarantee has misread it; the reader
   who reads it as a structural direction has read it correctly.
   The non-guarantee, too, points beyond itself. The tendency is not a guarantee; it is a
   structural direction that meets conditions it does not control. The conditions are real, and
   the direction is real; the two are not self-grounded. The non-guarantee points beyond itself
   to what makes the tendency possible, and to what makes the conditions possible. The
   framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal.
   It claims that the non-guarantee is real, and that the non-guarantee points beyond itself.
   The distinction is the distinction between the tendency and the ground of the tendency; it
   is kept throughout the book.



31.5        Is the Conflict Real?
The source of the apparent conflict has been identified. The question is now whether the conflict
is real, or whether it is the appearance that comes from running together the two distinctions.
      The chapter’s answer is: it is not real. The conflict is the appearance that comes from
treating the necessity of the tendency as if it were the necessity of the outcome, and the rigidity
of the identity as if it were the rigidity of the expression. Once the two distinctions are kept, the
conflict disappears.
      The claim is not that the conflict is merely verbal. It is that the conflict is the appearance
31.6. The Resolving Principle                                                                        327


that comes from a real distinction—the distinction between what an identity is and what its
expression realizes. The distinction is real; the conflict is the appearance that arises when the
distinction is not seen.
   The necessity of the tendency and the graded character of realization are compatible because
they are said of different things. The tendency is necessary; the realization is graded. To say
that the tendency is necessary is not to say that every realization is necessary, or that every
realization is at the maximal degree. To say that the realization is graded is not to say that the
tendency is not necessary, or that the identity is not rigid. The two statements say different
things, and they are both true.
   The compatibility is not a triviality. It would be a triviality if the tendency and its realization
were obviously different, as a direction and a destination are obviously different. But the
framework’s account of expression has established that the realization is the expression of the
tendency; it is not a separate thing alongside the tendency, but the tendency’s own realization
in a realm. The compatibility is a structural fact about the relation between tendency and
realization, and the framework’s task is to state it.

   Remark 31.5 (The Conflict Is Felt Because the Relation Is Close)

   The conflict is felt because the relation between tendency and realization is close: the
   realization is the tendency’s own expression, not a separate thing. If they were entirely
   separate, no one would think to confuse them; but because the realization is the tendency’s
   expression, it is easily mistaken for the tendency itself. The felt conflict is the residue of this
   closeness. The framework’s task is not to separate the tendency from its realization—they
   are not separate—but to distinguish them, so that the necessity of the one is not mistaken
   for the necessity of the other.
   The felt conflict, too, points beyond itself. The conflict is felt because the language does
   not distinguish the two; the distinction is real, and the language is partial. The felt conflict
   points beyond itself to what makes the tendency and the realization possible, and to what
   makes the distinction possible. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does
   not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the felt conflict is real, and that the
   felt conflict points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the felt conflict
   and the ground of the tendency; it is kept throughout the book.



31.6      The Resolving Principle

The resolution of the apparent conflict is stated in a principle. It is the framework’s application
of category-relative predication to the specific case of tendency and success.

   Principle 31.1 (Tendency Is Not Success)

   (T) The necessity of the tendency to express does not entail the necessity of the realization
   of any manifestation at any particular degree of structural fidelity, nor the necessity that
   a manifestation be realized in every realm.
328                                                             Chapter 31. Tendency and Success


      The principle is (T): it is argued from the definition of the tendency and the definition of
the degree of structural fidelity, both of which are established in the chapter on expression. The
argument is given in the next section. The principle’s status is therefore the status of its premises;
a reader who accepts the two definitions should accept the principle, and a reader who rejects
one of the definitions has a reason to reject the principle.
      The principle has two components, which the reader should keep distinct.

First component: no necessity of realization. The tendency does not entail the realization
of any particular manifestation. An identity tends to express itself, but the expression may be
realized at a lower degree, or not realized at all, depending on the receiving realm’s capacity and
the structural conditions of the moment. The tendency is necessary; the realization is conditional.

Second component: no necessity of universal realization. The tendency does not entail
that the identity is manifested in every realm. An identity may be manifested in one realm and
not in another, depending on the capacity of the realms and the structural relations among them.
The tendency is necessary; the universal realization is not.
      The two components together yield the resolution. The tendency is necessary; the realization
is graded; the two are compatible because they are said of different things. The apparent conflict
is the appearance that comes from running together the necessity of the one with the necessity
of the other.

   Remark 31.6 (The Principle Is Category-Relative Predication Applied)

   The principle is an application of the principle of category-relative predication, established
   in the chapter that opened the resolution of tensions. The principle says that the predicate
   “necessary” is said of the tendency in one respect, and the predicate “graded” is said of
   the realization in another respect. The two predicates are not said of the same respect,
   and the distinction of respects is what removes the apparent conflict. The reader who has
   understood the principle of category-relative predication will find the present principle a
   particular case of it; the reader who has not is directed to the chapter that establishes it.
   The principle, too, points beyond itself. The principle is the structure of the resolution; it
   is not the ground of the relation between tendency and realization. The principle points
   beyond itself to what makes the tendency possible, and to what makes the realization
   possible. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the
   ground is unreal. It claims that the principle is a real structural principle, and that the
   principle points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the principle and
   the ground of the relation; it is kept throughout the book.



31.7       The Argument
The argument for the resolution proceeds in four steps.

Resolution of the Apparent Conflict.        1. A tendency is a structural direction of what an iden-
        tity is; the degree of structural fidelity of a manifestation is a result of what the tendency
31.7. The Argument                                                                                329


      meets in a receiving realm. These are different kinds of structural fact.

   2. A tendency that is necessary in the first sense can meet a realm of low structural capacity,
      or be structurally hindered; the result is then a manifestation realized at a lower degree of
      structural fidelity, or not realized at all.

   3. Identity is rigid; the expression it tends to is graded in its fidelity. The grading belongs to
      the relation of identity to manifestation, not to the identity.

   4. Hence the necessity of the tendency and the structural possibility of unrealized or under-
      realized expression are compatible, and so are rigid identity and graded expression.


   The argument’s force is in step (1). If the tendency and the degree of structural fidelity were
the same kind of structural fact, the necessity of the one would be the necessity of the other,
and the conflict would be real. The framework’s account of expression is what blocks this: the
tendency is a structural direction, and the degree of fidelity is a result. The two are different
kinds of structural fact, and their difference is what makes the resolution possible.
   Step (2) applies the distinction to the particular case: the tendency can meet a realm of low
capacity, or be hindered, and the result is a manifestation at a lower degree, or no manifestation.
Step (3) states the distinction between the rigidity of the identity and the grading of the expression.
Step (4) states the conclusion: the two pairs—necessity and realization, rigidity and grading—are
compatible because they are said of different respects.

   Remark 31.7 (The Argument Is Relative to Its Premises)

   The argument depends on the definitions of the tendency and the degree of structural
   fidelity, both established in the chapter on expression. A reader who denies either definition
   has a reason to reject the resolution, and the framework does not pretend otherwise. The
   argument’s value is not that it proves the resolution without assumptions; it is that it
   makes the assumptions visible, and shows exactly what follows from them.
   The premises, too, point beyond themselves. The premises are the structural conditions of
   the resolution; they are not the ground of the relation between tendency and realization.
   The premises point beyond themselves to what makes the tendency possible, and to what
   makes the realization possible. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does
   not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the premises are real structural premises,
   and that the premises point beyond themselves. The distinction is the distinction between
   the premises and the ground of the relation; it is kept throughout the book.

   Remark 31.8 (Agreement with the Chapter on Expression)

   The present chapter’s resolution is the same as the distinction stated in the chapter on
   expression, where the necessity of the tendency was distinguished from the degree of
   structural fidelity. Neither chapter says more than that. A tendency that is necessary does
   not thereby guarantee the realization of any particular manifestation at any particular
   degree of structural fidelity. The reader who has read the chapter on expression will
330                                                               Chapter 31. Tendency and Success


   recognize the distinction; the reader who has not is directed to it.



31.8        Scope and Vulnerability
The resolution is valid for the respects named, and the scope must be stated with precision.
      The resolution says that the tendency is necessary and the realization is graded, and that the
two are compatible because they are said of different respects of the relation between identity and
manifestation. It does not say that every tendency is realized, or that every identity is manifested
in every realm. It says that the tendency is structural and the realization is conditional, and
that the two are compatible.
      The resolution rests on the definitions of the tendency and the degree of structural fidelity ((A),
established in the chapter on expression), and on the principle of category-relative predication
((A), established in the chapter that opened the resolution of tensions). The resolution’s force is
no greater than the force of these commitments; a reader who rejects either of them has a reason
to reject the resolution, and the framework does not pretend otherwise.
      The resolution is not relativism. The tendency is necessary, and the realization is graded, by
the structure of the relation between identity and manifestation, not by the observer’s choice.
The framework’s claim is that the relation has the structure the framework describes, and that
the predicates are appropriate to the structure. A reader who reads the resolution as a form of
relativism has misread it; a reader who reads it as a structural claim has read it correctly.
      The resolution would be put in question by two things.


First challenge. A case in which the necessity of a tendency could be shown to carry with it
the realization of its outcome at a particular degree of structural fidelity. If such a case could be
given, the tendency would guarantee the realization, and the distinction between the two would
be empty. The framework does not claim that no such case can be constructed; it claims that
none has been constructed that survives the distinction between the tendency and the outcome,
and it argues that none can be.


Second challenge. A case in which the degree of structural fidelity could not be separated
from the tendency, so that to speak of the tendency at all would require speaking of a particular
degree of realization. If such a case could be given, the tendency would be inseparable from the
outcome, and the resolution would fail. The framework holds that the two can be separated, and
it states the resolution at exactly the strength its arguments support.

   Remark 31.9 (The Resolution Is Not a Promise of Realization)

   The resolution does not promise that every tendency will be realized, or that every identity
   will be manifested at a high degree of structural fidelity. The tendency is necessary; the
   realization is conditional. A manifestation that is realized at a low degree of structural
   fidelity is a manifestation in which the tendency met unfavorable conditions; it is not a
   manifestation in which the tendency was eliminated. The reader who reads the resolution
31.9. Consequences                                                                                331


   as a promise of realization has misread it; the reader who reads it as a distinction between
   the tendency and its outcome has read it correctly.
   The non-promise, too, points beyond itself. The non-promise is the structural fact that
   the tendency is necessary and the realization is conditional; it is not the ground of the
   relation. The non-promise points beyond itself to what makes the tendency possible, and
   to what makes the realization possible. The framework does not describe the ground, and
   it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the non-promise is real, and
   that the non-promise points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the
   non-promise and the ground of the relation; it is kept throughout the book.


   Remark 31.10 (The Terminology of “Success” and “Failure”)

   The title uses the words “success” and “failure,” and the words must be fixed. In ordinary
   language, they carry evaluative weight: success is good, failure is bad. In this chapter, they
   are used in a purely structural sense. Success names the degree to which a manifestation
   satisfies the fidelity condition of viability; failure names the limit case in which that degree
   is zero. Neither term carries a value, an end, or a good; no normative or ethical claim
   is made in this chapter. The reader who imports an evaluative sense into the words has
   misread the chapter; the reader who reads them as structural terms has read it correctly.
   The structural terms, too, point beyond themselves. The terms name the degree of fidelity;
   they do not name the ground of the relation. The terms point beyond themselves to what
   makes the tendency possible, and to what makes the realization possible. The framework
   does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims
   that the terms are real structural terms, and that the terms point beyond themselves. The
   distinction is the distinction between the terms and the ground of the relation; it is kept
   throughout the book.



31.9     Consequences
The resolution has three consequences. They are stated here, with their status.


First consequence: the structural possibility of under-realization. An identity’s
expression may be realized at less than full structural fidelity; its tendency can be structurally
hindered, and light can be lodged in a realm unreturned. The under-realization is not a failure
of the tendency; it is a structural outcome of the tendency’s meeting with a realm of limited
capacity. The distinction between under-realization and failure is structural: the tendency is not
eliminated in under-realization, it is hindered. ((T))


Second consequence: the reality of graded realization. Expression can be realized at
various degrees of structural fidelity. This degree is a component of viability, as established
in the part of the book that treated the foundation. The graded character of realization is
not an imperfection of expression; it is a structural feature of the relation between an identity
332                                                           Chapter 31. Tendency and Success


and its manifestations. The manifestation that is realized at a lower degree is not a defective
manifestation; it is a manifestation whose relation to its source is at a lower degree. ((T))


Third consequence: hindrance and reduced fidelity differ. A tendency may be struc-
turally hindered so that no manifestation is realized in some realm; or a manifestation may be
realized at a low degree of structural fidelity. These are different structural outcomes. The first
is the absence of a manifestation; the second is the presence of a manifestation at a low degree.
The two are often run together, but they are distinct, and the framework’s account of expression
distinguishes them. ((T))
      The three consequences are not separate. They are three aspects of one structural fact: the
tendency is necessary, the realization is graded, and the relation between them is the relation of
expression. The first names the possibility of under-realization; the second names the reality of
grading; the third names the distinction between hindrance and reduced fidelity.

   Remark 31.11 (The Consequences Are Structural, Not Evaluative)

   The three consequences are structural, not evaluative. The framework does not claim that
   under-realization is bad, or that grading is a defect, or that hindrance is a failure in any
   evaluative sense. It claims that the three are structural features of the relation between
   tendency and realization, and that the framework’s account of expression, viability, and
   hindrance is built on them. A reader who reads the consequences as evaluations has
   misread them; a reader who reads them as structural facts has read them correctly.
   The consequences point beyond themselves. The consequences are the structural features
   of the relation between tendency and realization; they are not the ground of the relation.
   The consequences point beyond themselves to what makes the tendency possible, and
   to what makes the realization possible. The framework does not describe the ground,
   and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the consequences are
   real structural consequences, and that the consequences point beyond themselves. The
   distinction is the distinction between the consequences and the ground of the relation; it
   is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the relation as the will that nothing can hinder,
   and as the wisdom through which every realization is what it is. The framework does not
   claim that its consequences are that will, and it does not claim that the will is unreal. It
   claims that the consequences are real structural consequences, and that the consequences
   point beyond themselves.



31.10        What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
      First, the chapter does not develop the full account of how the degree of structural fidelity
is to be measured in a given case. The definition of the degree is stated, and the argument for
its distinction from the tendency is given, but the operational question of how to measure the
degree in a particular manifestation is left for the parts of the book that develop the framework’s
31.11. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                333


applications. The present chapter has distinguished the tendency from its outcome; the later
parts develop the measurement of the outcome.
   Second, the chapter does not develop the relation between the tendency and the framework’s
account of light. Light is the conveyor of effect; the tendency is the structural direction of an
identity toward expression; the relation between them is developed in the parts of the book that
treat light and expression together. The present chapter has distinguished the tendency from its
outcome; the later parts develop the relation to light.
   Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether every under-realization is a
hindrance in the strict sense, or whether some under-realizations are structural features of the
realm rather than hindrances of the tendency. The distinction between hindrance and under-
realization is stated, but its application to particular cases is left for the parts of the book that
treat the specific realms and their rules.
   Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of the tendency. It claims
to have described the structure of the tendency, and the structure points beyond itself to the
ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the
structure of the tendency and the ground of the tendency; it is kept throughout the chapter, and
it is stated here as the chapter’s explicit limit.
