A Question for Reflection
Consider a case in which something did not fully become what it tended to be—a seed that
did not become a tree, a person who did not become what she might have been, a work that
was never finished. What is the difference between the tendency that was not realized and the
tendency that was eliminated? Is there a sense in which the tendency is still there, even when its
realization is not?

The next chapter turns to the tension between relation and order. The resolution uses the same
principle—category-relative predication—applied to a different tension. The present chapter
has distinguished the tendency to express from the degree of its realization; the next chapter
distinguishes the mediating function of a realm from its mode of existence, and shows that a
realm can be both mediating and independently real.
Chapter 32

Relation and Order


Scope. This chapter resolves the apparent tension between two structural descriptions of the
barzakhic realms—that they are relational and that they are ordered levels of being. It uses the
principle of category-relative predication, established in the part of the book that opened the
resolution of tensions, and applies it to this final tension. It states the two concepts; it identifies
the source of the apparent conflict; it argues that the conflict is not real, but comes from running
together the function of a realm with its mode of existence; it states and argues the resolving
principle—function is not dependence—and draws its consequences. With this chapter, the part
of the book that resolves the apparent tensions is complete. Its claims are structural; where
the chapter is silent on questions of value, the silence is not a denial but a recognition that
the structural description is not the whole of what can be said. Where the chapter speaks of
“function,” “mediation,” “realization,” or “structural relation,” these are structural terms; their
sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and in the parts of the book that treated the
realms and their rules.


32.1      A Scene
Consider a bridge. It spans a river; it connects two banks. Its function is to relate: to make
it possible for something to pass from one side to the other. Ask what the bridge is, and the
answer is the function: it is a structure whose being consists in connecting. Take away the two
banks, and there is no bridge; a bridge with nothing to connect is not a bridge but a piece of
architecture without a purpose. The bridge seems to be nothing but its function of relating.
    Now ask a different question. Is the bridge a thing? Does it have a mode of existence of its
own? The answer is yes. The bridge is made of stone and steel; it has weight, span, load-bearing
capacity; it can be inspected, repaired, replaced; it can outlast the towns on either bank. The
bridge has properties that are not properties of its function: its material, its structure, its
capacity, its history. To say that the bridge is a relation between two banks is not to say that
the bridge is nothing but a relation. The bridge is a level of reality—a structure with its own
rules and its own possibilities—that also performs a function of relating.
    The same structure appears wherever a thing is both relational and real. Consider a translator.
Her function is to relate: to make it possible for something to pass from one language to another.
But she is not nothing but her function. She has a mind, a history, a style, a practice; she can
be studied as a person, as a professional, as a historical figure. Her function of relating is one
thing about her; her mode of existence is another. Neither reduces to the other.
    The scene poses a question. How can something be both a relation between other things
and a level of reality in its own right? If a thing is a relation, it seems to be nothing but the
relating; if it is a level, it seems to be something more than the relating. The present chapter

                                                 334
32.2. The Question                                                                             335


argues that the two are not exclusive: a thing can be a relation in its function and a level in its
mode of existence, and the two are compatible because they are different respects of one thing.
The argument is the final application of the principle of category-relative predication, and it
completes the part of the book that resolves the apparent tensions of the framework.

   Remark 32.1 (The Bridge Points Beyond Itself)

   The bridge is both a relation and a level; the framework’s claim is that the two are
   compatible because they are said of different respects of one realm. But the bridge is not
   self-grounded. The relation is the relation the bridge performs; it is not the ground of the
   relation. The level is the level the bridge is; it is not the ground of the level. The bridge
   points beyond itself to what makes the relation possible, and to what makes the level
   possible. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is
   not described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the bridge and
   the ground of the relation and the level; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the relation and the level as the one who is the
   source of every relation and every level, and as the one in whose knowledge the relation
   and the level are what they are. The framework does not claim that its structural bridge
   is that one, and it does not claim that the one is unreal. It claims that the bridge is a
   real structural bridge, and that the bridge points beyond itself. The reader who identifies
   the structural bridge with the one is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is
   free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a
   question for another inquiry.




32.2      The Question

The preceding chapters of this part have used the principle of category-relative predication to
resolve the tension between rigidity and dynamism, the tension between unity and multiplicity,
the tension between intensity and breadth, and the tension between tendency and success. Each
resolution has had the same form: the two predicates that appeared to conflict were said of
different respects of one thing, and the distinction of respects removed the contradiction.
   The present chapter uses the principle to resolve the final tension. The tension concerns the
barzakhic realms—the three realms whose mode of existence includes mediating, transforming,
or regulating relations between other realms. Two structural descriptions of these realms appear
to conflict.



First description: the barzakhic realms are relational. Each hub is defined by its
function: the Hub of Decree apportions measure, the Hub of Signification carries structure
into meaning, the Hub of Realization actualizes what is possible. The function is a relating; it
holds between other realms. The barzakhic realms are, in this description, relations between the
fundamental realms.
336                                                                Chapter 32. Relation and Order


Second description: the barzakhic realms are ordered levels. Each hub is an indepen-
dently real level of being, with rules and structural possibilities of its own. The independence of
the barzakhic realms was argued in the part of the book that gave the arguments; each hub has
a mode of existence that is not reducible to the mode of its neighbors. The barzakhic realms are,
in this description, levels of reality.
      The apparent conflict is: how can a realm be both a relation and a level? If it is a relation, it
seems to be nothing but the relating, and nothing but the relating is not a level. If it is a level,
it seems to be something more than the relating, and something more than the relating is not a
relation. The two descriptions appear to exclude each other.
      The present chapter argues that they do not. The two descriptions concern different questions
about one realm: what it does for other realms, and what it is in itself. The two questions are
distinct, and an answer to one is not an answer to the other. Once the distinction is kept, the
apparent conflict disappears.
      Two aspects of the question must be distinguished.

The conceptual aspect. What are the two concepts, exactly? The chapter states them
precisely, so that the apparent conflict can be located in the concepts themselves.

The structural aspect. What makes the two concepts compatible? The chapter argues that
the compatibility is a consequence of a structural fact about the barzakhic realms: their function
of relating is a feature of their mode of existence, not the whole of it.
      The chapter proceeds as follows. It states the two concepts. It identifies the source of the
apparent conflict. It argues that the conflict is not real. It states the resolving principle and
argues for it. It states the scope of the resolution and what would challenge it. It draws the
consequences. It closes the part with what it does not establish and with the epistemic status of
its claims.


32.3        The Two Concepts
The two concepts are stated in definitions, which restate the definitions given in the parts of the
book that treated the realms and the arguments.

   Definition 32.1 (Relation (as Function of a Barzakhic Realm))

   (A) The relation of a barzakhic realm is its function: the regulation, conditioning, or
   transformation of a relation between two other realms by the hub’s own mode of operation.
   The relation is what the hub does for the realms it mediates. (The definition restates the
   account of mediation given in the part of the book that treated the realms.)


   Definition 32.2 (Order (as Mode of Existence of a Barzakhic Realm))

   (A) The order of a barzakhic realm is its mode of existence: the level of being it is in its
   own right, with rules and structural possibilities of its own. The order is what the hub is
   in itself, not merely what it does for others. (The definition restates the principle of the
32.4. The Source of the Apparent Conflict                                                      337


   independence of the barzakhic realms, argued in the part of the book that treated the
   realms.)


   The two definitions are stated as commitments, because each restates a principle established
earlier. Neither is new in this chapter; the chapter’s task is not to establish them, but to show
that they can be held together.
   The apparent conflict is easy to state. The relation of a hub is its function; the function is a
relating; a relating is between two terms. The order of a hub is its mode of existence; the mode
of existence is a level; a level is not between two terms. The first makes the hub a relation; the
second makes the hub a level. The two seem incompatible.
   The apparent conflict is not a verbal quibble. It is a real tension, and it has been felt by
every reader who has followed the framework to this point. The reader who has accepted the
functional account of the hubs, and has also accepted their independent reality, has accepted two
principles that seem to contradict each other. The present chapter’s task is to show that the
seeming is only seeming.

   Remark 32.2 (The Two Analyses Point Beyond Themselves)

   The two analyses—the structural and the existential—are real analyses; the framework’s
   claim is that the structural analysis describes the architecture of the realms, and the
   existential analysis describes what can be realized in them, and the two are complementary.
   But the two analyses are not self-grounded. The analyses are the analyses of the realms;
   they are not the ground of the realms. The analyses point beyond themselves to what makes
   the architecture possible, and to what makes the realization possible. The framework’s
   claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the
   framework. The distinction is the distinction between the analyses and the ground of the
   realms; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the realms as the one through whom the levels are
   what they are, and as the one in whose knowledge the architecture and the realization
   are what they are. The framework does not claim that its analyses are that one, and
   it does not claim that the one is unreal. It claims that the analyses are real structural
   analyses, and that the analyses point beyond themselves. The reader who identifies the
   analyses with the one is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so;
   the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a question for
   another inquiry.



32.4     The Source of the Apparent Conflict
The apparent conflict has a source, and the source can be identified. It comes from running
together the function of a realm with its mode of existence.


The function of a realm. The function is what the realm does for other realms. It is a
structural relation between the realm and the relations it mediates. The function is real, and it
338                                                               Chapter 32. Relation and Order


is essential to what the hub is; but it is not the whole of what the hub is.


The mode of existence of a realm. The mode of existence is what the realm is in itself. It
is a level of being, with rules and structural possibilities that are not the rules and possibilities
of its neighbors. The mode of existence is real, and it is what makes the hub a realm rather than
a mere relation; but it is not the whole of what the hub is either.
      The two are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart. The distinction was drawn
in the part of the book that treated the realms, where it was stated that a barzakhic realm’s
mediating function does not make it dependent in existence, and in the part of the book that
gave the arguments, where it was argued that the hubs are not reducible to functions of their
neighbors. The present chapter applies the distinction to the specific tension between relation
and order.
      If the two are run together, the function is mistaken for the whole of the hub, and the hub
is treated as if it were nothing but its function. Or the mode of existence is mistaken for the
whole of the hub, and the hub is treated as if it were a level unrelated to its neighbors. Neither
mistake is warranted. The hub is both: a level whose mode of existence includes the function of
mediating. The function is a feature of the mode of existence, not an alternative to it.

   Remark 32.3 (The Distinction Is Not a Division)

   The distinction between function and mode of existence is not a division of the hub into
   two things. The hub is one thing; the function and the mode of existence are two aspects
   of it. The function is what the hub does; the mode of existence is what the hub is. The
   two are aspects of one realm, not two realms. A reader who reads the distinction as a
   division of the hub has misread it; a reader who reads it as a distinction of aspects has
   read it correctly.
   The distinction, too, points beyond itself. The distinction is the structural distinction of
   function and mode of existence; it is not the ground of the hub. The distinction points
   beyond itself to what makes the function possible, and to what makes the mode of existence
   possible. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the
   ground is unreal. It claims that the distinction is a real structural distinction, and that the
   distinction points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the distinction
   and the ground of the hub; it is kept throughout the book.


   Remark 32.4 (The Function Is Not Accidental)

   The function of the hub is not accidental to its mode of existence. The hub is not a
   level that happens, by accident, to mediate; it is a level whose mode of existence includes
   mediating. The function is essential to the mode of existence, and the mode of existence
   is what makes the function possible. The two are internally related: what the hub is, is
   partly what it does, and what it does is partly what it is. The distinction is not between an
   essential function and an accidental mode of existence, or between an accidental function
   and an essential mode of existence; it is between two aspects of one essential structure.
32.5. Is the Conflict Real?                                                                     339


   The internal relation, too, points beyond itself. The internal relation is the structural fact
   that the function and the mode of existence are aspects of one essential structure; it is not
   the ground of that structure. The internal relation points beyond itself to what makes
   the structure possible, and to what makes the internal relation possible. The framework
   does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims
   that the internal relation is real, and that the internal relation points beyond itself. The
   distinction is the distinction between the internal relation and the ground of the structure;
   it is kept throughout the book.



32.5     Is the Conflict Real?
The source of the apparent conflict has been identified. The question is now whether the conflict
is real, or whether it is the appearance that comes from running together the function and the
mode of existence.
   The chapter’s answer is: it is not real. The conflict is the appearance that comes from
treating the function as if it were the whole of the hub, or the mode of existence as if it were the
whole of the hub. Once the two aspects are distinguished, the conflict disappears.
   The claim is not that the conflict is merely verbal. It is that the conflict is the appearance
that comes from a real distinction—the distinction between what the hub does for other realms
and what it is in itself. The distinction is real; the conflict is the appearance that arises when
the distinction is not seen.
   The function and the mode of existence are compatible because they are said of different
respects of the same realm. To say that the hub is relational is to say that it performs a function
of mediating; to say that the hub is a level is to say that it has a mode of existence of its own.
The two statements say different things, and they are both true. The hub is both relational and
ordered, because it is a level whose mode of existence includes the function of relating.
   The compatibility is not a triviality. It would be a triviality if the function and the mode
of existence were obviously different, as a thing’s work and a thing’s substance are obviously
different. But the framework’s account of the barzakhic realms has established that their mode
of existence includes mediating; the mediating is not an add-on to the level, it is essential to it.
The compatibility is a structural fact about the relation between function and mode of existence
in a barzakhic realm, and the framework’s task is to state it.

   Remark 32.5 (The Conflict Is Felt Because the Relation Is Close)

   The conflict is felt because the relation between function and mode of existence is close:
   the function is essential to the mode of existence, not an add-on to it. If they were entirely
   separate, no one would think to confuse them; but because the function is essential to the
   mode of existence, it is easily mistaken for the whole of the realm. The felt conflict is the
   residue of this closeness. The framework’s task is not to separate the function from the
   mode of existence—they are not separate—but to distinguish them, so that the one is not
   mistaken for the other.
340                                                                  Chapter 32. Relation and Order


      The felt conflict, too, points beyond itself. The conflict is felt because the language does
      not distinguish the two; the distinction is real, and the language is partial. The felt conflict
      points beyond itself to what makes the function and the mode of existence possible, and
      to what makes the distinction possible. The framework does not describe the ground, and
      it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the felt conflict is real, and that
      the felt conflict points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the felt
      conflict and the ground of the hub; it is kept throughout the book.




32.6        The Resolving Principle

The resolution of the apparent conflict is stated in a principle. It is the framework’s application
of category-relative predication to the specific case of the barzakhic realms.

      Principle 32.1 (Function Is Not Dependence)

      (T) That a realm has the function of mediating between other realms does not entail
      that it lacks independent existence. Given the independence of the barzakhic realms, the
      mediating function is a part of its mode of existence and not the whole of it.


      The principle is (T): it is argued from the distinction between function and mode of existence
(stated in the present chapter) and from the principle of the independence of the barzakhic
realms (argued in the part of the book that treated the realms, and again in the part of the book
that gave the arguments). The argument is given in the next section. The principle’s status is
therefore the status of its premises; a reader who accepts the two premises should accept the
principle, and a reader who rejects one of them has a reason to reject the principle.
      The principle has two components, which the reader should keep distinct.



First component: function is not dependence. A realm can have a mediating function
and still be independently real. The two are not the same, and the first does not entail the
negation of the second. The function is what the realm does; the independence is what the realm
is.



Second component: function is part of the mode of existence. The mediating function
of a barzakhic realm is a feature of its mode of existence, not an alternative to it. The hub is
what it is partly because it does what it does; the mode of existence includes the function, not
as an accident, but as an essential feature.
      The two components together yield the resolution. The barzakhic realms are relational in
their function and ordered in their mode of existence, and the two are compatible because the
function is part of the mode of existence.
32.7. The Argument                                                                              341


   Remark 32.6 (The Principle Is Category-Relative Predication Applied)

   The principle is an application of the principle of category-relative predication, established
   in the chapter that opened the resolution of tensions. The principle says that the predicate
   “relational” is said of the hub in one respect (its function), and the predicate “ordered” is
   said of the hub in another respect (its mode of existence). The two predicates are not said
   of the same respect, and the distinction of respects is what removes the apparent conflict.
   The reader who has understood the principle of category-relative predication will find the
   present principle a particular case of it; the reader who has not is directed to the chapter
   that establishes it.
   The principle, too, points beyond itself. The principle is the structure of the resolution;
   it is not the ground of the hub. The principle points beyond itself to what makes the
   function possible, and to what makes the mode of existence possible. The framework does
   not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that
   the principle is a real structural principle, and that the principle points beyond itself. The
   distinction is the distinction between the principle and the ground of the hub; it is kept
   throughout the book.



32.7      The Argument
The argument for the resolution proceeds in four steps.

Resolution of the Apparent Conflict.      1. In the structural analysis, a barzakhic realm is de-
      scribed by the relations it regulates among other realms: it is what it does for them.

   2. In the existential analysis, it is described by what it is and what can be realized or occur
      in it: a level with its own rules and structural possibilities.

   3. The two descriptions concern different questions about one realm, and neither excludes the
      other.

   4. Hence the barzakhic realms are both mediating and independent.



   The argument’s force is in step (3). If the two descriptions concerned the same question,
they could not both be true, and the conflict would be real. The framework’s account of the
barzakhic realms is what blocks this: the two descriptions concern different questions, and their
answers are compatible. The first answers “what does the realm do?”; the second answers “what
is the realm?” The two are distinct, and the distinction is what makes the resolution possible.
   Step (1) states the structural analysis: the hub is described by the relations it regulates. Step
(2) states the existential analysis: the hub is described by what it is and what can be realized in
it. Step (3) draws the distinction between the two analyses. Step (4) states the conclusion: the
two are compatible because they answer different questions.
342                                                            Chapter 32. Relation and Order


   Remark 32.7 (The Two Analyses)

   The structural analysis describes the architecture: the realms and what relations they bear.
   The existential analysis describes what can be realized in the realms and what structural
   possibilities they admit. They are not independent of one another, and neither reduces
   to the other. Neither analysis makes a normative or ethical claim; both are descriptions
   of structure. The reader who reads the two analyses as two different realms has misread
   them; the reader who reads them as two ways of describing one realm has read them
   correctly.
   The two analyses, too, point beyond themselves. The analyses are the descriptions of the
   realm; they are not the ground of the realm. The two analyses point beyond themselves
   to what makes the architecture possible, and to what makes the realization possible. The
   framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal.
   It claims that the two analyses are real structural analyses, and that the analyses point
   beyond themselves. The distinction is the distinction between the analyses and the ground
   of the realm; it is kept throughout the book.


   Remark 32.8 (The Argument Is Relative to Its Premises)

   The argument depends on the distinction between the two analyses (stated in the present
   chapter) and on the principle of the independence of the barzakhic realms (argued in the
   part of the book that treated the realms, and again in the part of the book that gave the
   arguments). A reader who denies either premise has a reason to reject the resolution, and
   the framework does not pretend otherwise. The argument’s value is not that it proves the
   resolution without assumptions; it is that it makes the assumptions visible, and shows
   exactly what follows from them.
   The premises, too, point beyond themselves. The premises are the structural conditions of
   the resolution; they are not the ground of the hub. The premises point beyond themselves
   to what makes the function possible, and to what makes the mode of existence possible.
   The framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is
   unreal. It claims that the premises are real structural premises, and that the premises
   point beyond themselves. The distinction is the distinction between the premises and the
   ground of the hub; it is kept throughout the book.



32.8       Scope and Vulnerability

The resolution is valid for the respects named, and the scope must be stated with precision.
      The resolution says that the barzakhic realms are relational in their function and ordered
in their mode of existence, and that the two are compatible because the function is part of the
mode of existence. It does not say that every realm has a mediating function, or that every level
of being is a barzakhic realm. It says that, for the barzakhic realms, the two descriptions are
compatible.
      The resolution rests on the distinction between function and mode of existence (stated in
32.8. Scope and Vulnerability                                                                 343


the present chapter), and on the independence of the barzakhic realms ((A), established in the
part of the book that treated the realms, and argued again in the part of the book that gave the
arguments). The resolution’s force is no greater than the force of these commitments; a reader
who rejects either of them has a reason to reject the resolution, and the framework does not
pretend otherwise.
   The resolution is not relativism. The function and the mode of existence are fixed by the
structure of the barzakhic realms, not by the observer’s choice. The framework’s claim is that the
realms have the structure the framework describes, and that the two predicates are appropriate
to the structure. A reader who reads the resolution as a form of relativism has misread it; a
reader who reads it as a structural claim has read it correctly.
   The resolution would be put in question by two things.



First challenge. A case in which whatever has a mediating function is by that fact dependent
for its existence on what it mediates between. If such a case could be given, the function would
entail the dependence, and the independence of the barzakhic realms would fail. The framework
does not claim that no such case can be constructed; it claims that none has been constructed
that survives the distinction between function and mode of existence, and it argues that none
can be.



Second challenge. A case in which the rules of a barzakhic realm are derivable from the rules
of its neighbors, so that the hub is reducible to a function of the fundamental realms. If such a
case could be given, the order of the hub would collapse into the order of its neighbors, and the
hub would no longer be a level. The framework holds that the rules are not so derivable, and it
states the resolution at exactly the strength its arguments support.


   Remark 32.9 (The Resolution Is Not a Ranking)

   The resolution does not rank the two descriptions. It does not say that the structural
   analysis is more important than the existential analysis, or vice versa. It says that the
   two are distinct, and that the distinctness resolves the apparent conflict. A reader who
   looks for a ranking will not find one; a reader who accepts the distinctness will find the
   resolution clear. The framework’s claim is structural, not evaluative.
   The absence of ranking, too, points beyond itself. The absence of ranking is the structural
   consequence of the distinctness of the two descriptions; it is not the ground of the hub.
   The absence of ranking points beyond itself to what makes the two descriptions possible,
   and to what makes their relation possible. The framework does not describe the ground,
   and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the absence of ranking is
   real, and that the absence points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between
   the absence of ranking and the ground of the hub; it is kept throughout the book.
344                                                              Chapter 32. Relation and Order


   Remark 32.10 (The Resolution Is Not a Reduction of Order to Relation)

   The resolution does not reduce order to relation. It does not say that the barzakhic realms
   are really just relations, and that their being levels is an appearance. It says that the two
   are compatible because the function is part of the mode of existence. The order of the
   hub is real; the relation of the hub is real; the two are aspects of one realm. A reader who
   reads the resolution as a reduction of order to relation has misread it; a reader who reads
   it as a distinction of aspects has read it correctly.
   The non-reduction, too, points beyond itself. The non-reduction is the structural fact that
   order and relation are distinct aspects of one realm; it is not the ground of the realm.
   The non-reduction points beyond itself to what makes the order possible, and to what
   makes the relation possible. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does
   not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the non-reduction is real, and that
   the non-reduction points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the
   non-reduction and the ground of the hub; it is kept throughout the book.



32.9       Consequences
The resolution has three consequences. They are stated here, with their status.


First consequence: the reality of the barzakhic realms. The barzakhic realms are real
as levels, and they are real as mediators. The two realities are not in competition; they are two
aspects of one reality. The first names what the hub is; the second names what the hub does.
Both are real; neither is an appearance of the other. ((T))


Second consequence: the structural possibility of realization in the barzakhic realms.
It follows from the independence of the barzakhic realms that identities can be realized in them,
and that structural relations can obtain among those realizations, as in other realms. This is a
consequence of the principle, and it has its status. Which identities, if any, are realized in them,
and through what structural relations, is not argued here and remains an open philosophical
question. The consequence is a structural claim about realization, not a claim about conscious
subjects, agents, or purposes; no normative or ethical consequence follows from it. ((S))


Third consequence: the unity of the framework. The structural analysis and the
existential analysis are complementary. The first describes the architecture of the realms; the
second describes what can be realized in them. Neither reduces to the other, and neither is
complete without the other. The unity of the framework is the unity of the two analyses, not the
reduction of one to the other. ((T))
      The three consequences are not separate. They are three aspects of one structural fact: the
barzakhic realms are both mediating and independently real. The first names the reality; the
second names the realizability; the third names the unity of the two analyses. Together, they
state what the resolution of the apparent conflict amounts to.
32.10. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                    345


   Remark 32.11 (The Consequences Are Structural, Not Evaluative)

   The three consequences are structural, not evaluative. The framework does not claim
   that the barzakhic realms are more valuable as levels than as mediators, or vice versa. It
   claims that the three are structural features of the relation between function and mode of
   existence in the barzakhic realms, and that the framework’s account of realization, of the
   unity of the two analyses, and of the completeness of the seven realms is built on them. A
   reader who reads the consequences as evaluations has misread them; a reader who reads
   them as structural facts has read them correctly.
   The consequences point beyond themselves. The consequences are the structural features
   of the relation between function and mode of existence; they are not the ground of the
   hub. The consequences point beyond themselves to what makes the reality possible, to
   what makes the realizability possible, and to what makes the unity of the two analyses
   possible. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the
   ground is unreal. It claims that the consequences are real structural consequences, and
   that the consequences point beyond themselves. The distinction is the distinction between
   the consequences and the ground of the hub; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the hub as the one who is the source of every level
   and every relation, and as the one in whose knowledge the level and the relation are
   what they are. The framework does not claim that its consequences are that one, and it
   does not claim that the one is unreal. It claims that the consequences are real structural
   consequences, and that the consequences point beyond themselves.



32.10      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
   First, the chapter does not settle the question of which identities, if any, are realized in the
barzakhic realms. The consequence that realization in them is structurally possible is stated,
but the particular identities and relations are not argued for here. The question is marked as an
open philosophical question, and its development is left for later parts of the book.
   Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of the relation between the two analyses.
The structural analysis and the existential analysis are distinguished, and their compatibility is
argued, but the detailed account of how they interact—how the architecture of a realm conditions
what can be realized in it, and how what is realized in a realm conditions the architecture of the
realms that relate to it—is deferred to the parts of the book that treat the system as a whole.
   Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the distinction between function
and mode of existence applies to realms other than the barzakhic ones. The distinction is stated
for the barzakhic realms, and its application to the fundamental realms is not argued here. The
framework’s claim is that the distinction is structural for the barzakhic realms, not that it is
universal across all realms.
   Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of the relation between
function and mode of existence. It claims to have described the structure of the relation, and
the structure points beyond itself to the ground that the framework does not describe. The
346                                                                   Chapter 32. Relation and Order


distinction is the distinction between the structure of the relation and the ground of the relation;
it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is stated here as the chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing whose function is to relate—a translator, a bridge, a diplomat, a ritual. Is the
thing nothing but its function, or is it something more? If it is something more, what is the
relation between what it is and what it does? What does your answer tell you about the relation
between relation and order?

framework makes of them.

Derivative Concepts

Chapter 33

Time and Eternity


Scope. This chapter opens the part of the book that develops the derivative concepts—the
concepts that follow from the principles established in the preceding parts. It defines time as
realm-relative succession; distinguishes timelessness from eternity and from temporal persistence;
argues that the expression of an identity is never completed; and states the three properties of
time. Its claims are structural; where the chapter is silent on questions of theology or value,
the silence is not a denial but a recognition that the structural description is not the whole of
what can be said. Where the chapter speaks of “time,” “succession,” “eternity,” “timelessness,”
“beginninglessness,” “endlessness,” or “expression,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed
by the definitions in this chapter. The words “eternity,” “beginninglessness,” and “endlessness”
have histories in theology and in classical metaphysics; those histories do not enter the definitions.
The traditional name “Eternal Creation” is retained only as a historical label for a structural
claim, not as a theological doctrine.



33.1      A Scene

Consider an hour. It is not the same as another hour. An hour spent waiting for a delayed train,
with nothing to do and no one to talk to, is not the same as an hour spent in conversation with
a friend, or an hour of deep sleep, or an hour in which a difficult problem is finally solved. The
clock measures the same sixty minutes in each case; the experience of the hour is not the same.
If we said that each hour had the same duration, we would be speaking of the clock’s measure; if
we said that each hour had a different duration, we would be speaking of the hour as it is lived.
    The two statements are both true, and they are not the same statement. The clock measures
the succession of stages by which changes are realized; the experience measures the density of
what is realized in each stage. The two are different measures of the same temporal span, and
the difference is not a defect in either. It is a structural feature of the relation between time and
what is realized in time.
    Now consider a longer span. A mountain exists for millions of years; a mayfly for a day. The
mountain’s changes are imperceptible across a human lifetime; the mayfly’s entire life is lived in
a single afternoon. If we said that the mountain and the mayfly had the same duration, we would
be speaking of duration in some absolute sense; if we said that they had different durations, we
would be speaking of duration in the sense of what is realized in each. The two statements are
both true, and they are not the same statement. The mountain’s duration is long in the sense
of the succession of stages; the mayfly’s duration is short in the same sense. But the density
of what is realized in each may be different: the mountain’s changes are slow and massive; the
mayfly’s changes are fast and various.

                                                350
33.2. The Question                                                                             351


   The scene poses a question. What is time, such that it can be measured in two ways—by the
clock’s succession and by the density of what is realized? And what is the relation between time
and the realms in which things are realized? The present chapter answers these questions. Its
answer is a structural account of time, and its principal contribution is the distinction among
three concepts that are easily confused: timelessness, eternity, and temporal persistence.

   Remark 33.1 (The Hour Points Beyond Itself)

   The clock and the experience measure two different aspects of the same temporal span;
   the framework’s claim is that both measures are real, and that the difference between
   them is a structural feature of the relation between time and what is realized in time. But
   the two measures are not self-grounded. The measures are the measures of the temporal
   span; they are not the ground of time. The measures point beyond themselves to what
   makes time possible, and to what makes the realization possible. The framework’s claim
   is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework.
   The distinction is the distinction between the measures and the ground of time; it is kept
   throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of time as the one for whom a day is like a thousand
   years of what is counted, and as the one who is not measured by succession. The Quranic
   verse that the traditions cite in this connection is the verse of the measure of the day:
   “And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count” (Qur’an
   22:47). The framework’s structural reading is that the density of what is realized in a
   temporal span is not the same as the succession of the span; the verse is cited as structural
   evidence, not as a ground of justification. The framework does not claim that its structural
   measure is the measure of the day with the Lord, and it does not claim that the measure
   is unreal. It claims that the measure is a real structural feature, and that the feature
   points beyond itself.



33.2     The Question

The preceding parts of the book have established the framework’s principal structures. The
part that treated the foundation established the four-column framework. The part that treated
the realms established the seven realms. The part that treated the fixed elements established
identity and manifestation. The part that treated the fluid element established light. The part
that treated the governing dynamics established the twenty-two rules of the seven realms. The
part that gave the arguments established the arguments for the framework’s principles. The part
that resolved the apparent tensions showed that the principles are compatible with one another.
   The present part turns to the derivative concepts. These are the concepts that follow from
the framework’s principles—concepts that the framework does not introduce as primitives, but
derives from what it has already established. The first of these is time.
   The question is: what is time? The framework has spoken of time throughout the preceding
parts—in the definition of the Material Manifestation, in the distinction between the temporal
and the atemporal, in the account of succession in the higher realms. But it has not yet given a
352                                                                 Chapter 33. Time and Eternity


definition of time, and it has not yet distinguished the concepts that are easily confused with it.
      Two aspects of the question must be distinguished.


The definitional aspect. What is time, exactly? The chapter defines time as realm-relative
succession, and it argues that the definition does not presuppose what it defines.


The structural aspect. How does time relate to the realms? The chapter argues that time
is not of one kind in all realms, and that the difference among kinds of time follows from the
difference among realms.
      The chapter proceeds as follows. It defines time. It states the principle of time, and the table
of the realms’ relation to time. It defines the density of time. It states the three properties of
time. It defines beginninglessness and endlessness. It states the principle of the non-completion
of expression. It distinguishes timelessness from eternity and from temporal persistence. It closes
with what it does not establish and with the epistemic status of its claims.


33.3        The Nature of Time
The framework defines time through succession, change, and realization, and it then uses the
journey of light to explain why succession differs from realm to realm. The order of the definition
is deliberate: a rate is a measure relative to succession, and a definition of time through a rate
would presuppose what it defines. The definition proceeds from the more basic concepts to the
more derived.

   Definition 33.1 (Time)

   Time in a realm is the order of succession of the stages by which changes are realized
   there. A realm has time to the extent that such succession is possible in it.

      The definition does not presuppose what it defines. It defines time through succession, change,
and realization—concepts that are not themselves temporal in the way time is. Succession is
the order in which stages follow one another; change is the difference between one stage and the
next; realization is the occurrence of a change in a realm. The three concepts are structural, not
temporal, and the definition uses them to define time.
      The definition’s content is precise. Time is not a container in which things happen; it is the
order of the stages by which they happen. A realm has time to the extent that stages can follow
one another in it. A realm in which no stages can follow one another has no time; a realm in
which stages can follow one another has time, and the kind of time it has is fixed by the kind of
succession that is possible in it.

   Remark 33.2 (Time Points Beyond Itself)

   Time is the order of succession of the stages by which changes are realized; the framework’s
   claim is that time is real, and that time is realm-relative, and that the kind of time in a
   realm is fixed by the kind of succession that is possible in it. But time is not self-grounded.
33.4. The Principle of Time                                                                     353


   Time is the order of the stages; it is not the ground of the stages. Time points beyond
   itself to what makes succession possible, and to what makes realization possible. The
   framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described
   by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between time and the ground of time;
   it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of time as the one who is the originator of time, and as
   the one who is not subject to the succession that time measures. The framework does not
   claim that its structural time is that originator, and it does not claim that the originator
   is unreal. It claims that time is a real structural order, and that the order points beyond
   itself. The reader who identifies the structural time with the originator is free to do so;
   the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the
   identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.

   Remark 33.3 (Rate Without Presupposing Time)

   A rate of one succession is its ratio to another succession taken as reference: how many
   stages of the first occur per stage of the second. It is therefore relative, and does not
   presuppose an independent time. The rate of light’s journey between two manifestations
   is the ratio of the stages of that journey to the stages of a reference succession in the same
   realm. The rate is a structural fact about the two successions, not a fact about time as an
   independent quantity.
   The rate, too, points beyond itself. The rate is the ratio of two successions; it is not the
   ground of the successions. The rate points beyond itself to what makes the successions
   possible, and to what makes their ratio possible. The framework does not describe the
   ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the rate is a real
   structural fact, and that the rate points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction
   between the rate and the ground of the successions; it is kept throughout the book.



33.4     The Principle of Time
The definition of time raises four questions, and the principle answers them in turn.

   Principle 33.1 (Time Is Realm-Relative Succession)

   (E) Succession is not of one kind in all realms. Its kind is fixed by what is successive in
   the realm and by how the effect of light passes there. The journey of light is the concept
   by which the difference of kinds of succession is explained.

   The principle is (E): it is a structural estimate, not a derivation from the definition of time.
The estimate would be revised if a different account of the relation between the realms and their
kinds of succession did the same explanatory work.
   The table states the kind of time, if any, in each of the seven realms.

   Remark 33.4 (The Journey of Light as an Image)

   The journey of light from one manifestation to another is an image of how effect passes
   from one manifestation to another. It explains, and does not define. The image is not an
   argument; it is a way of seeing what the principle states. The reader who finds the image
   helpful will find the principle clearer; the reader who does not will find the principle still
   standing on its own.
   The image, too, points beyond itself. The image is the image of the journey; it is not
   the ground of the journey. The image points beyond itself to what makes the journey
   possible, and to what makes the effect pass possible. The framework does not describe
   the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the image is
   a real structural image, and that the image points beyond itself. The distinction is the
   distinction between the image and the ground of the journey; it is kept throughout the
   book.

   Remark 33.5 (The Table Is Not a Ranking)

   The table is not a ranking of the realms by their proximity to time. It is a description
   of the kind of succession, if any, that is possible in each realm. The First Determination
   has no succession; the Material Manifestation has the most articulated succession. The
   difference is structural, not evaluative. The realm with no succession is not less real than
   the realm with the most succession; it is a realm of a different kind, with a different mode
   of existence.
   The table, too, points beyond itself. The table is the description of the kinds of succession;
   it is not the ground of the realms. The table points beyond itself to what makes each
   realm what it is, and to what makes its kind of succession what it is. The framework does
33.5. The Density of Time                                                                       355


   not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that
   the table is a real structural table, and that the table points beyond itself. The distinction
   is the distinction between the table and the ground of the realms; it is kept throughout
   the book.

   Remark 33.6 (The Realms of Time Point Beyond Themselves)

   Each realm has its own kind of succession; the framework’s claim is that the kind of
   succession is fixed by the realm’s mode of existence, and that the difference among the
   kinds of succession follows from the difference among the realms. But the realms of time
   are not self-grounded. The realms are the realms of succession; they are not the ground of
   the succession. The realms of time point beyond themselves to what makes each realm
   what it is, and to what makes its kind of succession what it is. The framework’s claim is
   that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework.
   The distinction is the distinction between the realms of time and the ground of the realms;
   it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the realms as the one who determines the measure
   of each thing, and as the one in whose knowledge the times of things are what they are.
   The framework does not claim that its realms of time are that one, and it does not claim
   that the one is unreal. It claims that the realms of time are real structural realms, and
   that the realms point beyond themselves. The reader who identifies the realms with the
   one is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework
   takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



33.5     The Density of Time
The definition of time raises a further question. The same succession can be more or less dense;
the same span can be filled with more or less of what is realized. The framework distinguishes
this aspect of time in a definition.

   Definition 33.2 (Time Density)

   The density of time in a realm is the degree of presence of what is realized there per stage
   of succession.

   The definition states a measure, not a substance. The density is the degree of presence per
stage, not a quantity of time in itself. The same succession can be more or less dense; the same
span can have more or less of what is realized. The density is a structural feature of the relation
between time and what is realized in time.

   Remark 33.7 (The Claim)

   (E) In realms of greater unity, succession is less pronounced and presence greater. “Denser”
   therefore means “more presence per succession.” How this is to be made exact is an open
356                                                               Chapter 33. Time and Eternity


   philosophical question ((Q)): the framework fixes the concept, and does not give a formula.
   The claim is an estimate, and it would be revised if a different account of the relation
   between density and unity did the same explanatory work.
   The claim, too, points beyond itself. The claim is the claim about the density of time; it
   is not the ground of the density. The claim points beyond itself to what makes the density
   possible, and to what makes the presence possible. The framework does not describe the
   ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the claim is a real
   structural claim, and that the claim points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction
   between the claim and the ground of the density; it is kept throughout the book.



33.6       The Three Properties of Time
The three essential properties of light, established in the part of the book that treated the fluid
element, have three temporal aspects.

Descending time. The succession of generating manifestations. The aspect of time that
corresponds to light’s descent from identity to manifestation.

Ascending time. The succession of returns. The aspect of time that corresponds to light’s
return from manifestation to identity.

Reflective time. The succession by which manifestations connect. The aspect of time that
corresponds to light’s reflection among manifestations.
      The three are aspects of one temporal process, not three times. The process is the process of
expression; the three aspects are the three directions in which the process runs. The framework’s
claim is that time, like light, has the three directions; the three are not three kinds of time, but
three directions of one time.

   Remark 33.8 (The Three Properties Are Not Three Times)

   The reader who reads the three temporal aspects as three separate times has misread the
   framework’s account. The three are aspects of one process, distinguished by what they
   connect: descending time connects identity and manifestation; ascending time connects
   manifestation and identity; reflective time connects manifestation and manifestation. The
   process is one; the aspects are three; the directions are three. The unity of the process is
   what makes the three aspects aspects of one time.


   Remark 33.9 (The Three Properties Point Beyond Themselves)

   The three temporal aspects—descending, ascending, reflective—are real structural aspects
   of one temporal process; the framework’s claim is that time, like light, has the three
   directions, and that the three are directions of one time. But the three aspects are not
   self-grounded. The aspects are the aspects of the process; they are not the ground of the
33.7. Beginninglessness and Endlessness                                                         357


   process. The three aspects point beyond themselves to what makes the process possible,
   and to what makes the three directions possible. The framework’s claim is that the
   pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The
   distinction is the distinction between the aspects and the ground of the process; it is kept
   throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the process as the one who is every day in a matter,
   and as the one whose affair is not bounded by the succession of the days. The Quranic
   verse that the traditions cite in this connection is the verse of the daily affair: “Every day
   He is in a matter” (Qur’an 55:29). The framework’s structural reading is that the process
   of expression is never completed, and that the process has three directions; the verse is
   cited as structural evidence, not as a ground of justification. The framework does not
   claim that its three aspects are the daily affair of the one, and it does not claim that the
   affair is unreal. It claims that the three aspects are real structural aspects, and that the
   aspects point beyond themselves.



33.7     Beginninglessness and Endlessness

Two further definitions are needed to state the principle that follows.

   Definition 33.3 (Beginninglessness)

   Beginninglessness is the structural property of having no first stage of succession.


   Definition 33.4 (Endlessness)

   Endlessness is the structural property of having no last stage of succession.


   Remark 33.10 (Structural Use of the Terms)

   The terms “beginninglessness” and “endlessness” are structural labels in this book. They
   name the absence of a first and a last stage of succession. They do not name a divine
   attribute, a theological doctrine of the world’s eternity, or a metaphysical property of a
   creator. In the First Determination there is no succession, so beginning and end cannot
   be told apart there; the two properties are distinguished only where succession arises. The
   framework uses the two terms only to make this structural distinction, and attaches no
   theological or evaluative content to either.
   The terms, too, point beyond themselves. The terms name the structural properties of
   succession; they do not name the ground of succession. The terms point beyond themselves
   to what makes succession possible, and to what makes the absence of a first and last stage
   possible. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the
   ground is unreal. It claims that the terms are real structural terms, and that the terms
   point beyond themselves. The distinction is the distinction between the terms and the
   ground of succession; it is kept throughout the book.

33.8       The Non-Completion of Expression
The distinction between beginninglessness and endlessness bears on a principle about expression,
which the framework states as a consequence of the principle of expression established in the
part of the book that gave the arguments.

   Principle 33.2 (The Non-Completion of Expression)

   (T) Expression is never completed: no stage of manifestation exhausts the identity and
   ends the tendency to express. (The traditional name for this claim is “Eternal Creation”;
   the framework uses the structural name.)


Argument for the Principle.       1. Every identity tends to express itself, necessarily (the principle
        of expression, established in the part of the book that gave the arguments).

  2. Every manifestation is partial: none exhausts the identity (the definition of manifestation,
        established in the part of the book that treated the fixed elements).

  3. An identity not exhausted by any manifestation still has the tendency to express after each
        one.

  4. Hence there is no stage at which expression is complete. Expression does not come to an
        end.


      The argument uses the necessity of the tendency and the partiality of manifestation; it does
not use the claim that the identity is infinite. Its force is that the tendency, being structural, is
not exhausted by any manifestation, and that no manifestation, being partial, can exhaust it.
      One may picture the outcome as an imbalance between descending and ascending light:
descending effect is never fully returned in a manifestation. The picture illustrates; the argument
is the one above. A more detailed claim, that expression has a structural dynamic and a structure
of its own, is a commitment and is not argued here.

   Remark 33.11 (The Non-Completion Points Beyond Itself)

   The non-completion of expression is a real structural feature; the framework’s claim is
   that no stage of manifestation exhausts the identity, and that expression does not come
   to an end. But the non-completion is not self-grounded. The non-completion is the non-
   completion of the expression; it is not the ground of the expression. The non-completion
   points beyond itself to what makes the tendency possible, and to what makes the expression
   possible. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed
   to is not described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the
   non-completion and the ground of the expression; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the non-completion as the one who is every day in
   a matter, and as the one whose affair is never exhausted. The Quranic verse that the
   traditions cite in this connection is the verse of the daily affair: “Every day He is in a
33.9. Timelessness, Eternity, and Temporal Persistence                                          359


   matter” (Qur’an 55:29). The framework’s structural reading is that the expression of an
   identity is never completed, and that the non-completion is a structural feature of the
   tendency; the verse is cited as structural evidence, not as a ground of justification. The
   framework does not claim that its structural non-completion is the daily affair of the one,
   and it does not claim that the affair is unreal. It claims that the non-completion is a real
   structural feature, and that the feature points beyond itself.


   Remark 33.12 (The Word “Creation” as a Structural Label)

   The word “creation” is a structural label for the never-completed expression of an identity.
   The traditional name “Eternal Creation” is retained as a historical label for the structural
   claim that expression is never completed; it is not the theological doctrine of divine
   creation. The framework uses the structural name and marks the traditional name as a
   historical label; the two are not the same, and the reader who reads the traditional name
   as a theological doctrine has misread the framework’s use of it.
   The structural label, too, points beyond itself. The label names the structural feature; it
   does not name the ground of the feature. The label points beyond itself to what makes the
   expression possible, and to what makes the non-completion possible. The framework does
   not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that
   the label is a real structural label, and that the label points beyond itself. The distinction
   is the distinction between the label and the ground of the expression; it is kept throughout
   the book.



33.9      Timelessness, Eternity, and Temporal Persistence
The definition of time and the principle of non-completion together require a distinction among
three concepts that are easily confused.

   Definition 33.5 (Three Concepts)

       1. Timelessness: having no succession at all.

       2. Eternity: being without beginning and end in a way not bounded by succession. (A
         structural concept; not a theological attribute.)

       3. Temporal persistence: lasting through succession.

   The three concepts are distinct, and the framework’s account of the realms depends on
distinguishing them.

   Remark 33.13 (They Are Not One)

   The First Determination is timeless and eternal. The Structural Determination is eternal
   without being merely timeless: its laws have no beginning or end, yet there is an order of
   entailment among them, a before and after of implication and not of time. Material things
360                                                              Chapter 33. Time and Eternity


  have temporal persistence. To call something eternal is therefore not to say that it is
  timeless; to call something timeless is not to say that it lasts through time. All three terms
  are structural; none names a divine attribute, a theological doctrine, or an evaluative
  property.
  The distinction is important because the framework’s account of the seven realms depends
  on it. The First Determination is what it is because it is timeless; the Structural
  Determination is what it is because it is eternal without being timeless; the Material
  Manifestation is what it is because its things are temporally persistent. To confuse the
  three is to lose the distinctions that make the seven realms distinct.


  Remark 33.14 (Eternity Is Not the Same as Timelessness)

  The word “eternity” is often used, in ordinary language, as if it meant “timelessness”—as if
  an eternal thing were a thing outside time altogether. The framework’s use of the word is
  different: eternity is being without beginning and end in a way not bounded by succession.
  A thing can be eternal in this sense and still have an order of entailment among its stages
  (as the Structural Determination does). The distinction is structural: eternity is not the
  same as timelessness, and the two are distinguished where the realms are distinguished.


  Remark 33.15 (Eternity Points Beyond Itself)

  The three concepts—timelessness, eternity, temporal persistence—are real structural
  concepts; the framework’s claim is that the three are distinct, and that the distinction is
  what makes the seven realms distinct. But the three concepts are not self-grounded. The
  concepts are the concepts of the relation between time and what is realized; they are not
  the ground of the relation. The three concepts point beyond themselves to what makes
  the relation possible, and to what makes the realms possible. The framework’s claim is
  that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework.
  The distinction is the distinction between the concepts and the ground of the relation; it
  is kept throughout the book.
  The traditions speak of the ground of the relation as the one who is the First and the Last,
  the Manifest and the Hidden, and as the one who is not bounded by the succession of the
  days. The Quranic verse that the traditions cite in this connection is the verse of the First
  and the Last: “He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden” (Qur’an 57:3).
  The framework’s structural reading is that the eternity of the higher realms is not the
  timelessness of the First Determination, and that the temporal persistence of the material
  realm is not the eternity of the higher realms; the verse is cited as structural evidence, not
  as a ground of justification. The framework does not claim that its three concepts are the
  names of the one, and it does not claim that the names are unreal. It claims that the three
  concepts are real structural concepts, and that the concepts point beyond themselves.
33.10. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                          361


33.10       What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
    First, the chapter does not argue for the definition of time from principles more basic than it.
The definition is stated as a definition; its justification is its fruitfulness in what follows. A reader
who finds the definition unpersuasive has a reason to propose a different one; the framework
states the definition at exactly the strength it has.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of how the density of time is to be
measured in a given case. The definition of density is stated, and its relation to unity is estimated,
but the operational question of how to measure density in a particular realm is left for later
parts of the book. The present chapter has distinguished density from succession; the later parts
develop its measurement.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the temporal aspects of light’s
three properties exhaust the temporal structure of the realms. The three aspects are the ones
the framework has identified; whether a fourth exists is a question the framework leaves open.
The framework’s claim is that the three are structurally distinct and that they correspond to the
three properties of light, not that no further aspect could be found.
    Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of time. It claims to have
described the structure of time, and the structure points beyond itself to the ground that the
framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of time
and the ground of time; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is stated here as the chapter’s
explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection

Consider a span of time you have lived through—an hour, a year, a decade. Was the span more
or less dense at some points than at others? What filled the dense parts, and what left the sparse
parts empty? What does your answer tell you about the relation between the clock’s succession
and the density of what is realized?

The next chapter turns to death and birth. It defines death as the zeroing of the manifestation
functions of an identity in a realm—not as the destruction of the identity—and it defines birth as
the emergence in the Material Manifestation of a group of manifestations connected to a single
identity. The present chapter has defined time and distinguished the three concepts that are
easily confused with it; the next chapter applies the distinction to the beginning and the ending of
manifestation in a realm.

Death and Birth


Scope. This chapter defines death and birth as structural conditions of an identity’s manifestation
in a realm, and it states the balance criterion as a structural measure of the relation between
an identity and the light it receives. Its claims are structural; where the chapter is silent on
questions of value or religion, the silence is not a denial but a recognition that the structural
description is not the whole of what can be said. Where the chapter speaks of “death,” “birth,”
“balance,” “viability,” “return,” or “veil,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the
definitions in this chapter and in the parts of the book that treated the fixed elements, the
fluid element, and the resolution of tensions. Each names a structural relation, and the chapter
attaches no evaluation to what it describes.


34.1        A Scene
Consider a song that is not being sung. The score is on the shelf; the performers are at home;
the hall is dark. No sound is being produced; no voice is raised; the song, as a heard thing, is
absent. And yet the song is not gone. It can be sung tomorrow; it can be sung a hundred years
from now; it can be sung by someone who has never heard it, from the score alone. The song’s
manifestations in sound have ceased; the song has not.
    Now consider the same song being sung. The first note is sounded; the performance begins.
Something that was not there a moment ago is now there: a group of sounds, connected to the
song, appearing in time. The sounds are new; the song is not. The song was there before the
performance; it will be there after; the performance is the song’s appearance in sound, not its
creation.
    The scene is one instance of a structural relation. Whenever an identity ceases to be manifested
in a realm, its manifestations in that realm go to zero; the identity itself does not go to zero.
Whenever an identity begins to be manifested in a realm, a group of manifestations appears;
the identity does not appear, because it was already there. The ending and the beginning are
structural conditions of manifestation, not of identity. And the two are not the same as the
ending and the beginning of the identity itself.
    The scene poses a question. What is it for a manifestation to cease? Is the ceasing the
destruction of the identity, or is it a structural condition of the identity’s expression? And what
is it for a manifestation to begin? Is the beginning the creation of the identity, or is it the
appearance of an identity that was already there? The present chapter answers these questions.
Its answer is the framework’s account of death and birth, and its principal contribution is the
distinction among four kinds of death and the definition of the balance criterion as a structural
measure of the relation between an identity and the light it receives.
