364                                                                 Chapter 34. Death and Birth


   Remark 34.1 (The Song Points Beyond Itself)

   The song is the same song across the pause and the beginning of its performance; the
   framework’s claim is that the identity is conserved across the changes of its manifestations,
   and that the manifestation is a product, not the identity. But the conservation is not
   self-grounded. The conservation is the conservation of an identity; it is not the ground of
   the identity. The conservation points beyond itself to what holds the identity in being
   through the pause and through the performance, and to what makes the manifestation
   possible. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed
   to is not described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the
   conservation and the ground of the conservation; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the conservation as the one who preserves what is,
   and as the one whose face remains when every thing upon the earth passes. The Quranic
   verse that the traditions cite in this connection is the verse of the passing of all things:
   “Every one upon it will pass away, and there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner
   of Majesty and Honor” (Qur’an 55:26–27). The framework’s structural reading is that
   the identity is conserved while the manifestations pass; the verse is cited as structural
   evidence, not as a ground of justification. The framework does not claim that its structural
   conservation is the face of the one, and it does not claim that the face is unreal. It claims
   that the conservation is a real structural feature, and that the feature points beyond itself.



34.2       The Question
The preceding chapters of this part have established the framework’s account of time and the
concepts that are easily confused with it. The distinction among timelessness, eternity, and
temporal persistence was drawn (the previous chapter); the principle of the non-completion of
expression was argued; and the structural account of time as realm-relative succession was stated.
      The present chapter turns to death and birth. The two concepts are structural consequences
of the framework’s account of manifestation. The previous chapters have established that an
identity is manifested in a realm when it appears according to the realm’s capacity, aptitude,
and constraints; they have established that the manifestation is not the identity, and that the
identity is conserved across the changes of its manifestations; and they have established that
expression is never completed. The present chapter asks what happens when manifestation in a
realm ceases, and what happens when manifestation in a realm begins.
      The question is not idle. In ordinary language, death is spoken of as the end of a life, the
end of a thing, the destruction of what was. If the framework’s account of identity conservation
is correct, death cannot be the destruction of the identity; it must be something else. The
chapter’s task is to say what that something else is, and to distinguish the kinds of death that
the framework’s ontology makes visible.
      Two aspects of the question must be distinguished.

The structural aspect. What is death, and what is birth? The chapter defines both as
structural conditions of an identity’s manifestation in a realm, and it states the four kinds of
34.3. The Concept of Death                                                                         365


death that the framework’s ontology distinguishes.

The evaluative aspect. Is death a loss? Is birth a gain? The chapter does not answer these
questions, and it explicitly declines to answer them. The questions are normative, and they
belong to an independent inquiry; the framework states the structural relations, and it leaves the
evaluation to the reader.
   The chapter proceeds as follows. It defines death. It states the singularity of ontological
death. It distinguishes four kinds of death. It defines returning light. It defines birth. It defines
the veil. It states the balance criterion. It applies the criterion to a specific case, and states what
the application does and does not show. It closes with what it does not establish and with the
epistemic status of its claims.


34.3         The Concept of Death
The chapter’s first task is to define death. The definition is structural, and it is stated as a
principle.

   Principle 34.1 (Death as the Zeroing of Manifestation Functions)

   (A) Death, in a realm, is the zeroing of the output of an identity’s manifestation functions
   in that realm. It is not the destruction of the identity.

   The principle is (A): it is adopted as a commitment of the framework. It is supported by
the framework’s account of identity conservation (the part of the book that treated identity
established that identity is invariant under all temporal transformations of its manifestations),
and by the framework’s account of manifestation (the part of the book that treated the fixed
elements established that manifestation is a product of identity and receiving realm, not the
identity itself). The principle would be refuted by a case in which the zeroing of an identity’s
manifestation functions is also the destruction of the identity; the framework does not claim that
no such case can be described, but it argues that none can be coherently described, given the
distinction between identity and manifestation.
   Three questions follow from the principle, and the chapter answers them in turn.

First question: is death the death of a manifestation or of the identity? It is the
ceasing of manifestation in a realm. The identity is conserved (the part of the book that treated
the fixed elements established the conservation of identity). The death of a manifestation is not
the death of the identity.

Second question: does the end of manifestation in one realm end the possibility of
manifestation in others? Not by itself. The possibility of manifestation in another realm is a
separate matter, governed by that realm’s capacity and the identity’s tendency (the principle of
the non-necessity of downward passage, argued in the part of the book that treated the realms).
An identity can be manifested in one realm and not in another; the ceasing of manifestation in
one realm does not entail the ceasing of manifestation in every realm.
366                                                                 Chapter 34. Death and Birth


Third question: is death in one realm consistent with the identity’s continuing in
another? Yes. This is what conservation, together with the distinction of the persistence of
identity from the continuity of manifestation, requires. The identity is one; its manifestations in
different realms are many; the ceasing of one manifestation does not touch the identity, and does
not touch the manifestations in other realms.
      The ascending light associated with the ceased manifestations ceases; reflective light, which
connects other manifestations, continues. This distinction is developed in the section on returning
light, below.

   Remark 34.2 (The Principle Is Structural, Not Metaphorical)

   The principle’s use of “zeroing” is structural, not metaphorical. The output of an identity’s
   manifestation functions in a realm is a quantity of effect that the identity produces in
   that realm; to say that the output is zeroed is to say that the effect has ceased, not that
   the identity has ceased. The two are different, and the framework keeps them apart.
   The reader who reads “zeroing” as a metaphor for destruction has misread the principle;
   the reader who reads it as a structural description of the cessation of effect has read it
   correctly.


   Remark 34.3 (The Principle Does Not Deny the Reality of Death)

   The principle does not deny that death is real. It denies that death is the destruction of
   the identity. The death of a manifestation is a real event; the ceasing of an effect is a real
   change in the realm; the loss of a manifestation is a real loss in the order of the realm.
   What the principle denies is that the real event is the destruction of the identity. The
   reader who reads the principle as a denial of the reality of death has misread it; the reader
   who reads it as a denial of one interpretation of death (the interpretation that death is
   destruction) has read it correctly.


   Remark 34.4 (Death Points Beyond Itself)

   Death is the zeroing of the output of an identity’s manifestation functions; the framework’s
   claim is that the zeroing is real, and that the identity is not destroyed. But the zeroing is
   not self-grounded. The zeroing is the ceasing of a manifestation; it is not the ground of
   the identity. The zeroing points beyond itself to what holds the identity in being when its
   manifestation has ceased, and to what makes the identity possible. The framework’s claim
   is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework.
   The distinction is the distinction between the zeroing and the ground of the identity; it is
   kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the identity as the one in whose hand is the holding of
   every thing, and as the one who remains when every manifestation passes. The framework
   does not claim that its structural zeroing is that holding, and it does not claim that the
   holding is unreal. It claims that the zeroing is a real structural event, and that the event
   points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the zeroing with the holding is free to do
34.4. The Singularity of Ontological Death                                                      367


   so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no position on
   the identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



34.4     The Singularity of Ontological Death
The principle states that death is the zeroing of manifestation functions. But the zeroing is not
instantaneous; it is the limit of a process. The framework distinguishes the process from the
threshold, and it names the threshold.

   Definition 34.1 (The Singularity of Ontological Death)

   The singularity is the threshold at which the cost of restoring an existing manifestation in
   a realm exceeds the cost of bringing about a new one there. Cost, in the framework’s sense,
   is the demand that an expression makes on the capacity of a realm; the singularity is the
   point at which that demand, for restoration, exceeds the demand for a new manifestation
   of the same identity in the same realm.


   The singularity is a threshold of manifestation, not of identity. The identity is conserved
across the threshold; what is at stake at the threshold is the manifestation, not the identity.

   Remark 34.5 (Not a Line at the Level of Identity)

   Identity admits no degrees (the principle of identity rigidity, established in the part of the
   book that treated identity). At the level of manifestation the approach to the singularity is
   a gradient: output declines and the cost of restoration rises. The singularity is a threshold
   of manifestation, not of identity. The gradient has a limit; the identity does not.


   Remark 34.6 (Status)

   The singularity is (A) as a structural postulate that follows from the economy of expression
   and the definition of death. What the exact comparison of costs would be, for a given case,
   is a conceptual question the framework leaves open ((Q)). The singularity is a structural
   threshold, not a value.


   Remark 34.7 (The Singularity Points Beyond Itself)

   The singularity is the threshold at which the cost of restoring a manifestation exceeds the
   cost of producing a new one; the framework’s claim is that the threshold is real, and that
   the threshold is a threshold of manifestation, not of identity. But the threshold is not
   self-grounded. The threshold is the threshold of the manifestation; it is not the ground of
   the identity. The threshold points beyond itself to what holds the identity in being when
   the manifestation has crossed the threshold, and to what makes the identity possible. The
   framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal.
   It claims that the threshold is a real structural threshold, and that the threshold points
368                                                                 Chapter 34. Death and Birth


   beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the threshold and the ground of
   the identity; it is kept throughout the book.



34.5       Kinds of Death
Death is said of a realm, and so there are as many kinds as there are realms and manifestations
in them. The framework distinguishes four.

First kind: death in the Material Manifestation. The output of material manifestation
functions has gone to zero. The body has ceased its activity; the physical processes that sustained
the manifestation have stopped. The identity is not destroyed; its material manifestation is.

Second kind: death of the vital manifestation. The vital forms of an identity’s material
manifestation have ceased. The body has died, but in addition the vital organization (the
metabolism, the self-regulation, the living structure) has ceased. The distinction from the first
kind is that the first is the ceasing of material activity in general; the second is the ceasing of
the specifically vital form of that activity.

Third kind: loss of the self-model. The pseudo-identity that the subject holds of itself
has ceased to be produced. This is a death in the Relational Manifestation. The subject’s
self-reconstruction is no longer generated; the subject no longer appears to itself as a subject.
The identity is not destroyed; the self-model is.

Fourth kind: death of all manifestation. The manifestation functions of an identity in
every realm have ceased. Even this is not the destruction of the identity. The identity is conserved;
the manifestations in every realm are not.
      The four kinds are not exhaustive in the sense that no other kind could be described; they
are the kinds the framework has identified. They overlap in various ways: one may be dead in
one realm and manifested in another; the loss of the self-model may occur while the material
manifestation continues, or vice versa.

   Remark 34.8 (Overlap)

   They can overlap in various ways. One may be dead in one realm and manifest in another.
   Whether a case is a case of the fourth kind is not usually decidable by observation; the
   framework states the fourth kind as a structural possibility, not as an empirical prediction.


   Remark 34.9 (The Four Kinds Are Not a Hierarchy)

   The four kinds are not ranked by severity or by importance. The first is the ceasing of
   material activity; the fourth is the ceasing of activity in every realm. The difference is
   structural, not evaluative. The framework states the four kinds because the framework’s
   ontology distinguishes the realms; it does not claim that one kind of death is worse than
34.6. Returning Light                                                                              369


   another, or that one is more real than another.


   Remark 34.10 (The Four Kinds Point Beyond Themselves)

   The four kinds of death are four structural aspects of one relation between an identity
   and its manifestations; the framework’s claim is that the four are distinct, and that each
   names a different ceasing. But the four kinds are not self-grounded. The kinds are the
   kinds of ceasing; they are not the ground of the identity. The four kinds point beyond
   themselves to what makes the identity possible, and to what holds the identity in being
   when its manifestations cease. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that
   what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction
   between the kinds and the ground of the identity; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the identity as the one who preserves what is,
   and as the one whose knowledge of the identity is not interrupted by the ceasing of its
   manifestations. The framework does not claim that its four kinds are that preservation,
   and it does not claim that the preservation is unreal. It claims that the four kinds are real
   structural kinds, and that the kinds point beyond themselves. The reader who identifies
   the four kinds with the preservation is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is
   free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a
   question for another inquiry.



34.6     Returning Light
The principle of death states that the ascending light associated with the ceased manifestations
ceases, while reflective light continues. The framework names the continuing light, and its
definition is the subject of the present section.

   Definition 34.2 (Returning Light)

   Returning light is the light that continues after the pause of an expression, and refers back
   to its source through what the identity left in other manifestations.

   The definition states a structure, not a process. The structure is that of a light that continues
after the manifestation has ceased, and that refers back to the source through the traces the
source left in other manifestations. The traces are not the source; they are what the source left
behind. The returning light is the light that carries the effect of the traces back to the source,
without the source being manifested in the realm of the traces.

   Remark 34.11 (A Sketch of the Mechanism)

   (E) An identity’s expression leaves traces in other manifestations (effects, records, relations).
   When other identities take up these traces, reflective light is generated; when they are
   affected, it may become ascending light, which refers to the source. It is a return through
   other manifestations and not a direct return. The sketch is offered as an estimate; its
370                                                                   Chapter 34. Death and Birth


   details are left for the chapters that treat the specific realms and their rules.


   Remark 34.12 (Returning Light Is Not a Metaphor)

   The term “returning light” is not a metaphor for memory, legacy, or influence. It is a
   structural term, defined in the present chapter, and its sense is fixed by the definition. The
   reader who reads the term as a metaphor for the psychological phenomenon of remembering
   has misread it; the reader who reads it as a structural description of a light that continues
   after the pause of an expression has read it correctly. The two may be related—memory
   is a manifestation in which returning light may appear—but they are not the same, and
   the framework keeps them apart.


   Remark 34.13 (Returning Light Points Beyond Itself)

   Returning light is the light that continues after the pause of an expression, and refers back
   to its source through what the identity left in other manifestations; the framework’s claim
   is that the returning light is real, and that the returning light is a structural feature of the
   relation between identity and manifestation. But the returning light is not self-grounded.
   The returning light is the light of the traces; it is not the ground of the identity. The
   returning light points beyond itself to what makes the return possible, and to what holds
   the identity in being when its manifestation has ceased. The framework’s claim is that
   the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The
   distinction is the distinction between the returning light and the ground of the identity; it
   is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the return as the one to whom the ascending light
   returns, and as the one who receives what the traces carry. The framework does not claim
   that its structural returning light is that receiving, and it does not claim that the receiving
   is unreal. It claims that the returning light is a real structural feature, and that the feature
   points beyond itself. The reader who identifies the returning light with the receiving is
   free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them is free to do so; the framework takes no
   position on the identity, because the identity is a question for another inquiry.



34.7        The Concept of Birth
The chapter’s next task is to define birth. The definition is structural, and it is the counterpart
of the definition of death.

   Definition 34.3 (Birth)

   Birth is the emergence in the Material Manifestation of a group of manifestations connected
   to a single identity.


      The definition states a structure. The structure is that of a group of manifestations, appearing
in the Material Manifestation, connected to a single identity. The identity is not created; it is
34.7. The Concept of Birth                                                                      371


manifested in a new group of material appearances. The appearances are new; the identity is
not.
   Three features of the group are distinguished.


First feature: multiplicity. The manifestations are many; the identity is one. The group is
a group because its members are connected to one another through their common source.


Second feature: subjection to the rules of the Material Manifestation. The man-
ifestations are subject to the rules of the realm in which they appear: causality, temporality,
discreteness (the rules of the Material Manifestation, established in the part of the book that
treated the governing dynamics). The birth is a birth in the Material Manifestation, and the
manifestations are subject to the Material Manifestation’s rules.


Third feature: coordination. One manifestation plays the part of a principal channel
between the identity and the others. The coordination is structural; it is what makes the group
a group, not merely an aggregate of unconnected appearances.

   Remark 34.14 (Birth Is Not the Creation of Identity)

   The definition does not say that birth is the creation of an identity. It says that birth is
   the emergence of a group of manifestations connected to a single identity. The identity
   is conserved across the birth; what appears is the manifestation, not the identity. The
   reader who reads birth as the creation of an identity has misread the definition; the reader
   who reads it as the emergence of a group of manifestations has read it correctly.


   Remark 34.15 (Birth Points Beyond Itself)

   Birth is the emergence in the Material Manifestation of a group of manifestations connected
   to a single identity; the framework’s claim is that the birth is real, and that the identity
   is not created. But the birth is not self-grounded. The birth is the emergence of the
   manifestations; it is not the ground of the identity. The birth points beyond itself to what
   holds the identity in being before the birth, and to what makes the identity possible. The
   framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described
   by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the birth and the ground of
   the identity; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the birth as the one who brings forth from the womb,
   and as the one who knows the identity before its manifestation begins. The Quranic verse
   that the traditions cite in this connection is the verse of the bringing forth: “And Allah has
   brought you out from the wombs of your mothers, not knowing anything” (Qur’an 16:78).
   The framework’s structural reading is that the birth is the emergence of the manifestations,
   not the creation of the identity; the verse is cited as structural evidence, not as a ground
   of justification. The framework does not claim that its structural birth is the bringing
   forth of the one, and it does not claim that the bringing forth is unreal. It claims that the
   birth is a real structural event, and that the event points beyond itself.
372                                                                  Chapter 34. Death and Birth


34.8       The Veil

The concept of birth raises a further question. When an identity is manifested in the Relational
Manifestation, what is its condition? The framework names the condition, and the definition is
the subject of the present section.

   Definition 34.4 (The Veil)

   The veil is the state of an identity in the Relational Manifestation in which its world there
   has not yet been articulated.


      The definition states a structural condition, not a task. The condition is that of an identity
whose world in the Relational Manifestation has not yet been articulated; the articulation is
what the identity’s manifestation in that realm requires.

   Remark 34.16 (A Structural Condition)

   The veil is a structural condition of realization in the Relational Manifestation, not
   a deviation from a norm. An identity realized in that realm begins with its world
   unarticulated there; the articulation is a structural feature of the relation between the
   identity and the receiving realm, not a task assigned to it. What the articulation consists
   in, and how it proceeds, is a conceptual question the framework leaves open ((Q)).


   Remark 34.17 (The Veil Is Not a Metaphor for Ignorance)

   The veil is not a metaphor for ignorance, or for the limitations of a subject’s knowledge. It is
   a structural condition of the relation between an identity and the Relational Manifestation
   in which it is realized. The reader who reads the veil as a metaphor for epistemological
   limitation has misread it; the reader who reads it as a structural condition of realization
   has read it correctly.


   Remark 34.18 (The Veil Points Beyond Itself)

   The veil is the state of an identity in the Relational Manifestation in which its world there
   has not yet been articulated; the framework’s claim is that the veil is a real structural
   condition, and that the articulation is what the identity’s manifestation in that realm
   requires. But the veil is not self-grounded. The veil is the condition of the manifestation;
   it is not the ground of the identity. The veil points beyond itself to what makes the
   articulation possible, and to what opens the veil. The framework’s claim is that the
   pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The
   distinction is the distinction between the veil and the ground of the identity; it is kept
   throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the opening of the veil as the one who inspires the
   soul with its lewdness and its piety, and as the one who discloses to the soul what it did
   not know. The Quranic verse that the traditions cite in this connection is the verse of the
34.9. The Balance Criterion                                                                    373


   inspiration: “By the soul and He who proportioned it, and inspired it with its lewdness
   and its piety” (Qur’an 91:7–8). The framework’s structural reading is that the identity
   begins with its world unarticulated, and that the articulation is a structural condition
   of realization; the verse is cited as structural evidence, not as a ground of justification.
   The framework does not claim that its structural veil is the inspiration of the one, and it
   does not claim that the inspiration is unreal. It claims that the veil is a real structural
   condition, and that the condition points beyond itself.



34.9     The Balance Criterion

The concept of returning light raises a further question. What is the measure of the relation
between an identity and the light it receives? The framework states the measure in a definition.

   Definition 34.5 (The Balance Criterion)

   The balance of an identity in a realm is the extent to which the descending light it has
   received is preserved or returned, less the extent to which it has become sediment:

                 Balance = (received light preserved) + (ascending light given)
                             − (received light become sediment).


   The definition states a measure, not a value. The balance is the measure of the relation
between the identity’s manifestations and the light they receive; it is not a measure of the
identity’s worth or importance. The three components of the balance are the three aspects of
the relation: the light that has been preserved, the light that has been returned, and the light
that has become sediment.
   The concept of sediment, which appears in the definition, is stated here in the minimal
form the balance criterion requires. Sediment is light that has descended into a realm and not
ascended, and that has become lodged: light that persists beyond the activity that carried it, is
not integrated into the relations of its realm, and lays a lasting claim on that realm’s capacity.
The full treatment of sediment is given in the part of the book that treats expression cost and
sediment.

   Remark 34.19 (What Balance Is, and What Lack of Balance Is)

   Balance is a state of the relation of an identity’s manifestations to the light they receive.
   A lack of balance is a reduction of structural viability (more is lodged than returned),
   not a decay of the identity. The line between reduced structural viability and death is
   not sharp at the level of manifestation (it is the gradient to the singularity); at the level
   of identity there is no such line. And it is possible that an identity remains while its
   capacity to manifest in a given realm is lost: this is a structural feature of the relation,
   not a valuation of it.
374                                                               Chapter 34. Death and Birth


  Remark 34.20 (Three Thresholds)

  Three thresholds can be distinguished in the balance.

      1. High balance: received light has been preserved or returned; little sediment.

      2. Balance near zero: neither returned nor lodged; the structural possibility of return
        remains.

      3. Low balance: more has been lodged than returned.

  They are states of balance and not places. The framework states the thresholds to make
  the balance criterion usable; it does not claim that the thresholds are precise, or that
  every case falls clearly into one of the three.


  Remark 34.21 (Status of the Criterion)

  The criterion is (A) as a structural definition. How its quantities are to be compared in a
  given case is left open as a conceptual question ((Q)). The framework does not claim that
  the balance can be measured in every case; it claims that the balance is the measure the
  framework uses, and that it is structural, not evaluative.


  Remark 34.22 (The Balance Criterion Points Beyond Itself)

  The balance is the extent to which the descending light an identity has received is preserved
  or returned, less the extent to which it has become sediment; the framework’s claim is that
  the balance is real, and that the balance is a structural measure of the relation between an
  identity and the light it receives. But the balance is not self-grounded. The balance is the
  measure of the relation; it is not the ground of the identity. The balance points beyond
  itself to what makes the preservation possible, to what makes the return possible, and
  to what weighs the balance. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that
  what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction
  between the balance and the ground of the identity; it is kept throughout the book.
  The traditions speak of the ground of the balance as the one who weighs the deeds, and
  as the one whose scales are the measure of what is preserved and what is returned. The
  Quranic verse that the traditions cite in this connection is the verse of the scales: “Then
  as for one whose scales are heavy, he will be in a pleasant life” (Qur’an 101:6–7). The
  framework’s structural reading is that the balance is a structural measure of the relation
  between an identity and the light it receives; the verse is cited as structural evidence, not
  as a ground of justification. The framework does not claim that its structural balance is
  the scales of the one, and it does not claim that the scales are unreal. It claims that the
  balance is a real structural measure, and that the measure points beyond itself.
34.10. An Application of the Balance Criterion                                                  375


34.10      An Application of the Balance Criterion
The balance criterion can be applied to any identity realized in a realm. The following application
illustrates the structural criterion; it does not derive any normative consequence from it.

   Remark 34.23 (The Structural Application)

   Premise (a) ((E)): in an identity realized in the Material Manifestation whose light received
   has had little time to lodge as sediment and little withheld from return, the received light
   is largely preserved or returned. Given (a), the balance criterion yields a positive balance.
   The result does not follow from the criterion alone; it follows from the criterion together
   with (a). Premise (a) is not argued here; it is stated as an estimate.


   Remark 34.24 (Implications)

   Three implications follow.

      1. The positive balance is a result of the criterion and (a), not of an external exception.

      2. The framework does not say that the loss of such an identity is slight or severe; it
         says only that the identity is conserved and that its balance, given (a), is positive.
         It does not say that nothing has ceased in the Material Manifestation, where a
         manifestation has ceased.

      3. No normative or ethical consequence follows from this application. The framework
         states structural relations, not obligations, duties, or goods. What follows for action,
         if anything, is a separate inquiry that the framework does not undertake.

   The implications, too, point beyond themselves. The implications are the structural
   consequences of the balance criterion; they are not the ground of the identity. The
   implications point beyond themselves to what makes the balance possible, and to what
   weighs the balance. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim
   that the ground is unreal. It claims that the implications are real structural implications,
   and that the implications point beyond themselves. The distinction is the distinction
   between the implications and the ground of the identity; it is kept throughout the book.

   The application illustrates what the balance criterion is for: it is a measure of the relation
between an identity and the light it receives, and the measure can yield a result in a given case,
given an estimate of the case. The application does not settle the question of what the result
means; that question belongs to a separate inquiry, and the framework does not undertake it.


34.11      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
   First, the chapter does not develop the full account of how the balance criterion is to be
measured in a given case. The definition is stated, and its use is illustrated, but the operational
376                                                                 Chapter 34. Death and Birth


question of how to measure the balance in a particular manifestation is left for later parts of the
book. The present chapter has stated the criterion; the later parts develop its measurement.
      Second, the chapter does not settle the question of what follows for action, if anything. The
framework states structural relations, not obligations, duties, or goods. The reader who wishes
to know what the framework implies for practice is directed to a separate inquiry; the framework
does not undertake it.
      Third, the chapter does not develop the relation between the four kinds of death beyond the
distinctions stated above. How the four kinds interact in a given case, whether one kind entails
another, and what the conditions of each kind are—all these are questions that the framework
leaves for later parts. The present chapter has distinguished the four kinds; the later parts
develop them.
      Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of death and birth. It claims
to have described the structure of death and birth, and the structure points beyond itself to the
ground that the framework does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the
structure of death and birth and the ground of the identity; it is kept throughout the chapter,
and it is stated here as the chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Consider something that has ceased to be manifested in one realm but continues in another—a
person who has died but whose work continues to influence others; a language that is no longer
spoken but is studied from texts; a tradition that has ended but whose traces remain. What has
ceased, and what has continued? What does your answer tell you about the relation between the
zeroing of a manifestation and the conservation of an identity?

The next chapter turns to self-awareness, consciousness, and awareness. It defines the three
concepts as structural relations between a manifestation and its identity and the light it receives,
and it distinguishes them from one another. The present chapter has defined death and birth as
structural conditions of manifestation; the next chapter defines the three concepts by which the
34.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter     377


manifestation regulates its relation to its source.
Chapter 35

Self-Awareness, Consciousness, and Awareness


Scope. This chapter is a structural analysis. It defines three concepts—self-awareness, conscious-
ness, awareness—as structural relations between a manifestation and its identity and the light
it receives, and it distinguishes them from one another. Its claims are structural; where the
chapter is silent on questions of value or psychology, the silence is not a denial but a recogni-
tion that the structural description is not the whole of what can be said. Where the chapter
touches on the limits of a subject’s self-knowledge and on the levels at which a manifestation is
structurally determined, these are structural descriptions; no claim about values, goods, freedom,
choice, responsibility, or psychological health is intended or entailed. The words “self-awareness,”
“consciousness,” and “awareness” have histories in psychology and in philosophy of mind; those
histories do not enter the definitions given here, and the structural sense the definitions give
them is the sense the book uses.



35.1      A Scene

Consider three things that happen when you drink a glass of water. You reach for the glass; you
feel its coolness; you notice that you are thirsty. Three things, and each is different.
   The first is the act: the reaching, the lifting, the drinking. Your body regulates itself to bring
the water to your mouth, to swallow, to satisfy the thirst. The regulation is not something you
decide; it happens, and you can, at most, direct it. The mechanism of regulation is the first
thing.
   The second is the feeling: the coolness of the glass, the wetness of the water, the quenching
of the thirst. The feeling has an intensity; it is stronger or weaker, clearer or duller, more or less
present. The intensity of the connection between you and the water is the second thing.
   The third is the noticing: you notice that you are thirsty; you notice that you are drinking;
you notice that the water is cool. The noticing is not the act and not the feeling; it is the
reception of what the act and the feeling make available. The regulation of reception is the third
thing.
   The three are easily confused. In ordinary language, we speak of “being aware” of the water
and “being conscious” of the thirst and “knowing” that we are drinking, as if they were the same.
But they are not the same. The act of reaching for the glass can happen without the noticing;
the feeling of coolness can happen without the noticing; the noticing can be present without the
act being deliberate. The three are distinct, and the framework keeps them apart.
   The scene poses a question. What are the three, exactly, and how do they relate? The
framework’s answer is that they are three structural relations between a manifestation and its
identity and the light it receives: self-awareness is the mechanism of regulation; consciousness is

                                                 378
35.2. The Question                                                                               379


the intensity of connection; awareness is the regulation of reception. The present chapter states
the answer, and distinguishes the three from one another.

   Remark 35.1 (The Three Acts Point Beyond Themselves)

   The three acts—the regulation of the connection, the intensity of the connection, the
   regulation of reception—are distinct, and the chapter argues that each is a structural
   relation. The framework’s claim is that the three relations are real, and that the analysis
   of the manifestation requires all three. But the three acts are not self-grounded. The
   acts are the acts of a manifestation; they are not the ground of the manifestation. The
   three acts point beyond themselves to what makes the manifestation possible, and to
   what makes the three relations possible. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is
   real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction is
   the distinction between the three acts and the ground of the manifestation; it is kept
   throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the three acts as the one who proportioned the soul
   and inspired it with its lewdness and its piety, and as the one in whose knowledge the
   regulation and the reception are what they are. The Quranic verse that the traditions cite
   in this connection is the verse of the inspiration: “By the soul and He who proportioned
   it, and inspired it with its lewdness and its piety” (Qur’an 91:7–8). The framework’s
   structural reading is that the manifestation regulates its connection to its source, and that
   the regulation has an intensity and a reception; the verse is cited as structural evidence,
   not as a ground of justification. The framework does not claim that its structural acts
   are the inspiration of the one, and it does not claim that the inspiration is unreal. It
   claims that the three acts are real structural relations, and that the relations point beyond
   themselves.



35.2      The Question

The preceding chapters of this part have developed the framework’s derivative concepts. The
previous chapter defined death and birth as structural conditions of manifestation. The chapter
before that defined time and the three concepts that are easily confused with it.
   The present chapter turns to a different kind of derivative concept. The previous chapters
have described the manifestation from the outside: what it is, when it begins, when it ceases, how
it relates to time. The present chapter describes the manifestation from the inside, considered
under its structural aspects: what it is for a manifestation to regulate its relation to its identity,
what it is for the connection to have an intensity, what it is for a manifestation to regulate its
reception of light.
   The question is: what are self-awareness, consciousness, and awareness? The three terms are
often used interchangeably in ordinary language, and they are often conflated in the philosophical
literature. The framework distinguishes them, and the distinction is the chapter’s principal
contribution.
   Two aspects of the question must be distinguished.
380                                   Chapter 35. Self-Awareness, Consciousness, and Awareness


The structural aspect. What are the three, exactly? The chapter defines them as structural
relations, and distinguishes them by what they relate.

The systematic aspect. How do the three relate to one another? The chapter argues that
they are three aspects of one structure, distinguished by level: a mechanism, a degree, and a
specific activity.
      The chapter proceeds as follows. It states the distinction that is easily forgotten. It defines
the three concepts. It states what each is not. It states the relations among them. It distinguishes
them by level. It states the structural limits of self-knowledge. It states the two levels at which a
manifestation is structurally determined. It closes with what it does not establish and with the
epistemic status of its claims.


35.3        The Forgotten Distinction
The three concepts are often used as if they were one. A person is said to be “self-aware” when
she knows what she is doing; she is said to be “conscious” when she is awake and responsive; she
is said to be “aware” of something when she notices it. The three uses overlap, and the overlap
is what makes the distinction easy to forget.
      The framework’s claim is that the three are not the same, and that the forgetting of the
distinction has consequences. If self-awareness, consciousness, and awareness are conflated, the
framework cannot state what each is; the difference between the regulation of a connection and
the intensity of the connection, or between the intensity of the connection and the regulation of
reception, is lost. The present chapter recovers the distinction, and states the three concepts in
their structural specificity.
      The distinction is not a novelty of the framework. The three concepts are distinguished, in
various ways, in the philosophical and psychological literature; the framework’s contribution is
to state them as structural relations, and to distinguish them by what they relate. The reader
who has read the earlier parts of the book will recognize the vocabulary; the reader who has not
will find the definitions in the next section.


35.4        The Three Concepts
The three concepts are stated in definitions.

   Definition 35.1 (Self-Awareness)

   (A) Self-awareness is the mechanism of regulating the connection between a manifestation
   and its identity: the activity by which a manifestation adjusts how much descending light
   it receives, how much reflective light it emits, and how much ascending light it returns.

   Definition 35.2 (Consciousness)

   (A) Consciousness is the intensity of the connection between a manifestation and its
   identity.
35.4. The Three Concepts                                                                       381


   Definition 35.3 (Awareness)

   (A) Awareness is the regulation of a manifestation for the reception of reflective light and
   intra-category light.

    The three definitions are stated as commitments, because each is a specific structural notion
introduced in the present chapter. The definitions are not derived from the framework’s earlier
principles; they are the framework’s proposals for what the three concepts are.
    Each definition says what the concept is not, as well as what it is.


Self-awareness is not a degree and not a particular reception. It is the general
mechanism of regulation. It is the activity by which the manifestation adjusts its relation to its
identity, not the degree to which the relation holds, and not the particular reception of any given
light.


Consciousness is not a mechanism and not an activity. It is a degree of connection. It
is the intensity with which the connection between manifestation and identity holds, not the
mechanism by which the connection is regulated, and not the activity of receiving any given
light.


Awareness is not the whole of regulation. It is the part of regulation concerned with the
reception of reflective and intra-category light. It is not the mechanism of regulation as a whole
(which is self-awareness), and it is not the degree of connection (which is consciousness).

   Remark 35.2 (The Three Are Not the Same)

   The three definitions are different, and the difference is structural. Self-awareness is a
   mechanism; consciousness is a degree; awareness is a specific activity of regulation. The
   first is the how; the second is the how much; the third is the of what. The three answer
   different questions, and an answer to one does not answer the others. The reader who
   reads them as three names for one thing has misread the chapter; the reader who reads
   them as three distinct structural relations has read it correctly.


   Remark 35.3 (The Three Concepts Point Beyond Themselves)

   The three concepts—self-awareness, consciousness, awareness—are real structural relations;
   the framework’s claim is that the manifestation regulates its connection to its source, and
   that the regulation has a mechanism, a degree, and a specific activity. But the three
   concepts are not self-grounded. The concepts are the concepts of the relation between
   the manifestation and its identity; they are not the ground of the relation. The three
   concepts point beyond themselves to what makes the relation possible, and to what makes
   the three aspects possible. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that
   what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction
   between the concepts and the ground of the relation; it is kept throughout the book.
382                                   Chapter 35. Self-Awareness, Consciousness, and Awareness


   The traditions speak of the ground of the relation as the one who knows the secret and
   the hidden, and as the one whose knowledge of the manifestation is not interrupted by
   the manifestation’s regulation of itself. The Quranic verse that the traditions cite in
   this connection is the verse of the hidden: “He knows the treachery of the eyes and
   what the breasts conceal” (Qur’an 40:19). The framework’s structural reading is that the
   manifestation’s self-awareness is a regulation of its connection, not a complete knowledge
   of the connection; the verse is cited as structural evidence, not as a ground of justification.
   The framework does not claim that its three concepts are the knowledge of the one, and it
   does not claim that the knowledge is unreal. It claims that the three concepts are real
   structural relations, and that the relations point beyond themselves.



35.5       The Relations Among the Three
The three concepts are distinct, but they are related. The framework states the relations in a
remark, and the remark is the chapter’s principal contribution to the systematic account of the
three.
      Self-awareness is the genus; awareness is a species of it (the regulation of reception); con-
sciousness is a dimension of it (the intensity of the connection that it regulates).
      The relation can be stated in a sentence. Self-awareness is the how; consciousness is the how
much; awareness is the of what. The three are aspects of one structure, distinguished by the
question they answer.

   Remark 35.4 (The Relations Are Kept the Same in Every Later Use)

   The relations stated in this section are kept the same in every later use of the three terms.
   When the book speaks of self-awareness, it means the mechanism of regulation; when it
   speaks of consciousness, it means the intensity of connection; when it speaks of awareness,
   it means the regulation of reception. The reader who keeps the relations in mind will find
   the framework’s later uses of the three terms consistent; the reader who does not will find
   them puzzling.


   Remark 35.5 (The Relations Are Structural, Not Psychological)

   The relations are structural, not psychological. They state how the three concepts are
   related as structural relations between a manifestation and its identity and the light it
   receives; they do not state how the three are related in the psychology of a subject. The
   two may be related—a psychological subject may have the structural relations that the
   framework describes—but they are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart.
   The relations, too, point beyond themselves. The relations are the relations among the
   three concepts; they are not the ground of the relation between the manifestation and
   its identity. The relations point beyond themselves to what makes the three concepts
   possible, and to what makes their relation possible. The framework does not describe the
   ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the relations are
35.6. Self-Awareness: The Mechanism of Regulation                                                 383


   real structural relations, and that the relations point beyond themselves. The distinction is
   the distinction between the relations and the ground of the relation; it is kept throughout
   the book.



35.6      Self-Awareness: The Mechanism of Regulation
Self-awareness is the mechanism of regulation. It is the activity by which a manifestation adjusts
its relation to its identity.
    The mechanism has three channels: the descending channel (reception), the reflective channel
(emission), and the ascending channel (return). Each channel is a structural direction of light,
established in the part of the book that treated the fluid element: descending light is the flow
of effect from identity to manifestation; ascending light is the flow of effect from manifestation
to identity; reflective light is the flow of effect among manifestations. The mechanism of self-
awareness adjusts the manifestation’s relation to each channel: how much descending light it
receives, how much reflective light it emits, how much ascending light it returns.
    The mechanism operates in the realms in which manifestations occur. It operates in the
Material Manifestation (the manifestation’s regulation of its relation to its material conditions); in
the Hub of Realization (the manifestation’s regulation of its actualization); and in the Relational
Manifestation (the manifestation’s regulation of its relations to other manifestations). The
mechanism does not operate in the realms in which there are no manifestations; in the First
Determination, there is nothing to regulate; in the Structural Determination, there is nothing to
regulate; in the Hub of Decree and the Hub of Signification, the regulation is structural, not the
regulation of a manifestation.

   Remark 35.6 (The General and Human Senses)

   In the sense of the definition, self-awareness belongs to any manifestation that regulates
   its connection to its source. It is therefore wider than the reflexive reference of a subject
   to its own self-model, which is the human sense. The book uses the wide sense unless it
   says otherwise; the human sense is a special case of it in the Relational Manifestation.
   The reader who reads “self-awareness” in the narrow sense has read a special case; the
   reader who reads it in the wide sense has read the general concept.


   Remark 35.7 (Self-Awareness Is Not Reflexive Consciousness)

   Self-awareness is not the same as reflexive consciousness—the subject’s consciousness
   of its own consciousness. Reflexive consciousness is a specific act of consciousness in
   the Relational Manifestation; self-awareness is the general mechanism of regulation that
   operates across the realms. The two are related (the human self-awareness includes
   reflexive consciousness as a special case), but they are not the same, and the framework
   keeps them apart.
   Self-awareness, too, points beyond itself. The mechanism is the mechanism of regulation;
   it is not the ground of the regulation. The mechanism points beyond itself to what makes
384                                   Chapter 35. Self-Awareness, Consciousness, and Awareness


   the regulation possible, and to what makes the manifestation possible. The framework
   does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims
   that the mechanism is a real structural mechanism, and that the mechanism points beyond
   itself. The distinction is the distinction between the mechanism and the ground of the
   regulation; it is kept throughout the book.



35.7       Consciousness: The Intensity of Connection
Consciousness is the intensity of the connection between a manifestation and its identity.
      The connection is the fact that light holds between them. The intensity is how strongly it
holds. The two are different: a connection could be present with low intensity. Consciousness is
the second.

   Remark 35.8 (Degree, and Whether Experience Is Required)

   Consciousness is not binary; it is a matter of degree. Whether it also requires a particular
   kind of experience—something it is like to be the manifestation—is not decided by this
   definition. The framework gives a structural account and leaves that question open ((Q)).
   The reader who reads consciousness as necessarily involving experience has imported a
   claim the framework does not make; the reader who reads it as a degree of connection has
   read the definition.

   Remark 35.9 (Consciousness Is Not Self-Awareness)

   Consciousness is not self-awareness. Self-awareness is the mechanism of regulation; con-
   sciousness is the degree to which the connection holds. The mechanism can operate at
   any degree of connection; the degree can be high or low while the mechanism operates.
   The two are distinct, and the framework keeps them apart.
   Consciousness, too, points beyond itself. The intensity is the intensity of the connection;
   it is not the ground of the connection. The intensity points beyond itself to what makes
   the connection possible, and to what makes the manifestation possible. The framework
   does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims
   that the intensity is a real structural feature, and that the intensity points beyond itself.
   The distinction is the distinction between the intensity and the ground of the connection;
   it is kept throughout the book.



35.8       Awareness: The Regulation of Reception
Awareness is the regulation of a manifestation for the reception of reflective light and intra-category
light.
      The definition states a specific activity of regulation. The activity is the manifestation’s
regulation of its reception of light—specifically, of the light that connects manifestations to one
another (reflective light) and of the light that has descended into the realm and not ascended
35.9. An Analogy                                                                               385


(intra-category light). The regulation is the manifestation’s way of adjusting what it receives,
and how it receives it.
   Awareness is a species of self-awareness. Self-awareness is the general mechanism of regulation;
awareness is the part of regulation concerned with the reception of reflective and intra-category
light. The two are related, but they are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart.

   Remark 35.10 (Awareness Is Not Consciousness)

   Awareness is not consciousness. Consciousness is the intensity of the connection between
   manifestation and identity; awareness is the regulation of reception. The connection can
   have high intensity while the regulation of reception is minimal; the connection can have
   low intensity while the regulation of reception is intense. The two are distinct, and the
   framework keeps them apart.


   Remark 35.11 (Awareness Is Structural, Not Phenomenological)

   Awareness is structural, not phenomenological. It is the regulation of reception, not the
   experience of reception. A manifestation can be structurally aware of another without
   being phenomenologically aware of it; the structural relation is the condition of possibility
   of the phenomenological state, not the state itself. The reader who reads awareness as a
   phenomenological state has misread the chapter; the reader who reads it as a structural
   relation has read it correctly.
   Awareness, too, points beyond itself. The regulation of reception is the regulation of the
   reception; it is not the ground of the reception. The regulation points beyond itself to
   what makes the reception possible, and to what makes the manifestation possible. The
   framework does not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal.
   It claims that the regulation is a real structural activity, and that the regulation points
   beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the regulation and the ground of
   the reception; it is kept throughout the book.




35.9      An Analogy

An analogy may help to fix the three concepts.
   A production manager adjusts what goes into a process. The adjustment is the mechanism
of regulation (self-awareness). The intensity of the process is how fully it runs; the intensity is
the degree of connection (consciousness). The adjusting of the inputs is a particular activity of
management; the activity is the regulation of reception (awareness).
   The analogy suggests three roles. It misleads if it suggests three agents: in the framework,
they are three aspects of one structure, and self-awareness is not a separate agent apart from the
manifestation. The analogy is offered as an aid to understanding, not as a substitute for the
definitions.
386                                  Chapter 35. Self-Awareness, Consciousness, and Awareness


   Remark 35.12 (The Analogy Is Not the Argument)

   The analogy is not the argument. The three concepts are established by their definitions
   and by their relations; the analogy is a way of seeing what the definitions state. The
   reader who finds the analogy helpful will find the definitions clearer; the reader who does
   not will find the definitions still standing on their own.
   The analogy, too, points beyond itself. The analogy is the analogy of the three roles; it
   is not the ground of the three roles. The analogy points beyond itself to what makes
   the three roles possible, and to what makes their relation possible. The framework does
   not describe the ground, and it does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that
   the analogy is a real structural analogy, and that the analogy points beyond itself. The
   distinction is the distinction between the analogy and the ground of the roles; it is kept
   throughout the book.




35.10        The Structural Limits of Self-Knowledge

Self-awareness raises a further question. Can a subject know its own identity? The framework
distinguishes the structural limits of self-knowledge, and the definition is the subject of the
present section.

   Definition 35.4 (The Structural Limits of Self-Knowledge)

   The structural limits of self-knowledge are the limits that follow, for any finite subject,
   from the impossibility of super-identity: a subject can form only pseudo-identities of its
   own identity, never the identity as such.


      The definition states a consequence of the impossibility of super-identity, applied to the
subject’s own identity. The impossibility was established in the part of the book that treated the
foundation; the present section applies it to the specific case of the subject’s relation to its own
identity.
      The subject’s knowledge of its own identity is subject to the same structural constraints as
its knowledge of any other identity: it has access to manifestations, not to the identity itself, and
its reconstructions are pseudo-identities of increasing or decreasing adequacy.

   Remark 35.13 (A Structural Condition, Not a Psychological One)

   The subject’s knowledge of its own identity is subject to the same structural constraints
   as its knowledge of any other identity. This is a structural feature of the relation between
   a finite subject and any identity, including its own. The framework makes no claim about
   whether this structural condition is experienced as estrangement, conflict, or well-being;
   that is a separate question, and no normative or psychological consequence follows from
   the structural description.
35.11. Two Levels of Structural Determination                                                    387


   Remark 35.14 (Self-Knowledge Is Not Privileged)

   The subject’s knowledge of its own identity is not privileged. The subject has access to its
   own manifestations, as it has access to the manifestations of other identities; it does not
   have direct access to its own identity, any more than it has direct access to the identity
   of another. The framework’s account of self-knowledge is therefore continuous with its
   account of knowledge in general: both are reconstructions from manifestations, both are
   partial, both are fallible. The reader who expects a special privilege for self-knowledge
   will not find it in the framework; the reader who expects the same structural constraints
   as knowledge in general will find them.
   Self-knowledge, too, points beyond itself. The limits of self-knowledge are the limits of the
   finite subject’s reconstruction; they are not the limits of the identity. The limits point
   beyond themselves to what makes the identity possible, and to what knows the identity
   without reconstruction. The framework does not describe the ground, and it does not
   claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the limits are real structural limits, and
   that the limits point beyond themselves. The distinction is the distinction between the
   limits and the ground of the identity; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the identity as the one who knows what is in the
   breasts, and as the one who knows the self better than the self knows itself. The Quranic
   verse that the traditions cite in this connection is the verse of the signs in the selves:
   “And in yourselves; will you not then see?” (Qur’an 51:21). The framework’s structural
   reading is that the subject’s self-knowledge is a reconstruction from manifestations, not a
   direct access to the identity; the verse is cited as structural evidence, not as a ground of
   justification. The framework does not claim that its structural limits are the knowledge of
   the one, and it does not claim that the knowledge is unreal. It claims that the limits are
   real structural limits, and that the limits point beyond themselves.



35.11      Two Levels of Structural Determination
The concept of self-awareness raises a final question. At what levels is a manifestation structurally
determined? The framework distinguishes two levels, and the definition is the subject of the
present section.

   Definition 35.5 (Two Levels of Structural Determination)

   First level: the identity’s nature and the rules of the realm in which it is manifested
   determine the range of manifestations structurally available to it. Second level: the
   specific configuration of light and of other manifestations to which the manifestation is
   related determines which of the structurally available manifestations is realized.

   The two levels are distinct, and the distinction is what allows the framework to state what is
determined at each level.
   The first level gives the range: the identity’s nature and the rules of the realm fix what mani-
festations are structurally possible. The second level selects within the range: the configuration
388                                  Chapter 35. Self-Awareness, Consciousness, and Awareness


of light and other manifestations fixes which of the possible manifestations is realized. The two
levels are compatible because they describe different aspects of one structural relation: the first
gives the range, the second selects within it.

   Remark 35.15 (Compatibility of the Two Levels)

   The two levels are compatible because they describe different aspects of one structural
   relation: the first gives the range, the second selects within it. The first does not determine
   the second, and the second does not violate the first. They are two levels of structural
   description, not two kinds of causation. The framework’s claim is structural: every
   manifestation is determined at both levels, and the two levels are compatible.


   Remark 35.16 (The Two Levels Point Beyond Themselves)

   The two levels—the range and the selection—are real structural levels; the framework’s
   claim is that every manifestation is determined at both levels, and that the two levels
   are compatible. But the two levels are not self-grounded. The levels are the levels of the
   manifestation; they are not the ground of the manifestation. The two levels point beyond
   themselves to what makes the range possible, and to what makes the selection possible.
   The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not
   described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the two levels and
   the ground of the manifestation; it is kept throughout the book.
   The traditions speak of the ground of the two levels as the one who determines the measure
   of each thing, and as the one in whose knowledge the range and the selection are what
   they are. The framework does not claim that its two levels are that determination, and
   it does not claim that the determination is unreal. It claims that the two levels are real
   structural levels, and that the levels point beyond themselves. The reader who identifies
   the two levels with the determination is free to do so; the reader who distinguishes them
   is free to do so; the framework takes no position on the identity, because the identity is a
   question for another inquiry.


   Remark 35.17 (No Claim About Freedom, Choice, or Responsibility)

   The framework makes no claim about freedom, choice, or responsibility. Those concepts
   belong to an independent inquiry and are not part of the present framework. The framework
   asserts a structural claim: every manifestation is determined at both levels, and the two
   levels are compatible. What the framework does not assert is any thesis about the will,
   agency, or moral standing of the subject; those questions are outside its scope. The reader
   who looks for a position on free will will not find one; the reader who looks for a structural
   account of determination will find it.
   The absence of a claim about freedom, too, points beyond itself. The absence is the
   structural consequence of the framework’s scope; it is not the ground of the subject. The
   absence points beyond itself to what makes the subject possible, and to what the subject’s
   freedom and responsibility are for. The framework does not describe the ground, and it
35.12. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                     389


   does not claim that the ground is unreal. It claims that the absence is real, and that the
   absence points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the absence and
   the ground of the subject; it is kept throughout the book.



35.12      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
   First, the chapter does not settle the question of whether consciousness requires experience.
The definition states consciousness as the intensity of connection; whether the intensity must be
accompanied by something it is like to be the manifestation is a question the framework leaves
open.
   Second, the chapter does not develop the relation between the three concepts and the
framework’s account of light beyond what the definitions state. The three concepts are defined in
terms of light’s channels (descending, ascending, reflective, intra-category); the detailed account
of how the channels operate in each realm is left for later parts of the book.
   Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the three concepts exhaust the
structural relations between a manifestation and its identity. The three are the ones the framework
has identified; whether a fourth exists is a question the framework leaves open.
   Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of self-awareness, con-
sciousness, and awareness. It claims to have described the structure of the three concepts, and
the structure points beyond itself to the ground that the framework does not describe. The
distinction is the distinction between the structure of the three concepts and the ground of the
relation; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is stated here as the chapter’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a moment in which you did something without noticing it, or noticed something
without doing anything about it, or did something and noticed it at the same time. In each case,
390                                  Chapter 35. Self-Awareness, Consciousness, and Awareness


which of the three—the mechanism of regulation, the intensity of connection, the regulation of
reception—was at work? What does the answer tell you about the distinction among the three?

The next chapter turns to expression cost and sediment. It defines the cost of expression, states
the principle of ontological economy, states the variational principle of viability, and defines
sediment as intra-category light that has become lodged. The present chapter has defined the three
concepts by which a manifestation regulates its relation to its source; the next chapter defines the
cost that the regulation bears and the sediment that the regulation leaves.
