Scope. This chapter completes the framework’s treatment of the derivative concepts. It defines
the cost of expression, states the principle of ontological economy and the variational principle of
viability, distinguishes three aspects of cost, defines sediment as intra-category light that has
become lodged, distinguishes the three layers of sediment, and states the three structural forms
of integration. Every term in the chapter is structural; no normative, ethical, or evaluative claim
is made. Where the chapter speaks of “cost,” “economy,” “optimum,” “sediment,” “integration,”
or “transformation,” their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and in the parts of the
book that treated the fluid element, identity, and viability. Cost names a structural feature of
the relation between an identity and its receiving realm: the demand that expression makes on a
finite capacity.


36.1      A Scene
Consider a house that has been lived in for a hundred years. Every generation that lived in it
left something behind. In the attic, there are boxes of letters that no one has opened in decades.
In the basement, there are tools from a trade that no one in the family practices anymore. In
the walls, there are pipes that were installed, replaced, and abandoned; the abandoned ones are
still there, rusting, no longer connected to anything. The house has absorbed the lives that were
lived in it, and what it has absorbed has not all been processed.
   Some of what the house absorbed is active. The letters, when they are read, still speak; the
tools, when they are understood, still tell of the trade; the pipes, when they are inspected, still
show the shape of the plumbing that was. What has been absorbed can be integrated: it can
be brought into the network of relations that the house holds, and it can become part of what
the house is. Some of what the house absorbed is not active. The rust in the abandoned pipes
does not speak; the dust in the unopened boxes does not tell; the mold in the walls does not
show the shape of anything. What has been absorbed can also not be integrated: it persists, it is
not connected to anything, and it lays a claim on the house’s capacity that the house cannot
discharge.
   The scene is one instance of a structural relation. Whenever an identity expresses itself in a
realm, the expression leaves something behind, and what is left behind is either integrated into
the realm’s relations or lodged in it. The framework names the lodged light, and the process of
integration, and the cost that the whole relation bears.
   The scene poses a question. What is it for light to be lodged? What is it for light to be
integrated? And what does the relation between the identity and its realm cost, such that the
light can be lodged rather than integrated? The present chapter answers these questions. Its
principal contributions are the definition of cost, the distinction among its three kinds and three

                                                391
392                                                   Chapter 36. Expression Cost and Sediment


aspects, the definition of sediment, the distinction among its three layers, and the statement of
the three structural forms of integration.
      With this chapter, the framework’s treatment of the derivative concepts is complete. The
concepts developed in this part—time and eternity, death and birth, the three-fold distinction of
self-awareness, consciousness, and awareness, and the economy of expression cost and sediment—
are all derived from the principles established in the preceding parts, and none adds a new
foundation.


36.2       The Question
The preceding chapters of this part have developed the framework’s derivative concepts. The
previous chapter defined the three concepts by which a manifestation regulates its relation to its
source. The chapter before that defined death and birth as structural conditions of manifestation.
The chapter before that defined time and the three concepts that are easily confused with it.
      The present chapter turns to a further derivative concept. The previous chapters have
described the manifestation in its relation to time, to death and birth, and to its own regulation.
The present chapter describes the manifestation in its relation to what it costs—what the
expression of an identity demands of the capacity of its receiving realm, and what is left behind
when the demand is met.
      The question is: what does expression cost? The framework has spoken of the capacity of a
realm, of the constraints that a realm imposes on what can appear in it, and of the balance of an
identity in a realm. The present chapter states what the cost of expression is, and how cost is
distinguished from what the cost produces.
      Two aspects of the question must be distinguished.

The cost aspect. What is the cost of expression, and what kinds of cost are there? The chapter
defines the cost, distinguishes three kinds (realization, cognition, maintenance and recovery), and
distinguishes three aspects (extent, reach, duration).

The sediment aspect. What is left behind when expression has occurred? The chapter
defines sediment, distinguishes three layers (cognitive, affective, ontological), and states the three
structural forms of integration.
      The chapter proceeds as follows. It states the cost of expression. It states the principle of
ontological economy. It states the variational principle of viability. It distinguishes the aspects of
cost. It defines sediment. It distinguishes the three layers of sediment. It states the integration of
sediment. It distinguishes sediment from transformation and from loss of identity. It closes with
an account of the continuations that belong to later parts of the book and with the epistemic
status of its claims.


36.3       The Cost of Expression
The chapter’s first task is to state the cost of expression. The concept is philosophical: cost is
what the expression of an identity demands of the capacity of its receiving realm. Three costs
36.4. The Principle of Ontological Economy                                                     393


are distinguished, and the distinction must not be collapsed.


First kind: the cost of realization. What it takes for a manifestation to come to be. The
conditions that the realm must supply for the manifestation to be realized: the material, the
relations, the structural possibilities that the manifestation’s realization requires.


Second kind: the cost of cognition. What it takes to know or reconstruct a manifestation—
to form a pseudo-identity of it. The conditions that a subject must satisfy in order to reconstruct
the manifestation from its appearances: the observation, the comparison, the inference that the
reconstruction requires.


Third kind: the cost of maintenance and recovery. What it takes to keep, or to regain,
the capacity to manifest. The conditions that the realm must sustain for the manifestation to
continue, and the conditions that must be restored if the manifestation is to be recovered after a
lapse.
   The three costs are related; they are not the same without an argument. The cost of
realization is what the manifestation demands in order to be; the cost of cognition is what its
reconstruction demands in order to be known; the cost of maintenance and recovery is what
its continuation or restoration demands in order to persist. The three are distinct, and the
framework keeps them apart.

   Remark 36.1 (The Cost Is Not a Single Quantity)

   The three costs are not three components of one quantity that could be added up. They
   are three kinds of demand on the capacity of the realm, and their relation is not simply
   additive. How they stand to one another in a given case is a conceptual question the
   framework leaves open ((Q)). The framework’s claim is that the three are distinct; their
   sum is not the total cost.

   Remark 36.2 (Cost Is Structural, Not Evaluative)

   “Cost” in this chapter names what is demanded of the capacity of a realm for an expression
   to be realized, known, and kept. The demand is a structural feature of the relation between
   an identity and its receiving realm, and the framework’s account of expression, viability,
   and sediment is built on this feature. Nothing in the account implies that less cost is
   better or that more cost is worse; the framework relates cost to fidelity and recoverability,
   not to a scale of goods. The relation among cost, fidelity, and recoverability is what the
   framework’s account of viability states.



36.4     The Principle of Ontological Economy

The distinction among the three costs leads to a principle about the cost as such.
394                                                  Chapter 36. Expression Cost and Sediment


   Principle 36.1 (Ontological Economy)

   (A) Every realization, every reconstruction, and every maintenance of expression bears a
   cost that cannot be wholly removed. Cost is a structural feature of the relation between
   an identity and its receiving realm; it is not a value, a burden to be minimized as an end,
   or a good.


      The principle is (A): it is adopted as a commitment of the framework. Its support is the
structure of the relation between an identity and its receiving realm: the realm has finite capacity,
and no appearance is free of what it asks of that capacity. The principle would be refuted by a
case in which a realization, reconstruction, or maintenance of expression demands nothing of the
receiving realm’s capacity; the framework argues that none can be coherently described, given
the finite capacity of every realm.
      The principle has three components, which the reader should keep distinct.


First component: cost is irreducible. Cost belongs to the relation between an identity and
its receiving realm. A realm has finite capacity, and no appearance is free of what it asks of that
capacity. The cost cannot be eliminated; it can only be distributed, deferred, or transformed.


Second component: cost is a family of demands. Cost is not a single quantity. The three
kinds distinguished above are three ways in which expression asks something of capacity. Their
relation is not simply additive; how they stand to one another in a given case is not fixed in
advance.


Third component: complete reconstruction is structurally unavailable. Complete
reconstruction is impossible (the impossibility of super-identity, established in the part of the
book that treated the foundation), and it would demand unbounded cost. The framework states
this as a structural limit, not as a deficiency to be overcome.

   Remark 36.3 (The Economy Is Structural, Not Economic)

   The economy at issue is structural: it names what expression demands of a finite capacity,
   not a system of exchange or a market. The framework uses the word because the structural
   feature is analogous to what economy studies; it imports no assumption of economic theory.
   The structural economy is a statement about the relation between expression and finite
   capacity, and it is to be read at that level.



36.5       The Variational Principle of Viability

The principle of ontological economy raises a further question. Given that cost is irreducible,
what is the structural optimum of expression? The framework states the optimum in a principle.
36.6. The Aspects of Cost                                                                          395


   Principle 36.2 (Variational Principle)

   (A) For any identity and any receiving realm, the structural optimum of expression is the
   point at which cost is minimized subject to the constraints of fidelity and recoverability.
   There is no single structural optimum across realms; each is indexed to the realm and to
   the identity.


    The principle is (A): it is adopted as a commitment of the framework. Its support is the
structure of the relation between cost, fidelity, and recoverability: the three are the components
of viability (established in the part of the book that treated the foundation), and the structural
optimum is the point at which the cost is as low as it can be while fidelity and recoverability are
still satisfied.
    The principle’s claim is precise. Cost alone is not the criterion of viability. Cost can be lowered
by lowering fidelity: a thinner manifestation is cheaper and is a less complete reflection of the
source. Viability is the three-fold structural relation of fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability.
Cost and fidelity are therefore taken together: the structural optimum is the least cost consistent
with fidelity.

   Remark 36.4 (Cost Alone Is Not Viability)

   The criterion is fidelity-constrained cost, not cost alone. Viability has three components—
   fidelity, sustainability, recoverability—and the structural optimum is the point at which
   cost is as low as it can be while these are satisfied. A cheap manifestation with low
   fidelity is not at the optimum; it is simply cheap. The framework’s claim is structural:
   the optimum is indexed to the relation among the three components, not to cost taken in
   isolation.

   Remark 36.5 (No Single Structural Optimum)

   The structural optimum depends on the receiving realm, its capacity, and the identity.
   The principle states a family of structural optima, each indexed to a context. There is no
   single structural optimum across realms, because the realms differ in capacity, and the
   identities differ in their essential determination. The framework’s claim is structural: for
   any given identity and realm, there is a structural optimum; across identities and realms,
   there is no single optimum.



36.6       The Aspects of Cost
The cost of expression can be described under three aspects. The three are constitutive aspects
of one notion, a demand on capacity, and not an arbitrary list.


First aspect: extent. How much of the realm’s capacity is taken. The extent is the quantity
of capacity that the manifestation demands: how much material, how many relations, how many
structural possibilities.
396                                                    Chapter 36. Expression Cost and Sediment


Second aspect: reach. How much cognition and attention it takes to hold it. The reach
is the quantity of reconstruction that the manifestation demands: how much observation, how
much comparison, how much inference is required to form a pseudo-identity of it.


Third aspect: duration. How long it must be kept up. The duration is the quantity of time
that the manifestation demands: how long the capacity must be sustained for the manifestation
to continue.
      The three aspects are distinct, and their relation is not fixed in advance. A manifestation can
be high in extent and low in reach and short in duration (a large material object that is easily
recognized and soon gone); or high in reach and low in extent and long in duration (a subtle
relation that demands much reconstruction, occupies little capacity, and persists). The three
aspects answer different questions, and an answer to one does not answer the others.

   Remark 36.6 (The Phenomenological Aspect)

   The demand on capacity has a phenomenological aspect: it can be lived as fatigue,
   depletion of attention, and the sense of being overwhelmed. This is a description of how
   the demand is experienced, not a normative claim about how it ought to be met. The
   evaluation of the experience belongs to other inquiries; the framework’s claim is that the
   demand has an aspect that can be experienced.


   Remark 36.7 (The Three Aspects Are Not Three Quantities)

   The three aspects are not three quantities that could be added up. They are three
   dimensions of one demand on capacity, and their relation is not simply additive. How they
   stand to one another in a given case is a conceptual question the framework leaves open
   ((Q)). The framework’s claim is that the three are distinct; their combination is not the
   total cost.



36.7        The Definition of Sediment
The cost of expression is what expression demands. The sediment is what expression leaves
behind. The chapter’s next task is to define the sediment.
      The concept of intra-category light was defined in the part of the book that treated the fluid
element. Intra-category light is light that has descended into a realm and has not ascended:
effect that has arrived and not returned. The sediment is a species of intra-category light.

   Definition 36.1 (Sediment)

   Sediment is intra-category light that has become lodged: light that has descended and not
   ascended, persists beyond the activity that carried it, is not integrated into the relations
   of its realm, and lays a lasting claim on that realm’s capacity.

      The definition states a structure. The structure is that of a light that has descended, has not
ascended, and has become lodged. The lodging is characterized by three marks: persistence (the
36.8. The Three Layers of Sediment                                                                397


light persists beyond the activity that carried it), non-integration (the light is not integrated
into the relations of its realm), and a lasting claim on capacity (the light continues to demand
capacity that the realm cannot discharge).

   Remark 36.8 (The Criterion of Sediment)

   The criterion is lodging: persistence, non-integration, and a lasting claim on capacity.
   The three marks are three aspects of one structure—lodging—and hold or fail together.
   Sediment is thus a species of intra-category light; the integration of sediment is the return
   of lodged light to the relations of its realm.


   Remark 36.9 (Not Every Unreturned Light Is Sediment)

   Sediment is a narrower class than unreturned light. Light that is still in the course of its
   return, or that has been integrated, is intra-category light but not sediment. The three
   marks of lodging separate sediment from the wider class. Sediment names lodged light, by
   the three marks; intra-category light is the wider class within which sediment is a species.



36.8      The Three Layers of Sediment

The definition of sediment applies across the realms. The framework distinguishes three layers of
sediment, according to the realm in which the lodging occurs and the kind of relations in which
the lodging is embedded.


First layer: cognitive sediment. The sediment is in the Relational Manifestation. The
lodged light is meanings that have not been integrated into the network of relations. The meanings
persist, but they are not connected to the meanings that the identity’s other expressions have
produced; they lay a claim on the identity’s capacity for meaning that the identity’s relations do
not discharge.


Second layer: affective sediment. The sediment is in the Relational Manifestation. The
lodged light is experiences of feeling that have not been worked through. The feelings persist,
but they are not integrated into the relations that the identity’s other expressions have produced;
they lay a claim on the identity’s capacity for feeling that the identity’s relations do not discharge.


Third layer: ontological sediment. The sediment is in the Material Manifestation. The
lodged light is material forms that conflict with the structure of the identity. The forms persist,
but they are not integrated into the material relations that the identity’s other expressions have
produced; they lay a claim on the identity’s capacity for material manifestation that the identity’s
relations do not discharge.
   The three layers are distinct, and the distinction is structural. The first two are in the
Relational Manifestation; the third is in the Material Manifestation. The first is cognitive; the
second is affective. The three layers are not ranked by severity or by importance; they are
398                                                    Chapter 36. Expression Cost and Sediment


distinguished by the realm in which the lodging occurs and by the kind of relations in which the
lodging is embedded.

   Remark 36.10 (The Order of the Layers)

   A common pattern is that cognitive sediment gives rise to affective, and affective to
   ontological, and that deeper layers are harder to process. This is a possible pattern ((E))
   and not a necessity of logic: the framework does not show that the layers must arise in
   that order or that every case follows it. The pattern is stated as an estimate, not as a
   universal.

   Remark 36.11 (The Layers Are Distinguished Structurally)

   The three layers are distinguished structurally, not evaluatively: by the realm in which the
   lodging occurs and by the kind of relation in which the lodging is embedded. The cognitive
   sediment is in the Relational Manifestation; the ontological sediment is in the Material
   Manifestation. The framework’s ontology distinguishes the realms; the three layers follow
   from that distinction. The difference among them is structural, not a ranking.



36.9        The Integration of Sediment
The definition of sediment raises a further question. Can sediment be integrated? The framework’s
answer is that it can, and the answer is stated in a structural account of the forms of integration.
      Sediment can be integrated into the relations of its realm. Integration is the process by which
lodged light is returned to the network of relations from which it was separated. Three structural
forms of integration are distinguished.


First form: identification. The recognition of lodged light as lodged. The discernment of
sediment by the three marks of lodging (persistence, non-integration, and a lasting claim on
capacity). The first form is the recognition that the light is not on its way back, and that it is
claiming capacity that the realm cannot discharge.


Second form: structural recognition. The recognition that lodging is a structural condition
of the relation between an identity and its realm, not a deviation from a norm. The second form
is the recognition that the lodging is not a failure of the identity or of the realm, but a structural
feature of the relation between them. The lodging is what the relation produces when the light
does not return.


Third form: return. The re-entry of lodged light into the network of relations of its realm,
through expression in some form. The third form is the re-entry of the light into the network from
which it was separated; the light becomes active again, and its claim on capacity is discharged.
      The three forms are structural descriptions of integration, not prescriptions. The framework
states that integration is possible; the modes of integration, and the order in which they may
occur, are an open question ((Q)).
36.10. Sediment, Transformation, and Loss of Identity                                           399


   Remark 36.12 (Integration Is Structural Transformation)

   Integration is structural transformation, not elimination. The lodged light is returned to
   the relations of its realm; the light becomes active, and its claim on capacity is discharged.
   What integration produces is the transformation of sediment into integrated light; the
   sediment is not removed but integrated. The framework’s claim is structural: integration
   is the return of lodged light to the relations of its realm.


   Remark 36.13 (No Terminal State)

   Sediment accumulates; there is no final state in which it is absent. This is a structural
   feature of the relation between an identity and its realm, not a task to be completed.
   The framework claims the possibility of integration, within a structure in which sediment
   continues to arise.



36.10       Sediment, Transformation, and Loss of Identity
The concept of sediment is related to two other concepts that are easily confused with it:
transformation and loss of identity. The chapter states the distinctions.

First concept: sediment. Lodged light in a realm, with the three marks of lodging (persistence,
non-integration, and a lasting claim on capacity). The sediment is a feature of the relation
between an identity and its realm; it is not a feature of the identity.

Second concept: transformation. A change of manifestation or structure that the identity’s
allowable class permits, with no loss of identity. The transformation is a change in the manifesta-
tions; it is not a change in the identity. The identity is conserved across the transformation, as
the framework’s account of conservation established.

Third concept: loss of identity. A change in which the identity ceases to be the identity it
was. The loss of identity is not a matter of degree; the principle of identity rigidity established
that identity admits no degrees. Sediment and transformation can alter the structural viability
of manifestations; neither is, by itself, a loss of identity.
   The three concepts are distinct, and the distinctions are structural. Sediment is a feature of
the relation between identity and manifestation; transformation is a change in the manifestations;
loss of identity is a change in the identity. The three answer different questions, and an answer
to one does not answer the others.

   Remark 36.14 (Sediment Threatens Viability, Not Identity)

   The accumulation of sediment does not entail loss of identity. An identity can be surrounded
   by sediment, can be hindered by sediment, can have its capacity for manifestation reduced
   by sediment, and still be the identity it was; the conservation of identity (established in
   the part of the book that treated identity) is what makes this possible. Sediment threatens
400                                                    Chapter 36. Expression Cost and Sediment


   the viability of the relation; the identity itself is conserved.

   Remark 36.15 (Transformation Is Not Loss)

   A transformation of manifestations is not a loss of identity. The manifestations may change
   in structure, in realm, in mode; the identity is conserved. The distinction was drawn in
   the part of the book that resolved the tension between rigidity and dynamism; the present
   section applies it to the specific case of sediment and transformation. Transformation is a
   change in the manifestations with the identity conserved.



36.11        Limits and Continuations
Three continuations belong to later parts of the book, and they are indicated here so that the
reader knows where the present chapter’s account is taken up.
      First, the measurement of cost in a given case. The definition of cost is stated, and the three
kinds and three aspects are distinguished; the operational question of how to measure the cost
in a particular manifestation is developed in later parts of the book, where the framework’s
applications are developed.
      Second, the practical achievement of integration in a given case. The three structural forms
of integration are stated; the question of how integration is achieved in a particular relation is
left open. The framework states the possibility, not the method.
      Third, the relation between sediment and the balance criterion beyond what the definition
of viability states. The balance criterion, stated in the chapter that treated death and birth, is
the framework’s measure of the relation between an identity and the light it receives; the fuller
account of the relation between balance and sediment is developed in later parts.

A Question for Reflection
Consider something you have carried with you for a long time—a habit, a memory, a commitment,
a grief. Is it integrated into the rest of your life, or has it become lodged? What would it take for
it to be integrated? What does your answer tell you about the relation between what expression
costs and what expression leaves behind?

With this chapter, the framework’s treatment of the derivative concepts is complete. The next part
turns to the boundaries of philosophy and to the conclusion. The principles have been established,
the tensions resolved, the derivative concepts developed; the next part draws the boundary of the
framework’s claims and identifies the questions that remain open.
         Part IX

Boundaries and Conclusion




           403
Chapter 37

The Boundaries of Philosophy


Scope. This chapter states the boundaries of the framework and identifies the philosophical
questions it leaves open. It is a structural and meta-philosophical analysis: it says what the
framework does, what it does not do, and where its limits lie. Every term in the chapter is
structural or meta-philosophical; its claims concern the framework’s structure and its limits.
No normative, ethical, or evaluative claim is made, and no claim is made about the truth or
falsehood of any particular revelation. Where the chapter speaks of “open questions,” “limits,”
“boundaries,” or “revelation,” the terms are structural or meta-philosophical; no claim about
values, goods, or ends is intended or entailed.



37.1       A Scene

Consider a map. A map is not the territory it represents; it is a representation of the territory,
drawn for a purpose, at a scale, with a selection of what to include and what to leave out. A
topographic map shows elevation but not population; a political map shows borders but not
climate; a road map shows routes but not soil. Each map is accurate in its own terms, and
none is the territory. The map has a boundary—the edge of the sheet, the region it covers, the
features it represents—and the boundary is not a defect. It is what makes the map useful.
      Now consider philosophy. A philosophical framework is not the world it describes; it is a
description of the world, drawn for a purpose, at a level of abstraction, with a selection of what
to include and what to leave out. The framework developed in this book describes the structure
of identity and manifestation, the architecture of the seven realms, the character of light, the
rules of the contexts, and the concepts that follow from these. It does not describe everything; it
describes what its purpose requires, and it leaves out what its purpose does not.
      The scene poses a question. What are the boundaries of the framework? Where does its
description stop being useful, and where does it begin to be misleading? And what are the
questions it leaves open—the questions that its principles make visible but do not settle? The
present chapter answers these questions. Its answer is a statement of boundaries, and its principal
contribution is the enumeration of the open questions that the framework’s principles make
visible but do not resolve.
      The scene is the framework’s own scene. The book that precedes this chapter has described
the structure of identity and manifestation; the present chapter asks what the structure is for,
and what it is not for. The question is not idle. A framework that did not know its boundaries
would claim more than it can support, and its claims would be vulnerable to the very criticisms it
should have anticipated. The framework’s honesty about its limits is part of what the framework
is.

37.2. The Question                                                                              405


37.2     The Question

The preceding parts of the book have established the framework’s principles, resolved the
apparent tensions among them, and developed the derivative concepts. The part that treated
the foundation established the four-column framework; the parts that followed established the
seven realms, the fixed elements, the fluid element, the governing dynamics, the arguments, the
resolution of tensions, and the derivative concepts.
   The present part turns to the boundaries. The question is not what the framework claims; the
preceding parts have said what it claims. The question is what the framework is for, and what it
is not for; what it makes possible, and what it leaves to other inquiries; what it establishes, and
what it leaves open.
   Two aspects of the question must be distinguished.


The coherence aspect. What can be said of the framework as a whole? The chapter states
what can be said: the framework is coherent, its definitions are fixed, its arguments state their
premises, and its statuses are declared. The statement is not a claim that the framework is
closed or beyond revision; it is a claim about what the framework has achieved, at the strength
its arguments support.


The boundary aspect. What are the framework’s limits? The chapter states three principles
that fix the boundary—the autonomy of philosophical justification, the internal definition of the
framework’s concepts, and the non-export of meaning. It states the relation between philosophy
and revelation, and it identifies the open questions the framework leaves.
   The chapter proceeds as follows. It states the coherence of the existing architecture. It states
the framework’s role as a conceptual foundation. It states the three principles of the boundary.
It states the relation between philosophy and revelation. It identifies the open questions in three
groups: conceptual, argumentative, and metaphysical. It states the future of metaphysics, as the
framework sees it. It closes with a concluding note and with the epistemic status of its claims.



37.3     The Coherence of the Existing Architecture

Over thirty-five chapters, the book has built an architecture. What can be said of it is that
it is coherent: its definitions are fixed, its arguments state their premises, and its statuses are
declared. This is not a claim that it is closed or beyond revision. A philosophical architecture is
always open to correction, and the present chapter says what that means and what remains open.
   The coherence of the architecture is not a claim that every principle is true. It is a claim that
the principles are mutually consistent, that each is stated with its status, and that the arguments
for each are given in the chapters that establish them. A reader who rejects a principle has a
reason to reject the corresponding part of the architecture; the framework states the principles
and their statuses, so that the reader knows which parts are in question.
406                                                  Chapter 37. The Boundaries of Philosophy


   Remark 37.1 (Coherence Is Not Completeness)

   Coherence is not completeness. The framework is coherent in the sense that its principles
   are mutually consistent and its arguments are stated; it is not complete in the sense that
   every question it raises is answered. The open questions that this chapter identifies are
   the questions the framework raises but does not settle. The framework’s coherence is
   compatible with its incompleteness; the two are different virtues, and the framework has
   the first without claiming the second.


   Remark 37.2 (Coherence Is Not Finality)

   Coherence is not finality. A coherent framework can be revised; a framework that is not
   coherent cannot be revised, because there is no single structure to revise. The framework’s
   coherence is what makes revision possible; it is not a claim that no revision will ever
   be needed. The reader who finds a principle unpersuasive has a reason to revise the
   architecture; the framework invites the revision, and its coherence is what makes the
   invitation meaningful.



37.4     The Framework as a Conceptual Foundation
The framework supplies primitives, abstractions, and invariants for the structural description of
being and knowing. The supply is the framework’s role, and the role is stated in a remark.

Primitives. The framework’s primitives are identity, manifestation, light, realm, context,
expression, and cost. Each is defined in its proper place; each is used throughout the framework
as a term whose sense is fixed by its definition.

Abstractions. The framework’s abstractions are the four fundamental and three barzakhic
realms, the pseudo-identity, intra- category light and sediment, category-relative predication,
reflection, returning light, and signature. Each is a structural concept that the framework
introduces to describe a class of relations; each is defined by the framework’s principles.

Invariants. The framework’s invariants are identity rigidity and conservation, non-duplicability,
non-reduction of identity to manifestations, essential homogeneity of manifestation, non-necessity
of downward passage, expression as structural necessity, and the limits of the observer. Each
is a structural principle that the framework establishes; each is used as a fixed point in the
framework’s arguments.

   Remark 37.3 (The Role of the Framework)

   The role of the framework is to give fundamental principles and distinctions for the
   structural description of being and knowing. The phrase “philosophical operating system”
   would suggest a directive role; the structural role described above is the foundational role,
   and it is to be distinguished from any directive role. Value, normativity, and ethics belong
37.5. The Three Principles of the Boundary                                                      407


   to other inquiries.


   Remark 37.4 (The Framework’s Role Is Foundational, Not Directive)

   The framework’s role is foundational, not directive. It describes the structure of identity
   and manifestation; physics, chemistry, biology, and the other empirical inquiries answer
   their specific questions by their own methods. The framework states the conditions under
   which the inquiries can develop; the authority of those inquiries comes from their own
   methods. The distinction is structural: the framework’s role is foundational, and the
   inquiries it describes answer the specific questions by the methods proper to them.


   Remark 37.5 (Description and Prescription)

   The framework describes structure; it does not prescribe conduct. The distinction has been
   stated at the outset of the book (Introduction, “A Note on Description and Prescription”),
   and it is restated here because it bears on the framework’s role as a conceptual foundation.
   A structural description is not a normative prescription, but neither is it irrelevant to one.
   The description of the structure of identity and manifestation provides an ontological basis
   on which a normative prescription may be built; it does not itself supply that prescription,
   and it does not replace it. The relation between the two is one of grounding, not of identity:
   the description states what is, the prescription states what ought to be, and the transition
   from the first to the second requires a further premise that the description alone does not
   supply.
   Questions of ethics, value, and guidance belong to a different inquiry. The framework’s
   role is to describe the structure of identity and manifestation; the description of this
   structure provides the ontological basis on which a normative prescription may be built.
   The prescription itself belongs to the inquiry that undertakes it. A reader who seeks a
   normative theory will find it in that inquiry; a reader who seeks the structural ground on
   which a normative theory may be built will find that ground here.



37.5     The Three Principles of the Boundary
Three principles fix the boundary of the framework. They are stated here, with their statuses,
and they are the framework’s declaration of what it does and does not do.

   Principle 37.1 (Autonomy of Philosophical Justification)

   (A) The validity of a philosophical principle, within the domain of philosophy, does not
   depend on confirmation from outside philosophy. Autonomy is not exclusivity: the
   principle’s claim is about the method of philosophical justification, not about the extent
   of reality. Other domains have their own validity, and the principle’s internal autonomy is
   compatible with the reality of those domains.

   The principle was stated in the introduction to the book, and it has been observed throughout.
408                                                  Chapter 37. The Boundaries of Philosophy


Its statement here is its formal declaration, and its role is to fix the boundary: philosophical
justification is internal to philosophy, and no principle of the framework is justified by appeal to
an outside authority.
      The principle separates two things that are easily run together: autonomy and exclusivity.
Autonomy says that philosophy’s justification is internal to philosophy; exclusivity would say
that philosophy is the only domain of valid discourse. The framework holds the first and denies
the second. Philosophy is autonomous in its own domain; it does not claim that its domain is the
whole of reality. The question of telos, and the question of revelation, belong to other domains;
the framework neither subordinates those domains to philosophy nor subordinates philosophy to
them. The relation is one of distinction of domains, not of hierarchy of domains.

   Principle 37.2 (Internal Definition)

   (A) The concepts of the framework are defined and justified within its own system, from
   its premises.


      The principle states what the framework’s practice has been: every technical term is defined
within the book, and no argument depends on the reader’s acquaintance with any tradition. The
principle’s role is to fix the boundary of the framework’s vocabulary: the framework’s terms have
the sense the framework gives them, and no outside use of the terms determines their sense here.

   Principle 37.3 (Meaning Is Not Exported)

   (A) The use of a word or concept in another domain does not determine its philosophical
   sense here.

      The principle states what the framework’s practice has been: where a word has a use in
another domain, that use does not enter the framework’s definitions. The principle’s role is to
fix the boundary of the framework’s vocabulary against the vocabulary of other domains: the
framework’s terms are not hostage to the uses of the same words elsewhere.

   Remark 37.6 (Relation to Other Domains)

   Philosophy and other fields of inquiry are different undertakings, each answerable to its
   own standards. The book does not subordinate a field to philosophy or philosophy to a
   field. What is said in it is to be judged by the coherence, the discriminating power, and
   the strength of its own arguments. The relation is one of coexistence, not of hierarchy.


   Remark 37.7 (Where a Conflict Is Felt)

   If someone judges that a philosophical principle here is mistaken, the ground for revising
   it is a philosophical one: incoherence with other commitments, a better rival commitment,
   or the showing that the principle does no work. A principle is not revised because a
   statement made outside philosophy appears to differ from it. The framework does not
   claim that philosophy is immune to criticism from outside; it claims that the criticism, to
   be effective, must engage the framework’s own standards.
37.6. Philosophy and Revelation                                                                 409


37.6      Philosophy and Revelation

The distinction of domains that the previous section stated has a specific application that deserves
its own treatment: the relation between philosophy and revelation. The application is important
because the framework’s method is philosophical, and the reader who comes to it from a religious
tradition may wonder how the framework’s structural claims stand to what revelation reports.
The two belong to distinct domains, and the distinction is worth stating explicitly.
   Philosophy and revelation are two distinct domains, each with its own method and its own
kind of claim. Philosophy proceeds by argument: it states premises, draws inferences, and
assesses conclusions by coherence and explanatory power. Revelation proceeds by report: it
states what is disclosed, and it is received on the authority of the discloser. The two methods
are different, and the difference is not a deficiency in either. A philosophical argument is not a
revelation, and a revelation is not a philosophical argument; each is assessed by the standard
appropriate to its kind.
   The distinction of domains has three consequences for the framework, and each must be
stated.


First consequence: the framework’s principles are established by philosophical
argument. The framework’s principles are established by philosophical argument, and its
claims are philosophical claims, assessed by philosophical standards. What revelation reports
belongs to revelation’s own domain; the framework describes the structure that revelation’s
reports concern, and it does so by philosophical argument.


Second consequence: revelation’s truth belongs to revelation’s own inquiry. What
revelation reports belongs to revelation’s own domain, and the assessment of its truth belongs
to the inquiry that revelation itself authorizes. A reader who holds that revelation is true
and a reader who holds that it is false are both free to hold their positions; the framework’s
structural claims are compatible with either, because they concern the structure of identity and
manifestation, not the content of revelation’s reports.


Third consequence: the framework’s structural claims and revelation’s reports are
compatible. The framework’s structural claims and revelation’s reports can be held together
without contradiction, provided the two are kept in their proper domains. The framework
describes the structure of identity and manifestation; revelation reports the telos and the norms
that the structure serves. A reader can hold both. What the framework excludes is the confusion
of the two: the treating of a structural claim as if it were a revelation, or the treating of a
revelation as if it were a structural claim. The confusion is what the distinction of domains is
meant to prevent.
   The relation between philosophy and revelation is therefore one of complementarity, not of
rivalry. The two are not competitors for the same territory; they are different inquiries into
different aspects of the same reality. Philosophy asks how the structure of what is holds together;
revelation reports what the structure is for. The first does not entail the second, and the second
410                                                   Chapter 37. The Boundaries of Philosophy


does not replace the first. A complete account of reality would need both; the framework offers
the first.

   Remark 37.8 (Revelation and the Philosophical Method)

   Revelation is a report, and its authority is the authority of the discloser, not of an argument.
   The framework’s method is argumentative, and the assessment of revelation’s truth belongs
   to the inquiry that revelation itself authorizes. The framework describes the structure
   that revelation’s reports concern; the comparison of its structural claims with the reports
   of a particular revelation belongs to a different genre from the systematic reconstruction
   this book offers, and the separate treatise on the dialogues undertakes part of it. The
   comparison is not an argument for or against either side, and the framework’s principles
   do not depend on it.


   Remark 37.9 (The Framework’s Method and the Question of Truth)

   The framework’s method is the method of philosophy, and the question of revelation’s
   truth belongs to the inquiry that revelation itself authorizes. The framework’s claim about
   revelation is that the domain is real and distinct; it is not a claim that the question of
   truth is undecidable, and it is not a position on any particular answer. A philosophical
   claim about a domain and a philosophical abstention about a domain are different things:
   the framework makes claims about its own domain and abstains from claims about others,
   and the abstention is a consequence of its method, not a position on the matter.



37.7         The Open Questions: Conceptual
The framework’s principles make visible a set of questions that the framework does not settle.
The questions are philosophical, and they are marked with the appropriate status. They fall into
three groups. The first group is conceptual: the questions about the framework’s concepts and
their relations.


First question: the structural conditions of joint realizability of viabilities. Under
what structural conditions can two viabilities be jointly realized in the same realm? The
framework states the structural conditions of joint realizability; it makes no claim about which of
two competing viabilities ought to be preferred, nor about any normative ranking among them.
((Q))


Second question: the structural boundary between the reduction of viability and
the singularity. Where does a reduction of structural viability become the singularity? The
framework distinguishes the gradient of viability from the threshold of the singularity, but the
exact boundary is left open. ((Q))


Third question: the conceptual relation of light and expression. What exactly is it for
expression to be a conveying of light? The framework states that light is the conveyor of effect
37.8. The Open Questions: Argumentative                                                       411


and that expression is the enactment of the identity; the exact conceptual relation between the
two is left open. ((Q))


Fourth question: the relation between structural light and the divine light of the
traditions. What is the relation between the framework’s “structural light”—the condition
of possibility of relation—and the “divine light” of the theological traditions? The framework
states its structural sense and marks it as a homonym, not a synonym, of the theological sense
(Chapter 12, Remark on Structural and Theological Light); the exact relation between the two
senses is left open. ((Q))
   These four questions are conceptual: they concern the framework’s concepts and their
relations. They are the questions the framework raises but does not settle, and they are stated
at exactly that strength.

   Remark 37.10 (Why These Questions Are Open)

   The four questions are open because the framework does not have the resources to settle
   them at the strength its arguments support. The framework’s claim is that the questions are
   real questions—that they arise from the framework’s principles—and that the framework’s
   principles make them visible without answering them. A reader who settles one of the
   questions has extended the framework; a reader who shows that the question is not real
   has shown a limit of the framework’s formulation.



37.8        The Open Questions: Argumentative

The second group is argumentative: the questions about the framework’s arguments and their
premises.


Fifth question: the relation among self-awareness, consciousness, awareness, and
the subject. What is the relation among the three structural concepts and the subject? The
framework defines the three concepts, but the relation among them and the subject is left open,
including the question whether consciousness requires experience. ((Q))


Sixth question: the conceptual foundations of the thresholds and of the balance
criterion. What are the conceptual foundations of the thresholds and of the balance criterion?
The framework states the criterion and the thresholds; their conceptual foundations are left open.
((Q))


Seventh question: whether the principle of contextual manifestational capacity and
the criterion of manifestational adequacy can be given independent definition and
support. The framework states the principle and the criterion as proposals; whether they can
be given independent definition and support is left open. ((Q))
412                                                  Chapter 37. The Boundaries of Philosophy


Eighth question: the relation among the aspects of cost. What is the exact relation
among the three aspects of cost—extent, reach, and duration? The framework distinguishes the
three, but their relation is left open. ((Q))


Ninth question: the bridge between structural description and normative prescription.
How can the structural description of the framework serve as the basis for a normative prescription?
The framework states that description grounds prescription without replacing it (Remark on
Description and Prescription, and the Introduction’s note on the same subject), but the exact
form of the bridge—what further premise is needed, and what kind of premise it must be—is left
open. ((Q))
      These five questions are argumentative: they concern the framework’s arguments and their
premises. They are the questions the framework raises but does not settle, and they are stated
at exactly that strength.

   Remark 37.11 (Why These Questions Are Open)

   The five questions are open because the arguments for the relevant principles are given
   at the strength they have, and the arguments do not settle the further questions. The
   framework’s claim is that the arguments are given, that their premises are stated, and that
   the further questions are questions that the arguments raise but do not settle. A reader
   who strengthens an argument, or who shows that a premise can be given independent
   support, has extended the framework; a reader who shows that an argument is invalid has
   shown a limit of the framework’s formulation.



37.9       The Open Questions: Metaphysical

The third group is metaphysical: the questions about the framework’s ontology and its structural
claims.


Tenth question: the structural possibility and ontological standing of the realization
of identities in the barzakhic realms. What is the structural possibility and ontological
standing of such realization? The framework states the structural possibility; the ontological
standing is left open, and the question is marked as speculation where specific. ((S))


Eleventh question: the particular direct relations among realms. What are the
particular direct relations among the realms? The framework states that direct relations are
possible (the non-necessity of downward passage); the particular relations are left open. ((Q))


Twelfth question: whether the doctrine that identity is more than signature can be
given further support. The doctrine is a commitment of the framework; whether it can be
given further support—by argument, or by showing that a framework without it explains the
same things as well—is left open. ((Q))
37.10. The Future of Metaphysics                                                               413


   These three questions are metaphysical: they concern the framework’s ontology and its
structural claims. They are the questions the framework raises but does not settle, and they are
stated at exactly that strength.

   Remark 37.12 (Why These Questions Are Open)

   The three questions are open because the framework’s ontology is stated at the strength
   its arguments support, and the further questions are questions that the ontology raises but
   does not settle. The framework’s claim is that the ontology is stated, that its structural
   claims are argued, and that the further questions are questions that the ontology raises but
   does not resolve. A reader who settles one of the questions has extended the framework;
   a reader who shows that the question is not real has shown a limit of the framework’s
   ontology.



37.10      The Future of Metaphysics
The future of the framework depends on the capacity of the system itself to pose, analyze, and
resolve metaphysical questions: to sharpen its definitions, strengthen its arguments, and remove
what does not cohere. It is not a future that waits upon developments in other domains. The
framework’s claim is that philosophy’s development is internal to philosophy; the framework’s
future is the future of its own capacity to refine itself.

   Remark 37.13 (The Living Architecture)

   The architecture is not a static hierarchy in which higher principles simply dictate to lower
   ones. When a conceptual difficulty appears at one level, it can lead to refinement of a
   principle at another, and the refined principle in turn changes what can be said below.
   This is what keeps the system revisable. The framework is a living architecture, not a
   finished monument.

   Remark 37.14 (The Future Is Not the Future of Science)

   The framework’s future is not the future of science. The two are different undertakings,
   each answerable to its own standards. The framework does not wait upon science to
   answer its questions; science does not wait upon the framework to answer its questions.
   The two coexist, and each develops by its own methods. The framework’s future is the
   future of its own capacity to pose, analyze, and resolve metaphysical questions; it is not
   the future of any other domain.



37.11      Limits and Continuations
Three continuations belong to the framework’s extensions and to other inquiries, and they are
indicated here so that the reader knows where the present chapter’s account ends.
   First, the open questions the chapter identifies remain open. They are stated at the strength
the framework’s arguments support; the settlement of any one of them belongs to an extension
414                                                    Chapter 37. The Boundaries of Philosophy


of the framework. A reader who answers one of the questions extends the framework.
      Second, the three principles of the boundary are stated, and their roles are distinguished.
The detailed account of how they interact—whether one is more basic than another, whether
they are independent, what follows from their combination—belongs to a separate inquiry. The
present chapter states the principles; the interaction remains open.
      Third, the relation between the framework’s boundaries and the boundaries of other philosoph-
ical frameworks, and between the framework’s boundaries and those of other inquiries—including
revelation—belongs to a comparative inquiry. The chapter states the framework’s boundaries and
its relation to other domains; the specific comparison is a different question, and it is developed
in the separate treatise on the dialogues.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a question the framework raises but does not settle—one of the twelve open questions, or
a question of your own. What would it take to settle it? Would the settlement be a new principle,
a new argument, or a new concept? And consider a question that belongs to revelation—a
question of telos, or of the truth of what revelation reports. What does the difference between
the two kinds of question tell you about the relation between the framework’s boundaries and its
future?

The next chapter concludes the book. It states the architecture and its open questions, and it
offers a final statement of what the framework is and what it is not. The present chapter has
stated the boundaries; the next chapter states the conclusion that the boundaries make possible.
Chapter 38

Conclusion: The Architecture and Its Open Questions


Scope. This chapter concludes the book. It states what the framework has established, what it
has not established, and what it leaves open. It is a structural and meta-philosophical analysis: it
says what the framework is, and what it is not. Its claims are structural; where the chapter speaks
of “architecture,” “open questions,” or “horizon,” these are structural terms. The framework’s
task is the description of structure; the questions of values, goods, and ends belong to distinct
inquiries that the framework is designed to serve, not to replace.


38.1     A Scene
Consider a cathedral that has been under construction for centuries. Each generation added
something: a chapel, a tower, a stained-glass window, a restoration. The cathedral is not finished;
it is not meant to be finished in any single generation’s lifetime. It is a work that continues, and
each generation that works on it sees more of what it is than the generation before.
   The comparison is not perfect. A cathedral is a physical thing, and its construction has
a terminus that the framework’s construction does not. But the comparison has one point:
the framework, like the cathedral, is not offered as a finished monument. It is offered as an
architecture that the present book has built to a certain point, and that the inquiry that follows
will continue to build. The book’s final chapter states where the construction stands, what it has
built, and what remains to be built.
   The scene poses a question. What has the framework established? What has it not established?
And what does it leave open? The present chapter answers these questions. Its answer is a
statement of the architecture, its boundary, and its open horizon. It is the book’s closing, and it
is the inquiry’s continuation.


38.2     The Unfinished Inquiry
Philosophy has always been an inquiry, often a fractured one. This book offers a language for
part of it. Its architecture proceeds from the four-column framework of cognition, to the seven
realms, to identities and manifestations, to light, to the rules of the realms, to the arguments, to
the resolution of tensions, to the derivative concepts, to the boundaries of philosophy, and to the
open horizons.
   The architecture is the book’s contribution, and it is offered as a contribution to an inquiry
that continues. The reader who has followed the argument from beginning to end has seen the
architecture built, part by part, each part presupposing only what has come before. The reader
who has entered in the middle has seen one part in its context. Both readers have seen the same
architecture, and both are invited to continue the inquiry that the architecture makes possible.

                                                415
416                           Chapter 38. Conclusion: The Architecture and Its Open Questions


   Remark 38.1 (The Inquiry Is Not Finished)

   The inquiry is not finished. The book states its claims at the strength its arguments
   support, and it states the questions it does not settle. The reader who finds a claim
   unpersuasive, or a question unresolved, has located a place where the inquiry continues.
   The framework’s honesty about its incompleteness is part of what the framework is.


   Remark 38.2 (The Inquiry Is Not Fractured by the Framework)

   The inquiry is not fractured by the framework. The framework offers a language for part
   of philosophy; the philosophical inquiry has other languages and other voices, and the
   framework is one contribution among them. The framework is offered in the hope that it
   helps; it is not offered as the final word.



38.3       The Central Question
The central question of the book is not “What is identity?” but “How does an identity express
itself in manifestations, in many realms, while remaining one?”
      The distinction between the two questions is not small. The first asks for a definition; the
second asks for a structure. The first has been answered in many ways, each of which captures an
aspect and misses another. The second is the question the framework’s architecture is designed
to answer, and its answer is not a definition but an account of the relations among identity,
manifestation, light, and realm.
      The framework’s answer is that the identity expresses itself through light, in manifestations,
across realms, according to the rules of the realms, while remaining one because it is a single
source whose unity is not the unity of its products. The classical paradoxes of identity are
dissolved, not solved, by showing where levels have been run together: the persistence of a thing
with its manifestations, the unity of a source with the plurality of its products, the rigidity of
identity with the dynamism of expression.
      This is a metaphysical result. It concerns the structure of identity and manifestation; the
questions of value belong to distinct inquiries that the framework is designed to serve. The reader
who has followed the argument has seen the result, and the reader who has not is directed to the
chapters that establish it.


38.4       Three Conclusions
The book has established three conclusions. They are stated here as the framework’s principal
contributions, with their statuses.


First conclusion: identity and manifestation are two distinct levels. The manifestation
is not the identity and not unrelated to it; it is a real appearance in its own realm, homogeneous
in essence with its source. The distinction is what dissolves the classical paradoxes of identity;
the framework’s account of conservation, non-duplicability, and expression is built on it. ((T))
38.5. The Boundary of the Framework                                                              417


Second conclusion: the plurality of manifestations is compatible with the unity of
identity, and that unity is not the aggregate of appearances. Aggregating manifestations,
even compatible ones, does not reach the numerical unity of the source. The unity is the unity
of a source, not the unity of a pattern shared by many things; the plurality is the plurality
of products, not the plurality of sources. The framework’s account of expression, of recursive
manifestation, and of the impossibility of super-identity is built on this distinction. ((T))


Third conclusion: viability is a structural relation between an identity and its
manifestations in a realm, and not a criterion for counting identities or fixing
their nature. It is the three-fold structural character of that relation—fidelity, sustainability,
recoverability—and it admits of degrees, where identity does not. Viability is a descriptive
concept: it names a structural character of the relation between identity and manifestation, and
the inquiry into value is a distinct inquiry that the framework is designed to serve, not to replace.
The framework’s account of expression cost, of sediment, and of the balance criterion is built on
this concept. ((A))
   The three conclusions are not separate. They are three aspects of one result: identity is one,
its manifestations are many, and the relation between them is the relation of expression, which
viability measures. The first names the distinction; the second names the compatibility; the third
names the measure. Together, they state what the framework has established.

   Remark 38.3 (The Conclusions Are Structural)

   The three conclusions are structural features of the relation between identity and man-
   ifestation. They do not rank identity above manifestation, or unity above plurality, or
   viability as a good; they state the structural order through which the framework’s account
   of the relations is built. The framework’s account of the relations, and its account of
   expression, cost, and sediment, are built on these structural features.


   Remark 38.4 (The Conclusions Are Relative to Their Premises)

   The three conclusions are (T) or (A) relative to the premises on which they rest. The first
   is (T) relative to the definitions of identity and manifestation; the second is (T) relative to
   the principle of expression and the impossibility of super-identity; the third is (A) as a
   commitment of the framework. A reader who rejects one of the premises has a reason to
   reject the corresponding conclusion, and the framework states the premises so that the
   reader knows which conclusion is in question.



38.5     The Boundary of the Framework
The framework’s domain is metaphysics. Its subject is the structure of identity and manifestation,
the architecture of realms, the character of light, the rules of the contexts, and the derivative
concepts that follow from these. Questions of how anything ought to be, what is good, what is
right, and what is worth pursuing belong to ethics, value, and normativity—distinct inquiries
that the framework is designed to serve, not to replace.
418                          Chapter 38. Conclusion: The Architecture and Its Open Questions


      The boundary is not a deficiency. It is what the framework is: a description of structure.
Where the framework reaches its limit, the limit is marked, and the question is marked as open
((Q)), belonging to the inquiry that undertakes it. The boundary is what makes the framework
useful: it tells the reader what to expect, and what not to expect, from the framework’s claims.

   Remark 38.5 (The Boundary Is Structural, Not Arbitrary)

   The boundary is structural, not arbitrary. It follows from the framework’s method: the
   framework’s principles are established within philosophy, from philosophical arguments,
   and they concern the structure of being and knowing, not the norms of action or the
   values of life. The boundary is what the framework’s method requires, not an arbitrary
   limitation imposed from outside.


   Remark 38.6 (The Boundary Is a Distinction of Undertakings)

   The boundary is a distinction of undertakings, not a ranking. Metaphysics and ethics
   are different inquiries, each answerable to its own standards. The framework is one of
   them—a structural description of being and knowing—and the ethical and normative
   inquiries belong to their own domains. The framework’s claim is that the two are different
   undertakings, not that one is superior to the other.



38.6       The Humility of the Philosopher
The book ends in humility, grounded in the limits of the observer. It is a proposal. Even the
claim that there are four fundamental grades of multiplicity is an estimate. The inquiry continues
not because a final answer has been found, but because a precise question has been put.
      The humility is not a rhetorical gesture. It is a structural consequence of the framework’s
account of the observer. The observer is finite; the contexts are not finite in number; the
manifestations are products of identity and receiving realm; the effects are conveyed through
configurations. Together, these facts make exhaustive knowledge impossible, and they make
every claim a claim at a certain strength, to be revised as the inquiry continues.

   Remark 38.7 (The Humility Is the Recognition of a Structural Limit)

   The humility is the recognition of a structural limit, not a denial that knowledge is real.
   The framework claims that complete knowledge is impossible for a finite observer, and
   that partial knowledge, at a certain strength, is what such an observer can achieve. The
   limit is structural: it belongs to the relation between a finite observer and an identity, not
   to the identity itself, and not to the object of knowledge.


   Remark 38.8 (The Humility Is Not Despair)

   The humility is not despair. The framework claims that the inquiry continues, and that
   each generation that works on the framework sees more of what it is than the generation
   before. The humility is the recognition that the work is not finished; it is not a denial
38.7. Final Remarks                                                                           419


   that the work is worth doing.



38.7     Final Remarks
The book is offered as an independent philosophical system. Its worth is to be measured by its
coherence, by the discrimination its distinctions make possible, and by the strength of its own
arguments, and by nothing outside them.
   The framework is a description of the structure of identity and manifestation. The inquiry
into how anything ought to be, what is good, what is right, and what is worth pursuing belongs
to ethics, value, and normativity—distinct inquiries that the framework is designed to serve, not
to replace.
   The reader who has followed the argument from beginning to end has seen the architecture
built, part by part, each part presupposing only what has come before. The reader who has
entered in the middle has seen one part in its context. Both readers have seen the same
architecture, and both are invited to continue the inquiry that the architecture makes possible.

   Remark 38.9 (The Book Is a Proposal)

   The book is a proposal, not a finished system. Its worth is to be measured by what it
   makes possible: the questions it raises, the distinctions it draws, the arguments it states.
   A reader who finds the proposal useful has found what the book offers; a reader who does
   not has located a place where the inquiry continues.


   Remark 38.10 (The Inquiry Continues)

   The inquiry continues. The book has stated what it has established, what it has not
   established, and what it leaves open. The open questions are real questions, and they
   are invitations to the reader to continue the inquiry that the framework makes possible.
   The book’s final word is not an answer but a question: what will the reader make of the
   framework, and what will the framework make of the reader?
