Appendix A

Viability Metaethics: A Prospectus


Scope. This appendix is a prospectus for a dependent treatise, Viability Metaethics: The
Architecture of Moral Systems. It states what the treatise will undertake, what it will not
undertake, and how it is related to the framework of this book. It is not a treatment of the
subject; it is a map of the treatment. Its claims are structural; where the appendix is silent on
questions of value, the silence is not a denial but a recognition that the structural description is
not the whole of what can be said.



A.1      What Viability Metaethics Is

Viability metaethics is a metaethical inquiry. It does not ask what is good, right, or obligatory;
it asks what a moral system is, what its fundamental entities are, how those entities depend on
one another, and what formal structures a moral system can take. Its subject is the architecture
of moral systems, not their content.
   The distinction between metaethics and ethics is the distinction between the structure of a
system and the system’s claims. Ethics states what ought to be; metaethics states what a system
of oughts is, and how it is built. The present appendix is a prospectus for the second; it does not
undertake the first.

   Remark A.1 (The Name)

   The name “viability metaethics” does not mean that the framework regards viability as
   the good. It means that the framework borrows, selectively and explicitly, the tools and
   concepts of the philosophy of viability developed in this book, and uses them to describe
   the architecture of moral systems. The borrowing is methodological, not normative: the
   framework does not claim that a moral system is good because it is viable, and it does not
   claim that viability is the end that a moral system serves. Whether viability has value,
   and what value it has, is a question the treatise will leave to another inquiry.




A.2      The Position of Viability Metaethics in the Four-Level Ar-
         chitecture

The framework of this book distinguishes four levels of inquiry, and viability metaethics belongs
to the second.

                                                423
424                                               Appendix A. Viability Metaethics: A Prospectus


      Level      Domain                         Function

      1          Philosophy                     Produces general principles: ontology, epistemol-
                                                ogy, logic.
      2          Viability Metaethics           Describes the architecture of moral systems: the
                                                fundamental entities, the order of priority among
                                                them, the formal space of possible systems.
      3          Foundational Ethics            Produces normative principles that refer to the
                                                architecture described at level 2.
      4          Applied Ethics                 Produces judgments in particular cases, within
                                                the principles of level 3.

      Viability metaethics is neither philosophy (level 1) nor foundational ethics (level 3) nor applied
ethics (level 4). It is the level at which the architecture that foundational ethics presupposes is
described. Its relation to philosophy is one of borrowing: it takes from the philosophy of viability
the analytical tools it needs. Its relation to foundational ethics is one of grounding: it provides
the structural conditions that foundational ethics presupposes. The two relations are distinct,
and the treatise keeps them apart.

   Remark A.2 (The Intermediate Position)

   The position of viability metaethics is intermediate, and the intermediate position is not a
   compromise. It is a structural necessity: a normative system presupposes an architecture,
   and the architecture cannot be described from within the system. A metaethical inquiry
   describes the architecture from a standpoint that is neither the system nor the philosophy
   that the system borrows from. The intermediate position is the position from which the
   architecture is visible.


A.3        The Three Tasks of Viability Metaethics
Viability metaethics has three tasks, and the treatise will undertake them in order.

Task 1: Identifying and Defining the Fundamental Entities. The first task is to identify
the entities that every moral system presupposes, and to define them without circularity. The
entities include the individual, the effect, the act, the self and the other, the domain of ethics,
and the moral system. Each is defined structurally, and the definition of each is assessed by the
criterion that no definition may take its explanatory core from an entity that is itself derived
from what is being defined.

Task 2: Mapping the Order of Priority. The second task is to map the relations of
priority among the fundamental entities. The relations are of three kinds: methodological priority
(philosophy with respect to ethics), explanatory priority (ethics with respect to culture, society,
politics, and art), and definitional priority (the individual with respect to the collective). The
map is the sieve through which moral systems are assessed: a system that defines its fundamental
entities by their derivatives does not pass through the sieve.
A.4. The Two-Level Formal Structure                                                             425


Task 3: Describing the Formal Space of Possible Moral Systems. The third task is to
describe the formal space of possible moral systems, not to choose among them. A moral system
can be per-member or per-group at the level of its foundational function; it can be act-based
or rule-based; it can be monistic or pluralistic. The treatise describes each type, its formal
properties, and its structural costs. The choice among them is a normative choice, and it belongs
to foundational ethics, not to metaethics.

    Remark A.3 (The Tasks Are Distinct)

   The three tasks are distinct, and the treatise will not run them together. Task 1 is
    definitional; Task 2 is structural; Task 3 is taxonomic. A reader who wishes to assess the
    treatise can assess each task separately, and the treatise states the status of each claim it
    makes.



A.4       The Two-Level Formal Structure
The treatise will state the formal structure of a moral system in two levels. The first level
determines the domain; the second level determines the status.


Level 1: The Domain. The first level specifies which acts fall within the domain of moral
evaluation. It is stated as a function that takes a set of possible acts and a set of contexts and
returns the subset of acts that are candidates for moral evaluation in those contexts. At this
level, no judgment of good or bad is made; the level determines only what is a candidate for
judgment.


Level 2: The Status. The second level assigns a status to each act in the domain: obligatory,
forbidden, or permitted. The status is a function of the act and the context; it is not an intrinsic
and permanent property of the act. The status is what a moral system assigns, not what the act
is in itself.
    The two levels are distinct, and the distinction is what allows the treatise to describe a moral
system without committing itself to the system’s content. A system that assigns different statuses
to the same act in different contexts is a system with a context-relative Level 2; a system that
assigns the same status to the same act regardless of context is a system with a context-invariant
Level 2. Both are possible; the treatise describes both, and chooses neither.

    Remark A.4 (The Formal Structure Is Not a Normative Claim)

   The formal structure is not a normative claim. The treatise does not say that a system
    ought to have a Level 1 and a Level 2; it says that every system that has been examined
    can be described in terms of the two levels. The description is structural, not prescriptive.
   A reader who takes the formal structure as a normative claim has misread the treatise; a
    reader who takes it as a description of the form of a moral system has read it correctly.
426                                              Appendix A. Viability Metaethics: A Prospectus


A.5       The Core Principles

The treatise will state five core principles, each of which describes a structural feature of
metaethical inquiry. The principles are stated here in summary form; the treatise will develop
them in detail.

  1. The sieve, not the food. Metaethics produces no value judgments; it produces criteria
        by which systems are distinguished as consistent or inconsistent with the architecture it
        describes.

  2. Discovery, not translation. Metaethics discovers and organizes its own concepts; it does
        not translate philosophy wholesale into ethics.

  3. Ethics is derived, not impure. Ethics is grounded in philosophy but is not reducible to it.
        The relation is one of origin, not of contamination.

  4. The will is trans-categorical. If the will were located in one of the categories, the distribution
        of light would be meaningless, and structural attribution would be impossible. The trans-
        categorical character of the will is the condition of possibility of any attribution and any
        subsequent evaluation.

  5. Inclusion, not restriction to agents. The domain of ethics is not restricted to agents (those
        who possess a will); it is restricted to those who can be affected. A river, an ecosystem,
        and an institution can be affected. The condition of entry is twofold: a change in the space
        of manifestation of an identity, and the origin of that change in a will.

   Remark A.5 (The Principles Are Structural)

   The five principles are structural. They describe what metaethical inquiry is and how it
   proceeds; they do not prescribe what a moral system ought to contain. A reader who takes
   the principles as prescriptions has misread them; a reader who takes them as descriptions
   of the form of metaethical inquiry has read them correctly.



A.6       The Boundary of Metaethics

The treatise will stop where content begins. The choice between per-member and per-group, the
assignment of moral weight to an ecosystem relative to a human being, the criteria by which the
obligatory, the forbidden, and the permitted are produced—these are all tasks of foundational
ethics, not of metaethics.
      Metaethics shows only that these choices are possible, what structural costs each has, and
which axioms each is consistent with. It does not make the choices. The distinction between the
possible and the chosen is the distinction between metaethics and foundational ethics, and the
treatise keeps it throughout.
A.7. The Relation to This Book                                                                427


   Remark A.6 (The Boundary Is Not a Limitation)

   The boundary is not a limitation of the treatise. It is the condition of its precision. A
   treatise that claimed to make metaethical choices and foundational choices by a single
   method would be claiming more than its method can deliver. The boundary is what makes
   the metaethical claims assessable: the reader knows exactly what kind of claim is being
   made, and therefore what kind of criticism is appropriate.


   Remark A.7 (The Ground Beyond the Boundary)

   The metaethical architecture is real, and the treatise’s claim is that the architecture is
   invariant and describable. But the architecture is not self-grounded. The architecture
   points beyond itself to the ground that the treatise does not describe. The traditions speak
   of the ground of the ethical order as the command through which the order is established,
   and as the wisdom through which the order is sustained. The framework does not claim
   that its architectural description is that command or that wisdom, and it does not claim
   that they are unreal. It claims that the architecture is real, and that the architecture
   points beyond itself. The distinction is the distinction between the architecture and the
   ground of the architecture; it is kept throughout the treatise.



A.7     The Relation to This Book

Viability metaethics is a dependent treatise. It presupposes the framework of this book, but it is
not a part of it. The present book is a work of metaphysics; the dependent treatise is a work of
metaethics. The two are related as the body of the book is related to a domain of inquiry that
the body makes possible, not as the body is related to a part of itself.
   The treatise will develop the metaethical framework in a systematic form: it will state the
definitions, the priority map, the formal structure, the taxonomy, and the open questions. It will
not repeat the framework of this book; it will presuppose it. The reader who wishes to assess
the treatise is directed to this book for the framework, and to the treatise for the metaethical
development.

   Remark A.8 (The Direction of Dependence)

   The dependence runs from this book to the treatise, not from the treatise to this book.
   The book’s claims do not depend on the treatise; the treatise’s claims depend on the book.
   The relation is one of grounding, not of mutual support. The reader who accepts the book
   should accept the framework that the treatise presupposes; the reader who does not accept
   the book is not addressed by the treatise.



A.8     What This Appendix Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this appendix are deliberately deferred.
428                                               Appendix A. Viability Metaethics: A Prospectus


      First, the appendix does not develop the treatise’s arguments. It states the tasks, the formal
structure, the core principles, and the boundary; it does not argue for them. The arguments are
the subject of the treatise.
      Second, the appendix does not settle the question of which moral system the architecture
favors. The architecture is compatible with several systems; the choice among them belongs to
foundational ethics, and the appendix does not make the choice.
      Third, the appendix does not address the relation between the metaethical architecture and
the ethical realities that the traditions name. The architecture points beyond itself to those
realities; the appendix states the pointing, and leaves the realities to the inquiry that undertakes
them.
      Fourth, the appendix does not claim to have described the ground of the metaethical
architecture. It claims to have described the structure of the architecture, and the structure
points beyond itself to the ground that the appendix does not describe. The distinction is the
distinction between the architecture and the ground of the architecture; it is kept throughout
the appendix, and it is stated here as the appendix’s explicit limit.

architecture is most easily overlooked, and why? What does its being overlooked tell you about
the relation between the architecture and the system?

Appendix B

A Structural Anthropology: Nafs and Ruh


Scope. This appendix is a structural description of the human subject, using the framework’s
structural vocabulary. It defines nafs as the exigency of the material category, ruh as the light of
identity from the higher category, and the self as the meeting-point of the two. It describes the
three structural stages of the nafs, and it states the structural consequence for the self’s task.
It is not a scriptural exegesis, not a theological anthropology, and not an ethical prescription.
Where it cites scriptural verses, the citation is offered as structural evidence, not as a ground of
justification.


B.1      What This Appendix Is and Is Not
This appendix is a structural description. It uses the vocabulary of the framework—category,
light, identity, manifestation, the self, the material realm, the higher realms—to describe the
human subject. The description is offered as a structural account; it does not claim to exhaust
what the human subject is, and it does not claim to replace the inquiries that undertake the
subject from other angles.
    The appendix is not a scriptural exegesis. Where it cites a verse, the citation is offered as
structural evidence: the verse is cited because it describes the same structure that the framework
describes, not because the framework’s structure is derived from the verse. The framework’s
claim is established by its own arguments, stated in the body of the book; the verses are cited to
show that the structure is not the invention of the framework.
    The appendix is not a theological anthropology. It does not claim to describe the essence of
the soul, the mode of its creation, or its relation to the divine. Those questions belong to other
inquiries, and the appendix neither answers them nor forecloses them.
    The appendix is not an ethical prescription. It describes a structural condition of the human
subject; it does not prescribe what the subject ought to do. The distinction between the structural
description and the ethical prescription is the distinction between what the self is and what the
self ought to be; the appendix keeps the distinction throughout.

   Remark B.1 (The Appendix Presupposes the Framework)

   The appendix presupposes the framework of this book, and it uses the framework’s
   structural vocabulary. It does not repeat the framework’s arguments; it applies them
   to the human subject. The reader who has not read the body of the book will find the
   appendix compressed; the reader who has read the body will find the appendix a natural
   extension of the framework’s claims about identity, light, and the realms.

B.2. The Vocabulary of the Appendix                                                              431


B.2       The Vocabulary of the Appendix

The appendix uses three terms in a technical sense, and the sense of each must be fixed at the
outset.


Nafs. The exigency of the material category. The nafs is the structural pull that the material
realm exercises on the self: the pull toward what is discrete, localized, and successive; the pull
toward self-preservation, appetite, and the immediate. The nafs is not a substance; it is a
structural exigency.


Ruh. The light of identity from the higher category. The ruh is the structural light by which
the self is connected to its source in the higher realms: the light of the identity that the self is,
and the light of the source from which the identity comes. The ruh is not a substance; it is a
structural light.


The self. The meeting-point of the two. The self is the structural locus at which the exigency
of the material category and the light of the higher category meet. The self is not reducible to
the nafs, and not reducible to the ruh; it is the point at which the two are related.
   The three terms are structural, and the appendix uses them in the structural sense. The
terms have histories in the traditions, and the appendix does not claim that its structural sense is
the only sense the terms can bear. It claims that the structural sense is the sense the framework
needs, and that the structural sense is sufficient for the appendix’s purpose.

   Remark B.2 (The Terms Are Not Substances)

   The nafs, the ruh, and the self are not substances. They are structural conditions. The
   nafs is an exigency, not a thing; the ruh is a light, not a thing; the self is a meeting-point,
   not a thing. The framework uses the terms as structural labels, and the reader who takes
   them as substances has misread the appendix. The distinction is the distinction between
   the structure and the substance; it is kept throughout.


   Remark B.3 (The Terms Are Related to the Framework’s Categories)

   The nafs is related to the Material Manifestation: it is the exigency that the material
   realm exercises on the self. The ruh is related to the light that the framework describes: it
   is the light by which the self is connected to the higher realms. The self is related to the
   Relational Manifestation: it is the locus at which the material exigency and the higher
   light meet, and at which the structural awareness that the Relational Manifestation makes
   possible is realized. The three relations are structural, and the appendix develops them in
   the sections that follow.
432                                         Appendix B. A Structural Anthropology: Nafs and Ruh


B.3        Nafs: The Exigency of the Material Category
The nafs is the exigency of the material category. The material category, as the body of the
book described it, is the realm of things that are discrete, localized, and successive; its rules are
causality, temporality, and discreteness. The nafs is the pull that this realm exercises on the self:
the pull toward the discrete, the localized, the successive; the pull toward what preserves the
material manifestation; the pull toward appetite, immediate satisfaction, and self-assertion.
      The nafs is not a defect. It is a structural exigency of the material manifestation, and
without it no living being would survive. A being that had no nafs would have no pull toward
self-preservation, no appetite for food, no response to threat. The nafs is the structural condition
of the material manifestation’s persistence.
      But the nafs is not the whole of the self. The self is not reducible to the nafs; the self is the
meeting-point of the nafs and the ruh. The nafs is the pull of the material category; the ruh is
the light of the higher category; the self is the locus at which the two are related.

   Remark B.4 (The Nafs Is Not Evil)

   The nafs is not intrinsically evil. It is the exigency of the material category, and the
   exigency is necessary for the material manifestation’s persistence. The traditions speak of
   the nafs as the source of temptation, and the framework does not deny that the nafs can
   be the occasion of disorder; but the framework’s claim is structural: the nafs is a structural
   exigency, and the exigency is necessary for the material manifestation’s persistence. What
   the nafs becomes—a source of order or a source of disorder—depends on the relation
   between the nafs and the ruh, not on the nafs alone.
   The Quranic verse that the traditions cite in this connection is the verse of the soul and its
   inspiration: “By the soul, and the proportion and order given to it; and its enlightenment
   as to its wrong and its right” (Qur’an 91:7–8). The verse describes the soul as given
   both its wrong and its right; the framework’s structural reading is that the nafs is the
   pull toward the material, and the ruh is the light toward the higher, and the self is the
   meeting-point at which the two are related. The verse is cited as structural evidence, not
   as a ground of justification.



B.4        Ruh: The Light from the Higher Category
The ruh is the light of identity from the higher category. The light, as the body of the book
described it, is the conveyor of effect between identities and manifestations; it is the condition of
possibility of relation. The ruh is the light by which the self is connected to its source in the
higher realms: the light of the identity that the self is, and the light of the source from which the
identity comes.
      The ruh is not the self, and it is not the nafs. The ruh is the light; the self is the meeting-point;
the nafs is the exigency. The three are distinct, and the self is the locus at which the three are
related.
      The ruh is not accessible to the self in the way that the nafs is accessible. The nafs is the
B.5. The Self as Meeting-Point                                                                   433


pull that the self feels; the ruh is the light by which the self is connected to its source, and the
light is not an object that the self can survey. The ruh is the condition of the self’s relation to
its source; it is not one of the things that the self encounters. The distinction is the distinction
between the condition of relation and the terms of relation; it is kept throughout.

   Remark B.5 (The Ruh Is Not a Substance)

   The ruh is not a substance. It is a light; it is the condition of possibility of the self’s
   relation to its source. The traditions speak of the ruh as breathed into the human being
   by the creator, and the framework does not deny the description; but the framework’s
   claim is structural: the ruh is the light of identity from the higher category, and the light
   is the condition of possibility of the relation, not a thing that enters into the relation.
   The Quranic verse that the traditions cite in this connection is the verse of the ruh: “They
   ask you about the ruh. Say: the ruh is from the command of my Lord” (Qur’an 17:85).
   The verse describes the ruh as from the command of the Lord; the framework’s structural
   reading is that the ruh is the light from the higher category, and that the light is not an
   object that the self can survey. The verse is cited as structural evidence, not as a ground
   of justification. The framework’s silence on what the ruh is in itself is not a denial of the
   ruh; it is the recognition that the ruh is the condition of the self’s relation to its source,
   and that the condition is not one of the things that the self can survey.




B.5     The Self as Meeting-Point

The self is the meeting-point of the nafs and the ruh. The nafs is the exigency of the material
category; the ruh is the light from the higher category; the self is the locus at which the two
are related. The self is not reducible to the nafs, and not reducible to the ruh; it is the point at
which the two are related.
   The self is not a substance. It is a structural locus. The self is the point at which the pull of
the material category and the light of the higher category meet; the meeting is what the self is.
The self is not a thing that has the meeting as a property; the self is the meeting.
   The self’s structural condition is the condition of a relation: the relation between the nafs
and the ruh. The relation is not a third thing; it is the relation between the two. The self is the
locus of the relation, and the locus is not a substance.

   Remark B.6 (The Self Is Not a Substance)

   The self is not a substance. It is a structural locus at which the relation between the nafs
   and the ruh is realized. The framework’s account of the self is structural: the self is not a
   thing that has a relation to the nafs and the ruh; the self is the relation. The reader who
   takes the self as a substance has misread the appendix; the reader who takes the self as a
   structural locus has read it correctly.
434                                     Appendix B. A Structural Anthropology: Nafs and Ruh


   Remark B.7 (The Self Is Not a Composite)

   The self is not a composite of the nafs and the ruh. A composite is a whole made of parts;
   the self is not a whole made of parts. The nafs and the ruh are not parts of the self; they
   are the two conditions whose relation the self is. The distinction is the distinction between
   a composite and a relation; it is kept throughout.




B.6       The Three Structural Stages of the Nafs

The traditions describe three stages of the nafs. The framework’s structural reading is that the
three stages describe three structural states of the relation between the nafs and the ruh, and
that the three states are distinguished by which of the two is dominant in the relation.


First stage: the commanding nafs (al-nafs al-ammara). The nafs is dominant; the ruh
is subordinated. The self is pulled by the material exigency, and the light of the higher category
is not effective in the relation. The self acts according to the pull of the material category, and
the pull is not checked by the light of the higher category.


Second stage: the self-reproaching nafs (al-nafs al-lawwama). The nafs and the ruh
are both effective, and the two are in tension. The self is pulled by the material exigency, and
the self is also lit by the light of the higher category; the pull and the light are both present, and
the two are not in harmony. The self reproaches itself, because the light of the higher category
makes the self aware of the pull of the material category, and the awareness is the occasion of
the reproach.


Third stage: the tranquil nafs (al-nafs al-mutma’inna). The ruh is dominant; the nafs
is harmonized. The self is lit by the light of the higher category, and the pull of the material
category is not eliminated but is harmonized with the light. The self is at peace, because the
two conditions of the self are in harmony.
      The three stages are not a temporal sequence that every self must traverse. They are
structural states of the relation between the nafs and the ruh; a self may be in one stage, in
another, or in a mixture of the three. The distinction among the three is analytical, and the
appendix uses it to describe the structural possibilities of the self’s relation to its source.

   Remark B.8 (The Three Stages Are Structural, Not Temporal)

   The three stages are structural states of the relation between the nafs and the ruh; they
   are not a temporal sequence that every self must traverse. The reader who reads the three
   stages as a temporal sequence has misread the appendix; the reader who reads them as
   structural states has read it correctly.
B.7. The Structural Task of the Self                                                             435


   Remark B.9 (The Three Stages Are Described in the Quran)

   The three stages are described in the Quran. The commanding nafs is described in the
   verse of Joseph: “I do not acquit myself; indeed, the nafs is commanding to evil, except
   what my Lord has mercy on” (Qur’an 12:53). The self-reproaching nafs is described in
   the verse of the resurrection: “I swear by the self-reproaching nafs” (Qur’an 75:2). The
   tranquil nafs is described in the verse of the dawn: “O tranquil nafs, return to your Lord,
   well-pleased and pleasing” (Qur’an 89:27–28). The framework’s structural reading is that
   the three verses describe three structural states of the relation between the nafs and the
   ruh; the verses are cited as structural evidence, not as a ground of justification.



B.7     The Structural Task of the Self
The structural task of the self is the harmonization of the nafs and the ruh. The task is not
the elimination of the nafs; the nafs is a structural exigency, and its elimination would be the
elimination of the condition of the material manifestation’s persistence. The task is not the
subordination of the ruh; the ruh is the light from the higher category, and its subordination
would be the subordination of the condition of the self’s relation to its source. The task is the
harmonization of the two: the nafs is not eliminated, and the ruh is not subordinated; the two
are brought into harmony.
   The task is structural, not ethical. The framework describes the task as the structural task of
the self; it does not prescribe what the self ought to do. The distinction between the structural
task and the ethical prescription is the distinction between what the self is and what the self
ought to be; the appendix keeps the distinction throughout.

   Remark B.10 (The Task Is Not War)

   The structural task of the self is not a war against the nafs. The traditions sometimes
   describe the task as a struggle (jihad) against the nafs, and the framework does not deny
   the description; but the framework’s claim is structural: the task is the harmonization of
   the nafs and the ruh, not the elimination of the nafs. The harmonization is the structural
   condition of the tranquil nafs; the elimination would be the elimination of the condition of
   the material manifestation’s persistence, and would not be a structural possibility for a
   self that is still manifested in the material realm.
   The distinction between the harmonization and the elimination is the distinction between
   the structural task and the structural impossibility; it is kept throughout.

   Remark B.11 (The Task Is Not a Prescription)

   The structural task is not a prescription. The framework describes the harmonization as
   the structural task of the self; it does not prescribe that the self ought to harmonize. The
   distinction is the distinction between the structural description and the ethical prescription;
   it is kept throughout. A reader who takes the structural task as a prescription has misread
   the appendix; a reader who takes it as a description of the structural condition of the
436                                       Appendix B. A Structural Anthropology: Nafs and Ruh


   tranquil nafs has read it correctly.



B.8        What This Appendix Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this appendix are deliberately deferred.
      First, the appendix does not claim to describe the essence of the self, the mode of its creation,
or its relation to the divine. Those questions belong to other inquiries, and the appendix neither
answers them nor forecloses them.
      Second, the appendix does not claim to be a scriptural exegesis. Where it cites a verse, the
citation is offered as structural evidence, not as a ground of justification; the framework’s claim
is established by its own arguments, stated in the body of the book, and the verse is cited to
show that the structure is not the invention of the framework.
      Third, the appendix does not prescribe what the self ought to do. It describes a structural
condition of the self; it does not prescribe the self’s conduct. The distinction between the
structural description and the ethical prescription is kept throughout.
      Fourth, the appendix does not claim to have described the ground of the self. It claims to
have described the structure of the self, and the structure points beyond itself to the ground
that the appendix does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of
the self and the ground of the self; it is kept throughout the appendix, and it is stated here as
the appendix’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a moment in which you felt pulled in two directions—toward what is immediate and
material, and toward what is higher and more lasting. What was the structure of that moment?
Was one pull dominant, or were the two in tension, or were the two in harmony? What does
your answer tell you about the relation between the nafs and the ruh in your own self?

Appendix C

A Structural Description of Religious Phenomena


Scope. This appendix is a structural description of two religious phenomena: tasbih (the movement
of the creature toward its source) and worship (the synchronization of the self’s awareness and
self-awareness). It defines the two phenomena in the framework’s structural vocabulary, describes
their structural features, and states the structural chain that the traditions associate with worship.
It is not a prescription, not a scriptural exegesis, and not a theological treatise. Where it cites
scriptural verses, the citation is offered as structural evidence, not as a ground of justification.



C.1      What This Appendix Is and Is Not

This appendix is a structural description. It uses the vocabulary of the framework—movement,
light, direction, awareness, self-awareness, synchronization—to describe two religious phenomena.
The description is offered as a structural account; it does not claim to exhaust what the phenomena
are, and it does not claim to replace the inquiries that undertake them from other angles.
   The appendix is not a prescription. It describes the structural features of tasbih and worship;
it does not prescribe that anyone ought to perform tasbih, or that anyone ought to worship. The
distinction between the structural description and the prescription is the distinction between what
the phenomena are and what one ought to do; the appendix keeps the distinction throughout.
   The appendix is not a scriptural exegesis. Where it cites a verse, the citation is offered as
structural evidence: the verse is cited because it describes the same structure that the framework
describes, not because the framework’s structure is derived from the verse. The framework’s
claim is established by its own arguments, stated in the body of the book; the verses are cited to
show that the structure is not the invention of the framework.
   The appendix is not a theological treatise. It does not claim to describe the essence of the
divine, the mode of the divine’s self-disclosure, or the relation between the divine and the world.
Those questions belong to other inquiries, and the appendix neither answers them nor forecloses
them.

   Remark C.1 (The Appendix Presupposes the Framework)

   The appendix presupposes the framework of this book, and it uses the framework’s
   structural vocabulary. It does not repeat the framework’s arguments; it applies them to
   the phenomena. The reader who has not read the body of the book will find the appendix
   compressed; the reader who has read the body will find the appendix a natural extension
   of the framework’s claims about light, awareness, and the realms.




                                                439
440                              Appendix C. A Structural Description of Religious Phenomena


C.2       The Vocabulary of the Appendix
The appendix uses three terms in a technical sense, and the sense of each must be fixed at the
outset.


Tasbih. The movement of the creature toward its source. The term is used in a structural
sense: it names the structural orientation of a manifestation toward the identity that it manifests,
and the structural movement by which the manifestation returns to its source. The movement is
not a spatial motion; it is a structural direction, the direction of ascending light.


Worship. The synchronization of the self’s awareness and self-awareness. The term is used
in a structural sense: it names the structural alignment of the self’s horizontal awareness (the
awareness of what is co-present) and the self’s vertical self-awareness (the awareness of the
self’s relation to its source). The synchronization is not a psychological state; it is a structural
alignment.


Virtue. A pattern of ascending light. The term is used in a structural sense: it names a stable
structural pattern in which the self’s ascending light is regularly returned to its source. The term
is not used in an ethical sense; it names a structural pattern, not a moral good.
      The three terms are structural, and the appendix uses them in the structural sense. The
terms have histories in the traditions, and the appendix does not claim that its structural sense is
the only sense the terms can bear. It claims that the structural sense is the sense the framework
needs, and that the structural sense is sufficient for the appendix’s purpose.

   Remark C.2 (The Terms Are Not Psychological)

   The three terms are not psychological terms. Tasbih is not a feeling of devotion; worship
   is not a state of mind; virtue is not a character trait. The three are structural conditions
   of the relation between the self and its source. The framework uses the terms as structural
   labels, and the reader who takes them as psychological states has misread the appendix.
   The distinction is the distinction between the structure and the psychological state; it is
   kept throughout.



C.3       Tasbih: The Movement Toward the Source
Tasbih is the movement of the creature toward its source. The movement is structural: it is the
direction of ascending light, from the manifestation back to the identity that it manifests. The
movement is not a spatial motion; it is the structural direction of the return.
      The framework distinguishes three modes of tasbih, corresponding to the three conditions of
the creature.


First mode: essential tasbih. The tasbih of a creature that has no self-awareness. The
creature moves toward its source by its very structure: the stone falls, the plant grows, the
C.3. Tasbih: The Movement Toward the Source                                                    441


animal responds, and the movement is the movement of the structure toward the source. The
creature does not choose the movement; the movement is the structure.


Second mode: chosen tasbih. The tasbih of a creature that has self-awareness. The creature
moves toward its source by the structure and by the choice: the self is aware of the movement,
and the self chooses to align its awareness with the movement. The movement is not merely the
structure; the movement is the structure enacted with the self’s awareness.


Third mode: transitional tasbih. The tasbih of a creature at the moment of transition
between realms. The movement is most intense at the boundaries: at dawn, at dusk, at the
moment of death, at the moment of birth. The structural intensity of the movement is a function
of the structural transition.
   The three modes are not three kinds of tasbih; they are three modes of a single structural
movement. The movement is one; the modes are three.

   Remark C.3 (The Modes Are Structural, Not Temporal)

   The three modes are structural conditions of the creature’s movement toward its source;
   they are not a temporal sequence that every creature must traverse. The reader who reads
   the three modes as a temporal sequence has misread the appendix; the reader who reads
   them as structural modes has read it correctly.


   Remark C.4 (The Quranic Description of Tasbih)

   The Quran describes tasbih as universal: “There is not a thing but glorifies Him with
   praise, but you do not understand their glorification” (Qur’an 17:44). The framework’s
   structural reading is that every manifestation is structurally oriented toward its source,
   and that the orientation is tasbih; the fact that the orientation is not understood by the
   observer does not make the orientation less real. The verse is cited as structural evidence,
   not as a ground of justification.
   The framework does not claim that the verse’s “glorification” is the same as its structural
   tasbih. The framework claims that the verse describes a structure that the framework’s
   structural tasbih also describes; whether the two descriptions are the same, or whether
   one is the reality and the other its structural expression, is a question the framework does
   not settle. The distinction is the distinction between the structural description and the
   reality it describes; it is kept throughout.


   Remark C.5 (The Eight Layers of Tasbih)

   The traditions describe eight layers of tasbih. The framework’s structural reading is
   that the layers are eight aspects of the structural movement toward the source: the
   movement itself, the function performed, the negation of deficiency, the response to glory,
   the transition between realms, the scientific discourse, the ethical release of sediment, and
   the atemporal movement. The eight layers are not eight kinds of tasbih; they are eight
442                              Appendix C. A Structural Description of Religious Phenomena


   aspects of a single structural movement.
   The framework does not claim that the eight layers exhaust what tasbih is; it claims that
   the eight layers describe the structural aspects of the movement, and that the aspects
   are what the framework’s structural vocabulary can articulate. The reader who wishes
   to develop the eight layers further is invited to do so within the framework’s structural
   condition.


C.4       Worship: The Synchronization of Awareness and Self-Awareness
Worship is the synchronization of the self’s awareness and self-awareness. The framework
distinguishes three terms in this connection, and the three must be kept apart.

Awareness. The regulation of the self for the reception of reflective light and intra-category
light. Awareness is horizontal: it is the self’s relation to what is co-present.

Self-awareness. The mechanism by which the self regulates its relation to its source. Self-
awareness is vertical: it is the self’s relation to the identity that it is and to the source from
which the identity comes.

Worship. The synchronization of the two. Worship is the structural alignment in which the
self’s horizontal awareness and the self’s vertical self-awareness are brought into harmony. The
alignment is not a state; it is a structural relation.
      Worship has five structural elements, and the framework describes them as follows.

First element: system. Worship is a system, not a single act. The system is a repeated
structure; the repetition is what makes the synchronization stable.

Second element: synchronization. Worship aligns two things that are usually misaligned:
the self’s awareness and the self’s self-awareness. The alignment is the structural core of worship.

Third element: the two kinds of knowledge. Worship presupposes both the horizontal
knowledge (the knowledge of what is co-present) and the vertical knowledge (the knowledge of
the self’s relation to its source). Without the two kinds of knowledge, the synchronization is not
possible.

Fourth element: behavior change. Worship changes behavior: the synchronization produces
a change in the self’s structural pattern, from a pattern of sediment to a pattern of ascending
light.

Fifth element: shared context. Worship creates a shared context for a group of actions:
the five daily prayers, the fast, the pilgrimage, the almsgiving. The shared context is what makes
worship social, not merely individual.
C.5. The Chain: Knowledge, Worship, Taqwa, Virtues                                              443


   Remark C.6 (Worship Is Not a Psychological State)

   Worship is not a psychological state. It is a structural synchronization of the self’s
   awareness and self-awareness. The synchronization may be accompanied by psychological
   states, but the states are not the synchronization. The framework’s claim is structural; the
   reader who reads worship as a psychological state has misread the appendix; the reader
   who reads it as a structural synchronization has read it correctly.

   Remark C.7 (The Quranic Description of Worship)

   The Quran describes worship as the purpose of creation: “I did not create the jinn and the
   human being except to worship Me” (Qur’an 51:56). The framework’s structural reading
   is that the human being is created with the structural capacity for synchronization, and
   that the synchronization is worship; the verse is cited as structural evidence, not as a
   ground of justification.
   The framework does not claim that the verse’s “worship” is the same as its structural
   synchronization. The framework claims that the verse describes a structure that the
   framework’s structural synchronization also describes; whether the two descriptions are
   the same, or whether one is the reality and the other its structural expression, is a question
   the framework does not settle. The distinction is the distinction between the structural
   description and the reality it describes; it is kept throughout.



C.5      The Chain: Knowledge, Worship, Taqwa, Virtues
The traditions describe a chain that connects knowledge, worship, taqwa, and virtues. The
framework’s structural reading is that the chain describes the structural sequence by which the
self’s relation to its source is transformed from a pattern of sediment to a pattern of ascending
light.

First link: knowledge (ma’rifah). The first link is the vertical knowledge: the self’s
awareness of its relation to its source. Without the vertical knowledge, the synchronization is
not possible; the self does not know what it is aligning with what.

Second link: worship (’ibadah). The second link is the synchronization itself: the alignment
of the self’s awareness and self-awareness. The synchronization is the structural core of the chain;
without it, the knowledge remains abstract, and the virtues remain unrealized.

Third link: taqwa. The third link is the structural preservation of the synchronization: the
self’s structural pattern is preserved against the pull of the material exigency. Taqwa is not a
feeling of fear; it is the structural preservation of the alignment.

Fourth link: virtues (fada’il). The fourth link is the structural pattern that results from
the preservation: the self’s ascending light is regularly returned to its source, and the regular
return is the virtue. The virtues are not moral goods; they are structural patterns.
444                                Appendix C. A Structural Description of Religious Phenomena


      The chain is structural, not temporal. The four links are not four stages that the self
must traverse in sequence; they are four aspects of a single structural transformation. The
transformation is the transformation of the self’s relation to its source, from a pattern of sediment
to a pattern of ascending light.

   Remark C.8 (The Chain Is Not a Prescription)

   The chain is not a prescription. The framework describes the chain as the structural
   sequence of the transformation; it does not prescribe that the self ought to traverse the
   sequence. The distinction between the structural description and the prescription is the
   distinction between what the transformation is and what the self ought to do; the appendix
   keeps the distinction throughout.


   Remark C.9 (The Chain Is a Structural Description, Not a Promise)

   The chain is a structural description, not a promise. The framework does not claim that
   every self that traverses the chain will achieve the transformation; the transformation
   depends on the structural conditions of the self’s relation to its source, and those conditions
   are not fully under the self’s control. The framework describes the structural sequence; it
   does not promise the outcome. The distinction is the distinction between the structural
   description and the outcome; it is kept throughout.



C.6        The Shared Context of Worship
Worship is not only individual; it is also social. The framework describes the social dimension
structurally: worship creates a shared context for a group of actions, and the shared context is
what makes the synchronization collective.
      Three examples of the shared context are worth noting.


First example: the five daily prayers. The five daily prayers create a shared rhythm for
the community. The shared rhythm is a structural pattern; it is what makes the individual
synchronizations collectively aligned.


Second example: the fast. The fast creates a shared experience for the community. The
shared experience is a structural pattern; it is what makes the individual abstinences collectively
aligned.


Third example: the pilgrimage. The pilgrimage creates a shared journey for the community.
The shared journey is a structural pattern; it is what makes the individual journeys collectively
aligned.
      The shared context is not a psychological state; it is a structural condition. The framework’s
claim is structural: worship creates a shared context, and the shared context is what makes the
synchronization collective. The reader who reads the shared context as a psychological state has
misread the appendix; the reader who reads it as a structural condition has read it correctly.
C.7. What This Appendix Does Not Establish                                                     445


   Remark C.10 (The Shared Context Is Not a Collective Subject)

   The shared context is not a collective subject. The shared context is a structural condition
   of the individual synchronizations; it is not a subject that has its own awareness or
   self-awareness. The framework does not claim that the community is a subject; it claims
   that the community provides a structural condition for the individual synchronizations.
   The distinction is the distinction between the structural condition and the subject; it is
   kept throughout.



C.7     What This Appendix Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this appendix are deliberately deferred.
   First, the appendix does not claim to be a scriptural exegesis. Where it cites a verse, the
citation is offered as structural evidence, not as a ground of justification; the framework’s claim
is established by its own arguments, stated in the body of the book, and the verse is cited to
show that the structure is not the invention of the framework.
   Second, the appendix does not claim to prescribe what anyone ought to do. It describes the
structural features of tasbih and worship; it does not prescribe that anyone ought to perform
tasbih, or that anyone ought to worship. The distinction between the structural description and
the prescription is kept throughout.
   Third, the appendix does not claim to describe the essence of the divine, the mode of the
divine’s self-disclosure, or the relation between the divine and the world. Those questions belong
to other inquiries, and the appendix neither answers them nor forecloses them.
   Fourth, the appendix does not claim to have described the ground of the phenomena. It
claims to have described the structure of the phenomena, and the structure points beyond itself
to the ground that the appendix does not describe. The distinction is the distinction between
the structure of the phenomena and the ground of the phenomena; it is kept throughout the
appendix, and it is stated here as the appendix’s explicit limit.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a moment in which you were fully present to what you were doing—a conversation, a
prayer, a walk. Was the moment a moment of synchronization, in the sense the appendix has
described? What was aligned with what? And what does your answer tell you about the relation
between awareness and self-awareness in your own experience?

With this appendix, the three appendices are complete. The first is a prospectus for a metaethical
treatise; the second is a structural description of the human subject; the third is a structural
description of certain religious phenomena. None of the three is part of the metaphysical body of
the book, and each states its own limits explicitly. The appendices are offered as proposals and
descriptions, not as doctrines, and the reader who wishes to develop them further is invited to do
so within the framework’s structural conditions.

A Note on the Code System
Each source in this bibliography is assigned a code of the form [Cn-m], where n is the number of
the chapter in which the source is cited, and m is the number of the source within that chapter.
A source cited in more than one chapter appears under each chapter in which it is cited, with
a distinct code in each chapter. This allows the reader to locate every citation in its chapter
context, and it allows the footnotes in the text to identify a source by code, name, and the
passage cited.
   The codes used in the footnotes of this book are of the same form. When the text contains a
footnote of the form [C11-1], the reader will find the corresponding entry in the section of this
bibliography headed “Chapter 11.” The entry contains the full bibliographic description of the
source, and the footnote contains the specific passage cited.
   Two codes in this bibliography—[C12-1] and [C17-1]—are cross-references to the separate
treatise on the dialogues with the philosophical traditions. They are listed in their proper places
and are marked as cross-references; the separate treatise contains its own bibliography, with its
own codes.

Qur’anic Citations
The Qur’anic verses cited in the body of the book are cited as structural evidence: they describe
structural relations that the framework also describes, and they are quoted where the framework’s
structural vocabulary meets the vocabulary of the tradition. The framework’s principles are
established by philosophical arguments, and the verses are not premises of those arguments. The
interpretation of the verses belongs to the inquiry that revelation authorizes; the framework cites
them at the structural level and leaves their interpretation to the domain that undertakes it
(Chapter 36, Section on Philosophy and Revelation).
