This bibliography lists the sources cited in the body of the book. The separate treatise on the
dialogues with the philosophical traditions contains its own bibliography, with its own codes,
covering the primary and secondary sources for the comparative treatment of the traditions
Bibliography                                                                                  451


discussed there. The two bibliographies are distinct: the present bibliography records the sources
the framework cites, and the separate treatise’s bibliography records the sources the comparative
treatment cites. The body of the book states the framework’s own claims; the separate treatise
compares them with the traditions.
Glossary of Terms


A Note on the Glossary

This glossary collects the technical terms of the framework, with the definition or principle that
fixes each term’s sense, and a cross-reference to the place in the book where the term is defined.
The cross-references use the labels of the definitions and principles stated in the chapters; the
reader who wishes to see a definition in its context is directed to the chapter and section where
it appears.
    The terms are listed alphabetically. A term that has more than one definition, or that is
defined in more than one place, is listed with each definition, distinguished by the place of
definition.
    The glossary collects the terms of the metaphysical body of the book. The terms introduced
in the three appendices—nafs, ruh, tasbih, worship, and the other structural terms of the
appendices—are collected in a separate section (“Terms of the Appendices”), which marks them
as belonging to the appendices and not to the metaphysical body.



A

Accuracy
A rule of the Hub of Signification: the signification of structure into meaning preserves the
distinctions among the structural features of what it signifies. (Principle 17.6)

Active connection structure
A structure that always is, is a structure of connection, has edges that are activated or deac-
tivated according to rules, and itself does not move. Light is an active connection structure.
(Definition 13.1)

Actualization
The dimension in which the relation among identity, manifestation, and realm is quantified as
energy. (Definition 15.1)

Awareness
The regulation of a manifestation for the reception of reflective light and intra-category light; a
species of self-awareness. (Definition 35.3)

Awareness (as rule of the Relational Manifestation)
A rule of the Relational Manifestation: the manifestations are characterized by structural
awareness, in the sense of Definition 35.3. (Principle 16.11)



                                               452
Glossary of Terms                                                                              453


B
Balance criterion
The extent to which the descending light an identity has received is preserved or returned, less
the extent to which it has become sediment. (Definition 34.5)

Barzakhic realm
An independently real ontological level whose mode of existence includes mediating, transforming,
or regulating relations between other realms. (Definition 8.1)

Beginninglessness
The structural property of having no first stage of succession. (Definition 33.3)

Birth
The emergence in the Material Manifestation of a group of manifestations connected to a single
identity. (Definition 34.3)


C
Capacity (of a realm)
What a realm’s mode of existence permits to appear in it and what it constrains. (Definition 7.2)

Category-relative predication
The principle that metaphysical predicates are not absolute, but are defined relative to a realm
and to a respect. (Principle 28.1)

Causality
A rule of the Material Manifestation: the material manifestations are causally connected; every
material event has a cause, and every cause produces an effect. (Principle 16.12)

Cognitive context
The frame in which something is cognized; fixed by the question being asked. Distinguished from
existential context. (Definition 10.3)

Configuration-dependence
The manifestation of an identity in a context depends on what passes through the fluid element of
the context, and this in turn depends on the whole configuration of the context. (Definition 27.1)

Consciousness
The intensity of the connection between a manifestation and its identity. (Definition 35.2)

Consistency (as criterion of context validity)
A valid context is consistent in all its overlaps with other valid contexts. (Principle 6.4)

Context
The background in which cognition occurs; determines what counts as a fixed element, what
counts as a fluid element, and which dynamics governs. (Definition 2.4)
454                                                                              Glossary of Terms


Context (cognitive and existential)
An existential context is the realm in which a manifestation is realized, with its capacity and
constraints; a cognitive context is the frame in which something is cognized. (Definition 10.3)

Context-dependence
The fixedness or fluidity of an element depends on the cognitive context, not on the element’s
essence. (Principle 5.1)

Contextuality
A rule of the Relational Manifestation: the meaning of a manifestation depends on its context; it
is not fixed independently of the context. (Principle 16.10)

Continuation of realization
A rule of the Hub of Realization: the realization of the manifestations of an identity preserves
the conditions of realization across stages, so that the realization of further manifestations in the
same realm remains structurally possible. (Principle 17.10)

Conveyor principle
No explanation of how one fixed element bears on another is complete unless it invokes a fluid
element: a carrier, medium, signal, or process by which the effect passes. (Principle 4.1)

Cross-checkability
A valid context is one whose fixed and fluid elements can be identified and distinguished from at
least one other valid context. (Principle 6.2)


D
Death
The zeroing of the output of an identity’s manifestation functions in a realm; not the destruction
of the identity. (Principle 34.1)

Defining invariants
The features that constitute an identity’s determination: those that distinguish it from its
alternatives and are fixed by what it is. Taken as primitive in the framework. (Definition 9.2)

Degree of structural fidelity
The extent to which a manifestation preserves the essential determination of its source. Not
necessary; an identity can be realized at varying degrees of structural fidelity. (Definition 18.2)

Descent
The appearance of an identity in a lower realm in the mode of that realm, without the identity
going from one realm to another. Not to be confused with travel. (Principle 13.4)

Desire to find
The structural relation by which an identity is rendered legible in the reflection of its expression
in another identity’s expression. Not a mental state. (Theorem 24.1)
Glossary of Terms                                                                               455


Determinate capacity
Every differentiated realm has a determinate capacity: its mode of existence permits certain
manifestations and constrains others. (Principle 7.2)

Discreteness
A rule of the Material Manifestation: the material manifestations are separate from one another;
they occupy distinct positions in space and time. (Principle 16.14)

Duplication (qualitative and numerical)
Qualitative duplication produces a second thing that shares the first thing’s signature. Numerical
duplication of an identity would produce two distinct things, each of which is that very identity.
(Definition 9.6, Definition 23.1)

Dynamism
Identity is in a state of expression, continually manifesting, multiplying its manifestations, and
bringing about new ones. (Definition 28.2)


E
Endlessness
The structural property of having no last stage of succession. (Definition 33.4)

Energy
The quantity of the relation between identity, manifestation, and realm—in the dimension of
actualization. Not a column; a relational feature that appears in three columns. (Definition 15.1,
Principle 15.1)

Encompassment (in light)
We are not floating in light—we are encompassed in light. Light has taken us up, not that we
have taken up light. (Principle 14.4)

Essential feature
A feature of an identity that belongs to its defining invariants. (Definition 10.2)

Essential homogeneity (of manifestation)
A manifestation is essentially homogeneous with its source insofar as it preserves the source’s
essential determination. (Principle 10.2)

Estimate, not knowledge
We can estimate, from the properties of light in material manifestation, something about higher
levels, but we cannot know. (Principle 14.7)

Eternity
Being without beginning and end in a way not bounded by succession. A structural concept; not
a theological attribute. (Definition 33.5)

Existential context
The realm in which a manifestation is realized, with its capacity and constraints. (Definition 10.3)
456                                                                             Glossary of Terms


Expression
The structural tendency of every identity to express itself, with three moments: manifestational
descent, plurality, ontological novelty. (Principle 18.1)


F
Fallacy of super-identity
A record formed by aggregating manifestations drawn from contexts whose elements are not
mutually translatable is not a reconstruction of the identity; it is a context-confounded record.
(Principle 9.2)

Fidelity
A rule of the Hub of Signification: the act of signifying preserves the identity of the struc-
ture signified, so that the structure produced by the signification is the structure signified.
(Principle 17.7)

Finitude of the subject
Every cognizing subject is finite: at any time it occupies finitely many contexts, and in any finite
span it completes only finitely many acts of reconstruction. (Principle 1.2)

First Determination
The fundamental realm of pure unity. There is no multiplicity, no change, and no succession in
it. (Definition 7.3)

Fixed element
An entity selected as an invariant term within a given explanatory cognition. (Definition 2.1)

Fluid element
An entity that conveys effect; an edge in the network of cognition, connecting fixed elements to
one another. (Definition 2.2)

Formality
A rule of the Structural Determination: the structural laws concern the form of the manifestations,
not their content. (Principle 16.8)

Foundational fluid element
Light is not one of the fluid elements, but the foundational fluid element that appears in the
mode of each cognitive apparatus. (Principle 14.2)

Four-column framework
The framework of analytical roles for explanatory cognition: fixed elements, fluid elements,
governing dynamics, context. (Principle 3.1)

Function is not dependence
That a realm has the function of mediating between other realms does not entail that it lacks
independent existence. (Principle 32.1)
Glossary of Terms                                                                               457


Fundamental realm
An independently real mode of existence within which a specific mode of manifestation, activity,
and interaction is possible. (Definition 7.1)


G
Governing dynamics
A rule that explains how fluid elements affect fixed elements. (Definition 2.3)

Grade of multiplicity
A qualitatively distinct way in which many things can stand to one another, as opposed to a
merely quantitative difference of how many there are. (Definition 19.1)


H
Harmony
A rule of the Hub of Decree: the multiplicity produced by the specification of unity is structurally
coherent—its elements are structurally compatible with one another. (Principle 17.4)

Hub
A barzakhic realm; not merely a passage between two realms. (Definition 8.1)

Hub of Decree
The barzakhic realm of determination of measure. Its mode of existence is the allotment to
each identity of the extent, the limit, and the proportion within which it will express itself.
(Definition 8.4)

Hub of Realization
The barzakhic realm of actualization. Its mode of existence is the realizing of what is possible as
something concrete. (Definition 8.6)

Hub of Signification
The barzakhic realm of signification as a mode of existence. Its mode of existence is that of
structures standing as signs. (Definition 8.5)


I
Identity
That which remains invariant under a specified class of allowable transformations. “Structure” here
is the principle of distinction and unity, not necessarily an arrangement of parts. (Definition 9.1)

Identity conservation
Identity is invariant under all temporal transformations of its manifestations. (Principle 9.5)

Identity rigidity
Identity does not admit of degrees. A structure either is invariant under the specified transfor-
mations, or it is not. (Principle 9.4)
458                                                                              Glossary of Terms


Identity-preserving transformation
A transformation whose resulting state remains within the range of structural possibilities
compatible with the identity’s defining invariants. (Definition 9.3)

Independence from qualitative similarity
The principle of non-duplicability is independent of the degree of qualitative similarity between
things. (Principle 23.2)

Indivisibility
A rule of the First Determination: the First Determination is beyond division; there are no parts,
no components, no distinctions. (Principle 16.4)

Infinity of contexts
Given the openness assumption, the cognitive contexts in which an identity can be cognized are
not finite in number. (Principle 5.2)

Intensity (of a manifestation)
The degree to which a manifestation confirms the source as a whole, in its unity (the completeness
of reflection). (Definition 30.1)

Intra-category light
Light that has descended into a realm and has not ascended. (Chapter 13; see also the definition
of sediment at Definition 36.1)

Invariance
A rule of the First Determination: the First Determination is invariant under all transformations.
(Principle 16.2)

Invariance is not composition
That an identity is invariant does not entail that it is composed of several parts. (Principle 9.1)


L
Light
The fluid element: the conveying of effect between identity and manifestation, a process with
three essential properties (descending, ascending, reflective). (Principle 12.1, Principle 12.2)

Light as active structure
Light is an active structure, not a traveler. Light does not move; the edges of the structure,
according to the rules of the realms, connect different nodes. (Principle 13.1)

Light as condition of every fluid element
Light is the condition of possibility of every fluid element. (Principle 15.5)

Light as condition of possibility of relation
Light is not a relation—it is the condition of possibility of relation. (Principle 12.2)
Glossary of Terms                                                                               459


Light as foundational fluid element
Light is the foundational fluid element that appears in the mode of each cognitive apparatus.
(Principle 14.2)

Light as the only window
We have no direct access to higher levels; the only thing that reaches us from higher levels is
light, in its descended version in material manifestation. (Principle 14.6)

Light primary, energy secondary
Light is the carrier; energy is the quantity carried. (Principle 15.2)


M

Manifestation
The contextually realized appearance of an identity according to the ontological capacity, aptitude,
and constraints of the receiving realm. (Definition 10.1)

Manifestational adequacy
A proposed criterion: the context chosen for the study of a manifestation, and the realm to which
a manifestation is attributed, must have the capacity and aptitude for the kind of appearance
attributed to it. (Principle 6.5)

Manifestational capacity (contextual)
The form that a manifestation takes in a realm is fixed jointly by the source identity and by the
capacity of the realm. Proposed; not yet assigned a status. (Principle 10.1)

Material Manifestation
The fundamental realm of material multiplicity. Its mode of existence is that of things that are
discrete, localized, and successive. (Definition 7.6)

Mediation
The structural regulation or conditioning of a relation between two realms by a realm whose
mode of existence includes that function. (Definition 8.1)

Minimality (as criterion of context validity)
A valid context is the smallest context that can still explain the phenomenon. (Principle 6.3)

Mixed nature
A barzakhic realm has a mixed nature when its mode of existence shows features of both of its
neighboring realms without being identical with either. (Definition 8.3)

Multiplicity
The manifestations of an identity are many: they are multiple, they arise and pass away, they
differ in structure and in realm. Their multiplicity is the multiplicity of products, not the
multiplicity of sources. (Definition 29.2)
460                                                                             Glossary of Terms


N
Necessity
A rule of the Structural Determination: the structural laws could not be otherwise, given the
identity they express. (Principle 16.7)

Non-completion of expression
Expression is never completed: no stage of manifestation exhausts the identity and ends the
tendency to express. (The traditional name “Eternal Creation” is retained as a historical label
for the structural claim; the framework uses the structural name.) (Principle 33.2)

Non-duplicability
Identity cannot be copied. Signatures, pseudo-identities, and information can be duplicated;
identity cannot. (Principle 9.6)

Non-necessity of downward passage
The presence or effect of an identity in a lower realm does not require that the identity pass
existentially through every realm that lies between. (Principle 7.3)

Non-reduction of identity to manifestations
An identity is not identical with the aggregate of its manifestations, nor with their compatible
aggregate. (Principle 9.3)

Non-sequential connectivity
The conveyor principle does not require that the connection between two fixed elements pass
through all intermediate fixed elements. (Principle 4.2)

Non-travel of light
Light does not travel. (Principle 13.2)


O
Ontological economy
Every realization, every reconstruction, and every maintenance of expression bears a cost that
cannot be wholly removed. (Principle 36.1)

Openness of relations
For every cognitive context C and every manifestation m that an identity has in C, there is a
cognitive context C ′ in which m is itself a fixed element, related by fluid elements and dynamics
that are not available in C. (Definition 5.1)

Order (as rule of the Hub of Decree)
The specification of unity into multiplicity is structurally ordered: it follows the structural
articulation of the realms. (Principle 17.3)

Order (as mode of existence of a barzakhic realm)
The level of being a barzakhic realm is in its own right, with rules and structural possibilities of
its own. (Definition 32.2)
Glossary of Terms                                                                               461


P
Pair 2 as the medium of relation
Dynamics and fluid element form the medium of the relation. (Principle 14.1)

Perspective
The structural position of an observer within a cognitive context: the point from which, the
means by which, and the conceptual structure through which a manifestation is apprehended.
(Definition 10.4)

Plurality of manifestations (distinct from plurality of identities)
The plurality of the manifestations of one identity is not a plurality of identities, and recursive
manifestation is not numerical multiplication of the identity. (Principle 29.1)

Preservation of the realized
A rule of the Hub of Realization: the realization of the manifestations of an identity preserves the
structural conditions on which the manifestation of the entities at stake depends. (Principle 17.9)

Primary cognitive apparatus
A cognitive apparatus whose fixed elements are general and whose fluid element is foundational.
(Definition 14.1)

Proportion
A rule of the Hub of Decree: the specification of unity into multiplicity preserves the unity of the
First Determination in the very act of differentiating it. (Principle 17.2)

Proportion in realization
A rule of the Hub of Realization: the realization of the manifestations of an identity distributes
the conditions of realization proportionally to the structural requirements of those manifestations.
(Principle 17.8)

Pseudo-identity
The observer’s approximation of an identity, constructed from the available manifestations: an
estimate of a signature, not a rival identity. (Definition 9.5)


R
Realm
An independently real mode of existence within which a specific mode of manifestation, activity,
and interaction is possible. (Definition 7.1, Definition 8.1)

Recursive manifestation
The structure by which a manifestation realized in one realm can itself be the occasion for further
manifestations of the same identity, in the same realm or another, without the identity being
multiplied. (Definition 29.3)
462                                                                            Glossary of Terms


Reducibility
A candidate fifth column is reducible when its role in explanation can be reassigned to one of the
four columns without loss. (Definition 3.1)

Relational Manifestation
The fundamental realm of relational multiplicity. Its mode of existence is that of things that
exist in relation to one another through meaning and significance. (Definition 7.5)

Relationality
A rule of the Relational Manifestation: the manifestations exist only in relation to one another;
they have no independent existence. (Principle 16.9)

Relation (as function of a barzakhic realm)
The regulation, conditioning, or transformation of a relation between two other realms by the
hub’s own mode of operation. (Definition 32.1)

Returning light
The light that continues after the pause of an expression, and refers back to its source through
what the identity left in other manifestations. (Definition 34.2)

Rigidity
Identity is invariant under all allowable transformations of its manifestations, and admits no
degrees. (Definition 28.1)

Rules of being vs. rules of transition
The rules of the fundamental realms are rules of being; the rules of the barzakhic realms are
rules of transition. (Principle 17.1, Principle 16.1)


S
Secondary cognitive apparatus
A cognitive apparatus whose fixed elements are specific and whose fluid element is derived.
(Definition 14.2)

Sediment
Intra-category light that has become lodged: light that has descended and not ascended, persists
beyond the activity that carried it, is not integrated into the relations of its realm, and lays a
lasting claim on that realm’s capacity. (Definition 36.1)

Self-awareness
The mechanism of regulating the connection between a manifestation and its identity: the activity
by which a manifestation adjusts how much descending light it receives, how much reflective
light it emits, and how much ascending light it returns. (Definition 35.1)

Signature
The structural description of an identity’s invariance: what can be read off, compared, recorded,
and reproduced about the pattern. (Definition 9.4)
Glossary of Terms                                                                                463


Singularity (of ontological death)
The threshold at which the cost of restoring an existing manifestation in a realm exceeds the
cost of bringing about a new one there. (Definition 34.1)

Structural Determination
The fundamental realm of general multiplicity. Its mode of existence is that of law: what is
general, formal, and necessary with respect to an identity. (Definition 7.4)

Structural duality (of expression)
Intensity and breadth are two measures of one expression, not two quantities on one scale.
(Principle 30.1)

Structural fluidity
“Fluid element” is an analytical role—not an ontological essence. Light plays the role of conveyor,
so it is the fluid element. (Principle 13.3)

Super-identity
A subject’s claim to have known, or to be able to know, all manifestations of an identity in all
contexts. (Definition 6.1)


T
Temporality
A rule of the Material Manifestation: the material manifestations occur in time; they have a
past, a present, and a future. (Principle 16.13)

Tendency to express
The tendency to express is necessary. Every identity, by its nature, tends toward expression. The
tendency cannot be structurally unrealized; it can only be structurally hindered. (Definition 18.1)

Tendency is not success
The necessity of the tendency to express does not entail the necessity of the realization of any
manifestation at any particular degree of structural fidelity, nor the necessity that a manifestation
be realized in every realm. (Principle 31.1)

Time
Time in a realm is the order of succession of the stages by which changes are realized there.
(Definition 33.1)

Time density
The degree of presence of what is realized in a realm per stage of succession. (Definition 33.2)

Time is realm-relative succession
Succession is not of one kind in all realms; its kind is fixed by what is successive in the realm
and by how the effect of light passes there. (Principle 33.1)

Timelessness
Having no succession at all. (Definition 33.5)
464                                                                               Glossary of Terms


Trans-categorical substance
A substance that comes before the distinction substance/accident/process/relation—not after it.
(Definition 12.1)

Truthfulness
A rule of the Hub of Signification: the signification carries the structural features of the structure
it signifies, so that the meaning produced is a faithful sign of that structure. (Principle 17.5)


U
Unity (as rule of the First Determination)
The First Determination is pure unity. (Principle 16.5)

Unity (as characteristic of identity)
An identity is one: it is a single source, a single invariance, a single thisness. Its unity is the
unity of a source, not the unity of an aggregate. (Definition 29.1)

Unity of the rules (fundamental)
The rules of the four fundamental realms are not independent; they are related by the structure
of the realms. (Principle 16.15)

Unity of the rules (barzakhic)
The rules of the three barzakhic realms are not independent; they are related by the structure of
the transition from unity to multiplicity. (Principle 17.11)

Universality
A rule of the Structural Determination: the structural laws apply to all manifestations of a given
identity, regardless of context. (Principle 16.6)

Unknownness
The unknownness of same-context identities is the structural condition of possibility of reflection,
not a defect. (Theorem 25.1)


V
Variational principle
For any identity and any receiving realm, the structural optimum of expression is the point at
which cost is minimized subject to the constraints of fidelity and recoverability. (Principle 36.2)

Veil
The state of an identity in the Relational Manifestation in which its world there has not yet been
articulated. (Definition 34.4)

Viability
The structural character of the relation between an identity and its manifestations in a realm,
measured by fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability; a descriptive concept that names a
structural character of the relation, not a value or an end. (Definition 6.2)

Cross-References to the Separate Treatise

Dialogues with the philosophical traditions
The comparative treatment of the framework with the philosophical traditions (Ibn Sina,
Suhrawardi, Ibn Arabi, Mulla Sadra, Plato and Plotinus, Proclus, Kant and Hegel, White-
head, the Upanishads and Buddhism, and Kashmir Shaivism) is given in a separate treatise,
to be published independently. The comparison is historical and comparative; it carries no
justificatory weight for the framework’s principles. (See the Preface, and the notes at Chapter 12
and Chapter 17.)



Terms of the Appendices

The following terms are introduced in the three appendices. They belong to the appendices, not
to the metaphysical body of the book; their sense is fixed within the appendix that introduces
them, and their use is confined to that appendix. The section is marked separately so that the
reader can see at once which terms belong to the metaphysical body and which belong to the
appendices.


Appendix A: Viability Metaethics

Viability metaethics
A metaethical inquiry into the architecture of moral systems: what a moral system is, what its
fundamental entities are, how those entities depend on one another, and what formal structures
a moral system can take. (Appendix A)

Four-level architecture
The architecture of the inquiries that viability metaethics belongs to: philosophy (level 1),
viability metaethics (level 2), foundational ethics (level 3), applied ethics (level 4). (Appendix A)


Appendix B: Structural Anthropology (Nafs and Ruh)

Nafs
The exigency of the material category: the structural pull that the material realm exercises on
the self, toward what is discrete, localized, and successive. A structural exigency, not a substance.
(Appendix B)

Ruh
The light of identity from the higher category: the structural light by which the self is connected
to its source in the higher realms. A structural light, not a substance. (Appendix B)

Self (as meeting-point)
The structural locus at which the exigency of the material category (nafs) and the light of the
higher category (ruh) meet. A structural locus, not a substance. (Appendix B)
466                                                                                Glossary of Terms


Commanding nafs (al-nafs al-ammāra)
The first of the three structural stages of the nafs: the nafs is dominant and the ruh is subordinated;
the self acts according to the pull of the material category. (Appendix B)

Self-reproaching nafs (al-nafs al-lawwāma)
The second of the three structural stages: the nafs and the ruh are both effective and in tension;
the self reproaches itself. (Appendix B)

Tranquil nafs (al-nafs al-mut.ma’inna)
The third of the three structural stages: the ruh is dominant and the nafs is harmonized; the self
is at peace. (Appendix B)

Structural task of the self
The harmonization of the nafs and the ruh: not the elimination of the nafs, and not the
subordination of the ruh. A structural task, not an ethical prescription. (Appendix B)


Appendix C: Structural Description of Religious Phenomena

Tasbih
The movement of the creature toward its source: the structural direction of ascending light, from
the manifestation back to the identity that it manifests. A structural direction, not a spatial
motion. (Appendix C)

Essential tasbih
The tasbih of a creature that has no self-awareness: the creature moves toward its source by its
very structure. (Appendix C)

Chosen tasbih
The tasbih of a creature that has self-awareness: the creature moves toward its source by the
structure and by the choice, aligning its awareness with the movement. (Appendix C)

Transitional tasbih
The tasbih of a creature at the moment of transition between realms: the movement is most
intense at the boundaries (dawn, dusk, death, birth). (Appendix C)

Worship
The synchronization of the self’s awareness and self-awareness: the structural alignment in
which the self’s horizontal awareness and its vertical self-awareness are brought into harmony. A
structural synchronization, not a psychological state. (Appendix C)

Virtue
A pattern of ascending light: a stable structural pattern in which the self’s ascending light is
regularly returned to its source. A structural pattern, not a moral good. (Appendix C)

The chain
The structural sequence that the traditions associate with worship—knowledge (ma’rifah), worship
(’ibādah), taqwa, virtues (fad.ā’il)—read as four aspects of a single structural transformation:
Glossary of Terms                                                                             467


the transformation of the self’s relation to its source from a pattern of sediment to a pattern of
ascending light. (Appendix C)

Shared context of worship
The structural condition that the social forms of worship—the five daily prayers, the fast, the
pilgrimage, the almsgiving—provide for the individual synchronizations. A structural condition,
not a collective subject. (Appendix C)


Comparative Glossary of Terms
This glossary is not a glossary of the framework’s terms in the strict sense; it is a comparative
glossary, added for the reader who comes to the framework from a religious or traditional
vocabulary, and who wishes to see where the framework’s terms stand in relation to the terms
of that vocabulary. The comparison is offered as an aid to dialogue, not as a means of proof.
The framework’s principles do not depend on the comparison, and the comparison carries no
justificatory weight.
   The comparison is with the vocabulary of the Islamic tradition, as it appears in the Qur’an
and in the classical commentaries, and in Nahj al-Balagha and its commentaries. The choice of
this vocabulary is not a claim that it is the only vocabulary worth comparing; it is a choice made
because the reader who comes to this book from the Islamic tradition is likely to recognize the
terms, and because the structural kinships are particularly visible there. The reader who comes
from a different tradition is invited to construct the analogous comparison; the framework’s
terms are structural, and they can be compared with the vocabulary of any tradition that has a
structural or metaphysical dimension.
   The comparisons are of four kinds, and the kind is marked for each entry. The four kinds are:

  1. Homonymy: the framework’s term and the tradition’s term share a name, but not a
      meaning. The two are distinguished, not identified.

  2. Structural kinship: the framework’s term and the tradition’s term describe structurally
      similar roles, without either being reducible to the other.

  3. Distinction of domains: the framework’s term and the tradition’s term answer different
      questions, and the difference is one of domain, not of truth or falsity.

  4. Open question: the relation between the framework’s term and the tradition’s term is
      left open, and the framework takes no position on it.

   The glossary is organized alphabetically by the framework’s term. For each term, the
framework’s sense is given, the traditional term is given, the kind of comparison is marked, and
a brief explanation is added. The explanations are not arguments; they are descriptions of the
comparison, offered at the strength the comparison supports.

Descent (nuzūl)
Framework: the appearance of an identity in a lower realm in the mode of that realm, without
468                                                                               Glossary of Terms


the identity going from one realm to another (Principle 13.4). Tradition: nuzūl (descent), as in
the descent of the Qur’an (nuzūl al-Qur’ān) or the descent of angels (nuzūl al-malā’ika). Kind:
structural kinship, with a distinction of domain. Explanation: both the framework’s descent
and the tradition’s descent describe the appearance of a higher reality in a lower mode. But the
framework’s descent is structural and timeless; the tradition’s descent is an event in time, and its
description belongs to revelation. The two are not the same, and neither reduces to the other.

First Determination
Framework: the fundamental realm of pure unity, with no multiplicity, change, or succession
(Definition 7.3). Tradition: the 'aql al-awwal (first intellect) of the philosophers, or the .sādir
al-awwal (first emanation) of the Neoplatonists. Kind: structural kinship, with a distinction
of domain. Explanation: both the framework’s First Determination and the tradition’s first
intellect describe the first level at which determination takes form. But the framework’s First
Determination is defined structurally, without reference to emanation or to a hierarchy of
intellects; the tradition’s first intellect is defined within a cosmological scheme that the framework
does not adopt. The two are structurally parallel, but they are not the same.

Identity (huvı̄yat or 'ayn)
Framework: that which remains invariant under a specified class of allowable transformations
(Definition 9.1). Tradition: huvı̄yat (identity, ipseity) in the philosophical and mystical vo-
cabulary, or 'ayn (the concrete entity, the this) in the vocabulary of the philosophers. Kind:
structural kinship, with a distinction of domain. Explanation: both the framework’s identity
and the tradition’s huvı̄yat name what makes a thing the thing it is. But the framework’s identity
is defined by invariance under transformations, whereas the tradition’s huvı̄yat is often defined by
the thing’s concrete individuality, which the framework distinguishes from identity as “signature”
or as “primitive thisness” (Chapter 23). The two are related but not identical.

Light (nūr)
Framework: the structural condition of possibility of relation, which is not legible in the same
way that it makes relation legible (Principle 12.2). Tradition: nūr (light), as in the verse “God
is the light of the heavens and the earth” (Qur’an 24:35), and as in the Suhrawardian and Sadrian
accounts of light as a mode of existence. Kind: homonymy, with an open question about the
relation between the two senses. Explanation: the framework’s light and the tradition’s light
share a name, and they have a structural kinship (both make relation legible), but they are
not the same: the framework’s light is structural, the tradition’s light is divine or ontological.
Whether the two are related is an open question; the structural sense and the theological sense
are distinct, and the relation between them belongs to a different inquiry (see the Remark on
Structural and Theological Light in Chapter 12, and the open question in Chapter 36).

Manifestation (tajallı̄ or zuhūr)
Framework: the contextually realized appearance of an identity in a receiving realm, according
to that realm’s capacity, aptitude, and constraints (Definition 10.1). Tradition: tajallı̄ (self-
disclosure, manifestation) in the mystical vocabulary, or zuhūr (appearance) in the philosophical
vocabulary. Kind: structural kinship, with a distinction of domain. Explanation: both the
framework’s manifestation and the tradition’s tajallı̄ describe the appearance of a higher reality
Glossary of Terms                                                                                 469


in a lower mode. But the framework’s manifestation is the appearance of an identity in a
receiving realm, with the realm’s capacity as a co-determinant; the tradition’s tajallı̄ is often the
self-disclosure of the divine, and its description belongs to revelation or to mystical experience.
The two are structurally parallel, but they are not the same.

Realm ('ālam)
Framework: an independently real mode of existence within which a specific mode of manifes-
tation, activity, and interaction is possible (Definition 7.1). Tradition: 'ālam (world, realm),
as in the 'awālim (worlds) of the cosmological vocabulary, or as in the 'ālam al-amr (world
of command) and 'ālam al-khalq (world of creation) of the Qur’anic vocabulary (Qur’an 7:54).
Kind: structural kinship, with a distinction of domain. Explanation: both the framework’s
realm and the tradition’s 'ālam name a level of reality. But the framework’s realms are defined
structurally, as modes of existence, whereas the tradition’s 'awālim are often defined within a
cosmological or theological scheme, and their description belongs to revelation or to traditional
cosmology. The two are structurally parallel, but they are not the same.

Source
Framework: the point at which determination begins (Remark 7.5); not a being, a person,
or a deity. Tradition: al-mas.dar al-awwal (the first source) in the philosophical vocabulary,
or the divine essence (al-dhāt) in the theological vocabulary. Kind: homonymy, with an open
question about the relation between the two senses. Explanation: the framework’s source is a
structural term, defined by its role in the architecture of determination; the tradition’s source
is a metaphysical or theological term, defined by its relation to the divine. The two share a
name, but they are not the same. Whether they are related is an open question, and the relation
between the two belongs to a different inquiry (see Remark 7.5).

Time (zamān or dahr)
Framework: the order of succession of the stages by which changes are realized in a realm
(Definition 32.1). Tradition: zamān (time) in the philosophical vocabulary, or dahr (eternity,
time) in the Qur’anic and mystical vocabulary. Kind: structural kinship, with a distinction of
domain. Explanation: both the framework’s time and the tradition’s zamān name the order
of succession. But the framework’s time is realm-relative, and its definition is structural; the
tradition’s zamān is often defined in relation to motion or to the divine, and its description
belongs to physics or to metaphysics of a different kind. The two are structurally parallel, but
they are not the same.

Viability
Framework: the structural character of the relation between an identity and its manifestations
in a realm, measured by fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability (Definition 6.2); a descriptive
concept that names a structural character of the relation, not a value or an end. Tradition:
.salāh. (soundness, viability) or i'tidāl (balance, equilibrium) in the ethical and cosmological
vocabularies. Kind: distinction of domains, with a structural kinship. Explanation: the
framework’s viability is a descriptive concept; it states a condition on the relation between
an identity and its manifestations, and it names a structural character of that relation. The
tradition’s .salāh. is often a normative concept; it states what is good or fitting, and it carries a
470                                                                              Glossary of Terms


value. The two are related (both concern the soundness of a relation), but they are not the same,
and the inquiry into the normative sense of .salāh. belongs to the domain that the framework
serves, not to the framework itself.

   Remark C.11 (What the Comparative Glossary Is For)

   The comparative glossary is not a claim that the framework’s terms are the same as the
   tradition’s terms, and it is not a claim that the framework is derived from the tradition.
   It is a claim that the two vocabularies can be compared, and that the comparison is
   useful for the reader who wishes to locate the framework in relation to the tradition. The
   comparison is offered at the strength of a structural kinship, not at the strength of an
   identity. The framework’s terms stand on their own; the tradition’s terms stand on their
   own; and the relation between the two is a question for another inquiry—one that the
   framework neither undertakes nor forecloses.

   Remark C.12 (What the Comparative Glossary Is Not For)

   The comparative glossary is not a means of proof. It is not offered as evidence for the
   framework, and it is not offered as evidence against the tradition. A reader who finds
   that the framework’s terms are structurally parallel to the tradition’s terms has found a
   kinship, not a justification; a reader who finds that they diverge has found a distinction,
   not a refutation. The framework’s principles are justified by their own arguments, and the
   tradition’s claims are justified by their own sources. The comparison is an aid to dialogue,
   and it is offered in that spirit.



Terms Used Without a Formal Definition
Attribute
A category used in the framework’s discussion of the deadlock of light, alongside substance,
process, and relation. Not given a formal definition; used in Chapter 12 to characterize one of
the four available categories.

Causality, temporality, discreteness
The three rules of the Material Manifestation. See under their individual entries.

Fluidity
Used in two senses: kinetic fluidity (having flow, moving, traveling) and structural fluidity (having
the capacity to convey). The framework uses the second. See Principle 13.3.

Higher and lower
Ordinal positions in the architecture of expression. Higher means more unified or more general;
lower means more multiple or more particular. Not existential routes, causal priorities, or degrees
of reality. (See the remark at Chapter 7.)

Legibility
The recognizability of a relation as a relation between these terms. The term is structural, not
Glossary of Terms                                                                              471


metaphorical; developed in Chapter 12.

Reflection
In the framework’s account of light, the making-legible of the source in a manifestation. Developed
in Chapter 13 in connection with the three properties of light.

Shadow
Reflection limited by the capacity of the receiving realm. Developed in Chapter 13 as the
counterpart of complete reflection.

Source (of a manifestation)
The identity that appears in a manifestation. Not a higher realm. (See the remark at Chapter 10.)

Thisness (primitive)
The doctrine that an individuating feature is not qualitative, and that it distinguishes one thing
from an exact qualitative duplicate. Developed in Chapter 23.

The open questions the framework leaves are collected in Chapter 36; they are not principles of
the framework but questions that its principles make visible, and they are therefore not counted
among the entries of this index. The count of (Q) entries in the table is zero for that reason.
      The count is approximate in the following sense: some principles are restated in more than
one chapter (Identity Conservation is stated in Chapter 9 and restated in Chapter 22; Non-
Duplicability is stated in Chapter 9 and restated in Chapter 23; Impossibility of Super-Identity
is stated in Chapter 6 and restated in Chapter 26). Each restatement is counted separately,
because each is a separate entry in the tables above. A reader who wishes to see the full set of
principles as a system is directed to the dependency maps at the end of Parts I and VI, and to
the summaries at the end of Parts V, VII, and VIII.


Note on the Counts
The count of (A) entries is large because many of the framework’s principles are foundational
commitments: the definitions, the twenty-two rules of the realms, and the independence principles
are all (A). The count of (T) entries is smaller because the framework’s arguments are concentrated
in Part VI, and the principles argued there are the ones the framework’s case depends on. The
count of (E) entries is small because the framework uses the estimate status sparingly; the count
of (S) entries marks the framework’s speculative extensions; and the count of (Q) entries in the
tables is zero because the open questions are collected in Chapter 36, where they are stated as
questions the framework leaves open, not as principle entries of the index.
      The count is offered as a summary of the index’s structure. A reader who wishes to challenge
the framework will find the entries arranged by status: the (A) entries are the commitments
the framework makes; the (T) entries are the arguments the framework gives; and the (E), (S),
and proposed entries mark the points where the framework’s claims are most open to revision.
The arrangement makes the challenge possible: the reader can see at a glance which claims are
argued, which are commitments, and which are marked as open.
Index of Arguments


A Note on the Index
This index lists the arguments of the framework, organized by part and chapter. Each entry
gives the name of the argument, its epistemic status, and a cross-reference to the chapter and
section in which it is stated.
   The entries are listed in the order in which they appear in the book, not alphabetically, so
that the reader can follow the development of the framework’s case from its foundation to its
conclusion. A reader who wishes to locate an argument by name is directed to the General Index.
   An argument is listed as Proof where a complete argument is given from stated premises. It
is listed as Argument where the argument is given at a lower degree of completeness, or where
the argument is relative to named commitments. The status labels are those introduced in
the Introduction: (T) (argued), (E) (estimate), and “conditional” (the argument establishes a
conditional, not its antecedent). An argument that supports a (A) principle is marked “(T)
relative to (A)” or “relative to premises.”
   The index covers the metaphysical body of the book. The three appendices—the prospectus
for a viability metaethics, the structural anthropology of nafs and ruh, and the structural
description of religious phenomena—are applications of the framework’s structural vocabulary
and contribute no formal arguments to the framework’s case; they are noted in their own places
and are not indexed here.
   Two features of the framework’s case are worth noting. First, the arguments are distributed
across the book: the foundation’s arguments are in Part I, the fixed elements’ arguments in
Part III, the fluid element’s arguments in Part IV, the governing dynamics’ arguments in Part V,
and the fullest case in Part VI. Second, several arguments are stated more than once, in different
forms, in different chapters; each statement is counted separately below, so that the reader can
see the framework’s case at each point where it is made. The reader who wishes to see the
framework’s case as a whole is directed to the dependency maps at the end of Parts I and VI,
and to the summaries at the end of Parts V, VII, and VIII.

Summary of Statuses
The following table summarizes the arguments in the index, by status. The counts are the counts
of the present index; a restated argument is counted at each chapter in which it is stated, so that
the table reflects the framework’s case as it is actually made across the book.

                Status                                              Count

                (T) (Argued)                                        33
                (T) relative to (A) or premises                     16
                (E) (Estimate)                                      1
                Conditional                                         1

                Total arguments                                     51

Some arguments are stated more than once, in different forms, in different chapters: the
transcendental argument for conservation is stated in Chapter 9 and developed further in
Chapter 22; the argument for the impossibility of super-identity is stated in Chapter 6 and given
a second, independent argument in Chapter 26. Each restatement is counted separately, because
each is a distinct entry in the tables above.


Note on the Counts
The count of (T) entries is large because most of the framework’s arguments are proofs from
stated premises. The count of (T) relative to (A) entries reflects the structure of the framework’s
case: some arguments depend on the framework’s foundational commitments, and the index
records the dependence explicitly. The argument for the irreducibility of the barzakhic realms,
for example, is a proof relative to the premise that rules of regulation are not derivable from
rules of what is regulated, and that premise is itself a (A) commitment. The count of (E) entries
is small because the framework offers a single estimate—the support for the sufficiency half of
the four-column principle—and does not multiply estimates. The count of conditional entries
is one because the framework gives a single conditional argument—the conditional argument
from the desire to find—and the conditional is retained as a statement of what expression is a
condition of, not as independent support for the principle of expression.
   The count is offered as a summary of the index’s structure. A reader who wishes to assess the
framework’s case will find the entries arranged by status in the tables above: the (T) entries are
486                                                                          Glossary of Terms


the arguments the framework gives; the (T) relative to (A) entries are the arguments that depend
on the framework’s commitments; and the (E) and conditional entries mark the points where the
case is stated at a lower strength. The arrangement makes the assessment possible: the reader
can see at a glance which claims are argued at full strength, which depend on commitments, and
which are stated at a lower strength.
      The reader who wishes to see the framework’s case as a whole, rather than as a list of
arguments, is directed to the dependency maps at the end of Parts I and VI. The dependency
maps state, for each principle, which arguments depend on it and what is lost if it is rejected;
the index states, for each argument, its status and its place. The two are complementary: the
index locates the arguments; the dependency maps state their structure.
Index of Formalizations


A Note on the Index
This index lists the formalizations of the framework: the symbolic notation, the formal expressions,
and the formal structures (reductio, dilemma, transcendental argument) that appear in the book.
Its purpose is to make the framework’s formal apparatus visible in one place.
   The framework uses formalization sparingly. Every principle appears first in full philosophical
prose, and only then in symbolic form. The symbols abbreviate the prose, and the prose carries
the principle; the entries of the index are few, and each is cross-referenced to the prose that it
abbreviates.
   The index covers the metaphysical body of the book. The three appendices—the prospectus
for a viability metaethics, the structural anthropology of nafs and ruh, and the structural
description of religious phenomena—are applications of the framework’s structural vocabulary
and contain no formalizations of the kind indexed here; they are noted in their own places and
are not indexed here.
   The index has two parts. The first part, Symbolic Notation, lists the symbols used in the book,
with their meaning and the chapters in which they appear. The second part, Formalizations by
Chapter, lists the formal expressions and formal structures, organized by the chapter in which
they appear. A third part, The Status of Formalization, states what the framework’s formal
apparatus is.

      Remark C.13 (On the Use of Two Symbols for Light)

   The book uses two symbols for light: L (capital L) and L (script L). The first is used in
      the formal skeleton of Part IV and in the principles of Chapter 14; the second is used
      in the formal skeleton of Part IV’s summary, in Chapter 15, and in the theorems of
      Chapter 14 that are stated in fully symbolic form. The two symbols denote the same
      thing—light in its formal role—and the difference is typographic, not semantic; the two
      are used interchangeably in the formal expressions of the book.


      Remark C.14 (On the Use of the Quantifiers)

   The universal and existential quantifiers are used in the book in their standard senses:
      ∀x means “for all x,” and ∃x means “there exists an x.” The negation ¬ is used in its
      standard sense. The conditional → and the biconditional ↔ are used in their standard
Glossary of Terms                                                                               489


    senses. The book uses only the standard logical symbols, and the formal expressions are
    transparent to a reader who knows them.



Part II: Formalizations by Chapter
The following sections list the formal expressions and formal structures of the book, organized by
the chapter in which they appear. Each entry gives the formal expression, its prose counterpart,
and the definition or principle it abbreviates.


Chapter 5: Context-Dependence and the Infinity of Contexts

The sequence of contexts
C0 , C1 , C2 , . . .; m0 , m1 , m2 , . . .
The sequence of cognitive contexts and manifestations generated by the argument for the infinity
of contexts. Each Cn+1 contains an element mn that is not a fixed element of Cn or of any earlier
context. The formal expression abbreviates the argument at Principle 5.2.

The formal structure of the generative proof
∀n : ∃mn such that mn ∈ Cn+1 and mn ∈
                                    / {m0 , . . . , mn−1 }
The formal structure of the generative proof: for every stage n, there is a manifestation mn that
is an element of the next context and not of any earlier one. The expression summarizes the
argument; it is not a separate premise.


Chapter 13: Light — Active Structure, Not Traveler

The active connection structure
C ↓ (a, b) ↔ EdgeActive(a, b)
The descending edge from a to b is active if and only if the edge between them is active. The
expression abbreviates the re-reading of the three properties of light (descending, ascending,
reflective) as directions of one structure. The formal expression is stated in the formal skeleton
of Part IV (Chapter 15), where the three properties are re-read; the prose is in Section 13.9.


Chapter 14: The Place of Light

Encompassment in light
∀x : Knows(x, L) → Encompassed(x, L)
For every subject x, if x knows light, then x is encompassed in light. The expression abbreviates
the principle of encompassment at Principle 14.4, and it is stated in the formal skeleton of Part IV
(Section 15.11).

The impossibility of complete knowledge of light
¬∃x : KnowsCompletely(x, L)
There is no subject x that knows light completely. The expression abbreviates the principle at
Principle 14.5, and it is stated in the formal skeleton of Part IV.
490                                                                               Glossary of Terms


Light as the only window
∀x : Accessible(x, Lhigher ) → Ldescended
For every subject x, if higher light is accessible to x, then what is accessible is light in its
descended version. The expression abbreviates the principle at Principle 14.6, and it is stated in
the formal skeleton of Part IV.

Chapter 15: Consequences — Energy and Explanation
Light as condition of possibility of relation
∀a, b : Rel(a, b) → (Readable(Rel(a, b)) ↔ L(a, b))
For any a and b, if a is related to b, then the relation is legible if and only if light holds between
them. The expression abbreviates the principle at Principle 12.2, and it is stated in the formal
skeleton of Part IV.

Every explanation requires a conveyor
∀Expl : Possible(Expl) → ∃Ψ
For every explanation, if the explanation is possible, then there exists a fluid element. The
expression abbreviates the principle at Principle 15.3, and it is stated in the formal skeleton of
Part IV.

Without light, no explanation
¬L → ¬∃Expl
If there is no light, then there is no explanation. The expression abbreviates the principle at
Principle 15.4, and it is stated in the formal skeleton of Part IV.

Light primary, energy secondary
L primary; E secondary
Light is primary; energy is secondary. The expression abbreviates the principle at Principle 15.2,
and it is stated in the formal skeleton of Part IV.

Chapter 23: The Non-Duplicability of Identity
The logic of numerical identity
I1 = I, I2 = I ⇒ I1 = I2
If I1 is identical with I, and I2 is identical with I, then I1 is identical with I2 . The expression
abbreviates the proof of non-duplicability at Principle 23.1. The argument’s force is that the
supposition of two numerically distinct things each being the same identity is contradictory.

Chapter 26: The Impossibility of Super-Identity (Detailed)
The diagonal argument
Suppose S has surveyed C1 , . . . , Cn and claims that these are all the contexts in which I is
manifested. The survey is itself a cognition in some context CS . By openness, the manifestations
of I in the surveyed contexts, and the survey’s own results, are fixed elements of further contexts
not among C1 , . . . , Cn . So the survey is incomplete, and completing it generates the same
situation again.
Glossary of Terms                                                                                  491


The formal structure of the diagonal argument at Principle 27.1. The argument’s form is that of
a diagonal construction: whatever list of contexts is offered, a context outside the list can be
constructed from the list itself.

Chapter 33: Death and Birth
The balance criterion


Balance = (received light preserved)+(ascending light given)−(received light become sediment)


The balance of an identity in a realm is the extent to which the descending light it has received
is preserved or returned, less the extent to which it has become sediment. The expression
abbreviates the definition at Definition 34.5.


Part III: Formal Structures
The framework uses three formal structures, each of which appears in more than one chapter.
The structures are stated here in their general form, with cross-references to the chapters in
which they are used.

The Reductio
The reductio is the framework’s most common formal structure. It proceeds by supposing the
negation of what is to be proved, deriving a contradiction, and concluding that the supposition
is false. The framework uses the reductio in the following places:

The Dilemma
The dilemma is used in one place: the argument for non-duplicability from the identity of
indiscernibles (Principle 23.1). The argument has two horns—the identity of indiscernibles holds,
or it does not—and in both horns, the conclusion follows. The dilemma’s force is that it removes
the dependence of the principle on the identity of indiscernibles, without settling the dispute
over the principle itself.

The Transcendental Argument
The transcendental argument is used in two places: the argument for the necessity of expression
(Principle 18.1, Chapter 18), and the argument for the conservation of identity (Principle 22.1,
Chapter 22). Both arguments proceed from the possibility of experience to its condition. The
first proceeds from the experience of manifestation to the condition of expression; the second
proceeds from the experience of temporal continuity to the presumption of sameness.

The Counting Argument
The counting argument is used in one place: the argument for the minimality of the three hubs
(Chapter 20). The argument counts the distinctions between the four grades of multiplicity (three
distinctions), and concludes that three functions of mediation are required. The argument’s force
is arithmetic: four grades have three distinctions between them, not two and not four.


Part IV: The Status of Formalization
The framework uses formalization at a specific strength, and the strength is stated here. For-
malization here means brief notation, explicit formulation of principles, dependency tables, and
epistemic labels. It does not mean full formal proof, axiomatic derivation, or mathematical
formulation; the aim is precision of presentation, not justification.
      Three consequences follow, and they are stated here as a closing note on the index.

First consequence: the prose is primary. Every principle appears first in full philosophical
prose, and only then in symbolic form. The prose carries the principle; the symbol abbreviates it.
The symbols can be set aside without loss of the principle; the prose cannot be set aside without
loss. The index is a guide to the symbols; the prose is the substance.
Glossary of Terms                                                                               493


Second consequence: the symbols are few. The book uses a small number of symbols,
each of which is introduced with its meaning. The reader follows the formal expressions without
any special training, because the expressions are translatable into the prose that surrounds them,
and the translations are given in the chapters.


Third consequence: formalization summarizes, and the argument justifies. The
formal expressions summarize the principles they abbreviate, and they are offered at the strength
the principles’ arguments support. The argument for a principle is the place where the principle
is assessed; the symbolic form presents the principle in abbreviated form. A principle is justified
by its argument, and the symbolic form is a way of seeing the principle.

   Remark C.15 (The Index and the Framework’s Formal Apparatus)

   The index makes the framework’s formal apparatus visible in one place, so that the reader
   can see at a glance what the framework formalizes and what it leaves in prose. The
   formalization is present in the framework at the places the index records, and the index
   notes its presence.


   Remark C.16 (The Formalization Is Sparse)

   The formalization is sparse because the framework’s subject—the structure of identity and
   manifestation—is not naturally formal. The subject is structural, but not mathematical;
   the framework’s precision is philosophical, not computational. The formalization serves
   the precision where it can, and the prose carries the rest. The formalization is stated at
   the strength its purpose requires; a reader who wishes for more formalization is invited to
   provide it.

The count is small, and the smallness is the point. The framework uses formalization where it aids

The index is a guide to what is formalized. The prose is the substance; the formalization is the
abbreviation.
The Four-Column Map of the Book


A Note on the Map
The four-column framework is the first principle of the entire book. Its principle states that every
explanatory cognition requires four analytical roles—fixed elements, fluid elements, governing
dynamics, and context—and that if any one of the four is absent, the cognition is incomplete as
an explanation. This map shows, for each part and each chapter, which of the four roles the
chapter develops.
   The framework is stated in its own place, in Part I, and developed in the parts that follow;
the map is a guide to the structure that these parts build. It is offered as an aid to the reader
who wishes to know, before reading a chapter, what the chapter is about, in the framework’s
own vocabulary.
   The map makes the first principle of the book visible across the whole of the book: the reader
can see, as she reads, that the framework is a structure the chapters themselves articulate. The
chapters build the framework part by part, and the map traces this articulation.


Part I: The Four Columns in the Framework
The four columns are the analytical roles of explanatory cognition. They are not the content
of a single chapter; they are the organizing principle of the entire module. The following table
states what each column is, and which part of the book develops it.

  Governing dynam- The rule that explains how fluid ele- Part V (Chapters 16–17)
  ics                    ments affect fixed elements
  Context                The background in which cognition oc- Part II (Chapters 7–8), for

      Part I develops the framework as a whole; it is the part in which the four columns are
introduced and argued for. The reader who wishes to understand the four columns should read
Part I in full; the reader who wishes to see one column in isolation should read the corresponding
part that follows.

   Part II develops the context column in its existential sense: the seven realms are the contexts
in which manifestations are realized. The distinction between the cognitive context (fixed by the
question) and the existential context (fixed by the realm) was drawn in Part I; Part II develops
the second.

   Part III develops the fixed elements: identity and manifestation, the two entities that the
framework’s explanations hold invariant. The two chapters are the framework’s account of what
is related, before the medium of relation (Part IV) and the rule of the medium (Part V) are
developed.

Part IV: Fluid Elements (Chapters 11–15)


       Chapter          Column            What It Develops

   Part IV develops the fluid element: light, in its role as the conveyor of effect between identity
and manifestation. The five chapters move from the problem (Chapter 11) to the proposal
(Chapter 12), from the proposal to its sharpening (Chapter 13), from the sharpening to its place
in the framework (Chapter 14), and from the place to its consequences (Chapter 15). The part
is the framework’s most extended treatment of a single column.

      Part V develops the governing dynamics: the twenty-two rules that govern how light operates
in the seven realms. The two chapters distinguish the rules of being (the rules of the fundamental
realms) from the rules of transition (the rules of the barzakhic realms), and they show that the
rules are related by a single structure.

      Part VI develops the arguments for the framework’s principles. It does not develop a single

Part VI address a specific column (Chapters 19, 20, 22, 23, 26); others address the framework
as a whole (Chapters 18, 21, 24, 25). The part is the framework’s case, not the framework’s
structure.

   Part VII resolves the apparent tensions among the framework’s principles. It does not develop

The part is the framework’s demonstration that the four columns do not conflict, and that the
apparent conflicts are consequences of running together distinctions the framework has drawn.

   Part VIII develops the concepts that follow from the framework’s principles. It does not

make possible. The part is the framework’s application of its own principles to the derivative
concepts, and it is the part in which the framework’s reach is most visible.

      Part IX states the boundaries of the framework and concludes the book. It does not develop
a column; it reflects on the framework as a whole, on what it does and does not claim, and on
the questions it leaves open. The part is the framework’s self-reflection, and it is the part in
which the framework’s honesty about its limits is most explicit.

      The three appendices apply the framework’s structural vocabulary to specific domains. Each
marks at its beginning its relation to the metaphysical body of the book; each is offered as a
proposal or a structural description, and each carries its own epistemic status. The map places
them after the nine parts because they presuppose the framework that the parts build: they
apply the framework, and they do not develop a column of it.

Part V: The Map’s Scope
The map shows the framework’s architecture, and it shows how the four columns are distributed
across the book. Its scope is complemented by two further indexes, and the reader should know
them.


First: the arguments of the book. Each chapter’s column is shown in the map, and the
arguments each chapter gives for it are indexed separately in the Index of Arguments; the reader
who wishes to see the framework’s case is directed there.


Second: the dependencies among the principles. The map shows which column each
chapter develops; the dependencies among the principles are stated in the dependency maps at
the end of Parts I and VI; the reader who wishes to see the framework’s structure is directed
there.
   The map is a guide to the book’s architecture; the book itself is the substance, and the map
is the guide. It is offered as an aid to the reader who wishes to know, before reading a chapter,
what the chapter is about, in the framework’s own vocabulary.


A Note on the Map and the First Principle
The map is a statement of the framework’s first principle in the form of the book’s structure.
The first principle says that every explanatory cognition requires four columns; the map shows
that every part of the book is a study of one or more of those columns, and that no part of the
book does without them. The map is a demonstration of the book’s own claim, made visible in
the book’s own structure.
   The reader who has followed the map from beginning to end has followed the book’s first
principle from its statement (Part I) to its applications (Parts II–VIII) to its boundary (Part IX),
and from the parts to the three appendices that extend the framework’s structural vocabulary to
specific domains. The map is the book’s first principle, seen from above.
504                                                            The Four-Column Map of the Book


Summary
The map is stated in three views: by part, by column, and in a visual summary. The three views
are the same map, seen from three directions. The first view (by part) is the map in the book’s
order; the second view (by column) is the map in the framework’s order; the third view (visual
summary) is the map at a glance.
      The map is offered as a statement of the framework’s first principle in the form of the book’s
structure, and as an aid to the reader who wishes to follow one column through the whole book.
The map is a guide to the book’s architecture; the book itself is the substance.

The horizon is open. The inquiry continues.
